title: York County voters could abolish treasurer position in November
text:
Voters in York County could decide in November to get rid of a part-time elected treasurer position that officials have said serves little purpose in its current form.
If voters approve the referendum question this fall, the treasurer would instead be appointed by county officials.
It’s an issue that has county officials at odds over the duties of the treasurer and the consequences of potentially abolishing the position. A majority of county commissioners say it’s an unnecessary extension of the county Finance Department, while the former treasurer said keeping the position could save taxpayers some money.
But the current treasurer — who is not seeking to keep the job, no matter how residents vote Nov. 3 — thinks it’s a way for elected officials to gain control and remove a layer of public oversight.
‘IT’S JUST A FORMALITY’
The state statute governing the elected treasurer position doesn’t outline specific finance background requirements, but York County Commission Chair Richard Dutremble and County Manager Gregory Zinser say making it an appointed position would be a way to professionalize the budget process by establishing finance qualifications.
“Basically, the treasurer’s position now in county government is obsolete,” Dutremble said.
The responsibilities of the elected treasurer, Dutremble said, lost value once the county established a finance director and a Finance Department, which make decisions on investments, operating budgets and debts.
The finance director position was created in early 2007 after untimely audits and accounting errors led to a $1.2 million fund balance deficit. Since then, the county’s financial status has steadily improved. It gets audited three times a year — once for finances, and once each for state and federal compliance. The auditing firm used by York County has given the county an “A” rating.
The county’s current treasurer, Stacy Kilroy, whose term expires on Dec. 31, isn’t running again. She was appointed to serve out the term in 2024 by Gov. Janet Mills after previous treasurer and former Biddeford City Councilor Bobby Mills stepped down. (The two Millses are not related.)
Kilroy argued this week that finance and treasury are two “completely different subjects.”
“The intent of the treasurer’s position was, of course, to record finance, but also to be in the idea of town rule,” Kilroy said, adding that the four-person finance team isn’t composed of elected officials. To her, they’re responsible only to the county manager “and their pension.”
But Dutremble and Zinser described the position as “ceremonial” and said the budget goes through three approvals: first the county manager, then the county commissioners and finally the county’s budget committee.
“It’s just a formality so they can sign papers and stuff like that,” Dutremble said of the treasurer position, noting that state law requires counties to have a treasurer, regardless of how they’re chosen.
The treasurer is given a $500 annual stipend for the part-time role, Commissioner Justin Chenette said, and a potential difference in pay for an appointed treasurer is yet to be determined. But he thinks the commissioners could hesitate to allocate more money to the role because, ideally, they’d appoint someone who is already doing budget work for the county. Dutremble said he’d propose no increase to that stipend.
Bobby Mills, who is seeking to return to the treasurer position, said he’s running to save taxpayers money. Getting rid of the $500 stipend wouldn’t save the county any money when it already has a deputy treasurer, a full-time finance department position that he said pays almost $100,000 a year.
“Saving $500 is, like, ludicrous,” he said. “It’s not about money. It’s about serving the people.”
He says he would instead propose getting rid of the full-time deputy position and performing those duties under the $500 stipend — something he tried to do when he was first elected in 2018.
A SECOND ATTEMPT AT CHANGE
This isn’t the first time York County has considered abolishing the elected position. In 2018, commissioners approved the same ballot question, which asks, “Shall the position of elected county treasurer be abolished and replaced with a treasurer appointed by the county commissioners?”
But it failed by a wide margin when it was brought to voters, 70% of whom voted “no.”
Dutremble thinks officials made a mistake back then by not properly explaining the duties of the treasurer and why the position should be abolished.
“I think the knowledge surrounding that of the statutory role is rather unknown,” he said. “The existing treasurer isn’t even on the bank accounts and hasn’t been in quite some time.”
York is one of three Maine counties considering this change this fall; voters in Franklin and Washington counties will see similar questions on their ballots. Three other counties — Androscoggin, Cumberland and Knox — already appoint their treasurers.
State law generally requires treasurers to be an elected county resident, but there’s an exception that allows county commissioners to abolish the elected position and replace it with an appointed role, so long as voters approve such a change.
Four of the five York County commissioners have said they support the change.
Chenette, the sole commissioner opposed, said it’s not something residents are asking for. To him, abolishing the elected position would mean losing public agency and oversight into the budget process.
“I’m unclear what has changed between the last referendum and this fall to warrant more taxpayer money going towards a referendum that no one asked for,” Chenette said. “Instead, we really need to be looking at ways of making the county treasurer role more effective in the community.”
He’d rather see the position reformed, with an elected treasurer who involves the public more directly in the process.
Kilroy said the budget process is a lot less complicated than officials are making it seem.
“The county budget could be done on a cocktail napkin,” she said. “This is just a way for the county manager to gain control of a position so that nobody is looking at the various county commissioners.”
Zinser disagrees, because the treasurer plays no statutory role in the budget process. No matter what, final budget approval will still have to go through the budget committee, which remains an elected body.
Mills is seeking a nonconsecutive term as treasurer and will be the sole candidate listed for the position on the Nov. 3 ballot. But if the referendum to abolish the elected treasurer’s role is approved, then one will be appointed internally and that vote won’t matter.
Editor’s note: This story was updated on Oct. 1 to clarify Bobby Mills’ stance about eliminating the elected treasurer position.

title: Freeport residents will vote to decide whether landlocked ship gets to sea
text:
A citizens’ petition calling for the launch of an 80-ton ship that’s been landlocked in a Freeport neighborhood for decades has enough valid signatures to appear on town ballots in November.
The question asks residents if they would approve a temporary boat launch in the zoning district containing 0 Shore Drive, the planned site to launch the Island Rover.
In the process, it would exempt temporary boat launches from certain town environmental and zoning requirements.
Harold Arndt started building the Island Rover more than 30 years ago using scrap materials he got through his job at Bath Iron Works. His dream was to take a group of college students on a trip to the Arctic while showing them creative ways to reuse materials.
But that didn’t happen. Arndt, now in his 80s, and his business partner have been in legal battles with the town for years. The story was the focus of a documentary in 2023.
Some neighbors have opposed the launch off Lower Flying Point Road, worried about coastal erosion, the well-being of wildlife and that the ship could get stuck in the mud.
Last year, the Freeport Coastal Waters Commission denied a temporary boat launch for the roughly 90-foot schooner in the residential area — where the water in Raspberry Cove’s mudflat only reaches a depth of about 6 feet at the highest astronomical tide — for environmental reasons, including possible impacts to the cove’s coastal species.
This is the second time a citizens’ group has circulated a petition aimed at launching the Rover. In June, they failed to gain enough valid signatures to get the issue on the ballot.
Freeport’s town clerk validated this round of signatures on Sept. 29. Supporters gathered 812 valid signatures — 744 were required.
Town Clerk Christine Wolfe said Thursday that the Town Council will set a public hearing to discuss the referendum at its next meeting, on Oct. 6. The public hearing is planned for a special meeting on Oct. 15.
The council cannot take any action on the referendum at this hearing, Wolfe said. It had the opportunity to vote on the proposed ordinance in August, but instead chose to send it through the referendum process.
The issue has spurred lawsuits, starting in 2004 when town officials accused the shipbuilder of violating rules against “manufacturing use” in a residential zone. The town has also claimed that it is the legal owner of the vessel and the property it sits on.
Most recently, Arndt sued Freeport in February, claiming the town has spent more than 20 years fighting him in court to get the schooner removed, imposing thousands of dollars in fines, while rejecting his efforts to launch the ship.

title: Man bleeds out, dies after punching through window at former elementary school, family says
text:
JACKSON, Miss. (WLBT/Gray News) - A Mississippi family is grieving a loved one who they say died after he punched through a window and seriously injured himself, possibly out of grief.
Jackson Public Schools says district law enforcement officers responded Sunday to the former Lake Elementary School. Upon arrival, they found a man with severe injuries who later died.
The man’s mother identified him as 38-year-old David Bridges. His family says Bridges punched through a window. The glass cut a main artery, and he bled out.
Bridges’ family says he was dealing with grief, and that may have led to the incident.
Loved ones gathered a few blocks from the building Monday afternoon to remember Bridges and share his legacy.
“An outspoken person, a respectful person, a loving person, but as humans, you know, we all got our share of flaws. But overall, he was a great person, a genuinely good person,” Calesha Esco said.
WLBT reached out to the Hinds County coroner for more information about the circumstances surrounding Bridges’ death.
JPS reported the building only sustained minor damage and that the area was secured and cleaned. The district said operations continued as normal Monday.
While the facility is a former elementary school, JPS currently uses it for its Re-Engaging for All to Progress or REAP Program, which provides an alternative pathway to a high school diploma for students who are at risk of dropping out of high school.

Fisherman trapped under massive fallen boulder uses Siri to call for help: ‘It’s a miracle’
text:
PORTLAND, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) - An Oregon man on a fishing trip was trapped under a large boulder when it fell on him. His family is now sharing details of his rescue as he faces a long recovery.
Joe Little, 28, was fishing alone early Saturday morning on the Hammond Marina jetty in Astoria when his grandmother says a rock he had sat on several times before began to move.
“He said that he felt it start to move, and he put his feet down to stop it. But the boulder was huge. He slipped down, and it just went over him,” said Kelly Simonson, Little’s grandmother.
Trapped under the boulder and located below the high tide water line, Little knew he needed help quickly. His mother says his Bluetooth earbuds stayed connected when he fell, so he asked Siri to call 911.
Just after 7 a.m., Warrenton police and fire crews were dispatched to the jetty.
Police Sgt. Dylan McCoy says responders were able to narrow down Little’s location by honking their car horns. A dispatcher who was listening on the phone with Little would ask whether he could hear the horn nearby.
McCoy says the rocky terrain was too hazardous for responders to safely walk through, so they launched a drone. Three minutes later, McCoy spotted Little. Only part of his upper body and his feet were visible.
Responders then had to figure out how to free him. The rocky terrain and the size of the boulder made the rescue difficult. According to McCoy, Warrenton Fire devised a plan to remove some of the smaller rocks under Little rather than trying to move the larger boulder.
“They removed some of the smaller ones, and that allowed them to move him from underneath the extremely large boulder which had trapped him,” McCoy said.
A U.S. Coast Guard helicopter arrived at the scene shortly before 9 a.m. Crews hoisted Little from the jetty and transferred him to awaiting emergency medical personnel at Coast Guard Air Station Astoria.
Little is now at a Portland hospital, where he is being treated for severe facial injuries, including a broken jaw.
“His face got smashed. He’s almost unrecognizable,” his mother said. “It’s a miracle that my son is alive.”
Little was scheduled to undergo facial reconstruction surgery Thursday, a procedure expected to last about eight hours. His family has set up an online fundraiser to help with medical expenses.

title: It’s time for Mainers to put country first
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Many old-time Mainers, from all political parties, say they support Sen. Susan Collins because she brings money back to the state as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee. There is also a certain nostalgia many Mainers feel. “She’s done well for us in the past” and “she’s independent.” In truth, Collins has cost us more by following Donald Trump’s policies.
Collins has voted with Trump 95% of the time, resulting in extreme financial pain for most Mainers as well as Americans across the country. The war in Iran, tariffs, inflation, steep cost increases to gas and diesel, heat and groceries, the ballooning deficit, rising interest and mortgage rates, unaffordable housing, reduced SNAP benefits and $3 billion in Medicaid funding cuts in Maine alone to take effect in January — together with out-of-control immigration officers. These all have resulted from Trump’s policies, most of which Susan Collins has supported.
Until the Senate and the House are flipped, the unrestrained chaos, financial devastation and erosion to democracy will continue. What happens nationally affects Mainers too. It is time for Mainers to vote to push back against the impacts of Trump’s worst behaviors and put the country back on track. It’s time to put personal nostalgia aside, recognize that perfect is the enemy of good, and vote Susan Collins out and Troy Jackson in.
How will everyone feel if the Senate stays in Trump’s Republican control because Maine reelected Collins?
Susan Duncan
Phippsburg

title: Court denies motion to find Lindsay Clancy not guilty
text:
Court denies defense attorney's motion to find Lindsay Clancy not guilty in murder of 3 children
The Plymouth Superior Court in Massachusetts denied a motion Thursday that would have found Lindsay Clancy not guilty in the murder of her three children. 
Clancy's defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, argued Tuesday, the first hearing after her mistrial, that the prosecution failed to prove she caused their deaths. 
"Where does she say she did this?" Reddington said in court on Tuesday.
"The Court finds that the evidence, when viewed in the light most favorable to the Commonwealth and with the reasonable inferences permitted to be drawn, was sufficient to have satisfied any rational trier of fact beyond a reasonable doubt as to the essential element of the defendant's criminal responsibility," a court document announcing the motion stated.
Previous coverage in player above: Surprising twist in Lindsay Clancy case
The court stated several reasons why the motion was denied, including the issue of criminal responsibility.
Massachusetts District Judge Jim Barretto responded to Reddington's motion Tuesday.
"I almost don't know what to make of it," Barretto responded during a live interview with sister station WCVB. "I've heard hundreds, if not thousands, of motions for required finding of not guilty. I never expected this: Attorney Reddington, while arguing that motion, actually asserted that Lindsay Clancy -- or that there was no evidence that -- Lindsay Clancy killed her children."
Barretto continued, "That was a bedrock fact which he himself virtually conceded throughout the entire trial."
Video below: Judge reflects on hearing
Clancy, 36, was accused of killing her three children — 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan — at their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home on Jan. 24, 2023. Her defense argued she was not criminally responsible because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time of the killings.
A mistrial was declared Sept. 4 after jurors told the judge they were hopelessly deadlocked, with an 11-1 split in favor of acquittal after seven days of deliberations.
Reddington's unexpected argument was part of his renewed motion for a required finding of not guilty, and in his speech to the judge he traced the origins of that motion back to his pretrial request to split the trial into two parts. Back in April, the defense offered to admit to the killings and argued the only "live issue" for the court to decide was Clancy's state of mind.
Tuesday, however, Reddington argued differently.
Video below: Reddington disputes evidence
"As this woman sits in front of you today, I suggest to the court they did not prove probable cause, and they certainly did not prove that she was not acting at the time of the psychosis and should be found not guilty," Reddington said.
Prosecutor Shanan Buckingham said this is the first time the defense is arguing that there is no evidence Clancy committed the crime of killing her children.
"I suggest to you that the entire record is voluminous as to the information supporting the fact that she did this," Buckingham said.
Buckingham argued that the facts support premeditation and extreme cruelty/atrocity, which are the standards that must be met to prove first-degree murder.
After hearing both arguments, Judge William Sullivan said he would take the motion to dismiss under advisement.
If Sullivan grants Reddington's motion and enters a required finding, Barretto said the case would end without a retrial.
Background of the Clancy case:
- Lindsay Clancy, 36, faces three murder charges in the 2023 deaths of her children, Cora, Dawson and Callan.
- She also jumped from a second-floor window, leaving her partially paralyzed.
- In a civil case, Lindsay Clancy alleges a "catastrophic failure" of multiple medical providers in diagnosing and treating her psychiatric condition.
- Her trial began July 20. Although her legal team offered to stipulate to the deaths of the children, she has pleaded not guilty.
- She is being held at Tewksbury State Hospital.
This case involves issues of mental health. If you or someone you know needs help, you can talk with the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline by calling or sending a text message to 988, or you can chat online here.

title: A plumber, a dentist and the pilot are praised as heroes in FlyDubai near-disaster
text:
A plumber, a dentist and the pilot are praised as heroes in FlyDubai near-disaster
A dentist and other passengers wrestled with a violent copilot. A plumber seized the controls of the plane as it plunged toward the desert. And that's after the captain managed to open the cockpit door while being stabbed, helping to save all 174 people on board the Israel-bound flight.
Warning: The above video is graphic in nature. Viewer discretion is advised
As the U.S. ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, put it: "Hollywood isn't creative enough to come up with stories like this."
The FlyDubai co-pilot who officials said nearly crashed was barred from flying by his native Oman over concerns he had adopted extremist views, a person familiar with the matter said Saturday.
The co-pilot was subsequently hired by the United Arab Emirates-based airline, the person said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss the ongoing investigation. It was not immediately clear to what extent he was vetted when he was hired in the Emirates. Oman’s move to bar the co-pilot from flying was first reported by the Wall Street Journal.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warmly embraced the plumber shortly after the passengers’ arrival in Tel Aviv late Wednesday, and later posted a five-star review for Yaniv Hayoun’s professional services, calling him "a hero who has saved many lives."
"He can help you too — I highly recommend him!" Netanyahu added on X.
Hayoun was among several Israelis recommended for the Presidential Award for Civilian Heroism, while Indian Capt. Smit Machchhar was praised by Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi as "a HERO."
India's Modi lauds the pilot’s courage
Capt. Smit Machchhar, who is from India’s financial hub of Mumbai, was seriously injured in Wednesday's attack. Passengers described how the pilot still managed to open the cockpit door, allowing them to enter and restrain the attacker as the Boeing 737 descended sharply, according to witnesses and Israeli authorities.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Thursday called Machchhar a hero.
“In the face of the gravest danger and despite being seriously injured, he showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others. His valor helped save hundreds of lives and avert a great tragedy,” Modi wrote on X.
Modi also praised the captain for demonstrating ”patience, presence of mind and courage,” saying his “actions prevented another 9/11-like attack from happening." He said he had spoken with Machchhar's parents and wife and that the pilot was undergoing treatment.
One met the prime minister wearing a bloody shirt
Many of the details emerged in a rush shortly after the passengers, most of them Israeli, landed back home to cheers and waving flags.
Hayoun, apologizing for his bloody shirt, within minutes was telling the prime minister and journalists what happened.
There had been little time for him and the others to think. Passengers screamed after spotting the copilot stabbing the captain, and the flight from Dubai, in the United Arab Emirates, to the Israeli city of Tel Aviv began a steep dive. Some believed they were about to die.
A handful of Israelis reacted, hurtling up the aisle after the badly wounded captain managed to open the cockpit door. That was crucial, as cockpit doors are typically locked to prevent hijackings.
They had to struggle, Hayoun said, with the captain’s body resting against it.
The plumber seized the controls, just like in the movies
Hayoun said the copilot appeared to be trying to damage the plane’s controls. He grabbed the copilot, and others began struggling with the man.
Hayoun then tackled the controls. He had no training, but he remembered what he had seen in movies.
"I asked him, 'How did you know how to do that?' And he said, 'Well, I, I watched these air disaster films,'" Netanyahu told Fox News on Thursday.
It was not clear who among the passengers had security experience, though military service is compulsory for most men and women in Israel.
By another turn of events, there were others on board who knew how to fly a plane.
Netanyahu and Flydubai confirmed that reserve pilots who were in the passenger area managed to regain control of the aircraft, issued a mayday call, and sought a place to land.
A dentist treated the wounded pilot
The handful of Israeli passengers grappled with the copilot for several minutes before subduing him and binding his hands with the cord from a set of headphones.
One of them, Dr. Shota Musayev, a dentist, also attended to the captain, who appeared to have lost a lot of blood. "He was just praying the whole time and was in contact with me, and I was afraid we would really lose him," Musayev said.
In a video that Musayev shot and shared with The Associated Press, the captain lay on the floor of the cabin, saying his head was in pain.
Musayev later told journalists he and the other responders knew they'd had just seconds to act before a "critical event."
But even with the copilot bound and subdued, they were scared that other attackers might be on the plane. They sent other people around the cabin to stand by.
Finally, just about an hour after the plane issued a distress call, it made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
Now, investigators from across the region are working to understand what led to the attack. The copilot still has not been publicly identified.
Associated Press reporter Areej Hazboun in Jerusalem contributed.

Cardiac ICU nurse bikes across New England for healthcare worker mental health
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - An endurance athlete and cardiac intensive care unit nurse is biking hundreds of miles across New England to support healthcare worker mental health and suicide prevention.
Jenn Walsh began a 926-mile bicycle ride this week in Madawaska, with plans to finish the journey on Cape Cod. Walsh is raising funds and awareness through the Dr. Lorna Breen Heroes Foundation.
Walsh stopped in Bangor along her route, noting that demands placed on healthcare professionals remain high and that she hopes to reduce the stigma associated with seeking mental health support.
“The strongest thing someone can do is take a step back,” Walsh said. “And in healthcare, we’re kind of taught the opposite—it’s just to keep pushing and pushing and pushing. And in sport, you kind of do that too.”
Walsh is scheduled to finish the ride this weekend at Race Point Beach in Provincetown, Massachusetts.
Donations to support the ride and foundation can be made through Walsh’s GoFundMe campaign.

title: States and cities sue over Trump's EPA eliminating rule that limits emissions from power plants
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — States and cities sued the Trump administration Thursday for repealing rules that limit planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions from power plants fueled by coal and natural gas.
Twenty-one states, led by New York, are challenging the Environmental Protection Agency’s power plant rule. The coalition also includes Pennsylvania’s governor, the District of Columbia, New York City, Chicago and the city and county of Denver. They argue that “gutting one of the country’s most significant climate protections” will set the nation back decades and worsen the climate crisis.
The EPA announced last month it’s revoking the Biden-era rule, and said it is taking a separate but related step to prevent future administrations from regulating climate pollution from power plants.
New York Attorney General Letitia James said the federal government is showing “callous disregard” for Americans’ health and the environment, and future generations will pay the price. Power plants that burn fossil fuels are a major source of planet-warming pollution.
“Dismantling these protections is a betrayal of American families, and the stakes are too high to allow this administration to once again put profits over people,” James said in a statement Thursday.
The EPA did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the lawsuit. However, it has said the repeal would save the industry more than $300 billion in costs and help “unleash” American energy. EPA Assistant Administrator Aaron Szabo said in September that it will allow utilities to “make the best decision for the ratepayers based on cost and cost savings, instead of being required to shut down facilities.”
The coalition is petitioning the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia to review the EPA’s decision and strike down the repeal. It says the EPA unlawfully abandoned the pollution limits without properly considering reasonable alternatives or the enormous health and climate costs of allowing more pollution into the atmosphere. The coalition also told the EPA it intends to sue over the agency’s failure to regulate pollution from many gas-fired power plants.
The rule change for power plants, first proposed last year, represents a fundamental shift from efforts by Democratic Presidents Joe Biden and Barack Obama to address climate change and regulate carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases that trap the sun’s heat. Environmental groups say it will come at a cost to Americans’ health and further degrade the environment.
The separate rule proposed last month could prevent future administrations from regulating greenhouse gas emissions from power plants. The proposal, expected to be made final next year, follows on EPA’s action earlier this year revoking a scientific finding that long has been the central basis for U.S. action to regulate greenhouse gas emissions and fight climate change.
The coalition includes the states of New York, Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, North Carolina, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Washington, and Wisconsin.
___
McDermott reported from Providence, R.I.

title: Video shows moment cat was reunited with owner after apartment fire
text:
'The sweetest cat': Video shows moment tabby was reunited with owner after Massachusetts apartment fire
Dozens of people were displaced after a five-alarm fire tore through a mixed-use building in Somerville, Massachusetts, on Wednesday evening.
Warren Thanes, who lives in the building, said he was on his way home when he saw the flames.
"I was sitting waiting for someone to go in there and get my cat," Thanes said. "My cat is so precious to me and my partner; we need our cat. And I don't know what's going on. They told me to wait patiently."
Firefighters were eventually able to walk out of the building with Thanes' 13-year-old gray tabby cat, Naz.
Chelsea firefighter Alex Lozada, who helped find Naz, said they began the search for the cat once the flames were put out.
"It was tough to find. It was like hidden in the closet, dark cat, dark closet, and we almost left, and I saw the yellow eyes pop out and I was like, 'I found it.'"
Thanes said he and his partner are heading somewhere safe while firefighters put out the blaze.
"(It's) the only thing that matters when a tragedy like this happens," Warren said, as Lozada handed him Naz.

Four buildings were damaged, each containing 8 apartments.
"We had to pull all the ceilings on the top floor, and I had a number of crews on the roof to get the roof open to let the fire vent itself," Somerville Fire Chief Charles Breen said. "It's just been a tremendous amount of work."
According to the Red Cross, 43 people were displaced as a result of the fire.

title: Obituary: Phyllis Elaine (Rollins) Pratt
text:
PLEASANT RIDGE PLANTATION – Phyllis Elaine (Rollins) Pratt, 96, passed away on Sept. 21, 2026, at Maplecrest Rehabilitation Center in Madison, Maine. She was born June 8, 1930, on Pleasant Ridge Plantation and lived there until August of 2022. She was the daughter of Avery L. Rollins and Ruth H. (Beane) Rollins Flanders.
Phyllis attended elementary school at Pleasant Ridge and Kittery, Maine. She graduated from Bingham High School in 1948. Phyllis and George were married on Oct. 30, 1948. They were married for 73 years.
Phyllis worked at Quimby Veneer Mill and as a CNA at the Somerset Rehabilitation & Living Center, both in Bingham Maine.
Phylis enjoyed traveling with her husband, George, with their pickup and camper. She enjoyed rides in the country, summers “at camp” on Embden Lake and trips to Lost Pond.
Phyllis is survived by her daughters Darlene Paine and Elaine Philbrook; grandchildren, Randi Paine and her husband Chris Pupke, Dustin Paine, Brittany Rumery and husband Ben Rumery, Kyle Philbrook; great-grandson Benson Rumery, great-granddaughter Belle Rumery; brother-in-law Wallace Pratt.
Phyllis was predeceased by her husband Geogre; her parents; brother Dennis Rollins and wife Charlene; son-in-law David Paine; brother-in-law Mardel Pratt and wife Gloria, sister-in-law, Barbara Petley and husband Charles, sister-in-law, Marjorie Adams and husband Clayton, and sister-in-law, Claire Pratt.
Phyllis will be remembered by family and friends for loving her life on “The Ridge” and the outdoors. She will be greatly missed by all who knew her.
There will be a graveside service at the Robinson Cemetery in Moscow, Maine on Oct. 2, 2026, at 11 a.m.

title: Pro-Collins PAC takes out $2M ad buy attacking Troy Jackson
text:
A political action committee connected to an alleged pay-to-play scheme has resumed its spending on behalf of Republican Sen. Susan Collins.
The Pine Tree Results PAC on Tuesday reported nearly $2 million in new spending on television ads attacking Democratic challenger Troy Jackson. It was the PAC’s first expenditure since late August and it follows a recent report from ProPublica alleging that its chair, Scott Reed, discussed concealing an illegal donation from a defense contractor to a different committee that backed Collins’ 2020 reelection.
Reed, a longtime Washington lobbyist with close ties to Collins and her husband, Tom Daffron, has denied those allegations to The New York Times. Collins, who has called the ProPublica report offensive and outrageous, told reporters on Capitol Hill last week that Reed is a man of integrity.
In 2020, Reed ran the 1820 PAC, which spent nearly $12 million backing Collins’ reelection. Campaign finance filings show that the Pine Tree Results PAC has nearly doubled that spending this cycle.
The new PAC is funded by an array of well-heeled donors and dark money groups.
This story appears through a media partnership with Maine Public.

title: Mortgage rate forecast: October 2026
text:
Mortgage rate forecast: October 2026
Mortgage rates surged in September, and they’ve reached their highest point since May 2024. The run-up in rates has left many consumers feeling less than eager to dive into the housing market.
The war in Iran sent oil prices soaring in recent months. Higher energy prices translate to both higher inflation and rising 10-year Treasury yields. And both of those things exert upward pressure on mortgage rates.
As of Sept. 30, the average 30-year mortgage rate was 7.38%, according to Bankrate’s weekly lender survey.
“With inflation still running well above target and no sustained relief from lower oil prices, the path of least resistance for rates remains higher,” says Nicole Rueth, senior vice president at CrossCountry Mortgage.
Will mortgage interest rates go down?
Most housing economists say mortgage rates are likely to stay elevated. The Mortgage Bankers Association and Fannie Mae both call for rates to stay near 7% for the rest of 2026 — although their latest forecasts were issued before the late September jump in mortgage rates and Treasury yields.
Mortgage rates are nothing if not volatile, though, and other factors are pushing them higher — especially the war in Iran.
Current mortgage rate trends
The median national home price clocked in at $429,100 in August, up 1.6% from a year earlier, according to the National Association of Realtors. But home sales volumes remain muted by the recent spike in mortgage rates.
“For the housing market, this increase in mortgage rates acts as a significant headwind,” says Lisa Sturtevant, chief economist at Bright MLS. “Sellers are having to adjust their pricing expectations and offer more concessions to buyers.”
Bankrate’s weekly mortgage rate averages differ slightly from the statistics reported by Freddie Mac, the government-sponsored enterprise that buys mortgages and packages them as securities. Bankrate’s rates tend to be higher because they include origination points and other costs, while Freddie Mac removes those figures and reports them separately. However, both Bankrate and Freddie Mac report similar overall trends in mortgage rates.

What to do if you’re getting a mortgage this year
- Shop around. With rates elevated, it’s more important than ever to shop around for a mortgage. Bankrate’s Hidden Homeownership Tax research found that 87% of Americans overpaid for their home loans in 2025 because they settled for the first offer they got. For the typical borrower, that added up to $3,343 in extra costs each year. The stakes are only higher when mortgage rates are rising quickly.
- Improve your credit score. The lowest mortgage rates go to borrowers with the highest credit scores, usually at least 780. A lower credit score won’t prevent you from getting a loan, but it can make all the difference between getting the best possible rate and more costly borrowing terms.
- Save up for a bigger down payment. Putting more money down upfront can help you obtain a lower mortgage rate, and if you put down at least 20% of the purchase price, you’ll avoid mortgage insurance, which adds costs to your loan. If you’re a first-time homebuyer and can’t cover a 20% down payment, there are loans, grants and programs that can help. Eligibility requirements vary by program but often depend on factors like your income.
- Understand your debt-to-income ratio. Your DTI ratio compares how much money you owe to how much money you make, specifically your total monthly debt payments against your gross monthly income. Not sure how to figure out your DTI ratio? Bankrate has a calculator for that.
Frequently asked questions
-  How are mortgage rates determined? Mortgage rates aren’t set by any one entity; they come from a complex mix of economic factors. Lenders typically set their rates based on the return they need to make a profit after accounting for risks and costs. The Federal Reserve gets a lot of attention, but it doesn’t directly set mortgage rates, either. The closest proxy for mortgage rates is the 10-year Treasury yield: Historically, the typical 30-year mortgage rate has been about 2 percentage points higher than the 10-year Treasury yield. But since the pandemic, that spread has been closer to 3 percentage points.
-  When should I refinance my mortgage? Deciding when to refinance is based on many factors. If rates have fallen since you took out your mortgage, refinancing might make sense. A refi can also be a good idea if you’ve improved your credit score and could lock in a lower rate.

title: Maine artist debuts first solo exhibition at Woolwich gallery
text:
Sarah Bouchard Gallery in Woolwich presents Jennifer Brou’s solo debut, featuring a stunning series of 14 large-scale graphite drawings, from Oct. 3 through Nov. 7. An opening reception for ‘Somewhere Still’ is from 3-5 p.m. Saturday at the gallery, 13 Nequasset Pines Road. RSVP is required to [email protected].
Brou’s work delivers the viewer deep into the forest for an emotional encounter with stillness, shadow and a supreme reverence for the natural world. Her practice is based on the ritual of wandering. Whether isolated in the woods or deeply invested in a drawing, she allows herself to become lost in the process. Brou uses photography and rendering from direct observation to record her subjects and bring them to her studio, where she combines them with imagined elements. Drawing in this manner is both a wandering and a search for stillness; a translation and distillation of place into an accumulation of marks.
Brou is an artist, designer and educator based in South Portland. Her multifaceted studio practice includes knitwear design, drawing and photography. Jennifer currently teaches in the Foundation and Continuing Studies Programs at Maine College of Art & Design.
Her drawings have been exhibited at the Center for Maine Contemporary Art, Sarah Bouchard Gallery, Taymour Grahne Projects, Zero Station, University of New England, Easthaus Gallery, Buoy Gallery, Institute of Contemporary Art at Maine College of Art & Design, and Cicada.

title: Fisherman trapped under massive fallen boulder uses Siri to call for help: ‘It’s a miracle’
text:
PORTLAND, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) - An Oregon man on a fishing trip was trapped under a large boulder when it fell on him. His family is now sharing details of his rescue as he faces a long recovery.
Joe Little, 28, was fishing alone early Saturday morning on the Hammond Marina jetty in Astoria when his grandmother says a rock he had sat on several times before began to move.
“He said that he felt it start to move, and he put his feet down to stop it. But the boulder was huge. He slipped down, and it just went over him,” said Kelly Simonson, Little’s grandmother.
Trapped under the boulder and located below the high tide water line, Little knew he needed help quickly. His mother says his Bluetooth earbuds stayed connected when he fell, so he asked Siri to call 911.
Just after 7 a.m., Warrenton police and fire crews were dispatched to the jetty.
Police Sgt. Dylan McCoy says responders were able to narrow down Little’s location by honking their car horns. A dispatcher who was listening on the phone with Little would ask whether he could hear the horn nearby.
McCoy says the rocky terrain was too hazardous for responders to safely walk through, so they launched a drone. Three minutes later, McCoy spotted Little. Only part of his upper body and his feet were visible.
Responders then had to figure out how to free him. The rocky terrain and the size of the boulder made the rescue difficult. According to McCoy, Warrenton Fire devised a plan to remove some of the smaller rocks under Little rather than trying to move the larger boulder.
“They removed some of the smaller ones, and that allowed them to move him from underneath the extremely large boulder which had trapped him,” McCoy said.
A U.S. Coast Guard helicopter arrived at the scene shortly before 9 a.m. Crews hoisted Little from the jetty and transferred him to awaiting emergency medical personnel at Coast Guard Air Station Astoria.
Little is now at a Portland hospital, where he is being treated for severe facial injuries, including a broken jaw.
“His face got smashed. He’s almost unrecognizable,” his mother said. “It’s a miracle that my son is alive.”
Little was scheduled to undergo facial reconstruction surgery Thursday, a procedure expected to last about eight hours. His family has set up an online fundraiser to help with medical expenses.

title: Massachusetts man charged with cyberstalking podcaster and former Trump official Katie Miller
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A Massachusetts man was arrested Thursday in a federal case alleging he cyberstalked conservative podcaster and former Trump administration official Katie Miller, targeting her dozens of times with menacing phone calls and messages, according to court papers.
Authorities say the man contacted Katie Miller at least 40 times over the course of several weeks, sometimes leaving disturbing voicemails and text messages about her and her husband, Stephen Miller, who serves as White House deputy chief of staff. He also sent messages to phone numbers for her parents, according to prosecutors.
John Anthony Proia III, 41, is charged with one count of cyberstalking. An attorney listed for him didn’t immediately respond to an email seeking comment on Thursday.
The court documents do not identify the victim by name, but a person familiar with the matter confirmed that it is Katie Miller. The person spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss non-public parts of the investigation.
“Those who use technology to harass, intimidate or torment others should understand that attempts to anonymize their criminal conduct will not shield them from prosecution,” Leah Foley, the U.S. Attorney for Massachusetts, said in an emailed statement. “We will find you, and we will hold you accountable.”
The investigation contributed to upheaval inside the FBI’s Washington field office, where two top counterterrorism supervisors were recently reassigned by the office’s leader in part because of dissatisfaction over their handling of and approach to the Miller probe, according to multiple people familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss non-public personnel changes.
Darren Cox, the assistant director in charge of the Washington office, said in a statement that the reassignments were not ordered by Director Kash Patel and that the moves were a personnel decision “based on our constant evaluation of mission needs. Any suggestion otherwise is false.”

title: Astronaut Jessica Meir says growing up in Maine sparked her curiosity for space
text:
ISS (WABI) - NASA astronaut Jessica Meir, who has been aboard the International Space Station since February, says her upbringing in northern Maine helped inspire her path to space.
Meir grew up in Caribou and credits the state’s natural landscape with sparking her passion for science and discovery early in life.
“Growing up in Maine surrounded by pine trees with my mom, who was Swedish and had this close affinity and bond with nature, I was very curious about the world around me, especially the natural world, going out into the forest, and looking at the plants and animals,” Meir said. “I think that’s what sparked my curiosity for exploration. I also, of course, had this incredible night sky. I didn’t appreciate it at the time, of course, because that’s just all that I knew, but the density of stars that you can see from northern Maine is quite extraordinary because there is not a lot of light pollution. I started saying I want to be an astronaut by the time I was 5 years old.”
Throughout her career, Meir has spent more than 430 combined days in space and completed seven spacewalks. Looking ahead, she hopes to return to space as part of NASA’s Artemis program, which aims to send astronauts back to the moon in early 2028.
“I do remember in Mrs. Blanchard’s class in first grade, we were asked what we wanted to be when we grew up,” Meir said. “I distinctly remember drawing a picture of an astronaut standing on the surface of the moon. So hey, maybe that Artemis mission will help prove that dream true.”
Meir and her fellow astronauts on SpaceX Crew-12 are scheduled to begin their return to Earth on Monday, Oct. 5, following the handover to SpaceX Crew-13, which launched from Florida on Thursday morning.

title: Maine DHHS awards child development grant to out-of-state, private equity-backed firm
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A Maine organization that has provided training and assistance to educators for decades could close its doors after the state awarded a multimillion dollar contract to an out-of-state company backed by private equity and venture capital firms, officials confirmed Wednesday.
Maine Roads to Quality was created in 1999 by the Catherine Cutler Institute at the University of Southern Maine to offer professional development to child care providers across the state. The organization provides guidance to more than 10,000 Maine child care providers each year.
For much of its existence, Maine Roads has been funded by contracts provided by Maine’s Department of Health and Human Services. That lifeline evaporated last week.
The state offered a pair of contracts worth an estimated $10 million over two years to Shine Early Learning, a New York-based company that offers similar services to childcare centers, home-based providers and public schools in more than 30 states.
“The University of Southern Maine was notified on Sept. 21 that its proposals for two state contracts supporting the Maine Roads to Quality Professional Development Network were not selected for continued funding, thus ending a nearly three-decade partnership,” Samantha Warren, spokesperson for the University of Maine System, said in a statement.
Maine Roads employs more than 30 people. Warren said “layoffs are expected” without a renewal of the DHHS contracts.
The contracts specify Shine Early Learning must employ at least 10 staff members in Maine. Shine Early Learning’s proposals also specify it plans to use artificial intelligence to do much of the work Maine Roads’ human staffers currently perform.
The company plans to implement an “AI-powered family navigation assistant,” an AI-assisted employee vetting tool and an AI agent that will manage a provider registry, according to its applications.
Lindsay Hammes, a spokesperson for DHHS, noted the company has only been offered conditional awards and that no contracts have been ratified yet. The full value of the new contracts “will become public once they are finalized,” she said.
Shine Early Learning underbid Maine Roads by some $2 million between the two contracts, according to documents obtained by the Portland Press Herald. The company did not respond to a request for comment prior to publication.
One contract is for coaching, credentialing, and training of early childhood educators and care providers. The other is for providing a DHHS-approved training plan “designed to improve quality” of child care services and early childhood educators, according to the state’s request for proposals.
Those services have historically been housed under a single contract, Warren said.
When state offices ask for contract bids, they score each of the proposals on a scale from 0 to 100. Shine Early Learning’s bid for the coaching contract received a 97, while its proposal for the training plan got a perfect 100.
Maine Roads received about 73 points on each of its proposals. DHHS said the scores were issued in accordance with the processes laid out in its requests for proposals, but did not specify how Shine Early Learning received such high marks.
Shine Early Learning’s website touts the company’s “data-driven services and solutions” to “accelerate child and family outcomes.”
The company is owned by Acelero, Inc. — a firm seeded with a “strategic investment” from BlackRock, one of the world’s largest private equity companies. Several members from BlackRock and other venture capital firms who invested in Acelero subsequently joined the company’s board, according to a 2022 news release.
The private equity company’s investment in Acelero, and Shine Early Learning by extension, was made with the goal of “extending Acelero’s footprint and deepen(ing) its impact across communities,” BlackRock’s senior portfolio manager said at the time.
BlackRock handles more than $11 trillion in assets. The firm has been criticized for being “too big to fail,” purchasing everything from electric grids to billions’ of dollars of real estate across the country.
Activists have scrutinized BlackRock for investing in companies contributing to climate change and mass surveillance. The United Nations in 2025 issued a report saying BlackRock is complicit in Israel’s genocide in Gaza due to its investments in several weapons manufacturers.
In Maine, BlackRock acts as one of the primary investment managers for Maine’s Public Employee Retirement System.
Maine Roads plans to appeal DHHS’ decision on the contracts issued to Shine Early Learning, said Warren, the UMaine system spokesperson.
“In the meantime, the university is committed to continuing to provide high-quality services for Maine’s early childhood education community through the end of the current contract and supporting potentially affected employees, many of whom have served the field through the program for more than 15 years,” she said.

title: Former fraternity leader gets jail time after pledge died of alcohol poisoning
text:
FLAGSTAFF, Ariz. (KPHO/Gray News) — A former Northern Arizona University fraternity leader was sentenced Wednesday in connection with the death of an 18-year-old pledge.
Carter Eslick, 20, was sentenced to 60 days in jail. He pleaded guilty to a felony hazing charge in connection to the Jan. 31 death of Colin Martinez. Martinez died from alcohol poisoning at an off-campus house party.
Along with the jail time, Judge Stacy Krueger ordered Eslick to serve three years of probation.
Eslick could face an additional 305 days behind bars if he fails to meet probation conditions, which require him to deliver anti-hazing presentations and file court updates every six months.
Eslick’s friends and family speak during hearing
The hearing began with mitigation testimony from five of Eslick’s friends and family members, who attested to his character while warning about the dangers of fraternity culture.
“While trying to teach my children these things, I realized I failed to teach him or explain to them, and in those gaps, toxic influence and toxic communities have stepped in,” Cody Eslick, Carter’s father, said.
Eslick also addressed the court directly, offering an apology to Martinez’s loved ones.
“I am so incredibly deeply sorry for the events that happened on Jan. 31, and I take full responsibility for the hand I played in that ritual,” Eslick said. “And if I had known that one day somebody’s life could be in my hands, there is no way in hell I would have ever looked that way.”
Defense attorneys and Eslick’s mother noted that he served as a designated driver the night of the party and left around 11 p.m. However, prosecutors said Eslick still provided the alcohol and the rules for the fatal drinking game.
Martinez’s parents appeared remotely via Zoom to describe the grief they have endured since their son’s death.
“Every morning since Jan. 31, our families have awakened to the reality that he is not coming home,” Chris Martinez, Colin’s father, said. “No parent should ever have to bury their child.”
The Martinez family said they were not seeking extended prison time, focusing instead on accountability and reform within Greek life.
AZFamily reported that Krueger grew emotional while explaining why jail time was necessary. She noted that while she took Eslick’s character and certain mitigating steps into account, such as reducing the initial alcohol supply and removing blindfolds from the game, Martinez still lost his life.
“Not one person speaking out,” Krueger said. “No one caring more about the well-being of others over their desire to fit in. You know, Mr. Eslick, I look at those steps, and those steps that you took, they do go both ways, because it does tell me you were well aware this was [dangerous].”
The former Delta fraternity leader was originally facing more serious charges, but he pleaded guilty last month to one count of hazing as part of an agreement. As part of the plea agreement, Eslick would face probation, not prison time.
What led to Martinez’s death?
On Jan. 31, Flagstaff police officers responded to an off-campus Delta Tau Delta house and found Martinez unresponsive. He was pronounced dead at the scene.
Investigators said an invite-only dinner was hosted the prior evening as part of spring 2026 rush. A pledge told police that recruits had pillowcases placed over their heads while being taken to the house.
Pledges were told to play drinking games where they drank large amounts of vodka. During the drinking games, court papers say the four pledges, including Martinez, drank around 3.5 liters of vodka.
Witnesses later recalled Martinez snoring unusually and gagging without vomiting. Around 3 a.m., several people searched online for “symptoms of alcohol poisoning,” shifted his position, and checked his pulse and breathing. However, 911 was not called until about six hours later.
An autopsy showed that Martinez had a blood alcohol level of 0.425%, more than five times the legal limit and generally considered deadly
3 members arrested, 1 indicted
Northern Arizona University suspended the fraternity following Martinez’s death. Delta Tau Delta’s national leadership team later voted to close the school’s chapter.
Police initially arrested three executive board members — Eslick, Ryan Creech and Riley Cass — on hazing charges.
The Coconino County Attorney’s Office said in a statement that “after an independent review of the evidence and law,” it indicted Eslick.
According to the Associated Press, Eslick was the pledge master at the time and responsible for welcoming the fraternity’s new members.

title: Waldoboro man cops to lesser charges in kidnapping and drug cases
text:
WISCASSET, Maine — A 44-year-old Waldoboro man was sentenced Wednesday to 18 months in prison after he pleaded to lesser criminal charges in a case where a man said he was held against his will for a week, beaten and threatened with death.
Russell W. Hardin pleaded guilty in Lincoln County Superior Court to trafficking in cocaine and no contest to felony theft and terrorizing. Charges of kidnapping, elevated aggravated assault, robbery and criminal threatening with a dangerous weapon were dismissed.
A no contest plea results in a conviction but allows the defendant to contest the allegations in any civil matter. Defense attorney Ben Tucker said his client knows he could have been found guilty at a trial but that he disputed some of the allegations about the theft and terrorizing charges.
The plea agreement reached with the Maine attorney general’s office on the drug charge called for a sentence of six years in prison with all but 18 months suspended, three years probation and a $400 fine. The district attorney’s office handled the non-drug charges and agreed to lesser concurrent sentences.
The prosecutor said the district attorney’s office had tried to contact the victim but got no response back on the sentence that was being recommended.
Hardin and two co-defendants have been held since their arrests April 15 following a raid at the Reef Road home in Waldoboro.
The grand jury in Lincoln County issued the indictments May 12 against Andonis Morel Tavarez, 18, of Waldoboro and formerly of New York; Shane R. Jones, 38, of South Thomaston; and Hardin of Waldoboro. They were each charged with kidnapping, elevated aggravated assault, robbery, theft, criminal threatening with a dangerous weapon and terrorizing.
The indictment alleges Hardin threatened the male victim with a shotgun. Tavarez is alleged to have threatened the victim with a knife. And Jones is alleged to have threatened the victim with a propane tank.
The police report filed in court by the Waldoboro Police Department states that the offenses occurred from March 23 through March 31. The victim was not from the area and was a passenger in a car that broke down on Wagner Bridge Road in Waldoboro. The vehicle was towed, and the driver said he knew some people who lived at the Reef Road home.
While there, the occupants would not let him leave and made him do chores. The victim said he was asked if he would help deal drugs for them, according to the affidavit. The victim refused and he was accused of being a “cop or FBI.” He was then beaten on multiple occasions. They also stole his belongings including his cellphone, a laptop and clothes.
The victim said on one of the days at the house, he awoke to a shotgun pointed at his face by Hardin, a pistol aimed at him by someone called “Skinny,” a propane tank held by a Shane, and a breaker bar held by a Lulu, according to the affidavit. He said Hardin, Skinny and Shane started beating him from all sides. They then dragged him to the back door and discussed how they might kill him and dispose of his body, according to the police report.
They then confined him in a back-room addition and held him in a chair and beat him intermittently over the next two days.
Eventually, Shane came to get him and told him to get out. The victim left and went to MaineHealth Lincoln Hospital in Damariscotta. The hospital contacted police at the victim’s request and he gave a statement to an officer.
The victim said he witnessed drug sales occurring at the house and saw a couple assaulted.
In the early morning hours of April 15, the Waldoboro Police Department, with assistance from the Maine State Police tactical team, the Lincoln County Sheriff’s Office, Maine Drug Enforcement Agency, and the Maine Warden Service, executed a search warrant at the Reef Road home based on the kidnapping investigation.
Police said as a result of a search warrant subsequently executed there, Hardin, Jones and Tavarez were arrested for the kidnapping. Lauren Elaine Curtis, 26, of Tenants Harbor was arrested for kidnapping, robbery, aggravated assault, criminal threatening and theft.
Curtis was not indicted as part of the May grand jury, according to the court.
Other people were arrested as part of the drug investigation.
Glenn A. Hardin, 72, was charged for outstanding unrelated warrants. He is the owner of the house and father of Russell Hardin. A defense attorney told the court earlier this year that the older Hardin suffers from dementia. Yendy Zenzof Rodriguez, 25, of Massachusetts and Tavarez were charged for aggravated trafficking of scheduled drugs and two charges of unlawful trafficking in scheduled drugs.
Seized at the house were 66 grams of methamphetamine, 48 grams of crack cocaine, 67 grams of fentanyl and about $4,500 in cash.
Assistant District Attorney Jeffrey Baroody told the court at the younger Hardin’s hearing on Sept. 30 that police had received information beginning in January that drug trafficking was occurring out of the Reef Road house and that Hardin was allowing two out-of-state drug dealers to stay at the home.
Tavarez is represented by attorney Andrew Wright of Brunswick. Jones is represented by attorney David Paris of Bath. Curtis is represented by attorney Benjamin Hutchinson of Portland.

title: AARP survey finds most older adults lack confidence in online privacy
text:
Maine (WABI) - A new survey from AARP highlights how artificial intelligence is changing the online safety landscape.
The survey of more than 600 older adults, conducted by Senior Planet from AARP, found just 7% feel very confident about protecting their data online.
The survey also found 70% are not very confident or not at all confident about what they should or should not share with AI tools.
“We don’t want people to stop using technology. It’s really important for us to stay part of the mainstream and learn these tools, but we do want people to become informed, we use them and just be a little bit more cautious and use that common sense we all have,” said Tom Kamber, executive director of Older Adults Technology Services, AARP.
AARP has unveiled a new guide for privacy and security best practices. Recommendations include limiting what apps can access, regularly checking privacy settings on devices and accounts, and staying mindful of what you share on the web.
People can visit seniorplanet.org/privacy-and-security to better understand how to protect their privacy and security while using the internet.

title: Bobby Charles has received lobbyist money. But he’s trying to make an ‘Augusta’ distinction.
text:
He may run a firm that has lobbied in Washington, D.C., since the turn of the century, but in his bid to become Maine’s next governor, Republican Bobby Charles has said he is rejecting money from “Augusta lobbyists.”
Charles first made that pledge in June, when he called on Democrat Hannah Pingree and independent Rick Bennett to join him in also not accepting donations from Central Maine Power or “AI data center companies.”
He has occasionally left out the “Augusta” distinction, such as during an interview this summer. But he reiterated it in his latest digital ad, released Wednesday, in which he calls Augusta a “crime scene” and accuses Pingree and her family of profiting off her years leading Gov. Janet Mills’ policy and innovation office.
“I’m the only candidate in this race who has rejected Augusta lobbyist money,” Charles says in the ad.
But Charles has received money from lobbyists who live outside of Maine. He has received more than $13,000 in donations from current or former lobbyists and their family members, according to campaign finance records.
Still, Charles’ campaign, which has raised more than $1.8 million since launching last year, reiterated Wednesday that lobbyist donations to his campaign have not come from “Augusta lobbyists.”
That pledge has not changed the fact that Pingree, a former Maine House speaker from North Haven, has consistently led Charles by double digits in independent polling of the race to succeed Mills, a Democrat who is termed out of office after this year. Additionally, Charles has not received help from the Republican Governors Association in the form of ad spending — a sign that national leaders do not view the Maine race as very competitive.
Scrutiny over campaign donations across Maine’s high-profile races for the Blaine House, U.S. Senate and 2nd Congressional District is nothing new, though it ticked up this week when Pingree’s campaign said it would return $300 it received earlier this year from a former attorney for Jeffrey Epstein after the Portland Press Herald asked for comment on the donation.
Charles’ firm, The Charles Group, has lobbied on Capitol Hill for decades, though the Leeds lawyer and former assistant U.S. secretary of state says it mostly focuses on conducting studies, providing management guidance and evaluating performance for clients. Charles’ lobbying ties drew criticism even from his Republican primary opponents earlier this year, including Jonathan Bush, who dubbed him “Lobby Charles.”
Campaign finance records show he received contributions such as $4,150 from Van Hipp Jr. and his wife. Hipp Jr., a former South Carolina Republican Party chair, has a lobbying role as chair of American Defense International, a Washington-based consulting firm.
Among other donors, Rob Hartwell, a Virginia-based lobbyist and former chief of staff to several Republican members of Congress, chipped in $250. Bob Carlstrom, a former lobbyist who joined Charles in serving in former President Ronald Reagan’s administration, gave Charles more than $2,600. And Barry Caldwell, a former lobbyist for Cigna and other firms, donated $1,000.
Bennett, a former Maine Republican Party chair and state senator from Oxford who has been mired in the single digits in polls, and Pingree, who previously led Mills’ policy office and is the daughter of Democratic U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, mostly wrote off Charles’ pledge as performative. Each of them has received donations from people who work for lobbying firms that operate in Augusta, such as Preti Flaherty and Mitchell Tardy Jackson.
The lobbyist donations are not the only point of contention among the candidates. The Maine Democratic Party filed a complaint Thursday morning with the state’s ethics commission against Charles. The complaint said Charles reported 46 contributions totaling more than $25,000 over the legal contribution limit, including donors who gave thousands of dollars more than the $2,075 maximum amount allowed under law.
Charles gave the similar “no Augusta lobbyist” donations line in a campaign ad he released last week, featuring him and his daughter walking by apple trees while referring to Mills and Pingree as “Augusta’s bad apples.”
While not producing TV ads like Pingree, who has led the field in raising more than $4.2 million, Charles has projected confidence at his chances after he also used an array of lower-budget digital ads and social media videos to win a crowded Republican primary in June.
The three gubernatorial candidates will face off Thursday evening in a debate hosted by the Maine State Chamber of Commerce at Cross Insurance Arena in Portland.

title: Aging Untold: Depression in older adults doesn’t always look like sadness
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we break down the hidden warning signs of depression in older adults and explain when to seek professional help.
Plus, we explore how older Americans are turning passion projects and hobbies into profitable side hustles to boost their budgets.
We also visit a Memphis bakery on a mission to provide employment, training and a vital second chance for families experiencing homelessness.
When an older adult is living with depression, it might not look like the way you would expect.
The signs might include irritability, withdrawal or suddenly sleeping all day rather than tears or sadness. Depression can also mask itself as declining memory.
Depression can be tied to grief, but physical and chemical factors matter just as much, according to the Aging Untold experts.
Help is available, and aging expert Amy O’Rourke said people who have Medicare or a Medicare Advantage plan can have an annual wellness visit that includes a depression screening.
Deciding whether to get a vaccine as an older adult is a personal choice, especially if you have a chronic condition or a weaker immune system.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the starting point is understanding the purpose of a vaccine in the first place.
Gerontologist Sam Cradduck said the value of a shot isn’t only measured by the disease it prevents, but by what you’re going to prevent it from stealing from you.
We are breaking down the factors to consider when weighing whether to get shots, including flu, shingles and RSV vaccines.
Some people who are looking to make some extra income are turning to side hustles.
Rob Macgregor, who has a full-time job running a small car dealership in Phoenix, also gives golf lessons. He connects with students through a platform that matches people looking for lessons in all kinds of activities, including pickleball, tennis and guitar, with instructors.
Find out more about how this works, the most popular side hustles and what people say they earn by doing them.
A bakery in Memphis serves more than bread, croissants, cupcakes and cookies. It also serves opportunities for people who need a fresh start.
Lucy J’s provides jobs and training opportunities for people experiencing homelessness, according to head baker and executive director Josh Burgess.
Burgess’ wife, Tracy Burgess, is executive director of Dorothy Day House, a Memphis nonprofit that provides temporary housing and support services, including jobs at Lucy J’s.
“Probably the most important thing is that it’s more than just housing,” Tracy Burgess said. “It’s important for families to find employment that will sustain them long term.”

title: Depression in older adults doesn’t always look like sadness
text:
(Aging Untold) — Depression in older adults doesn’t always show up as tears or sadness. Sometimes it looks like irritability, withdrawal or suddenly sleeping all day.
The Aging Untold experts are breaking down the signs, why this generation is especially at risk and what to do about it.
The signs are often mistaken for something else
“I think some of the most common signs you do see with people, really are withdrawal — they just lack interest in anything. A lot of times they’ll just sleep. I have people tell me, ‘I’ve just slept for 36 hours,’ or they will turn to substance abuse, or they just kind of look disheveled,” Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
She added that depression in older adults can also mask itself as declining memory.
“A lot of times in the older person, it may show up as kind of memory starting to go, as well. It may not come about the way that you think it is,” Rogers said.
It’s not “normal aging” — and it’s not rare
The experts pointed to a sobering statistic on suicide rates and older adults.
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the highest rate of suicide in 2024 was among adults 80 and older.
“We have an epidemic going on of depression, and it’s not normal aging,” Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, said. “That’s the problem — so many people think, ‘Well, you should be sad, you’re old,’ or ‘You should expect to lose your spouse or leave your home.’”
She noted that the compounding nature of loss in later life makes it harder to cope.
“There’s a lot of loss, and there’s not a lot of friendship that still exists once you start losing so many. So you lose your partner that you’re bouncing things off of, you lose that comfort, and then you’ve got to deal with all these other things,” Cradduck said.
Hormones, nutrition and lost purpose play a role too
Depression isn’t only tied to grief. Physical and chemical factors matter just as much.
“It’s not the most common reasons that people think either — hormonal shifts are a big thing, or vitamins, nutrient deficiencies and all that. That can affect mood and things like that as well. And then that loss of purpose — that’s a big deal,” Rogers said.
Treatment works — and it’s more accessible than people realize
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke shared a client’s story of how getting help changed his outcome entirely.
“I had a client that was so depressed, one of those that couldn’t get out of bed, and he went to the hospital for treatment for depression, and the outcome was miraculous. He got his life back. He lived independently. The family was blown away. And it really taught me a lesson about really being proactive about getting this depression under control.”
Cost doesn’t have to be a barrier, either. O’Rourke said people who have Medicare or a Medicare Advantage plan can have an annual wellness visit with a screening for depression.
“A lot of people will say, ‘I can’t afford it.’ Well, if you’ve got Medicare or a Medicare Advantage plan, you’ve got an annual wellness visit. They do a depression screening and you can get mental health help. There’s not a visit limit — I’m going to be a mythbuster here. There’s not a visit limit.”
The real cost is not getting help
Rogers pushed back on the idea that mental health treatment is optional or too expensive to pursue.
“I don’t think people realize the worst outcome they can come up with. They think, ‘I can’t afford to get help.’ You can’t afford not to,” Rogers said.
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose added a pointed comparison: “Can you afford dementia? And do you want some of these other things to happen to you? If you can, turn it around.”
It’s time to retire the stigma
The experts said depression deserves the same treatment as any other medical condition.
“Don’t be ashamed. That’s no different than your heart getting help, you know? You go to the heart doctor. That’s no different than your knees, so your brain is just as important, if not more, because it’s controlling everything else,” Rogers said.
Cradduck also called out the “bootstraps” mindset that keeps people from seeking treatment.
“We have this mindset about mental health that the person that’s suffering can just pull their bootstraps up, that they can just get over it, that if you would just choose to be happy, if you would choose to get out of bed, if you choose to do it different... We have to realize that there becomes a chemical imbalance. Depression isn’t just, ‘I’m going to change my mood’ — it’s the chemicals in my brain have changed. And maybe I need an antidepressant. Maybe I need some help to get through this. But if I don’t get through this, the outcome is not OK.”
That same stigma, the experts said, often applies to medication.
“This is a temporary thing that you’re doing to get yourself up and going, and then you might have the energy to go walking or do something that makes your energy level get higher,” O’Rourke said.
“You notice people don’t have a stigma around taking high blood pressure meds,” Rogers added.
Where to start
“I would start with your medical doctor. I think therapy’s a great answer, but also getting out and being social and finding purpose and fun again — it’s really important. And remember, you’re showing other people how to live as well and how to cope,” Ambrose said.
She closed with encouragement for anyone weighing whether to seek help: “Here’s your opportunity to make the rest of the years that you have left your best years. ... They’re the only years you have left.”
Resources
- The Friendship Line: 1-800-971-0016
  - The Friendship Line provides crisis support for people who are 60 and up.
- National Institute on Aging: Depression and Older Adults
- National Suicide and Crisis Lifeline
  - If you are facing mental health struggles or emotional distress, dial 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline anytime.
Key takeaways
- Depression doesn’t always look like sadness. In older adults, it can show up as irritability, withdrawal, sudden changes in sleep or a decline in hygiene.
- Depression is treatable. Getting help can protect memory and cognitive function.
- Help is covered and accessible. Start with your doctor. Medicare and Medicare Advantage plans include an annual wellness visit with a depression screening, and there’s no visit limit on mental health care.
- Treatment is not something to be ashamed of. Seeking help for depression should be treated the same as seeking care for the heart, knees or blood pressure.
- Contributing factors go beyond grief. Hormonal shifts, nutrient deficiencies and loss of purpose can all affect mood.

title: A community celebration of music, autumn and giving
text:
DAMARISCOTTA — Just like that, with autumn, we leave our old selves behind with a newer version of ourselves and our community. The season ignites fresh new beginnings giving way to exciting opportunities. The soundscapes and renewal that Autumn brings come our way through music, song and spoken word on Saturday, Oct. 3 from 1:30 to 4:30 p.m. in the long barn at Inn Along the Way’s, Chapman Farm, 741 Main St. in Damariscotta. With the arrival of October, Applefest and Pumpkinfest, cooler weather, the changing color of leaves and a natural shift in routines, Damariscotta’s Open Mic, celebrating music and verse, embodies fall’s harvest and spirit.
This vibrant afternoon of live music is a by-donation fundraiser, supporting the mission and community programs of the Inn Along the Way. Local performer sign-up begins at 1 p.m. Artist performances, Inn tours, labyrinth and meadow walks plus the ambiance in the Inn’s newly renovated, handicapped accessible long barn, are all part of bringing people together through music and shared purpose.
Musicians and performing artists from all genres and generations this is your opportunity to step onto the DOM autumn stage beginning at 1:30 p.m. Guests can expect an eclectic mix of folk, jazz, blues and storytelling all performed in a relaxed and welcoming barn setting. There’s magic in watching neighbors take the stage and hearing voices you didn’t know were right in your own backyard. All are welcome — whether to perform, listen, dance or simply enjoy the day.
Once each open mic performer has had the opportunity to step onto the Main stage The Rusty Hinges Trio (John Couch, Dan Townsend and Bob Ryan) will bring their unique blend of eclectic music from Midcoast Maine with a repertoire ranging from classic rock to country, bluegrass to the blues, folk to oldies-but-goodies. Their songs, mostly Americana, with the occasional Celtic tune thrown in among the many favorites with tight harmonies, great instrumentation and irresistible rhythms and more come to the main stage around 3 p.m.
The Inn Along the Way is a collaborative community offering older adults and those seeking temporary relief from the responsibilities of caregiving, an environment of support, purpose and sustainability in a multigenerational and mutually interdependent setting. The IAW model is a unique and innovative community design in which older adults will, in the years to come, be able to live interdependently in a neighborhood-style setting of small, environmentally friendly homes. Plans are currently underway to build two interconnected respite cottages.
For more about DOM participation or the IAW’s Say Hello to Autumn musical fundraiser schedule please contact Sylvia Tavares at 207-766-8469 or sylviatavares502@gmail.com.
