title: Witnesses to Christa Pike’s failed execution say their view was blocked multiple times
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WVLT/Gray News) - Witnesses to the failed execution of Christa Pike said their view of her attempted execution was often obscured, raising questions about Tennessee’s already scrutinized execution process.
Several witnesses were told by Tennessee’s Department of Correction that they would be granted access to watch Pike’s execution for the murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer.
During a news conference, witnesses confirmed TDOC staff had closed a curtain over the viewing window multiple times, blocking their view of the room where Pike was being put to death.
Tennessee’s official execution witness policy does not mention when, if at all, a curtain is supposed to be drawn over the window.
One witness to the failed execution outlines how often the curtain came down. Times are reported in Eastern time.
- 7:41 p.m. - Witnesses enter the viewing chamber
- 8:26 p.m. - Curtains open for the first time
- 8:46 p.m. - Curtains close for the first time
- 8:49 p.m. - Curtains open
- 9:05 p.m. - Curtains close
- 9:53 p.m. - Witnesses escorted out of viewing room
Another witness said, “I cannot mention enough how much happened behind a closed curtain as Christa Pike was still alive. A lot of this execution, or attempted execution, happened when we could not see what was going on.”
Tennessee is required by state law to allow media to witness an execution. Those witnesses act as representatives for the public and enable checks and balances when the state decides to execute someone in the public’s name.
Pike’s legal team said it had not been given an update on her condition after she was taken from the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution to a nearby hospital.
“The Tennessee Department of Correction followed every step of the State’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General’s Office,” the Tennessee Department of Correction said in a statement. “The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening. Christa Pike has been transported to an off-site medical facility.”
The failed execution marked the end of a chaotic day for Pike, Tennessee and several federal authorities.
Less than an hour before Pike was originally supposed to be executed at 11 a.m. Wednesday, the 6th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals granted a stay pausing her execution. That pause then prompted a response from the state, which asked the U.S. Supreme Court to intervene and allow the execution to continue.
Pike was convicted in 1996 in the “Job Corps Murder,” a name that came about because both Pike and Slemmer were members of the Job Corps at the time of the 1995 killing. Prosecutors have said in testimony that Pike conspired with two others, 17-year-old Tadaryl Shipp and 18-year-old Shadolla Peterson, to kill Slemmer over relationship issues. During the case, it was discovered that the offenders had carved a pentacle into Slemmer’s chest and taken a piece of her skull as a souvenir of the grisly murder.
There is no word on what the next steps will be in Pike’s planned execution.

title: Aroostook’s only warming shelter faces deficit even with new state boost
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The warming shelter operated seasonally by Homeless Services of Aroostook is getting $112,000 from MaineHousing but, at 25% less funding than last year, that may not be enough.
The Augusta-based housing agency awarded $2.72 million in grants yesterday to 12 of Maine’s warming sites, including half of those in Bangor.
The news comes as cooler temperatures foretell the winter to come, which make housing and heating greater challenges for Maine’s most vulnerable. It’s the most MaineHousing has offered in its five years of warming center grants, and means 474 beds will be available each night throughout Maine.
Presque Isle — the only warming shelter north of Bangor — offers space for 15 people from November through April. Homeless Services of Aroostook Executive Director Kari Bradstreet is glad for the help, but it’s also the lowest such grant the shelter has gotten and will mean cutting other costs.
“Funding wise, it’s the lowest amount we’ve received. Last year, we got $148,500,” Bradstreet said Wednesday. “We’re looking at a $36,000 deficit for a service we spent $148,500 on last year, so there are concerns. We’ll be looking at ways to cut.”
The organization once allowed people to stay in the dining room of its Sister Mary O’Donnell Homeless Shelter during cold weather. Two years ago, after purchasing a nearby building, it opened a separate warming shelter.
Beds are offered on a first-come, first-served basis from 7 p.m. to 7 a.m. Participants can have a warm meal, coffee, a shower and a cot, and staff will do their laundry if needed, Bradstreet said. In the mornings breakfast and snacks are available.
The space is a no-barrier shelter. The only requirement is safe behavior, which Bradstreet defined as being nonviolent and able to function safely with other people.
The shelter doesn’t just serve the unhoused, but anyone in Aroostook County who needs a warm space. Bradstreet thinks the rising cost of utilities and home heating oil will spur more to seek its warmth.
“We helped a woman last year who didn’t have any firewood. She stayed with us for a few weeks and we were able to get her some firewood through [a program], and she was able to return back to her home,” Bradstreet said. “I think we’re going to see more of those situations this year.”
Home heating oil prices hit a record high last week owing to the war with Iran, going over $6 a gallon, Maine Public reported earlier this week.
Shelters can use the funding for staffing, supplies, transportation, extended hours and other operating costs.
The funding comes from the state’s Emergency Housing Relief Fund, appropriated by the Legislature as part of the state’s two-year budget and directed to MaineHousing to help the unhoused or those in need of warming spaces, MaineHousing Communications Director Scott Thistle said.
Six shelters received an amount equivalent to $7,515 per bed while others received less. That’s normal because it’s a competitive grant and applicants ask for what they think they’ll need, Thistle said.
“Grants are done on a competitive process, so they’re not all the same,” he said. “We understand that the need is great throughout the state of Maine. Our role is really to try to be fair and equitable and try to distribute these funds in a way that will help the most people as possible.”
MaineHousing issues a request for proposals each year and chooses applicants based on where funds will help the most, he said. There’s always more demand than there is funding available, which is a standing challenge.
The 12 Maine shelters receiving grant funding also include: Alter L/A, Lewiston; Augusta Overnight; Bangor Area Homeless Shelter; Brick Church, Bangor; Healthy Acadia, Ellsworth; HOME Inc., Orland; Mid-Maine Homeless Shelter, Waterville; Seeds of Hope, Biddeford; Seeds of Hope, Portland; State Street Church, Portland; and Tedford Housing, Brunswick.
As Homeless Services of Aroostook works to cut costs, it also depends on community donations, Bradstreet said. Besides financial contributions, community members, churches and organizations have often prepared meals for warming shelter participants.
For information on how to help, contact Homeless Services at 207-764-4125 or visit them on the web or on Facebook.
For participants who want the help, staff will work with them on referrals to the homeless shelter or other services, Bradstreet said. But the first goal is to get people under a warm roof.
“Warming doesn’t require them to engage in services,” Bradstreet said. “It’s really just to keep people safe and alive.”

title: Annual Maine Public Health Conference Focuses on Getting ‘Back to the Basics’
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - To cultivate mental, spiritual and physical health, we often have to go back to the basics.
That’s what happened Thursday as public health leaders gathered at the Augusta Civic Center for the annual Maine Public Health Association conference.
This year’s theme, “Nourish to Flourish,” focused on strengthening fundamental building blocks across the state.
A key focus: food access.
“The things we heard from people that they need are more access to quality and affordable health care, especially in rural areas. Safe and affordable housing. Making sure that there’s economic opportunity for people living in these far-flung parts of Maine,” said Matt Wellington, associate director of the Maine Public Health Association. “How do we make sure folks can have a happy and healthy life in those areas as well?”
One group promoting that access at Thursday’s conference was the Maine Federation of Farmers’ Markets, which targets food insecurity through SNAP bonus bucks and Senior Farm Share.
“Farmers markets, as they currently exist even without our intervention, are public health institutions,” said Jimmy DeBiasi, executive director of the Maine Federation of Farmers’ Markets. “They’re helping folks access more fresh produce, connect with their neighbors, socialize, and learn about new foods.”
For Maine’s tribal nations, the conversation goes beyond access—centering on the right to shape their own food systems.
“Specifically as Indigenous people, and working towards food sovereignty within our Wabanaki homelands, and really giving our people a choice to the kinds of foods that they have access to and the way that they want to shape their own food systems,” said Keyana Pardilla, director of the Our Sacred Relations division at Wabanaki Public Health and Wellness.
Pardilla explains displacement onto reservations—often food deserts—creates high food insecurity risks, noting “food as medicine” has always been an Indigenous value.
With record turnout, organizers say it proves a shared drive to tackle Maine’s health challenges together.

title: New ICE guidance sets tighter rules for traffic stops, memo shows
text:
New ICE guidance sets tighter rules for traffic stops and bans high-speed chases, memo shows
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers have been ordered not to engage in high-speed car chases and to make vehicle stops only if they have completed specific training, according to an internal memo obtained by The Associated Press.
The guidance follows more than a dozen encounters since last year in which ICE agents fired their guns, resulting in fatalities and injuries, including one deadly shooting in Biddeford, Maine.
The memo, which is dated Wednesday, states officers are not authorized to chase vehicles that fail to pull over. Instead, the officers should take down the vehicles' information for further investigation.
Under the guidance, all officers at the scene of vehicle stops must wear and activate their body cameras. In addition, only officers who have completed one of five specific agency training courses can conduct vehicle stops. Officers who have not completed the training courses can only participate in vehicle stops "in a support capacity" as passengers and cannot be the drivers of any of the vehicles involved.
The guidance says ICE officers can continue to use a technique known as pinning, which is defined as "using a vehicle or physical barrier to trap or stop a car," but only if they have received special training. Similarly, only trained officers can use spike strips that deflate tires to prevent drivers from fleeing.

title: Obituary: Margaret Lee Algazi
text:
DAVIS, Calif. – Margaret Algazi, a longtime resident of Davis, died Sunday, Aug. 30, 2026, from complications related to congestive heart failure. She was born on Feb. 1, 1938 in Portland, the second daughter of John and Edythe Foley. When Margaret was still very young, her parents divorced and she, Edythe, and her sister Eileen moved 30 miles north to Lewiston, to be closer to Edythe’s sister.
When Edythe contracted tuberculosis in 1944 and was confined to a sanatorium, Margaret and sister Eileen were sent to live at St. Joseph’s Orphanage in Lewiston. The orphanage was run by Sisters of Charity of Ste. Hyacinthe, a congregation of French-speaking nuns from Quebec. While at St. Joseph’s, Margaret excelled as a student, took up the piano and learned the Canadian French dialect spoken by the sisters.
After six years in the sanatorium, Edythe was well enough to return home and to reunite with her daughters in Lewiston, where the girls attended public schools. Margaret was a member of the Lewiston High School class of 1956 and was active in the debating and science clubs. She graduated one of the top 10 students in her class and one of only four high school students across New England to receive a Kiwanis Club Scholarship.
In the fall of 1956, Margaret enrolled at Bates College in Lewiston. At Bates, she joined the off-campus students’ club where she met and befriended Betty Chadburn, who became her stepsister when Betty’s father and Margaret’s mother married. While a student at Bates, Margaret had a summer job collecting water samples from the Androscoggin River, which runs through Lewiston, under the supervision of Professor Walter Lawrance. At that time, the river was heavily polluted by the effluents from paper mills. Margaret graduated with her BS in chemistry in 1960.
After graduating from Bates, Margaret left Maine for Boston, where there were more job opportunities for chemists. She found work as a research assistant at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge. Margaret often took her meals at the dining hall in the Graduate House, which was frequented by international students. There, she met Ph.D. student Raphael Algazi, originally from France. She and Raphael were able to converse in French, which Margaret had learned in the orphanage. They hit it off and, in 1963, married. They welcomed their first son, Andre, in 1964.
After finishing his Ph.D., Raphael accepted a position on the faculty of the Department of Electrical Engineering at the University of California, Davis, and the family moved to Davis. In 1966, the family settled in their newly-built home on Willow Lane, where Margaret lived for the rest of her life. In 1967, Margaret and Raphael welcomed a second son, Alain.
After a few years a stay-at-home mom, Margaret decided to pursue a master’s degree in chemistry at UC Davis, which she completed in 1973. In the mid-1970s, Margaret worked in the Department of Vegetable Crops, where she applied her analytical chemistry skills to analyzing tomato samples to identify compounds associated with better tasting fruit.
In the 1980’s, Margaret became active in the volunteer-led Friends of the UC Davis Arboretum. She loved learning and teaching about plants and led popular tours of the arboretum’s collections from different regions of the world. She joined the Friends’ plant propagation group and helped plan and run the group’s annual plant sale. Margaret served as the organization’s president from 1986 – 1988, during which time she organized a popular series of lectures on topics related to botany and horticulture. She leveraged her knowledge and love of plants in landscaping her yard, whose lasting beauty is a legacy of her passion for plants and her eye for design.
Throughout her life, the state of Maine held a special place in Margaret’s heart. After several visits, the family acquired a lakeside camp in the early 2000s, where they enjoyed summer family vacations for several years. Throughout her life Margaret enjoyed keeping up with extended family in Maine and buying gifts from there. In the 1990s, Margaret re-discovered ice skating, one of her favorite pastimes as a youth in Maine. She continued to skate and take lessons until around 2020.
Margaret’s grandchildren, Ryan and Claire, were a a great source of joy for her and she was a loving, attentive grandmother. She organized wonderful family birthday celebrations for them and looked forward to their annual stays in Davis.
Margaret loved books and reading, and she left behind an extensive library. Cooking was another of her lifelong passions, and she led a re-design of her kitchen in 2004 to provide more space to prep and cook meals, as well as store the many kitchen implements and gadgets she collected (and used!). The family has many memories of Margaret’s delicious, eclectic dinners.
Margaret is survived by her husband, Raphael of Davis; son André and his partner Hillary Campbell of Davis; son Alain, daughter-in-law Gail Shibata, and grandchildren, Ryan and Claire of San Francisco. Margaret’s death has left a hole in the hearts of her family, who are greatly comforted by being together during this difficult time. They are also grateful for the love and support of extended family and friends.
A private memorial service will be held at the Algazi home in Davis at a date to be determined.
Donations in Margaret’s name may be made to the UC Davis Arboretum and Public Garden through https://give.ucdavis.edu/AARB/RDSDONR-RMEMO (please specify that your gift is in memory of
Margaret Algazi).

title: 82-year-old pilot injured when ‘last of its kind’ airplane flips at Brunswick airport
text:
An 82-year-old from Windham, New Hampshire, was injured Thursday when the rare plane he was piloting flipped over at Brunswick Executive Airport in Brunswick.
The crash was reported at about 12:30 p.m.
The two-seat, open cockpit plane, a 1939 Kinner Sportwing, was headed to the Owls Head Transportation Museum, executive director John Bottero confirmed on Thursday. According to Brunswick police it had started its flight in Lawrence, Massachusetts.
Police said the plane flipped over on touchdown. Bottero said he heard that the plane was taxiing when something happened with the brakes and it went over its nose onto its back.
The pilot was the only occupant and was treated at the scene for minor injuries, police said.
Bottero said the plane was expected to be “a flying example” and probably still will be.
“Most of these things are well worth restoration,” he said. “It was restored by the gentleman who was donating it. So I have every confidence that it will most likely fly again.”
Bottero identified the plane as one that appears in a 2019 video, in which it is described as the “last of its kind.” Owner David DeVries, whose age and residence match those of the pilot in Thursday’s crash, appears in the video and talks about finding the plane in a dilapidated wooden hanger, covered in droppings. “Even with all that, I thought it was the most beautiful plane I ever saw.”
DeVries said he contacted every registered owner of a Kinner Sportwing and believes his is the only remaining flying example.
The crash is being investigated by the Federal Aviation Administration.

title: Lethal drug that failed to execute Christa Pike was already under scrutiny
text:
(AP) - The lethal drug administered in Tennessee’s failed attempt to execute Christa Pike has been used in multiple states that carry out the death penalty and by the U.S. government after President Donald Trump resumed federal executions during his first term.
Pike, 50, remained alive Wednesday after two doses of pentobarbital were administered, according to her attorneys and media witnesses. On Thursday afternoon, her legal team confirmed that she was still alive and receiving “life-saving medical care.”
Tennessee officials haven’t explained yet what went wrong.
Republican Gov. Bill Lee ordered a third-party review to determine what happened and said another scheduled execution in Tennessee will not take place this year.
What is pentobarbital?
Pentobarbital is a barbiturate, a class of drugs that depresses the central nervous system.
Approved medical uses include sedation, short-term treatment of insomnia, preparation for anesthesia and emergency control of certain severe seizures. It is also used in veterinary euthanasia.
In an overdose, it can produce coma, suppress breathing and cause circulatory collapse and death.
Why is it used in executions?
For years, lethal injections commonly used three drugs: an anesthetic, a paralytic that stopped breathing and potassium chloride to stop the heart.
That method drew criticism because if the anesthetic failed, the paralytic could prevent a prisoner from communicating pain. It also became difficult to maintain after drugmakers restricted distribution for executions.
The pentobarbital protocol was adopted at the federal level during Trump’s first term to replace a three-drug mix used in the 2000s.
As with Tennessee’s guidelines, the federal death penalty protocol calls for administering a 5-gram dose of pentobarbital; in medical settings, patients typically receive a fraction of a gram.
Trump resumed the federal death penalty after an informal moratorium during previous administrations. The federal government used pentobarbital in 13 executions between 2020 and 2021, contributing to making Trump the most prolific execution president in over 130 years.
During the Biden administration, the Justice Department stopped executions with pentobarbital after a government review raised concerns about the potential for “unnecessary pain and suffering.”
After Trump came back to power, the Justice Department in 2026 reauthorized the use of lethal injections with pentobarbital.
How do guidelines vary in different states?
Georgia and Texas use a similar protocol to Tennessee, administering a second dose only if the first is unsuccessful. South Carolina, which turned to pentobarbital in 2024, automatically gives inmates two 5-gram doses spaced about 10 minutes apart.
Lawyers for people on death row have argued that giving such a large dose twice was proof the condemned were dying a lingering death, still conscious and feeling like they were drowning when fluid rushed into their lungs.
But a South Carolina Department of Corrections attorney said inmates are unconscious in well under a minute and can’t feel anything. The heart may show an occasional flicker on a monitor, but that’s because it is the last organ to use the body’s stored oxygen and has residual electrical impulses.
When past lethal injection executions have gone wrong, it is usually because an IV line can’t be properly inserted and the execution is stopped before the drugs are given. There have also been cases of violent reactions or prolonged time passing before death when a new combination of drugs is used.
Wednesday’s failed pentobarbital execution appeared to be the first time problems happened with that drug. Witnesses frequently report that inmates stop breathing and become still less than a minute after getting the drug.
What have experts said about the drug?
Experts quoted in the 2025 federal review argue pentobarbital can cause pulmonary edema, a buildup of fluid in the lungs that may create a sensation of suffocating.
The review concluded that “there remains significant uncertainty about whether the use of pentobarbital as a single drug lethal injection causes unnecessary pain and suffering” and advised that the government should “err on the side of humane treatment.”
Other specialists quoted in a report released by the second Trump administration said a lethal dose causes unconsciousness before that occurs.

title: New ICE guidance bans high-speed car chases and sets tighter rules for traffic stops
text:
New ICE guidance bans high-speed car chases and sets tighter rules for traffic stops
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers have been ordered not to engage in high-speed car chases and to make vehicle stops only if they have completed specific training, under new internal guidance issued after several drivers were shot in encounters with ICE.
A memo sent to officers in ICE’s Enforcement and Removal Operations division and obtained by The Associated Press warned they are not authorized to chase vehicles that fail to pull over under any circumstances. Instead, officers should take down the vehicles’ information for further investigation, according to the memo signed by ICE’s executive associate director Marcos D. Charles and dated Wednesday.
The new guidance comes after ICE-initiated vehicle stops have repeatedly escalated when drivers have refused to cooperate or tried to flee. ICE agents have fired their guns during more than a dozen such encounters since last year, killing at least four people and wounding several others.
President Donald Trump's administration has faced internal tension over how to handle traffic stops, which are seen as particularly high-risk encounters.
After fatal shootings of drivers in Maine and Texas in July, ICE officers were directed to temporarily pause most vehicle stops. But the next day, Trump went on social media to direct the agency to continue traffic stops, calling them “one of ICE’s most important and effective Crime Fighting tools.”
ICE has faced intense pressure from the White House to deport more people who are in the country illegally, and its arrests have reached record numbers. At the same time, the agency's rapid hiring spree last year resulted in some poorly vetted and trained officers hitting the streets.
ICE and the Department of Homeland Security had no immediate comment on the policy guidance.
The new memo outlines steps intended to improve the safety of vehicle stops for ICE officers, drivers they are targeting, their passengers and the public.
The memo told ICE’s field office directors that they must ensure vehicles used for traffic stops have lights and sirens that let the public know they are law enforcement vehicles when activated. All officers on the scenes of vehicle stops must wear and activate their body cameras, under the guidance.
In addition, only officers who have completed one of five specific agency training courses can conduct vehicle stops. Officers who have not completed the training courses can only participate in vehicle stops “in a support capacity” as passengers and cannot be the drivers of any of the vehicles involved.
The guidance says ICE officers can continue to use a controversial technique known as pinning, which is defined as “using a vehicle or physical barrier to trap or stop a car,” but only if they have received special training. Similarly, only trained officers can use spike strips that deflate tires to prevent drivers from fleeing.
The memo came the day that courtroom testimony highlighted ways in which two ICE officers involved in a vehicle stop, pursuit and shooting that wounded a delivery driver in Austin last month would not have complied with the new guidance.
During a bond hearing for Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, testimony showed that the officer who shot him wasn’t wearing a body-worn camera. The ICE officer who did have a camera was driving in a separate car and turned it off during the pursuit.
Prosecutors presented surveillance video that showed an ICE agent chasing Garces Perez at high speeds through residential streets after he fled an initial traffic stop.
Garces Perez faces federal assault charges after investigators say he struck an ICE officer with his driver’s side mirror. That officer then shot into Perez's vehicle, lodging a bullet in his back, officials say.
Attorneys for Garces Perez have called the charges against him “retaliation” and have argued that the camera footage was inconclusive because it didn’t fully capture the moment when he allegedly tried to flee.
Associated Press reporter Anna Wilder contributed to this report from Austin, Texas.

title: 🍁🐶 STELLA IS BACK! Maine’s Favorite Leaf-Jumping Dog Is Showing Off Her Epic Fall Moves!
text:
Maine Social Media Star Stella the Dog Shows Off Epic Leaf Jumps
Maine’s coolest dog is already having a great fall!
Stella is a spirited English yellow Lab who lives with her family in Freeport, Maine. She’s a legit star, too. In fact, she’s so famous that she has her own YouTube channel, with more than 151,000 subscribers.
Like her fellow Maine canine Tatum, Stella proves that you don’t have to be human to become a social media superstar!
Stella also has an impressive following on Facebook, where she has more than 1 million followers.
She’s on TikTok, too, where she has more than 837,000 followers. Combined, her videos have racked up a staggering 53 million views. Incredible!
And if you just can’t get enough of Stella the Dog, you can also follow her on Instagram.
Stella Loves Her Leaves
Stella absolutely loves being outside, especially when there are humongous piles of leaves covering the ground.
Watching her run like she was shot out of a cannon before launching herself through the air and into an awe-inspiring mountain of leaves is endlessly entertaining.
Best of all, there are no sound effects or music in the video clips. You can actually hear Stella smash through the leaves with the greatest of ease!
With that in mind, her owners put together a compilation of some of her coolest leaf jumps every fall.
Stella’s leaf-jumping tradition goes all the way back to when she was a puppy. Her owner, Jody Hartman, first noticed that she would launch herself into freshly raked piles of leaves completely on her own.
And Jody doesn’t simply rake the leaves and call it a day. He dries them with a hair dryer, covers them to keep them dry, “fluffs” them up, and does whatever else is necessary to create the perfect pile for Stella’s epic dives.
She’s been jumping into leaves every autumn for more than 10 years now. Even as an older dog, her enthusiasm hasn’t dimmed much at all.
Stella Even Made the CBS Evening News
Steve Hartman’s “On the Road” series is a much-loved part of the CBS Evening News. In the popular series, Hartman travels across America, sharing inspiring stories and profiles of interesting people and places.
A few years ago, he made a stop in Maine to meet Stella and learn more about the dog who has turned leaf jumping into an annual tradition.
And honestly, once you see Stella launch herself into those leaves, it’s pretty easy to understand why she became a star.

title: High school teacher fired after offering students extra credit in return for cash donations, reports say
text:
(Gray News) - An Iowa high school teacher has been fired for offering students extra credit in return for cash donations to her personal GoFundMe account.
Stephanie Mullaley, a teacher at a high school in the Clinton Community School District, told students in spring 2026 that she had set up a GoFundMe page to raise money for what she described as “personal education goals,” the Iowa Capital Dispatch reported.
Mullaley allegedly told her students that she had set up a the fundraiser to help pay for her education, adding that if they made cash donations to her account they could earn extra credit toward their grade in her class.
Some students in the class contributed funds to the GoFundMe account, according to Administrative Law Judge Duane Golden. Because of the extra credit incentive, students felt pressured to donate money to the GoFundMe.
Donations, she allegedly wrote would be used to pay for “transportation, including flights, buses, and boats, food and hotel accommodations.”
She was fired on May 29, 2026, for allegedly violating the district’s ethics policy.
Golden denied Mullaley’s request for unemployment benefits, ruling that her conduct amounted to job-related misconduct and demonstrated a “willful or wanton disregard” of her employer’s interests, rendering her ineligible for benefits.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch could not reach Mullaley for comment.
The account had a fundraising goal of $1,800 and netted $140 through six donations ranging from $5 to $50 before activity on the account was paused.

title: Couple accused of shooting, killing son-in-law in public park
text:
DUBLIN, Calif. (AP) — A California couple has been charged with murder after authorities say they shot their son-in-law to death Saturday in a public park, days before he and the couple’s daughter were set for a hearing in a bitter divorce case.
Shili Chen and Shouyong Zhang, both 77, were due in court Wednesday for an arraignment on the charges. The Associated Press was not able to reach an attorney for the couple prior to the court appearance. Their daughter, Candice Jang, could not be reached, though she appeared virtually at Wednesday’s hearing.
Jonathan McKinsey, a 40-year-old gaming engineer for The New York Times, was shot to death in the parking lot of a sports complex in Dublin, east of San Francisco. A police sergeant was driving nearby and saw him on the ground as witnesses began calling 911 and pointing out the couple, who were still near the scene, Dublin Police Services said in a news release.
Court records show McKinsey’s killing came during a contentious divorce with Jang and a custody battle over the couple’s three young children. In petitions for restraining orders filed last year, the couple accused each other of physical, emotional and psychological abuse going back more than a decade. McKinsey, who is transgender, alleged that both Jang and her parents were verbally and physically abusive regarding a gender transition he underwent years ago.
In his petition for a protection order, McKinsey alleged that Chen had directed anti-LGBTQ slurs at him and his oldest child.
He also accused Jang of being physically and emotionally abusive during medical procedures related to his transition. He alleged Zhang punched him in the chest while he was recovering from double mastectomy surgery.
Victim had been charged with misdemeanor child abuse
McKinsey was arrested last October and charged with misdemeanor child abuse for allegedly hitting their oldest son. Police said he acknowledged having slapped the child. Prosecutors also charged him with endangering their youngest child after deputies responded to the family’s home to talk with him and found their 2-year-old had been left home alone, according to court documents.
McKinsey pleaded not guilty to the charges and alleged in court records that he had been set up by his wife, who had left the house without telling him the child was sleeping in a crib upstairs. He was released from jail on the condition that he complete 12 parenting classes. At the time of his killing, McKinsey was out on bail and had been trying to enter a mental health diversion program.
It was also in October that Jang obtained a domestic violence protection order against McKinsey.
Jang said in her filing that in 2010 McKinsey had grabbed her by the forearms during one argument and caused her to hit the corner of a coffee table, fracturing a vertebra in her upper back. She also said that in 2023 she called the police to their home after McKinsey pushed their oldest son hard on the head. Jang also accused McKinsey of emotionally abusing her mother.
Victim filed a competing protective order request
McKinsey in December filed his own request for domestic violence protection against Jang, alleging years of abuse that included her hitting him in the head with a frying pan. He later filed for divorce and sought more time with the three children, noting that he had been limited to two hours of supervised visits per week since last fall, Alameda County court documents show.
In late August, McKinsey was granted unsupervised visits in public twice a week.
The killing occurred a week before a hearing was scheduled in McKinsey and Jang’s divorce case. The couple had been married since July 2011.
McKinsey joined The New York Times in January 2023. He was director of engineering for New York Times Games and based in the San Francisco Bay Area, the paper said. A spokesperson declined to comment further.

title: SNAP benefit changes are in effect for millions of recipients. Here’s what you need to know
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray News) - Millions of Americans who depend on the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program will be seeing changes Thursday, including a slight cost-of-living increase.
Every year on Oct. 1, the federal government adjusts its monthly SNAP benefits to account for inflation.
For the upcoming fiscal year, the maximum SNAP benefit for a one-person household will rise by about $8 per month, while the maximum benefit for a household of four will increase by about $29 per month.
Those numbers translate to a maximum monthly benefit of $306 for a single-person household and $1,023 for a household of four.
Federal officials note that benefits vary based on different household circumstances, and residents in Alaska, Hawaii, Guam and the U.S. Virgin Islands will see higher maximums.
The inflation adjustments are intended to help families with the rising cost of food.
Food prices in the United States have increased by about 2.7% between August 2025 and August 2026, according to the United States Department of Agriculture.
The USDA reported earlier this year that more than 37 million people received SNAP benefits, with the program also seeing a drop of nearly 5 million recipients from a year earlier.
More information for those interested in applying for SNAP benefits can also be found online.

title: Human remains found at UC Davis Health Sacramento
text:
Human remains found at UC Davis Health Sacramento campus
Human remains from unidentified burials were discovered by construction crews at UC Davis Health's Sacramento campus earlier this year, officials said.
University officials said the remains were uncovered in February during excavation for construction along X Street near Stockton Boulevard.
Following historical and archaeological investigations, it was revealed that the area overlapped with the former site of the Sacramento County Hospital cemetery, which operated from the 1880s to the 1920s, according to officials.
The remains were from 77 previously unknown burials at the site and are being stored at a secured facility. Officials said the remains varied in condition, with some "consisting of relatively complete skeletal remains" and others having "bone fragments."
University officials said there is no evidence the recovered remains were Native American. Gravestones, grave markers or other materials identifying specific individuals were not uncovered.
There was an earlier discovery of 72 people's remains near the site, which were also believed to be associated with the former hospital cemetery. Those remains were reinterred in St. Mary's Cemetery in Sacramento with approval from the Sacramento Superior Court, officials said.
"The discovery of older human remains is relatively common in historic regions like Sacramento," the university said in a statement. "UC Davis Health is coordinating with appropriate public agencies and the Sacramento County Cemetery Advisory Commission to process the discovery, handling, and reinterment through the standard legal and archeological protocols."
Anyone who has questions or information on the remains is encouraged to contact UC Davis Health Government and Community Relations at community.relations@health.ucdavis.edu or 916-734-5441 by close of business on Nov. 3.

title: Woman told Cornell police 2 years ago she was 100% confident she was raped, transcript shows
text:
ITHACA, N.Y. (AP) - A woman who filed a lawsuit saying she was sexually assaulted by seven men at a Cornell University fraternity house told police weeks after the incident that she could “say with 100% confidence I was raped,” according to a report by CBS New York, which said it obtained a transcript of her interview with investigators.
The transcript, which has not been publicly released, raises new questions surrounding the local district attorney’s decision not to prosecute anyone at the time.
In recent days, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten has maintained the woman’s first account to police didn’t include allegations that she was drugged, incapacitated beyond the ability to consent, or forced into sex. Yet, he also said he had reopened the investigation based on new information in the woman’s lawsuit, which was filed this month.
Cornell has agreed to bring in outside lawyers to independently investigate how the university handled the woman’s allegations, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul announced Wednesday.
The woman initially went to Cornell’s campus police about three weeks after the alleged attack that began on Oct. 19, 2024, then went back on Nov. 14 and 15, 2024, to be interviewed.
“Yes. It was coercion, yes,” she told a campus police officer, according to the transcript obtained by CBS. According to CBS News, she said she was “completely and totally incapacitated” before some of the sexual abuse.
The woman acknowledged she had been drinking alcohol and used drugs the night she visited the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024, and that she had gaps in her memory.
She also told police she was comfortable with an initial sexual encounter with two of the men, but not with what happened later, when other men began to enter the room.
“And then, of course, I was being hit at the same time. Physically hit very, very hard,” she told police, according to the transcript. “I can say with 100% confidence I was raped,” it said she told investigators.
The woman, identified only by the pseudonym Jane Doe in the lawsuit, filed a complaint Sept. 16 saying she was sexually assaulted at the Chi Phi fraternity house after being pressured into snorting ketamine, smoking marijuana and drinking alcohol. She became completely incapacitated while fraternity members were sexually assaulting her, she said.
Van Houten didn’t immediately respond to emails and phone messages from The Associated Press on Wednesday, but he told CBS News he never saw the transcript of the woman’s interview when his office declined to bring charges, and relied instead on a statement written by a campus police officer but signed by the accuser.
Van Houten has released a summary of that statement, with some of her direct quotes included. He has defended his office’s decision not to do additional investigation after the woman first came forward.
“There were no question marks. There was no additional need to find information because we had all of the information that the police collected from Jane Doe through her very detailed, very comprehensive statement that she provided,” Van Houten told CNN earlier this week.
Cornell University first publicly disclosed that it was investigating the woman’s allegations on Nov. 8, 2024, the same day she first went to police. The school sent students an email warning them that a person had reported they had been sexually assaulted at a fraternity house and coerced into consuming drugs. Cornell suspended the Chi Phi fraternity the same day.
In another public statement to students in late November 2024, Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff said campus police were investigating “deeply disturbing allegations of drug abuse and sexual violence” at the fraternity house.
Later, Cornell appointed a task force designed to address sexual assault on campus. But with the district attorney’s decision not to pursue charges and the university’s internal disciplinary investigation shielded from the public, attention on the matter waned.
Cornell said in a statement this week that it supported the decision to reopen the criminal investigation, adding that its own investigation had led to some students being disciplined or expelled. The Chi Phi chapter remains barred from campus, but the university has declined to release more information on discipline for individual students, citing privacy rules.
Earlier this week, Hochul called for a new investigation into the university’s handling of the matter. In a post on social media Wednesday, she said she had spoken with Kotlikoff and he “agreed to bring in outside counsel for an independent investigation.” Cornell confirmed it had agreed but declined additional comment.
“This culture has to stop. And in New York, we’re going to do everything we can to stop it,” Hochul said.

title: Federal report says pilots weren’t warned about wind before Amazon cargo plane crashed in Miami
text:
(AP) - Despite regulations requiring it, an air traffic controller failed to tell the pilots of an Amazon cargo plane about the potential for strong tailwinds as they landed in Miami, careening off the runway and killing five people last month, according to a preliminary report Thursday from the National Transportation Safety Board.
Just four minutes before clearing the plane for landing, an air traffic controller had provided a wind advisory to a different flight, noting gusts of up to 25 mph (40 kph) from the south. But the controller “did not issue information about the wind” to the pilots of the Amazon cargo plane, the report said.
According to federal regulations, “both wind direction and velocity were required to be stated when authorizing use of a runway when a tailwind component exists,” the NTSB report said.
The airplane, carrying packages of contact lenses for Amazon, came in fast after a flight from Puerto Rico and barreled roughly 1,200 feet (366 meters) past the end of the runway at Miami International Airport on Sept. 6. It smashed into a van carrying workers for a company that cleans airplanes. Five people who were in the van died. Two others in the van sustained serious injuries, as did the driver of a car that was hit by the plane. The two pilots had minor injuries.
A summary of cockpit voice recordings previously released by the NTSB said one of the pilots repeatedly warned his counterpart that they were going too fast as they approached for landing and after touchdown. But the fellow pilot never gave “a consistent verbal response” to the warnings, the NTSB has said. The two pilots had flown together for the first time just earlier that day, according to the preliminary NTSB report.
The cockpit audio recordings also captured a series of automated warnings from the plane about the speed of descent and the approaching terrain.
The plane was well down the runway when its right and nose landing gear first touched down, reducing how much distance it had on the runway to stop. Experts have said strong winds from approaching storms could have created a tailwind that helped propel the plane forward.
After the crash, Amazon suspended its partnership with 21 Air, which operated the plane. The North Carolina carrier had flown packages for Amazon since 2024. The Boeing 767 that crashed was 32 years old and originally built to carry passengers. It was converted to a cargo plane in June 2016, the preliminary NTSB report said.
The Miami crash came less than a year after a UPS cargo plane crashed at Louisville’s Muhammad Ali International Airport after losing its engine while accelerating down the runway. That crash killed all three pilots and 12 people on the ground. Twenty-three more were injured.

title: Mountain Valley soccer is the Varsity Maine Boys Team of the Week
text:
Editor’s note: Each week during the fall sports season, Varsity Maine will highlight a boys and girls team of the week. The teams, picked by staff members, will take into account several factors, including success stories, bounce-back efforts and notable accomplishments, among others. Athletes, coaches and athletic directors can nominate teams by emailing sports editor Bill Stewart at [email protected] or Varsity Maine editor Lee Horton at [email protected].
Varsity Maine Boys Team of the Week: Mountain Valley boys soccer
The Falcons didn’t enter the fall as an expected contender in Class C South. In fact, in the past three years, the team has totaled four wins.
But after eight games, the Falcons own a 4-2-2 record and sit at No. 2 in the C South Heal point standings, just below defending state champion Hall-Dale (6-1).
“Last year, we only won one game. It was tough,” said Mountain Valley coach JT Taylor. “Sometimes you’ve got to take your licks before you can get to where you need to be.”
Last week, the Falcons picked up a 2-1 win over Maranacook and a 4-3 victory in a Class C/D crossover against Buckfield. Mountain Valley opened its season by showing it can hang with the division’s best teams, falling 2-1 to Mt. Abram.
“It’s so much more fun,” said Mountain Valley senior Cash Provencher. “We’re starting to become the team that other teams (don’t) want to play. … Change your expectations about us and watch out in the future.”
The Falcons still have a tough road ahead, including matches with Hall-Dale on Oct. 14 and Monmouth Academy in the regular-season finale on Oct. 19.

title: Man indicted in Lincoln Loon Festival crash that injured family of four
text:
LINCOLN, Maine (WABI) - A man charged with operating under the influence of methamphetamine and hitting a family of four walking on a sidewalk in Lincoln during the town’s Loon Festival this summer was indicted by a Penobscot County grand jury.
Carl Hartley, 58, of Mattawamkeag, is charged with aggravated criminal mischief, criminal OUI, driving to endanger, failure to stop for an officer, and violating conditions of release.
Arrest followed July crash
Hartley was arrested on July 18 after police said he struck a couple and their two young children near the intersection of Main Street and West Broadway.
Lincoln police officers and firefighters pulled 24-year-old Jasmine Drew from under the vehicle. She was hospitalized with serious injuries.
Her fiancé and their daughters, a 5-year-old and a 3-month-old, were treated for non-life-threatening injuries.
Second arrest days later
Hartley was arrested days later after police said he fled from officers following reports of erratic driving and ended up striking a police cruiser. The officer was temporarily trapped but not hurt.
Hartley is additionally charged with criminal OUI, driving to endanger, reckless conduct with a dangerous weapon, and unlawful possession of scheduled drugs.

title: 35% of undergraduate women at Cornell University say they have been sexually assaulted on campus
text:
ITHACA, N.Y. (WTSM) — More than a third of undergraduate women polled in a Cornell University survey reported experiencing nonconsensual sexual contact since arriving on campus, according to data released by Cornell.
Cornell has surveyed its student body since 2021 to learn more about sexual assaults on campus.
Survey results show increase since 2023
Cornell’s 2025 Survey of Sexual Assault and Related Misconduct found 35% of undergraduate women and 15% of the entire student body polled reported experiencing nonconsensual sexual contact since coming to Cornell. In 2023, that total number was 11%.
Laura Palumbo, communications director for the National Sexual Violence Resource Center, said the surveys provide information beyond campus safety reports or reports made to campus law enforcement.
“They can tell us a lot more about what’s happening on a campus than just looking at the number of campus safety reports or reports that have come through to campus law enforcement,” Palumbo said.
Survey participation declined
Only 15% of students invited to Cornell’s 2025 survey participated, less than half the respondents from two years earlier. Palumbo said that raises questions about whether students believe sharing their experiences will lead to change.
Fraternity investigation raises questions
In the case of an investigation into Cornell fraternity members allegedly raping and drugging a student, the district attorney has said the survivor’s initial account differed from allegations made later.
Palumbo said changes or additional details in a survivor’s account aren’t necessarily unusual following trauma.
“It’s very normal for survivors to, one, delay their disclosure. And then as they are ready to come forward, it’s very normal for survivors to not have a linear recollection of their traumatic experience, especially if there were intoxicants involved,” Palumbo said.
University and criminal investigations differ
The case has also raised questions about the difference between university and criminal investigations. Palumbo said Title IX proceedings, which mandate universities to respond to, investigate and resolve reports of sexual assault, are separate from criminal investigations conducted by law enforcement.
Cornell’s own survey found only 23% of respondents who experienced nonconsensual sexual contact contacted a formal resource.
“It’s not at all clear where that breakdown may have happened in this case, but I will tell you that is something that survivors commonly struggle with,” Palumbo said.

title: When running the Maine marathon, remember the journey
text:
Editor’s note: Assistant Sports Editor Scott Martin is training to run the Maine Marathon on Sunday. He has a goal and it’s within reach. He has been sharing his ups and downs and everything in between for what it takes to be ready to run 26.2 miles.
I took off my hydration vest and dropped it on the pavement next to my car at the Wainwright Sports Complex in South Portland. Three hours and 55 minutes after leaving this spot on Sept. 19, and nearly 10 months after signing up for the 2026 Maine Marathon, peak training was over. I was too tired and sore to celebrate, but as I leaned on my Subaru Impreza and chugged a vanilla protein shake, I couldn’t help but grin.
Training for my first marathon in seven years was not perfect, but training never is, and despite hiccups caused by illness, insomnia, work and other stress, I was able to do enough speed work and run enough miles to be prepared for a successful race on Sunday. For that, I am grateful.
The time on the clock when I finish will not be the sole factor in determining if my race was a success. There are way too many things that could happen that are out of my control to let my time alone determine if it was a good day or not.
My list of goals for the marathon on Oct. 4 has a number of times (A: 3:47:45; B: 3:49:44 — a PR; C: 3:59:59 — sub 4), but also has things like, “Don’t be a jerk,” “try to have fun,” and “don’t do anything crazy.”
If I accomplish those last three things and cross the finish line healthy, even if I don’t accomplish any of my time goals, race day will be a success.
Really, when I dropped my hydration vest in that parking lot, I had already won. I spent a lot of time this year (Garmin tells me I ran about 76 hours since July 1) working toward this goal. I ran more miles and harder workouts than I have since the COVID pandemic derailed my running habit. When I tore my calf on March 31, 2021, it started a cascade of health issues that forced me to stop running for nearly two months at the end of 2022.
I have spent the last four years building myself to this point. Making it to the starting line and having the opportunity to run a marathon is a huge win.
Maybe you think I am giving myself an out if I am unable to run my goal time. Maybe I am. I have a lot of doubts, despite what my running friends and my coaches tell me, about my ability to average 8:41 per mile for 26.2 miles. I ran close to that pace for 11 miles on Sept. 12, but it filled me with more questions than confidence.
“This feels so fast. Can I really do this for 26.2 miles? Am I fit enough? Will my achy knees put up with this?”
That’s just how my brain works. Confidence has never been my default. Doubt and pessimism are.
When I told my coach, Dan Frey of Finish Strong Physical Therapy and Endurance, about my doubts, he reminded me just how different the situation will be on race day.
“If you push aside race-day anxiety, that’s the only hard part about it,” Frey said. “It’s a supported race. There’s people running with you. There are people cheering you on. All of these things arguably make (the race) easier (than the workouts and the long runs).”
I’ll try to remember that on race day. I will also try to remember all the fun I had with my friends running this summer. Training has been a shared experience with a group of people I’ve grown quite fond of. What happens in the race won’t ruin what has happened over the last 10 months.
I hope I reach my goal in the race. I would love to erase the chalkboard in my apartment with 3:47 written on it because I finally ran that time after 12 years of trying. Even if I don’t, I’ll do my best to enjoy it, to not be a jerk, and remember the journey to get here.
Because no matter how long it takes to run 26.2 miles, the journey has been a lot longer.

title: Judge overturns Trump's decision to fire court-appointed US attorney in Seattle
text:
SEATTLE (AP) — A judge on Thursday overturned President Donald Trump’s decision to fire the court-appointed top U.S. prosecutor in Seattle, the latest development in a legal tug-of-war over the administration’s efforts to control who occupies the powerful Justice Department posts.
The 17 active and senior judges in the Western District of Washington unanimously named Roger Rogoff, a former judge and veteran prosecutor, U.S. attorney in July, after Trump failed to fill the post with a nominee confirmed by the U.S. Senate.
The president fired Rogoff less than an hour later. Rogoff sued, and in a ruling Thursday, U.S. District Judge Stanley Bastian found the termination unlawful and reinstated him.
Bastian noted that when presidents fail to fill a U.S. attorney post with a nominee confirmed by the Senate, federal law authorizes the judges of that district to appoint someone “until the vacancy is filled.”
“It does not say ‘until the president fires the person selected,’” Bastian said.
He concluded: “Mr. Roger Rogoff is the United States attorney for the Western District of Washington and has been the rightful holder of that office since July 15, 2026, when he took the oath of office.”
The Justice Department said in a written statement it disagreed with the decision and would appeal.
Rogoff is the latest in a series of judicially appointed U.S. attorneys to be ousted by the Trump administration, and he is believed to be the first to sue over the removal, setting up a direct legal battle over the issue.
Presidents normally appoint U.S. attorneys, the top federal prosecutor in each judicial district. The positions require Senate confirmation, except in temporary appointments, which can last up to 120 days. When temporary appointments expire before a nominee is confirmed, the judges in a judicial district can name a U.S. attorney.
But under Trump, the Justice Department has sought to leave unconfirmed prosecutors in their positions indefinitely, often through novel personnel maneuvers. Trump named Charles Neil Floyd, who previously served as an immigration judge, interim U.S. attorney in Seattle in October 2025 but never forwarded his nomination to the Senate.
When Floyd’s time as interim U.S. attorney expired, Trump simply shifted his title, a tactic the administration has also tried in other federal judicial districts: It named him first assistant U.S. attorney, while leaving the top post empty.
Trump last month nominated Pete Serrano, the first assistant U.S. attorney in eastern Washington, to be the U.S. attorney in Seattle. But Serrano has not been confirmed, and his nomination is opposed by Washington’s senior Democratic senator, Patty Murray.
“Today’s ruling is an important victory for the rule of law and the people in Western Washington who deserve a U.S. attorney that answers to the law, not Donald Trump,” Murray said in a written statement Thursday.
Bastian is the chief judge in eastern Washington. He heard the case because the judges in western Washington were recused.
In December, Alina Habbaresigned as the top federal prosecutor for New Jersey after an appeals court said she had been serving in the post unlawfully.
Lindsey Halligan, who pursued indictments against a pair of Trump’s adversaries, left her position as an acting U.S. attorney in Virginia after a judge concluded her appointment was unlawful and that indictments she brought against James and former FBI Director James Comey must be dismissed.
The judges there named James Hundley, who had handled criminal and civil cases for more than 30 years, but the administration fired him. It also fired a court-appointed U.S. attorney in northern New York.

title: High schools Thursday: Leavitt girls soccer beats Winthrop
text:
Sophia Poulin deposited three goals and Reese Bilodeau added two scores to lead Leavitt to a 6-1 girls soccer victory over Winthrop, which played most of the game shorthanded, on Thursday in Turner.
“What a crazy game,” Hornets coach Connor Cyr said.
Poulin scored twice in the first half, the second on a penalty kick after a Winthrop player received a red card for an intentional handball in the penalty box with 47 seconds left before halftime, putting the Ramblers (3-4) down a player the rest of the game.
Winthrop’s Harper Stasulus netted a shorthanded goal with 29 minutes remaining to cut the Hornets’ lead to 2-1, but a few minutes later the Ramblers lost their goalie to a red card when she was called for a trip on a breakaway, forcing Winthrop to play 9-vs.-11 for the remainder of the match.
Bilodeau then scored to goals off assists from Eris Cloutier and Poulin. Poulin added her third goal on another penalty kick, and Leavitt (4-5) sophomore Khloe Nadeau capped the scoring with four minutes to play.
Hornets goalie Jillian York finished with five saves.
CAPE ELIZABETH 3, POLAND 0: Pippi Hooper’s two goals paced the Capers (8-1) to a road win over the Knights (8-1-1) in a matchup of the fifth- and 10th-ranked teams in the Varsity Maine poll on Thursday in Poland.
Haisel McGeachey opened the scoring two minutes into the game with a goal from 25 yards out. Hooper scored her first goal four minutes later, and added her second midway through the second half off an assist by Addie Miller.
Poland’s goalies combined for eight saves — seven by Payton Blake and one by Adalyn Martin.
LINCOLN ACADEMY 2, GRAY-NEW GLOUCESTER 1: Ysabelle Bhe and Rowan Coffin scored to lead the Eagles (7-1) to an overtime win over the Patriots (3-6) in Gray.
Ainsley Harris scored with an assist from Bri Burbank for Gray-New Gloucester.
Natalie Hanna made five saves in the win, while Mallory Hardiman stopped four shots for the Patriots.
BOYS SOCCER
LISBON 1, RICHMOND 0: JT Hoyle scored on a header off a direct kick by Nolan Parker in the first half, and the Greyhounds (4-3-2) made that goal stand up in a win over the Bobcats (1-7-1) at Richmond.
LEAVITT 3, WINTHROP 1: Jacob Gibbs netted two second-half goals to pace the Hornets (5-1-2) past the Ramblers (3-6) in Winthrop.
Leavitt’s Everett Michaud opened the scoring with a goal from 30 yards out in the first half. Goalie Luke Horn made six saves.
Korbin Littler scored Winthrop’s goal.
LINCOLN ACADEMY 3, GRAY-NEW GLOUCESTER 1: Peter Norian scored twice in the first half as the Eagles (7-2) took a 3-0 lead on their way to a win over the Patriots (2-6) in Newcastle.
Norian scored with 19 minutes left in the first half on volley from 25 yards. Vito Gazzi made it 2-0 after a feed from George Siegel two minutes later. Norian added his second goal with a volley on a pass from James Hanley.
Hobey Duffy scored in the second half for Gray-New Gloucester.
MT. BLUE 2, BANGOR 0: Sam Dorr and Quin Lawless tallied second-half goals, and the Cougars (4-2-2) beat the Rams (2-6-1) in Farmington.
Stevie Davis and Quin Hoeft each got an assist. Mt. Blue keeper Ollie Cormier made four saves.
Jack Fitzgerald made 10 saves for Bangor.
FIELD HOCKEY
BREWER 2, OXFORD HILLS 0: Paced by goals from Alleia Richards and Ella Davis, the Witches (4-4) defeated the Vikings (3-6-1) in Paris.
Emily Kane need only one save for the shutout.
Oxford Hills goalie Kya Smith made two saves. Anna Fitts had a defensive save.

title: Woman Dies After Sedan And Pickup Collide On Moosehead Trail
text:
Updated as of 10/02/2026
The Penobscot County Sheriff's Office has identified the three individuals involved in a deadly crash that took place just before 7 PM on Wednesday, September 30th.
According to authorities, 67-year-old Kendall Thompson of Dixmont was driving a Chrysler sedan, with 68-year-old Patricia Thompson in the passenger's seat. They were heading east on or near Route 7 near Plymouth Pond. 69-year-old Timothy Malo of Newport was driving his Hyundai Santa Cruz west when the vehicles collided.
"An early investigation indicates Malo's vehicle crossed the center line and struck the Thompson's vehicle in the eastbound lane. As a result of the crash, both vehicles left the roadway and came to rest in Plymouth Pond. All three occupants were transported to the hospital; sadly, Mrs. Thompson passed away from her injuries sustained during the crash."
The Sheriff's office is still looking into the matter and trying to "determine what charges will be filed in this investigation."
We will update this story once those decisions are made.
A crash reconstruction team, along with members of the Penobscot County Criminal Investigation Division, spent hours at the scene of a deadly motor vehicle crash Wednesday evening.

The call came into dispatchers at the Penobscot County RCC just before 7 PM and emergency personnel from the Bangor PD, the Sheriff's Department and Plymouth Fire Department responded immediately.
The Penobscot County Sheriff's Office says the crash occurred in the area of 1789 Moosehead Trail in Plymouth.
"The preliminary investigation indicates that a small sedan was traveling eastbound on Moosehead Trail when it was struck by a pick-up truck traveling westbound. After the collision, both vehicles exited the roadway on opposite side of the road and into Plymouth Pond. Upon arrival, emergency services immediately began treating the patients involved."

The driver's injuries were determined to be serious but not life-threatening. The passenger, however, succumbed to her injuries and passed away at the hospital.
The operator of the pickup truck, a 69-year-old man, was also taken into the hospital and treated for injuries that were non-life-threatening.

title: NFL Week 4 schedule, predictions and more
text:
NFL Week 4 schedule, predictions and more
NFL Week 4 schedule, predictions and more
After three weeks of the NFL season, things are starting to take shape. But there's still a lot of games to be played.
Video above: The Patriots did not come ready to play against Jacksonville
There are five teams still unbeaten: Bills, Vikings, Chiefs, Raiders and 49ers; and five teams still searching for their first win: Titans, Texans, Buccaneers, Dolphins, Chargers.
Something has to give this week with the Kansas City Chiefs and Las Vegas Raiders squaring off in a meeting of the unbeatens.
Here's a look at what's ahead this week, with predictions by Matthew Peaslee of the Hearst National Team. Peaslee went 8-8 in his Week 3 predictions and sits at 29-19 on the year.
All game times are in Eastern Standard Time.
Thursday, Oct. 1
Pittsburgh Steelers (2-1) vs. Cleveland Browns (2-1), 8:15 p.m.
The rivalry is being renewed, and it couldn't come at a better time for the home-standing Browns. The Browns have won two straight games in the past two weeks and three of the last five meetings against the Steelers. The overall series is led by Pittsburgh, 83-65-1. The teams come into this matchup with identical records and similar offenses that have yet to impress so far. Pittsburgh likely pulls out a low-scoring win.
Prediction: Steelers 13, Browns 10
Sunday, Oct. 4
Indianapolis Colts (1-2) vs. Washington Commanders (1-2), 9:30 a.m.
It'll be an early wake-up call Sunday as this one kicks off in London, England. Whoever can score first has the easiest path to victory, as both defenses have struggled in the first three weeks. Marcus Mariota has a chance to expand his game on the international stage after throwing for three touchdowns last week. Look for him to replicate that performance against the Colts.
Prediction: Commanders 38, Colts 33
Tennessee Titans (0-3) vs. Baltimore Ravens (2-1), 1 p.m.
Robert Saleh won a Super Bowl as a member of the Seattle Seahawks in 2014. He hasn't done much winning as the head coach of NFL football teams. He's 0-3 in his first three weeks with Tennessee and he never had a winning record when leading the New York Jets in four seasons. It's probably too early to pull the plug, but another loss is on the horizon and things look bleak the rest of the season.
Prediction: Ravens 40, Titans 13
New England Patriots (1-2) vs. Buffalo Bills (3-0), 1 p.m.
Two of the most dominant teams in the AFC East meet up to see who has the fast track to a division crown. In a quarterback duel between Drake Maye and Josh Allen, the Bills' signal caller has the upper hand. But the Patriots can unleash a strong running attack to take some pressure off Maye, who hasn't performed as well as he did last year. This game comes down to the defenses and Greg Rousseau is Buffalo's standout defensive end who is an early frontrunner for Defensive Player of the Year. Forcing a turnover will turn the tide in a close game.
Prediction: Bills 28, Patriots 24
New York Jets (1-2) vs. Chicago Bears (2-1), 1 p.m.
Case Keenum, 38, stole the headlines across the league last week with an epic performance and locker room speech. Keenum and Tyson Bagent both have played this year with Caleb Williams out and they both have proven to be capable replacements. The Bears defense has improved from week to week, making this one of the NFC's most balanced teams.
Prediction: Bears 24, Jets 10
Jacksonville Jaguars (2-1) vs. Cincinnati Bengals (2-1), 1 p.m.
The Jaguars dominated the Patriots last week and the Bengals just couldn't pull it out in Pittsburgh. Joe Burrow won't have that at home and despite Trevor Lawrence's best efforts, it won't be enough to knock off the Bengals. Ja’Marr Chase has too much firepower, despite Jacksonville having one of the AFC's best defenses.
Prediction: Bengals 38, Jaguars 33
Dallas Cowboys (1-2) vs. Houston Texans (0-3), 1 p.m.
Deep in the heart of Texas, two teams are looking to avoid the basement. The Texans have lost all three games and they were even the favorites in two of them. This isn't the start that was expected in Houston, but there's plenty of time to turn things around — starting this week. Dak Prescott has been performing well enough for the Cowboys to be better than 1-2, it's the defense that has dropped the games thus far. C.J. Stroud is due for a better game than he's had so far and if Nico Collins makes his first appearance this week, that should be enough for a Houston win.
Prediction: Texans 22, Cowboys 17
Arizona Cardinals (1-2) vs. New York Giants (2-1), 1 p.m.
The Giants made the biggest move of the week, acquiring former first-round pick J.J. McCarthy in a trade with the Minnesota Vikings. Jameis Winston is still the starter, though, but bringing in McCarthy gives New York more options and shows the Giants aren't giving up on this season. While the Cardinals may be better than their record indicated with Jacoby Brissett playing well at quarterback, the Giants can do something special and start 3-0 at home.
Prediction: Giants 28, Cardinals 24
Los Angeles Rams (1-2) vs. Philadelphia Eagles (2-1), 1 p.m.
The Rams and Eagles are both looking to bounce back from primetime losses when they meet up on Sunday afternoon. The Los Angeles defense blew a huge second-half lead to the Broncos, and the Eagles were dominated by the Bears. If the Rams are true Super Bowl contenders, like they were predicted to be in the offseason, they need to pull off this road win. Matthew Stafford and Davante Adams are keeping things going on offense to make up for the defense's disappointing start.
Prediction: Rams 36, Eagles 28
Green Bay Packers (1-2) vs. Tampa Bay Buccaneers (0-3), 1 p.m.
Baker Mayfield is out and Jalon Daniels is in at quarterback for the Buccaneers. The Packers also have a sizable list of injured players, and Josh Jacobs is still out on the Commissioner’s Exempt List. Green Bay has enough left in the tank to prove it can still hang atop the NFC North, and it'll help get things back on track with a road win here in Week 4. Jordan Love needs to throw the ball better, but he will still be the best offensive player on the field in Tampa.
Prediction: Packers 30, Buccaneers 24
Miami Dolphins (0-3) vs. Minnesota Vikings (3-0), 4:05 p.m.
Video below: Antonio Brown's plea deal hearing delayed
Kyler Murray is sparking the Vikings' offense, and Jordan Addison is helping his cause. The Vikings are equally strong on defense, leading the NFL with 14 sacks. It'll be a long day for Miami quarterback Malik Willis — and a long season for the Dolphins, who could be the first 0-17 team in history (the 2008 Detroit Lions and 2016 Cleveland Browns both went 0-16).
Prediction: Vikings 44, Dolphins 13
Kansas City Chiefs (3-0) vs. Las Vegas Raiders (3-0), 4:25 p.m.
This should be the most anticipated matchup of the weekend. The Chiefs are the Chiefs, as per usual and the Raiders can prove they are for real with a statement-making victory. A fourth win would surpass the Las Vegas win total of 2025. Brock Bowers has burst onto the scene and is turning into a top tight end and one of Kirk Cousins' favorite targets. But is he the next Travis Kelce? He and his Raiders can prove the doubters wrong this week. The Raiders lead the NFL with nine takeaways, giving the up-and-coming offense more chances.
Prediction: Raiders 27, Chiefs 24
Los Angeles Chargers (0-3) vs. Seattle Seahawks (2-1), 4:25 p.m.
Don't worry, Dolphins, the Chargers will soon join you on the losing streak. The Seahawks are heavily favored, just like the Vikings are, against their winless opponent. Seattle can't face an upset like they did last week against Washington. The offense for the Chargers just hasn't clicked with Justin Herbert at quarterback and Mike McDaniel at offensive coordinator. Drew Lock has shown he is the right man for the job at quarterback for the Seahawks and Jaxon Smith-Njigba is always helping his case.
Prediction: Seahawks 38, Chargers 17
Denver Broncos (2-1) vs. San Francisco 49ers (3-0), 4:25 p.m.
The 49ers have the league's best offense, but they have yet to play a team as talented as the Broncos. However, their defense is suspect and the offense rallied last week. Denver had arguably the best win last week and will be riding that high into Northern California. Key injuries to Nick Bosa and Mike Evans may slow down the 49ers, while the Broncos' Jaylen Waddle is proving himself to be a star.
Prediction: Broncos 30, 49ers 28
Detroit Lions (2-1) vs. Carolina Panthers (1-2), 8:20 p.m.
Detroit has a great offense and a suspect defense. Carolina has a string of injuries that may slow it down in front of a big night crowd. The Lions' Jahmyr Gibbs is the favorite to win the NFL’s Offensive Player of the Year, and he should keep that up this week while the Panthers' offense has cooled down from its hot start in Week 1.
Prediction: Lions 27, Panthers 21
Monday, Oct. 5
Atlanta Falcons (1-2) vs. New Orleans Saints (1-2), 8:15 p.m.
If the Saints didn't turn the ball over, they could be 3-0. Their offense is further hampered this week with injuries to lineman Kelvin Banks Jr. and running back Travis Etienne Jr. The Falcons need Michael Penix Jr. to play better, and he will this week. Bijan Robinson can also carry the load and start to turn things around before the season slips away.
Prediction: Falcons 24, Saints 14

title: The Lincoln County News
text:
Lois M. Lane, 79, of New Harbor, passed away peacefully in the early morning hours of Sept. 29, 2026 with her son Chris by her side. Born on Oct. 14, 1946, Lois was the daughter of Leverett and Ethel May Chase.
In 1962, Lois married Erlyn “Buddy” Lane at her family home in Pemaquid Beach. Many joked that the marriage would not last a year. Fifty years later, after weathering life’s challenges and celebrating its successes together, many would agree there were no two people more destined to share a life than Bud and Lois.
Together, they built a life filled with love and happiness on Pemaquid Point, where they raised their two sons, Alec and Chris, and enjoyed the company of countless cherished friends.
After working various jobs around the Pemaquid area, Lois found her calling when she joined the New Harbor office of J. Edward Knight Insurance. She spent more than 30 years serving her community, a role she loved because it allowed her to help others and connect with the people she knew and cared about.
In addition to her parents, Lois was predeceased by her beloved husband and lifelong partner, Erlyn “Buddy” Lane; her son, Alec Lane; and her brother, Paul Chase.
Those who knew Lois will remember her radiant smile, warmth, kindness, and caring nature. She treasured the time spent with family and friends and enjoyed reading, painting, traveling, camping, and making memories with those she loved most.
Lois leaves behind a legacy of love, compassion, strength, and generosity. She is survived by her son, Chris Lane; her brother-in-law, Denis Lane; her nieces, Dawn Michelle Stryffeler, Debbie Crum, and Bronwen Lane; and her nephews, Darryl Walizer, Darrin Walizer, and Caleb Lane.
In her later years, as she courageously faced the challenges of dementia, Lois was a resident of Riverside at Chase Point Assisted Living Memory Care on the MaineHealth Miles Campus. Her family extends their heartfelt gratitude to the unforgettable caregivers and staff whose compassion, kindness, and dedication brought comfort and dignity to her life.
Chris would also like to recognize the team at CHANS Home Health & Hospice. Their dedication ensured that Lois experienced a graceful, compassionate, and gentle final chapter of life. Just as importantly, they helped Chris navigate the many challenges that accompanied her illness, allowing him to focus his time and energy on being a son rather than a caregiver alone.
Finally, Chris wishes to recognize Dr. Allen Teel and the ElderCare Network of Lincoln County, whose guidance and support helped not only Lois, but Buddy as well, as they navigated the early stages of dementia.
In lieu of flowers, those wishing to make a donation in Lois’s memory are encouraged to consider the ElderCare Network of Lincoln County, founded by Dr. Allen Teel.
Chris would also like to share a personal request. If you know a caregiver, do not wait for them to ask for help. More often than not, they will not. Caregivers often feel they are already placing a burden on others, making it difficult to ask for assistance.
The gift of time, even a few minutes, can mean the world. Giving a caregiver five or 10 minutes for a walk, a worry-free cup of coffee, or simply a moment alone can provide much-needed relief and support.
You might also consider volunteering with one of the organizations that helped Lois along her journey. Through this experience, Chris was forever humbled and profoundly changed by the residents, families, caregivers, and professionals he met. Their kindness and compassion left a lasting impact for which he will always be grateful.
A time of visitation will be held from 3-5 p.m. on Friday, Oct. 9, 2026 at the Strong-Hancock Funeral Home in Damariscotta. She will be laid to rest privately with Erlyn in the New Harbor Cemetery.
Arrangements are under the direction and care of the Strong-Hancock Funeral Home, 612 Main St., Damariscotta, ME 04543. Condolences and messages for his family may be expressed by visiting stronghancock.com.
Lois will be deeply missed by all who knew and loved her.
