title: ‘Like I won the lottery’: Army veteran battling leukemia surprised with mortgage-free home
text:
RICHMOND HILL, Ga. (WTOC/Gray News) - A retired Army veteran who suffered severe injuries during his military service and is now battling leukemia received a life-changing surprise: a brand-new, mortgage-free home.
Retired Army Chief Warrant Officer Steve Smith and his wife, Jenifer, were welcomed into their custom, three-bedroom home in the Del Webb Savannah at Heartwood community during an emotional ceremony surrounded by community leaders, veterans and family.
“It’s like you literally go out, get a lottery card, and you’re like, ‘I won,’” Smith said.
Service and life-altering injuries
Smith enlisted in the U.S. Army in 1990, dedicating 13 years of service before being medically and honorably discharged in 2003.
While deployed to Kuwait that same year, Smith was performing a high-altitude night parachute jump when his chute became entangled and partially collapsed. Unable to deploy his reserve chute in time, he plummeted roughly 200 feet to the ground in a semi-assisted fall.
The impact fractured bones across his back, shoulders, collarbone, femur, pelvis and right arm, leaving him with permanent paralysis in his hand. He also lives with a traumatic brain injury, post-traumatic stress disorder, hearing and vision loss, tinnitus and ongoing mobility complications. Smith has since been diagnosed with leukemia.
“To be injured in the way I was, it was a mental blow, because you feel like you can no longer be who you were,” Smith said.
For years, the couple faced mounting questions about the future.
“It’s surreal, you dream, you think, ‘What’s gonna happen?’” Jenifer Smith said.
Built for accessibility and family
The home was gifted through a partnership between national nonprofit Building Homes for Heroes and PulteGroup’s Built to Honor program.
The house was constructed with specialized accommodations for Smith’s physical recovery, featuring zero-entry doorways, a roll-in shower and full main-level living spaces.
PulteGroup Coastal Carolinas Division President Matthew Raines said crews wanted to ensure the home was completely stress-free from day one.
“We’re gonna provide them a fully furnished house, move-in ready, with things in the pantry,” Raines said, noting the home includes “the amazing things that they put throughout this house to make your life wonderful, easier, happier.”
During the ceremony, U.S. Rep. Buddy Carter presented Smith with an American flag that previously flew above the U.S. House of Representatives.
“A community that cares about each other, and that’s why we’re here today,” Carter said. “We’re here to welcome home Steve and Jenifer Smith, a true American hero.”
For the Smiths, Richmond Hill offers not just physical stability, but proximity to loved ones. The home splits the distance between family living in Virginia and Florida.
“Being able to go an hour and a half to go see them, that means everything to me, it really does,” Smith said.

title: Rapper Rick Ross denied special treatment in court as judge tells him ‘I don’t know who you are’
text:
MIAMI BEACH, Fla. (Gray News) — Rapper Rick Ross, born William Leonard Roberts, is facing charges for an alleged domestic violence issue in August.
But the judge Ross appeared in front of Thursday did not know who he was.
Brad Horenstein, Ross’ lawyer, wanted his client’s release expedited.
“Mr. Roberts is a celebrity, and so I don’t know...” Horenstein said.
“What does that mean?” the judge responded.
“I don’t know to whatever degree your honor can, but I’d ask that that his release be expedited. He’s in a red jumpsuit and for purposes of his safety. I don’t know what your honor can do, but, I don’t know,” Horenstein said.
The judge then said hello to Ross and said he would not get special treatment.
“Hi, Mr. Roberts. I have no idea who you are, except as somebody here in the court who’s going to be treated fairly just like everybody else here,” she said.
Ross faces a felony charge of battery by strangulation, as well as a misdemeanor battery charge, according to online court records.
An attorney for Ross, 50, said in a statement that Ross is being wrongfully accused by an ex-girlfriend whose motivations are unclear.
Jail records showed that Ross was being held Thursday morning on $5,000 bail. He was later released. An arraignment is scheduled for Oct. 22.

title: States and cities sue over EPA cutting rule that limits emissions from coal and gas power plants
text:
States and cities sue over EPA cutting rule that limits emissions from coal and gas power plants
States and cities sued the Trump administration Thursday for repealing rules that limit planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions from power plants fueled by coal and natural gas.
Twenty-one states, led by New York, are challenging the Environmental Protection Agency's power plant rule. The coalition also includes Pennsylvania's governor, the District of Columbia, New York City, Chicago and the city and county of Denver. They argue that "gutting one of the country's most significant climate protections" will set the nation back decades and worsen the climate crisis.
The EPA announced last month it's revoking the Biden-era rule, and said it is taking a separate but related step to prevent future administrations from regulating climate pollution from power plants.
New York Attorney General Letitia James said the federal government is showing "callous disregard" for Americans' health and the environment, and future generations will pay the price. Power plants that burn fossil fuels are a major source of planet-warming pollution.
"Dismantling these protections is a betrayal of American families, and the stakes are too high to allow this administration to once again put profits over people," James said in a statement Thursday.
The EPA said Thursday it does not comment on pending litigation. However, it said in announcing the repeal that it would save the industry more than $300 billion in costs and help “unleash” American energy. EPA Assistant Administrator Aaron Szabo said in September that it will allow utilities to “make the best decision for the ratepayers based on cost and cost savings, instead of being required to shut down facilities.”
The coalition is petitioning the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia to review the EPA's decision and strike down the repeal. It says the EPA unlawfully abandoned the pollution limits without properly considering reasonable alternatives or the enormous health and climate costs of allowing more pollution into the atmosphere. The coalition also told the EPA it intends to sue over the agency's failure to regulate pollution from many gas-fired power plants.
The suit comes as the Supreme Court prepares to hear a landmark case in which the city and county of Boulder, Colorado, are suing oil and gas companies to force them to help pay for damage caused by disasters linked to climate change.
The case is part of a wave of climate change litigation around the country and the world with billions of dollars at stake. The high court will hear the case on Monday, the first day of its new term.
The rule change for power plants, first proposed last year, represents a fundamental shift from efforts by Democratic Presidents Joe Biden and Barack Obama to address climate change and regulate carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases that trap the sun’s heat. Environmental groups say it will come at a cost to Americans’ health and further degrade the environment.
The separate rule proposed last month could prevent future administrations from regulating greenhouse gas emissions from power plants. The proposal, expected to be made final next year, follows EPA’s action earlier this year revoking a scientific finding that long has been the central basis for U.S. action to regulate greenhouse gas emissions and fight climate change.
Abre’ Conner, the NAACP’s director of environmental and climate justice, hailed the lawsuit.
“When the federal government retreats, our state and local elected officials have an obligation to step up,” Conner said. “We cannot allow the Trump administration to give passes to polluters when we know the outcome will mean our communities will suffer.”
The coalition includes the states of New York, Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, North Carolina, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Washington and Wisconsin.
McDermott reported from Providence, R.I.

title: Video captures scary moment when roller coaster gets stuck at vertical drop
text:
'Oh, we're stuck now': Video captures scary moment when roller coaster gets stuck at vertical drop
Riders in Texas experienced a frightening moment after a roller coaster paused in a vertical position for nine minutes during the amusement park's opening weekend, forcing riders to evacuate.
It happened at the new amusement park COTALAND in Austin, Texas, on its Circuit Breaker roller coaster. The ride has a "tilt" feature where it pivots and pauses at a high point of the ride before resuming. The ride stopped for nine minutes, causing riders to evacuate and walk down approximately 100 steps to get down, KXAN reported.
"Maybe it's just a little delayed," Nicholas Thomas, who had already ridden the ride multiple times, told KXAN. "One second turns into two seconds turns into three seconds, and that’s when I realized, like, 'Oh, we're stuck now.'"
The roller coaster paused again for about two minutes at the same spot on Sunday before the ride resumed. No one was hurt in either of the incidents.
The Circuit Breaker has been operating since October 2025 and reaches up to 130 feet high, according to KTBC.
The amusement park is on the property of the Circuit of the Americas racetrack.
The roller coaster is at the center of a lawsuit filed in May based on a December malfunction when it was stuck for nearly an hour, according to reports.

text:
74-year-old woman sues hospital after wrong leg is amputated
A 74-year-old woman filed a lawsuit against a hospital in Ohio after she says surgeons amputated the wrong leg.
On Sept. 19, 2025, Sharon Jacks underwent surgery at Selby General Hospital to remove her right leg as part of treatment for skin cancer, but when she woke up, she realized her healthy left leg had been removed, according to the lawsuit filed in Washington County, Ohio.
Jacks later underwent surgery at a different hospital to remove her right leg, leaving her as a double amputee.
Due to the error, the lawsuit claims Jacks "suffered severe physical injury, permanent disability, pain and suffering, emotional distress, humiliation, loss of enjoyment of life."
Jacks alleges medical negligence and battery against nine defendants, including the hospital and her doctors and surgeons.
She is seeking unspecified punitive and compensatory damages.

title: Bakery pairs pastries with a path to employment
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
MEMPHIS, Tenn. (Aging Untold) — Lucy J’s, a bakery in Memphis, is providing jobs and training opportunities for people who need a fresh start, according to head baker Josh Burgess.
Burgess is also Lucy J’s executive director. The bakery is named after his daughter and eldest son.
“Our fresh bread is some of the best in the city,” Burgess said. “Our sourdough and our cheddar jalapeno bread are very, very popular. We have the best cinnamon roll in the world.”
The bakery also sells savory and sweet pockets, croissants, cupcakes and cookies.
Jobs for families in need
The jobs pave a path forward for many of Lucy J’s employees.
“Just depends on what they need, and we try to find a slot for them to fill,” Burgess said.
Josh Burgess’ wife, Tracy Burgess, is executive director of Dorothy Day House, a Memphis nonprofit that provides temporary housing and support services, including jobs at Lucy J’s, for families experiencing homelessness.
“There is a huge need here in the city, and it really is an invisible problem,” Tracy Burgess said. “They have to be able to sustain their family life after they move out.”
Dorothy Day House was founded in 2006 and named after a late journalist who advocated for the poor. The organization operates three locations in Memphis for families working toward stability while gaining a network of support.
“Probably the most important thing is that it’s more than just housing,” Tracy Burgess said. “It’s important for families to find employment that will sustain them long term.”
Living wage and expansion plans
Lucy J’s provides jobs for some Dorothy Day House families and pays workers $15 an hour.
“It’s just a community that needs help,” Josh Burgess said. “And they’re here to help us, and we’re here to help them.”
With steady demand for Lucy J’s baked goods at groceries, restaurants and food trucks, Josh and Tracy Burgess hope to raise money to expand the bakery and hire more workers.
“It’s a big mission that we’re trying to tackle, and we could use everybody’s help,” Josh Burgess said. “Come in, buy something, donate if they’re available, volunteer if they’re available, and just become part of the community.”

title: Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens Named One of America’s Most Underrated Attractions
text:
Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens Named One of America’s Most Underrated Attractions
The Maine staple was named among the most underrated and underappreciated attractions in the country.
👇 KEEP READING: 19 Maine News Stories That Went National in the Last 20 Years 👇
Stasher compared 665 selected U.S. attractions using Tripadvisor ratings and an equally weighted online popularity score based on Wikipedia views and TikTok and Instagram post totals.
Attractions qualified as underrated if they had strong visitor ratings but relatively low online popularity, while highly popular attractions with ratings below 4 out of 5 were classified as overrated.
Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens ranked fourth on the study’s list of underrated attractions, with an online popularity index of 30.9.
Its Tripadvisor rating of 4.9 out of 5 was the highest among the top 10 attractions on that list.
Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens is a public botanical garden in Boothbay, covering more than 300 acres of gardens and natural areas along Maine’s coast.
Visitors can explore plant displays, woodland and waterfront trails, a children’s garden and outdoor art installations.
And there you have it! The gardens’ strong visitor rating compared with their relatively modest online popularity helped place them near the top of the study’s underrated list.

title: New ICE guidance bans high-speed car chases and sets tighter rules for traffic stops, a memo shows
text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers have been ordered not to engage in high-speed car chases and to make vehicle stops only if they have completed specific training, under new internal guidance issued after several drivers were shot in encounters with ICE.
A memo sent to officers in ICE’s Enforcement and Removal Operations division and obtained by The Associated Press warned they are not authorized to chase vehicles that fail to pull over under any circumstances. Instead, officers should take down the vehicles’ information for further investigation, according to the memo signed by ICE’s executive associate director Marcos D. Charles and dated Wednesday.
The new guidance comes after ICE-initiated vehicle stops have repeatedly escalated when drivers have refused to cooperate or tried to flee. ICE agents have fired their guns during more than a dozen such encounters since last year, killing at least four people and wounding several others.
President Donald Trump’s administration has faced internal tension over how to handle traffic stops, which are seen as particularly high-risk encounters.
After fatal shootings of drivers in Maine and Texas in July, ICE officers were directed to temporarily pause most vehicle stops. But the next day, Trump went on social media to direct the agency to continue traffic stops, calling them “one of ICE’s most important and effective Crime Fighting tools.”
ICE has faced intense pressure from the White House to deport more people who are in the country illegally, and its arrests have reached record numbers. At the same time, the agency’s rapid hiring spree last year resulted in some poorly vetted and trained officers hitting the streets.
ICE and the Department of Homeland Security had no immediate comment on the policy guidance.
The new memo outlines steps intended to improve the safety of vehicle stops for ICE officers, drivers they are targeting, their passengers and the public.
The memo told ICE’s field office directors that they must ensure vehicles used for traffic stops have lights and sirens that let the public know they are law enforcement vehicles when activated. All officers on the scenes of vehicle stops must wear and activate their body cameras, under the guidance.
In addition, only officers who have completed one of five specific agency training courses can conduct vehicle stops. Officers who have not completed the training courses can only participate in vehicle stops “in a support capacity” as passengers and cannot be the drivers of any of the vehicles involved.
The guidance says ICE officers can continue to use a controversial technique known as pinning, which is defined as “using a vehicle or physical barrier to trap or stop a car,” but only if they have received special training. Similarly, only trained officers can use spike strips that deflate tires to prevent drivers from fleeing.
The memo came the day that courtroom testimony highlighted ways in which two ICE officers involved in a vehicle stop, pursuit and shooting that wounded a delivery driver in Austin last month would not have complied with the new guidance.
During a bond hearing for Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, testimony showed that the officer who shot him wasn’t wearing a body-worn camera. The ICE officer who did have a camera was driving in a separate car and turned it off during the pursuit.
Prosecutors presented surveillance video that showed an ICE agent chasing Garces Perez at high speeds through residential streets after he fled an initial traffic stop.
Garces Perez faces federal assault charges after investigators say he struck an ICE officer with his driver’s side mirror. That officer then shot into Perez’s vehicle, lodging a bullet in his back, officials say.
Attorneys for Garces Perez have called the charges against him “retaliation” and have argued that the camera footage was inconclusive because it didn’t fully capture the moment when he allegedly tried to flee.
___
Associated Press reporter Anna Wilder contributed to this report from Austin, Texas.

title: SpaceX launches 4 astronauts on a fast track to the International Space Station
text:
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. (AP) — Four astronauts pulled up at the International Space Station on Thursday after launching on an eight-hour express that set a U.S. speed record.
The fresh arrivals include a Canadian whose wife will give birth while he’s away.
SpaceX launched commander Jessica Watkins and her crew for NASA after a three-week delay to fix their Dragon capsule’s leaking fuel system. Thick clouds threatened all morning to halt the countdown but in the end, the skies cleared enough to allow for a safe liftoff.
Although their stay at the International Space Station will last a long six months, the flight there was the quickest yet not only for Elon Musk’s company, but any American entity, including NASA. The space station’s convenient location when the astronauts launched enabled the fast transit.
With the late morning liftoff from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Watkins became the first Black woman to lead a crew to orbit. A geologist who worked with NASA’s Mars rover Curiosity a decade ago, Watkins is making her second trip to the space station following a lengthy stay in 2022.
“Thanks for an amazing ride,” Watkins radioed following liftoff.
The others are newcomers to space: NASA’s Luke Delaney, a retired Marine; Canada’s Joshua Kutryk, a colonel in the Royal Canadian Air Force; and Russia’s Sergey Teteryatnikov, a former submariner. They will replace four astronauts who have been living at the orbiting laboratory since February.
This was the 13th crew launched by SpaceX for NASA, not counting 2020’s test flight. All four embrace their Crew-13 designation that pays homage in their mission patch to Apollo 13. The harrowing 1970 moonshot ended with the astronauts’ safe return.
References to the number 13 abounded Thursday. Watkins and her crew rode to the launch pad in black Teslas bearing plates that read “Lucky 13.” What’s more, they carried up a small crocheted golden dragon named Lucky with a four-leaf clover around its neck.
“We figured it wouldn’t hurt to bring a little of our own luck just in case, but clearly we don’t need it,” Watkins said from orbit, noting they were “four of the luckiest humans on or off planet Earth.”
Kutryk will become the fourth man to become a father while orbiting Earth. Wife Heather is due to give birth to their third child in late November. The Canadian Space Agency promises plenty of support for the entire family when the big day comes.
“A lot of life-changing things can happen over six months,” NASA manager Dana Weigel said on the eve of liftoff, noting that the space agency will do its best to keep Kutryk looped in to his family.
In 2004, NASA provided a radio link between space station astronaut Mike Fincke and his wife’s delivery room during the birth of their daughter. Five years later, Randy Bresnik, commander of next year’s Artemis III mission, dialed in to his wife’s hospital from orbit.
The happy news traveled more slowly for Austrian astronaut Franz Viehbock. His daughter was born a few hours after he launched to the Soviet Union’s Mir space station in 1991. He was not informed until the next day.
SpaceX, meanwhile, is on a roll. Three hours after Crew-13 blasted off, SpaceX launched a Falcon rocket from California with more than 100 mini satellites. Another Falcon was set to soar late Thursday night from Florida, with a classified satellite for the National Reconnaissance Office. All this comes the same week that the company’s massive Starship reached orbit for the first time.

title: Greenville's historic Masonic temple will be rebuilt after devastating fire
text:
Greenville’s historic Masonic temple will rise from the ashes.
The Masonic Hall on Pritham Avenue was gutted in an early morning fire in December.
Over the past nine months, the Columbia-Doric Lodge No. 149 has worked and prepared to rebuild, and site preparations started Wednesday, according to the Moosehead Historical Society.
Interior demolition begins next week and is expected to take three weeks.
The restoration, being done by E.W. Littlefield Inc. and Sons, will preserve the hall’s four brick walls and exterior appearance.
“Keeping those four walls means a great deal to the lodge and to the community,” Luke Muzzy, a lodge member and executive director of the Moosehead Historical Society, said in a Wednesday statement. “We’re happy to tell people that the temple will be rebuilt and will still look very much like the building they remember.”
Crews will be restoring the roof, windows and entrance to their former appearance. The same goes for the upstairs lodge room.
But some changes are coming to the historic property, including moving the kitchen from the basement to the first floor, which, along with a ramp, will make breakfasts, dinners and gatherings more accessible to the public. The basement will then become space for lodge members, according to the historical society.
The fire broke out at the Masonic Hall about 1:07 a.m. on Dec. 15, 2025.
When firefighters arrived, they discovered heavy flames, and video and photos from the scene showed flames roaring up from the lodge’s roof.
Investigators concluded that the fire began in the basement kitchen. But the extent of the damage has prevented the fire marshal’s office from determining the blaze’s cause.
The lodge has loomed over Pritham Avenue since its construction in 1929, paid for by merchant Arthur Crafts.
There is currently no timeline for the completion of the reconstruction.

title: Tracks displayed at old Gilead train station
text:
GILEAD — The old Gilead train station has new tracks running to it — complete with a bumper stop and a whistle post.
The train station building, moved twice since its original location next to the St. Lawrence and Atlantic Railroad tracks, has been sitting at its most recent home on Depot Street since 2011, according to Lin Chapman of the Gilead Historical Society. The oldest known railroad depot in Maine, it serves as a museum of local rail history and receives regular tourist visitors who pass by on nearby Route 2 in the summer.
The society maintains the building, along with an old schoolhouse next door.
In 2022, a railroad baggage car was added at the station site. Chapman said the car was restored by Cruiser Solutions of New Hampshire, working initially with the only original parts — the iron remains of the car, including the wheels. A replica wooden frame was built to attach to them. The baggage car was originally donated by Stephen and Lise McLain a few years before the restoration began.
In August, society members and volunteers from two states placed cast-off rails and ties on a bed of gravel next to the train station to simulate train tracks.
They didn’t have to go far to get them. The St. Lawrence and Atlantic Railroad tracks run just on the other side of Depot Street from the station.
Historical society member Hugh Chapman, Lin’s husband, said that following some rail work, the railroad company had left old rails and ties behind, sitting next to its tracks. The society members asked if they could have them, and the company agreed.
In early August, the volunteers dragged them across the street, and historical society trustee Peter Risbara placed them with his tractor on gravel from Daniels Landscaping of Gorham, New Hampshire.
Then came the additions that might not be familiar to people other than rail enthusiasts, though they likely have seen them along tracks.
A whistle post, white with the black letter “W” on it, was donated by Steve Hastings a few years ago. It had first been placed next to the station building, but was relocated to be next to the new tracks.
Whistle posts let train engineers know when to sound their whistle when approaching a crossing.
And then the biggest, and most likely heaviest, addition followed. It was a bumper stop, donated by Paul and Marsya Robert of Bethel. It had come into their possession when they bought the property of George and Danna Nickerson, formerly of Bethel, who moved out of town a few years ago. Hugh Chapman said George Nickerson had brought it home from where he worked, at the P.H. Chadbourne Mill in Bethel. The mill was next to the St. Lawrence and Atlantic track there.
A bumper stop sits at the end of a rail siding and is the last line of defense in case an engineer slightly misjudges his speed and distance when moving rail cars onto the siding. The bumper stop keeps the last car from dropping off the end of the rails.
Hugh Chapman estimated its weight at at least 1,700 pounds. Moving it from Bethel was no easy task, he said. Enlisted to help was Robert Chapman of Chapman Scrap Metal Recycling of Milan, New Hampshire. He brought a large truck, loaded the bumper stop, and brought it to Gilead.
The track section, bumper stop and whistle post lend more of a railroad context to the station building, which Hugh Chapman said people unfamiliar with railroads might not otherwise recognize.
Now all the track display needs, Lin Chapman said, is something “such as a putt putt (a small motorized vehicle used by maintenance crews) or a hand pump track car.”
Alison Aloisio is a freelance writer.

title: DC judge permanently dismisses case charging ex-Olympian with vandalizing Reflecting Pool
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A judge in the nation’s capital agreed on Thursday to permanently dismiss a criminal case charging a former Olympian with vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a move that could prevent federal prosecutors from reviving the case under political pressure from President Donald Trump.
D.C. Superior Court Judge Todd Edelman ordered the dismissal of David Hearn’s case with “prejudice,” which would block U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro’s office from refiling the felony charge against him. The judge ruled nearly a month after hearing attorneys’ arguments.
Hearn’s lawyers say Trump administration officials have continued to falsely accuse the Maryland resident of vandalizing the reflecting pool despite Pirro’s decision to drop the case on July 31. Trump responded by saying Pirro “choked” and “folded like an umbrella.”
In a court filing in July, Pirro said new evidence produced by the Interior Department showed Hearn wasn’t responsible for damage to the pool’s lining. Pirro’s office attributed the damage instead to a botched installation by a contractor as well as a rush to complete the project in time for this summer’s America 250 celebration in Washington.
Pirro’s admission was an embarrassing setback for the White House. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum has backed Trump’s claims that vandals damaged the pool.
Hearn has said he was on a bike ride on June 19 when he reached in to examine the pool’s newly peeled coating and briefly touched a chunk attached to the side of the pool. But he said he obeyed a park worker’s command to let go of it.
Hearn was charged with one count of property destruction, which carries a maximum prison sentence of 10 years. His lawyers questioned whether prosecutors properly presented the grand jury with adequate evidence to support the charge and the amount of damage alleged by the government.
Hearn, 67, of Bethesda, Maryland, competed in three Summer Olympics, earning his best finish, ninth, at the 1996 Atlanta Olympic Games, the U.S. Olympic and Paralympic Committee says on its website.
Trump, a Republican, appointed Pirro, a former Fox News host, to serve as the top federal prosecutor for the District of Columbia. Edelman was nominated to the bench by Democratic President Barack Obama.
Hearn’s attorneys said the ruling is “a victory for the rule of law and for an innocent American seeking justice” and allows Hearn to “move forward with his life as he deserves.”
“This administration chose to pursue an unjust prosecution against Mr. Hearn. It should not get repeated chances to wield the power of criminal prosecution against someone who should never have been prosecuted,” the lawyers said in a statement.

title: Troy Jackson says sorry for comments on Jewish Mainers’ views on Gaza war
text:
Troy Jackson told media outlets across the country that he was sorry for saying Jewish Mainers “don’t like to” call Israel’s war against Hamas in Gaza a genocide, “only because they’re Jewish and what that means to them with the Holocaust.”
Jackson made the initial comments to News Center Maine on Tuesday. He called the three-year war — which began with Hamas terrorist attacks on Oct. 7, 2023, and has since resulted in the killing of 70,000 Palestinians by Israeli forces in Gaza — a genocide, and continued on to say Jewish Mainers “don’t like to use that term.”
“I apologize for the pain that caused,” Jackson said in a statement. “Mainers hold a range of deeply considered views, and I promise I will always listen and work to approach these conversations with the care and respect they deserve.”
Jackson reiterated his belief that “what’s happening in Gaza is a genocide.”
“In trying to acknowledge that, I misspoke and made a generalization about Jewish Mainers’ views that doesn’t reflect what I meant to say,” his statement continued.
In the News Center Maine interview, Jackson also called Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, a war criminal. The International Criminal Court, to which the U.S. is not a signatory, issued an arrest warrant against Netanyahu in 2024 for starving people in Gaza as a means of war and ordering the killing of civilians.
A United Nations commission first found that Israel was committing genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza strip in September 2025. More than 64,000 children have been killed or injured in Gaza since October 2023, the U.N. said in August.
Like his predecessor for the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate, Graham Platner, Jackson’s use of the word “genocide” to describe Israel’s actions in Gaza is part of a larger call to stop arms funding to Israel. Brown University found that the U.S. sent $21.7 billion in military aid to Israel from October 2023 to September 2025 — for which Republican Sen. Susan Collins, Jackson’s incumbent opponent, has consistently voted.
“I don’t want the United States sending money, a blank check to (Netanyahu) anymore, watching young children, innocent people die,” Jackson told News Center Maine. “I mean, I just disagree with that.”

title: Nokomis field hockey stays hot with win over Lawrence
UMaine men’s hockey seeking bounceback season as it prepares for opening weekend
text:
University of Maine sixth-year hockey coach Ben Barr isn’t one to reap praise unless it is thoroughly deserved.
Yet, even though the 2026-27 Black Bear team hasn’t played a game yet, he is already touting the players’ work ethic and culture.
“I told the guys that we’re sleeping well at night because they’re working hard every day. That doesn’t mean we’re going to go out and win just because we work hard,” said Barr. “There’s another level to that. But we know we will be in the fight with the work ethic they have established so far. They haven’t had a bad practice yet.”
The team first got together in July for the optional six-week training regimen in Orono.
“It is an unbelievably fun group to be around which is really cool for our staff,” Barr said. “The guys care about each other and that has been in evidence since the first day they got here in July. They’re good dudes.”
Last season, the work ethic wasn’t up to the standard Barr established and that was one of the primary reasons the team finished with a disappointing 18-14-3 record, which included a dismal showing in a 5-0 loss to Boston College in the Hockey East quarterfinals. The team went 12-11-1 in league play during the regular season.
His previous two teams had gone a combined 47-20-8 overall and 27-14-7 in league regular season play and earned back-to-back NCAA Tournament appearances for the first time since the 2005-06 and 2006-07 seasons. The Black Bears won the Hockey East tournament in 2024-25 for the first time since 2004.
“We’re trying to find the soul of our program again,” Barr said. “That blue collar work ethic that we need to bring every single night so our opponents know it is going to be one of the hardest games they’ve played in all year.”
“I love this group,” said senior center and alternate captain Sully Scholle. “There isn’t another group of guys I would rather go into battle with. You know the guys next to you are giving their all.”
“You couldn’t have a tighter group of guys,” agreed senior center and alternate captain Max Scott. “We have a great culture. We’re going to play a great style of hockey that I know the Maine fans are going to love. We’re going to get it done out there.”
Scott’s 1,073 career faceoff wins between Brown and UMaine is third most among active players. His 54.8 percent faceoff success rate is third among active players with at least 750 faceoff wins.
The Black Bears were picked to finish seventh among 11 teams in the Hockey East preseason coaches poll.
On paper, it’s understandable to see why the Black Bears have been picked so low. There are question marks in all areas, so they will need some of their 15 newcomers to be impactful right away.
This team may not be as talented as last year’s, but it hopes to compensate with work ethic, grit, depth and chemistry. This team will be bigger and older and will win more puck battles and be a much tougher team to play against.
They have lost their top four scorers in defenseman Brandon Holt (6 goals, 26 assists), right wing Josh Nadeau (17 goals, 13 assists), left wing Justin Poirier (18 goals, 11 assists) and right wing Miguel Marques (10 goals, 13 assists).
Holt was chosen the league’s best defensive defenseman, a first team All-American and an All-Hockey first teamer and Nadeau was also a first teamer.
The Black Bears have lost players who produced 52.6 percent of their goals and 53.1 percent of their assists.
“We’re going to be a hard-nosed team,” said senior left wing and team captain Owen Fowler. “We may have lost some point-getters from last year, but I will honestly take the group we have in the locker room now any day of the week.”
Fowler, selected the league’s best defensive forward last year, is the only returnee who scored double-digit goals a year ago as he had a career-high 12 to go with 10 assists in 34 games.
His five career shorthanded goals makes him the Hockey East leader among active players.
Scholle (7 goals, 11 assists) and Scott (5 goals, 13 assists) were next with 18 points apiece and senior right wing Charlie Russell had 6 goals and 9 assists. Junior right wing Thomas Pichette, sophomore center Jaden Lipinski, sophomore left wing Will Gerrior, junior center Oskar Komarov and sophomore center Brock James are the other returning forwards.
All of the forwards have the potential to elevate their point productions, and that’s what the team will need because you aren’t likely to get a 20-goal season from any one of them.
They have seven incoming forwards including four transfers, and they will be called upon to contribute to a team that will seek to have good scoring balance and depth..
Robert Morris transfer Tanner Klimpke had 41 goals and 39 assists in 103 career games and was an All-Atlantic Hockey America second team pick last season. UMass Lowell transfer Lee Parks had 14 goals and 14 assists in 69 career games; Alaska-Anchorage’s Judah Makway had 3 goals and 3 assists in 33 games a year ago; and Arizona State’s Sam Alfano had 6 goals and 11 assists in 35 games.
Freshmen Rowan Calvert, Ross Campbell and Mason Fleece had 31, 28 and 25 goals for their respective junior teams.
The three returning defensemen were all regulars as freshmen a year ago: Lukas Peterson, Jeremy Langlois and Lois Usereau. Each improved as they gained more experience, and they all can supply offense.
The defense corps will have a promising group of newcomers who will all have legitimate shots to earn regular minutes.
Dru Krebs has 142 pro games under his belt between the ECHL (140 games) and American Hockey League (2). Providence College transfer Alex Bales, Ohio State transfer Chris Romaine and former CCHA All-Rookie team pick Isa Parekh from Bemidji State all have plenty of experience.
They will also have two freshmen in Ludvig Lafton from Dubuque in the United States Hockey League and Dante Siciliano from Brooks in the British Columbia Hockey League.
In goal, the Black Bears desperately need a bounceback year from senior Albin Boija, who slumped to a 2.59 goals-against average and an .899 save percentage after going 1.82 and .928 en route to second team All-American status two years ago.
He leads all active goaltenders in Division I in career wins (43) and shutouts (10).
He is getting seriously challenged for the starting job by fellow Swede Petter Wickstrom Stumer, who had a 2.64 GAA and a .921 save percentage in 12 games for Canisius a year ago. The 6-foot-6-inch Stumer had a 72-save gem in a 4-3 win over Lindenwood.
Lindenwood transfer Colin Ronan is the No. 3 goalie.
Barr said the makeup of the roster is a lot different than a year ago.
“Last year, we were playing 10 or 11 freshmen every night. This year, we have a lot of new faces, but many of them are transfers with college experience so the maturity level is different, which is a good thing,” said Barr.
“Every single player in our locker room is fully capable of being a good player at this level,” he added. “There isn’t much separation between players, which drives the competition level up. They know they are all fighting for a job.”
Fowler pointed out that the coaches brought in more size and that will help them wear teams down.
“We have guys over six feet who will forecheck (aggressively) and the opposing defensemen will definitely feel it each weekend. That will be a big part of our team this year,” Fowler said.
UMaine will open its 50th season this weekend on the road against a Holy Cross team from Atlantic Hockey America that went 18-18-2 a year ago, 14-10-2 in league play.
They will play on campus at the Hart Center Rink in Worcester, Massachusetts, at 7 p.m. Friday and then at the DCU Center at 7 p.m. Saturday.
Holy Cross was picked to finish fourth in the AHA preseason poll.
They will be led by Matt Kursonis (6 goals, 15 assists), Noah Eyre (8 goals, 12 assists) and goalie Danick Leroux (12-9-1, 2.58, .908).

title: Former fraternity leader gets jail time after pledge died of alcohol poisoning
text:
FLAGSTAFF, Ariz. (KPHO/Gray News) — A former Northern Arizona University fraternity leader was sentenced Wednesday in connection with the death of an 18-year-old pledge.
Carter Eslick, 20, was sentenced to 60 days in jail. He pleaded guilty to a felony hazing charge in connection to the Jan. 31 death of Colin Martinez. Martinez died from alcohol poisoning at an off-campus house party.
Along with the jail time, Judge Stacy Krueger ordered Eslick to serve three years of probation.
Eslick could face an additional 305 days behind bars if he fails to meet probation conditions, which require him to deliver anti-hazing presentations and file court updates every six months.
Eslick’s friends and family speak during hearing
The hearing began with mitigation testimony from five of Eslick’s friends and family members, who attested to his character while warning about the dangers of fraternity culture.
“While trying to teach my children these things, I realized I failed to teach him or explain to them, and in those gaps, toxic influence and toxic communities have stepped in,” Cody Eslick, Carter’s father, said.
Eslick also addressed the court directly, offering an apology to Martinez’s loved ones.
“I am so incredibly deeply sorry for the events that happened on Jan. 31, and I take full responsibility for the hand I played in that ritual,” Eslick said. “And if I had known that one day somebody’s life could be in my hands, there is no way in hell I would have ever looked that way.”
Defense attorneys and Eslick’s mother noted that he served as a designated driver the night of the party and left around 11 p.m. However, prosecutors said Eslick still provided the alcohol and the rules for the fatal drinking game.
Martinez’s parents appeared remotely via Zoom to describe the grief they have endured since their son’s death.
“Every morning since Jan. 31, our families have awakened to the reality that he is not coming home,” Chris Martinez, Colin’s father, said. “No parent should ever have to bury their child.”
The Martinez family said they were not seeking extended prison time, focusing instead on accountability and reform within Greek life.
AZFamily reported that Krueger grew emotional while explaining why jail time was necessary. She noted that while she took Eslick’s character and certain mitigating steps into account, such as reducing the initial alcohol supply and removing blindfolds from the game, Martinez still lost his life.
“Not one person speaking out,” Krueger said. “No one caring more about the well-being of others over their desire to fit in. You know, Mr. Eslick, I look at those steps, and those steps that you took, they do go both ways, because it does tell me you were well aware this was [dangerous].”
The former Delta fraternity leader was originally facing more serious charges, but he pleaded guilty last month to one count of hazing as part of an agreement. As part of the plea agreement, Eslick would face probation, not prison time.
What led to Martinez’s death?
On Jan. 31, Flagstaff police officers responded to an off-campus Delta Tau Delta house and found Martinez unresponsive. He was pronounced dead at the scene.
Investigators said an invite-only dinner was hosted the prior evening as part of spring 2026 rush. A pledge told police that recruits had pillowcases placed over their heads while being taken to the house.
Pledges were told to play drinking games where they drank large amounts of vodka. During the drinking games, court papers say the four pledges, including Martinez, drank around 3.5 liters of vodka.
Witnesses later recalled Martinez snoring unusually and gagging without vomiting. Around 3 a.m., several people searched online for “symptoms of alcohol poisoning,” shifted his position, and checked his pulse and breathing. However, 911 was not called until about six hours later.
An autopsy showed that Martinez had a blood alcohol level of 0.425%, more than five times the legal limit and generally considered deadly
3 members arrested, 1 indicted
Northern Arizona University suspended the fraternity following Martinez’s death. Delta Tau Delta’s national leadership team later voted to close the school’s chapter.
Police initially arrested three executive board members — Eslick, Ryan Creech and Riley Cass — on hazing charges.
The Coconino County Attorney’s Office said in a statement that “after an independent review of the evidence and law,” it indicted Eslick.
According to the Associated Press, Eslick was the pledge master at the time and responsible for welcoming the fraternity’s new members.

title: Jay approves $52,188 boiler for wastewater facility
text:
JAY — The Select Board approved spending $52,188.07 from a joint capital reserve account for a new propane-fired condensing boiler at the Livermore Falls wastewater treatment facility.
The new boiler will replace an oil-fired system that has used an average of about 5,000 gallons of heating oil per season, with the more efficient propane system expected to substantially reduce fuel use and operating costs.
Mark L. Holt, superintendent of the Livermore Falls and Jay sewer departments, presented the request to the board Sept. 28. Because the expenditure comes from a joint capital reserve account for the Livermore Falls wastewater treatment facility, both towns must approve it under their interlocal wastewater treatment agreement.
Livermore Falls approved the expenditure Sept. 15, Holt said.
The project was put out to sealed bid, with proposals submitted by ABT of Wilton, Central Maine Plumbing & Heating of Livermore and A. Maurais & Son of Jay. Holt said both towns use the three companies to supply and maintain municipal heating systems. Maurais initially suggested installing a condensing boiler instead of replacing the existing equipment with a conventional cast-iron boiler. The other two contractors were given an opportunity to bid on the alternative system. Maurais submitted the lowest proposal for both options.
“The decision to install a condensing boiler was based on its efficiency compared to the cast-iron boiler,” Holt said in a follow-up email.
Maurais estimated the condensing boiler would save just over $6,000 annually compared with a cast-iron propane boiler, Holt said.
Part of the difference comes from the new boiler’s ability to adjust its output to match heating demand rather than always operating at full capacity.
“Instead of starting and running at the full 1,000,000 BTU capacity and burning the maximum amount of fuel, it can run at an idle, burning 1/10th as much fuel to produce only the BTUs required to heat the space,” Holt said.
At the Sept. 28 meeting, Holt estimated that continuing to use heating oil could cost about $25,000 per year, while the propane condensing system could cost roughly $6,100 annually to operate, based on past fuel use. He told the board the resulting savings would allow the new equipment to pay for itself relatively quickly.
Holt later clarified that the calculation was based on an average annual consumption of about 5,000 gallons of No. 2 heating oil. “The fuel savings are considerable,” Holt told the board.
The boiler is expected to last 25 years or more, according to the information presented to the board.
A. Maurais & Son has ordered the new boiler, Holt said, and the equipment is expected to arrive in about two to three weeks.

title: Farmington library launches seed exchange
text:
FARMINGTON — Farmington Public Library has launched a garden seed exchange program aimed at helping local residents grow food, support plant biodiversity and build community interest in gardening.
The library is collecting still-viable vegetable, herb and flower seeds in their original packaging this fall, with plans to distribute the donated seeds free to local library cardholders next spring.
Seed collection boxes are available at Farmington Public Library, Root Down Market in New Sharon and the Franklin County Cooperative Extension office at 138 Pleasant St. in Farmington.
Organizers hope gardeners who receive seeds will donate leftover seeds after the next growing season, creating an ongoing community exchange.
“This community seed exchange program is designed to promote sustainable gardening, foster local food resilience and preserve plant biodiversity,” program coordinator Patti Millette said. “In this time of constantly rising food prices and the scarcity of less processed food, it has become more important than ever to consider growing your own food.”
The program was funded by the Greater Franklin County Food Council.
For more information, contact Farmington Public Library at 207-778-4312 or [email protected].

title: Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens Named One of America’s Most Underrated Attractions
text:
Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens Named One of America’s Most Underrated Attractions
The Maine staple was named among the most underrated and underappreciated attractions in the country.
👇 KEEP READING: 19 Maine News Stories That Went National in the Last 20 Years 👇
Stasher compared 665 selected U.S. attractions using Tripadvisor ratings and an equally weighted online popularity score based on Wikipedia views and TikTok and Instagram post totals.
Attractions qualified as underrated if they had strong visitor ratings but relatively low online popularity, while highly popular attractions with ratings below 4 out of 5 were classified as overrated.
Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens ranked fourth on the study’s list of underrated attractions, with an online popularity index of 30.9.
Its Tripadvisor rating of 4.9 out of 5 was the highest among the top 10 attractions on that list.
Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens is a public botanical garden in Boothbay, covering more than 300 acres of gardens and natural areas along Maine’s coast.
Visitors can explore plant displays, woodland and waterfront trails, a children’s garden and outdoor art installations.
And there you have it! The gardens’ strong visitor rating compared with their relatively modest online popularity helped place them near the top of the study’s underrated list.

title: Would ‘Medicare for All’ increase federal spending by roughly $3 trillion annually?
text:
Yes.
“Medicare for All” would increase federal spending by roughly $3 trillion annually, according to some estimates.
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Troy Jackson says he supports the idea, which would replace most private health insurance with federally funded “single-payer” coverage, in which the government pays most medical bills.
A 2019 Urban Institute study estimated that a comprehensive single-payer system would increase federal spending by $2.8 trillion annually, largely replacing expenditures by employers, households and states.
The Congressional Budget Office subsequently projected $1.5 trillion to $3 trillion in additional annual federal health care subsidies by 2030, depending on the program’s design.
But higher federal spending doesn’t necessarily mean higher overall costs: A recent Yale University analysis, which has not yet been peer-reviewed, estimated that Medicare for All could reduce total annual U.S. health spending by more than $1 trillion and save an estimated 114,000 lives a year.
This fact brief is responsive to conversations such as this one.
The Maine Trust for Local News partners with Gigafact to produce fact briefs — bite-sized fact checks of trending claims. Read our methodology to learn how we check claims.

title: ‘Digger’ Explained: Tom Cruise’s Character, the Twist, and What That Ending Means
text:
‘Digger’ Explained: What You Need to Know About Tom Cruise’s Strange New Film
The following post contains SPOILERS for Digger. If you complain that it ruins the movie you might just get squished by a rogue glacier.
From the moment Warner Bros. unveiled the first look for Digger, cinephiles speculated that something was going on with the film that wasn’t immediately obvious from its trailer. I even heard speculation from multiple sources that Digger, starring Tom Cruise as a brash billionaire whose reckless attitude causes an environmental calamity, was actually a secret musical.
That wasn’t quite right — but it was a lot closer to the truth about Digger than I certainly expected. Even after you see the film, the exact specifics of what is real and what is fiction here is a little hazy. So let’s break down exactly what transpires in the latest mind bender from director Alejandro González Iñárritu.
Who Is Digger?
In Digger, Tom Cruise plays Digger Rockwell, an obscenely wealthy oil tycoon with a cartoonish accent and a hideous combover. He’s expanded his deeply American business to every corner of the globe. As the movie begins — and as he attempts to prolong the life of his dying cat — Digger’s team at a drilling platform near Greeland has made a troubling discovery. A crack in a glacier is rapidly expanding, causing the release of methane and imperiling Digger’s entire operation in the region. His safety experts recommend they shut the platform down and investigate. Unconcerned about the potential hazards, Digger bullies his employees into continuing their work. A few minutes later, the platform has exploded and everyone aboard is dead.
Much of the rest of the film follows Digger and a few of his employees — most notably an environmental scientist named Dr. Ganesh (Riz Ahmed) as they race to contain the literal and metaphorical fallout of this disaster. A massive chunk of the glacier nicknamed “Judy” is dislodged in the explosion, and it heads out to the open ocean; if it reaches mainland Europe, Ganesh warns that it could cause thousands upon thousands of deaths and cause trillions of dollars in property damage. At the same time, Digger seeks to insulate himself from criticism. If he can’t control nature, he explains he can at least “control the narrative” around the ultimate responsibility for this accident.
Ah, but that’s just part of the film. About 30 minutes into Digger’s story, the entire reality of the story breaks down, as Iñárritu reveals that everything we have seen in Digger to that point is actually a very elaborate stage play, one in which the role of Digger Rockwell is played by an actor named Curtis Markson — also portrayed by Tom Cruise.
Who Is Curtis Markson?
As soon as Digger breaks the fourth wall — in the form of a model tree toppling over in the background of a scene between Digger and U.S. President Compson (John Goodman) — Cruise drops Digger’s Southern fried accent, and returns to his natural speaking voice. We never see him without his Digger hair and prosthetic makeup, but we follow him backstage where he engages in FaceTime-style phone calls (conducted on a high-tech vanity mirror) with his wife. Their converstions gradually reveal that Cruise’s actually an actor named Curtis Markson, who is playing the role of Digger Rockwell in a play called Fossil Fools. The first 30 minutes of Digger are the play’s final dress rehearsal before its first performance in front of an audience.
So Digger Is Character in a Play?
Yes ... and no. That first fourth-wall break establishes that most of what we are watching is a play performed by actors. But the specifics of the play’s origins, and the details of when and where this play is being performed, are left vague until Digger’s final act, when a monologue delivered by actor Jesse Plemons reveals that Fossil Fools is a satire based on real events that actually occurred decades earlier within the reality of the film.
In other words: Digger Rockwell was a real person, and his careless business practices resulted in the creation of “Judy,” a massive iceberg did cause catastrophic harm across Europe and to the Earth’s ecosystem at large. While society still exists, and plays like Fossil Fools do as well, Digger’s final moments reveal that the world outside the theater where this production is staged is a drowned, ruined, dystopian nightmare, complete with flooded streets, gray skies, and jackbooted soldiers patroling what’s left of civilization.
Think of Fossil Fools as this future’s version or something like Hamilton or Evita; a fictional interpretation of historical people and events.
So Digger Is Not a Musical?
Sadly, no. But the rumor that the film was a musical wasn’t completely off-base. The trailers for Digger were hiding something — namely, the fact that the whole Digger Rockwell storyline is actually a play performed by actors within this dystopian future.
(Honestly, the film may have played better if it was a musical. It might have been easier to accept the heightened reality of Digger’s play-with-a-film — which is wildly unrealistic at times — if it more fully dove into the realm of fantasy with elaborate musical numbers.)
What’s the Deal With Curtis’ Daughter?
Every time Iñárritu goes backstage of Fossil Fools, Markson stresses out about his missing daughter. He speaks to her over the phone early in the film while she���s about to take a flight, but then at some point while he’s rehearsing, she disappears. Markson and his wife exchange frantic calls while they try to locate her, while referring to a terrible hurricane that’s affecting flights all over the world. (Someone refers to it as a “Category 6 storm,” a designation that does not currently exists, one of the early clues that Digger actually takes place in the future.) In Digger’s final scenes, after Curtis and the cast finish their first performance of Fossil Fuels, his wife appears in person and reveals that their daughter has been found and is safe, thanks in part to Jesse Plemons’ character Kenny.
Those are the events depicted onscreen. What do they have to do with the story of Digger Rockwell, and why are they included in Digger? That’s open to interpretation.
Thematically, the search for Curtis’ daughter may be related to what Digger says during his big monologue before that European tribunal investigating Judy. During that speech, Digger both admits his company’s fault in the tragedy while pointing the blame back on society for demanding cheap oil in order to fuel their easy lives. He explicitly mentions that people are too concerned with their day-to-day survival and comfort to worry themselves with future issues like energy sustainability and environmental devastation. The storyline involving Curtis Markson’s daughter is an echo of that; even as he prepares for this big performance, his most immediate concern involves his daughter.
The other potential reading of the daughter character is metatextual. Tom Cruise doesn’t discuss his private life very much in interviews, but he has several children, including his daughter Suri with his ex-wife Katie Holmes. Suri is now 20 years old — close to the age of Curtis Markson’s daughter in Digger. The more the film invites us to peak behind the curtain of Fossil Fools and see this actor’s backstage life, the more the audience might be inclined to try and place Cruise’s own biography atop Curtis’ life story. Certainly it’s interesting to speculate about the parallels between the two. (And the differences; Curtis is married, Cruise is not.)
Who Is Jesse Plemons’ Character?
During Digger’s backstage scenes, Curtis repeatedly encounters a mysterious man referred to as a producer of Fossil Fools. It’s only at film’s climax, as the tensions between Curtis and the play’s director reach a breaking point, that the producer fully introduces himself.
He’s not just some wealthy backer of the show; he was actually a witness to the events depicted in Fossil Fuels. A handful of scenes in the play involving Digger and his family feature a young boy with bright red hair. This is Kenny, the son of Digger’s half-sister Emma (Sandra Hüller). Plemons plays the adult version of Kenny, Digger’s nephew.
As the cast and crew debate whether Fossil Fools is accurate to the real historical disaster, Plemons steps forward to reassure them that their work is good, and funny, and above all truthful. He explains that he backed the new production of the play (it is supposedly considered a cult classic in this dystopian society) because of a sense of familial guilt about the role his uncle played in the destruction of the world’s ecosystem. He wants Digger and the rest to look ridiculous because, well, they were ridiculous. (That’s at least according to Kenny. It’s left the audience to determine how Kenny’s own motives might influence his actions — just as Digger’s motives affect the way he responds to Judy.)
What Does the End of the Movie Mean?
Digger’s penultimate scene show Digger Rockwell’s final days. After his role in the Judy fiasco is exposed, he and his family are exiled to another of his company’s oil rigs in the middle of the ocean. President Compson dies, and his bumbling Vice President (Michael Stuhlbarg) replaces him; he eventually cuts off support of the disgraced businessman. Digger and his family are left to subsist on the meager supplies left in their compound’s refrigerator. Instead of slowly starving to death, a delusional Digger jumps into the ocean and drowns.
That concludes Fossil Fools. The movie’s last few minutes reveal the extent to which the real Digger’s actions contaminated the Earth. As the play’s audience leaves the theater, some sort of alarm sounds, and the attendees all put on gas masks before venturing out into a world that is mostly submerged in dirty water, and patroled by jackbooted soldiers. It’s too late for Fossil Fools’ patrons — but I imagine Iñárritu would like us to heed Digger’s warning and ensure our future descendents don’t end up the same way.

title: Rapper Rick Ross charged with battery after domestic violence accusation
text:
MIAMI BEACH, Fla. (AP) — Rapper Rick Ross was arrested in Miami Beach early Thursday and charged with battery related to a domestic violence accusation, authorities said.
Ross, whose legal name is William Roberts II, faces a felony charge of battery by strangulation, as well as a misdemeanor battery charge, according to online court records.
An attorney for Ross, 50, said in a statement that Ross is being wrongfully accused by an ex-girlfriend whose true motivations are unclear.
“The ex did not even file a police report until a month after the claimed incident allegedly took place,” defense attorney Steve Sadow said in the statement. “Mr. Roberts is innocent and has pled not guilty to the charges. He respectfully requests that his friends, fans and the general public not prejudge the situation and allow the judicial process to run its course.”
Jail records showed that Ross was being held Thursday morning on $5,000 bail. An arraignment is scheduled for Oct. 22.
Ross is a longtime South Florida resident who gained prominence in 2006 with his debut single “Hustlin.”
The rapper and entrepreneur helped put Miami on the musical map in the early 2000s, when most hip-hop fans looked to Atlanta and Houston as Southern rap headquarters. “Hustlin'” was certified platinum twice by the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) and sparked a bidding war for Ross. He eventually signed with Def Jam Records, headed by Jay-Z.
Ross’ debut album, “Port of Miami,” also went platinum, debuting at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 chart. It was the first in a series of chart-toppers, including 2008’s “Trilla” and 2009’s “Deeper Than Rap.” He has been nominated for nine Grammy Awards.
In 2008, he founded the influential label Maybach Music Group (MMG), boosting the careers of signees like Wale, Meek Mill and French Montana.
His most recent album, “Set In Stone,” was released in July. ___
This story was first published Oct. 1, 2026. It was updated Oct. 1, 2026, to remove information about an unrelated prior case involving Rick Ross because details weren’t immediately clear.

title: Who’s afraid of Bobby Charles?
text:
Sam Patten has worked for Maine’s last three Republican senators, including Susan Collins’ first electoral campaigns, is a former managing editor of The Maine Wire and is the author of “Dangerous Company: The Misadventures of a Foreign Agent.”
Given the publicly available polling on Maine’s gubernatorial race going into the fall campaign season, it appears likely that Democrat Hannah Pingree is favored to win. So, with their nominee’s comfortable lead of more than 10 points, why is the state Democratic Party launching such furious attacks on Republican nominee Bobby Charles?
CNN recently released results of a poll that showed more than half — 52% — of likely
voters favoring Hannah Pingree as opposed to 39% saying they plan to vote for Bobby Charles (the poll did not include independent Rick Bennett, a former Republican). Last month, a Fox poll pegged Pingree at 49% compared to Charles’ 38% and Bennett’s 9%.
The answer is strikingly simple: it is not enough just to defeat Bobby Charles. In order to perpetuate their now eight-year stranglehold on power in the state, Maine Democrats must crush everything Charles represents, and to bury his call that Augusta actually be accountable for a change.
Taking a page out of an authoritarian’s handbook, the Democrats seem intent on obliterating Charles altogether — and stigmatizing those who might support him in November.
Charles’ sister authored an op-ed that was published in these pages on Sept. 9 and announced her intention to vote for Pingree. Based on a deeply personal revelation, the op-ed argued that her brother is too divisive and not sufficiently supportive of women to merit her vote.
It was a political body blow, reminiscent of women coming forward this summer alleging they’d been assaulted by then-Democratic senatorial nominee Graham Platner. While emotionally charged and undeniably brave in terms of public disclosure, there was something about both events that felt very political. After all, the synchronized press conference was held at the state Democrats’ Portland office.
Many of us disagree about politics around the family dinner table, but this was very different.
Also consider the peculiar press conference they staged late last month in a Portland park where one usually must tread carefully to avoid stepping on used hypodermic needles. It was there that former Maine CDC Director Nirav Shah — who but for ranked-choice voting would be squaring off against Charles this November — and two other Democrat-aligned public health figures inveighed against the Republican’s pledge to cut the state budget by $4 billion and insisted he would eliminate benefits for Maine’s senior citizens.
How dare he, Dr. Shah then seemed to sneer.
Then there is the candidacy of Rick Bennett itself. Fashioning himself a latter-day Bill
Cohen by walking around the state to put himself in various communities, Bennett —
once a chairman of the state GOP — seems to be a pressure release valve for old-
fashioned Maine Republicans who just wish people could be nice again and want to feel
good about their vote. But Bennett’s single-digit showing shows us how much times have
changed.
Why is he even running, I asked in a Maine Wire column a year ago, when sheer mathematics so
clearly indicated he has no path to victory? There are only two explanations I can
imagine today: either he wants to make a point, as Lindsey Graham did when he ran for
president in 2016 on the sole platform of defeating ISIS, or he wants to help someone
siphon away votes.
The only way to know which of these is Bennett’s motivation is to wait until Pingree announces her cabinet. “Look, Republicans,” Bennett’s candidacy seems to say, “this is what you are supposed to look like, pay attention!”
Maybe Maine Democrats are just so much better organized and resourced than their erstwhile counterparts at the state GOP that they can afford to spend as much attention on systematically attacking Charles as they have. But the persistence of their effort points to something different.
Cutting taxes and fighting crime are the wrong priorities, this effort insists. Despite the double-digit advantage Pingree seems to enjoy, crushing everything Charles stands for is important. Because, despite the breezy prettiness of Maine’s bucolic coast, they are afraid to discuss the rot that consumes Augusta today. Very afraid.

title: Jay approves $52,188 boiler for wastewater facility
text:
JAY — The Select Board approved spending $52,188.07 from a joint capital reserve account for a new propane-fired condensing boiler at the Livermore Falls wastewater treatment facility.
The new boiler will replace an oil-fired system that has used an average of about 5,000 gallons of heating oil per season, with the more efficient propane system expected to substantially reduce fuel use and operating costs.
Mark L. Holt, superintendent of the Livermore Falls and Jay sewer departments, presented the request to the board Sept. 28. Because the expenditure comes from a joint capital reserve account for the Livermore Falls wastewater treatment facility, both towns must approve it under their interlocal wastewater treatment agreement.
Livermore Falls approved the expenditure Sept. 15, Holt said.
The project was put out to sealed bid, with proposals submitted by ABT of Wilton, Central Maine Plumbing & Heating of Livermore and A. Maurais & Son of Jay. Holt said both towns use the three companies to supply and maintain municipal heating systems. Maurais initially suggested installing a condensing boiler instead of replacing the existing equipment with a conventional cast-iron boiler. The other two contractors were given an opportunity to bid on the alternative system. Maurais submitted the lowest proposal for both options.
“The decision to install a condensing boiler was based on its efficiency compared to the cast-iron boiler,” Holt said in a follow-up email.
Maurais estimated the condensing boiler would save just over $6,000 annually compared with a cast-iron propane boiler, Holt said.
Part of the difference comes from the new boiler’s ability to adjust its output to match heating demand rather than always operating at full capacity.
“Instead of starting and running at the full 1,000,000 BTU capacity and burning the maximum amount of fuel, it can run at an idle, burning 1/10th as much fuel to produce only the BTUs required to heat the space,” Holt said.
At the Sept. 28 meeting, Holt estimated that continuing to use heating oil could cost about $25,000 per year, while the propane condensing system could cost roughly $6,100 annually to operate, based on past fuel use. He told the board the resulting savings would allow the new equipment to pay for itself relatively quickly.
Holt later clarified that the calculation was based on an average annual consumption of about 5,000 gallons of No. 2 heating oil. “The fuel savings are considerable,” Holt told the board.
The boiler is expected to last 25 years or more, according to the information presented to the board.
A. Maurais & Son has ordered the new boiler, Holt said, and the equipment is expected to arrive in about two to three weeks.

title: Here’s what to know about political sign regulations in central Maine
text:
Across central Maine, more and more political signs are popping up in yards and along the region’s roads.
But what are the specific rules governing sign placement? And what happens if signs are tampered with?
Here are some key things to know.
WHERE CAN I PUT SIGNS?
Different rules apply to signs on private and public property.
Signs in the public right of way are prohibited from being placed on traffic control signs or devices, public utility poles or fixtures, rotary traffic islands, trees in the public right of way, control-of-access areas —areas where access is limited or prohibited— or medians less than 6 feet wide.
To avoid causing traffic hazards, signs in the public right of way cannot be placed along interstates, within 660 feet of the nearest edge of the interstate system or in a place that can be seen from an interstate highway.
In general, the Maine Department of Transportation will remove signs on either public or private property where they might block a driver’s sight line or cause traffic hazards.
Signs on private property must be outside of the right of way on public ways; how far that is depends on the road. People can contact their MaineDOT region office for more information.
Temporary signs on public property bearing the same or similar messages — like those supporting political candidates — must be placed at least 30 feet from one another.
Signs cannot be placed on public property within 250 feet of a polling location on election day.
WHEN CAN I PUT SIGNS UP?
Signs may be posted in rights of way six weeks before a primary or general election, and they must be removed in the week after the election.
Temporary signs can be placed within the public right of way for as long six weeks from Jan. 1 to June 30 and from July 1 to Dec. 31.
Signs on private property are not subject to any time restrictions.
HOW BIG CAN THEY BE?
Signs on private property are limited to 50 square feet. Temporary signs in the public right of way are limited to 4 feet by 8 feet.
Signs in the public way must be labeled with the name and address of the individual or organization that placed the sign and the date it was placed there.
Kelly Weissenfels, who is town manager and town clerk in Litchfield, said having contact information on signs is helpful, because if signs are placed improperly or are not collected after elections, those people can be alerted.
“I think (the rules) are broad enough to allow for plenty of freedom in placing signs,” Weissenfels said.
WHAT HAPPENS IF SIGNS ARE TAMPERED WITH?
Removing, damaging or disturbing a sign placed in the public right of way without authorization is a civil violation with a fine of up to $250.
Stealing a sign from private property is considered theft, a class E crime, while intentionally damaging or destroying the property of another would be considered criminal mischief, a class D crime.
Valerie Hanson, Pittston’s town clerk, said the town had to remove a political sign from a town road last year due to inappropriate content. Hanson said she’s surprised the town doesn’t receive more reports of people tampering with others’ political signs after hearing stories of theft and damage to signs in other towns.
WHERE CAN I LEARN MORE?
For more information about sign placement rules and town-specific restrictions, contact your local election official, who is generally a city or town clerk. More information about specific Maine laws regarding signs is available on the Maine State Legislature website.

title: Drug Trafficking Investigation Underway In Cornish After Main Street Bust
text:
Cornish Woman Arrested After Authorities Say They Found Her With Cash, Guns & $5K In Drugs
A woman from Cornish has been arrested after a multi-agency drug bust netted guns, cash, and $5K worth of illegal product in York County.
Read More: Maine State Police Search For Suspect After Skowhegan Drug Stop
The Maine Department of Public Safety says 52-year-old Adele Rogers was taken into custody Thursday afternoon after MDEA agents and the Maine State Police Tactical Team searched a property at 355 Main Street in Cornish and found a multitude of drugs and drug paraphernalia.
Authorities say they've had their eye on the area, suspecting that a drug trafficking organization had set up in the small York County town.
During their several-month investigation, evidence was collected and surveillance completed enough for a judge to issue law enforcement agents a warrant.
"The search resulted in the seizure of 49.5ggw Cocaine HCL, diverted Hydrocodone pills, $1760.00 in suspected drug proceeds and three firearms. Rogers was taken into custody without incident at the residence...The estimated street value of the drugs seized is $5000."
We're told Rogers is facing four counts of aggravated drug trafficking and is being held at the York County Jail on $50,000 cash bail.
Read More: Ellsworth, Maine Police Arrest Suspect In 2024 Terrorizing Case
Authorities say the drug trafficking activity in Cornish is still under investigation, and they expect to arrest more people in connection with this case.
They ask community members to remain vigilant and report any suspicious or drug-related activity to authorities. You can call the MDEA Tip Line directly at 1-800-452-6457 or reach out to them by texting MDEA to TIP411.
