title: Judge keeps Venezuelan delivery driver shot by ICE in Texas in custody for alleged assault
text:
Judge keeps Venezuelan delivery driver shot by ICE in Texas in custody for alleged assault
A Venezuelan delivery driver who was shot in his car by a federal immigration agent in Texas will remain in custody on charges that he assaulted an officer while trying to evade arrest, a federal judge ruled Wednesday.
Judge Dustin Howell said that the case against Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, should proceed after prosecutors presented body-worn camera footage of the encounter in Austin, in which Garces Perez allegedly struck a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer with his driver's side mirror.
Garces Perez is charged with one count of assaulting, resisting and impeding a federal officer and faces up to 20 years in prison if convicted. His case has sparked widespread outrage across the Texas capital city and brought renewed criticism from Democrats of President Donald Trump’s aggressive crackdown on immigration.
Garces Perez appeared in court in a wheelchair and wearing a sling on his arm
With a bullet still lodged in his back, Garces Perez appeared in court in a wheelchair. His attorneys said he still urgently needs medical care, 10 days after being shot. He also wore a sling on his arm and needed help putting on a headset to listen to a translation of the proceedings.
The defense called the charges against Garces Perez “retaliation” and argued that the camera footage was inconclusive because it didn't fully capture the moment when he allegedly tried to flee.
The hearing also included testimony from Homeland Security Investigations Special Agent Rick Bazan, who signed the criminal complaint charging Garces Perez with assault. The defense argued that Bazan, whose agency is the investigative arm of ICE, could not confirm whether the ICE agent was actually hit by the car mirror since no federal investigators interviewed the agent directly. Bazan also couldn't explain why the officer allegedly struck by the mirror was not wearing a body-worn camera.
Footage provided Wednesday in court shows officers pulling Garces Perez over Sept. 20 in Austin, where he was making deliveries for DoorDash.
The video showed Garces Perez giving officers his driver's license through a crack in his window and then asking in Spanish if he could park his car so that a relative could come retrieve it. The officer demanded Garces Perez get out of the car multiple times, to which he asked if he could park his own car so a family member could come retrieve it. After a back and forth, Garces Perez abruptly and rapidly drove off.
Prosecutors show video but not of the shooting itself
Prosecutors presented a video from cameras at a nearby business showing the ensuing high-speed chase through residential streets. The shooting itself was not captured on the footage shared in court.
The federal officer who shot Garces Perez wasn’t wearing a body-worn camera. The immigration officer who did have a camera was driving in a separate car and turned the camera off during the pursuit.
Garces Perez said he was struck by a law enforcement SUV and spun around before he was shot. Federal officers told investigators, however, that Garces Perez attempted to strike an officer with his car at the end of the chase before the unidentified officer fired his weapon.
The accusations against Garces Perez recall previous claims made by immigration agents after other high-profile shootings, similarly accusing drivers of weaponizing their vehicles. In a handful of cases, the allegations have been undermined or walked back after the release of body-worn camera footage, drawing renewed scrutiny about the DHS’s reliance on vehicular stops to execute arrests.
The man's lawyer accuses ICE of denying him medical treatment
Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, one of Garces Perez's immigration attorneys, accused ICE of denying him medical treatment for his bullet wound.
“ICE’s conduct has been so egregious that physicians, nurses, medical ethicists and health advocates have come together to demand his release,” she said outside court after the hearing.
Garces Perez entered the U.S. in 2024 using CBP One, a program begun under President Joe Biden that allowed migrants to schedule appointments with U.S. authorities to be considered for asylum. President Donald Trump ended the program on his first day back in office.
Garces Perez was an asylum seeker and had a valid work permit, according to his lawyer. She said a judge later issued a deportation order after Garces Perez missed an immigration court hearing because the notice had been sent to a former address.
Judge Howell said he denied Garces Perez bond on the basis that he could be a flight risk to Venezuela, where he has a child.
His attorneys have filed a lawsuit seeking to prevent his removal from the U.S.

title: Thousands of eligible Mainers to automatically receive discounts on electric bills
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Thousands of low-income Mainers are slated to receive automatic discounts on their monthly electric bills.
Gov. Janet Mills announced on Thursday that $40 million in electricity discounts and other services would be distributed among eligible Maine households through the state’s Low Income Assistance Program, and many will be enrolled automatically this year.
Amounts vary by income, but eligible Central Maine Power customers could see discounts anywhere between 25% and 81%, while Versant customers could get between 17% and 83% off monthly, according to the announcement.
To qualify, customers must have a household income at or below 150% of the federal poverty guidelines. About 44,000 Maine ratepayers participated in the program last year, according to the announcement, but officials determined that roughly another 23,000 were eligible.
To increase participation, many households will now be enrolled automatically.
The Maine Department of Health and Human Services will use information from programs like SNAP and MaineCare to determine automatic eligibility, the announcement states. Those participating in the federally funded Home Energy Assistance Program will also be automatically enrolled in the program.
“Beneficiaries will have their information securely shared with participating utilities” to have the discounts applied to their monthly bills, the announcement said. Mainers not already participating in a DHHS program can apply for the Low Income Assistance Program.
The roughly $40 million in funding for the program is a leap from $22.5 million in 2025, with an additional $7.5 million being approved in a recent supplemental budget for this year. However, the program is largely funded by a ratepayer monthly surcharge of about $2, according to the announcement, with further support from New England Clean Energy Connect.
The monthly nature of the discount is also new to the program. Previously, program participants were given lump sums to offset their costs.
The program is part of “SupportLink,” a Mills initiative implemented through DHHS that connects Maine households with discounts and other forms of relief they are eligible for, unless they opt out, the announcement states.
“Maine families are being pushed to the brink by the president’s whipsaw tariffs and his reckless war in Iran,” Mills said of President Donald Trump in a written statement. “At a time when every dollar matters, my administration is making it easier for vulnerable Mainers to lower their electric bills without unnecessary paperwork or bureaucratic hurdles.”
SupportLink currently includes nine electric utilities, as well as Efficiency Maine and the Portland Water District, according to the announcement.
Mills credited the participating utilities as well as Maine’s Public Advocate, Public Utilities Commission, DHHS and MaineHousing for making the automatic process possible.
Leaders of those state entities praised the move in statements that were included in Thursday’s announcement.
Ian Yaffe, director of the Maine DHHS’ Office for Family Independence, said it’s “a meaningful step toward making services easier to access.”
“Families should not have to navigate multiple applications or send paperwork from one agency to another when we can securely share the information needed to connect them with help,” Yaffe stated.
Maine Public Advocate Heather Sanborn said it will “provide meaningful, predictable support” for struggling Mainers, while Dan Brennan, director of MaineHousing, said it will “help take some of the complications and pressures off our most vulnerable households.”
Eligible households can expect the discounts to begin taking effect on or soon after their November bill, according to the announcement, which notes the timing could be off due to electric bills not always following the calendar month.

title: Maine gubernatorial hopefuls trade barbs in first televised debate
text:
The first televised debate between the three candidates vying to become Maine’s next governor featured several testy exchanges, many of which involved Republican Bobby Charles.
The hourlong debate, hosted by the Maine Chamber of Commerce and moderated by News Center Maine, sought to cover a wide range of topics, including taxes, state revenue, housing, substance use, energy costs and healthcare. But moderators had trouble keeping the candidates on topic and within their allotted time.
The forum was an opportunity for Charles and independent Rick Bennett to shake up a race in which Democrat Hannah Pingree has been the clear front-runner in polling and fundraising.
Bennett, a longtime Republican who unenrolled from the party when he entered the race in June, repeatedly went after Charles, accusing him of not understanding the state budgeting process, and attacking his record serving in the U.S. State Department under President George W. Bush.
“It’s hard to digest all I’ve just heard here, particularly from Bobby Charles,” Bennett, 63, said about 20 minutes into the debate in response to a question about state spending.
“He just doesn’t simply understand how the fiscal process works, which doesn’t surprise me because inspector generals and auditors at the federal government cited him dozens of times for mismanagement of federal spending.”
Bennett was referring to a Bangor Daily News article about how federal audits raised concerns about poor management, spending and ineffectiveness during Charles’ 18-month tenure leading the Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs.
“The Bangor Daily News doesn’t always report the facts,” Charles shot back. “We showed them, ‘Hey, here is the unbelievable record,’ and they decided that they’re gonna take the little paragraph down here that didn’t look like it was the best paragraph.”
Charles, meanwhile, portrayed himself as a political outsider. He said Bennett and Pingree are part of the current political system that has led to the present affordability and housing crises. And he said he’d use his experience as a former investigator to conduct a top-to-bottom review of state agencies to root out fraud and waste.
“I find it ironic that two people who’ve served both 30 years and 25 years are saying that we need to fix the system,” Charles said.
After one exchange, Pingree, who was flanked by both men, said, “This is why we need women in charge.” The line drew laughter and applause from the audience.
Throughout the night, Pingree and Bennett tried to put Charles on the defensive.
At one point, Pingree referred to Bennett as “my friend.” She later called out Charles’ previous work as a federal lobbyist and repeatedly highlighted his support for President Donald Trump, whose low approval rating is creating headwinds for Republicans across the county.
“(Charles is) somebody who has supported Donald Trump at every turn,” Pingree said. “His tariffs, his war in Iran, his big, beautiful bill that has cut our healthcare system. We’re facing economic headwinds because of this president.”
Later, Charles, a 66-year-old Leeds lawyer and former assistant U.S. secretary of state, sought to distance himself from Trump on tariffs and the Iran war.
“I have been very clear, at the outset, that the hitting of the nuclear program was great (but), I do not agree with him right now, in terms of the extended engagement over there,” Charles said about Iran. “I’ve never met the guy (Trump), but I have appealed publicly that we need to get back to the negotiating table and get tariffs down.”
It’s unclear whether the debate will change the trajectory of the race.
Pingree, a 49-year-old Democrat from North Haven who led a policy office under Gov. Janet Mills and is the daughter of U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, has held a steady lead in both fundraising and polling.
Pingree led Charles 48% to 36% in a New York Times/Portland Press Herald/Siena poll released last week, while Bennett drew 8%.
The Democrat has a significant money advantage as well. She has raised more than $4.3 million, compared to Charles’ $1.8 million and Bennett’s nearly $924,000.
The candidates will meet for three more debates, including one Thursday hosted by Maine Public, News Center Maine and the Portland Press Herald. WGME CBS 13 will host a debate on Oct. 13, followed by WMTW the next day.

title: When running the marathon, remember the journey
text:
Editor’s note: Assistant Sports Editor Scott Martin is training to run the Maine Marathon on Sunday. He has a goal and it’s within reach. He has been sharing his ups and downs and everything in between for what it takes to be ready to run 26.2 miles.
I took off my hydration vest and dropped it on the pavement next to my car at the Wainwright Sports Complex in South Portland. Three hours and 55 minutes after leaving this spot on Sept. 19, and nearly 10 months after signing up for the 2026 Maine Marathon, peak training was over. I was too tired and sore to celebrate, but as I leaned on my Subaru Impreza and chugged a vanilla protein shake, I couldn’t help but grin.
Training for my first marathon in seven years was not perfect, but training never is, and despite hiccups caused by illness, insomnia, work and other stress, I was able to do enough speed work and run enough miles to be prepared for a successful race on Sunday. For that, I am grateful.
The time on the clock when I finish will not be the sole factor in determining if my race was a success. There are way too many things that could happen that are out of my control to let my time alone determine if it was a good day or not.
My list of goals for the marathon on Oct. 4 has a number of times (A: 3:47:45; B: 3:49:44 — a PR; C: 3:59:59 — sub 4), but also has things like, “Don’t be a jerk,” “try to have fun,” and “don’t do anything crazy.”
If I accomplish those last three things and cross the finish line healthy, even if I don’t accomplish any of my time goals, race day will be a success.
Really, when I dropped my hydration vest in that parking lot, I had already won. I spent a lot of time this year (Garmin tells me I ran about 76 hours since July 1) working toward this goal. I ran more miles and harder workouts than I have since the COVID pandemic derailed my running habit. When I tore my calf on March 31, 2021, it started a cascade of health issues that forced me to stop running for nearly two months at the end of 2022.
I have spent the last four years building myself to this point. Making it to the starting line and having the opportunity to run a marathon is a huge win.
Maybe you think I am giving myself an out if I am unable to run my goal time. Maybe I am. I have a lot of doubts, despite what my running friends and my coaches tell me, about my ability to average 8:41 per mile for 26.2 miles. I ran close to that pace for 11 miles on Sept. 12, but it filled me with more questions than confidence.
“This feels so fast. Can I really do this for 26.2 miles? Am I fit enough? Will my achy knees put up with this?”
That’s just how my brain works. Confidence has never been my default. Doubt and pessimism are.
When I told my coach, Dan Frey of Finish Strong Physical Therapy and Endurance, about my doubts, he reminded me just how different the situation will be on race day.
“If you push aside race-day anxiety, that’s the only hard part about it,” Frey said. “It’s a supported race. There’s people running with you. There are people cheering you on. All of these things arguably make (the race) easier (than the workouts and the long runs).”
I’ll try to remember that on race day. I will also try to remember all the fun I had with my friends running this summer. Training has been a shared experience with a group of people I’ve grown quite fond of. What happens in the race won’t ruin what has happened over the last 10 months.
I hope I reach my goal in the race. I would love to erase the chalkboard in my apartment with 3:47 written on it because I finally ran that time after 12 years of trying. Even if I don’t, I’ll do my best to enjoy it, to not be a jerk, and remember the journey to get here.
Because no matter how long it takes to run 26.2 miles, the journey has been a lot longer.

title: Acadia Chamber gears up for festival season on the Quietside
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
SOUTHWEST HARBOR — The Acadia Chamber of Commerce is in overdrive, gearing up for Oktoberfest and the Finish Line Festival, both right around the corner.
Acadia Chamber President Holly Masterson and Vice President Jeff Prentice updated the board on the upcoming festivities in Southwest Harbor and Tremont at its last meeting.

title: Frances Perkins Center to Wrap Up Visitor Season With Events Starting Oct. 3
text:
The Frances Perkins Center is planning festivities to mark the end of the visitor season at the Frances Perkins National Monument, including a pumpkin walk, guided grounds tours, and other seasonal activities.
Located in Newcastle, the national monument includes the ancestral home of Frances Perkins, the first woman to serve in a U.S. presidential cabinet and a principal architect of Franklin D. Roosevelt’s New Deal policies.
Visitors can explore the site’s self-guided exhibit in the historic barn and learn more about Perkins’ life, work, and enduring legacy. The welcome center and barn exhibit are open from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. Wednesday through Sunday until Sunday, Oct. 11.

title: Personal bankruptcy filings up nearly 50% since 2022, analysis finds
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Personal bankruptcy filings have jumped nearly 50% since 2022, according to a new LendingTree analysis, as inflation on housing, insurance, groceries and health care, combined with high interest rates, pushes families deeper into credit card debt.
About 1,400 people a day are now turning to the courts for relief. The biggest spikes are in the South, and most filings are the more severe Chapter 7 bankruptcies, which wipe out many debts but also significantly damage credit.
Matt Schulz, with LendingTree, said reaching the point of filing for bankruptcy typically follows a long period of financial strain.
“Anytime you’re talking about bankruptcy, it’s a really big deal, because bankruptcy is generally the end of a long, difficult period that somebody has faced over the course of months or years, and they’ve decided that they really have no other choice,” Schulz said.
Schulz said filing for bankruptcy can create financial challenges that last seven to 10 years. He recommends addressing missed or late payments as early as possible.
“It’s a whole lot easier to go to a creditor when you are saying, ‘Hey, I think I may be late with a payment this month or in the coming months,’ than to go to them and say, ‘Hey, I haven’t paid you in three months, can you help me?’” Schulz said.
Schulz said it is easy to feel powerless when facing serious debt, but resources are available. Creditors can be contacted directly, and nonprofit credit counselors are available for guidance at any time. Schulz said third-party organizations, including local government programs and religious organizations, may also be able to help.

title: Woman killed, two people hurt after crash sends vehicles into a pond in Plymouth
text:
Woman killed, two people hurt after crash sends vehicles into a pond in Plymouth, Maine
A woman is dead and two people are hurt after a crash ended in a pond in Plymouth.
The Penobscot County Sheriff's Office says the crash happened at about 6:39 p.m. Wednesday on Moosehead Trail Highway, near the intersection with Loud Road. Moosehead Trail Highway is also Route 7.
Deputies say a small sedan was headed east when it was hit by an oncoming pickup truck. Both vehicles then ended up in Plymouth Pond.
Emergency crews were able to get both people in the car and the sole person in the truck out. All three were taken to the hospital.
The driver of the car, a 67-year-old man, was being treated for what police said are serious but non-life-threatening injuries. A 68-year-old woman who was a passenger in the car died at the hospital.
The 69-year-old man who was driving the truck was being treated for what police said were non-life-threatening injuries.
Police did not release the names of any of the people involved.
The cause of the crash was under investigation late Wednesday.

title: Chellie Pingree’s going after Trump. Why are so few of us listening?
text:
Hardly anyone seems to be paying attention to the increasingly sharp and powerful case made by Rep. Chellie Pingree against President Trump. They should.
Pingree, a Democrat who represents Maine’s 1st District, rips into Trump daily on an astonishing variety of issues, never mincing words. The House representative has been more or less screaming about the importance of saving America while we still can.
Consider just a handful of her many comments in the past two months.:
On corruption: “Trump’s personal wealth has ballooned by more than $2 billion in just the past 18 months, thanks to a combination of insider trading, shady crypto schemes, and brazen backroom deals. He’s the most corrupt president in history — and it ain’t close.”
On farming: “Trump says he wants to help American farmers but then plans to flood the American market with foreign beef. There is nothing ‘America First’ about his dumbass plan.”
On using tax money for campaign ads: “Let’s be clear: It is ILLEGAL to pay for campaign ads with taxpayer money. Period. … He really does see himself as above silly things like ‘the law’ and ‘campaign ethics.’”
On Iran: Trump “casually threatening to ‘annihilate’ another country in front of the entire U.N. General Assembly. What he’s saying would constitute war crimes. And this man has the nuclear codes. It’s astounding how hellbent he is on violating domestic and international law practically every time he opens his mouth. American foreign policy cannot revolve around destabilizing global peace and stability, the world economy, and our role as the leader of the free world. Horrifying.”
On the Kennedy Center: “Trump says the Kennedy Center is bankrupt and that only he can save it. BULLSHIT. The only problem with the Kennedy Center is Donald J. Trump.”
On the Arch: “Republicans are sitting back and letting Trump desecrate the hallowed landscape of Arlington National Cemetery. This hideous, massive vanity project is such an affront to veterans and Gold Star families. … Republicans in Congress could stop this and every other vanity project Trump is obsessed with. They need to grow a damn spine and remember their duty to the taxpayer. Pathetic.”
Pingree isn’t just concerned, not even very concerned. She’s actively trying to shake this nation from its torpor and get people riled up enough to prevent Trump from destroying what generations before him have built.
Pingree told me this week, “Whether it’s social media rants made with AI slop or threatening to annihilate entire civilizations, none of what Trump is saying and doing is normal or OK. I will keep speaking out, calling attention to this administration’s abuses and incompetence, and making sure people have the information they need to act.”
Maine’s independent senator, Angus King, issues eloquent statements opposing the president’s most stupid proposals and projects. King’s words are more measured, in keeping with the rational debate of our country at its best.
Regrettably, this isn’t a moment for polite disagreement. With so much at stake, Pingree has become too damn angry for calm appeals.
“My hope is that speaking out, consistently and plainly, helps turn justified frustration into engagement, organizing and, ultimately, change at the ballot box in November,” Pingree said.
Why she isn’t getting through to more people, I don’t know. As far as I’m concerned, Pingree is a hero in these dark times.

title: Nokomis field hockey is the Varsity Maine Girls Team of the Week
text:
Editor’s note: Each week during the fall sports season, Varsity Maine will highlight a boys and girls team of the week. The teams, picked by staff members, will take into account several factors, including success stories, bounce-back efforts and notable accomplishments, among others. Athletes, coaches and athletic directors can nominate teams by emailing sports editor Bill Stewart at [email protected] or Varsity Maine editor Lee Horton at [email protected].
Varsity Maine Girls Team of the Week: Nokomis field hockey
Entering a game Wednesday at Camden Hills, the Nokomis field hockey team was off to a 6-1 start, including recent victories over Maine Central Institute and Erskine Academy by a combined margin of 10-0.
The Warriors were atop the Class B North Heal point standings, with notable victories over sixth-ranked Gardiner and second-ranked Cony.
“Our schedule has been really tough, but it’s been really fun,” said Nokomis sophomore Maeve Rush. “I think we’ve learned a lot about our game play from playing harder games.”
Nokomis has routinely been a contender in recent seasons but was put in a tough spot in August when coach Shaunessy Saucier left the program to become the head coach at Husson University.
The school moved quickly to hire former Nokomis standout Lauren Neal (formerly Lauren Burke), who played at Merrimack College from 2020-23.
“I’d say (the transition) has been interesting, but I don’t think it could have gone any smoother,” Neal said. “I think I got blessed to have a really good group of girls and a supportive staff. The parents have also been super supportive.”
The schedule doesn’t let up on the Warriors. They were supposed to play back-to-back games this week against unbeaten opponents, but a road game against two-time defending Class B champion Belfast was postponed Monday and will be made up Oct. 10. On Wednesday, Nokomis was visiting Camden Hills (9-0), the No. 1 team in Class A North.
“There’s just so much talent on this team,” Rush said. “I think we’re going to make some waves this season.”

title: Driver charged in May crash that killed Cape Elizabeth swimmer
text:
The driver has been charged in the crash that killed former Cape Elizabeth High School swimming star Keegan McKenney.
Burton Elijah Brinkman, 22, of Marietta, Georgia, was arrested and charged with felony death by vehicle last week in a North Carolina court. He was also charged with felony serious injury by vehicle due to the injuries sustained by another passenger, according to court documents.
Brinkman was driving while “subject to an impairing substance,” according to the arrest warrant. He was released on $25,000 bail following his arrest on Sept. 24, according to court records.
McKenney was a passenger in a BMW that ran off the road and collided with a tree in Charlotte in the early morning hours of May 10, according to the Charlotte-Mecklenburg Police Department. The other passenger was transported to the hospital. Police said at the time that they were investigating whether speed or impairment were factors.
McKenney was a senior at Queens University in Charlotte and a member of the swim team, specializing in the individual medley and butterfly.
In Cape Elizabeth, he held school records in the 200 individual medley, 100 butterfly, 100 freestyle, 200 freestyle, 500 freestyle and in relays. At his senior year state meet in 2022, he was named Performer of the Meet, breaking a meet record, helping Cape Elizabeth win the state title for the first time since 2015 and beating a school record that had been set in 1983.
McKenney was named the Varsity Maine Male Swimmer of the Year in 2022, and was also on the USA Swimming Scholastic All-America Team.

title: Couple accused of shooting, killing son-in-law in public park
text:
DUBLIN, Calif. (AP) — A California couple has been charged with murder after authorities say they shot their son-in-law to death Saturday in a public park, days before he and the couple’s daughter were set for a hearing in a bitter divorce case.
Shili Chen and Shouyong Zhang, both 77, were due in court Wednesday for an arraignment on the charges. The Associated Press was not able to reach an attorney for the couple prior to the court appearance. Their daughter, Candice Jang, could not be reached, though she appeared virtually at Wednesday’s hearing.
Jonathan McKinsey, a 40-year-old gaming engineer for The New York Times, was shot to death in the parking lot of a sports complex in Dublin, east of San Francisco. A police sergeant was driving nearby and saw him on the ground as witnesses began calling 911 and pointing out the couple, who were still near the scene, Dublin Police Services said in a news release.
Court records show McKinsey’s killing came during a contentious divorce with Jang and a custody battle over the couple’s three young children. In petitions for restraining orders filed last year, the couple accused each other of physical, emotional and psychological abuse going back more than a decade. McKinsey, who is transgender, alleged that both Jang and her parents were verbally and physically abusive regarding a gender transition he underwent years ago.
In his petition for a protection order, McKinsey alleged that Chen had directed anti-LGBTQ slurs at him and his oldest child.
He also accused Jang of being physically and emotionally abusive during medical procedures related to his transition. He alleged Zhang punched him in the chest while he was recovering from double mastectomy surgery.
Victim had been charged with misdemeanor child abuse
McKinsey was arrested last October and charged with misdemeanor child abuse for allegedly hitting their oldest son. Police said he acknowledged having slapped the child. Prosecutors also charged him with endangering their youngest child after deputies responded to the family’s home to talk with him and found their 2-year-old had been left home alone, according to court documents.
McKinsey pleaded not guilty to the charges and alleged in court records that he had been set up by his wife, who had left the house without telling him the child was sleeping in a crib upstairs. He was released from jail on the condition that he complete 12 parenting classes. At the time of his killing, McKinsey was out on bail and had been trying to enter a mental health diversion program.
It was also in October that Jang obtained a domestic violence protection order against McKinsey.
Jang said in her filing that in 2010 McKinsey had grabbed her by the forearms during one argument and caused her to hit the corner of a coffee table, fracturing a vertebra in her upper back. She also said that in 2023 she called the police to their home after McKinsey pushed their oldest son hard on the head. Jang also accused McKinsey of emotionally abusing her mother.
Victim filed a competing protective order request
McKinsey in December filed his own request for domestic violence protection against Jang, alleging years of abuse that included her hitting him in the head with a frying pan. He later filed for divorce and sought more time with the three children, noting that he had been limited to two hours of supervised visits per week since last fall, Alameda County court documents show.
In late August, McKinsey was granted unsupervised visits in public twice a week.
The killing occurred a week before a hearing was scheduled in McKinsey and Jang’s divorce case. The couple had been married since July 2011.
McKinsey joined The New York Times in January 2023. He was director of engineering for New York Times Games and based in the San Francisco Bay Area, the paper said. A spokesperson declined to comment further.

title: Tom Cruise’s Most Extreme Onscreen Transformations
text:
Tom Cruise’s Most Extreme Transformation in Movies
Tom Cruise has been a star for more than 40 years. And in that time, there have been few more instantly recognizable faces in movies than his. He’s Maverick. He’s Ethan Hunt. He’s Jim Eyeswideshut. (That’s who he played in that one, right?) He’s not exactly the type of actor who disappears into his characters. He’s Tom freaking Cruise.
But over the years, Cruise has also tried to transform his unmistakable persona to suit certain roles. An ancient vampire and a hair-metal legend can’t both look like Jim Eyeswideshut; that just won’t do. So let’s a take a tour through some of Cruise’s most dramatic onscreen metamorphoses.
Born on the Fourth of July (1989)
Just three years after he became a megastar in Top Gun, Cruise boldly played against his budding type as an hotshot action hero in the biopic Born on the Fourth of July, based on the memoir of the same name by Vietnam War veteran Ron Kovic. After Kovic was wounded in combat, he became an anti-war activist; to play him, Cruise embraced the real Kovic’s look, donning thinning hair and a bushy mustache. The transformation earned him some of the best reviews of his career and an Academy Award nomination for Best Actor. (Cruise ultimately lost the Oscar that year to Daniel Day-Lewis in My Left Foot.)
Interview WIth the Vampire (1994)
It’s pretty wild to consider that Tom Cruise and Brad Pitt have been A-listers for decades, and the only time their paths crossed on the big screen was in Scenes From a Vampire Marriage. With long, blonde locks and an astonishing array of frilly shirts, Cruise’s vampire Lestat bites his way through American history, guzzling gallons of blood as the centerpiece of Neil Jordan’s extravagant horror drama.
READ MORE: ScreenCrush’s Full Review of Digger, Starring Tom Cruise
Vanilla Sky (2001)
For a good amount of the twisty Vanilla Sky, Cruise looks exactly how you think of him in your mind’s eye: The chiseled features, the perfect hair. Ah, but there are some surprises in store for viewers of this Cameron Crowe thriller, including a car accident that for a time scars Cruise’s face beyond repair. In other scenes, Cruise wears an eerie and featureless prosthetic mask. (I think he calls the mask “Vanilla Sky.” Frankly, I’m still fuzzy about why that’s the film’s title.)
Collateral (2004)
Admittedly, Collateral is the least “extreme” of the transformations on this list. But when else have you seen the eternally boyish Cruise — who’s currently doing the Digger press tour with a full head of thick dark hair — as a silver fox? The striking shift from his usual onscreen persona suited Michael Mann’s dark crime thriller, with Cruise potraying one of the rare villains in his career, the ruthless assassin Vincent.
Tropic Thunder (2008)
When Ben Stiller first approached Tom Cruise about being in Tropic Thunder, he wanted him for the role of dunderheaded action hero Tugg Speedman. Cruise wasn’t interested, but he suggested that Stiller add a character that wasn’t in that early draft — a monstrous Hollywood executive who could antagonize the other characters. Stiller loved the idea, and then asked Cruise to play the part of the odious exec, Les Grossman. Cruise agreed on two conditions: He needed to be given big prosthetic hands and a fake belly, and he had to be allowed to dance on camera. After a makeup test, Stiller agreed to both conditions.
Rock of Ages (2012)
Movie stars and rock stars are very different breeds. To play legendary hair metal frontman Stacee Jaxx in the film adaptation of the Broadway musical Rock of Ages, Cruise reinvented his look yet again, donning ’80s-tastic hair, dark eyeliner, enough ink to keep a tattoo shop in business for a year, and a wardrobe full of bandanas, bracelets, and leather pants. The film was not a hit, but Cruise got surprisingly good reviews for the way he saw a million faces and rocked them all.
Digger (2026)
Cruise’s first non-action movie in many years gives him gray hair, a combover, jowls, and a big belly — not to mention a cartoonish Southern accent — as Digger Rockwell, an oil baron whose reckless drilling in the Arctic sets off an environmental calamity. Does all of the makeup — which supposedly took six hours to apply in the early days of Digger’s production — add anything to the story? That’s debatable. It certainly doesn’t make you forget you’re watching Tom Cruise at the center of this surreal film. But it is a less energetic manifestation of the same impulse behind Cruise clinging to the exterior of a plane or swinging from the Burj Khalifa: A self-sacrificial commitment to doing whatever it takes to entertain an audience.

title: October holiday sales: What to buy now, what to wait for
text:
October holiday sales: What to buy now, what to wait for
Amazon, Target, and Walmart are launching October sales events. Here's what to buy early and what to hold off on until Black Friday.
October holiday sales: What to buy now, what to wait for
Amazon, Target, and Walmart are launching October sales events. Here's what to buy early and what to hold off on until Black Friday.
Major retailers are kicking off the holiday shopping season early this year, with Amazon, Target, and Walmart hosting sales events in October.
Walmart's deal event runs from Oct. 5 through Oct. 11, while Amazon and Target will hold their sales on Oct. 6 and 7.
"It used to be that Cyber Week was the be-all and end-all, but now October's gotten a lot more competitive," said Brie Schwartz, editorial commerce director at Good Housekeeping.
Starting in October also may help shoppers spread out the cost of holiday gifts.
PwC's latest Holiday Outlook found that consumers expect to spend an average of $708 on gifts this year. Buying a few gifts earlier could allow shoppers to divide that cost among multiple paychecks.
Schwartz recommended buying toys early, as popular items may sell out quickly.
"If you see something at a good price that you know your kid will like, I wouldn't wait until Cyber Week," she said.
The NeeDoh advent calendar, for example, is available through an invite-only purchase process on Amazon, making it a product shoppers may want to monitor early.
"The toy mania has gotten crazy," Schwartz said. "You don't want to miss the opportunity to get something that will just be, frankly, totally sold out."
However, Schwartz advised waiting on certain categories, like TVs and large appliances, unless they are urgently needed.
"TVs, the big appliances, if you need something now, you'll still see decent discounts. But if you're remodeling your kitchen in six months, hold off on buying the fridge. If you don't need a new TV, I would say hold off on that as well," Schwartz said.
Shoppers concerned about return policies may also benefit from waiting until closer to the holidays, as retailers often extend return windows during that time.
At Walmart, most items purchased now through Dec. 31 are returnable through Jan. 31. Target offers a 90-day return window for most items and a full year for Target-branded products with a receipt. Amazon's standard return window is 30 days.
Electronics may have shorter return windows, ranging from two weeks to 30 days depending on the product. Shoppers are encouraged to read the fine print to avoid surprises.

title: Renee Good’s family sues US government, immigration officials over her killing
text:
MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — Renee Good’s family sued the U.S. government and several immigration officials Thursday, alleging wrongful death and other violations of federal law in the 37-year-old woman’s killing by an immigration officer during a federal crackdown in Minneapolis.
The two lawsuits were filed by Good’s partner, Becca Good, and Renee’s brother Brent Ganger.
One lawsuit, filed against “the United States of America,” alleges the wrongful death of Renee Good under Minnesota law predicated on claims of battery, assault, false imprisonment, intentional infliction of emotional distress and negligence that caused her death.
The other lawsuit alleges a conspiracy to interfere with civil rights. It names as defendants: Jonathan Ross, the immigration officer who shot her; White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller; former Homeland Security head Kristi Noem; former U.S. Border Patrol commander-at-large Gregory Bovino, Corey Lewandowski, President Donald Trump’s campaign manager, and others.
Renee Good, a mother of three, was fatally shot Jan. 7 as protests against immigration raids flared across the city. According to Becca Good, her partner stopped their car in a street to support neighbors during an immigration operation.
Bystander video shows Renee Good in the driver’s seat of a red SUV blocking part of the road and repeatedly honking her horn.
Two immigration officers get out of a truck, their faces covered, and one orders Good to get out of the car. She reverses briefly, then turns the steering wheel as the officer says again, “get out of the car.”
Almost simultaneously, Becca Good, standing in the street, shouts: “Drive, baby, drive!”
One officer standing in front of the vehicle pulls his weapon and fires into the windshield. He lurches back as the car turns away from him. The officer, who is now very close to the open window on the driver’s side, opens fire two more times, fatally shooting Renee Good, according to an analysis of the videos by The Associated Press and others.
Federal officials at the time said the officer acted in self-defense and that Good had engaged in “an act of domestic terrorism.”
The killing of Good and another U.S. citizen, Alex Pretti, in Minneapolis just weeks later sparked outrage across the country and calls to rein in immigration enforcement. At least 10 people have died in encounters with immigration officers during President Donald Trump’s second term.
In July, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer with a history of violent behavior fatally shot a 25-year-old Colombian man, Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, in his car in Biddeford, Maine. Durán Guerrero was not the target of an immigration enforcement action.
Last week, immigration enforcement agents shot and wounded a Venezuelan delivery driver in Austin, Texas. Wilber Rafael Garces-Perez, 28, survived but was charged with sideswiping an officer with his car mirror and later attempting to strike an officer with the vehicle.
Becca and Renee Good were not legally married, according to a family lawyer, but referred to one another as wives. They had only recently relocated to Minneapolis from Kansas City, Missouri.
In social media accounts, Renee Good described herself as a “poet and writer and wife and mom.” On Pinterest, a profile picture shows her smiling and holding a young child, alongside posts about tattoos, hairstyles and home decorating.
In an interview shortly after her death, Renee Good’s mother, Donna Ganger, told The Associated Press: “She had this way of making you feel special and loved that I didn’t even understand that until we lost her.”

title: Senator introduces bill to protect workers during AI boom
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Artificial intelligence has become a recent hot topic of debate on Capitol Hill, as lawmakers consider how to move forward with the quickly changing technology. Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly (D) is one lawmaker proposing legislation that supports humans while also considering the relevance of the tech.
“This is something we have to tackle immediately,” Kelly said.
What to do about the rise and evolution of artificial intelligence has become a sticking point on Capitol Hill. With the technology both a benefit and a possible risk, Kelly says it’s important to get ahead of the trend.
“You know when I used to fly the space shuttle, the master alarms flashing on the instrument panel, you gotta take action. You look at the data, you come up with a plan, you execute the plan. That’s this moment with this technology,” Kelly said.
Kelly said AI has integrated itself into Americans’ everyday lives while also posing a risk to workers, who could soon see their positions filled by technological advancements.
Kelly introduced the Make AI Work for Americans Act, legislation that would guarantee companies benefiting most from AI invest in workers and pay their fair share, mitigating damage from technology poised to replace the human workforce.
“There are estimates out there that possibly millions of Americans lose their jobs because of this technology. We have to have an answer for that,” Kelly said.
The legislation is one proposal amid increased debate on artificial intelligence. The debate comes the same week President Donald Trump hosted top tech leaders at the White House to praise the development of what he calls “super intelligence.”
Kelly said any evolution must come with strict guardrails and should not rely on companies to self-police. He said that begins with an understanding of the basic workings of AI.
“So we can introduce good legislation that will work,” Kelly said.

title: Rapper Rick Ross pleads not guilty to strangulation charge
text:
MIAMI BEACH, Fla. (AP) — Rapper Rick Ross was arrested in Miami Beach early Thursday and charged with battery related to a domestic violence accusation, authorities said.
Ross, whose legal name is William Roberts II, faces a felony charge of battery by strangulation, as well as a misdemeanor battery charge, according to online court records.
An attorney for Ross, 50, said in a statement that Ross is being wrongfully accused by an ex-girlfriend whose true motivations are unclear.
“The ex did not even file a police report until a month after the claimed incident allegedly took place,” defense attorney Steve Sadow said in the statement. “Mr. Roberts is innocent and has pled not guilty to the charges. He respectfully requests that his friends, fans and the general public not prejudge the situation and allow the judicial process to run its course.”
Jail records showed that Ross was being held Thursday morning on $5,000 bail. An arraignment is scheduled for Oct. 22.
Ross is a longtime South Florida resident who gained prominence in 2006 with his debut single “Hustlin.” He also has a home outside of Atlanta in Fayette County on a property he calls “The Promise Land.”
The rapper and entrepreneur helped put Miami on the musical map in the early 2000s, when most hip-hop fans looked to Atlanta and Houston as Southern rap headquarters. “Hustlin’” was certified platinum twice by the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) and sparked a bidding war for Ross. He eventually signed with Def Jam Records, headed by Jay-Z.
Ross’ debut album, “Port of Miami,” also went platinum, debuting at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 chart. It was the first in a series of chart-toppers, including 2008’s “Trilla” and 2009’s “Deeper Than Rap.” He has been nominated for nine Grammy Awards.
In 2008, he founded the influential label Maybach Music Group (MMG), boosting the careers of signees like Wale, Meek Mill and French Montana.
His most recent album, “Set In Stone,” was released in July.

title: Hand-picking potatoes remains family tradition on Aroostook County farm
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
NEW SWEDEN, Maine (WAGM) - An old tradition of hand-picking potatoes is still alive on a farm in Aroostook County, where kids are filling barrels much like generations before them.
Leo Rossignol said he started picking potatoes as a 5-year-old.
“Back then, it was three and four weeks,” Rossignol said.
Rossignol is now back in the fields with his two grandchildren, who spend their harvest break picking potatoes together. From 8 a.m. to 3 p.m., kids are in the fields filling baskets full of potatoes.
“Last year, his sister, once she back to school, they asked her what they did on the break. She says, I picked potatoes. And she was the only one in her class that did. She was pretty proud of that. So she felt good,” Rossignol said.
Rossignol said the work is hard but gives him time with his grandchildren.
“Well, right now for me, it’s special because I do it for them. I feel too old to do it,” Rossignol said.
Organic potato operation spans 25 to 30 acres
The operation is on Sven Bondeson’s farm in New Sweden. Bondeson said it takes a lot of hands to keep the tradition going on his roughly 25 to 30 acres of organic potatoes.
“There’s a few people here that are adults that come out, you know, with their grandkids or kids, but they wouldn’t come out either if their kids were in school. So yeah, that’s a big deal for me,” Bondeson said.
About 15 to 20 kids are picking on any given day this year. The potatoes picked feed people from the local area to as far as Portland. The kids gather Lehighs, caribou russets, Kennebecs, reds and a few fingerlings.
Bondeson said the quality of the potatoes on his farm reflects the work.
“I get less bruising and seems to work better for me,” Bondeson said.
Tradition has changed over time
Rates are higher and days are shorter than when Rossignol was 5 years old. But Rossignol said the experience is still something worth passing down.
“Well, they’re lucky because they got a chance to say they pick potatoes by hand. Not many kids feel alive that chance to know,” Rossignol said.
Bondeson said he will keep the hand-picking tradition going as long as kids keep showing up during school break.
“You know, and obviously school break will play a factor into that over, you know, over the course of time. But yes, as long as I can still get the kids and everybody else that come out and pick and we’ll keep doing it,” Bondeson said.

title: Ex-firefighter wanted by FBI for child porn may have faked his death, investigators say
text:
Ex-firefighter wanted by FBI for child porn may have faked his death, investigators say

Charles Johnathen Harris, of Modesto, was believed to have been killed in a boating accident in Suisun Bay on April 4, 2023, the FBI said. Law enforcement said Harris' death warrants further scrutiny.
A federal warrant for Harris' arrest was issued on April 21, 2023, and he was charged with failure to appear.
Jail records show Harris, who also goes by "Chuck" and "Charlie," is a former firefighter. He is 5 feet 10 inches tall, has blue eyes and red hair.

title: Nokomis field hockey is the Varsity Maine Girls Team of the Week
text:
Editor’s note: Each week during the fall sports season, Varsity Maine will highlight a boys and girls team of the week. The teams, picked by staff members, will take into account several factors, including success stories, bounce-back efforts and notable accomplishments, among others. Athletes, coaches and athletic directors can nominate teams by emailing sports editor Bill Stewart at [email protected] or Varsity Maine editor Lee Horton at [email protected].
Varsity Maine Girls Team of the Week: Nokomis field hockey
Entering a game Wednesday at Camden Hills, the Nokomis field hockey team was off to a 6-1 start, including recent victories over Maine Central Institute and Erskine Academy by a combined margin of 10-0.
The Warriors were atop the Class B North Heal point standings, with notable victories over sixth-ranked Gardiner and second-ranked Cony.
“Our schedule has been really tough, but it’s been really fun,” said Nokomis sophomore Maeve Rush. “I think we’ve learned a lot about our game play from playing harder games.”
Nokomis has routinely been a contender in recent seasons but was put in a tough spot in August when coach Shaunessy Saucier left the program to become the head coach at Husson University.

“I’d say (the transition) has been interesting, but I don’t think it could have gone any smoother,” Neal said. “I think I got blessed to have a really good group of girls and a supportive staff. The parents have also been super supportive.”

title: The Lincoln County News
text:
Other than profiles on the candidates facing each other in the upcoming election, readers might notice a trend in stories featured on the front page.
This week, four stories explore the impact of those in the community that we have lost. Whether that is longtime Bristol resident Sandra Lane, who will soon be getting a playground named in her honor, or Edgecomb firefighter Gavin Martin, whose family now honors him through a nonprofit organization, we can reflect on how a person’s work in life can continue beyond their time on Earth.
In Lin-Manuel Miranda’s Broadway production “Hamilton,” the end of the musical features Alexander Hamilton moments before his death. In this moment, listeners hear him questioning what a person’s legacy means and how it is shaped. He asks himself if one moment from his life will define how he is remembered forever. In the song this is featured in, “The World Was Wide Enough,” he gives one of the best analogies of what a legacy is.
“Legacy! What is a legacy? It’s planting seeds in a garden you never get to see. I wrote some notes at the beginning of a song someone will sing for me,” Hamilton sings.
When reflecting on these words, we can look at those we highlight this week and see how some of the work they started they never got to see and how it is our responsibility to continue it. Now, we find ourselves faced with the question: How do we honor someone’s legacy?
In her obituary, Sandra Lane is remembered as “the best bus driver ever.” Those who remember her think of her kindness and dedication to Bristol; some of our employees here at The Lincoln County News had her as their bus driver. She served on the Bristol Parks Commission for 13 years. The new playground planned for Pemaquid Beach Park was originally her idea and the continuation of the construction an indicator of the impact she left and the love for her community, carried on by those currently on the board. Even though she is not here to see what will come out it, children for years to come will play on the playground and hopefully experience the same joy Lane brought to the people she met.
Recently, Dresden lost a pillar of their community: Shari Lilly, who was the secretary of more than 10 committees and boards. The longtime Dresden resident is remembered for her kindness and dedication to the town. Numerous town officials shared memories and thoughtful words about someone who is often recognized as the person who kept the town organized and running.
Lilly leaves behind a legacy of generosity, thoughtfulness, and wisdom. Whoever takes on the role of town secretary next has big shoes to fit and will hopefully be as involved a Lilly was.
In December 2025, 21-year-old Edgecomb firefighter Gavin Martin died in a car crash in Whitefield. Since his passing, his family founded the Gavin Martin Foundation, a nonprofit organization dedicated to giving back to first responders and other community groups Martin cared about. This includes monetary donations, as well as fire trainings in both Maine and New Jersey.
Martin’s parents said the organization not only keeps his memory alive, but continues his passion for giving back to the people around him. His mother, Monika, recalled how when he moved to Maine from New Jersey by himself, he always checked in on his older neighbors and got as involved with the community as his could. His father, Joel, is now a part-time volunteer firefighter with the Edgecomb Fire Department.
Martin’s life inspired others to continue on after grief and honor his legacy through service.
Earlier this month, the former owner of what would one day become Red’s Eats died at 95. Allen Crosby Pease is often remembered as “everybody’s ideal of a judge” after serving as the Maine District Court chief judge. People said this about him because he would never lose his temper, even if there was cause to. The man who is remembered as kind and patient is the one who bought the hot dog stand that would become Red’s Eats, selling the business in 1956. His son, Daniel, said he cannot think of a time when his father wasn’t “helpful and encouraging.”
While many might remember the man for the iconic food stand that visitors wait hours in line for, he is the perfect example of someone with a coat of many colors. His legacy is just as multifaceted, as he is known for his dedication to the court system, Wiscasset, and technology.
Legacy is not always the product of one singular action, but often the culmination of years of hard work, memories, and love. As said in “Hamilton,” a legacy is oftentimes work not only done for the betterment of oneself and the present but something that lasts long into the future. It is based on how we connect with others who will in turn continue to share said legacy.
We can look to Lane, Lilly, Martin, and Pease, and see four very different people who leave behind very different legacies, but all have something in common: love, connection, and a desire to leave things better than they found them.

title: Medical helicopter crash kills 2 people, leaves 2 hospitalized and 1 missing, report says
text:
A medical helicopter transporting a patient crashed off Catalina Island near Los Angeles, killing two people and leaving two hospitalized, authorities said Thursday. Rescuers continued searching for a fifth person who was aboard the aircraft and went missing after the Wednesday night crash.
The Coast Guard, firefighters and divers with the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department were among emergency personnel who searched through the night and into the afternoon.
The cause was not immediately clear. Coast Guard Capt. Stacey Crecy said the helicopter went down shortly after takeoff and hit the water a short distance from the island.
“We believe that the medical aircraft was transporting a person off the island for additional medical care on the mainland,” Crecy said.
Relatives of the missing person told ABC7 that the woman was being transported after having an allergic reaction. They also said her 20-year-old son went with her in the helicopter to help translate.
Sheriff Robert Luna said at an afternoon news conference that authorities were not yet identifying victims by name. But he described the two people that died as the male pilot and a female nurse. He also said another medic and a fourth person, a man, were hospitalized.
A memorial service was held on the island to honor the victims.
The crash came 11 days after a firefighting helicopter went down, killing two pilots in Yosemite National Park in California, and two weeks after a news helicopter crashed in Los Angeles, killing two people.
First responders were called to the Catalina crash shortly before 8 p.m. and pulled four people from the water. Two were pronounced dead at the scene, and two, in stable condition, were brought to hospitals on the mainland, the Los Angeles County Fire Department said.
Firefighters on the island were able to get to the scene quickly by boat, Crecy said.
The National Transportation Safety Board said it is investigating and identified the aircraft as a Eurocopter EC-135-P2. NTSB staff were expected to arrive on the scene later Thursday. The aircraft will be brought to a secure facility for evaluation, a board spokesperson said.
Authorities said the helicopter was submerged in 240 feet (about 70 meters) of water off Catalina, which is located about 22 miles (35 kilometers) off the mainland.
The helicopter landed on the island shortly after 7 p.m., following a 24-minute flight from an airport in Oceanside, according to the flight tracking service Flightradar24.
The helicopter was operated by REACH Air Medical Services of Sacramento.
“At this time, we are gathering information and coordinating with emergency responders and authorities,” the company said in a statement. “Our thoughts are with the families, loved ones and colleagues affected by this tragedy. We are focused on supporting our team and everyone impacted during this incredibly difficult time.”
The company said it was unable to share additional details out of respect for the people involved and the ongoing emergency response.

title: A look at the Dubai airline that made an emergency landing after a captain was stabbed
text:
A look at the Dubai airline that made an emergency landing after a captain was stabbed
A copilot on a flight to Israel stabbed a captain on Wednesday before passengers pushed their way into the cockpit and wrestled with the attacker. The FlyDubai plane fell rapidly, and a passenger said he grabbed the controls and pulled upward, like how he had seen on television. Other crew members soon took over, and the jetliner made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
It was not clear what motivated the attack. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Saudi Arabia arrested the copilot. The passengers from the flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv were met with cheers in Israel as they completed the journey on another flight Wednesday evening.
Here's a look at the airline in which the altercation took place.
Airline is owned by the Emirati government
FlyDubai, the sister airline to Emirates, is a government-owned carrier run by the United Arab Emirates that operates a fleet of 98 Boeing 737 aircraft, according to its website. The airline flies to the Mideast, Africa, Europe and Asia, including the Indian subcontinent.
In November 2020, FlyDubai began offering commercial flights between Tel Aviv and Dubai, a rare route at a time when other airlines in the region stopped flying to Israel, a UAE ally.
The airline reported carrying 15.7 million passengers in 2025 and reached a total revenue of AED 13.6 billion ($3.7 billion).
Stabbed captain helped passengers overpower attacker
In the chaos of the attack, the flight descended from 33,000 feet to 17,000 feet (around 10,000 meters to 5,100 meters) in about a minute, before making an erratic circle close to the Jordanian border and landing in Tabuk about an hour later, according to Flightradar24. Most of the plane’s rudder was ripped off the tail during the sudden drop.
Netanyahu identified the wounded captain as Smit Machchhar of India. The Indian Embassy in Saudi Arabia said Machchhar was in stable condition.
“Despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door, and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker — preventing a catastrophic midair disaster,” Netanyahu said on X. “He saved the lives of 174 people, including Israeli citizens and other nationals.”

A red leaf. A yellow leaf. Nudged them with my foot. To pick up the red leaf. Because I love to collect first leaves. After their final descent. Especially red ones. But they were stuck together. The yellow leaf came with the red one. One leaf but two colors? No. Two very different leaves. Separate stems and veins. But totally one. Like Siamese twin leaves.
I googled it. AI popped up. That guru on the summit with all the answers. Revered and promoted by our highest leaders. But AI didn’t really know. Some vague references to bugs and fungus. Didn’t answer the questions. Like that “expert” about something who is more into being an expert than providing answers. Uh oh. Two different leaves that were one leaf. And AI didn’t have the answers. Light headed. My confidence in the how the world works. Beginning to crumble.

title: Federal report says pilots weren't warned about wind before Amazon cargo plane crashed in Miami
text:
Despite regulations requiring it, an air traffic controller failed to tell the pilots of an Amazon cargo plane about the potential for strong tail winds as they landed in Miami, careening off the runway and killing five people last month, according to a preliminary report Thursday from the National Transportation Safety Board.
Just four minutes before clearing the plane for landing, an air traffic controller had provided a wind advisory to a different flight, noting gusts of up to 25 mph (40 kph) from the south. But the controller “did not issue information about the wind” to the pilots of the Amazon cargo plane, the report said.
According to federal regulations, “both wind direction and velocity were required to be stated when authorizing use of a runway when a tail wind component exists,” the NTSB report said.
The preliminary report did not list a cause of the crash. The ongoing investigation could take more than a year to complete.
The plane’s operator, 21 Air, said in a written statement Thursday that safety is “a core focus” of its organization.
“We are reviewing the information in the NTSB preliminary report closely, alongside our own internal safety and operational protocols, and we will take all appropriate action to improve our safety based on the facts as they are established,” the company said.
The airplane, carrying packages of contact lenses for Amazon, came in fast after a flight from Puerto Rico and barreled roughly 1,200 feet (366 meters) past the end of the runway at Miami International Airport on Sept. 6. It smashed into a van carrying workers for a company that cleans airplanes. Five people who were in the van died. Two others in the van sustained serious injuries, as did the driver of a car that was hit by the plane. The two pilots had minor injuries.
A summary of cockpit voice recordings previously released by the NTSB said one of the pilots repeatedly warned his counterpart that they were going too fast as they approached for landing and after touchdown. But the fellow pilot never gave “a consistent verbal response” to the warnings, the NTSB has said. The two pilots had flown together for the first time just earlier that day, according to the preliminary NTSB report.
The cockpit audio recordings also captured a series of automated warnings from the plane about the speed of descent and the approaching terrain.
The plane was well down the runway when it touched down, reducing how much distance it had on the runway to stop. Experts have said strong winds from approaching storms could have created a tail wind that helped propel the plane forward.
The pilots may have tried to abort the landing. Data from the plane show its wheel brakes were applied then released as the engines throttled to “go-around” thrust values before the brakes again were applied with about 415 feet (126 meters) of runway remaining.
The plane ran off the pavement while still traveling at 130 mph (209 kph), then struck some airport equipment and the cleaning crew’s van before crashing through a perimeter fence, hitting a car on a public road and coming to rest with its nose in a parking lot fence, the preliminary report said.
After the crash, Amazon suspended its partnership with 21 Air, which operated the plane. The North Carolina carrier had flown packages for Amazon since 2024. The Boeing 767 that crashed was 32 years old and originally built to carry passengers. It was converted to a cargo plane in June 2016, the preliminary NTSB report said.
The Miami crash came less than a year after a UPS cargo plane crashed at Louisville’s Muhammad Ali International Airport after losing its engine while accelerating down the runway. That crash killed all three pilots and 12 people on the ground. Twenty-three more were injured.
___
Associated Press transportation writer Josh Funk contributed from Omaha, Nebraska.

title: Georgia man charged in crash that killed star Maine swimmer
text:
A Georgia man has been arrested in the spring crash that left a star Maine swimmer dead.
Burton Brinkman, 22, of Marietta has been charged with death by vehicle and serious injury by vehicle, both felonies, according to WCB-TV in Atlanta.
Brinkman was allegedly under the influence while driving a BMW M3 north on Queens Road West in Charlotte, North Carolina, about 2:15 a.m. on May 10 when the sedan went off the road and hit a tree, according to WCB-TV and the Charlotte-Mecklenburg Police Department.
That crash killed 22-year-old Keegan McKenney and injured Brinkman’s other passengers, who firefighters had to free from the wreckage, the Charlotte-Mecklenburg Police Department said at the time.
McKenney was a standout swimmer at Cape Elizabeth High School, where he graduated in 2022. That year he helped Cape Elizabeth win its first state title since 2015 and beat a school record set back in 1983.
He was attending Queens College in Charlotte, where McKenney continued to swim competitively.
The crash remains under investigation.

title: DraftKings sued over alleged AI-targeted gambling promotions
text:
DraftKings faces proposed class-action lawsuit over alleged AI-driven gambling promotions
DraftKings, the online sportsbook and casino, faces a proposed class action lawsuit after customers read reports alleging the company used artificial intelligence to target vulnerable gamblers with promotions that encouraged them to bet more and lose more money.
Related video above: Carnegie Mellon professor discusses what bet to avoid and why
West Virginia gambler Daniel Vest brought the lawsuit, which was filed Wednesday in Massachusetts Federal Court. He is seeking to represent a nationwide class of users who were allegedly identified through an AI model as likely to be persuaded by incentives to keep gambling.
The lawsuit follows a recent New York Times report that said DraftKings worked over several years to analyze the behavior of gamblers, including their likelihood of stopping and their susceptibility to promotional offers. The company disputes these claims.
According to the lawsuit, users who were classified as "elastic" by the DraftKings model were sent extra emails, texts and app notifications. Those included extra promotions or incentives to keep them wagering. 
Vest's lawsuit claims that users were unaware of DraftKings' use of AI and alleges the practice is "both unfair and deceptive." It further alleges that DraftKings broke its contractual obligations and Massachusetts law.
"Despite its professed 'commitment to responsible play' and to 'ensur[ing] that [users] are playing responsibly,' (DraftKings), upon information and belief, uses AI, and has developed its Model, not to protect users but, rather, to target the most vulnerable among them," the lawsuit states.
Quoting the newspaper's report, the lawsuit cites an interview with a former DraftKings employee who said about the program: "It is as predatory as it sounds."
According to the lawsuit, Vest has wagered "thousands of dollars" on DraftKings annually for several years and observed an inundation of messages or offers from the company. He said that included "at least approximately 70" messages in the 30 days ending on Sept. 25.
The plaintiff is asking the court to certify the case as a class action, award damages, order disgorgement of money allegedly obtained through the challenged practices and prohibit DraftKings from using the alleged AI model to target users with additional gambling promotions, according to the complaint.
In a statement provided to sister station WCVB, the company disputed the claims contained in the lawsuit. 
"DraftKings does not use AI to target customers based on losses, nor do we use AI to target customers based on indicators of potential problem gaming. We intend to vigorously defend any potential lawsuits on the matter," a spokesperson said.

title: Farmington library launches seed exchange
text:
FARMINGTON — Farmington Public Library has launched a garden seed exchange program aimed at helping local residents grow food, support plant biodiversity and build community interest in gardening.
The library is collecting still-viable vegetable, herb and flower seeds in their original packaging this fall, with plans to distribute the donated seeds free to local library cardholders next spring.
Seed collection boxes are available at Farmington Public Library, Root Down Market in New Sharon and the Franklin County Cooperative Extension office at 138 Pleasant St. in Farmington.
Organizers hope gardeners who receive seeds will donate leftover seeds after the next growing season, creating an ongoing community exchange.
“This community seed exchange program is designed to promote sustainable gardening, foster local food resilience and preserve plant biodiversity,” program coordinator Patti Millette said. “In this time of constantly rising food prices and the scarcity of less processed food, it has become more important than ever to consider growing your own food.”
The program was funded by the Greater Franklin County Food Council.
For more information, contact Farmington Public Library at 207-778-4312 or [email protected].

title: After 3 months of work, home and decor boutique ready to go in downtown Brunswick
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
After nearly three decades of dreaming about opening a shop of their own, spouses Karen and Perry Schwarz are bringing that dream to life with the opening of Holy Chic Maison, a European-inspired home and gift boutique at 96 Maine St.in Brunswick.
The boutique officially opened its doors on Thursday; a grand opening and ribbon-cutting ceremony is next Friday, Oct. 9.
For the Schwarzes, Holy Chic Maison is the culmination of a dream that began early in their 31-year marriage. Throughout the years, they have worked together on a variety of creative ventures, including furniture, wreaths, artwork, and several years as vendors in an antique and craft mall. Karen, a lifelong painter and decorative artist, also launched a home décor business in 2008 after losing her job.
Through raising their family and navigating life’s many seasons, one thing remained constant: the dream of having a shop together. Now, at ages 56 and 57, they are finally doing it.
“We have dreamed of having a shop like this for as long as we’ve been together,” Karen Schwarz said in a prepared release. “We always knew we would find a way. It may have taken 30 years, but here we are. We couldn’t be more grateful to finally open our doors and share something we’ve poured so much of ourselves into.”
What began as a vision for a boutique quickly became a three-month labor of love.
After working all day at his construction management job, Perry would meet Karen at the shop in the evenings. Nearly every weekend, from early morning until late afternoon, the couple worked side by side — demolishing, repairing, painting, replacing carpet, refinishing furniture and completely reimagining the space.
Perry’s construction experience and the couple’s years of working together allowed them to tackle much of the transformation themselves, including a dramatic French-inspired feature wall that has become a centerpiece of the boutique.
Karen spent days stripping and refinishing an old wooden door, while the couple sourced and restored distinctive furnishings, including an antique counter from a local shop in northern Maine.
“We initially thought we could have it done in a month,” Karen said. “But once we got into it, we realized we had one chance to do this. We decided to go big. Every detail mattered to us.”

title: Groundbreaking held for Augusta supportive housing complex

title: Supreme Court to review immigrant detention policy
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The Supreme Court announced Thursday it will review the Trump administration’s policy of detaining immigrants who entered the country illegally without a bond hearing.
Previously, most immigrants who entered the country illegally were given a bond hearing, provided they did not have a criminal record, and were detained away from the border. The Trump administration has ended that practice, and the new policy is now before the Supreme Court.
The case revolves around a Brazilian citizen the Trump administration argues entered the country illegally two decades ago and applied for asylum in 2016. The man has never been charged with a crime besides illegal entry, but was placed in detention following a 2025 traffic stop and kept there.
In July, the Trump administration began the policy of mandatory detention without bond. The policy shift comes from a new interpretation of a 1990s immigration law.
Most lower courts have ruled that detaining immigrants indefinitely without a bond hearing is illegal, but the Fifth and Eighth circuit courts have upheld the new policy.
The high court is expected to hear the case in the next few months, with a decision expected by the end of June 2027.
