title: Judge denies defense motion asking Lindsay Clancy be found not guilty due to a lack of evidence
text:
BOSTON (AP) — The judge in the Lindsay Clancy murder case on Thursday refused to declare her not guilty, turning down a defense motion that had argued there wasn’t enough evidence to prove she was responsible for killing her three children.
On Tuesday, Clancy’s attorney Kevin Reddington tried to persuade Judge William Sullivan that prosecutors had not offered any proof that Clancy had killed her three children. Prosecutors argued there was plenty of evidence, calling Reddington’s claim “laughable.”
In his ruling, Sullivan said prosecutors had provided adequate evidence for a jury to decide whether Clancy was the person responsible for the killings.
“There was evidence introduced, both physical and circumstantial, that would permit a rational trier of fact to find beyond a reasonable doubt the elements of the charge of murder,” Sullivan wrote.
___
___
During that trial, Reddington didn’t dispute that Clancy killed the children at the family’s home in 2023. Instead, the defense sought to persuade the jury that the 36-year-old former labor and delivery nurse was not criminally responsible because of mental disease, a rare condition called postpartum psychosis.
Prosecutors acknowledged that Clancy, 36, had mental health problems that included months of treatment and a stay in a psychiatric hospital, but argued that she knew what she was doing when she strangled the children then tried to kill herself.
Clancy’s first trial ended Sept. 4 with a deadlocked jury. A judge declared a mistrial with the jury split 11 to 1 in favor of acquitting Clancy of murder charges.

title: Libra Foundation Gives $1.3 Million To Expand Outdoor Education
text:
The Libra Foundation will invest $1.3 million over the next two years to expand Maine Outdoor School for All, a statewide program that reached 1,675 students from 43 schools in its first year.
The gift will help University of Maine Cooperative Extension, which administers the program, expand opportunities for public school students to participate in interdisciplinary, experiential learning in natural settings.
“The Libra Foundation is pleased to support University of Maine Cooperative Extension as it expands this model throughout the state and works toward consistent, ongoing public funding,” said Jere Michelson, president and CEO of the Libra Foundation. “Sustained support can help make these experiences available to Maine students while strengthening connections to the natural resources and career pathways that are important to the state’s future.”

title: 15-year-old arrested in connection with Lewiston shooting
text:
15-year-old arrested in connection with Lewiston shooting
Lewiston police have arrested a 15-year-old boy in connection with a shooting in the city Sunday afternoon.
15-year-old arrested in connection with Lewiston shooting
Lewiston police have arrested a 15-year-old boy in connection with a shooting in the city Sunday afternoon.
Police said officers, detectives and task force officers continued investigating the Sept. 27 shooting in the area of Walnut and Shawmut streets. Investigators say they identified and located another person believed to be involved in the shooting.
The teenager was arrested Thursday afternoon and charged with attempted murder, a Class A felony, and reckless conduct with a dangerous weapon, a Class C felony, according to police.
A Juvenile Community Corrections Officer authorized a hold, and the teenager is being detained at the Long Creek Youth Development Center in South Portland.
The shooting was reported shortly before 3:25 p.m. Sunday. Police said officers found several shell casings near the intersection and learned a vehicle was seen leaving the area. Investigators previously identified a suspect vehicle using Flock cameras and located it downtown, where they found multiple bullet holes and detained 20-year-old Mohammud Osman.
Police charged Osman with reckless conduct with a dangerous weapon.
Police said no injuries were reported in connection with the Sept. 27 shooting, but the gunfire did cause property damage. The investigation remains ongoing.
The arrest comes as Lewiston police continue to investigate a series of recent shootings and other violent incidents involving juvenile suspects. Last week, police announced charges against two teenagers following a separate shooting near Knox and Maple streets.

title: FBI arrests Energy Department employee on charge of trying to support Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A Department of Energy electrical engineer has been arrested on charges of providing support to the Iranian-backed Houthi rebels, including by buying materials for homemade explosives and drones and traveling to Yemen, the Justice Department said Thursday.
Ashton Hamed Ellaboudy, 51, of Richland, Washington, was arrested Thursday and is due to make his first court appearance Friday. Court records do not list an attorney available to speak on his behalf.
The FBI says Ellaboudy had a goal of helping the Houthis improve their communications capabilities and traveled last September to Yemen, where the Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces are now engaged in renewed violence that has killed hundreds and displaced tens of thousands. The conflict began in 2014 when the Iran-backed rebels took over the capital, Sanaa, forcing the country’s government to settle into exile in Saudi Arabia.
Upon his return to the United States, authorities say, Ellaboudy told Customs and Border Protection officials that he was traveling back from Oman on a work trip and was part of a U.S. government mission to inspect defense facilities. But investigators interviewed Ellaboudy’s supervisor, who reported having no knowledge of any international travel or of an Energy Department missile inspection program that Ellaboudy would have been part of, an FBI affidavit said.
Ellaboudy himself was recorded telling FBI informants, whom officials had introduced into the investigation, that he had to be smuggled into and out of Yemen and that he had hoped to reach the country’s capital to make government-level connections, the affidavit says. He was ultimately unable to make it to Sanaa, the FBI said.
The FBI says investigators began looking into Ellaboudy after learning that he had purchased precursor chemicals commonly involved in the construction of homemade explosive devices, including acetone and sodium bisulfate, as well as parts used for drones.
During the course of the investigation, the FBI says, he communicated with multiple informants — including one who purported to be a Houthi colonel — and provided advice and assistance on communications equipment.
Ellaboudy is charged under a law that makes it a crime to provide material support to a group designated by the United States as a foreign terrorist organization, of which the Houthis are one.
“These allegations are so deeply disturbing that they almost defy imagination,” John Eisenberg, an assistant attorney general in charge of the Justice Department’s National Security Division, said in a statement.

title: Driver and school board member indicted
Obituary: Stephen T. Hughes
text:
AUBURN / NEW YORK CITY, N.Y. – Stephen T. Hughes passed away on Aug. 17, 2026. He was 83.
Steve lived a life marked by service to others — as an elected official, a trustee of the University of Maine, and an active member of several Episcopal parishes, most notably St. Bartholomew’s Church in New York City, N.Y. where he lived for the last 40 years of his life.
Born on July 26, 1943 to Albert W. “Beau” Hughes and Edith Bivens Hughes, Steve grew up in Auburn and graduated from Edward Little High School. He went on to attend Duke University in Durham, North Carolina, a state where members of his extended family lived. After being drafted, Steve served for two years in the United States Army before enrolling at the University of Maine.
At UMaine, Steve made many lifelong friends and served as president of the student body during a tumultuous era when the Vietnam War and the national debate surrounding it profoundly affected campus life. While still an undergraduate, he gained statewide recognition when Gov. Kenneth M. Curtis appointed him as the first student to serve as a trustee of the University of Maine.
Steve graduated from UMaine in 1970 and, while continuing his service as a trustee, attended the University of Maine School of Law. In 1974, voters in Auburn elected him to the Maine House of Representatives. He was reelected in 1976.
During his legislative career, Steve became closely identified with two landmark environmental measures. He sponsored legislation establishing Maine’s beverage-container deposit law, commonly known as the “Bottle Bill,” and championed the successful effort to eliminate most roadside billboards. Both measures helped shape Maine’s approach to environmental protection and preservation of its landscape and remain the law today. Steve was also a strong advocate for civil rights, reproductive freedom, and the rule of law.
After serving four years in the Legislature, Steve left Maine for New York City, N.Y. where he pursued a life of ministry. He enrolled at Union Theological Seminary and spent 15 years leading programs at the Cathedral Church of St. John the Divine. He later became deeply involved with St. Bartholomew’s Church, known as St. Bart’s, where he served in a variety of leadership roles for 25 years. His activities there were curtailed in later years by health issues related to COVID-19.
Throughout his life, Steve maintained a deep love of music, culture, and the arts. Blessed with an extraordinary tenor voice, he sang with numerous choirs in both Maine and New York. He also loved to travel and, over the years, explored much of the United States and Europe with his many friends.
Steve will be remembered for his lively conversation, intellectual curiosity, commitment to public and community service, love of music and the arts, and devotion to a wide circle of friends and an extended network of cousins scattered across the country.
Steve was predeceased by his parents, Albert W. “Beau” Hughes and Edith Bivens Hughes; and his brother, Nick Hughes.
A gathering of Steve’s Maine family and friends will be held 2 p.m., Sunday, Oct. 11, at Maple Hill Farm in Hallowell. A service celebrating Steve’s life will be held at 2 p.m. Nov. 6 at St. Bartholomew’s Church in New York City, N.Y. Interment will be in the Hughes family plot in Eno Presbyterian Church in Cedar Grove, N.C.
In lieu of flowers please donate to be made to the University of Maine Alumni Association. https://www.umainealumni.com/

title: Nearly 60 years after his adoption, man learns Grammy Award-winning musician Michael McDonald is his biological father
text:
ST. LOUIS (KMOV/Gray News) - A man who was placed for adoption as a baby nearly 60 years ago learned that his father is five-time Grammy Award winner Michael McDonald.
Michael Goessling said he always knew he was adopted and had a “wonderful childhood.”
“I could not pick two finer folks to raise me,” he said.
Goessling always wondered about his biological parents and said the mystery began unraveling after one of McDonald’s children took a 23andMe DNA test.
“Within 36 hours, he got an email notifying him, ‘Michael Gossling, half brother, St. Louis,’” Goessling said. “And that’s how this all began.”
On his 58th birthday, Goessling met his birth mother in person. Later, he spoke with his biological father over the phone. Goessling asked what he did for a living, and his biological father mentioned he was a musician preparing to tour through St. Louis that summer.
“And I said, ‘Are you Michael McDonald?’” Goessling said. “And he said, ‘Yeah, I’m afraid so.’”
Goessling’s biological mother and McDonald were 14 years old when Goessling was conceived.
McDonald is a singer-songwriter and Doobie Brothers member known for songs including “What a Fool Believes” and “I Keep Forgettin.’”
The fact that Goessling and McDonald share the same first name is purely coincidental.
McDonald and Goessling’s biological mother have remained close friends over the years.
McDonald described the emotional weight of not knowing what happened to his son.
“We always talked about him. And it always came down to our greatest fear was, how did life treat him?” McDonald said. “I always carried that guilt with me. But just to know that he was OK and that he had a good life, and a life certainly that I wouldn’t have been able to afford him at that time, was a great reward. The real rock stars in this story are his adoptive parents.”
Goessling and McDonald have since met in person.
“When he first saw me, he put his arms out, gave me a big old bear hug and told me he loved me, and I told him the same,” Goessling said.
The reunion also made McDonald a grandfather.
“Yeah, I’m still wrapping my head around that,” McDonald said with a laugh. “My daughter-in-law is just the daughter-in-law you’d hope for. And the kids are two of the greatest kids you’d ever meet. I’m just so proud of them.”

title: WATCH: Off-duty detective, deputy pull driver from burning truck moments before it explodes
text:
Off-duty detective, deputy pull disoriented driver from burning truck in Missouri moments before it explodes
Local law enforcement officers jumped into action earlier this month to rescue a man whose truck caught fire on a Missouri interstate.
The Clay County Sheriff's Office shared a post Wednesday detailing the rescue.
Detective Findley with the Kansas City Police Department had just gotten off work when he came across a truck engulfed in flames on Interstate 35 on Sept. 15.
Clay County Sheriff's Deputy Blatt was driving in the Claycomo area, which is in the Kansas City metropolitan area, when he saw the fire and pulled over to help. As Blatt stopped, Findley got the driver out of the truck.
Findley and Blatt worked together to pull the driver, who was disoriented, to safety. Their quick action may have saved the man's life, as the vehicle later exploded, the sheriff's office said.
The driver was taken to the hospital to be treated for burns to his legs.
"Without the intervention of Detective Findley and Deputy Blatt, it could have been much worse," the Clay County Sheriff's Office said.
"The smoke was getting thicker and heavier, and I couldn't see anything in front of me," Findley said.
He described the intense conditions as he approached the vehicle.
"It was hot when I got to the vehicle. I could start to see some flame coming, like, from the engine compartment, and almost the entire cab looked like it was full of just heavy black smoke," he said.
Findley said the man inside the truck was disoriented and experiencing a medical issue.
Clay County Sheriff's Deputy Chase Blatt was driving home northbound on I-35 when he noticed the black smoke and stopped to help.
"As I was coming around the curve on I-35, I saw the black smoke coming up," Blatt said.
The truck was engulfed in flames, and explosions erupted from the heat as the officers worked together to pull the man to safety.
"We pulled him back a couple more after we realized that flying on fire debris was coming from the vehicle," Blatt said.
Findley described the scene as "a very, kind of a frantic situation for a minute."
The officers said this type of rescue is not something they train for, but their instincts took over.
"It's more of an instinct that kicks in, and you just do what you have to do," Findley said.
The Clay County Sheriff's Office said the situation could have been much worse if the officers had not arrived when they did. A video of the aftermath showed the truck completely destroyed by the fire.
"If I would have been on the road 15, 20 seconds earlier, I would have been ahead of this and probably not seen it," Findley said.
Blatt expressed relief that they were able to get the man the help he needed.
"I'm glad we were able to get fire there and EMS there to help him out, make sure he got the medical attention he needed," Blatt said.

title: Americans are using buy now, pay later more than ever. Here’s what to know if you’re one of them
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Americans spent more than $160 billion last year using buy now, pay later plans, according to research published by Federal Reserve economists.
Experts say they’re increasingly seeing people use the plans for everyday expenses like groceries, bills, transportation and, sometimes rent.
“It has been very hard out there for a lot of people,” said Sara Rathner, NerdWallet’s credit card expert. “It’s a tough job market, and it’s a rough economy, and the cost of the things that we buy every day has been going up, in some cases more than people’s incomes.”
Pay-in-four plans, which generally allow consumers to pay for purchases in four installments over six weeks, accounted for about half of the $160 billion in buy now, pay later spending last year, according to the study. Use of those plans has increased nearly 80% since 2023.
The rest of the plans were either longer- or shorter-term loans.
How consumers are using buy now pay later
When Elizabeth Brown first used buy now, pay later, she had just started living by herself and was earning a salary that made it hard to afford basic expenses. She would buy groceries and, once she got her paycheck, pay for them through buy now, pay later. Six years later, things haven’t changed much.
“I used buy now, pay later so I can have the furniture I need. I have groceries in my fridge because of it. I don’t necessarily feel shameful for using it because at the end it’s very beneficial to me at this point of my life,” said Brown, 26, of Columbia, South Carolina, who works as a clinical service member at an optical store.
Buy now, pay later products have evolved. Rent now, pay later services are one form, which break rent into multiple payments.
“It isn’t really just a convenience element anymore; it really is becoming a cash flow challenge,” said Mark Elliott, chief customer officer at Happen Bank, a financial services company formerly known as Lending Club.
Jordan Williams, 28, first used buy now, pay later to get concert tickets to Hozier. Then, when she experienced financial hardship after her daughter was born, she started leaning on it to pay for some of her groceries.
“There’s just not a lot of resources, and that makes me angry because this shouldn’t be something I have to do,” said Williams, a lecturer and content creator from Greensboro, North Carolina. ”We should be able to just afford groceries. I feel angry and then I feel embarrassed.”
For a long time, Williams felt ashamed about having to use buy now, pay later for basic expenses. She now feels less alone after talking with other people who also have debt.
If you’re going to use buy now, pay later plans, here are some expert recommendations:
Read the fine print
The most well-known buy now, pay later product is pay-in-four, where you can pay back what you owe in four payments, one every two weeks, with a 0% annual percentage rate, or APR. However, not every buy now, pay later loan has the same terms. Before you commit to buying something using buy now, pay later, Ed deHaan, a professor at the Stanford Graduate School of Business, recommends that you read your contract carefully.
“So-called buy now, pay later products are popping up that are not good deals at all,” deHaan said. “Some of them charge hefty fees, both upfront and if you miss a payment.”
In general, if you miss a buy now, pay later payment, you can face fees, interest or the possibility of being banned from using the services in the future.
Know how it impacts your credit score
In the past, buy now, pay later loans didn’t impact your credit score, but that has changed. Buy now, pay later agencies now report credit lending activity to one of the three major credit bureaus, Equifax, Experian and TransUnion.
“Entering into a buy now, pay later plan for now isn’t going to affect your credit in any way, but missing a payment can, so that’s where you really want to be careful,” Rathner said.
Credit reporting depends on the company and its policies. For example, both Affirm and Klarna report to Experian and TransUnion. Afterpay does not report to any credit bureau.
Only borrow what you can pay back
Before purchasing something with buy now, pay later, deHaan recommends pausing to consider whether it’s an amount you can pay back.
“The general advice for credit is that it’s very easy to spend and hard to pay off,” deHaan said. “And most of us, many of us, are not good at making good predictions about what we will be able to pay in the future.”
When using buy now, pay later, Brown set herself a limit of $100 a month across payments, and she avoids signing up for payments every two weeks and instead chooses the monthly payment options.
Avoid stacking plans
As with credit cards, you can sign up for multiple buy now, pay later plans. These loans can quickly balloon until they become unmanageable. If you don’t want to risk snowballing into debt, avoid stacking buy-now, pay later loans, said Carla Sanchez-Adams, senior attorney at the National Consumer Law Center.
“Avoid multiple purchases because then it gets really hard to track, especially if they’re with different companies,” Sanchez-Adams said.
If you have to utilize multiple loans, make sure you keep track of the payment amounts and dates so you avoid late fees, she added.
Seek out additional resources
Looking into additional resources such as food banks, SNAP or hardship help programs in your area can be helpful, Rathner said.
“If you are stretched thin for affording food and going into debt to do so, it could be time to seek out additional help,” she said. “So this is hopefully less of a struggle for you and your family while you’re going through this difficult time.”
Seek help from a nonprofit credit counseling agency
If you’ve reached a point where you have too many buy now, pay later loans and maybe some credit card debt too, it might be time to seek help from a credit counseling agency. Two well-known resources for finding nonprofit credit counseling agencies are the National Foundation for Credit Counseling and the Financial Counseling Association of America. Both can help you connect with certified agencies and counselors.
“You have financial stress, you have work stress, you have family stress,” Rathner said. “Get help with the financial stress because that can help you feel more in control of this area of your life. And it can help take one step at a time toward paying down your debts and feeling more in control.”

title: Maine man faces drug trafficking charges after crashing into construction vehicle
text:
A Lisbon man faces drug trafficking charges after he allegedly crashed into a construction vehicle Wednesday night.
Demetrius Starks, 45, has been charged with aggravated cocaine trafficking, aggravated fentanyl trafficking, unlawful cocaine possession, unlawful fentanyl possession, illegal possession of a firearm, operating under the influence, criminal mischief and driving to endanger, according to the Auburn Police Department.
Starks was driving a black BMW near the intersection of Court Street and Minot Avenue in Auburn about 11:36 p.m. when he allegedly went over the median, through a sign and crashed into a construction vehicle.

Starks was taken to the Androscoggin County Jail.

title: The Food Detective: Opa, Part 2
Failed Tennessee execution renews the debate over death penalty methods
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — Tennessee officials haven’t explained yet what went wrong during the failed execution of Christa Pike, which was called off after she was given two doses of the drug meant to kill her.
It wasn’t clear if Pike was still alive on Thursday. She could be heard snoring loudly in the execution chamber Wednesday night more than an hour after the execution process began and nearly 30 minutes after a second dose of pentobarbital was administered.
Pike, who was sentenced to death for a gruesome 1995 murder, was taken by ambulance from the prison to a hospital, where she was being treated, her attorneys said.
May Martinez, whose daughter was murdered by Pike and her boyfriend and who traveled to Nashville to see the sentence carried out, told NBC News that “it was a mess.”
The failure, which one death penalty expert described as unprecedented, led Gov. Bill Lee to postpone Tennessee’s lone remaining execution this year and to order a review “to determine exactly what occurred.” It also raises questions again about the state’s procedures and its use of single-drug lethal injections.
“There are very few answers this morning. It’s very early. There are a lot of questions,” Lee told reporters Thursday at an unrelated event, noting he had received no updates on Pike’s condition. “The people of our state deserve to have those questions answered.”
“This is a tragedy. There is no one who wanted what happened last night to happen,” the governor said. He added: “It’s deeply disturbing to me that this has happened in this state.”
Pike, 50, had been scheduled for execution Wednesday morning for the killing she committed at age 18 and would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. An appeals court stopped the execution an hour before it was to start, but the U.S. Supreme Court overturned that stay hours later.
Officials gave Pike two doses of pentobarbital, her attorneys said in court filings late Wednesday.
The Tennessee Department of Correction said in a statement that it “followed every step of the State’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General’s Office.”
Tennessee changed its execution method two years ago
The state’s execution protocol calls for a secondary set of drug syringes to be administered “if the inmate is not deceased” after the first set. It does not spell out what happens if the subject is alive after the second set.
Tennessee announced in 2024 it was switching from a three-drug series for lethal injections to the single drug pentobarbital. That came more than two years after the state abruptly halted the execution of Oscar Smith and acknowledged it had failed to ensure its lethal injection drugs were tested properly.
Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said what Pike experienced is “singular and unparalleled.”
Seven other people have survived medical problems due to an execution team’s failure to access a vein to administer lethal injection drugs, but no one has stayed alive after receiving the drugs used in such executions, she said.
Executions in the U.S. have fallen sharply since the beginning of this century as public opposition has increased and so have concerns about costs and the drugs used in lethal injections. But the number of executions nearly doubled last year behind a record increase in Florida.
Pike would have been the 30th person executed in the U.S. this year.
Pike was awake in the execution chamber
Strapped to a gurney in the execution chamber, Pike described herself as at peace.
“I’m going to leave this world the way I spent most of my life and that is in love,” she said in her “last” words.
But she remained awake and at one point raised her head, asking prison officials if her arm was supposed to feel that way. An hour after officials first raised the execution chamber’s curtains, witnesses reported that a second dose of pentobarbital was administered.
Pike could still be heard snoring behind a closed curtain until the microphone was cut off almost 30 minutes later.
Lawyers for Pike filed an emergency motion late Wednesday with the Tennessee Supreme Court seeking to immediately halt and stay the execution, saying she was in “unnecessary agony” and the procedure violated her right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment. They also filed motions with two other courts.
It was the second time this year that Tennessee has been unable to complete an execution: In May state officials called off the lethal injection of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and killing three people in 1994, after executioners tried and failed for over an hour to place an IV to administer pentobarbital.
Pike and her boyfriend were convicted of the fatal stabbing and beating in 1995 of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a classmate at a job training facility in Knoxville. The killing gained attention because of a pentagram carved on Slemmer’s body, stoking fears of Satan worship during the “satanic panic” of the 1980s and 1990s.
Pike’s boyfriend wasn’t eligible for the death penalty because he was 17 at the time of the killing and received a sentence of life in prison. He was denied parole last year.
Pike’s case renews the debate over the death sentence
Pike did not deny committing the killing, but her supporters argued that the state should consider her age at the time, her mental illness and her allegations of severe sexual abuse.
Assistant Federal Defender Stephen Ferrell said Pike’s death sentence is an outlier because other 18-year-olds in Tennessee have had such sentences vacated.
After the killing, Pike was diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder. In her clemency petition, she said she only wanted to fight Slemmer but killed her in a frenzied attack when she couldn’t “put the brakes on.”
“It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” Pike said in a statement.
___
Associated Press writers Jeffrey Collins in Columbia, South Carolina, Ed White in Detroit, Russ Bynum in Savannah, Georgia, Hallie Golden in Seattle and Hannah Schoenbaum in Salt Lake City contributed.

title: Lincoln Academy golf wins tight battle for KVAC B title, state bid
text:
ROCKLAND — Considered the favorites to win the Kennebec Valley Athletic Conference Class B Shootout, the Lincoln Academy golf team had to work for it Thursday.
In the end, the Eagles did prevail, beating out Nokomis and Medomak Valley to win the conference title at Rockland Golf Club. The win secured Lincoln a spot in the Class B championships next Saturday at Natanis Golf Course in Vassalboro.
“Our boys have had a great season — they really have — and they did excellent today,” said Lincoln coach Todd Brackett. “Nokomis has a really good team, and they beat us in the regular season. Medomak, we have a good rivalry with them. We knew it was going to be close.”
Lincoln’s top-four players shot a combined nine-hole score of 162, beating out the Warriors (166) and the Panthers (167) in a tight battle for first. Belfast (181), Leavitt (183) and Erskine Academy (188) rounded out the team scoring.
Lincoln junior Drew Nichols (38) shot the second-best score of the day, finishing a stroke behind medalist Caden Chretien of Nokomis (37). Colin Mitchell shot a 39 for the Eagles to tie Medomak Valley’s Seb Mank and Joseph Wilcox for third.
“My short game was really solid,” Nichols said. “Off the tee, I was a little iffy — I actually topped my driver twice, so that was interesting — but with how good my short game was, I was able to get around the golf course. … I had a really rough go of it this season, so I’m glad I brought it around here.”
Max Blake added a 41 for Lincoln, while Dylan Lomas shot a 44. That was enough to outduel Nokomis, which also got a 42 from Atticus Haining, a 43 from Will Hayes and a 44 from Jake Paradis, and Medomak Valley, which got a 44 from Andrew Flanders and a 45 from Wyatt Hood.
“If anybody was going to steal it from us today, I thought it was going to be Medomak,” Brackett said. “Like I said, we just played great today. It was a good day for us out there.”
A warm October day that saw temperatures reach the upper 60s even on the coast made for an enjoyable round of golf. The winds from earlier in the week had largely subsided, though some stiffer gusts did arrive later into the afternoon.
Medomak Valley had the fortune of playing the round on its home course, though coach Kevin Richardson pointed out that changing greens throughout the week mitigated that advantage. Richardson, too, said the three-way race between Medomak Valley, Lincoln and Nokomis played out as expected.
“In all 10 regular-season matches that we played (until today), we had the medalist, which shows you that Lincoln and Nokomis both have some really good players,” Richardson said. “We played well all year, and I had a feeling we were going to play well today. We did, but it just wasn’t quite enough.”
Nokomis, Medomak Valley, Belfast, Leavitt and Erskine will still get chances to book berths at states at the KVAC qualifier Tuesday at Natanis. Lincoln can rest easy that its state championship participation is assured, though Nichols said the Eagles’ absence Tuesday will also have some drawbacks.
“We’d like to go to the qualifier to get that extra round in, but it’s also quite the plus that we get to have that auto-bid,” Nichols said. “We’re a good group of guys that play a lot and put the work in over the summer, so it feels great.”
Jason Thurston of Belfast tied for seventh individually, shooting a 42. James Brisson shot a 44 to lead Leavitt, while Blake Morrow and Nolan Pierce also shot 44s to lead Erskine.

title: What scares me about real estate in Maine right now
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Julia Bassett Schwerin of Cape Elizabeth has been a real estate broker since 2005.
The real estate market is approaching a balanced market where supply and demand are in equilibrium and moving away from the seller’s market it has been in since 2020. After the pandemic, demand surged, prices rose and inventory dropped, but now the number of homes for sale has finally started to recover.
My prediction is that prices, which have doubled the value of most homes over the last seven years, will soften as sellers spend some of their massive equity to attract fewer buyers, but will not result in anything like the crash we had in 2008.
The issue that does scare me is that the operating expenses of owning a home represent a larger contributor to the unaffordability of housing than the first cost, which is getting all the attention. Specifically, I am referring to the cost of heating and homeowner’s insurance.
Maine has been doing well transitioning off heating with oil, going from 70% down to 50% of homes burning oil in the last seven years, but oil costs are expected to increase 30% this winter compared to last due to the Iran war. Buyers of more efficient buildings using clean energy are much more able to benefit from paying less in fuel cost than the small increase in mortgage payments for better insulation and air sealing.
For help paying utility bills, check out the consumer assistance information on the websites of the Public Utilities Commission, the Office of the Public Advocate and Efficiency Maine.
Maine has also enjoyed affordable insurance until recent storms caused catastrophic damage. Unfortunately, rising sea levels and severe storms caused by climate change are being sidelined and smeared as a political wedge issue. The weather risks from a warming planet are raising insurance premiums for property both across the board in reinsurance rates and selectively in areas where flooding, wildfires, storms, droughts and pollution have caused damage and claims.
Models ranking address-level property risks from climate factors have been built by several firms and are being closely scrutinized by insurers who have their own databases on losses. As the property damage costs from increased global warming rise, so too will claims for reimbursement by the government; if and when the federal government is unwilling or unable to help people who incurred disaster losses, the private insurers will be left holding the bag.
According to data from the U.S. Senate Budget Committee, the rate of home insurance policy nonrenewal is rising in the U.S. and in Maine. If homeowners can’t afford insurance premiums big enough to share the costs of flood and storm damage with those unaffected, then they can’t afford to live in single-family homes and will have to share housing; the insurers must be doing the math that it’s better for their business to incentivize us to fortify our buildings against climate change than rachet up the premiums or stop renewing policies.
Here is the proof: the Maine Bureau of Insurance, which is responsible for regulating the insurance firms underwriting policies in the state, took it upon themselves to adopt a program designed in the hurricane and tornado belts by the Institute for Business and Home Safety.
Called Fortify, it collects money from insurers and distributes it to building owners in the form of substantial grants to add fortification to a new roof by sealing the roof deck and locking down the drip edge, measures proven in wind tunnel testing to keep the roof attached and the water out.
If insurers with sophisticated data think that enough increasingly scary weather is on its way to Maine to warrant adopting the program, shouldn’t we in the real estate and construction trades act like they are probably right?
What the heck are we doing here bickering about whether we should teach Realtors about sustainability, whether we should adopt stricter building energy codes that reduce emissions, or whether we need to take collective measures to make buildings more resilient to the risk of loss from worsening storms and floods? The answer is a resounding “yes.”
The real estate and construction industries can see this bubbling up like a manhole cover on a side street at the Portland Old Port during a sunny day king tide.
We need an all of us together approach to the transition to clean energy from fossil fuel combustion emissions in buildings, and we need it now.

title: The laws tied to the Susan Collins-Navatek allegations are ‘crystal clear.’ Enforcing them is another matter.
text:
The allegations of a “pay-to-play” scheme and bribery outlined in the recent ProPublica report on U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, and a contractor may not lead to any further consequences beyond serving as campaign fodder, but experts said the piece highlighted some key facts.
Existing laws are clear on banning such behavior, but it takes a federal agency to investigate any alleged wrongdoing, campaign finance experts noted.
That seems to be what happened with the case involving Hawaiian defense contractor Navatek, its former CEO-turned-convicted-felon Martin Kao and an illegal donation to a pro-Collins super PAC through a shell company. But an FBI investigation focusing on Collins and Kao — along with other potential corruption involving members of Congress — died after President Donald Trump returned to office in 2025 and purged the anti-corruption unit that had been handling the probe, ProPublica reported.
So it appears unlikely that more penalties will come as a result of the alleged interactions detailed in the Sept. 22 piece, though ProPublica said it was only “the first in a series of stories drawn from our reporting.” The fallout is instead mostly coming in the form of fresh criticism of Collins as she seeks a sixth term against former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson in a race that appears neck and neck ahead of the Nov. 3 election.
Still, the report opened up various questions regarding campaign finance and what is allowed in an American political system that both sides of the aisle agree is awash in money.
Collins and her campaign staff, who have never been charged in connection with Kao’s case, have bashed the new reporting as covering old allegations from Kao, who was sentenced to 87 months in prison last year after he pleaded guilty to funneling more than $200,000 to Collins’ 2020 reelection campaign and an affiliated super PAC that Collins and the PAC returned in light of the criminal proceedings against Kao.
But ProPublica rebutted the Collins camp’s criticism by noting its story focused on previously unreported claims Kao made between 2022 and 2024, and on how a trove of records and emails the news organization obtained show the FBI was still investigating Kao’s relationship with Collins, her staffers and employees of the super PAC up until early 2025.
The Portland Press Herald spoke with several campaign finance experts who have worked in law and for the federal government about various questions raised by the ProPublica reporting. Without rehashing all the details in the ProPublica story, the interviews revealed a few tweaks that could fix broader finance loopholes. But the experts agreed the existing laws in place to protect against pay-for-play schemes and bribery are clear. Enforcing them is another matter.
What are the laws on contractor donations and bribery of public officials? What are the penalties for breaking them? How easy it is to prosecute?
Both the Hatch Act amendments of 1940 and Federal Election Commission regulations ban federal government contractors from donating to — or promising to donate to — federal candidates, political parties, political committees and super PACs. Civil fines are common penalties, but prison sentences occur in more serious cases that also involve other violations.
Kao received his 87-month prison sentence in 2025 because of a series of violations, rather than illicit campaign donations. His crimes included COVID-19 pandemic wire fraud, money laundering and bank fraud, with a judge also ordering him to pay back about $12.8 million in Paycheck Protection Program funds he fraudulently obtained.
Anti-bribery statutes prohibit “quid pro quo” dealings and ban public officials from giving or receiving anything of value if it is given “with intent to influence” an official act or received “in return for being influenced.” A bribery conviction is punishable by up to 15 years in prison, but a separate case of giving a “gratuity” after the fact as “thanks” for an act, but not in exchange for it, can result in up to two years. A “gratuity” does not include campaign contributions.
The current laws make it “crystal clear that certain behaviors are unlawful,” said Erin Chlopak, who worked for the FEC in litigation and policy roles for nearly a decade and now serves as the nonprofit Campaign Legal Center’s senior director of campaign finance. The Campaign Legal Center had filed a complaint with the FEC after getting suspicious about what turned out to be the $150,000 straw donation to the pro-Collins super PAC in 2020 that Kao reportedly told PAC officials he would give through the “Society of Young Women Scientist and Engineers.”
But proving bribery is not easy, campaign finance experts noted, and Supreme Court rulings have narrowed what counts. For contractor violations, the FEC has lacked a four-member quorum during Trump’s second term and thus cannot start investigations or issue penalties.
“It is incredibly difficult for prosecutors to prove that sort of quid pro quo exchange,” said Eric Petry, counsel in the left-leaning Brennan Center for Justice’s Elections and Government Program. “And oftentimes, it really boils down to a ‘he said versus she said,’ which is really difficult for courts and juries to get to the bottom of.”
A jury in 2024 found former U.S. Sen. Bob Menendez, a New Jersey Democrat who was seeking reelection that year as an independent, guilty of acting as a foreign agent for Egypt amid a yearslong bribery scheme involving him, his wife and three New Jersey businesspeople. Menendez is appealing his 11-year prison sentence.
On the topic of illicit federal contractor donations, FEC commissioners were equally divided in 2024 and thus closed a complaint from the Campaign Legal Center that a federal contractor violated the law by giving more than $236,000 to a super PAC supporting Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis’ presidential campaign.
What are the gray areas? What about business leaders who donate and whose companies win contracts?
The ban on federal contractor donations does not apply to several categories of people, including stockholders, officers or employees of a corporation, and it does not apply to donations in state or local elections. And when it comes to campaign money, the U.S. Supreme Court’s Citizens United ruling in 2010 essentially paved the way for corporations to spend unlimited funds on elections.
Petry said Congress could seek to boost low levels of public trust in the government by at least expanding the federal contractor donation ban to cover those other affiliated individuals, such as stockholders and officers. He also flagged how federal contractors and corporations can give to presidential inauguration funds or projects such as Trump’s White House ballroom.
Other examples of giving are allowed and easier to spot, though experts noted that voters have cited them in surveys when expressing disgust with the amount of money floating around the political system.
New Balance’s owner and chairman, Jim Davis, gave $1 million to Collins’ super PAC last year. The senator proudly held one of the company’s shoes when announcing her reelection campaign in February. And earlier in September, she touted a nearly $60 million contract the company got to produce military footwear at its Skowhegan plant.
Did Collins actually call Kao to thank him?
Scott Reed, who leads the pro-Collins Pine Tree Results PAC, was mentioned repeatedly in the recent ProPublica piece because of Kao’s testimony, FBI records and emails showing his interactions with Kao. That included a 2019 meeting in Washington in which Reed allegedly asked Navatek executives for a $500,000 campaign donation after Collins had helped the company win a multimillion dollar Navy research contract in Maine.
ProPublica viewed an email in which Kao told Reed he planned to donate $150,000 through a shell company. “Very smart,” Reed replied.
(ProPublica reached out to Reed for comment, and he said via email that, “I understand Martin Kao is now sitting in federal prison,” along with saying he “never had any communications with Senator Collins (or) her staff about Martin Kao and/or Navatek.”)
Seven days after the super PAC cashed the check from Kao’s shell company, one of Reed’s subordinates emailed a Navatek lobbyist asking for Kao’s phone number and said Collins “would like to call Martin to thank him,” ProPublica reported.
The Collins campaign and its manager, Steve Abbott, responded last week by saying they do “not believe” the senator ever called Kao. When the Portland Press Herald asked Wednesday if Collins herself would comment on whether she called Kao, campaign spokesperson Blake Kernen said it “does not appear in any of our records that this call was made.”
“Neither Susan Collins nor anyone who worked for her believes that she made a call,” Kernen said.
Would a federal investigation get reopened?
Since the ProPublica story came out, The New York Times and Washington Post have also each reported that the FBI in 2025 shut down its investigation revolving around Reed, Kao and Collins. The Times reported that senior bureau officials questioned Kao’s truthfulness, but ProPublica said that by the end of 2024, agents had “enough evidence to pursue a sweeping bribery probe that could ensnare top lawmakers of both political parties.”
Campaign finance experts said a renewed investigation is unlikely under Trump, who is serving his second and final term through 2028. Craig Holman, a government affairs lobbyist for the left-leaning consumer advocacy group Public Citizen, has helped states such as Illinois, New Jersey and Connecticut write their own “pay-to-play” legislation but said the Justice Department has the chief responsibility to prosecute bribery or contractor-related corruption.
“It is very unfortunate, though not surprising, that the Trump administration would step in and stop that investigation,” Holman said. “They just accept this as normal behavior.”

title: Scattered Showers Friday. Pleasant Fall Weekend Ahead
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Clouds will increase overnight into Friday ahead of an incoming cold front. Overnight low temperatures remain mild, settling in the mid 50s to low 60s, patchy fog and a few spotty showers could develop across northern communities before daybreak. A Dense Fog Advisory has been issued for central and coastal Washington County.
Friday: Cold front tracks northwest to southeast
Showers push into northern and western Maine Friday morning as the cold front arrives. The front will slowly press toward the coast through Friday afternoon. As the showers nears the Interstate and coast, they will turn lighter and much more scattered.
Afternoon highs will depend heavily on the front’s timing:
- Mountains and North: Expect highs in the mid- to upper 60s behind earlier frontal passage.
- Foothills to Coast: Expect highs climbing into the upper 60s to mid-70s ahead of the front.
Expected Rainfall Totals:
- Northern Maine: Up to 0.25″, with isolated pockets reaching 0.50″.
- Down East & Coast: Lighter totals, ranging from a few hundredths up to 0.10″.
Weekend Outlook: Bright Saturday, crisp Sunday with northern frost
High pressure builds in quickly behind the departing front, setting up a crisp, pleasant fall weekend.
- Saturday: Plentiful sunshine with comfortable afternoon highs reaching the mid 60s—right at average for early October.
- Sunday: A chilly morning start with patchy frost possible across northern valleys as lows drop into the 30s. Sunday remains dry and bright through the afternoon with highs from the upper 50s to mid-60s before light shower chances return Sunday night into Monday.
First Alert 7-Day Forecast
TONIGHT: Increasing clouds with lows ranging from the mid 50s to the low 60s. Patchy fog is possible. SW wind 5-15 mph.
FRIDAY: Mostly cloudy skies with scattered showers moving from northwest to southeast. Highs will range from the mid 60s to the mid 70s. WSW wind10-20 mph.
SATURDAY: Sunny skies with highs in the low to mid 60s. NW wind 10-20 mph.
SUNDAY: Increasing clouds later in the day. Highs range from the upper 50s to the mid 60s.
MONDAY: Mostly cloudy with scattered showers possible. Highs in the 50s and low 60s.
TUESDAY: Mostly sunny with highs in the 50s. NW gusts to 30 mph.
WEDNESDAY: Frosty morning. Lots of sunshine with highs in the 50s and low 60s.

title: Dresden’s ‘Face of the Town’ Remembered for Kind and Giving Nature
text:
After lifelong Dresden resident Sharon “Shari” Lilly died after a battle with cancer, residents remembered her for her kindness and devotion to the town.
Having grown up in Dresden and attending the local school Bridge Academy, Lilly was already familiar with many residents before she started her work with various committees, which she balanced with her work as a housewife married to Gorham “Pean” Lilly.
Dresden Town Administrator Nicole Rogers knew Lilly all her life, both as her father’s cousin and her neighbor.
“She genuinely cared about people and she knew everybody in town,” Rogers said. “That’s probably why she was willing to give so much of her time to the community because she had some kind of tie to every person in Dresden.”
Rogers said she remembers Lilly’s kindness growing up and how she cared about people in town. Lilly congratulated her on life events and helped her apply for a scholarship through Bridge Academy Public Library.
The town will work with Lilly’s family to figure out if it can create something to honor her, Rogers said. She added it will be “strange” to think that Lilly will not be a presence in the town or office anymore. Besides visiting the office through her work, Lilly also stopped in to bring staff treats and to deliver presents to Rogers’ son around Christmas.
Lilly held the town positions of committee recording secretary and local health officer. Lilly also volunteered her time often as a member or trustee. Members of the community praised her work with the Dresden Planning Board, Dresden Sno-Valley Riders Snowmobile Club, Bridge Academy Public Library, Dresden Education Exploratory Committee, Dresden Historical Society, Dresden Board of Appeals, Maine Elver Fisherman Association, Dresden Comprehensive Plan Committee, Dresden Budget Review Committee, Dresden Select Board, Alewife Harvesters of Maine, Dresden Fire Association, Maple Grove Cemetery Association of Dresden, and a conservation committee that previously existed in Dresden.
Lilly was also known to bring food to events and provide permits for burning.
Dresden Select Board member Jeffrey Bickford said the list of organizations she was involved in may go on.
“If you were to ask me about somebody else in the town who would have a complete list, the person I would suggest to you that had that list would be Shari,” Bickford said. “If you wanted to know what something happened in a town select meeting in the early ‘90s she was the person you went to because she had all the books.”
Bickford said he first met Lilly when he moved to Dresden in 2017. Lilly was a poll worker during elections, and Bickford met her when he went to vote.
“She was extremely helpful,” Bickford said. “She knew everybody in town. It was pretty much like meeting the face of the town because everybody knew her. She was loved by everybody in town.”
Bickford said he got to know her better through working with the town on the select board. The two met at many town events.
“I don’t know that there was an event in the town of Dresden that didn’t coincide with Shari Lilly,” Bickford said.
Dresden Planning Board Chair Jeff Pierce said Lilly also kept track of when meetings in town were for board members. Sometimes this included rearranging meeting times so Lilly could attend them.
Pierce worked with Lilly since meeting her over 28 years ago when he first moved to town.
“She’s just one of those people who puts a smile on your face,” Pierce said. “Never had a coarse word for anybody. She always had a smile. She didn’t judge anybody.”
In her work, Lilly never missed meetings and took the most meticulous notes of “anybody who I’ve ever worked with,” Pierce said. While she did not interrupt meetings, she found ways to let Pierce know if he was missing anything, sometimes by passing him notes.
Pierce said “everybody” wanted her on their committee or board because it was easy to work with her. She remembered birthdays, had “fabulous” handwriting, and enjoyed the work. Pierce said she was also knowledgeable about the town itself.
“She knows more than most of the town forgot,” Pierce said.
After meetings, Pierce and Lilly would have fun socializing tell stories, and enjoy drinks, Pierce said. It is the friendship and honesty Pierce said he remembers from her.
“She was my friend, just plain and simple,” Pierce said. “If I was getting (expletive), she’d say, ‘Now Jeffrey, that ain’t nice.’ She’d have that calming voice and it’d be like, ‘Yeah, yeah, you’re right.’”
Former Dresden resident Joe Wiley, who worked with Lilly on several committees, said she was “very careful” to get notes right, even when members spoke over each other. At one point he had to fill in for her and said it was “extremely difficult” work. Wiley said committees seldom had to change minutes she created.
“She’s impossible to replace,” Wiley said. “I don’t think there’ll ever be anyone else like her that is 1as dedicated to the town for as long a period and is active in so many different organizations within the town.”
Dresden Planning Board member Steve Stone said Lilly was “community oriented.”
“She’s the type of person that every town would need to have,” Stone said. “A small town has a character of their own. They develop it through the families that are there. And she knew everybody, all the families. She was the person that would, if you needed something, she’d be there.”
During an instance when Stone had to fill in as chair of the planning board, Lilly sat at his left side and slid him papers with instructions, he said. As a joke, Stone called her “mother.” Stone added Lilly kept the meeting flowing correctly.
Stone said it will be impossible to replace Lilly’s place in the community.
“We’re going to have to try to figure out how we are going to deal with not having her around, as a secretary but not only that, but not having her around as the person that was with such a big heart,” Stone said.
Rick Graffam worked with Lilly on several committees and said her involvement impacted the town, as it is hard to get people involved.
“She’s very knowledgeable and she was just willing to help out wherever she could,” Graffam said. “That’s her giving nature, I believe.”
Dresden Select Board Chair Lisa Hewitt said she first met Lilly while working at the town office.
“When she first walked through the door, all I saw was this wonderful woman with the happiest attitude and I just knew from that moment we were going to become fast friends,” Hewitt said.
The two bonded through their work with multiple committees and getting lunch together, Hewitt said. One topic the two discussed was family, which Hewitt said Lilly cared about.
Lilly also shared memories of growing up in Dresden on Hatchs Corner and of activities she participated in such as bingo at Jewett Station. Hewitt said shortly before Lilly’s health began to decline, the two got lunch together.
“It was just nice to see her enjoy the fresh air, the ocean, just a great spot to eat,” Hewitt said. “And I think that is probably one of my favorite memories with Shari, was just seeing the pleasure in her enjoying herself, knowing unfortunately what was coming.”
Hewitt said Lilly worked right “to the end.” Rogers said even as her health deteriorated, she did not complain.
“She was going through a really tough time herself, she would just always say, ‘Other people have it worse,’” Rogers said. “I think she really lived that way. She was very kind and generous and truly cared about everybody.”

title: Duo accused of choking and assaulting man in Bangor parking lot
text:
A duo allegedly choked and assaulted a man Wednesday morning when he informed them that they couldn’t camp in a Bangor parking lot.
Ethan Cilley, 26, was charged with aggravated assault and Shelley Melanson, 36, was charged with aggravated assault and violating her conditions of release, according to Katy England, a spokesperson for the Bangor Police Department.
Cilley and Melanson were living in a car at a parking lot off Union Street, England said Wednesday morning.
Police found Cilley and Melanson about 3:01 p.m. and arrested them.
Cilley and Melanson were taken to the Penobscot County Jail, where they remained Wednesday morning, according to the jail’s website.

title: 🍁🐶 STELLA IS BACK! Maine’s Favorite Leaf-Jumping Dog Is Showing Off Her Epic Fall Moves!
text:
Maine Social Media Star Stella the Dog Shows Off Epic Leaf Jumps
Maine’s coolest dog is already having a great fall!
Stella is a spirited English yellow Lab who lives with her family in Freeport, Maine. She’s a legit star, too. In fact, she’s so famous that she has her own YouTube channel, with more than 151,000 subscribers.
Like her fellow Maine canine Tatum, Stella proves that you don’t have to be human to become a social media superstar!
Stella also has an impressive following on Facebook, where she has more than 1 million followers.
She’s on TikTok, too, where she has more than 837,000 followers. Combined, her videos have racked up a staggering 53 million views. Incredible!
And if you just can’t get enough of Stella the Dog, you can also follow her on Instagram.
Stella Loves Her Leaves
Stella absolutely loves being outside, especially when there are humongous piles of leaves covering the ground.
Watching her run like she was shot out of a cannon before launching herself through the air and into an awe-inspiring mountain of leaves is endlessly entertaining.
Best of all, there are no sound effects or music in the video clips. You can actually hear Stella smash through the leaves with the greatest of ease!
With that in mind, her owners put together a compilation of some of her coolest leaf jumps every fall.
Stella’s leaf-jumping tradition goes all the way back to when she was a puppy. Her owner, Jody Hartman, first noticed that she would launch herself into freshly raked piles of leaves completely on her own.
And Jody doesn’t simply rake the leaves and call it a day. He dries them with a hair dryer, covers them to keep them dry, “fluffs” them up, and does whatever else is necessary to create the perfect pile for Stella’s epic dives.
She’s been jumping into leaves every autumn for more than 10 years now. Even as an older dog, her enthusiasm hasn’t dimmed much at all.
Stella Even Made the CBS Evening News
Steve Hartman’s “On the Road” series is a much-loved part of the CBS Evening News. In the popular series, Hartman travels across America, sharing inspiring stories and profiles of interesting people and places.
A few years ago, he made a stop in Maine to meet Stella and learn more about the dog who has turned leaf jumping into an annual tradition.
And honestly, once you see Stella launch herself into those leaves, it’s pretty easy to understand why she became a star.

title: Groundbreaking held for Augusta supportive housing complex
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - “More than an apartment”- that’s how one developer described the vision for Riverland apartments.
It’s one of seven permanent supporting housing communities to be built as part of Gov. Janet Mills’ “Home for Good” initiative.
Ground broke Thursday afternoon on the first project: a complex in Augusta designed for 25 residents who are experiencing chronic homelessness.
The project is funded through the State of Maine and investors, alongside 30% of each resident’s monthly income once the building is complete.
Riverland will employ 13 full-time staff with 24/7 access to support and services for its residents.
During the event, Mills read a statement from a formerly unhoused individual who is now receiving services in a complex like Riverland.
“I think I’m a better person now to be honest. I have value now. I’m a human being again because I finally found a stable place to be,” she read.
Residents for Riverland will be selected through an assessment process through local service providers.
The apartment complex is expected to be completed in October of next year.

title: Cony and Lawrence square off in battle of unbeatens in high school football
text:
Class B North supremacy will be at stake Friday when a pair of 4-0 teams, Cony High of Augusta and Lawrence High of Fairfield, will square off in Fairfield at 7 p.m.
Two other 4-0 teams will be tested by 3-1 clubs as Hermon will travel to Rockland to face Oceanside/North Haven at 7 p.m. Friday, and Stearns/Schenck/Katahdin will entertain Washington Academy of East Machias.
Other Friday matchups include 3-1 Foxcroft Academy of Dover-Foxcroft entertaining 2-2 John Bapst of Bangor at 7 p.m. and 1-3 Orono awaiting 3-1 Spruce Mountain from Jay for a 6 p.m. kickoff.
In Fairfield, Lawrence will be looking to avenge a 46-14 loss to Cony a year ago, and the Bulldogs come into the contest with all four of its wins being by at least 13 points.
Lawrence topped Gorham 48-0, Fryeburg Academy 27-14, Skowhegan 29-13 and Mt. Blue of Farmington 49-6.
Cony, the reigning Class B North champ, has also beaten Fryeburg Academy (25-21), Skowhegan (42-35) and Mt. Blue (14-0) but only by a combined 25 points.

The Hawks own wins over Foxcroft Academy (24-0), Nokomis of Newport (28-6), Hampden Academy (56-0) and Medomak Valley of Waldoboro (51-6).

title: Gorham middle schoolers are leading an Anne Frank history exhibit
text:
GORHAM — Yanamarie DiVico, 13, stood confidently in front of a group of sixth graders seated in her middle school’s auditorium.
“Does anyone know what a dictator is?” she asked the group. The students weren’t sure. They leaned in closer to listen.
She and her fellow docent, Nora Emlet, were leading their younger classmates through an exhibit about Anne Frank and the history that framed the young Jewish diarist’s life.
They are among 20 eighth graders at Gorham Middle School who trained last week to become guides for “Anne Frank: A History for Today,” a museum exhibit now on view in the school’s auditorium. By the end of two full days with staff from the Anne Frank Center, they could recount Frank’s childhood, her years hiding from the Nazis in the “Secret Annex” in Amsterdam, the Holocaust and her death in a concentration camp.
“It’s definitely very heavy,” DiVico said.
All of the school’s 684 students will tour the exhibit. For many, it will be their first time learning about Hitler and the Nazi genocide of Jewish people and other groups from 1933 to 1945. It comes as antisemitism surges and as scholars push for more Holocaust education in the U.S.
Heather Whitaker, the Gorham Middle School alternative education teacher who organized the program, said learning about the past through Frank — a teenager who shared her observations and experiences of everyday life while in hiding — allows the students to connect with the history.
“The kids really become the leaders and take ownership in creating a more just world,” Whitaker said.
DiVico and Emlet shared stories in their presentation like expert historians. They encouraged their audience to come closer to the panels and ask questions.
The Anne Frank House in Amsterdam produced the exhibit panels. Staff there create them to send to schools around the world, allowing students to spread Frank’s story.
This set first made its way to Maine for a stay at Stearns Junior-Senior High School in Millinocket, and will go to Middle School of the Kennebunks next, Whitaker said.
The exhibit will be open to the public for tours and viewings on Friday, Oct. 2, from 5:30 to 7:30 p.m., Tuesday, Oct. 6, from 2:45 to 4 p.m. and Wednesday, Oct. 7, from 5:30 to 6:30 p.m.
“Everyone needs to know about (the Holocaust) so that it doesn’t happen again,” said student docent Jacob Philbrick.

title: One woman dead, two injured in Penobscot County crash
text:
A 68-year-old Dixmont woman was killed in a Plymouth crash on Wednesday evening that injured two men and left two vehicles in a pond.
She was identified Friday as Patricia Thompson, according to the Penobscot County Sheriff’s Office.
Thompson was a passenger in a small sedan driving eastbound on Moosehead Trail when the car was hit by a westbound pickup truck shortly after 6:30 p.m. on Wednesday. The crash caused both cars to leave the road and enter Plymouth Pond.
Patricia Thompson was taken to a hospital and died there from her injuries.
The driver of the sedan, Kendall Thompson, 67, also of Dixmont, was taken to a hospital with serious but non-life-threatening injuries, according to the sheriff’s office.
The 69-year-old man driving the pickup, identified Friday as Timothy Malo, of Newport, was also treated for injuries that weren’t believed to be life threatening.
It’s unclear what caused the crash, which spurred a significant emergency response Wednesday evening. The sheriff’s office says the investigation is ongoing.
Editor’s note: This story was updated on Oct. 1 to correct the date that the crash happened and on Oct. 2 to add the identities of the people involved.

title: Wiscasset Boys Force a Pair of Ties
text:
The Wiscasset boys soccer team tied Vinalhaven 1-1 on Monday, Sept. 28 in Vinalhaven. The Wolverines took a ferry over to the island despite the harsh weather and waves caused by a nor’easter that shut down all the other local high school sports events on Monday. The teams battled to a 1-1 tie in the inclement weather.
Vinalhaven striker Aidan Farnham sliced through a pair of Wiscasset defenders and struck a low shot into the right corner of the net to stake the Vikings to an early 1-0 lead.

title: Depression in older adults doesn’t always look like sadness
text:
(Aging Untold) — Depression in older adults doesn’t always show up as tears or sadness. Sometimes it looks like irritability, withdrawal or suddenly sleeping all day.
The Aging Untold experts are breaking down the signs, why this generation is especially at risk and what to do about it.
The signs are often mistaken for something else
“I think some of the most common signs you do see with people, really are withdrawal — they just lack interest in anything. A lot of times they’ll just sleep. I have people tell me, ‘I’ve just slept for 36 hours,’ or they will turn to substance abuse, or they just kind of look disheveled,” Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
She added that depression in older adults can also mask itself as declining memory.
“A lot of times in the older person, it may show up as kind of memory starting to go, as well. It may not come about the way that you think it is,” Rogers said.
It’s not “normal aging” — and it’s not rare
The experts pointed to a sobering statistic on suicide rates and older adults.
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the highest rate of suicide in 2024 was among adults 80 and older.
“We have an epidemic going on of depression, and it’s not normal aging,” Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, said. “That’s the problem — so many people think, ‘Well, you should be sad, you’re old,’ or ‘You should expect to lose your spouse or leave your home.’”
She noted that the compounding nature of loss in later life makes it harder to cope.
“There’s a lot of loss, and there’s not a lot of friendship that still exists once you start losing so many. So you lose your partner that you’re bouncing things off of, you lose that comfort, and then you’ve got to deal with all these other things,” Cradduck said.
Hormones, nutrition and lost purpose play a role too
Depression isn’t only tied to grief. Physical and chemical factors matter just as much.
“It’s not the most common reasons that people think either — hormonal shifts are a big thing, or vitamins, nutrient deficiencies and all that. That can affect mood and things like that as well. And then that loss of purpose — that’s a big deal,” Rogers said.
Treatment works — and it’s more accessible than people realize
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke shared a client’s story of how getting help changed his outcome entirely.
“I had a client that was so depressed, one of those that couldn’t get out of bed, and he went to the hospital for treatment for depression, and the outcome was miraculous. He got his life back. He lived independently. The family was blown away. And it really taught me a lesson about really being proactive about getting this depression under control.”
Cost doesn’t have to be a barrier, either. O’Rourke said people who have Medicare or a Medicare Advantage plan can have an annual wellness visit with a screening for depression.
“A lot of people will say, ‘I can’t afford it.’ Well, if you’ve got Medicare or a Medicare Advantage plan, you’ve got an annual wellness visit. They do a depression screening and you can get mental health help. There’s not a visit limit — I’m going to be a mythbuster here. There’s not a visit limit.”
The real cost is not getting help
Rogers pushed back on the idea that mental health treatment is optional or too expensive to pursue.
“I don’t think people realize the worst outcome they can come up with. They think, ‘I can’t afford to get help.’ You can’t afford not to,” Rogers said.
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose added a pointed comparison: “Can you afford dementia? And do you want some of these other things to happen to you? If you can, turn it around.”
It’s time to retire the stigma
The experts said depression deserves the same treatment as any other medical condition.
“Don’t be ashamed. That’s no different than your heart getting help, you know? You go to the heart doctor. That’s no different than your knees, so your brain is just as important, if not more, because it’s controlling everything else,” Rogers said.
Cradduck also called out the “bootstraps” mindset that keeps people from seeking treatment.
“We have this mindset about mental health that the person that’s suffering can just pull their bootstraps up, that they can just get over it, that if you would just choose to be happy, if you would choose to get out of bed, if you choose to do it different... We have to realize that there becomes a chemical imbalance. Depression isn’t just, ‘I’m going to change my mood’ — it’s the chemicals in my brain have changed. And maybe I need an antidepressant. Maybe I need some help to get through this. But if I don’t get through this, the outcome is not OK.”
That same stigma, the experts said, often applies to medication.
“This is a temporary thing that you’re doing to get yourself up and going, and then you might have the energy to go walking or do something that makes your energy level get higher,” O’Rourke said.
“You notice people don’t have a stigma around taking high blood pressure meds,” Rogers added.
Where to start
“I would start with your medical doctor. I think therapy’s a great answer, but also getting out and being social and finding purpose and fun again — it’s really important. And remember, you’re showing other people how to live as well and how to cope,” Ambrose said.
She closed with encouragement for anyone weighing whether to seek help: “Here’s your opportunity to make the rest of the years that you have left your best years. ... They’re the only years you have left.”
Resources
- The Friendship Line: 1-800-971-0016
  - The Friendship Line provides crisis support for people who are 60 and up.
- National Institute on Aging: Depression and Older Adults
- National Suicide and Crisis Lifeline
  - If you are facing mental health struggles or emotional distress, dial 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline anytime.
Key takeaways
- Depression doesn’t always look like sadness. In older adults, it can show up as irritability, withdrawal, sudden changes in sleep or a decline in hygiene.
- Depression is treatable. Getting help can protect memory and cognitive function.
- Help is covered and accessible. Start with your doctor. Medicare and Medicare Advantage plans include an annual wellness visit with a depression screening, and there’s no visit limit on mental health care.
- Treatment is not something to be ashamed of. Seeking help for depression should be treated the same as seeking care for the heart, knees or blood pressure.
- Contributing factors go beyond grief. Hormonal shifts, nutrient deficiencies and loss of purpose can all affect mood.
