title: AARP keeps Maine members informed
text:
As someone who has spent years working in civic engagement, I have seen firsthand what happens when people understand the power of their voice and use it.
In Maine, voters 50 and older are a powerful part of that voice. In the 2024 general election, they made up more than 59% of all voters in our state. That matters, not simply because of the size of this voting bloc, but because older Mainers consistently show up and participate in our democracy.
The issues important to older voters are also issues that touch entire families and communities. Social Security, affordable healthcare, support for family caregivers, housing and the ability to age with dignity and independence affect all of us, directly or through someone we love.
That is why staying informed matters. AARP provides information to help voters understand the issues and make their own decisions at the ballot box.
Democracy works best when people participate. When voters stay informed, ask questions, speak up, and ultimately vote, elected leaders and candidates listen.
Maine’s 50-plus voters have tremendous power. Let’s continue to use that power to strengthen our communities and help build a future where people of every generation can thrive.
Pious Ali
AARP Maine Volunteer
Portland

title: Rapper Rick Ross arrested in Florida on domestic violence charges
text:
Rapper Rick Ross arrested in Miami Beach on domestic violence charges
Rapper Rick Ross was arrested by Miami Beach police early Thursday on domestic violence charges, including felony battery by strangulation, according to Miami-Dade jail and court records.
Ross, whose legal name is William Leonard Roberts, was booked into the Turner Guilford Knight Correctional Center at 6:10 a.m. this Thursday.
The 50-year-old rapper faces one felony count of battery by strangulation and one misdemeanor count of battery stemming from a late-August altercation at his residence in the Star Island community of Miami. Both charges are listed as involving domestic violence.
The arrest affidavit says Ross and the alleged victim had been in a relationship for about a year and were living together at the time of the alleged incident.
The woman told investigators that on Aug. 28 she was awakened around 7:44 a.m. by Ross, who she said was angry because she had been tagged in a photo on Instagram. Police said Ross questioned her about whether she was lying to him and allegedly slapped her in the face.
Later that morning, according to the affidavit, Ross accused the woman of being involved with another person and continued questioning her while she was in a bathroom. The woman told police Ross struck her in the chest several times and restricted her breathing by grabbing and twisting the collar of the hoodie she was wearing.
The affidavit alleges Ross then grabbed the woman by her ponytail and slammed her against a wall before striking her in the face, causing a busted lip. The report states he then pushed her to the floor, turned on the shower and attempted to spray her with the shower head. The woman was eventually able to leave the bathroom and later gathered her belongings and left the residence after Ross left, according to the affidavit.
Police said the woman later provided detectives with a sworn statement and timestamped photographs of her injuries. Investigators also reviewed surveillance video from the residence that they said showed a friend arriving to pick her up and being turned away. According to the affidavit, Ross later posted a photo on his Instagram account showing the friend arriving at the property.
This arrest comes days after Ross' former girlfriend, Jazzma Kendrick, publicly accused him of physically abusing her. According to People.com, Kendrick alleged on social media that Ross injured her lip during an incident she said happened about a month earlier. Ross had not publicly responded to those allegations as of earlier this week.
Bond was listed at $5,000 on the battery by strangulation charge and $1,000 on the battery charge, for a total of $6,000. Jail records note that posted bond information may not reflect the current amount.
Ross has retained private attorney Bradley Horenstein, according to court information. His arraignment is scheduled for Oct. 22. Horenstein said Ross denies the accusations.
"All I can say is that the allegations are false. He's innocent. Everything is going to come out," Horenstein said. "We just ask that you allow the process to play out before rushing to judgment, because the truth will come in."
It was not immediately clear whether those allegations are connected to the ones mentioned in Thursday's arrest report.
Ross has had a long history of legal troubles, dating as far back as 2008 when he was arrested on charges related to the possession of guns and drugs.
Prior to his arrest Thursday, his most recent arrest came in 2015 when he and his bodyguard were arrested on kidnapping and battery charges. The two were accused of holding Ross' groundskeeper in a building on the rapper's 322-acre property in Fayette County, Georgia, and pistol-whipping him. That incident was allegedly related to money the groundskeeper owed to Ross.
The rapper struck a plea deal in that case, receiving a $10,000 fine and being sentenced to time served in jail after having already been in jail for a week. His conviction was erased after the payment of the fine.
Ross, a Miami-area native known for songs including "Hustlin'," "Blowin' Money Fast," and "The Devil Is a Lie," has been a prominent figure in hip-hop for two decades and is the founder of Maybach Music Group, among other business ventures.
Parts of this reporting come from WFOR in Miami, Florida, via CNN Newsource.

title: Most Americans blame Trump for high prices as midterms approach, a new AP-NORC poll finds
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Americans are deeply frustrated with President Donald Trump’s handling of the economy and rising prices, with most panning his performance and blaming his policies as higher costs threaten his party’s chances in November.
A new poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research finds that only 17% of U.S. adults approve of the Republican president’s handling of the cost of living. Just 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall, marking a new low.
A majority, 65%, of U.S. adults now blame Trump’s policies for persistently high costs more than factors outside of his control, signaling growing weariness over his aggressive use of tariffs and continued unhappiness with the war with Iran.
The dismal numbers come just weeks before midterm elections that will determine whether Republicans maintain control of Congress and while Trump is hitting the campaign trail with an aggressive schedule of rallies. But Trump — who has asked voters to pretend that he is on the ballot as he tries to bolster turnout — remains deeply unpopular, with even many Republicans faulting him for failing to deliver on promised relief.
“I was hoping it would be better or different, but it’s not really good,” said Robert Gault, 66, a retired factory worker from Bradford, Pennsylvania, who describes himself as a Republican.
“Our president, I thought, was going to help the country, and so far he has not really seemed to have done that with the economy or in general. He’s not really done what I was hoping he would,” said Gault. “He said, ‘Make America Great Again.’ And I have not seen him do that.”
Costs drag on Trump as the economic pain keeps coming
Over the last few months, Americans have grown more worried about being able to afford basics like groceries and gas. About half of U.S. adults now say they are “extremely” or “very” concerned about being able to fill their tanks, up from 39% in July. About half are also highly concerned about being able to afford food.
Prices are “extremely exorbitant. Just the cost of everything is going up as a result of fuel,” said Pedro Sanchez, 52, of Perris, California, who voted for Trump and works in law enforcement. “I used to have a lot more disposable income. I don’t have that any more. It’s gotten eaten up because of all these increases in the cost of everything.”
Trump’s current approval on the economy is a 14 percentage point drop from March 2025, just after he took office for the second time. His struggles on the issue mark a significant departure from his first term, when the economy was often a point of strength.
Trump spent much of the 2024 campaign hammering President Joe Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris, Democrats, on inflation and promising to lower prices. Now, there’s widespread disappointment with his performance. About 7 in 10 Americans say Trump’s handling of the cost of living has been “worse than expected.” That includes roughly half of Republicans, who are also broadly concerned about being able to afford groceries and gas.
“Groceries are just like kind of out of control. It seems like everything is going up,” said Bethany Lnenicka, 41, who operates a small farm in Fairfax, Iowa. “It’s just one thing and the next week it’s another thing. It’s just insane. And of course your income doesn’t go up.”
A political independent who typically votes Republican and has voted for Trump three times, Lnenicka said she had hoped his second term would be more like his first.
“I just do not feel like it has gotten a lot better,” she said.
About 6 in 10 Republicans disapprove of Trump’s handling of the cost of living, according to the new poll, up from about half in April.
“It definitely doesn’t feel like we have trended in the right direction,” agreed Kristen Slaven, 41, a mental health therapist who lives in Gluckstadt, Mississippi, and typically votes Republican. She said Trump is focused on the wrong things.
“Obviously wars don’t help. When they’re necessary, I understand. But our focus on renaming bodies of water and pieces of land, that’s just stupid to me when people can’t feed their family,” she said.
“I had hoped that it would be better,” Slaven added.
Some Republicans are still willing to cut Trump some slack
Despite their frustration, most Republicans, 67%, say factors outside of Trump’s control are more to blame for high prices.
“I think inflation is a very difficult thing to tackle,” said Fred Naumann, 51, a Republican and longtime Trump supporter who lives in Green Bay, Wisconsin.
Though he would like to see interest rates come down, Naumann, who works in the automotive industry, supports tariffs and the war with Iran, believing it was necessary.
Overall, however, most Americans, 69%, continue to say the war has not been worth fighting, up slightly from 64% in July. Only 28% approve of how Trump is handling Iran.
Americans are also unhappy with Trump’s trade wars. Only about 3 in 10 U.S. adults approve of how he is handling trade negotiations with other countries, down from about 4 in 10 in March. And 64% say he has “gone too far” on imposing new tariffs on other countries, up from 58% in January.
Overall, the picture is not better. Only about 3 in 10 Americans approve of how Trump is handling his job as president. And about 6 in 10 say the country as a whole is “much” or “somewhat” worse off than when he began his second term.
The issue on which Trump maintains relative strength is border security, with about half of Americans saying they approve of his performance.
Trump faces more blame than Biden did
Trump’s low grade on the economy rivals Biden’s 28% approval rating in June 2022, when there was record-high inflation during the COVID-19 pandemic.
But Americans were less likely to blame Biden in the lead-up to that year’s midterm elections, a sharp contrast with the solid majority who hold Trump responsible now. In October 2022, 44% of Americans said Biden’s policies were responsible for high prices, while 55% blamed factors outside of his control.
Sanchez, a Republican who voted for Trump, blames him, at least in part.
“I think he has a lot to do with it. This war in Iran, the tariffs that he’s placing on other countries, obviously are affecting us. Those two things are things he’s been directly involved in that directly affect the economy,” he said. “I think with Biden, a lot of the stuff was outside of his control. It was all the COVID and how that affected everything else. I don’t think that there was much that he could have done.”
He had high hopes for Trump’s return. Now, things seem worse than under Biden.
___
Colvin reported from New York.
___
The AP-NORC poll of 2,140 adults was conducted Sept. 24-28 using a sample drawn from NORC’s probability-based AmeriSpeak Panel, which is designed to be representative of the U.S. population. The margin of sampling error for adults overall is plus or minus 2.9 percentage points.

title: ‘America’s Most Wanted’ rerun leads to tip, arrest in hit-and-run after 29 years
text:
DES MOINES, Iowa (KCRG/Gray News) - Thanks to a rerun of “America’s Most Wanted,” police in Iowa have made an arrest in a deadly hit-and-run cold case from nearly 30 years ago.
The Des Moines Police Department announced a breakthrough Tuesday related to the case of 64-year-old Leslie Ruby, who was killed in a hit-and-run outside his Des Moines home on Sept. 29, 1997.
Ruby was a retiree, a grandfather and a veteran of the Korean War. Police say he was described by everyone who knew him as a very loving and caring family man.
Investigators were able to identify the suspect as then-28-year-old Gerardo Garcia-Michel, but police say he fled the state before he could be arrested.
Despite attempts to find Garcia-Michel, the case ran dry as investigators exhausted their leads.
The popular TV show “America’s Most Wanted” aired an episode on the Ruby case in 1998. Almost 29 years later, police say a rerun of that episode led someone to send a Crime Stoppers tip to investigators, saying Garcia-Michel was his neighbor.
That tip helped detectives find Garcia-Michel in New Jersey. He was arrested by U.S. Marshals, and Des Moines Police are working to extradite him to Iowa.
“It doesn’t matter if it’s 29 minutes or 29 days or 29 years after a crime. Getting answers for the family is one of the most important things that we can do,” Police Sgt. Paul Parizek said.

title: Animal Carving Class at The Carpenter’s Boat Shop Oct. 18
text:
The Carpenter’s Boat Shop will host an animal wood-carving class let by artist Eva Sturm-Gross from 2-5 p.m. on Sunday, Oct. 18.
The class will review basic knife safety as well as instruction on wood grain, surface design, using the band saw, sanding, and finishing.
Students will leave the workshop with a small carved animal and the confidence to carve at home using a few affordable tools.
The cost is $175, and registration is available online.

title: Aroostook County Toys for Tots Applications Open
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AROOSTOOK COUNTY, Maine (WAGM) - Applications have opened for Aroostook County’s Toy for Tots. Families in need of assistance affording presents for their children this holiday season can now apply. Aroostook County has seen costs rising. Everything from groceries to heating oil are becoming more difficult for families to afford. This holiday season Aroostook County Toys for Tots is expecting to distribute more toys to local kids than they did last year.
Kassandra Boyington-Ward, the Coordinator for Aroostook County Toys for Tots says: “I think that a lot of people are going to have more financial strain with oil, and gas prices rising, food prices. I’m hoping that we are able to reach more children this year. We served 1,544 children last year. I am expecting us to surpass that. I’m thinking around maybe 1,700 children.”
They are currently approving drop-off locations for donation boxes and hope to have them up next week. Drop-off boxes will include a QR code for locals to make monetary donations as well. Kassandra says their biggest challenge this year has been getting volunteers. “For the toy sorting we are always looking for volunteers. Those that are willing to travel, it is rewarding. We need them to be able to help distribute boxes, monetary donation cans that we have. “
Kassandra says sometimes it can be hard for families to ask for help. “I think it’s okay to accept community help and Toys for Tots help. During our presence at the Acadian festival, I had a gentleman come up and donate a decent donation and say that he was proud to give back because he had applied for his son several years back when he was having a hard time with finances.”
Families are eligible to receive toys based on income or if they receive medical or financial assistance. The deadline to apply is November 25th. You can apply through the Toys for Tots app or by visiting aroostook-me.toysfortots.org.

title: How to get or give help in Maine for housing, heating, food and more
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Across Maine, hundreds of nonprofits, churches and community groups offer help with food, household items and fuel assistance. Many of these programs cater to the most pressing needs in their communities and are often in need of support from those who can afford to donate.
If you are in need of help — or are in the position to offer support — below are some of the resources available.
Please send additional resource suggestions to [email protected].
HOW TO FIND HELP
Call 211 or go to 211Maine.org to connect with assistance programs near you. The service can also help with basic needs, such as directing people to shelter and transportation.
General Assistance is offered through town and city halls to help with rent, utilities and other expenses for people who qualify. Check with the town where you live for more information about how to apply.
The “Be There for Me” website helps parents and caregivers find a variety of support options, from housing and transportation to childcare and getting everyday items. Visit bethereforme.org to search for support.
FOOD ASSISTANCE
There are hundreds of food pantries and meal programs across the state. The Maine Food Access Map is an interactive tool to help people find resources near them.
To apply for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, visit a local Maine Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) Office for Family Independence, call 855-797-4357 or go to mymaineconnection.gov.
The federal Commodity Supplemental Food Program provides food boxes to low-income people 60 and older. For information about how to apply, visit the website for the Maine Department of Agriculture, Conservation & Forestry, which links to the local agencies that distribute the boxes.
HOUSING AND HEATING ASSISTANCE
The Home Energy Assistance Program (HEAP) helps qualified homeowners and renters pay for heating costs. Households are encouraged to apply for HEAP as soon as possible. Applications are handled by local Community Action Agencies. To apply online or to find information about how to apply by phone or in person, go to mainehousing.org.
Nearly two dozen wood banks operate across the state to provide households with firewood, including those in Cumberland, Freeport, Bethel, Kennebec County, Buxton, Waldo County and the Midcoast. For more information, visit the Maine Wood Banks website: woodbanks.org.
There are shelters in 11 counties for people experiencing homelessness. A list with contact information is available through MaineHousing. If you are currently homeless and need emergency shelter in Portland, call the 24/7 phone line at 207-761-2072. Veterans who are homeless or at risk can get immediate assistance by calling 800-377-5709 to connect with local programs.
The Maine Eviction Prevention Program helps cover past due rent and assistance for as long as a year to people who meet certain requirements. For more information, contact MaineHousing.
Pine Tree Legal Assistance provides free civil legal help to qualifying low-income Mainers with a variety of issues, including evictions and guidance on family matters. For more information, call 207-942-8322 or visit ptla.org.
HEALTHCARE ASSISTANCE
The Maine Medical Association maintains a list of clinics that offer free medical and dental care to people without insurance. To view the list and find contact information, visit mainephysicians.org.
The Maine Mobile Health Program’s mobile health clinics provide medical and behavioral health care on a sliding scale to farmworkers and others across the state. For more information, call 207-622-9252 or visit mainemobile.org.
HELP WITH HOUSEHOLD ITEMS
Several diaper banks operate in Maine. The Trinity Jubilee Center in Lewiston operates a diaper bank out of its food pantry and provides a 50-pack of diapers once a month. For more information, visit the website or call 207-782-5700.
In southern Maine, the Michael Klahr Jewish Family Services Diaper Bank in Portland does bi-monthly distributions. An essentials pantry also distributes household items that are not accessible with SNAP benefits. To sign up, call 207-772-1959.
For people with a case manager, help with furniture is available through Furniture Friends in Westbrook. Case managers can also request clothing and household items through Maine Needs in Portland.
HOW TO HELP
Maine Needs: The Portland nonprofit provides gently used clothing, boots, household items, diapers and other needed items to people across Maine and is accessed through case managers and social workers. Maine Needs accepts monetary donations and has detailed guidelines on its website for donating clothing and other requested items. It is also raising money to provide diapers through local food pantries to 8,500 babies. For more information, go to maineneeds.org
Keep ME Warm: The program, a partnership between United Way and community action agencies, is the only statewide fuel assistance fundraising effort in Maine. Donations support fuel assistance distributed across the state. To donate, visit uwsme.org/keep-me-warm.
Good Shepherd Food Bank: The Auburn-based nonprofit distributes food to more than 600 partner programs across the state. Good Shepherd accepts monetary donations to support its efforts. For more information, go to gsfb.org
Check with your local food pantry: Many local food pantries except donations of shelf-stable items, as well as money that can be used to buy food in bulk. Pantries also report a need for volunteers to help distribute and deliver food.
Furniture Friends: The Westbrook organization collects gently used furniture to give to community members who can’t afford to buy their own and who are referred through an agency or case manager. Information about how to donate furniture or money is posted on the Furniture Friends website. For more information, go to furniturefriends.org.

title: Ex-fraternity leader at Arizona university sentenced after pledge died of alcohol poisoning
text:
Ex-fraternity leader at Arizona university gets jail time after pledge died of alcohol poisoning
A former Northern Arizona University fraternity leader was sentenced to two months in jail Wednesday for his role in a hazing ritual that led to the death of a pledge.
Carter Eslick, 20, also received three years of supervised probation during a sentencing hearing in Coconino County Superior Court. Eslick had pleaded guilty to a felony hazing charge in the Jan. 31 death of Colin Daniel Martinez, 18, at an off-campus house.
An autopsy found Martinez died of alcohol poisoning with a blood-alcohol content of 0.425% — more than five times the state's legal limit for drivers 21 and over.
Martinez was among four Delta Tau Delta pledges who shared two bottles of vodka to ensure they vomited, according to court documents. Witnesses reported adjusting Martinez’s sleeping position and checking his pulse and breathing to look for signs of alcohol poisoning throughout the night, the documents said.
Martinez's parents appeared remotely in court, still grieving their son, and said they want accountability and reform within Greek life, Phoenix television station azfamily.com reported.
Eslick was the fraternity’s pledge master at the time and was responsible for welcoming new members. He apologized Wednesday to Martinez's family and said he takes “full responsibility for the hand I played in that ritual.”
Coconino County Attorney Ammon Barker said no sentence can undo the harm to the Martinez family.
“My hope is that this case helps people understand the serious dangers of hazing and encourages them to speak up and intervene before another family experiences this kind of loss,” Barker said in a statement.
Judge Stacy Krueger said Eslick knew what he did was dangerous and was troubled that no one spoke out against it.
Eslick could face additional jail time if he doesn't meet the conditions of probation, which include creating and delivering 305 anti-hazing presentations and keeping the court updated on his progress. He also can't use alcohol or drugs unless prescribed.
The university suspended the fraternity after Martinez’s death, and the national organization later closed the NAU chapter.

title: He travels the country foraging his food and medicine, here’s why
text:
HENDERSONVILLE, N.C. (InvestigateTV) — Robin Greenfield doesn’t buy his food. He finds it.
Greenfield is traveling the country foraging 100 percent of his food and medicine.
Greenfield said his lifestyle starts with his clothes, which are 100% compostable.
“This outfit is 100% homemade, natural fiber and natural dye,” Greenfield said. “I could just walk into those woods, die like a deer and there would be no littering.”
Fifteen years ago he changed the way he was living to minimize his impact on the earth and others. That starts with the food he eats.
During a 30-minute walk along a Hendersonville greenway, he found nearly a dozen edible plants.
“This right here is dock, this is a common edible,” Greenfield said.
Teaching others
Greenfield said he has spent the last decade learning and educating others about the grocery store that is in backyards.
“I think it is kind of revolutionary for people who think that food has to come from a grocery store, it has to cost money, but no food is growing all around us,” Greenfield said.
He doesn’t just eat plants.
He also forages meat anywhere he can find it, including roadkill. He fishes for his own food and forages starches like yams.
Health checkups
Greenfield checked with a doctor about whether this lifestyle is healthy. The doctor said he has no health concerns.
Greenfield doesn’t use a toothbrush or toothpaste because he only wants to use natural items. According to a dentist, he has some teeth staining, but no tooth decay.
His mission is to live in harmony with the earth and treat nature as a food pantry and pharmacy.
“A big part of that is through living simply. Just realizing what do I actually really need,” Greenfield said.
Greenfield’s lifestyle goes far beyond food and nutrition. He has sold almost all of his possessions and now lives below the federal poverty line on purpose.

title: Dual UK-Iranian national arrested over security incident at US-run air base in England
text:
Dual UK-Iranian national arrested over security incident at US-run air base in England
Police on Thursday arrested a dual U.K.-Iranian national on suspicion of plotting a terror attack following a security incident at a U.S.-run military air base in England that British authorities have linked to Tehran.
The 27-year-old man was arrested in London on Thursday, and police have searched two properties in the U.K. capital, Counter Terrorism Policing said in a statement.
A 26-year-old British national was interviewed by police “under caution,” which means the interview was recorded and can be used in future prosecutions.
On Sunday, five men, all British nationals in their 20s and from London, were arrested on suspicion of explosives and terror offenses close to the RAF Fairford air base, which has been used by American bombers to strike Iran. The suspects have since been released on bail.
Police say they found a quantity of an accelerant – gasoline – in three vans linked to the five suspects, but no explosives.
Vicki Evans, the senior national coordinator for counter terrorism policing, said the investigation “is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of inquiry.
“As we’ve made clear, we’re looking at all possible angles — including possible foreign state involvement,” she said.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the U.K. sees “strong indications” that Iran played a part in the incident. Iran denies involvement.
The base 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of London has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East, including this year’s war with Iran.
Top U.S. officials have criticized the decision to grant five suspects bail, with President Donald Trump saying “I wouldn’t have done that” and Secretary of State Marco Rubio saying a lot of people were “disturbed” by the move.
Burnham said authorities have the investigation under “the strongest grip and the closest control,” and British officials had been “talking to counterparts in the United States all week to explain what is happening here, how things are being done.”
U.K. officials say proxies linked to Iran have been behind a string of arsons and other attacks in Britain and other countries, many of them targeting the Jewish community and intended to sow fear. They have previously warned that Tehran could expand its targets in the U.K. if conflicts in the Middle East continue.

Coaching through kidney failure, one man uses football to keep fighting
text:
Coaching through kidney failure, David Finn uses football to keep fighting
An assistant football coach in Kentucky, David Finn, loves the game. It gives him purpose, a second family and a reason to keep pushing through dialysis as he waits for a kidney transplant.
A little more than two years ago, Finn learned his kidneys were failing.
“At the age I was, it was horrifying. I was scared and nervous, but through prayer and my family, I just put my hard hat on and went straight in,” Finn said.
Three days a week, Finn spends four hours in treatment. Dialysis is mentally, physically and emotionally draining, but he continues to show up as a coach and a father.
“I’m trying to raise my son to be a strong, independent man,” Finn said. “I don’t want him to ever see me stop pushing, so until I can’t push anymore, I’m going to push.”
Balancing football and family isn’t easy.
“The most challenging part is spending my time between myself, my son and my football team, my other kids, trying to give them all of me that I can, but still trying to maintain life for myself,” Finn said.
Football gives him an escape from the life-sustaining treatment.
“My coaching staff, those are my brothers,” Finn said. “Seeing them, seeing those kids, being at this school, what we’re accomplishing this year on the football field — it just makes my heart.”
Until he receives a kidney transplant, Finn will keep showing up for his son, his players and himself.
“Whatever you’re going through, it’s not over ... just keep pushing.”

title: Trump says Iran will be hit ‘very hard’ if it is behind copilot who tried to crash flight to Israel
text:
JERUSALEM (AP) — U.S. President Donald Trump said Thursday that if Iran is linked to the copilot who tried to crash an Israel-bound flight, the Islamic Republic would be struck “very hard” for the attempt on the lives of more than 180 people aboard the jet.
Trump issued the warning as investigators worked to determine why the copilot stabbed the flight’s captain, causing the FlyDubai plane to plummet before others on board stopped the attack and landed the airliner in Saudi Arabia.
The president was asked by reporters at the White House whether he had been briefed about any links between the pilot behind the attack and Tehran. He said, “We’re working on it right now.”
“I would say the answer, based on what I’m hearing, is yes, but we’re working on it right now,” Trump said. He did not elaborate about why he suspects Iran might be involved.
Asked if the U.S. would retaliate against Tehran if it was behind the attack, Trump said, “Oh they’ll be hit, very hard, don’t worry.”
“You just ask them,” he added. “They know what happened. They’ll be hit very hard.”
His remarks came as diplomatic efforts to end the war appear to have stalled.
Iranian officials indicated Wednesday that they received an official U.S. response to Tehran’s latest proposal to end the seven-month war, which Trump had publicly rejected just days earlier. The officials did not say what the response contained and whether it was a rejection.
Trump said in a Time magazine interview published Thursday that he will not accept proposals from Iran that “he wouldn’t have approved a year ago,” and left open the possibility of resuming bombing after the Nov. 3 election in the U.S.
Meanwhile, the American military has dispatched roughly 9,000 troops aboard a group of ships to the Middle East, a U.S. official said Thursday. That could mean three carriers will be in the region as soon as late October, according to the official, who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military operations.
Despite Trump’s public rebuff, mediators have continued working with Iran and the U.S. to try to broker a deal to end the fighting and open the Strait of Hormuz, according to officials who were not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity.
Passengers got into cockpit to take control of jet
Passengers on the plane — which was carrying 182 people, mostly Israelis, from the United Arab Emirates to Tel Aviv — have described how the bloodied Indian captain managed to open the cockpit door to let them in before they grappled with the copilot and stabilized a descent so sharp that the plane’s rudder was torn away.
“We felt helpless, suspended in midair, and I didn’t know who to turn to. But it was all instinct to survive,” Asaf Rajuan, who was among those who intervened, said in a statement shared by Israel’s presidency.
A regional official briefed on the investigation said the suspect, an Omani citizen, was under arrest and confirmed that Saudi authorities were working with countries, including Israel, to try to determine a motive. He said the UAE, the United States and Oman also were involved. Saudi Arabia said the copilot had been handed over to the UAE.
“All possible scenarios, from terrorism to mental disorders, are being looked into. Nothing is ruled out for now,” said the official, speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss an ongoing probe.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, without giving details, claimed the attacker underwent Islamist indoctrination. Asked who helped radicalize him, the prime minister told Fox News channel’s “Fox and Friends” he did not know.
When asked by AP how the prime minister knew the copilot underwent indoctrination, Netanyahu’s office said it would not comment.
Netanyahu told Fox that the suspect apparently got through a loophole in Israeli aviation rules that normally bar pilots from flying to Israel if they are from countries that do not have diplomatic relations with Israel, which Oman does not.
The copilot has not been publicly identified. Video shot inside the plane by Dr. Shota Musayev, a dentist who treated the captain, shows the copilot on his knees, with his hands tied behind his back.
Capt. Smit Machchhar, widely praised as one of the heroes of the flight, was recovering in the Emirati capital of Abu Dhabi, the Indian government said Thursday.
It was not clear what the copilot used as a weapon.
Israeli investigators will join the interrogation of the copilot
Israeli intelligence and security officials were in Saudi Arabia to help investigate the copilot, according to another regional official who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media.
Israel has requested that the copilot be sent to Israel for the investigation, though it was unclear if that request would be granted, the official said.
Saudi Arabia does not have formal diplomatic ties with Israel, but the countries have long cooperated on security and intelligence matters through alternative channels.
The UAE government said its own investigation team had begun looking into the attack and “whether it was linked to any terrorist purpose,” noting that Emirati authorities have jurisdiction because the plane is registered there and UAE law applies to crimes committed on board.
Asked if there is any indication of Iranian involvement, Netanyahu told Fox News it was “too early to say.”
Netanyahu earlier said he also spoke with the UAE’s president, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, who agreed that Israel would join the interrogation of the suspect.
On Wednesday, Trump told reporters at the White House that he and Netanyahu discussed the incident “at length” by phone. He said it seemed as though the copilot “was perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack job.”
Oman’s government has not commented.
Netanyahu had warned in recent days of heightened security threats, though he told CNN that Israel had received no specific warning. The country is a week away from the anniversary of the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel, which has triggered the war in Gaza, and weeks away from an election.
The Israeli Foreign Ministry said most of the people aboard the flight were from Israel, along with others from India and the UAE. The U.S. State Department said four passengers had American citizenship.
Someone in cockpit sent out discreet distress codes
Someone in the cockpit sent out two four-digit codes to discreetly signal distress while the plane flew erratically near the Jordanian border with Saudi Arabia, according to Flightradar24.com. The first code was “7700,” the universal “squawk” signal for an emergency, then “7500,” which indicates unlawful interference, including a possible hijacking.
The codes are used by pilots when speaking over the radio may not be possible or wise.
FlyDubai said Wednesday that the jet was secured by on-duty crew members “who diverted and landed the aircraft safely.” A regional official said the crew members were pilots in training. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media.
In the chaos that began about two and a half hours after takeoff, the Boeing 737 Max 8 descended from 33,000 feet to 17,000 feet (around 10,000 meters to 5,100 meters) in about a minute, before making an erratic circle close to the Jordanian border and landing in Tabuk, according to Flightradar24.
___
Magdy reported from Cairo. Price reported from Washington. Associated Press writers Josef Federman in Jerusalem and Laurie Kellman in London contributed to this report.

title: Obituary: George Adams Gilmore
text:
BRUNSWICK – George Adams Gilmore, a resident of Thornton Oaks, passed away on Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026 at Mid Coast Hospital.
George was born in Portland, Maine on April 15, 1935, the son of Martha Senter Gilmore, of Brunswick and David William Gilmore, a professor of European Languages at Rutgers University in New Brunswick, N.J., and a summer resident on Birch Island in Maine.
George grew up in Highland Park, N.J., a suburb of New Brunswick, and graduated from Highland Park High School in 1952, and was president of his class. George then attended Webb Institute of Naval Architecture in Glen Cove, Long Island, N.Y., where he graduated in 1957 with a B.S. in Naval Architecture and Marine Engineering.
George worked in the marine field until 1958 when he joined the U.S. Navy and was Brigade Commander at Naval Officer Training Command in Newport, R.I. He served as a submarine repair coordinator for two years at Pearl Harbor Naval Shipyard in Hawaii, and then two years as the Damage Control Officer on the USS Colahan, (a Bath built destroyer), in the Pacific Ocean during the Vietnam War.
George then attended Harvard Business School, graduating in 1964. He then worked in various marine design and management positions with locations in Bethesda, Md., Washington, D.C., and New York City, N.Y. In NYC, at Energy Transportation Corporation, he was co-author with two others in 1980 of the Society of Naval Architects and Marine Engineers technical paper “Service Experience with 125,000-m3 LNG Vessels of Spherical Tank Design.” George moved to Brunswick, Maine in 1985 where he became the manager of Senter’s Department Store, founded by his grandfather, until it closed in 1992.
After moving to Brunswick, he married Martha Kendall Gilmore. They were active members of the Maine State Music Theatre community. They also enjoyed time on Casco Bay and summers at Mere Point. While in Brunswick, George participated in several organizations including The Brunswick Rotary Club, Maine Merchants Association, Independence Association, and Brunswick-Topsham Land Trust. He was a member of First Parish Church.
George was predeceased by his wife, Martha Kendall Gilmore.
George is survived by three stepchildren, Kent (Lisa) Black, Daphne Brenner, Elizabeth Shortsleeve; step-grandchildren; and numerous cousins from the Senter Family.
Friends and family are invited to visit 10 a.m. Saturday Oct. 17, at First Parish Church, Maine Street, Brunswick. A funeral service will follow at 11 a.m. at the church. Committal will reunite him with his wife, Martha in Riverside Cemetery, Brunswick. Memories and condolences can be shared at http://www.brackettfh.com.
In lieu of flowers, please consider a donation to
First Parish Church
9 Cleaveland St.
Brunswick, ME 04011

title: Judge denies defense motion asking Lindsay Clancy be found not guilty due to a lack of evidence
text:
EDITOR’S NOTE: This story includes discussion of suicide. If you or someone you know needs help, the national suicide and crisis lifeline in the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988.
BOSTON (AP) — The judge in the Lindsay Clancy murder case on Thursday refused to declare her not guilty, turning down a defense motion that had argued there wasn’t enough evidence to prove she was responsible for killing her three children.
During Clancy’s first trial, which ended Sept. 4 with a deadlocked jury, her defense argued that she was not criminally responsible because of a mental disease, specifically a rare condition called postpartum psychosis. As such, the defense didn’t dispute that the 36-year-old former labor and delivery nurse carried out the killings at her family’s Massachusetts home in 2023.
However, in a hearing earlier this week, Clancy’s attorney Kevin Reddington tried to persuade the judge that prosecutors had not offered any proof that Clancy did it. Prosecutors argued there was plenty of evidence, calling Reddington’s claim “laughable.”
Prosecutors have yet to decide whether they will put the case in front of a jury for a second time. They could choose to retry her on first-degree murder charges or seek to try her only on lesser charges, including second-degree murder or manslaughter, or drop the case entirely.
In his ruling Thursday, Judge William Sullivan noted that for the purposes of his decision, he was required to analyze the evidence in the light most favorable to prosecutors — and that it was up to the jury, not the judge, to decide whether to believe expert witnesses for the defense who testified that Clancy was not responsible for her actions because of mental illness.
“There was evidence introduced, both physical and circumstantial, that would permit a rational trier of fact to find beyond a reasonable doubt the elements of the charge of murder,” Sullivan wrote.
At the first trial, prosecutors acknowledged that Clancy had mental health problems that included months of treatment and a stay in a psychiatric hospital, but argued that she knew what she was doing when she strangled the children — the youngest just 8 months old — then tried to kill herself.
Sullivan had declared a mistrial with the jury split 11 to 1 in favor of acquitting Clancy of murder charges.
In Tuesday’s hearing, Reddington suggested the entire case “was based on speculation” and listed shortcomings in the prosecution’s case. There was almost no police investigation, he claimed, and significant questions revolving around Clancy’s condition outside the night of the killings and her lack of memory of what happened.
At the trial, jurors heard testimony that Clancy said she heard voices instructing her to kill 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan Clancy. Her DNA was found on exercise bands used to strangle them. Before the trial, Reddington himself filed a motion in which he said Clancy was willing to stipulate, in writing, to her involvement in the children’s deaths.
“For the first time, the defendant is arguing that there is no evidence she did this,” Prosecutor Shanan Buckingham told the judge. “I’d suggest to you the entire record is voluminous as to information supporting the fact that she did this.”
Clancy remains charged with murder and is expected to stay at a psychiatric hospital until her case is resolved.
Clancy could have been sentenced to life in prison if convicted of murder. If acquitted, the judge could have ordered her confined to a mental health facility.
Her former husband, Patrick Clancy, who discovered the children’s bodies, has said in interviews that he forgives her. The livestreamed trial generated intense public interest and drew attention to maternal mental health after childbirth.

title: Dunlap, LePage take the debate stage for first time in 2nd Congressional District race
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Democrat Matt Dunlap and Republican Paul LePage went toe-to-toe Thursday night in their first debate in the 2nd Congressional District race.
LePage, 77, the former governor, and Dunlap, 61, the state auditor and former secretary of state, are just over a month away from the Nov. 3 election to decide who will succeed Democratic Rep. Jared Golden, who did not seek reelection.
A recent poll conducted by the University of New Hampshire Survey Center found Dunlap with a 51% to 45% edge over LePage, with 5% of respondents undecided.
Unsurprisingly, Dunlap and LePage disagreed on a number of topics during Thursday night’s debate televised by WMTW, but both continuously argued their agendas would be more effective in meeting a common goal: affordability.
Healthcare took the spotlight on many occasions throughout the debate. On questions regarding MaineCare, the state’s Medicaid program, LePage said he would attempt to raise reimbursement rates, while Dunlap said he supports expanding the program.
Early on, both candidates were asked what bill they’d introduce first, if elected. Dunlap said his first piece of legislation would focus on healthcare access and affordability, such as restoring tax subsidies for the Affordable Care Act. LePage said he would introduce a bill to increase access to dental care for veterans.
A number of Democratic candidates this cycle have made a Medicare for All system a cornerstone of their campaign, but Dunlap didn’t fully embrace it Thursday night. He highlighted some of the benefits and said he would “certainly encourage the country to go in that direction,” while cautioning it would take a long time to fully implement.
LePage, meanwhile, bashed the idea, claiming it would do away with private healthcare and services would get “rationed.”
They also disagreed on tariffs. Dunlap argued that the trade war with Canada is detrimental to American citizens, while LePage argued “we’ve gotten a bad deal for many years,” but the two allies need to come to a resolution.
The two differed even while finding common ground on several topics, including the war in Iran. Both, for instance, said they don’t support the war, but LePage said he doesn’t support a war powers act, while Dunlap does.
Both agreed that housing production could be boosted by better supporting those who make the housing. However, Dunlap said he’d help make finances more accessible for housing developments, while LePage said he’d focus on improving the permitting process and regulations.
Dunlap and LePage also agreed that caps on Social Security contributions should be raised, and that Congress should have at least some oversight on the development of artificial intelligence. They differed on data centers, with LePage saying that should be decided on the local level and Dunlap arguing federal, state and local governments need to work together on the issue.
Perhaps the most stark difference between the two candidates was their attitudes toward President Donald Trump.
Multiple times throughout the debate, including in his opening statement, LePage touted his ability to call upon Trump. He said the first thing he’d do, if elected, would be to request that Trump “put restrictions on sending diesel to foreign countries.” He also said he’d call him before the election to make that suggestion.
During a response to a question on the trade war with Canada, LePage suggested, “I can help the president because I can speak French to the prime minister.”
“I will be able to get into the Oval Office; my opponent will not,” LePage said.
As for Dunlap, he repeatedly critiqued Trump’s policies and argued Congress needs to reel the president in.
“The job of Congress is to provide oversight of the executive branch,” he said regarding the war in Iran.

title: Thomas Jefferson hair in Smithsonian Bible helps fuel strongest DNA evidence on Sally Hemings
text:
DNA evidence from Thomas Jefferson’s hair reveals strongest evidence yet about his relationship with Sally Hemings
Opening a Bible that once belonged to Thomas Jefferson, staff at the Smithsonian National Museum of American History in 2011 discovered a reddish-blond hair pressed between the pages. That hair, suspected to have belonged to Jefferson himself, launched a DNA investigation spanning more than a decade that's now providing a long-missing puzzle piece regarding Jefferson's relationship with Sally Hemings, an enslaved woman in his household.
Related video above: Presidential Bookworms! America’s Presidents and Their History With Books
After spending years reconstructing DNA fragments, scientists have revealed the most compelling evidence to date that Jefferson, a founding father of the United States, also fathered children with Hemings — a relationship that has been long rumored but never definitively proven. How that investigation unfolded is documented in the book "History by a Hair: Thomas Jefferson, Sally Hemings & Solving a 200-Year-Old Mystery," written by Richard Kurin, a distinguished scholar and ambassador-at-large at the Smithsonian, and published on Sept. 22.
Kurin is also senior author of a paper describing the methods that connected the former US president to Hemings' descendants, which involved delving deep into the genetics of the Jefferson and Hemings family trees. The paper, published September 21 on the preprint platform bioRXiv, has not yet been peer-reviewed.
In addition to testing the hair found in the Bible, the researchers also collected genetic material from multiple confirmed samples of Jefferson's hair, held in the collection of the Smithsonian. They compared that with DNA from descendants of multiple lineages: Jefferson and his wife Martha, Jefferson's brother Randolph, and two of Hemings' sons, Eston and Madison. (Hemings had four children who lived to adulthood, but only Eston and Madison claimed Jefferson as their father).
Matches in the DNA suggest the chance that Thomas Jefferson fathered at least one of Sally Hemings' children was 99.96%.
Previously, a genetic study from 1998 led by the late Eugene Foster, a retired pathology professor at Tufts University and the University of Virginia, claimed to prove Jefferson's parentage of Hemings' children. That study found a rare haplotype — a combination of genes — in the Y chromosomes of males descended from Thomas Jefferson's uncle. That same haplotype existed in descendants of Hemings, too. However, many experts questioned Foster's claim for one very important reason, Kurin told CNN.
"He didn't have Thomas Jefferson's DNA," Kurin said. "He didn't have something to directly compare living descendants of the Jefferson family to Madison Hemings and Eston Hemings and others that might have been the descendants of Thomas Jefferson." Critics of that the 1998 study said Foster's evidence merely connected Hemings' descendants to a male in the Jefferson lineage, and not necessarily to the former president.
"I thought, if we can get Thomas Jefferson's DNA, we could use that as the source of comparison to various descendants, and really firmly solve the question," Kurin said.
A 'dead end' hair
Kurin and his team were initially disappointed to find that the Bible hair wasn't the smoking gun that they thought it would be. To check whether the hair was Jefferson's, they compared its DNA with that of a living woman who was a direct descendant of Thomas Jefferson's mother along the family's female lineage. They expected to find identical mitochondrial DNA, which is genetic material specifically inherited from the maternal side. But their hopes were dashed when the two samples didn't match.
Still, they were able to access other hair samples that records attributed to Thomas Jefferson. These hairs, including a lock clipped at his deathbed, were in a packet provided by the Thomas Jefferson Foundation at Monticello, and had not previously been available for analysis. The scientists reconstructed and compared historic genome sequences of Jefferson and Hemings with DNA collected from 16 living individuals, including multiple descendants of Eston and Madison Hemings. These analyses found matches across genomes that linked Hemings descendants to Thomas Jefferson.
"What made this study so powerful is that researchers weren't just comparing two genomes," said Éadaoin Harney, a senior population geneticist at the 23andMe Research Institute. "Instead, they collected DNA samples from multiple people from different branches of the family tree."
In genetic analysis, larger sample pools provide more robust conclusions, said Harney, who was not involved in the new research. "By studying the patterns of DNA sharing across all of these individuals, it became possible to disambiguate exactly how the descendants of Sally Hemings were related to Thomas Jefferson," she told CNN in an email.
While the new book and paper focus on genomic data of well-known historical figures, these methods are also broadly useful for illuminating the obscured history of enslaved people, which has been a focus of Harney's own research. In a 2023 study of enslaved and free African Americans from Maryland, Harney used DNA analysis combined with other biomolecular and archaeological techniques to uncover individuals' ancestry and places of origin. The data also suggested links to people who still live in Maryland.
"Historical records are full of gaps, particularly when it comes to documenting the lives of people who occupied less privileged places in society," she said. "This is particularly true for enslaved Africans and African Americans, who are often only described in historical records as property."
Genetic analyses, such as those used in the new Jefferson study, can help restore connections that were lost because of slavery, Harney added. "The same tools can be applied to study the many enslaved people whose lives were never well documented, and help reconnect them with their descendants."
From rumor to confirmation
Whispers about Jefferson's sexual relationship with Hemings — who was 30 years his junior and a half-sister to his wife — have endured for more than 200 years. Initial rumors were fueled by local innuendo and supported by records aligning Hemings' pregnancies with Jefferson's presence at his plantation home of Monticello in Virginia. An article published in 1902 in the Richmond Recorder stated that "there is not an individual in the neighbourhood of Charlottesville who does not believe the story," regarding Jefferson fathering children with Hemings.
Though the conclusions of Foster's 1998 study were not universally accepted, that genetic evidence was compelling enough for the Thomas Jefferson Foundation to issue a statement two years later acknowledging "the strong likelihood that Thomas Jefferson and Sally Hemings had a relationship over time that led to the birth of one, and perhaps all, of the known children of Sally Hemings."
Finally laying that uncertainty to rest was enough of a motivation to keep Kurin and the other researchers going for more than a decade, despite their initial disappointment that the hair found in the Bible did not belong to Thomas Jefferson, he said.
"We had hit a dead end, but scientists are always looking for alternatives," he said. "I think we were propelled still by scientific and historical curiosity."
While the question of Jefferson's ancestry in Hemings' descendants may finally have been answered, another remains: Whose hair was pressed in Jefferson's bible? The researchers had collected enough of its fragmentary genetic data to know that it belonged to a female member of the Jefferson family, but that was all the information the team could learn, Kurin said.
"It's like a partial fingerprint," he explained. "That is still a lingering mystery."

title: Annual Maine Public Health Conference Focuses on Getting ‘Back to the Basics’
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - To cultivate mental, spiritual and physical health, we often have to go back to the basics.
That’s what happened Thursday as public health leaders gathered at the Augusta Civic Center for the annual Maine Public Health Association conference.
This year’s theme, “Nourish to Flourish,” focused on strengthening fundamental building blocks across the state.
A key focus: food access.
“The things we heard from people that they need are more access to quality and affordable health care, especially in rural areas. Safe and affordable housing. Making sure that there’s economic opportunity for people living in these far-flung parts of Maine,” said Matt Wellington, associate director of the Maine Public Health Association. “How do we make sure folks can have a happy and healthy life in those areas as well?”
One group promoting that access at Thursday’s conference was the Maine Federation of Farmers’ Markets, which targets food insecurity through SNAP bonus bucks and Senior Farm Share.
“Farmers markets, as they currently exist even without our intervention, are public health institutions,” said Jimmy DeBiasi, executive director of the Maine Federation of Farmers’ Markets. “They’re helping folks access more fresh produce, connect with their neighbors, socialize, and learn about new foods.”
For Maine’s tribal nations, the conversation goes beyond access—centering on the right to shape their own food systems.
“Specifically as Indigenous people, and working towards food sovereignty within our Wabanaki homelands, and really giving our people a choice to the kinds of foods that they have access to and the way that they want to shape their own food systems,” said Keyana Pardilla, director of the Our Sacred Relations division at Wabanaki Public Health and Wellness.
Pardilla explains displacement onto reservations—often food deserts—creates high food insecurity risks, noting “food as medicine” has always been an Indigenous value.
With record turnout, organizers say it proves a shared drive to tackle Maine’s health challenges together.

title: Walmart recalls nearly 4.5 million grill wire brushes. Here are the impacted brushes
text:
(Gray News) - Walmart is recalling nearly 4.5 million grill brushes because small metal wire bristles can detach, stick to grills or food, and cause severe internal injuries requiring surgery if swallowed.
The recall covers approximately 4,477,655 Expert Grill metal wire bristle brushes sold individually and as part of grilling tool sets, according to the Consumer Product Safety Commission.
The brushes feature black plastic or stainless steel handles, and several models include an attached metal scraper.
Products were sold at Walmart stores nationwide and online at Walmart.com from January 2021 through August 2026 for between $1 and $28.
No injuries or incidents have been reported, according to the CPSC notice.
Recalled models
The recall includes five specific models. Consumers can locate the model number on the product packaging or on a sticker or tag attached directly to the brush:
- EX5607031616002: Expert Grill 16-inch Steel Fiber Scrub Brush and Scraper for Grills (sold January 2025 to August 2026)
- EX5607031616003: Expert Grill Handheld Steel Fiber Scrub Brush with Ergonomic Handle for Grill Cleaning (sold January 2025 to August 2026)
- XG1310700206: Expert Grill 21-inch 3-Head Grill Brush with Stainless Steel Bristles and Soft-Grip Handle (sold January 2022 to August 2026)
- XG1136178597003: Expert Grill Long Handle Grill Brush with Scraper, 17.7-inch (sold January 2021 to August 2026)
- XG1410700124: Expert Grill Grilling Accessories BBQ Grill Tools Set, 10-Piece Stainless Steel Grill Kit (sold December 2023 to August 2026)
Refund and contact information
Consumers should immediately stop using the recalled brushes and contact Walmart to receive a full refund or store credit valid in stores or online. Customers will be instructed to either return the product to a store or discard it.
Walmart can be reached toll-free at 800-925-6278 from 7 a.m. to 9 p.m. CT Monday through Friday, or online through the company’s product recalls page.

title: Mountain Valley soccer is the Varsity Maine Boys Team of the Week
text:
Editor’s note: Each week during the fall sports season, Varsity Maine will highlight a boys and girls team of the week. The teams, picked by staff members, will take into account several factors, including success stories, bounce-back efforts and notable accomplishments, among others. Athletes, coaches and athletic directors can nominate teams by emailing sports editor Bill Stewart at [email protected] or Varsity Maine editor Lee Horton at [email protected].
Varsity Maine Boys Team of the Week: Mountain Valley boys soccer
The Falcons didn’t enter the fall as an expected contender in Class C South. In fact, in the past three years, the team has totaled four wins.
But after eight games, the Falcons own a 4-2-2 record and sit at No. 2 in the C South Heal point standings, just below defending state champion Hall-Dale (6-1).
“Last year, we only won one game. It was tough,” said Mountain Valley coach JT Taylor. “Sometimes you’ve got to take your licks before you can get to where you need to be.”
Last week, the Falcons picked up a 2-1 win over Maranacook and a 4-3 victory in a Class C/D crossover against Buckfield. Mountain Valley opened its season by showing it can hang with the division’s best teams, falling 2-1 to Mt. Abram.
“It’s so much more fun,” said Mountain Valley senior Cash Provencher. “We’re starting to become the team that other teams (don’t) want to play. … Change your expectations about us and watch out in the future.”
The Falcons still have a tough road ahead, including matches with Hall-Dale on Oct. 14 and Monmouth Academy in the regular-season finale on Oct. 19.

title: Girl, 11, will learn her fate in trial over brutal rape and assault of a 5-year-old
text:
CLEVELAND (WOIO/Gray News) - The trial for the 11-year-old girl accused in the brutal rape and assault of a 5-year-old girl wrapped up in Cuyahoga County Juvenile Court Wednesday afternoon.
Judge Kristin Sweeney will release her decision on Friday.
What happened
Prosecutors said the 11-year-old, addressed as M.H. in court, and a now 10-year-old boy attacked the girl in a field in Cleveland on Sept. 13, 2025.
The victim’s clothes were removed, according to testimony, and she was strangled with her own shirt.
The 10-year-old boy, addressed as M.B. during the trial, pleaded guilty Monday to attempted rape and felonious assault.
He testified against the 11-year-old girl Wednesday and described what he claims M.H. said while strangling the victim with a shirt.
“This is what bad girls get for following people,” said M.B.
He says M.H. also ordered him not to tell anyone about what happened.
“How were you feeling when she told you that?” asked the prosecution. “Scared,” said M.B.
He is scheduled to be back in court on Nov. 20 and could face probation or placement in a residential treatment facility.
Victim’s mom takes the stand
On Tuesday, the mom of the victim took the stand and testified that her daughter spent several weeks in the hospital following the attack.
She also described the emotional toll the attack has had on her little girl.
“When we left the hospital, she went through severe behavioral changes. She kept saying she’s not pretty anymore. She kept saying earth is a bad place,” said the mom.
Previous coverage:
- Children charged in brutal attack on 5-year-old Cleveland girl to undergo competency restoration
- Cleveland police connect kid suspects to beating; mother describes 5-year-old as ‘unrecognizable’
- Prosecutors charge 2 children, 9 and 10, in brutal attack on 5-year-old Cleveland girl
Case background
The Cleveland Division of Police Sex Crimes and Child Abuse Unit investigated the case.
In October 2025, prosecutors charged the 11-year-old girl and then nine-year-old boy with attempted murder, rape, felonious assault, kidnapping and strangulation.
On April 1, Judge Sweeney ordered the two children to undergo competency restoration before they could stand trial.
According to court records, a change in the 11-year-old’s placement was necessary to get a true assessment of her competency.
When a placement was not found, prosecutors requested she be held in the detention center during the restoration process.
The court said returning to her home was not in her best interest, and the Court Diagnostics Clinic provided competency restoration services at the detention center.
Both children were previously held on home detention.
After a period of court-ordered rehabilitation, the children were later found competent to stand trial.
