title: Manager Chad Tracy’s decisions questioned after Yankees eliminate Red Sox
text:
NEW YORK — With the Boston bats ice cold at Yankee Stadium again, a couple of quick hooks by Red Sox rookie manager Chad Tracy led to another early postseason exit.
And top starter Sonny Gray wasn’t happy about being lifted after only 70 pitches.
“I think I’m the best pitcher in the American League going through the order the third time. I think that’s a fact,” Gray said. “I would have liked to have been trusted in that moment.”
For the second consecutive season, the Red Sox were sent home for the winter by their biggest rivals as the New York Yankees rolled to a 9-2 victory Wednesday night and a two-game sweep of their Wild Card Series.
Boston was outscored 18-2 overall and left to lament a miserable finish to this roller-coaster ride of a season that included Tracy taking over when Alex Cora was fired in April.
Tracy’s decision-making came under scrutiny after both playoff games against the Yankees. In Boston’s 9-0 defeat a night earlier, Tracy pulled rookie starter Payton Tolle after 4 2/3 innings and 83 pitches in a 1-0 game.
Last year, the Red Sox won their Wild Card Series opener before losing to New York in a deciding Game 3 as they got overpowered by Cam Schlittler, who pitched another playoff gem against his hometown team Tuesday night.
“To have it end here two times in a row is tough,” shortstop Trevor Story said.
Facing a Yankees lineup missing injured slugger Aaron Judge, the Red Sox gave up 26 hits in two games despite a pair of effective performances from their starting pitchers.
At the plate, Boston mustered only seven hits and finally snapped a 26-inning postseason scoring drought that dated to last year when Willson Contreras homered just over the right-center fence in the sixth Wednesday.
“It’s obviously been an eventful year,” Tracy said. “In the moment right now you can’t think much more other than anything but the fact that we just lost a playoff series.”
Needing a victory to extend their season, the Red Sox sent Gray to the mound and the 18-game winner certainly gave them a chance. Boston trailed 1-0 in the fifth when the right-hander allowed a two-out single to Ben Rice that put runners at the corners.
Tracy then yanked Gray, eager to hand the ball to baseball’s best bullpen during the regular season.
“I felt good. You know, I felt crisp. I felt sharp. I felt like I was just out there competing. And yeah, I mean, I got clipped for a solo homer and then some singles, but I felt like I stayed on the attack throughout. I was just executing what I wanted to do,” Gray said. “I’m frustrated, for sure. You know, not ready for it to end. A lot of emotions.”
Asked about the move, Contreras put his finger over his lips to zip them shut.
“It’s not enough when you have talent or you have data or you have computers that’s telling you what to do, because this is baseball,” he said. “The data is here to help us, but at the end of the day you are going to have to need experience and veteran guys to win games.”
In both games of the series, Tracy gave the ball to left-handed reliever Erik Miller after taking out his starting pitcher.
On Tuesday, Rice greeted Miller with a 423-foot solo homer to straightaway center field.
On Wednesday, Tracy summoned Miller to face a different left-handed hitter, Cody Bellinger — who batted .274 against lefties this season and .259 versus right-handers. In fact, his .310 batting average against left-handers over the past two years was the best of any left-handed hitter in the majors.
Bellinger made Tracy and the Red Sox pay, lining an RBI single to right field.
“We’re struggling to score runs,” Tracy said. “And when you get in spots where you’re struggling to score runs and you’re already trailing, you feel like you’ve got to be aggressive and go.”
Back from a shoulder injury, ace starter Garrett Crochet entered in the sixth for his first outing since April 25 and first relief appearance since 2023 with the Chicago White Sox. The left-hander opened with a strikeout, but Spencer Jones reached safely on a wild pitch, and Crochet never got an out.
Bellinger’s three-run homer off right-hander Garrett Whitlock capped a six-run inning that made it 8-1, and the Red Sox were done. A bullpen that led the majors with a 3.00 ERA during the regular season finished this series with a 20.25 ERA after giving up 15 runs, 15 hits and seven walks in 6 2/3 innings, with a .484 opponents’ batting average.
Boston’s latest downfall in the Bronx was a crushing end to a wild 2026 season for the Red Sox, who stumbled to a 32-46 start. Tracy was the skipper at Triple-A Worcester before getting promoted to interim manager in Boston, and the team finally began to take off with a four-game sweep of the Yankees at Fenway Park in late June.
After clinching a wild-card spot last week, the Red Sox removed the interim tag and named Tracy the 49th manager in team history, signing him to a three-year contract that runs through the 2029 season, with a club option for 2030. The team also exercised the 2029 and 2030 options on chief baseball officer Craig Breslow.
“I wasn’t there for the highs and lows,” Crochet said. “For this team to do what it did do, to make it to this point, was nothing short of miraculous.”
Led by Gray and Contreras, among others, the Red Sox went on a 15-game winning streak in July that equaled a franchise record and used a 32-5 surge to climb back into contention. They became the fourth team in major league history to reach the postseason after falling 14 games under .500, and the first to qualify after losing as many as 44 of its first 75.
Gray, who can become a free agent after the World Series, went around the clubhouse to hug each of his teammates following Wednesday’s defeat.
“I’m proud of what we accomplished,” the pitcher said. “We were left for dead there for a while.”

title: Thousands of eligible Mainers to automatically receive discounts on electric bills
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Thousands of low-income Mainers are slated to receive automatic discounts on their monthly electric bills.
Gov. Janet Mills announced on Thursday that $40 million in electricity discounts and other services would be distributed among eligible Maine households through the state’s Low Income Assistance Program, and many will be enrolled automatically this year.
Amounts vary by income, but eligible Central Maine Power customers could see discounts anywhere between 25% and 81%, while Versant customers could get between 17% and 83% off monthly, according to the announcement.
To qualify, customers must have a household income at or below 150% of the federal poverty guidelines. About 44,000 Maine ratepayers participated in the program last year, according to the announcement, but officials determined that roughly another 23,000 were eligible.
To increase participation, many households will now be enrolled automatically.
The Maine Department of Health and Human Services will use information from programs like SNAP and MaineCare to determine automatic eligibility, the announcement states. Those participating in the federally funded Home Energy Assistance Program will also be automatically enrolled in the program.
“Beneficiaries will have their information securely shared with participating utilities” to have the discounts applied to their monthly bills, the announcement said. Mainers not already participating in a DHHS program can apply for the Low Income Assistance Program.
The roughly $40 million in funding for the program is a leap from $22.5 million in 2025, with an additional $7.5 million being approved in a recent supplemental budget for this year. However, the program is largely funded by a ratepayer monthly surcharge of about $2, according to the announcement, with further support from New England Clean Energy Connect.
The monthly nature of the discount is also new to the program. Previously, program participants were given lump sums to offset their costs.
The program is part of “SupportLink,” a Mills initiative implemented through DHHS that connects Maine households with discounts and other forms of relief they are eligible for, unless they opt out, the announcement states.
“Maine families are being pushed to the brink by the president’s whipsaw tariffs and his reckless war in Iran,” Mills said of President Donald Trump in a written statement. “At a time when every dollar matters, my administration is making it easier for vulnerable Mainers to lower their electric bills without unnecessary paperwork or bureaucratic hurdles.”
SupportLink currently includes nine electric utilities, as well as Efficiency Maine and the Portland Water District, according to the announcement.
Mills credited the participating utilities as well as Maine’s Public Advocate, Public Utilities Commission, DHHS and MaineHousing for making the automatic process possible.
Leaders of those state entities praised the move in statements that were included in Thursday’s announcement.
Ian Yaffe, director of the Maine DHHS’ Office for Family Independence, said it’s “a meaningful step toward making services easier to access.”
“Families should not have to navigate multiple applications or send paperwork from one agency to another when we can securely share the information needed to connect them with help,” Yaffe stated.
Maine Public Advocate Heather Sanborn said it will “provide meaningful, predictable support” for struggling Mainers, while Dan Brennan, director of MaineHousing, said it will “help take some of the complications and pressures off our most vulnerable households.”
Eligible households can expect the discounts to begin taking effect on or soon after their November bill, according to the announcement, which notes the timing could be off due to electric bills not always following the calendar month.

title: AARP poll shows close Maine Senate race, Pingree leading in governor’s contest
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AARP poll shows close Senate race in Maine, Hannah Pingree leading in governor’s race
Democrat Troy Jackson holds a 50% to 47% lead over Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins in a new AARP poll of likely Maine voters, while Democrat Hannah Pingree leads Republican Bobby Charles in the governor’s race.
AARP poll shows close Senate race in Maine, Hannah Pingree leading in governor’s race
Democrat Troy Jackson holds a 50% to 47% lead over Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins in a new AARP poll of likely Maine voters, while Democrat Hannah Pingree leads Republican Bobby Charles in the governor’s race.
The poll’s margin of sampling error is 3.1 percentage points, putting Jackson’s three-point advantage within the margin of error.
Swing voters over the age of 50 make up 20% of the 50+ electorate, which researchers noted is "really critical" in keeping Collins competitive in the race.
In the Governor's race, pollsters found Pingree with a clear 52% to 39% lead over Charles. Independent candidate Rick Bennett received 6%. Three percent were undecided.
"I think the results here really underscore the importance of 50+ voters," said Matt Hogan, one of the researchers commissioned by AARP. "They are especially likely to be ticket splitters."
The findings add to a series of close Senate polls. A University of New Hampshire poll released Sept. 24 found Jackson at 51% and Collins at 47%, a race researchers described as statistically tied.
The AARP survey found a sharp age divide in the Senate contest: Jackson led 60%-35% among voters younger than 50, while Collins led 53%-44% among voters 50 and older. In the governor’s race, Pingree led among both age groups, including 49%-42% among voters 50 and older.
Beyond the two big races in Maine, the poll also examined the broader political environment and found that most voters are "extremely motivated" to vote this year, with 82% rating themselves a 10 out of 10. Among voters 50+ this figure climbs to 87%.
Top Issues Motivating Voters
Rising prices and affordability were ranked as the biggest issues motivating people to vote this November; 44% of voters named the issue as one of their top two priorities.
Threats to democracy was ranked as the number 2 issue overall, driven by Democrats who have it as their top issue. Two issues were tied for 3rd place at 22%, immigration and taxes, both top issues for Republicans.
Among voters 50 and older, 47% said rising electricity costs had forced them to cut back on other essentials; 97% said it was important for elected officials to work to keep utility costs affordable. The poll noted that utilities like electricity are a higher concern in Maine than other battleground states this election cycle.
According to the poll, nearly 6 out of 10 older voters said they were worried about their financial situation. The rising price of gasoline and groceries are top concerns for voters both under and over the age of 50.
Key Issues for Voters 50+
Rising prices of everyday essentials is something 84% of voters 50+ are focused on heading into the November election.
When researchers asked older Mainers what other issues were the most important in deciding their vote, 81% of voters put down Social Security, including 45% who called it "extremely important."
Among older voters, 93% said they would vote for a candidate who makes sure they receive the Social Security they paid into.
"These are extremely high numbers," said Bob Ward, one of the researchers who conducted the poll. "So candidate who fights to make sure that workers get the Social Security they paid for and protects it from cuts, gets a massive boost across party lines."
The cost of health care also ranked high, with 80% of older voters selecting that issue.
Researchers surveyed 982 likely voters selected from Maine’s voter list by live interviews on cellphones and landlines, and by text messages leading to an online survey.

title: This city set a goal to end traffic deaths by 2050. Is it working?
text:
PHOENIX, Ariz. (InvestigateTV) — Experts have labeled car crashes as a public health concern. Every day, over 100 people in the United States are killed in a car crash.
But they also stress traffic collisions are preventable.
In 2021, the number of traffic-related deaths hit a record high of 43,230 in the country. Since then, there’s been a major shift toward improving road safety. In 2025, that number dropped to 36,640, one of the lowest rates in more than a decade.
In Phoenix, Arizona, the push is showing results, but also highlighting the limitations.
Phoenix recorded 278 traffic deaths in 2024, down from 307 the previous year, as the city’s Vision Zero program enters its third year with mixed results.
The city adopted Vision Zero in 2022 with the goal of eliminating all traffic deaths by 2050. Phoenix has one of the highest rates of traffic deaths among major U.S. cities.
Erik Gamino still struggles with the loss of his 13-year-old nephew JD, who was killed in July 2023 when Kyle Nobbley struck their car on Bell Road near 7th Street and fled the scene.
“It hurts a lot. I still go through the pain every day,” Gamino said.
Funding and staffing challenges
The city has spent $10 million annually on Vision Zero, improving dangerous intersections, adding lighting and building crosswalks and medians.
“These projects do make a difference. We can generally see at locations that we do see after a couple years that collision rates do come down,” said Carl Langford, traffic engineering supervisor.
However, the city continues to miss several goals, including reducing pedestrian-related fatal crashes, reducing nighttime crashes and increasing funding for road safety projects.
“Other strategies we are maybe lagging a little bit behind compared with what the plan was to begin with and some of that is potentially staffing shortages in some areas,” Langford said.
Police traffic unit reduced
Phoenix Police traffic unit has been reduced from more than 150 officers to about 40 due to staffing shortages, according to Councilwoman Debra Stark, who chairs the city’s Transportation, Infrastructure and Planning Subcommittee.
Phoenix installed 17 speed cameras — nine along road stretches and eight in school zones — as part of photo enforcement efforts.
The cameras have recorded more than 132,000 events as of May 31, with 17,600 of those resulting in traffic citations being mailed.
The program began issuing citations on March 25 after a 30-day trial period.
Officials say the system activates if you’re caught going 11 miles per hour over the speed limit. They say it’s not about making money, it’s about safety and slowing drivers down.
“Do I wish we had more money so that we could implement it quicker? You betcha. And that has been an issue,” Stark said.
When asked to grade the city’s Vision Zero performance, Stark said, “I would probably say a B.”
Family seeks justice, prevention
Nobbley took a plea deal in 2024, pleading guilty to manslaughter and failing to remain on scene. He was sentenced to eight and a half years in prison.
“It really doesn’t” bring closure, Gamino said of the sentence. “I feel like our justice system is not, it’s not right.”
Gamino got a tattoo of his nephew’s last heartbeat on his arm and hopes sharing their story can prevent other crashes.
“Just think about other people,” he said when asked what he wants other drivers to know.
Studies show speed, heavier vehicles, distracted driving and more people walking and biking contribute to traffic safety problems.
The city continues to apply for federal grants connected to Vision Zero despite uncertainty about future funding.

title: The laws tied to the Susan Collins-Navatek allegations are ‘crystal clear.’ Enforcing them is another matter.
text:
The allegations of a “pay-to-play” scheme and bribery outlined in the recent ProPublica report on U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, and a contractor may not lead to any further consequences beyond serving as campaign fodder, but experts said the piece highlighted some key facts.
Existing laws are clear on banning such behavior, but it takes a federal agency to investigate any alleged wrongdoing, campaign finance experts noted.
That seems to be what happened with the case involving Hawaiian defense contractor Navatek, its former CEO-turned-convicted-felon Martin Kao and an illegal donation to a pro-Collins super PAC through a shell company. But an FBI investigation focusing on Collins and Kao — along with other potential corruption involving members of Congress — died after President Donald Trump returned to office in 2025 and purged the anti-corruption unit that had been handling the probe, ProPublica reported.
So it appears unlikely that more penalties will come as a result of the alleged interactions detailed in the Sept. 22 piece, though ProPublica said it was only “the first in a series of stories drawn from our reporting.” The fallout is instead mostly coming in the form of fresh criticism of Collins as she seeks a sixth term against former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson in a race that appears neck and neck ahead of the Nov. 3 election.
Still, the report opened up various questions regarding campaign finance and what is allowed in an American political system that both sides of the aisle agree is awash in money.
Collins and her campaign staff, who have never been charged in connection with Kao’s case, have bashed the new reporting as covering old allegations from Kao, who was sentenced to 87 months in prison last year after he pleaded guilty to funneling more than $200,000 to Collins’ 2020 reelection campaign and an affiliated super PAC that Collins and the PAC returned in light of the criminal proceedings against Kao.
But ProPublica rebutted the Collins camp’s criticism by noting its story focused on previously unreported claims Kao made between 2022 and 2024, and on how a trove of records and emails the news organization obtained show the FBI was still investigating Kao’s relationship with Collins, her staffers and employees of the super PAC up until early 2025.
The Portland Press Herald spoke with several campaign finance experts who have worked in law and for the federal government about various questions raised by the ProPublica reporting. Without rehashing all the details in the ProPublica story, the interviews revealed a few tweaks that could fix broader finance loopholes. But the experts agreed the existing laws in place to protect against pay-for-play schemes and bribery are clear. Enforcing them is another matter.
What are the laws on contractor donations and bribery of public officials? What are the penalties for breaking them? How easy it is to prosecute?
Both the Hatch Act amendments of 1940 and Federal Election Commission regulations ban federal government contractors from donating to — or promising to donate to — federal candidates, political parties, political committees and super PACs. Civil fines are common penalties, but prison sentences occur in more serious cases that also involve other violations.
Kao received his 87-month prison sentence in 2025 because of a series of violations, rather than illicit campaign donations. His crimes included COVID-19 pandemic wire fraud, money laundering and bank fraud, with a judge also ordering him to pay back about $12.8 million in Paycheck Protection Program funds he fraudulently obtained.
Anti-bribery statutes prohibit “quid pro quo” dealings and ban public officials from giving or receiving anything of value if it is given “with intent to influence” an official act or received “in return for being influenced.” A bribery conviction is punishable by up to 15 years in prison, but a separate case of giving a “gratuity” after the fact as “thanks” for an act, but not in exchange for it, can result in up to two years. A “gratuity” does not include campaign contributions.
The current laws make it “crystal clear that certain behaviors are unlawful,” said Erin Chlopak, who worked for the FEC in litigation and policy roles for nearly a decade and now serves as the nonprofit Campaign Legal Center’s senior director of campaign finance. The Campaign Legal Center had filed a complaint with the FEC after getting suspicious about what turned out to be the $150,000 straw donation to the pro-Collins super PAC in 2020 that Kao reportedly told PAC officials he would give through the “Society of Young Women Scientist and Engineers.”
But proving bribery is not easy, campaign finance experts noted, and Supreme Court rulings have narrowed what counts. For contractor violations, the FEC has lacked a four-member quorum during Trump’s second term and thus cannot start investigations or issue penalties.
“It is incredibly difficult for prosecutors to prove that sort of quid pro quo exchange,” said Eric Petry, counsel in the left-leaning Brennan Center for Justice’s Elections and Government Program. “And oftentimes, it really boils down to a ‘he said versus she said,’ which is really difficult for courts and juries to get to the bottom of.”
A jury in 2024 found former U.S. Sen. Bob Menendez, a New Jersey Democrat who was seeking reelection that year as an independent, guilty of acting as a foreign agent for Egypt amid a yearslong bribery scheme involving him, his wife and three New Jersey businesspeople. Menendez is appealing his 11-year prison sentence.
On the topic of illicit federal contractor donations, FEC commissioners were equally divided in 2024 and thus closed a complaint from the Campaign Legal Center that a federal contractor violated the law by giving more than $236,000 to a super PAC supporting Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis’ presidential campaign.
What are the gray areas? What about business leaders who donate and whose companies win contracts?
The ban on federal contractor donations does not apply to several categories of people, including stockholders, officers or employees of a corporation, and it does not apply to donations in state or local elections. And when it comes to campaign money, the U.S. Supreme Court’s Citizens United ruling in 2010 essentially paved the way for corporations to spend unlimited funds on elections.
Petry said Congress could seek to boost low levels of public trust in the government by at least expanding the federal contractor donation ban to cover those other affiliated individuals, such as stockholders and officers. He also flagged how federal contractors and corporations can give to presidential inauguration funds or projects such as Trump’s White House ballroom.
Other examples of giving are allowed and easier to spot, though experts noted that voters have cited them in surveys when expressing disgust with the amount of money floating around the political system.
New Balance’s owner and chairman, Jim Davis, gave $1 million to Collins’ super PAC last year. The senator proudly held one of the company’s shoes when announcing her reelection campaign in February. And earlier in September, she touted a nearly $60 million contract the company got to produce military footwear at its Skowhegan plant.
Did Collins actually call Kao to thank him?
Scott Reed, who leads the pro-Collins Pine Tree Results PAC, was mentioned repeatedly in the recent ProPublica piece because of Kao’s testimony, FBI records and emails showing his interactions with Kao. That included a 2019 meeting in Washington in which Reed allegedly asked Navatek executives for a $500,000 campaign donation after Collins had helped the company win a multimillion dollar Navy research contract in Maine.
ProPublica viewed an email in which Kao told Reed he planned to donate $150,000 through a shell company. “Very smart,” Reed replied.
(ProPublica reached out to Reed for comment, and he said via email that, “I understand Martin Kao is now sitting in federal prison,” along with saying he “never had any communications with Senator Collins (or) her staff about Martin Kao and/or Navatek.”)
Seven days after the super PAC cashed the check from Kao’s shell company, one of Reed’s subordinates emailed a Navatek lobbyist asking for Kao’s phone number and said Collins “would like to call Martin to thank him,” ProPublica reported.
The Collins campaign and its manager, Steve Abbott, responded last week by saying they do “not believe” the senator ever called Kao. When the Portland Press Herald asked Wednesday if Collins herself would comment on whether she called Kao, campaign spokesperson Blake Kernen said it “does not appear in any of our records that this call was made.”
“Neither Susan Collins nor anyone who worked for her believes that she made a call,” Kernen said.
Would a federal investigation get reopened?
Since the ProPublica story came out, The New York Times and Washington Post have also each reported that the FBI in 2025 shut down its investigation revolving around Reed, Kao and Collins. The Times reported that senior bureau officials questioned Kao’s truthfulness, but ProPublica said that by the end of 2024, agents had “enough evidence to pursue a sweeping bribery probe that could ensnare top lawmakers of both political parties.”
Campaign finance experts said a renewed investigation is unlikely under Trump, who is serving his second and final term through 2028. Craig Holman, a government affairs lobbyist for the left-leaning consumer advocacy group Public Citizen, has helped states such as Illinois, New Jersey and Connecticut write their own “pay-to-play” legislation but said the Justice Department has the chief responsibility to prosecute bribery or contractor-related corruption.
“It is very unfortunate, though not surprising, that the Trump administration would step in and stop that investigation,” Holman said. “They just accept this as normal behavior.”

title: First National Bank Named A Best Place To Work In Maine
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
First National Bank has been named one of the 2026 Best Places to Work in Maine in the large employer category, which includes organizations with 250 or more U.S. employees.
This recognizes the bank among the state’s leading employers and reinforcing its commitment to creating a workplace where employees can grow, build meaningful careers, and make a difference in their communities.
The Best Places to Work in Maine program identifies and honors employers based on a research and survey process managed by Best Companies Group. Final rankings will be announced at the Best Places to Work in Maine awards celebration on Tuesday, Oct. 13.

title: Christa Pike is in critical condition after Tennessee’s failed execution attempt, her lawyers say
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — Christa Pike was in critical condition Thursday and receiving “lifesaving care” at a hospital, her lawyers said, a day after a failed attempt to execute her pushed Tennessee’s governor to halt further executions this year and order an independent review.
Pike, who was sentenced to death for a 1995 murder, was taken to a hospital Wednesday night after surviving a double dose of the drug Tennessee uses to execute prisoners.
“We don’t have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment,” attorney Randy Spivey said during a news conference. “But we know she is alive right now.”
The failed execution, which one death penalty expert described as unprecedented, led Republican Gov. Bill Lee to order a review, calling what happened “deeply disturbing” and indefinitely postponing Pike’s execution and another one that had been scheduled for this year. It also reignited the debate over the state’s execution procedures, including its single-drug lethal injections.
Spivey called the process cruel and torturous, saying he was “haunted” by watching and hearing Pike talking, singing and then snoring loudly during her more than 90 minutes in the death chamber. Her attorneys also said it was unclear if she might have suffered brain damage from being deprived of oxygen.
May Martinez, whose daughter was murdered by Pike and her boyfriend and who traveled to Nashville to watch the execution, was also upset.
“I didn’t get justice for my daughter,” Martinez told The Associated Press on Thursday.
“I watched the whole thing. She was awake. She was laughing. She was moving her head, moving her feet. She was trying to sit up,” Martinez said. “Didn’t work the first time they gave her a shot. It didn’t work the second time.”
A prolonged attempt ends in failure
It was not immediately clear what went wrong. Pike’s attorneys said there were a number of possibilities.
The execution team worked for an hour to administer the lethal drugs, said Spivey, who counted at least seven needles in her left arm.
During the struggle to locate a vein, Pike even suggested where they might find one, he said.
“Please try here, please try here,” Spivey recalled her saying. “She told them over and over, please try higher on my shoulder.”
At one point Pike asked prison officials if her arm was supposed to feel that way, though it’s unclear if it was after the first dose entered her body because officials don’t share that information.
Neither the initial nor the backup dose of pentobarbital worked. Pike was still snoring when the execution chamber’s microphone was cut off more than an hour into the attempt.
Another Pike attorney, Steve Ferrell, said she feared there would be complications because of a lifelong blood disorder that made it tough to get needles into her veins. “Throughout her life, she’s explained to us that she had trouble having blood drawn,” he said.
It was quite possible, Ferrell said, that the IV line didn’t enter her vein properly and the drug was filling her arm instead of entering her bloodstream.
Lee said it appeared prison staff followed procedure.
Attorneys seek commutation
Pike’s lawyers now want her death sentence to be commuted. Now age 50, she was sentenced to death for a murder she committed at 18. She would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.
An appeals court had stopped her execution an hour before it was scheduled to begin Wednesday morning, but the U.S. Supreme Court overturned that stay hours later.
It was the second time this year that the state was unable to complete an execution. In the other case, officials couldn’t find a suitable vein for an IV line so the drugs weren’t administered
Pentobarbital, the barbiturate Tennessee uses for executions, has been used to carry out death sentences in multiple states and by the federal government. But concerns have been raised about the potential for “unnecessary pain and suffering.”
Dr. Ervin Yen, an Oklahoma City anesthesiologist who has no link to Pike’s execution but has witnessed others, said it’s possible that if the prison staff was using a small vein, there could have been some burning, as mentioned by Pike’s attorneys.
“It just depends on the vein that you’re injecting it in and how fast you are injecting,” Yen said.
The state changed its execution method two years ago
In 2024, Tennessee switched from a three-drug series for lethal injections to a single drug, pentobarbital. That came about two years after the state abruptly halted the execution of Oscar Smith and acknowledged it had failed to ensure its lethal injection drugs had been tested properly.
Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said what Pike experienced is “singular and unparalleled” in that she survived long enough to be moved to a hospital.
Seven others have survived medical problems due to an execution team’s failure to access a vein to administer lethal injection drugs, but no one has stayed alive after receiving the drugs used in executions, she said.
Executions in the U.S. have fallen sharply since the beginning of this century, but the number nearly doubled last year behind a record increase in Florida.
Pike would have been the 30th person executed in the U.S. this year.
Awake in the death chamber
Strapped to a gurney, Pike described herself as at peace and said “I’m ready to be free. ... This is a happy day.”
But she remained awake, and at one point she complained about a feeling in her arm.
An hour after officials first raised the curtains, witnesses reported that a second dose of pentobarbital was administered. Pike could still be heard snoring behind a closed curtain until the microphone was cut off almost 30 minutes later.
Her lawyers filed an emergency motion with the Tennessee Supreme Court seeking to immediately halt and stay the execution, saying she was in “unnecessary agony” and the procedure violated her right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment.
Pike acknowledged her role in the killing
Pike and her boyfriend were convicted of the fatal stabbing of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a classmate. The killing stoked fears of Satan worship because of a pentagram carved on Slemmer’s body.
She didn’t dispute that she helped kill Slemmer, but supporters argued that her mental illness and allegations of severe sexual abuse should be considered. She was diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder after the killing.
“It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” she once said.
___
This story was updated to correct the spelling of Randy Spivey’s last name.
___
Associated Press writers Jeffrey Collins in Columbia, South Carolina, Ed White in Detroit, Russ Bynum in Savannah, Georgia, Hallie Golden in Seattle, Hannah Schoenbaum in Salt Lake City and John Seewer in Toledo, Ohio, contributed.

title: ICE is moving Maine detainees more quickly and farther away, report says
text:
Most people detained and processed by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in Maine are quickly moved out of state, according to a new analysis by an immigrant advocacy group.
After processing at the agency’s facility in Scarborough, 98% of the individuals detained this year amid the agency’s expanded efforts have been swiftly moved to facilities outside Maine, mostly in Massachusetts and New Hampshire, before commonly being transferred to sites in the South, the report says.
Detainees are also spending less time at any given facility, and so far this year, 90% of those processed in Scarborough have been moved within six hours of their initial detention.
The new data, which comes through public records requests to ICE from the Deportation Data Project and was analyzed by the Maine Immigrants’ Rights Coalition, underscores long-standing concerns by the attorneys and loved ones of those detained.
Those groups have argued that the agency swiftly moves detainees out of state, and even shifts them several times to several different facilities, making it harder to stay in contact or legally advocate.
ICE significantly grew its operations in Maine this year amid the Trump administration’s push to increase deportations. Immigration agents arrested hundreds during a surge in January, most with no criminal convictions, despite the agency’s claim that it only targets the “worst of the worst.”
In July, an agent in Biddeford fatally shot Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a 25-year-old father, who didn’t have a criminal history and wasn’t the target of enforcement that day, sparking widespread protest.
The Scarborough facility — ICE’s only one in Maine, since the agency pulled detainees from the Cumberland County Jail following criticism by the sheriff — has been the subject of frequent protest from residents advocating for its closure.
Hunter Cropsey, the programs and engagement manager at the coalition and a co-author of the report, said it was born out of requests from individuals in Scarborough who wanted more data to understand the relationship between the facility and their town.
The data also comes amid reports of a new forthcoming ICE facility in the Penobscot County town of Newport, although details remain scarce.
The report shows 293 detentions at the Scarborough facility between Jan. 1 and Aug. 5 of this year, a significant increase over prior years.
An analysis of data from 2024 to 2026 shows that while most people held at the Scarborough facility used to be held elsewhere in Maine after being processed, that shifted sharply in the last two years. Now, more than half go to Massachusetts as their next location, while 40% go to facilities in New Hampshire.
The most common next stops this year were in Plymouth, Massachusetts; Dover, New Hampshire; and Burlington, Massachusetts.
Later transfers often took detainees far from New England, primarily to Louisiana and Texas, but also to Arizona, Georgia and Ohio. Forty percent of those first processed in Scarborough spent some time in the Gulf states, according to the report.
After being processed in Maine, detainees this year spent time in a total of 30 facilities across 11 states, for an average of just 12.6 days at each site. That’s a significant change from 2024, when detainees spent an average of 46 days in a given facility.
Cropsey, the co-author, said the movement to those southern states is particularly notable because it’s less likely detainees would be released on bond and, statistically, an applicant’s likelihood of approval for asylum is lower.
But even just a move across the border to New Hampshire can cut off detainees from their support systems and their chances of a good legal defense, he said.
“This accelerated and widespread movement removes Mainers from their communities and support systems, creating severe hurdles for legal representation and family contact,” the report concludes. With planned increases in ICE enforcement and the proposed Newport facility, those patterns are likely to intensify, the report says.

title: Death Notice: Arlene E. (Towers) Cannon
Renee Good's family sues US government and immigration officials over her killing in Minneapolis
text:
Renee Good's family sues US government and immigration officials over her killing in Minneapolis
Renee Good's family sued the U.S. government and the architects of President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown on Thursday, saying “the time is absolutely now for accountability” after her killing in January by a federal agent in Minneapolis.
Good’s partner, Becca Good, and brother, Brent Ganger, accused the government and the Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer who shot into her SUV and killed her, Jonathan Ross, of unjustified and excessive use of force.
The Jan. 7 shooting, captured on bystander video, was “the predictable and intended product” of the Trump administration’s crackdown on Somali and other immigrants in Minnesota, an exercise that officials dubbed Operation Metro Surge, the lawsuit said.
“She was the love of my life,” Becca Good said at a news conference announcing the lawsuits. “I’m here today because last January, the whole world had to watch as our entire universe was destroyed — as the sunshine who was my amazing Renee was robbed from us, from her children, and from her community.”
Video below: Renee Good's partner says her "universe collapsed" after Good's killing
The killings of Good, a 37-year-old mother of three, and another U.S. citizen, Alex Pretti, in Minneapolis just weeks later sparked outrage across the country and calls to rein in immigration enforcement. At least 10 people have died in encounters with immigration officers during Trump’s second term.
The crackdown, a pillar of Trump’s second term, has prompted a slew of lawsuits filed by everyone from Chicago-area pastors to more than a dozen states and the cities of Minneapolis and St. Paul. Hundreds of protesters have been arrested, but few have been convicted of any crimes.
“What happened to Rene was completely senseless,” Ganger said. “And the fact that there’s been no accountability, no investigation, no expression of condolence, no change in policy is completely mind blowing.”
“The hole in my family and myself created by my sister’s passing is hauntingly apparent,” he added.
The lawsuits — one against the government, the other against Ross and officials including White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, ex-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and White House border czar Tom Homan — seek unspecified damages for wrongful death, conspiracy and other violations.
“Our government has become a grave and mortal threat to its own citizens,” the family’s lawyer, Antonio Romanucci said.
The Justice Department has not responded to an email seeking comment.
Officer shot Good as she turned her car away from him
Renee Good was killed while driving home with Becca on a street where masked federal immigration officers were conducting an enforcement operation, the lawsuits said. They had just dropped their six-year-old son off at school,
Renee stopped their SUV in the street and honked her horn to warn people about the operation while Becca got out and started recording video with her cellphone, the lawsuit said.
Bystander video shows Renee Good in the driver’s seat of a red SUV blocking part of the road and repeatedly honking her horn. Two immigration officers get out of a truck, their faces covered, and one orders Good to get out of the car. She reverses briefly, then turns the steering wheel as the officer says again, “get out of the car.”
Almost simultaneously, Becca Good, standing in the street, shouts: “Drive, baby, drive!”
GRAPHIC: New video shows ICE agent's perspective leading up to Renee Good's death
One officer standing in front of the vehicle pulls his weapon and fires into the windshield. He lurches back as the car turns away from him. The officer, who is now very close to the open window on the driver’s side, fires two more times, fatally shooting Renee Good, according to an analysis of the videos by The Associated Press and others.
Federal officials at the time said the officer acted in self-defense and that Good had engaged in “an act of domestic terrorism.”
Becca and Renee Good were not legally married, according to a family lawyer, but referred to one another as wives. They had only recently relocated to Minneapolis from Kansas City, Missouri.
“I don’t hate the people that took Renee from us,” Becca Good said.
“But what I want them to understand: Every single day they get to look at their children and their wives and their sisters and know what they took from our family. They took a mother away from her children. They know that. And they will carry it forever.”
Government tried to hide the truth, lawsuit says
The family’s wrongful death lawsuit against the U.S. government seeks damages for “the immense suffering” Good endured in the final moments of her life “and for the profound and permanent losses that her death has inflicted upon her family.”
The other lawsuit, against Ross and top federal immigration officials, paints Operation Metro Surge as a conspiracy to trample the civil rights of Somali and other immigrants and accuses the administration of targeting Becca instead of thoroughly investigating Good’s killing.
The government sought to hide evidence of what happened to Good, the lawsuit said, and senior officials were concerned that pursuing a civil rights investigation into the killing would undermine Trump’s claims that she had tried to kill an officer.
Operation Metro Surge, the lawsuit said, was a “carefully planned, coordinated effort” to make Somali and Hispanic immigrants “the object of aggression and abduction.” The crackdown, the lawsuit said, used intimidation, violence and the threat of arrest to intimidate neighbors and allies “who observed, documented and warned of that campaign.”
Other defendants include: Corey Lewandowski, a Trump campaign manager who also served as one of Noem’s advisers; former acting director of U.S. Immigrations and Customs Enforcement Todd Lyons; former U.S. Border Patrol commander Gregory Bovino; and 10 unnamed federal agents.
The news conference announcing the lawsuit was held in the atrium of University of St. Thomas School of Law, and dozens of law students stood on balconies of upper floors watching the family and lawyers speak.
“The time is absolutely now for accountability for the deep damage done by ICE and others,” Ganger said. “We will not be quiet. We will not go away.”
Good's partner acknowledges other lives lost in immigration crackdown
In social media accounts, Renee Good described herself as a “poet and writer and wife and mom.” On Pinterest, a profile picture shows her smiling and holding a young child, alongside posts about tattoos, hairstyles and home decorating.
In an interview shortly after her death, her mother, Donna Ganger, told The Associated Press: “She had this way of making you feel special and loved that I didn’t even understand that until we lost her.”
Good's partner noted the broader loss to communities nationwide.
“As we have tried to navigate our own massive loss, I am also devastated by how many other lives have been destroyed in this darkest of times,” Becca Good said in a news release Thursday. “So many other families are dealing with the loss of their loved ones; to everyone who has had to witness it — the pain of this moment extends far beyond our family. What happened to us should never happen to any family.”

title: From homemade bouquets to selling in supermarkets: Family opens flower shop after 20 years
text:
Family opens flower shop after 20 years of perseverance
A Dominican family in Pennsylvania has opened a flower shop inspired by their journey and a vision to serve the Hispanic community
Family opens flower shop after 20 years of perseverance
A Dominican family in Pennsylvania has opened a flower shop inspired by their journey and a vision to serve the Hispanic community
A Dominican family in Lancaster, Pennsylvania, has fulfilled a long-time dream by opening Rafaela’s Creations, a flower shop that debuted on Aug. 23 after years of hard work and community support.
A longtime dream takes root
"Her dream was to always open a flower shop," Selina Baez said about her mom.
The Baez family arrived in Lancaster from the Dominican Republic 20 years ago, starting from scratch. Reflecting on their early experiences, Selina Baez said. "When you first come, you feel like maybe you don't have the opportunity to do big things or create a business. We didn’t know a lot of Hispanics."
Meeting a gap in Hispanic grocery stores
The idea for the shop began when owner Matilde Baez noticed a lack of fresh flowers in local Hispanic grocery stores.
"I started visiting Hispanic supermarkets in the area and saw a need, because there were never flowers, never fresh flowers. We always had to go to big supermarkets to get a flower or bouquet we needed," Matilde Baez said.
She then pitched the idea of selling her homemade bouquets to those stores.
"From there, the idea was born to start making flowers for Hispanic supermarkets, for our Hispanic people," Matilde Baez said.
Today, the family sells their bouquets to 23 supermarkets across Lancaster, Harrisburg, York and Hazleton. These partnerships were just one part of their vision.
A business built petal by petal
"I'm really proud to be Dominican and opening a flower shop and, you know, representing Hispanics, and just the idea that you can do big things, doesn't matter where you come from," Selina Baez said.
The family’s dream of opening a brick-and-mortar shop is now blossoming before their eyes.
"You form a flower petal by petal. This space was formed petal by petal with our own effort, with the help of my children, with the help of my family," Matilde Baez said. "If it’s not a friend, it’s a neighbor. It’s your own family. Hispanics always have that — a big heart and mutual support."
The Baez family said they source many of their flowers from local vendors in Lancaster, while also conducting outreach in places like Ecuador and Miami. They said this outreach is a significant part of their business.

title: Stahl Award Presented To Town, Historical Society
text:
The Old Broad Bay Family History Association has given the Jasper J. Stahl Award to the Waldoborough Historical Society and the Waldoboro Cemetery Fund.
The Stahl Award recognizes individuals and groups within the Waldoboro community who work to preserve the genealogical and historical heritage of the town.
On July 31, Association President David Putnam presented a check for $250 dollars to Waldoborough Historical Society President Bill Maxwell in memory of the late Jean Lawrence, a former board member and honorary historian for the association and liaison to the historical society.

title: ‘Shouldn’t have taken 31 years’: Victim’s niece voices frustration before Christa Pike’s botched execution
text:
KNOXVILLE, Tenn. (WVLT/Gray News) - Colleen Slemmer’s niece said the process of executing Christa Pike should not have taken 31 years.
After learning the state was fighting to lift the stay, Seeley expressed both frustration with the delay and hope that the high court would finally deliver closure.
“It didn’t make sense how they stopped it an hour before she was supposed to go,” Seeley said. “I think that they had enough time out of the 31 years to be able to do this. Colleen is going to get justice today.”
Slemmer was 19 years old when she was killed in January 1995 after being lured to an isolated area on the University of Tennessee agricultural campus. Both Slemmer and Pike were enrolled in Job Corps at the time.
Pike and two co-defendants, Tadaryl Shipp and Shadolla Peterson, were convicted in 1996. Testimony showed the trio tortured Slemmer, carved a pentagram into her chest, and Pike kept a piece of Slemmer’s skull as a souvenir.
Members of Slemmer’s family traveled to the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville on Wednesday morning expecting the execution to take place, but the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals suddenly granted a stay.
Seeley said she spoke with her grandmother, May Martinez, by video call earlier in the day while the family prepared for what they hoped would be the end of a decadeslong legal fight.
Seeley’s mother, who was Slemmer’s sister, passed away in 2021, and Seeley’s stepfather traveled to the prison to stand in her place.
Seeley pushed back against Pike’s repeated legal attempts to overturn her death sentence or obtain clemency.
“It shouldn’t have taken 30, 31 years to be able to get this,” Seeley said. “Allowing somebody, what Christa did to my aunt, to allow her to live 31 years longer than her is heartbreaking.”
Tennessee officials were unable to execute Christa Gail Pike on Wednesday for the 1995 murder after administering two doses of a lethal drug.
Her attorneys filed an emergency motion to halt the execution, saying Pike was “still alive and snoring” after receiving the lethal injection Wednesday.
“The vein in my arm feels like it’s about to bust,” one witness recalled her saying.
The emergency motion filed Wednesday night stated that the execution was “causing Ms. Pike unnecessary agony and occurring in violation of [her] right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment.”

title: Meteor showers, planets, and the core of the Milky Way: Astronomical events for October 2026
text:
Meteor showers, planets, and the core of the Milky Way: Astronomical events for October 2026
The spookiest month is packed with things to see in the dark night skies
Meteor showers, planets, and the core of the Milky Way: Astronomical events for October 2026
The spookiest month is packed with things to see in the dark night skies
It’s the start of a supernatural season, and this month is packed with astronomical events to check out.
Related video above: Artemis II reveals a stunning view of the Milky Way
This month, we'll have plenty of chances to view the inner planets in the night sky and two separate chances to experience a meteor shower. We'll also have our last chance to observe the cosmic basket of stars that is our very own Milky Way Galaxy, and finish off the month with a Hunter's Moon.
Read below for the full list of astronomical events in October.
Oct. 4 — Saturn at opposition
This is the perfect time of year to spy the ringed planet. Saturn will be at opposition, which means it lies directly opposite the sun, rising during sunset and setting during sunrise. Saturn should be visible in the sky near its opposition and until its next solar conjunction, which is when it passes behind the sun in the sky. Its next solar conjunction is April 7, 2027.
Saturn will be visible with the naked eye, appearing as a bright, yellowish “star” that does not twinkle, just below the constellation Pisces. If you’d like to catch the planet’s rings, that will require a telescope.
Oct. 6 — Moon near Jupiter
Since the moon is the most prominent object in the night sky, it makes it super easy to find other objects nearby. This month, the king of planets nestles right next to the moon for a single morning — just look to the east in the pre-dawn sky and you should see a steady, cream-colored dot right next to the moon. If you look up from there, you should also be able to view Mars, just above the constellation Cancer. Bonus: if you make it out the morning of Oct. 5, Mars will instead sit closest to the moon.
Both Jupiter and Mars can be observed without equipment. However, if you would like to try to see some of Jupiter’s moons or even its Great Red Spot, you’ll need a basic telescope.
Oct. 8-9 — Draconid meteor shower
The Draconids are one of two annual meteor showers that fall in October. They are named for their radiant, or the point in the sky that they seem to originate from, the constellation Draco. The Draconids were previously called the Giacobinids, after the comet that causes the meteor shower, 21P/Giacobini-Zinner. In 1985, this comet also became the first to ever be explored by a space probe.
The Draconids are an occasional shower, according to NASA, and usually quite faint. Historically, they have been known to produce stunning meteor storms, which is when a comet throws off more than 1,000 meteors per hour. This has happened very rarely and inconsistently, with the next major Draconid meteor storm predicted for the year 2098, making the dragon a fickle beast. Still, if you find a good spot on a clear night, you may be able to catch a few streaks in the dark.
Oct. 10 — New moon (and the Milky Way core)
A new moon means a clear night, which means ideal conditions for stargazing. And that’s a good thing too, since this will be the last week to get a glimpse of the core of our Milky Way. It’s a stellar spread of many of the stars in our galaxy and appears as a brilliant crack in the night sky. The core should be visible shortly after nightfall, and you’ll have a few chances to try and catch it between Oct. 8-13. You can use this map to find a dark sky zone in your area for peak viewing conditions. Catch the core before it disappears from view for the winter.
Oct. 12 — Mercury at greatest elongation east
About every four months, we get a new chance to spot Mercury in the sky. Mercury can be challenging to view since it’s an inner-system planet that sits very close to the sun. The best chance to see it is during its greatest elongation, or the farthest distance from the sun from our perspective. Coming up is its greatest elongation east, meaning it will be farthest from the sun in our evening sky. We will have a quick chance to view Mercury shortly after sunset in the southwestern sky, just above the horizon and just beneath the constellation Libra.
Oct. 21-22 — Orionid meteor shower peaks
The second annual meteor shower of October, the Orionids are a more dependable shower than the Draconids. The Orionids’ radiant is the constellation Orion, specifically its bright star Betelgeuse. The meteors of the Orionids come from the debris of the comet Halley, which passes near Earth about every 76 years, but delivers two meteor showers to Earth’s atmosphere per year — the Orionids in the fall and the Eta Aquarids in May.
The Orionids are known to be bright and fast, and the fall weather usually makes for ideal conditions to view them. According to NASA, the Orionids can show up to 20 meteors per hour on a good night. The evening and early morning of Oct. 21-22 is just the peak — you may be able to see this shower anytime from Oct. 2 to Nov. 7.
Oct. 26 — Hunter’s Moon
The full moon of October is known as the Hunter’s Moon. According to The Old Farmer’s Almanac, the name "reflects the seasonal shift from gathering crops to preparing meat for winter," and was predominantly used in Anglo-Saxon cultures.
The Hunter’s Moon has some overlap with the Harvest Moon, sometimes being one and the same, depending on the seasonal cycle. For some American Indigenous peoples, the October full moon is the Harvest Moon (Cherokee, Passamaquoddy), while other native nicknames for the moon make mention of specific seasonal harvests. Other Indigenous names for the moon include the Falling Leaves Moon (Abenaki, Anishinaabe, Arapaho, Lakota), the Moon of the Wildcat (Choctaw), the Moon When the Birds Fly South (Cree), the Big Chestnut Moon (Creek), the Wilted Moon (Shawnee), and the Big Wind Moon (Zuni).

title: Millions in Amazon settlement payouts are rolling out. Are you eligible?
text:
(Gray News) - Automatic payments as part of an expanded federal settlement over billing and cancellation practices involving Amazon have reportedly started going out.
Last month, the Federal Trade Commission announced that Amazon was accelerating and widening consumer refund payouts stemming from a $2.5 billion deceptive enrollment settlement.
Under the historic September 2025 settlement of the FTC’s allegations, Amazon was required to pay up to $1.5 billion in redress to consumers harmed by the company’s deceptive Prime enrollment practices in addition to a $1 billion civil penalty.
According to the FTC, those automatic payments started rolling out Thursday via PayPal, Venmo or mailed check.
The eligibility requirement also expanded beyond low-use subscribers to include millions who used between 11 and 20 Prime benefits over a one-year period.
“The revised order will ensure more consumers who were harmed by Amazon’s deceptive enrollment and cancellation practices benefit from the FTC’s historic settlement,” Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, said.
Additionally, the individual payment cap could be as high as $200.
Those who have already cashed earlier checks could see an additional automatic supplemental payment of up to $149 starting in April 2027.
The settlement noted that customers do not have to file any claims or forms.
But the FTC warned that anyone reaching out claiming to be from the agency or asking for money or personal banking details to claim a refund is running a potential scam.

title: Wildflower Walk at Autumn View Preserve
text:
Thursday, Oct. 1 
In the early fall, you can still find wildflowers blooming in the meadows and woodlands of the Boothbay region. Join botanist and Boothbay Region Land Trust volunteer Lauren Stockwell for a leisurely guided walk at our newest preserve, Autumn View Farm from 10 to 11:30 a.m. As we explore the trails, Lauren will help participants identify a variety of common wildflowers and highlight the unique features and adaptations of each plant.
This is an easy-paced walk with uneven surfaces suitable for all ages with an interest in the natural world. The event is free and registration is required by filling out the form at https://bbrlt.org/event/fall-wildflower-walk-at-autumn-view-preserve/ or calling the BRLT office at 633-4818.

title: Lincoln Academy golf wins tight battle for KVAC B title, state bid
text:
ROCKLAND — Considered the favorites to win the Kennebec Valley Athletic Conference Class B Shootout, the Lincoln Academy golf team had to work for it Thursday.
In the end, the Eagles did prevail, beating out Nokomis and Medomak Valley to win the conference title at Rockland Golf Club. The win secured Lincoln a spot in the Class B championships next Saturday at Natanis Golf Course in Vassalboro.
“Our boys have had a great season — they really have — and they did excellent today,” said Lincoln coach Todd Brackett. “Nokomis has a really good team, and they beat us in the regular season. Medomak, we have a good rivalry with them. We knew it was going to be close.”
Lincoln’s top-four players shot a combined nine-hole score of 162, beating out the Warriors (166) and the Panthers (167) in a tight battle for first. Belfast (181), Leavitt (183) and Erskine Academy (188) rounded out the team scoring.
Lincoln junior Drew Nichols (38) shot the second-best score of the day, finishing a stroke behind medalist Caden Chretien of Nokomis (37). Colin Mitchell shot a 39 for the Eagles to tie Medomak Valley’s Seb Mank and Joseph Wilcox for third.
“My short game was really solid,” Nichols said. “Off the tee, I was a little iffy — I actually topped my driver twice, so that was interesting — but with how good my short game was, I was able to get around the golf course. … I had a really rough go of it this season, so I’m glad I brought it around here.”
Max Blake added a 41 for Lincoln, while Dylan Lomas shot a 44. That was enough to outduel Nokomis, which also got a 42 from Atticus Haining, a 43 from Will Hayes and a 44 from Jake Paradis, and Medomak Valley, which got a 44 from Andrew Flanders and a 45 from Wyatt Hood.
“If anybody was going to steal it from us today, I thought it was going to be Medomak,” Brackett said. “Like I said, we just played great today. It was a good day for us out there.”
A warm October day that saw temperatures reach the upper 60s even on the coast made for an enjoyable round of golf. The winds from earlier in the week had largely subsided, though some stiffer gusts did arrive later into the afternoon.
Medomak Valley had the fortune of playing the round on its home course, though coach Kevin Richardson pointed out that changing greens throughout the week mitigated that advantage. Richardson, too, said the three-way race between Medomak Valley, Lincoln and Nokomis played out as expected.
“In all 10 regular-season matches that we played (until today), we had the medalist, which shows you that Lincoln and Nokomis both have some really good players,” Richardson said. “We played well all year, and I had a feeling we were going to play well today. We did, but it just wasn’t quite enough.”
Nokomis, Medomak Valley, Belfast, Leavitt and Erskine will still get chances to book berths at states at the KVAC qualifier Tuesday at Natanis. Lincoln can rest easy that its state championship participation is assured, though Nichols said the Eagles’ absence Tuesday will also have some drawbacks.
“We’d like to go to the qualifier to get that extra round in, but it’s also quite the plus that we get to have that auto-bid,” Nichols said. “We’re a good group of guys that play a lot and put the work in over the summer, so it feels great.”
Jason Thurston of Belfast tied for seventh individually, shooting a 42. James Brisson shot a 44 to lead Leavitt, while Blake Morrow and Nolan Pierce also shot 44s to lead Erskine.

title: Decades-old fight over Down East gravel road is heading back to court
text:
This story appears as part of a collaboration to strengthen investigative journalism in Maine between the BDN and The Maine Monitor. Read more about the partnership.
MACHIASPORT, Maine — A shorefront road in Starboard at the Point of Maine remains at the center of a decadeslong dispute over its ownership and maintenance.
The town now faces a motion for a new trial filed in late August by Starboard residents Carmine and Christine DeFalco and Paula Aschettino, who previously alleged that Machiasport failed to comply with an agreement governing the road.
After a civil trial in May, the court issued a judgment in favor of Machiasport, finding that the town complied with an earlier ruling recognizing its ownership of the easement under certain regulatory conditions. The town announced the judgment on Facebook in July.
In their motion, filed in late August in the Business & Consumer Docket in Portland, Carmine DeFalco and the other plaintiffs allege that the town failed to disclose a relationship between District Court Judge Michael A. Duddy and Town Clerk Marcia Hayward, a key witness for Machiasport.
Portland lawyer Keith Richard of Archipelago Law Team filed the motion.
The road has gone by many names over the years, including Starboard Road, Starboard Island Road, Shore Road, Beach Road and Port Road.
In a July Facebook post, the town said that Duddy, who was appointed by then-Gov. Paul LePage in January 2017, had ruled in the town’s favor in the decadeslong dispute over the road’s ownership in Machiasport.
“We would like to share the news that the Court has found that the Town of Machiasport complied in all respects with the 1997 judgment governing its responsibilities for the Port Road in Starboard. The Court has entered a judgment in favor of the Town,” the post said.
The plaintiffs dispute that conclusion. They allege that the road’s deteriorating condition remains an ongoing problem and say the town has not fully complied with the 1997 settlement, which required it to follow an improvement plan developed with the assistance of James Beyer of the Maine Department of Environmental Protection to stabilize the right of way.
The improvement plan, which Carmine DeFalco provided to Monitor Local, requires the town to take steps to prevent erosion, including installing riprap in all areas not protected by natural bedrock. DeFalco told Monitor Local that the town had not completed that work on his property.
During a tour of the property, DeFalco pointed to locations where riprap had not been installed. He said the area is prone to flooding and erosion because of a steep granite ledge.
The question of ownership first became a legal issue in the late 1980s, when resident Bruce Sprague allegedly used a bulldozer to clear a stretch of his neighbor’s property and create the road he claimed was his right of way, according to court filings. Sprague died in 2005.
Court records and case files allege that the work was done without the property owner’s permission and did not comply with state and local laws, ordinances and environmental requirements enforced by agencies including the Maine Department of Environmental Protection.
Beyer, who works in the Department of Environmental Protection’s Division of Enforcement and Field Services within the Bureau of Land Quality, investigated the road’s compliance with the department’s standards and identified several concerns.
In an official letter, Jeffrey Lovitt, a lawyer who represented a group of landowners in lawsuits against Sprague during the 1990s, wrote, “While certainly the determination by the Department of Environmental Protection is not definitive as to the issue of legal access, at least there was a preliminary determination that Mr. Sprague had no legal right to use the ‘right of way.’”
By the mid-1990s, the initial lawsuit had run its course. Following a state investigation, the homeowners, Sprague and the town reached an agreement under which Machiasport would assume responsibility for the road’s right of way. At the time, the road was surveyed as a 16.5-foot-wide stretch of gravel running along the shoreline.
Under the agreement, Machiasport became responsible for correcting the environmental problems identified by the state as a condition of assuming responsibility for the right of way.
In July, the court issued a judgment in favor of the town in a lawsuit brought by the DeFalcos and their neighbor, Aschettino. The plaintiffs alleged that the town had violated the earlier agreement, including by failing to maintain the road.
Duddy found that the town had complied with all provisions of the Starboard improvement plan, which was drafted in 1994 and incorporated into the 1997 agreement. Those provisions included maintaining access to homes and property at the Point of Maine and Starboard Island, preventing erosion along Beach Road, and preserving historic Beach Road and Starboard Beach for future generations.
The plan also called for permanent riprap in areas not protected by natural bedrock. It specified using granite ledge with a weathered face from the Point of Maine to create a natural appearance, placing the granite in designated areas according to an approved cross-section plan, and installing filter fabric to prevent silting.
The plan required workers to dig a drainage ditch along the inland side of the road so water could flow into new culverts. It also called for removing a protruding ledge identified in the plan and blocking a natural drainage channel.
The first phase required the designated contractor to complete all work except the riprap installation as soon as the contractor could bring equipment to the site. The plan estimated that the work would take two days.
The second phase of the plan would be required only if there was not enough granite to complete the work. In that case, the remaining work, including the remaining riprap installation, would be completed the following year.
In a new motion filed by Carmine DeFalco, his wife, Christine, and their neighbor, Aschettino, Richard asserts that “a connection between the Town Clerk Marcia Hayward and the jurist in this matter” was not disclosed to the plaintiffs. The jurist is Duddy.
According to Richard, the plaintiffs became concerned after learning that Hayward and Duddy had been high school classmates several decades before the trial. The motion notes that Hayward served as a key witness for the town. It also states that Hayward and Duddy grew up in Calais, lived near each other and had family members who worked in law enforcement.
The plaintiffs’ motion argues that the connection required Duddy to recuse himself because, under state law and judicial standards, “A judge shall disqualify or recuse himself or herself in any proceeding in which the judge’s impartiality might be reasonably questioned.”
Richard argues that the court can and should revisit the judgment before entering it as final.
In an email shared with Monitor Local, Carmine DeFalco said he grew up in New Jersey and worked at the World Trade Center. He said he became a first responder after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks and later moved to Machiasport.
DeFalco said the attacks prompted him to seek a safer place for his family. When he bought a house in Starboard, he said, he believed the original agreement between the town and the Department of Environmental Protection had resolved questions about the right of way and road maintenance.
By the time he moved in, however, the town had expanded the road from the original 16.5-foot easement conveyed to the town to more than 30 feet, DeFalco said.
According to G.F. Johnston & Associates, a Southwest Harbor civil engineering and land-use consulting firm hired in 2022, the gravel roadway “is in active state of failure.” DeFalco claims the road’s condition led to subsequent flooding and damage to his property. He also alleges that the town placed easements on his land that overlap his beachfront property.
The town’s 1997 agreement states that Machiasport is responsible for preserving the beach and must “preserve the historic Beach Road and Starboard beach for future generations.” That provision remains a point of contention between the parties.
In April, Carmine DeFalco wrote to Maine State Fire Marshal Shawn Esler, alleging that the road violated “the Maine Infrastructure and Adaptation Fund funding requirements of safe, unobstructed, free of hazard and environmental impact passage.”
DeFalco said the road serves as the sole access point to a 600-acre housing development in Starboard’s historic district and lies in a flood zone.
“This appears to be a defiance of those stipulations and the mission statement of Selectmen for safe passage,” DeFalco wrote.
Monitor Local confirmed that the road lies in a regulated flood zone and appears in Zone VE on Federal Emergency Management Agency flood maps, which the town updated in 2017. According to FEMA, properties in Zone VE have a “26 percent chance of flooding over the life of a 30-year mortgage.”
Carmine DeFalco also asserts that no historic road ever crossed the shorefront portion of his property. Instead, he said, the historic road ran farther inland, above the present-day Beach Road. He cited old photographs of the property and historic maps to support his claim.
A clerk for the Washington County Superior Court confirmed that the town filed a response to the motion by the September deadline.
Hayward, the town clerk, and the town’s attorney, Stephen Wagner of the Bangor law firm Rudman Winchell, did not respond to requests for comment.

title: Cardiac ICU nurse bikes across New England for healthcare worker mental health
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - An endurance athlete and cardiac intensive care unit nurse is biking hundreds of miles across New England to support healthcare worker mental health and suicide prevention.
Jenn Walsh began a 926-mile bicycle ride this week in Madawaska, with plans to finish the journey on Cape Cod. Walsh is raising funds and awareness through the Dr. Lorna Breen Heroes Foundation.
Walsh stopped in Bangor along her route, noting that demands placed on healthcare professionals remain high and that she hopes to reduce the stigma associated with seeking mental health support.
“The strongest thing someone can do is take a step back,” Walsh said. “And in healthcare, we’re kind of taught the opposite—it’s just to keep pushing and pushing and pushing. And in sport, you kind of do that too.”
Walsh is scheduled to finish the ride this weekend at Race Point Beach in Provincetown, Massachusetts.
Donations to support the ride and foundation can be made through Walsh’s GoFundMe campaign.
