title: Dancing with hearts, they share the love with Portland
text:
You’ll know they’re out dancing in Portland’s Longfellow Square long before you see them.
First, you’ll hear drivers honking their horns in support. Next, their music will reach you — an upbeat mix of ’80s pop, contemporary club remixes and the occasional Beatles song. Then, you’ll see the group of about a half dozen members, jumping and swaying on the street corner with large, brightly-colored hearts in hand.
They hope that last, maybe, you’ll join them for a dance.
Gathering in either Longfellow Square or Congress Square Park three days a week with their tunes and hearts, Love Signs is partially an art installation, somewhat a demonstration, certainly a celebration and undoubtably a solid hour of exercise, said the group’s steadfast participants.
Love Signs sometimes gets misunderstood as a cult or as having religious or political aims. The goal is much more simple, said organizer Krista Love (yes, she legally changed her last name to Love a few years ago). They just want to draw attention to love.
“We’re saying yes and celebrating something that we wanna see more of in the world,” said Love.
While they can be met with indifference, more often Love Signs members see passerby reflect their message back to them with honks, peace signs, smiles and — by the brave, joyous few — an accompanying shimmy on the street.

title: Troy Jackson says sorry for comments on Jewish Mainers’ views on Gaza war
text:
Troy Jackson told media outlets across the country that he was sorry for saying Jewish Mainers “don’t like to” call Israel’s war against Hamas in Gaza a genocide, “only because they’re Jewish and what that means to them with the Holocaust.”
Jackson made the initial comments to News Center Maine on Tuesday. He called the three-year war — which began with Hamas terrorist attacks on Oct. 7, 2023, and has since resulted in the killing of 70,000 Palestinians by Israeli forces in Gaza — a genocide, and continued on to say Jewish Mainers “don’t like to use that term.”
“I apologize for the pain that caused,” Jackson said in a statement. “Mainers hold a range of deeply considered views, and I promise I will always listen and work to approach these conversations with the care and respect they deserve.”
Jackson reiterated his belief that “what’s happening in Gaza is a genocide.”
“In trying to acknowledge that, I misspoke and made a generalization about Jewish Mainers’ views that doesn’t reflect what I meant to say,” his statement continued.
In the News Center Maine interview, Jackson also called Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, a war criminal. The International Criminal Court, to which the U.S. is not a signatory, issued an arrest warrant against Netanyahu in 2024 for starving people in Gaza as a means of war and ordering the killing of civilians.
A United Nations commission first found that Israel was committing genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza strip in September 2025. More than 64,000 children have been killed or injured in Gaza since October 2023, the U.N. said in August.
Like his predecessor for the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate, Graham Platner, Jackson’s use of the word “genocide” to describe Israel’s actions in Gaza is part of a larger call to stop arms funding to Israel. Brown University found that the U.S. sent $21.7 billion in military aid to Israel from October 2023 to September 2025 — for which Republican Sen. Susan Collins, Jackson’s incumbent opponent, has consistently voted.
“I don’t want the United States sending money, a blank check to (Netanyahu) anymore, watching young children, innocent people die,” Jackson told News Center Maine. “I mean, I just disagree with that.”

title: Drug Trafficking Investigation Underway In Cornish After Main Street Bust
text:
Cornish Woman Arrested After Authorities Say They Found Her With Cash, Guns & $5K In Drugs
A woman from Cornish has been arrested after a multi-agency drug bust netted guns, cash, and $5K worth of illegal product in York County.
Read More: Maine State Police Search For Suspect After Skowhegan Drug Stop
The Maine Department of Public Safety says 52-year-old Adele Rogers was taken into custody Thursday afternoon after MDEA agents and the Maine State Police Tactical Team searched a property at 355 Main Street in Cornish and found a multitude of drugs and drug paraphernalia.
Authorities say they've had their eye on the area, suspecting that a drug trafficking organization had set up in the small York County town.
During their several-month investigation, evidence was collected and surveillance completed enough for a judge to issue law enforcement agents a warrant.
"The search resulted in the seizure of 49.5ggw Cocaine HCL, diverted Hydrocodone pills, $1760.00 in suspected drug proceeds and three firearms. Rogers was taken into custody without incident at the residence...The estimated street value of the drugs seized is $5000."
We're told Rogers is facing four counts of aggravated drug trafficking and is being held at the York County Jail on $50,000 cash bail.
Read More: Ellsworth, Maine Police Arrest Suspect In 2024 Terrorizing Case
Authorities say the drug trafficking activity in Cornish is still under investigation, and they expect to arrest more people in connection with this case.
They ask community members to remain vigilant and report any suspicious or drug-related activity to authorities. You can call the MDEA Tip Line directly at 1-800-452-6457 or reach out to them by texting MDEA to TIP411.

title: Enjoy the Warmth Today — Rain Arrives Friday
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - High pressure... centered to our south... will usher some warmer air into the region today. We’ll see a mix of sun and clouds for the day with temperatures climbing to the low to mid-70s away from the coast. Temperatures for coastal areas will be in the mid to upper 60s due to a southerly breeze off the ocean. A cold front will approach the state tonight. We’ll see partly to mostly cloudy skies for the night and most areas will stay dry but there will be an increasing chance for rain towards daybreak... mainly over northern and western locales. Temperatures will be on the warmer side tonight with lows in the mid-50s to low 60s.
A cold front will cross through the state during the day Friday. This will bring us a quick round of rainfall... first across the northern half of the state during the morning then spreading southward across the remainder of the state during the afternoon. There could be some heavier downpours in spots but overall the rain doesn’t look too impressive with most areas only seeing .10″ or less by Friday evening with higher amounts maybe closer to .5″ if we manage to see some heavier downpours. Despite the clouds and the rainfall... temperatures will still feel pretty good with highs in the 60s north and low to mid-70s elsewhere. Rain will move out Friday evening followed by clearing skies as the night progresses. Cooler... more seasonable air will move in behind the cold front for the upcoming weekend. High pressure will give us a beautiful day Saturday with sunshine and highs in the upper 50s to mid-60s. Sunday looks good too with partly to mostly sunny skies and temperatures in the mid-50s to low 60s for highs. Showers chances return to our forecast for Monday.

title: Dunlap, LePage take the debate stage for first time in 2nd Congressional District race
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Democrat Matt Dunlap and Republican Paul LePage went toe-to-toe Thursday night in their first debate in the 2nd Congressional District race.
LePage, 77, the former governor, and Dunlap, 61, the state auditor and former secretary of state, are just over a month away from the Nov. 3 election to decide who will succeed Democratic Rep. Jared Golden, who did not seek reelection.
A recent poll conducted by the University of New Hampshire Survey Center found Dunlap with a 51% to 45% edge over LePage, with 5% of respondents undecided.
Unsurprisingly, Dunlap and LePage disagreed on a number of topics during Thursday night’s debate televised by WMTW, but both continuously argued their agendas would be more effective in meeting a common goal: affordability.
Healthcare took the spotlight on many occasions throughout the debate. On questions regarding MaineCare, the state’s Medicaid program, LePage said he would attempt to raise reimbursement rates, while Dunlap said he supports expanding the program.
Early on, both candidates were asked what bill they’d introduce first, if elected. Dunlap said his first piece of legislation would focus on healthcare access and affordability, such as restoring tax subsidies for the Affordable Care Act. LePage said he would introduce a bill to increase access to dental care for veterans.
A number of Democratic candidates this cycle have made a Medicare for All system a cornerstone of their campaign, but Dunlap didn’t fully embrace it Thursday night. He highlighted some of the benefits and said he would “certainly encourage the country to go in that direction,” while cautioning it would take a long time to fully implement.
LePage, meanwhile, bashed the idea, claiming it would do away with private healthcare and services would get “rationed.”
They also disagreed on tariffs. Dunlap argued that the trade war with Canada is detrimental to American citizens, while LePage argued “we’ve gotten a bad deal for many years,” but the two allies need to come to a resolution.
The two differed even while finding common ground on several topics, including the war in Iran. Both, for instance, said they don’t support the war, but LePage said he doesn’t support a war powers act, while Dunlap does.
Both agreed that housing production could be boosted by better supporting those who make the housing. However, Dunlap said he’d help make finances more accessible for housing developments, while LePage said he’d focus on improving the permitting process and regulations.
Dunlap and LePage also agreed that caps on Social Security contributions should be raised, and that Congress should have at least some oversight on the development of artificial intelligence. They differed on data centers, with LePage saying that should be decided on the local level and Dunlap arguing federal, state and local governments need to work together on the issue.
Perhaps the most stark difference between the two candidates was their attitudes toward President Donald Trump.
Multiple times throughout the debate, including in his opening statement, LePage touted his ability to call upon Trump. He said the first thing he’d do, if elected, would be to request that Trump “put restrictions on sending diesel to foreign countries.” He also said he’d call him before the election to make that suggestion.
During a response to a question on the trade war with Canada, LePage suggested, “I can help the president because I can speak French to the prime minister.”
“I will be able to get into the Oval Office; my opponent will not,” LePage said.
As for Dunlap, he repeatedly critiqued Trump’s policies and argued Congress needs to reel the president in.
“The job of Congress is to provide oversight of the executive branch,” he said regarding the war in Iran.

title: FIRST ALERT WEATHER: Showers Return Friday, Much Cooler Weekend Ahead
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Good evening everyone and happy Thursday. We kicked off October on a warm note across northern Maine today, but changes are already beginning to take shape as our next cold front approaches from the west. Clouds will continue to build tonight, with scattered showers developing after midnight before becoming much more widespread Friday morning. Rainfall from this system will be welcome considering the ongoing drought, but totals remain fairly limited. Behind the front, noticeably cooler air settles into the region for the weekend, with another round of frost expected Saturday night into Sunday morning.
Showers will initially move into northwestern portions of the region overnight before spreading across the rest of Aroostook County Friday morning. The latest rainfall forecast from the Weather Prediction Center generally keeps totals around or below a quarter of an inch across northern Maine through the weekend. Locally higher amounts cannot completely be ruled out, but this does not look like a particularly significant rainmaker.
That means Friday’s rainfall is unlikely to provide much improvement to our ongoing drought conditions. Showers will be most widespread during the morning and early afternoon before gradually tapering off from northwest to southeast later in the day.
The latest Drought Monitor released Thursday shows no change across Aroostook County compared to last week, with the entire county remaining in moderate drought. While we have picked up some rainfall over the past week, it simply has not been enough to overcome the longer-term moisture deficit across the region. With Friday’s system only expected to produce relatively light rainfall, meaningful drought relief remains unlikely in the short term.
Friday will be the unsettled day of the upcoming stretch, with widespread showers expected, especially during the morning hours. Temperatures will still remain relatively mild, but once the cold front passes through, cooler and drier air quickly takes over.
Saturday looks much nicer weather-wise, with plenty of sunshine returning across northern Maine. The tradeoff will be cooler temperatures, with highs generally only reaching the mid 50s to around 60 degrees. Sunday starts off very chilly before a mixture of sunshine and clouds develops during the afternoon.
Saturday night will likely be one of the colder nights we’ve seen in a few days. Low temperatures across much of Aroostook County are expected to fall into the upper 20s and lower 30s, with widespread frost likely by Sunday morning. Anyone with sensitive vegetation still outside will want to keep that in mind heading into the weekend.
The cooler weather arrives just as fall colors continue to rapidly advance across northern Maine. Explore Fall’s latest foliage forecast shows peak color developing across a large portion of northern and western Aroostook County, including areas around Fort Kent and west toward the North Woods. Farther south and east, high to moderate color remains more common.
Saturday and much of Sunday should provide some good opportunities to get outside and enjoy the foliage, especially with dry weather and increasing sunshine expected. There may also be some urgency to enjoy the colors while they last, as another system early next week could bring both rain and increasingly gusty winds.
Foliage data courtesy of Explore Fall - ExploreFall.com
The temperature trend over the next several days really shows the transition deeper into fall. After highs in the upper 60s around Caribou Friday, temperatures fall back into the upper 50s Saturday before briefly recovering into the lower 60s Sunday. Another system arrives Monday, followed by a stronger push of cold air Tuesday, when highs may struggle to reach 50 degrees.
There is still considerable uncertainty surrounding Monday’s system and exactly how much rain it may produce. Confidence is increasing, however, that gusty west to northwest winds will develop behind it Tuesday. Current guidance suggests gusts over 35 mph may become possible, and with parts of northern Maine reaching peak foliage, those winds could result in significant leaf loss. We’ll continue to fine-tune those details over the next several days.
For more details on Friday’s showers, the chilly weekend ahead and our next system early next week, make sure to check out this evening’s First Alert Video Forecast attached to this article. Have a great evening!

title: Pennsylvania records a fifth measles death as the nation endures its worst year since 1991
text:
Pennsylvania records a fifth measles death as the nation endures its worst year since 1991
Pennsylvania health officials reported a fifth measles-associated death Wednesday as the U.S. endures its worst year for the disease since 1991.
Video: Get the Facts: Proposed changes to the childhood vaccine schedule
The Pennsylvania Department of Health said the person was from Lancaster County and was unvaccinated. The state did not provide any further information about the person who died. Lancaster County’s coroner, Dr. Stephen Diamantoni, said that his office did not handle the death and that state officials have not provided him with any details.
The state's other deaths have included an 18-year-old resident of Mifflin County, in the center of the state; a 40-year-old woman from Jefferson County, a rural area in western Pennsylvania; and two infants in Lancaster County, in the southeastern part of the state.
None of them were vaccinated, according to the state health department. The infants were too young for vaccinations, according to current recommendations.
The U.S. has now seen eight reported measles-associated deaths in the last two years — more than the combined total of reported deaths over the previous three decades.
Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak continues to grow, with 943 illnesses reported so far this year across 39 counties. The measles-associated deaths are the first reported in the state in 35 years, state officials say.
The nation eliminated the domestic spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but they have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks. Meanwhile, measles infections have been surging in recent years.
In November, international health officials will meet to determine if the U.S. and Mexico have lost their measles-free status.
The problem has been years in the making, as fewer kids get routine vaccines because of parental waivers, healthcare access issues and rampant disinformation. More recently, Trump administration health officials, including Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., have questioned and sown doubt about the established safety of vaccines at an unprecedented level while also defunding local efforts to improve vaccination rates.

title: Nashville Singer-Songwriter to Debut at Waldo Theatre Feb. 13
text:
Nashville-based singer-songwriter and multi-instrumentalist Gabe Dixon will make his debut at The Waldo Theatre in Waldoboro at 7:30 p.m. on Saturday, Feb. 13.
Born and raised in Tennessee, Dixon first emerged on the music scene in 1999 and has been penning honest and heartfelt songs that continue to garner fans and crowds across the globe.

title: Millions in Amazon settlement payouts are rolling out. Are you eligible?
text:
(Gray News) - Automatic payments as part of an expanded federal settlement over billing and cancellation practices involving Amazon have reportedly started going out.
Last month, the Federal Trade Commission announced that Amazon was accelerating and widening consumer refund payouts stemming from a $2.5 billion deceptive enrollment settlement.
Under the historic September 2025 settlement of the FTC’s allegations, Amazon was required to pay up to $1.5 billion in redress to consumers harmed by the company’s deceptive Prime enrollment practices in addition to a $1 billion civil penalty.
According to the FTC, those automatic payments started rolling out Thursday via PayPal, Venmo or mailed check.
The eligibility requirement also expanded beyond low-use subscribers to include millions who used between 11 and 20 Prime benefits over a one-year period.
“The revised order will ensure more consumers who were harmed by Amazon’s deceptive enrollment and cancellation practices benefit from the FTC’s historic settlement,” Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, said.
Additionally, the individual payment cap could be as high as $200.
Those who have already cashed earlier checks could see an additional automatic supplemental payment of up to $149 starting in April 2027.
The settlement noted that customers do not have to file any claims or forms.

title: Manager Chad Tracy’s decisions questioned after Yankees eliminate Red Sox
text:
NEW YORK — With the Boston bats ice cold at Yankee Stadium again, a couple of quick hooks by Red Sox rookie manager Chad Tracy led to another early postseason exit.
And top starter Sonny Gray wasn’t happy about being lifted after only 70 pitches.
“I think I’m the best pitcher in the American League going through the order the third time. I think that’s a fact,” Gray said. “I would have liked to have been trusted in that moment.”
For the second consecutive season, the Red Sox were sent home for the winter by their biggest rivals as the New York Yankees rolled to a 9-2 victory Wednesday night and a two-game sweep of their Wild Card Series.
Boston was outscored 18-2 overall and left to lament a miserable finish to this roller-coaster ride of a season that included Tracy taking over when Alex Cora was fired in April.
Tracy’s decision-making came under scrutiny after both playoff games against the Yankees. In Boston’s 9-0 defeat a night earlier, Tracy pulled rookie starter Payton Tolle after 4 2/3 innings and 83 pitches in a 1-0 game.
Last year, the Red Sox won their Wild Card Series opener before losing to New York in a deciding Game 3 as they got overpowered by Cam Schlittler, who pitched another playoff gem against his hometown team Tuesday night.
“To have it end here two times in a row is tough,” shortstop Trevor Story said.
Facing a Yankees lineup missing injured slugger Aaron Judge, the Red Sox gave up 26 hits in two games despite a pair of effective performances from their starting pitchers.
At the plate, Boston mustered only seven hits and finally snapped a 26-inning postseason scoring drought that dated to last year when Willson Contreras homered just over the right-center fence in the sixth Wednesday.
“It’s obviously been an eventful year,” Tracy said. “In the moment right now you can’t think much more other than anything but the fact that we just lost a playoff series.”
Needing a victory to extend their season, the Red Sox sent Gray to the mound and the 18-game winner certainly gave them a chance. Boston trailed 1-0 in the fifth when the right-hander allowed a two-out single to Ben Rice that put runners at the corners.
Tracy then yanked Gray, eager to hand the ball to baseball’s best bullpen during the regular season.
“I felt good. You know, I felt crisp. I felt sharp. I felt like I was just out there competing. And yeah, I mean, I got clipped for a solo homer and then some singles, but I felt like I stayed on the attack throughout. I was just executing what I wanted to do,” Gray said. “I’m frustrated, for sure. You know, not ready for it to end. A lot of emotions.”
Asked about the move, Contreras put his finger over his lips to zip them shut.
“It’s not enough when you have talent or you have data or you have computers that’s telling you what to do, because this is baseball,” he said. “The data is here to help us, but at the end of the day you are going to have to need experience and veteran guys to win games.”
In both games of the series, Tracy gave the ball to left-handed reliever Erik Miller after taking out his starting pitcher.
On Tuesday, Rice greeted Miller with a 423-foot solo homer to straightaway center field.
On Wednesday, Tracy summoned Miller to face a different left-handed hitter, Cody Bellinger — who batted .274 against lefties this season and .259 versus right-handers. In fact, his .310 batting average against left-handers over the past two years was the best of any left-handed hitter in the majors.
Bellinger made Tracy and the Red Sox pay, lining an RBI single to right field.
“We’re struggling to score runs,” Tracy said. “And when you get in spots where you’re struggling to score runs and you’re already trailing, you feel like you’ve got to be aggressive and go.”
Back from a shoulder injury, ace starter Garrett Crochet entered in the sixth for his first outing since April 25 and first relief appearance since 2023 with the Chicago White Sox. The left-hander opened with a strikeout, but Spencer Jones reached safely on a wild pitch, and Crochet never got an out.
Bellinger’s three-run homer off right-hander Garrett Whitlock capped a six-run inning that made it 8-1, and the Red Sox were done. A bullpen that led the majors with a 3.00 ERA during the regular season finished this series with a 20.25 ERA after giving up 15 runs, 15 hits and seven walks in 6 2/3 innings, with a .484 opponents’ batting average.
Boston’s latest downfall in the Bronx was a crushing end to a wild 2026 season for the Red Sox, who stumbled to a 32-46 start. Tracy was the skipper at Triple-A Worcester before getting promoted to interim manager in Boston, and the team finally began to take off with a four-game sweep of the Yankees at Fenway Park in late June.
After clinching a wild-card spot last week, the Red Sox removed the interim tag and named Tracy the 49th manager in team history, signing him to a three-year contract that runs through the 2029 season, with a club option for 2030. The team also exercised the 2029 and 2030 options on chief baseball officer Craig Breslow.
“I wasn’t there for the highs and lows,” Crochet said. “For this team to do what it did do, to make it to this point, was nothing short of miraculous.”
Led by Gray and Contreras, among others, the Red Sox went on a 15-game winning streak in July that equaled a franchise record and used a 32-5 surge to climb back into contention. They became the fourth team in major league history to reach the postseason after falling 14 games under .500, and the first to qualify after losing as many as 44 of its first 75.
Gray, who can become a free agent after the World Series, went around the clubhouse to hug each of his teammates following Wednesday’s defeat.
“I’m proud of what we accomplished,” the pitcher said. “We were left for dead there for a while.”

title: K-9 sniffs out nearly 450 pounds of cocaine at northern border
text:
LEWISTON, N.Y. (Gray News) — Federal border officers seized an estimated $6 million worth of cocaine after discovering 174 packages concealed under the floorboards of a commercial truck bound for Canada, authorities said.
On Sept. 22, U.S. Customs and Border Protection officers at the Port of Buffalo’s Lewiston Bridge border crossing encountered a 21-year-old Canadian man driving a commercial truck and trailer.
After an initial physical inspection of the trailer, officers found the floorboard had been modified. A CBP canine then searched the empty trailer and alerted to the presence of narcotics. The truck and trailer were escorted to a secondary inspection area.
A detailed search uncovered 174 vacuum-sealed packages of cocaine concealed inside the floor, which field-tested positive for the drug. The narcotics weighed approximately 450 pounds and had an estimated street value of $6 million.
“This significant seizure highlights the exceptional vigilance, advanced training and relentless dedication of our CBP officers and canine teams at the Lewiston Bridge border crossing,” said Sharon Swiatek, acting port director for the Area Port of Buffalo. “While a large focus of our border security mission is on inbound threats, our officers remain equally sharp during outbound operations to dismantle transborder criminal networks, disrupt the flow of dangerous narcotics and protect communities on both sides of the border.”
The case was referred to Homeland Security Investigations for further review.

title: Man arrested on suspicion of planning an attack on the Texas Capitol, authorities say
text:
Man arrested on suspicion of planning an attack on the Texas Capitol, authorities say
A 40-year-old man was arrested early Wednesday on suspicion of plotting to attack the Texas Capitol, authorities said.
The Texas Department of Public Safety said in a statement that it received “credible information about an individual planning a violent attack" for Thursday in Austin. Officials did not provide details about the alleged plot, citing an ongoing investigation.
The tip came in Tuesday evening, and SWAT officers made the arrest about 3 a.m. Wednesday at a residence in Converse, near San Antonio.
Benny Caldera Jr. was charged with making a terroristic threat against a public servant, a felony, the DPS statement said. He made bond, according to online court records in Bexar County, but DPS said later Wednesday that Caldera was in federal custody after being arrested by the FBI to face additional federal charges.
DPS did not provide further details, and the FBI's San Antonio press office did not immediately respond to an email late Wednesday seeking comment.
Messages were left seeking comment from John Bunk, an attorney listed for Caldera.
DPS notified state lawmakers about the threat and arrest early Wednesday. The Capitol remained open during regular operating hours.
Gov. Greg Abbott said DPS was assisted by the FBI in making the arrest.
"Texas will NOT tolerate threats of violence against our Capitol," the governor said in a statement on social media.

title: Death Notice: Elaine June (Moulton) Alley
Mt. Blue field hockey captain back in action after emergency surgery
text:
FARMINGTON — On a scenic fall day in the western Maine mountains, there was hardly a patch of grass untouched by Keira Adams’ stick.
Between being active in front of goal, running from sideline to sideline, and tracking back when needed, the Mt. Blue field hockey captain was as lively as could be Tuesday when the Cougars hosted Bangor. She hardly looked like a player who, early in fall practices, was in the hospital rather than with her teammates.
“I’ve learned to be grateful to be here and for what I have,” said Adams, who played the full 60 minutes for Mt. Blue in a 2-1 victory. “I’m healthy, my body is working, and I’m moving around fine. I’m just so lucky that I’m able to be out here.”
That was far from guaranteed six weeks ago after the senior underwent an emergency appendectomy on the second day of preseason. Midway through the season, Adams has learned to see not just field hockey but life from a new perspective.
The fall season started like any other for Adams with the first preseason practice on Aug. 17. That evening, however, she began feeling a sharp pain in her lower chest. Not knowing what was wrong, she initially chose to “tough it out” through the night.
By morning, though, the pain hadn’t subsided, and Adams knew something was seriously wrong. She went to MaineHealth Medical Center in Portland, where she learned she had an inflamed appendix that required removal. Adams was hospitalized for approximately 12 hours.
“I had never had surgery, so of course I was scared — I had to go under anesthesia, obviously, so I was nervous,” Adams said. “I did cry a lot because my thought was, ‘I don’t want to get it; I don’t want to be taken out of the season,’ but I had no choice, really.”
The appendectomy kept Adams away from the team for four days. Although she rejoined the Cougars for the second week of fall practices, she was not cleared to resume practicing until Sept. 14. That meant, for three weeks, all Adams could do was watch as her teammates practiced and competed.
That was a tough experience, but it was also one that provided a chance for personal growth. Not once, Mt. Blue coach Julie Lajoie said, did Adams sulk or give off a “poor me” attitude. Instead, she became an encouraging voice from the sidelines — and learned the game from a new perspective.
“You want the kids to find some way they can continue to grow, and she found some ways on her own and really contributed more in a verbal way,” Lajoie said. “She was almost like an assistant coach for us in a lot of ways. … I think she became a better captain for us in the process.”
Although Adams, who had been working on her stick skills at home, felt ready to play upon her Sept. 14 return, she was not immediately able. Under Maine Principals’ Association rules, players must take part in five on-field practices before being eligible for competition. Adams, unfortunately, had only practiced once.
The senior made her return in Mt. Blue’s home game against Oxford Hills on Sept. 19. It was a triumphant return for Adams. One minute into the second quarter, she scored the opening goal in the Cougars’ 3-0 win.
“It was the best feeling in the world,” Adams said. “When I was going through that month of waiting, I felt like I kind of lost myself as an athlete because this is my pride and joy. So, when I came back and scored, I really got that spark and that fire. It made me so happy and grateful.”
Her absence from the lineup early in the season left a hole for Mt. Blue. The Cougars lost seven seniors from a strong 2025 squad, so the experience of Adams, who scored four goals last season, looked crucial for a younger 2026 team. Instead, Mt. Blue was missing a player who senior Reese Nye called “the glue that holds us together.”
“It was hard for us to see in her pain like that, especially so early in her senior year, but we knew she was going to come back stronger, and she did,” said Nye, Adams’ best friend and a fellow captain. “She took what she learned from it and applied it back to her game and has improved even more.”
Although Adams admits she’s a bit more tired than usual following games as a result of missing preseason conditioning, she is completely pain-free. Her stamina will return with time, and after everything she’s experienced, Adams isn’t about to complain about what she can and can’t do.
“There was nothing I could do other than support my team and be positive, so I focused on that instead of being sad all the time,” Adams said. “Playing the sport and watching it are so different, so that taught me a lot. … It could have been so much worse, so like I said, I’ve just learned to be grateful.”

Charles releases personal financial disclosure after Democrats urged him to do so for months
The Maine Ethics Commission is submitting legislation to require candidates for governor to file a personal finance disclosure.
Republican candidate for governor Bobby Charles released his personal financial disclosure on Thursday morning after Democrats have urged him to do so for months.
Maine law requires candidates for office to file a financial disclosure, but gubernatorial candidates are exempt only the winning candidate has to file after being elected.
The Maine Ethics Commission is submitting legislation for lawmakers to consider that would require gubernatorial candidates to submit the same personal finance disclosure statement that is filed by legislative candidates.

Hannah Pingree's only recent stream of income came from her job in the Mills Administration as Director of Policy Innovation and the future.
Pingree's husband, Jason Mann, recorded income from North Haven Sustainable Housing as well as income from his work as a filmmaker. Pingree also disclosed one of her dependent children made more than $2,000 working at a restaurant on North Haven, the island the family lives on.

title: Christa Pike is in critical condition after Tennessee’s failed execution attempt, her lawyers say
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — Christa Pike was in critical condition Thursday and receiving “lifesaving care” at a hospital, her lawyers said, a day after a failed attempt to execute her pushed Tennessee’s governor to halt further executions this year and order an independent review.
Pike, who was sentenced to death for a 1995 murder, was taken to a hospital Wednesday night after surviving a double dose of the drug Tennessee uses to execute prisoners.
“We don’t have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment,” attorney Randy Spivey said during a news conference. “But we know she is alive right now.”
The failed execution, which one death penalty expert described as unprecedented, led Republican Gov. Bill Lee to order a review, calling what happened “deeply disturbing” and indefinitely postponing Pike’s execution and another one that had been scheduled for this year. It also reignited the debate over the state’s execution procedures, including its single-drug lethal injections.
Spivey called the process cruel and torturous, saying he was “haunted” by watching and hearing Pike talking, singing and then snoring loudly during her more than 90 minutes in the death chamber. Her attorneys also said it was unclear if she might have suffered brain damage from being deprived of oxygen.
May Martinez, whose daughter was murdered by Pike and her boyfriend and who traveled to Nashville to watch the execution, was also upset.
“I didn’t get justice for my daughter,” Martinez told The Associated Press on Thursday.
“I watched the whole thing. She was awake. She was laughing. She was moving her head, moving her feet. She was trying to sit up,” Martinez said. “Didn’t work the first time they gave her a shot. It didn’t work the second time.”
A prolonged attempt ends in failure
It was not immediately clear what went wrong. Pike’s attorneys said there were a number of possibilities.
The execution team worked for an hour to administer the lethal drugs, said Spivey, who counted at least seven needles in her left arm.
During the struggle to locate a vein, Pike even suggested where they might find one, he said.
“Please try here, please try here,” Spivey recalled her saying. “She told them over and over, please try higher on my shoulder.”
At one point Pike asked prison officials if her arm was supposed to feel that way, though it’s unclear if it was after the first dose entered her body because officials don’t share that information.
Neither the initial nor the backup dose of pentobarbital worked. Pike was still snoring when the execution chamber’s microphone was cut off more than an hour into the attempt.
Another Pike attorney, Steve Ferrell, said she feared there would be complications because of a lifelong blood disorder that made it tough to get needles into her veins. “Throughout her life, she’s explained to us that she had trouble having blood drawn,” he said.
It was quite possible, Ferrell said, that the IV line didn’t enter her vein properly and the drug was filling her arm instead of entering her bloodstream.
Lee said it appeared prison staff followed procedure.
Attorneys seek commutation
Pike’s lawyers now want her death sentence to be commuted. Now age 50, she was sentenced to death for a murder she committed at 18. She would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.
An appeals court had stopped her execution an hour before it was scheduled to begin Wednesday morning, but the U.S. Supreme Court overturned that stay hours later.
It was the second time this year that the state was unable to complete an execution. In the other case, officials couldn’t find a suitable vein for an IV line so the drugs weren’t administered
Pentobarbital, the barbiturate Tennessee uses for executions, has been used to carry out death sentences in multiple states and by the federal government. But concerns have been raised about the potential for “unnecessary pain and suffering.”
Dr. Ervin Yen, an Oklahoma City anesthesiologist who has no link to Pike’s execution but has witnessed others, said it’s possible that if the prison staff was using a small vein, there could have been some burning, as mentioned by Pike’s attorneys.
“It just depends on the vein that you’re injecting it in and how fast you are injecting,” Yen said.
The state changed its execution method two years ago
In 2024, Tennessee switched from a three-drug series for lethal injections to a single drug, pentobarbital. That came about two years after the state abruptly halted the execution of Oscar Smith and acknowledged it had failed to ensure its lethal injection drugs had been tested properly.
Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said what Pike experienced is “singular and unparalleled” in that she survived long enough to be moved to a hospital.
Seven others have survived medical problems due to an execution team’s failure to access a vein to administer lethal injection drugs, but no one has stayed alive after receiving the drugs used in executions, she said.
Executions in the U.S. have fallen sharply since the beginning of this century, but the number nearly doubled last year behind a record increase in Florida.
Pike would have been the 30th person executed in the U.S. this year.
Awake in the death chamber
Strapped to a gurney, Pike described herself as at peace and said “I’m ready to be free. ... This is a happy day.”
But she remained awake, and at one point she complained about a feeling in her arm.
An hour after officials first raised the curtains, witnesses reported that a second dose of pentobarbital was administered. Pike could still be heard snoring behind a closed curtain until the microphone was cut off almost 30 minutes later.
Her lawyers filed an emergency motion with the Tennessee Supreme Court seeking to immediately halt and stay the execution, saying she was in “unnecessary agony” and the procedure violated her right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment.
Pike acknowledged her role in the killing
Pike and her boyfriend were convicted of the fatal stabbing of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a classmate. The killing stoked fears of Satan worship because of a pentagram carved on Slemmer’s body.
She didn’t dispute that she helped kill Slemmer, but supporters argued that her mental illness and allegations of severe sexual abuse should be considered. She was diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder after the killing.
“It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” she once said.
___
This story was updated to correct the spelling of Randy Spivey’s last name.
___
Associated Press writers Jeffrey Collins in Columbia, South Carolina, Ed White in Detroit, Russ Bynum in Savannah, Georgia, Hallie Golden in Seattle, Hannah Schoenbaum in Salt Lake City and John Seewer in Toledo, Ohio, contributed.

title: Trump’s economic approval falls as he says White House has a ‘public relations’ problem
text:
Trump’s economic approval falls as he says White House has a ‘public relations’ problem
"I've done a very bad job of explaining how good the country is doing. We're doing better than any country in the world economically," Trump said. President Donald Trump is campaigning to address economic concerns as new polling shows declining approval for his handling of inflation and the cost of living.
Trump’s economic approval falls as he says White House has a ‘public relations’ problem
"I've done a very bad job of explaining how good the country is doing. We're doing better than any country in the world economically," Trump said. President Donald Trump is campaigning to address economic concerns as new polling shows declining approval for his handling of inflation and the cost of living.
President Donald Trump is hitting the campaign trail ahead of November's midterm elections, facing growing frustration over the economy as new polling shows his economic approval at a new low.
The president said he plans to spend little time in Washington, D.C., between now and November, focusing on convincing the public that his policies are working.
"I thought I was finished campaigning, but in order to help Republicans because we need the votes. We have to have the votes," Trump said.
Trump is embarking on a 32-day campaign push leading up to the midterms.
"I've done a very bad job of explaining how good the country is doing. We're doing better than any country in the world economically," Trump said.
Trump offered a similar assessment Wednesday, saying, "There's no economy like this economy. And the only thing we don't have is good public relations."
A new AP-NORC poll shows only 26% of Americans approve of Trump's handling of the economy, while just 17% approve of how he is handling the cost of living.
That comes after the Conference Board's Consumer Confidence Index fell to 81.9 in September, its lowest level since April 2014.
White House economic adviser Kevin Hassett said, "I don't think that the confidence survey is really about economics. I think it's about, are you satisfied with politics right now?"
Still, dissatisfaction extends into Trump's own party. About 52% of Republicans disapprove of his handling of the cost of living, according to the AP-NORC poll.
When asked what metric Americans should use to evaluate the economy, Hassett said, "Oh, well, I would recommend that they not look at any metric in the newspaper, that they look at their wallet and look at how their family's doing. It doesn't matter to a typical person unless when they open their wallet, they see that they're better off. And I think that right now the average American is way, way better off because of our policies."
The poll also shows more Americans blaming Trump's policies for high prices than blamed President Joe Biden's policies ahead of the 2022 midterm elections. About 65% now say Trump's policies are more responsible for persistently high costs than outside factors. In October 2022, 44% said Biden's policies were more responsible for high prices.
Among Americans' biggest concerns are food and gas prices. About half said they are highly concerned about being able to afford food, and about half said the same about filling their gas tanks.
Changes to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, also took effect Oct. 1.
Maximum benefit levels are increasing under the program's annual inflation adjustment. At the same time, states are now responsible for a larger share of the cost of administering SNAP, with their share rising from 50% to 75% under the tax and spending law Trump signed last year.
That shift does not directly reduce a family's SNAP benefit, but it significantly increases the share states must pay to operate the program.

title: EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin tours Wesmac Custom Boats in Surry
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
SURRY, Maine (WABI) - On Thursday, Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin stopped in Surry to tour Wesmac Custom Boats.
Zeldin’s visit to Downeast Maine comes months after Maine fisherman were granted an exemption from EPA regulations, allowing certain commercial fishing vessels to utilize Tier 3 engines instead of Tier 4.
Zeldin stated that he felt it was important to have these discussions in person as opposed to over the phone.
“It’s very eye-opening when you actually stand on the boat, you look at the size of the tier 3 engine, you visualize the size of a tier 4 engine, how that impacts the design, what kind of physical limitations currently exist for a boat. I mean, we were all standing on a boat that was 50 feet long, but we’re hearing first-hand stories of operating on boats that are even smaller. The smaller the boat gets, the even less it makes sense, the more difficulty and challenge faced by those putting the boat together, the impact for the user. And also the practicality when you think of operations of a boat. You can’t assume that these lobstermen are full throttle their entire trip. It’s very much not not that reality. And you want to make sure that you have an engine that makes the most, it’s designed to make the most amount of sense, and you’re not making bad assumptions on how that engine is operated,” said Zeldin.
Zeldin said that immediately following his discussion he was going to make phone calls to the Office of Air and Radiation and work through options moving forward.
“As far as options go, is it an updated rulemaking? Is it an updated exemption, an updated exemption process? Is it new guidance that needs to come out of the agency?” said Zeldin.
Zeldin said that there will be further conversations with the office of general counsel to ensure any decisions made are durable and won’t be overturned.

title: Supreme Court to review immigrant detention policy
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The Supreme Court announced Thursday it will review the Trump administration’s policy of detaining immigrants who entered the country illegally without a bond hearing.
Previously, most immigrants who entered the country illegally were given a bond hearing, provided they did not have a criminal record, and were detained away from the border. The Trump administration has ended that practice, and the new policy is now before the Supreme Court.
The case revolves around a Brazilian citizen the Trump administration argues entered the country illegally two decades ago and applied for asylum in 2016. The man has never been charged with a crime besides illegal entry, but was placed in detention following a 2025 traffic stop and kept there.
In July, the Trump administration began the policy of mandatory detention without bond. The policy shift comes from a new interpretation of a 1990s immigration law.
Most lower courts have ruled that detaining immigrants indefinitely without a bond hearing is illegal, but the Fifth and Eighth circuit courts have upheld the new policy.
The high court is expected to hear the case in the next few months, with a decision expected by the end of June 2027.

title: Aging Untold: Depression in older adults doesn’t always look like sadness
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we break down the hidden warning signs of depression in older adults and explain when to seek professional help.
Plus, we explore how older Americans are turning passion projects and hobbies into profitable side hustles to boost their budgets.
We also visit a Memphis bakery on a mission to provide employment, training and a vital second chance for families experiencing homelessness.
When an older adult is living with depression, it might not look like the way you would expect.
The signs might include irritability, withdrawal or suddenly sleeping all day rather than tears or sadness. Depression can also mask itself as declining memory.
Depression can be tied to grief, but physical and chemical factors matter just as much, according to the Aging Untold experts.
Help is available, and aging expert Amy O’Rourke said people who have Medicare or a Medicare Advantage plan can have an annual wellness visit that includes a depression screening.
Deciding whether to get a vaccine as an older adult is a personal choice, especially if you have a chronic condition or a weaker immune system.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the starting point is understanding the purpose of a vaccine in the first place.
Gerontologist Sam Cradduck said the value of a shot isn’t only measured by the disease it prevents, but by what you’re going to prevent it from stealing from you.
We are breaking down the factors to consider when weighing whether to get shots, including flu, shingles and RSV vaccines.
Some people who are looking to make some extra income are turning to side hustles.
Rob Macgregor, who has a full-time job running a small car dealership in Phoenix, also gives golf lessons. He connects with students through a platform that matches people looking for lessons in all kinds of activities, including pickleball, tennis and guitar, with instructors.
Find out more about how this works, the most popular side hustles and what people say they earn by doing them.
A bakery in Memphis serves more than bread, croissants, cupcakes and cookies. It also serves opportunities for people who need a fresh start.
Lucy J’s provides jobs and training opportunities for people experiencing homelessness, according to head baker and executive director Josh Burgess.
Burgess’ wife, Tracy Burgess, is executive director of Dorothy Day House, a Memphis nonprofit that provides temporary housing and support services, including jobs at Lucy J’s.
“Probably the most important thing is that it’s more than just housing,” Tracy Burgess said. “It’s important for families to find employment that will sustain them long term.”

title: How to get or give help in Maine for housing, heating, food and more
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Across Maine, hundreds of nonprofits, churches and community groups offer help with food, household items and fuel assistance. Many of these programs cater to the most pressing needs in their communities and are often in need of support from those who can afford to donate.
If you are in need of help — or are in the position to offer support — below are some of the resources available.
Please send additional resource suggestions to [email protected].
HOW TO FIND HELP
Call 211 or go to 211Maine.org to connect with assistance programs near you. The service can also help with basic needs, such as directing people to shelter and transportation.
General Assistance is offered through town and city halls to help with rent, utilities and other expenses for people who qualify. Check with the town where you live for more information about how to apply.
The “Be There for Me” website helps parents and caregivers find a variety of support options, from housing and transportation to childcare and getting everyday items. Visit bethereforme.org to search for support.
FOOD ASSISTANCE
There are hundreds of food pantries and meal programs across the state. The Maine Food Access Map is an interactive tool to help people find resources near them.
To apply for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, visit a local Maine Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) Office for Family Independence, call 855-797-4357 or go to mymaineconnection.gov.
The federal Commodity Supplemental Food Program provides food boxes to low-income people 60 and older. For information about how to apply, visit the website for the Maine Department of Agriculture, Conservation & Forestry, which links to the local agencies that distribute the boxes.
HOUSING AND HEATING ASSISTANCE
The Home Energy Assistance Program (HEAP) helps qualified homeowners and renters pay for heating costs. Households are encouraged to apply for HEAP as soon as possible. Applications are handled by local Community Action Agencies. To apply online or to find information about how to apply by phone or in person, go to mainehousing.org.
Nearly two dozen wood banks operate across the state to provide households with firewood, including those in Cumberland, Freeport, Bethel, Kennebec County, Buxton, Waldo County and the Midcoast. For more information, visit the Maine Wood Banks website: woodbanks.org.
There are shelters in 11 counties for people experiencing homelessness. A list with contact information is available through MaineHousing. If you are currently homeless and need emergency shelter in Portland, call the 24/7 phone line at 207-761-2072. Veterans who are homeless or at risk can get immediate assistance by calling 800-377-5709 to connect with local programs.
The Maine Eviction Prevention Program helps cover past due rent and assistance for as long as a year to people who meet certain requirements. For more information, contact MaineHousing.
Pine Tree Legal Assistance provides free civil legal help to qualifying low-income Mainers with a variety of issues, including evictions and guidance on family matters. For more information, call 207-942-8322 or visit ptla.org.
HEALTHCARE ASSISTANCE
The Maine Medical Association maintains a list of clinics that offer free medical and dental care to people without insurance. To view the list and find contact information, visit mainephysicians.org.
The Maine Mobile Health Program’s mobile health clinics provide medical and behavioral health care on a sliding scale to farmworkers and others across the state. For more information, call 207-622-9252 or visit mainemobile.org.
HELP WITH HOUSEHOLD ITEMS
Several diaper banks operate in Maine. The Trinity Jubilee Center in Lewiston operates a diaper bank out of its food pantry and provides a 50-pack of diapers once a month. For more information, visit the website or call 207-782-5700.
In southern Maine, the Michael Klahr Jewish Family Services Diaper Bank in Portland does bi-monthly distributions. An essentials pantry also distributes household items that are not accessible with SNAP benefits. To sign up, call 207-772-1959.
For people with a case manager, help with furniture is available through Furniture Friends in Westbrook. Case managers can also request clothing and household items through Maine Needs in Portland.
HOW TO HELP
Maine Needs: The Portland nonprofit provides gently used clothing, boots, household items, diapers and other needed items to people across Maine and is accessed through case managers and social workers. Maine Needs accepts monetary donations and has detailed guidelines on its website for donating clothing and other requested items. It is also raising money to provide diapers through local food pantries to 8,500 babies. For more information, go to maineneeds.org
Keep ME Warm: The program, a partnership between United Way and community action agencies, is the only statewide fuel assistance fundraising effort in Maine. Donations support fuel assistance distributed across the state. To donate, visit uwsme.org/keep-me-warm.
Good Shepherd Food Bank: The Auburn-based nonprofit distributes food to more than 600 partner programs across the state. Good Shepherd accepts monetary donations to support its efforts. For more information, go to gsfb.org
Check with your local food pantry: Many local food pantries except donations of shelf-stable items, as well as money that can be used to buy food in bulk. Pantries also report a need for volunteers to help distribute and deliver food.
Furniture Friends: The Westbrook organization collects gently used furniture to give to community members who can’t afford to buy their own and who are referred through an agency or case manager. Information about how to donate furniture or money is posted on the Furniture Friends website. For more information, go to furniturefriends.org.

title: South Portland and Windham girls soccer battle to draw
text:
WINDHAM — One season removed from failing to make the playoffs, the South Portland girls soccer team has quietly crept into Class A South relevance.
Thursday night at traditional power Windham, the Red Riots proved their promising start is neither fluke nor fancy by going toe-to-toe with the 2025 regional runner-up in a 1-1 tie.
South Portland sophomore striker Sasha Neff scored the tying goal on a powerful solo run and finish, and junior keeper Maizie Savage made a pair of brilliant saves in overtime.
The Red Riots are 6-1-2, with quality wins against Gorham and Thornton Academy. A season ago, they were 3-9-2 and finished 14th in the Heal point standings.
Windham, ranked No. 4 in the Varsity Maine Top 10, is 7-1-1.
“I think we’re a top contender. Windham beat us 6-1 last year, so we’re bouncing back from that,” Neff said. “I think it just shows we have grit. We can hang in there. We go down and we come back up and tie. We have the ability to do it.”
SOUTH PORTLAND IMPROVEMENT
South Portland, ranked eighth in the Varsity Maine poll, has 12 sophomores, six who start. Midfielder Maci Rauscher is the only senior. The group has gelled well under first-year head coach Jarrod Carnrick, who previously coached the St. Dominic Academy girls and, last season, the Poland boys.
Savage returned as one of the region’s top keepers, and her sisters (they are triplets) Reese and Charlie add a physical presence at outside back and center midfield, respectively. The back four of Reese Savage, center backs Rylin Small and Claire Phillips, and fullback Lauren Way made it difficult for Windham’s forwards to turn and shoot.
At the other end, Neff is a fast player with strong balance and shot-making skills. On her tying goal, scored with 20:08 to play in regulation, she showed her abilities. Collecting the ball near midfield, Neff ran hard down the left side with three Windham defenders unable to slow her, then cut to the middle and fired a shot past keeper Jennifer Schwarz.
“I think (this season) was like a whole factory reset for us,” Neff said. “We just came out with a whole new coach, a pretty young team, and I think we just have the mentality, the positivity, that we can do this.”
WINDHAM STILL A MAJOR THREAT
Windham showed it’s still a very tough team. The Eagles controlled most of the play in the first half and opened the scoring when Isabella Vassoler knocked in a well-placed diagonal free kick from Denali Momot with 28:37 left in the second half. That was the only time Windham was able to get to one of Momot’s 15 kicks on set pieces.
“We knew (South Portland) was going to be a great, competitive team,” Eagles coach Deb Lebel said. “We also have to finish our corners.”
STATISTICS
• South Portland: Sasha Neff (1 goal), Maizie Savage (6 saves), team (7 shots, 3 shots on goal, 1 corner kick)
• Windham: Isabella Vassoler (1 goal), Delani Momot (1 assist), Jennifer Schwarz (2 saves), team (12 shots, 7 shots on goal, 15 corner kicks)

title: Judge permanently dismisses case charging ex-Olympian with vandalizing Reflecting Pool
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A judge in the nation’s capital agreed on Thursday to permanently dismiss a criminal case charging a former Olympian with vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a move that could prevent federal prosecutors from reviving the case under political pressure from President Donald Trump.
D.C. Superior Court Judge Todd Edelman ordered the dismissal of David Hearn’s case with “prejudice,” which would block U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro’s office from refiling the felony charge against him. The judge ruled nearly a month after hearing attorneys’ arguments.
Hearn’s lawyers say Trump administration officials have continued to falsely accuse the Maryland resident of vandalizing the reflecting pool despite Pirro’s decision to drop the case on July 31. Trump responded by saying Pirro “choked” and “folded like an umbrella.”
In a court filing in July, Pirro said new evidence produced by the Interior Department showed Hearn wasn’t responsible for damage to the pool’s lining. Pirro’s office attributed the damage instead to a botched installation by a contractor as well as a rush to complete the project in time for this summer’s America 250 celebration in Washington.
Pirro’s admission was an embarrassing setback for the White House. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum has backed Trump’s claims that vandals damaged the pool.
Hearn has said he was on a bike ride on June 19 when he reached in to examine the pool’s newly peeled coating and briefly touched a chunk attached to the side of the pool. But he said he obeyed a park worker’s command to let go of it.
Hearn was charged with one count of property destruction, which carries a maximum prison sentence of 10 years. His lawyers questioned whether prosecutors properly presented the grand jury with adequate evidence to support the charge and the amount of damage alleged by the government.
Hearn, 67, of Bethesda, Maryland, competed in three Summer Olympics, earning his best finish, ninth, at the 1996 Atlanta Olympic Games, the U.S. Olympic and Paralympic Committee says on its website.
Trump, a Republican, appointed Pirro, a former Fox News host, to serve as the top federal prosecutor for the District of Columbia. Edelman was nominated to the bench by Democratic President Barack Obama.
Hearn’s attorneys said the ruling is “a victory for the rule of law and for an innocent American seeking justice” and allows Hearn to “move forward with his life as he deserves.”
“This administration chose to pursue an unjust prosecution against Mr. Hearn. It should not get repeated chances to wield the power of criminal prosecution against someone who should never have been prosecuted,” the lawyers said in a statement.

title: Witnesses describe Christa Pike ‘snoring’ and ‘looking around’ during botched execution attempt
text:
KNOXVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV/Gray News) - Christa Pike remains alive after officials attempted to execute her by lethal injection, with witnesses describing “haunting” moments during the failed attempt.
The state tried to execute her by lethal injection on Wednesday, but neither the initial nor backup dose of pentobarbital killed her.
“Christa is alive right now. We don’t have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment,” Spivey said during a news conference.
Witnesses say she was snoring when the execution chamber’s microphone was cut off more than an hour into the attempt.
Attorneys say at least seven needles were used in her left arm alone. They described her physical reactions, including ragged breathing, looking around and complaining of a burning sensation.
The failed execution amounted to “torture,” her lawyers said, and they called for her death sentence to be commuted.
“I’m haunted by last night,” he said. “What I saw last night is not something that should ever, ever happen again.”
Pike, 50, was sentenced to death for killing Colleen Slemmer in 1995.
Slemmer was 19 years old when she was killed after being lured to an isolated area on the University of Tennessee agricultural campus. Both Slemmer and Pike were enrolled in Job Corps at the time.
Pike and two co-defendants, Tadaryl Shipp and Shadolla Peterson, were convicted in 1996. Testimony showed the trio tortured Slemmer, carved a pentagram into her chest and Pike kept a piece of Slemmer’s skull as a souvenir.
Pike is currently receiving “life-saving medical care.”
