title: Weather Discussion 10/1/26
Federal scholarship for private school and homeschooling opening to most kids in at least 30 states
text:
Federal scholarship for private school and homeschooling opening to most kids in at least 30 states
Nearly all schoolchildren in at least 30 states can apply for a new federal scholarship next year to help pay for private school, homeschooling and other educational expenses, according to regulations proposed Thursday by the Trump administration.
The first national school choice scholarship program, the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit, will launch Jan. 1, establishing a taxpayer-funded incentive for families to choose private or homeschooling in participating states. Taxpayers who donate to an organization passing out the scholarships will receive a federal tax credit, a perk expected to further fuel the conservative school choice movement.
About 96% of children in those states should be eligible, according to the department. Children attending public schools could use the scholarships for extra learning expenses.
“Education freedom is the key to unlocking opportunity and success for our next generation of students,” said U.S. Secretary of Education Linda McMahon in a statement issued Thursday. The federal scholarship program, she said, will ensure “every child has access to the education they need, not one limited by ZIP code, family income, or government‑imposed barriers.”
School choice scholarships have been available for decades in conservative-led states and throughout the South, giving individual students taxpayer-funded grants ranging from a couple thousand dollars to more than $30,000 a year. In places where they are available to all students regardless of income, such as Florida and Arizona, the majority of students using the money were already in private or home school or were from affluent neighborhoods, an analysis by The Associated Press showed.
The federal program departs from most state programs by not forcing students to leave public school to qualify for a scholarship. Public school students could use the money for tutoring or special education therapies, although the Republican administration has not provided specific criteria for eligible expenses yet.
Regulators say they have set up the program in a way that will make it easier for poor students to apply, proposing to let students use proof of participation in a government assistance program in lieu of providing income documentation. Foster children would not have to provide any income verification when they apply, officials said.
Experiences with school choice scholarships in other states have shown barriers to using the programs go beyond paperwork hurdles. Many families often do not know scholarship programs exist. Federal officials have not said how they would tell taxpayers and students about the scholarships.
How the scholarship and tax credit will work
Taxpayers will have the chance to donate to a scholarship program in a participating state, even if they do not live there, starting Jan. 1. Individuals can donate up to $1,700 and receive a federal tax credit for the same amount in exchange. Federal officials propose a couple filing jointly could give as much as double that amount.
Scholarship organizations in each state would decide how much to grant to each child who applies, depending on available funds and student need. Children could qualify if they are in elementary through high school and their families earn up to three times the area's median income. For a family of four in Houston, for example, that equates to more than $300,000.
Scholarship recipients could use their funding to pay for religious or private school tuition, homeschooling costs, tutoring and special education therapies, books, computers and other expenses connected to enrollment or attendance, according to officials at the Treasury Department.
At least 30 states have opted in, and more may sign up
States could not turn to laws or regulations to narrow the uses for the scholarships or the type of organization that can grant them, federal officials said.
But states can choose whether to participate in the program.
According to the most recent Treasury Department list, as of mid-September these states are in for 2027: Alabama, Alaska, Arkansas, Colorado, Florida, Georgia, Idaho, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, New Hampshire, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Virginia, West Virginia and Wyoming.
Governors from Arizona, Minnesota, Wisconsin, and Oregon have said their states will not join, with some arguing these programs divert resources from public schools.
More than two dozen states have yet to say what they will do. In New York, Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul has been supportive, and the state is expected to sign up.
Governors deciding whether to participate face many competing objectives and interests. There is the opportunity to bring significant new education money to students who need extra support, such as tutoring or extra speech therapy that their public school does not provide. At the same time, large scholarship programs in states such as Florida and Arizona have accelerated a growing enrollment crisis in public schools.
Even so, the federal program is expected to bring taxpayer money for private school tuition to several states that have yet to embrace vouchers or education savings accounts.
Education advocates disagree on whether states should participate
In Massachusetts — a state with historically robust public school funding, caps on charter school expansion and no taxpayer funding for private school tuition — education advocates on both sides are lobbying the governor to take a stand and pushing the public to register their opinion.
The state’s association of school superintendents opposes the idea that districts should take advantage of the program by creating their own nonprofits to accept donations and distribute scholarships. Many big city school districts around the country already have their own foundations. In Massachusetts, where every municipality has its own district, the majority of the more than 300 school systems have no such entity.
“Districts face a significant disadvantage compared to the private school networks that already have elaborate fundraising and scholarship infrastructure in place,” reads the Massachusetts Association of School Superintendents’ position paper. The group said requiring families to apply for scholarships and, in many cases, prove income eligibility were “bureaucratic hurdles that will certainly leave behind our most vulnerable families.”
On the other side, former Boston City Councilor and former public schoolteacher Annissa Essaibi George has argued Boston Public Schools faces severe budget shortfalls and needs new streams of income.
And besides, she argued in an op-ed published in a neighborhood newspaper: “Massachusetts taxpayers will be eligible to take advantage of this program whether the governor opts in or not. The only question is whether those dollars come back to Massachusetts children, or instead flow to students in states that moved faster.”
In just a few years, after donations from taxpayers pick up, the IRS and the Treasury Department predict the program will direct nearly $26 billion into as many 2.2 million scholarships each year.
The federal tax-credit scholarship program was signed into law last year by President Donald Trump as part of his signature tax breaks and spending cuts bill. The public has 60 days to comment on the Treasury Department's proposed regulations.

title: Housing, heating and the shrinking margin
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
For Bonnie and Mark, the question last winter was not whether they could afford to heat their home. It was whether they could afford to keep up with everything else, too.
The Bath couple, both in their 70s, had already learned how quickly a household budget can change. After spending years raising their children, whom they adopted when they were in their 30s, they eventually sold their home so they could travel and spend more time visiting their children and grandchildren. When they returned to Maine, buying another home was no longer within their means, so they rented instead.
Mark, a retired middle school gym teacher and coach, has limited mobility. Bonnie had spent years as a stay-at-home mom and had not been working outside the home. About two years ago, she returned to the workforce, taking a retail job because their fixed incomes were no longer enough to cover their expenses. The additional income gave them some breathing room. There was no cushion of savings to fall back on. Then Bonnie fell and sustained a back injury.
She could no longer stand for long periods of time, which meant she could no longer work. The income disappeared, but the expenses did not. Rent still came due. Groceries still had to be bought. And when winter arrived, the heating oil tank still needed to be filled.
When Bonnie reached out to Tedford’s Warm Thy Neighbor program last winter, she was asking about heating assistance, but the concern behind that question was much bigger. She was worried about the rising price of oil, increasingly expensive groceries, the loss of her income, and what might happen if they fell behind on rent next. She was afraid they could end up facing eviction. She was also embarrassed to ask for help and wondered whether someone else might need it more.
Bonnie and Mark’s experience offers a glimpse into a problem that is increasingly difficult to see as a single, isolated expense. Housing, food, transportation, utilities and medical costs all draw from the same household budget. When one of those costs rises, something else has to give. The newly released 2026 Out of Reach report, published annually by the National Low Income Housing Coalition, puts some numbers around that pressure. In Maine, about 26% of households are renters, representing more than 153,000 households across the state.
A Maine household needs to earn $32.32 an hour to afford a modest two-bedroom rental at the state’s fair market rent without spending more than 30% of its income on housing. The average Maine renter earns $18.29 an hour. That is a difference of $14.03 an hour.
Those numbers describe a gap, but they cannot show what it feels like to live inside it. When rent takes up more of a paycheck, there is less left for a car payment, childcare, utilities, medication or the unexpected expense that inevitably comes along. Eventually, a household may have to decide which bills can wait. At Tedford, those decisions are often what bring a neighbor to us. Sometimes it is a past-due rent payment and the fear of losing a home. Sometimes it is a heating oil tank and the question of how to fill it without falling behind somewhere else. This year, that question is getting more expensive to answer.
As of Sept. 14, the Maine Department of Energy Resources reported that the statewide average price of heating oil had reached $5.77 a gallon, 74% higher than it was at the same time last year. For a household with a standard 275-gallon tank, filling it now costs $675 more than it did a year ago.
For a household already stretching its income to cover the basics, that $675 has to come from somewhere. It might mean less money for groceries, a car repair that gets postponed, a medical expense that has to wait, or a rent payment that becomes harder to make.
Last winter, Bonnie and Mark were one of 237 households who received heating assistance through Tedford’s Warm Thy Neighbor program. Funded entirely by community donations, the program provided more than $93,000 in heating assistance across 14 Midcoast towns. This winter, we expect more neighbors to need heating assistance, and we know it will cost more to help each household keep the heat on.
The need is already making itself known. Warm Thy Neighbor’s phone lines will not open for another three weeks, but emails and handwritten letters from neighbors are already arriving, asking when applications will be available and whether help with heating will be possible. Winter has not yet arrived, but for many Maine households, the calculations have already begun.
Katrina Webster is the director of development at Tedford Housing.

title: ICE is moving Maine detainees more quickly and farther away, report says
text:
Most people detained and processed by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in Maine are quickly moved out of state, according to a new analysis by an immigrant advocacy group.
After processing at the agency’s facility in Scarborough, 98% of the individuals detained this year amid the agency’s expanded efforts have been swiftly moved to facilities outside Maine, mostly in Massachusetts and New Hampshire, before commonly being transferred to sites in the South, the report says.
Detainees are also spending less time at any given facility, and so far this year, 90% of those processed in Scarborough have been moved within six hours of their initial detention.
The new data, which comes through public records requests to ICE from the Deportation Data Project and was analyzed by the Maine Immigrants’ Rights Coalition, underscores long-standing concerns by the attorneys and loved ones of those detained.
Those groups have argued that the agency swiftly moves detainees out of state, and even shifts them several times to several different facilities, making it harder to stay in contact or legally advocate.
ICE significantly grew its operations in Maine this year amid the Trump administration’s push to increase deportations. Immigration agents arrested hundreds during a surge in January, most with no criminal convictions, despite the agency’s claim that it only targets the “worst of the worst.”
In July, an agent in Biddeford fatally shot Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a 25-year-old father, who didn’t have a criminal history and wasn’t the target of enforcement that day, sparking widespread protest.
The Scarborough facility — ICE’s only one in Maine, since the agency pulled detainees from the Cumberland County Jail following criticism by the sheriff — has been the subject of frequent protest from residents advocating for its closure.
Hunter Cropsey, the programs and engagement manager at the coalition and a co-author of the report, said it was born out of requests from individuals in Scarborough who wanted more data to understand the relationship between the facility and their town.
The data also comes amid reports of a new forthcoming ICE facility in the Penobscot County town of Newport, although details remain scarce.
The report shows 293 detentions at the Scarborough facility between Jan. 1 and Aug. 5 of this year, a significant increase over prior years.
An analysis of data from 2024 to 2026 shows that while most people held at the Scarborough facility used to be held elsewhere in Maine after being processed, that shifted sharply in the last two years. Now, more than half go to Massachusetts as their next location, while 40% go to facilities in New Hampshire.
The most common next stops this year were in Plymouth, Massachusetts; Dover, New Hampshire; and Burlington, Massachusetts.
Later transfers often took detainees far from New England, primarily to Louisiana and Texas, but also to Arizona, Georgia and Ohio. Forty percent of those first processed in Scarborough spent some time in the Gulf states, according to the report.
After being processed in Maine, detainees this year spent time in a total of 30 facilities across 11 states, for an average of just 12.6 days at each site. That’s a significant change from 2024, when detainees spent an average of 46 days in a given facility.
Cropsey, the co-author, said the movement to those southern states is particularly notable because it’s less likely detainees would be released on bond and, statistically, an applicant’s likelihood of approval for asylum is lower.
But even just a move across the border to New Hampshire can cut off detainees from their support systems and their chances of a good legal defense, he said.
“This accelerated and widespread movement removes Mainers from their communities and support systems, creating severe hurdles for legal representation and family contact,” the report concludes. With planned increases in ICE enforcement and the proposed Newport facility, those patterns are likely to intensify, the report says.

Hannah Pingree holds double-digit lead over Bobby Charles in AARP poll
text:
Politics
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
Democrat Hannah Pingree leads Republican Bobby Charles by 13 points in a new AARP poll, the latest in a string of surveys showing her comfortably ahead in the race for governor.
Pingree, a former Maine House speaker from North Haven, led Charles 52% to 39% in the survey of 982 likely Maine voters taken Sept. 20-22 and released Thursday. Independent state Sen. Rick Bennett of Oxford had 6% with 3% undecided. The margin of error was plus or minus 3.1 percentage points.
The result fits a steady trend. Every public poll of the race has shown Pingree ahead by 8 to 13 points, and her lead has barely moved in that time. An average compiled by RealClearPolitics, which does not include the AARP poll, had her up by nearly 11 points through Tuesday.
Pingree leads across age groups in AARP’s poll. She led voters 65 and older by 14 points, the same group that favored Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins by 7 in her pivotal race against Democrat Troy Jackson. Pingree also led women 50 and older by 16. In the conservative 2nd Congressional District, she was tied with Charles.
Pingree is also the best-defined candidate. She was viewed favorably by 49% of voters and unfavorably by 38%. Charles was underwater at 33% to 40%, with 13% saying they had never heard of him.
Bennett, a former Maine Republican Party chair and longtime lawmaker, remains largely unknown, with 36% of voters saying they had never heard of him. But he ran second among older swing voters, getting 32% to Pingree’s 41% and Charles’ 13%. Maine’s ranked-choice voting system does not apply to general elections for state office.

title: Obituary: x
text:
CAPE ELIZABETH –
Constance Barbara Ortolani, 78, passed away on Sept. 22, 2026, surrounded by her family and near her longtime home of Cape Elizabeth, Maine. Connie was a teacher, dancer, mother, sister and friend. She was committed to her communities, dedicated to helping others, and a devoted Boston sports fan. 
Connie was born in the Back Bay Fens neighborhood of Boston, Mass., to Nicholas Rassias, a bartender and postal worker, and Christine Rassias, a hairdresser. Her family later moved to the Boston neighborhood of Jamaica Plain. Her brother, Peter, loved baseball and his big sister, but at the age of 11, he passed away from leukemia. Connie honored his spirit throughout her life by supporting the Dana Farber Cancer Institute.
Connie was a third-generation Greek American and was raised with a strong Greek tradition, including attending Hellenic school. Every year, she liked to attend Portland’s Greek festival for the mousaka, koulourakia cookies and, of course, the dancing.
As a young woman, Connie excelled at school and athletics, especially dance. She performed in the Nutcracker, cast as “one of the boys” because she was tall. A straight-A student, she attended Boston State College and received a Bachelor of Science in elementary education. Early in her career, she taught gym and health at Copley Square High School.
During college, Connie worked at an Anderson-Little clothing store. There, she met Philip Ortolani. For one of their first dates, they went to a Bruins game, where Connie fell in love with another Boston sports team, and also Philip. They got married in 1971, moved to Randolph, Mass., and started a family, having two children, Nikki and Alex.
In 1982, Philip was considering a job in southern Maine and brought Connie to see the Pine Tree State. Her response was lukewarm. Connie always called herself a “Boston Girl,” but she soon came to love Maine—its coastline, its birds, its lobster rolls, and its people.
She began teaching at local schools while also working as a dance instructor. In 1991, she got a master’s degree in special education from the University of Southern Maine with a near-perfect GPA.
Connie went on to teach at Hall School and later Lincoln Middle School, where she was known as a dedicated teacher with a talent for getting her kids to engage in lessons and respond to her. In the mid-2000s, she started working for Even Start, a literacy and education program to help families break out of poverty. She became a program director and child education specialist, further deepening her bonds with the local community and other educators. Her mother, Christine, also eventually moved to the area, allowing Connie and her family to be close to Christine in her final years.
After retiring, Connie took on volunteering. Some of it was formal, such as becoming a regular volunteer at soup kitchens and Reiche School, often working with children who were just starting to learn English. Some volunteering was informal, such as delivering a meal to a family or connecting them with a local furniture charity. Of this volunteering, she would always say that she “got back more than she gave.”
In 2015, Connie and her family were struck by tragedy. A car ran off the road and took Philip’s life, while injuring Connie. She stayed close to Philip by taking frequent trips to Fort Williams, where they loved to walk, and by hanging hearts around her home to keep him close.
Despite her loss, Connie went on to build an active life. In the mornings, she would often attend a dance, Zumba, or gym class, and then volunteer in the afternoon at a school or with the Wayside Food Programs. In the evenings and weekends, she’d often connect with a much-loved group of friends in the Portland area. They would go to plays, dance in Congress Square, and explore new restaurants. In her neighborhood, she’d go on “walk and talks,” where she always said she ended up doing more talking than walking. In these ways, she shared her spirit and love for life despite its hardships, and took solace in the strength and endurance of others.
She also hosted her children in Maine and took frequent trips to New York City, N.Y., to visit them, go to Broadway shows and museums, and attend holiday gatherings. She reveled in her role as grandmother to her grandson, Enzo, including taking him on a trip to Universal Studios and to basketball games in Brooklyn. In her final year, her daughter Nikki moved up to Maine, bringing Connie great happiness and comfort.
Even after being diagnosed with glioblastoma in June, Connie carried a smile on her face and always had a word of kindness or gratitude. She constantly said how lucky she was.
Connie is survived by her daughter, Nikki Ortolani of South Portland; son, Alex Ortolani, daughter-in-law, Kate, and grandson, Enzo of Brooklyn; and cousins Arthur and his wife Judy Carakatsane of Portsmouth, N.H., Michael and wife Pam Carakatsane of Lynnfield, Mass., and Bill and wife Sharon Carakatsane of Lowell, Mass.
To view Connie’s memorial page or to leave an online condolence for the family please visit http://www.hobbsfuneralhome.com
In lieu of flowers, donations can be made to the Dana Farber Cancer Institute (danafarber.jimmyfund.org) or
Wayside Food Programs (https://www.waysidemaine.org/home).

title: Worried about the tenor of Troy Jackson’s campaign

title: Maine needs more home sweet homes. How can we expedite the process?
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Almost exactly two years ago, a statewide housing analysis found that a staggering number of housing units were needed in Maine. According to the report, in order to make up for years of lagging construction and to meet our anticipated future need, Maine needed 80,000 housing units by 2030. Most of those units are needed within 50 miles of where I sit typing this in Brunswick, though there are pockets of housing needed in northern Maine and Bangor specifically.
To our good fortune, I have attended a number of groundbreakings and ribbon-cuttings in the Bath, Brunswick and Topsham region over the past year. In fact, it is not overstating to say that many of the most promising housing projects in Maine came from unique public-private partnerships in the communities covered by our Bath-Brunswick-Topsham Regional Chamber of Commerce.
That was on full display this week, as The Lupine, a 183-unit housing development, held a groundbreaking touting the partnership between Dave Holman’s team at Katahdin Property Management and the Town of Topsham. Dave’s remarks gave great credit to where credit was due, highlighting their partnership with Penobscot General Contractors, the Town of Topsham planning board, the Board of Selectmen, town staff, several designers, various subcontractors and the residents of Topsham for their feedback during the public meetings. Clay Maker of Penobscot General Contractors mentioned how supportive the partners have been and referenced a previous partnership for The Sandpiper that many of these same companies partnered on at Brunswick Landing. Each speaker mentioned the tremendous time and amount of work that went into this multiyear project.
That flashed me back to the ribbon-cutting at The Sandpiper, where Dave spoke again on how much Katahdin Property Management valued their partnerships with these subcontractors, the designers, the town residents and the town planning staff/town leadership — this time Brunswick and not Topsham, of course. Each speaker mentioned the tremendous time and amount of work that went into this multiyear project.
That made me think of the Ways, an incredible BIW-supported housing project that Bath Housing helped plan along with Developers Collaborative on Congress Avenue in Bath. This partnership is producing 84 units that will first go to shipbuilders working with BIW, but also could be home to other Bath employees should the units not get all gobbled up by BIW folks. This was an incredible groundbreaking event, as Developers Collaborative complimented their partnership with BIW, Bath Housing, the subcontractors, City of Bath employees, the city’s planning department and the residents of Bath.
Each speaker mentioned the tremendous time and amount of work that went into this multiyear project.
These projects are incredible, and incredibly needed, but a theme is arising. In each case, we are hearing stories — verging on parables — about how arduous, strenuous and, at times, seemingly insurmountable the obstacles to these projects were due to our process, licensing and more.
My question is: If we need 80,000 units by 2030, what can we do to make this process more efficient and easier for us to accept community investments and accelerate projects?
This is not a call for no oversight or no public input as those are critical pieces, but we do need this to happen quicker. The 183 units at the Lupine in Topsham is astounding, but this process took three years. Doing napkin math, in order to get to 80,000 units by 2030, we need 437 Lupine projects over roughly the next 222 weeks (which would get us to the end of December 2030). That’s roughly two Lupine-sized projects in Maine, or their equivalent, each week.
Greg Payne, senior advisor on housing policy from the Governor’s Office of Policy Innovation and the Future, was at the Lupine groundbreaking and mentioned a half-dozen other groundbreaking events in the coming month all around the state — which is excellent. Twenty-five units here, and 47 units there, and so. It all adds up, but it’s not quick enough.
We need to look at some efficiencies in the process.
For example, there are certain permits and licensing that require state signoff, but due to low staffing or limited bandwidth, some of these permits and licensing are taking three to six months for site review and approval. Yet in all cases, these permit requests are coming from vetted, insured and licensed contractors, who are doing, in some cases their 10th, or 30th, or 100th project of this kind. They know these required practices as well as the regulators and state agencies. So, could we create a process where if a developer who has already been approved for a similar project of that size and scope, can get express approval so they don’t have to wait three to six months? I’m not saying we cut corners, but maybe put some trust in the professional builders that they will continue to do their peak professional work just as they have for their past 30 projects?
And that’s just one example — I’m sure developers can come up with other efficiencies. I think we can find some at the municipal level, too. One positive for these new developments is that each success becomes a case study in how to approve a similar project the next time around, if we are willing to accept that the previous project was done correctly. What are the policies communities we need in place to meet these housing needs expeditiously?
These are the questions we need to be asking, and the answers will be vital. I was heartened last week as Midcoast Council of Governments convened a six-hour meeting around housing and a potential new housing-friendly community accreditation. It’s in the early stages, but it could be a possible solution. That’s really important work and something we all must engage in.
I don’t know the answers, but I’m excited to help work on them.
Thank you to the municipal employees for your unheralded work. Thanks also to the housing organizations, developers, designers, investors and contractors who are choosing to help our region grow one unit at a time. I hope we can all get behind your future investments to continue that growth for years to come.
Cory King is executive director of the Bath-Brunswick-Topsham Regional Chamber of Commerce.

title: A closer look at the candidates for the Portland City Council District 4 race
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Among the three City Council seats up for grabs this November, Anna Bullett is the only sitting councilor running for reelection. Jacob Viola, who ran unsuccessfully for an at-large seat in 2024, is also vying for the District 4 seat.
The district includes East Deering and parts of the Back Cove, Deering Center and North Deering neighborhoods. The Portland Press Herald spoke to each candidate ahead of the Nov. 3 election to ask why they are running and what their priorities are.
This is the second of three previews for City Council races that will run in the coming days. Read the preview of the at-large race here. Early voting in the state of Maine begins Oct. 5. For polling locations, or to request an absentee ballot, go to portlandmaine.gov/elections-voting.
ANNA BULLETT
When Anna Bullett walks her kids to school now, there are a series of recently-installed speed tables along Ocean Avenue meant to slow down traffic. She’s had constituents ask if the city can come to their street next.
“The number one issue at doors is safe streets,” she said. “It’s been great to hear that people want more and they want it urgently, which lights a fire under me.”
Bullett, 42, who was elected in 2023, is the senior director of health and nutrition at The Opportunity Alliance, which administersWIC and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program for Cumberland County.
She said her experience running government programs is why she entered local politics, and she wants to see the comprehensive approach Vision Zero takes to pedestrian safety be applied to other city issues like homelessness.
Bullett serves as chair of the public safety and health and human services committee, which has frequent policy discussions on the related issues of mental health and substance use.
She said city staff are now developing a comprehensive public safety plan that she hopes can provide a clearer direction for officials, but that she will oppose elements that are “not informed by science, evidence and personnel out in the field.”
Bullett said she disagreed with Mayor Mark Dion’s recent comments on the visibility of Portland’s substance use problem downtown.
“You can’t arrest yourself out of a problem unless there are the right systems in place after the fact, which we don’t have,” she said, adding that Portland needs to do a better job of including county and state officials on the issues.
She said police can arrest someone a dozen times, but if they don’t have a high enough charge to send someone to prison, “that’s out of our scope.”
Bullett wants to make decisions based on preparing Portland for the future. She pointed to an upcoming street lighting analysis as an important measure that affects both public and pedestrian safety. She’s also looking forward to reviewing a citywide facilities assessment so officials can make decisions about buildings where the community gathers.
She wants the city to think about climate resilience and public transit, particularly as it plans future housing development. During her first term, the council passed ReCode Portland, ambitious updates to the city’s zoning ordinances.
“I don’t want regressive policies,” she said. “I want to find ways to honor what Portland was but ensure we’re prepared for where it’s going.”
Bullett’s challenger for the District 4 seat has made communication part of his platform and has said he hears concerns about Bullett being non-responsive to constituents. When asked, Bullett said she doesn’t believe people who have interacted with her would have complaints about her engagement and problem-solving.
She said she does her best to keep up with messages from constituents and that if she doesn’t write back immediately, it’s often because she’s seeking accurate information from staff.
“City Council is a job I take seriously, as much as being a mom and a good boss and a good neighbor,” she said.
Bullett said she’s formed a lot of trusted relationships with city staff across departments over her term that can make a difference in addressing constituent problems.
“I feel like I’ve gotten a graduate degree the last three years, and now I need to put it to use,” she said.
JACOB VIOLA
Jake Viola comes from Italian immigrants and a line of commercial fishermen. His parents held down multiple jobs, and now that Viola, 35, has a child of his own, he wonders if Portland can still be a place where a fisherman’s kid can make it.
As he’s gone door-to-door during the campaign, he said, the top concerns being raised are property taxes, public safety and the responsiveness and direction of the City Council.
“I think (residents) see a lot of good intentions that have led to bad outcomes,” he said, referring to issues like Portland’s needle exchange program and inclusionary zoning policy, which requires large housing projects to have at least 25% affordable units.
Viola said that when he hears the police chief say opioid overdoses are on track for a 10-year-high, he questions whether current policies are working.
“Does it have to do with our approach to public safety and public health?” he said.
He also pointed out that while the city has seen a higher return rate for used syringes, the program eclipsed the 1 million mark last year, making the overall volume of needles on the streets a concern.
When asked about the broader public safety concerns downtown, Viola said there needs to be an “all hands on deck” response from the city, county and state.
He said recent council decisions have stonewalled or changed rules that have prevented new businesses from coming to Portland. While he said he’s agnostic to the specific example, he’s concerned for the precedent set by retroactive zoning that blocked the Portland Music Hall project and took away dollars that could alleviate the property tax burden.
He wants to streamline the permitting process to make it easier for more housing and accessory dwelling units to be built in the city.
Viola, who has degrees from Yale and Harvard, said he wants to use his experience from working in the Massachusetts’ governor’s office and an ability to “lower the temperature in the room” when talking about difficult issues.
He’s been campaigning on a “24-hour promise” to respond to questions or concerns from constituents within a day. He said being accessible to residents is the most important thing a councilor should do, and that it “became clear” while campaigning “that doesn’t exist right now.”
Viola has been posting a series of videos on social media that highlight local businesses. He said owners tell him it’s hard to operate a business in Portland, and that it’s difficult to get in touch with City Hall.
He wants to get to a place with constituents where, even if he or the city does something they don’t agree with, “they understand where I’m coming from and they feel respected in the process.”
“I think that’s missing right now,” he said.

title: Presque Isle Apple Crisp sale draws steady crowd, sells out before noon
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Volunteers sold almost 1,000 pre-ordered cups of apple crisp as part of an annual fundraiser for the Central Aroostook Chamber of Commerce.

“The warmth of those apples and the sweetness of the whipped cream and the crunch, you know, that’s so good... The apple crisp sold at $6 a cup this year, up a dollar from last year. A steady flow of residents stopped by to buy a cup or two of their own.

title: Former Dallas officer convicted of killing Black man in his apartment granted parole
text:
The former white Dallas police officer convicted of killing a Black man in his apartment that she mistook for her own was granted parole Thursday after serving seven years of her 10-year sentence.
The Texas Board of Pardons and Parole, which is appointed by Gov. Greg Abbott, rejected Amber Guyger’s initial parole request in 2024 but approved her case over the objections of the victim’s family the first time she was eligible to return.
Guyger was convicted of murder in the 2018 killing of Botham Jean, an accountant from the Caribbean island nation of St. Lucia, who had been eating a bowl of ice cream when Guyger entered his home and shot him.
The shooting drew widespread attention because of the strange circumstances and because it was one in a string of shootings of Black men by white police officers. Guyger’s sentencing hearing also included a stunning courtroom scene when Jean’s brother and the Black judge presiding over the case embraced the sobbing officer.
During her murder trial, Guyger said that after a long shift at work and still in uniform, she walked up to Jean’s apartment — which was on the fourth floor, directly above hers on the third — and found the door unlocked. She said she thought the apartment was her own and that Jean was an intruder when she drew her service weapon and entered.
Civil rights attorney Lee Merritt said Jean’s family “strongly opposed this parole.”
“They stood up again and again to ask that the full sentence be served. A 10-year sentence was already a fraction of what was lost. Releasing Ms. Guyger after seven years makes that loss feel even smaller in the eyes of the system. It is not smaller,” Merritt said.
In 2024, a jury awarded Jean’s family nearly $100 million in a federal civil trial.
In granting her release, the board said it reviewed a “plethora” of information in her case.
The board said Guyger’s record did not include a documented pattern of violent or assaultive arrests or convictions, and showed she has participated and completed programs in her prison treatment plan to get and keep a job when she is released. It said she also “maintained a satisfactory institutional adjustment.”
The board said the state prison system will determine when she is released. Texas Department of Criminal Justice officials did not immediately respond to requests for comment Thursday.

title: Father of newborn triplets kidnapped, murdered in case of mistaken identity, authorities say
text:
SAN JOAQUIN COUNTY, Calif. (KCRA) - Three suspects wanted in the kidnapping and murder of a California father who authorities say was a victim of mistaken identity have been identified.
Avtar Singh, a 57-year-old father of newborn triplets, was kidnapped Feb. 17 from a Sikh temple in Tracy. His body was found three days later more than 100 miles away.
Investigators with the San Joaquin County Sheriff’s Office believe Singh was a victim of mistaken identity. On Wednesday, they identified the three suspects indicted in connection with his death as 25-year-old Alberto Alencastro, 20-year-old Alfonso Segura and 22-year-old Barnabe Segura.
All three suspects have been indicted on charges that include murder with special circumstances and kidnapping. The men are from Vallejo, have ties to Mexico and remain at large.
Surveillance footage showed Singh had been kidnapped by three people in a white crossover-style SUV. The suspect vehicle was identified by Flock license plate reader technology, tracked to Vallejo and seized on Feb. 19, the sheriff’s office said.
Authorities say Singh was not the intended target of the kidnapping but instead mistaken for someone else. Between Feb. 25 and Feb. 27, investigators traveled to Canada to interview the man identified as the intended target. He and his family had been receiving threats related to a stolen trailer, the sheriff’s said.
Investigators say that stolen trailer was enough for the three suspects to want to chase him down and kill him.
Singh had lived on the Sikh temple’s grounds with his wife and children. San Joaquin County Sheriff Patrick Withrow remembered him as a pillar in his community.
“He was such a good person. He cooked for everybody at the temple, and he took care of anything that was broken,” Withrow said. “This man was taken from a place of worship in broad daylight because of a theft that had nothing to do with him.”
Withrow says investigators made a promise to Singh’s wife.
“We gave her our word then and we give her our word now that we will not let this go by without finding these individuals,” he said.
The three suspects all face a life sentence without the possibility of parole. The Sikh community is offering a $50,000 reward for information that may lead to their arrests.

title: What scares me about real estate in Maine right now
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Julia Bassett Schwerin of Cape Elizabeth has been a real estate broker since 2005.
The real estate market is approaching a balanced market where supply and demand are in equilibrium and moving away from the seller’s market it has been in since 2020. After the pandemic, demand surged, prices rose and inventory dropped, but now the number of homes for sale has finally started to recover.
My prediction is that prices, which have doubled the value of most homes over the last seven years, will soften as sellers spend some of their massive equity to attract fewer buyers, but will not result in anything like the crash we had in 2008.
The issue that does scare me is that the operating expenses of owning a home represent a larger contributor to the unaffordability of housing than the first cost, which is getting all the attention. Specifically, I am referring to the cost of heating and homeowner’s insurance.
Maine has been doing well transitioning off heating with oil, going from 70% down to 50% of homes burning oil in the last seven years, but oil costs are expected to increase 30% this winter compared to last due to the Iran war. Buyers of more efficient buildings using clean energy are much more able to benefit from paying less in fuel cost than the small increase in mortgage payments for better insulation and air sealing.
For help paying utility bills, check out the consumer assistance information on the websites of the Public Utilities Commission, the Office of the Public Advocate and Efficiency Maine.
Maine has also enjoyed affordable insurance until recent storms caused catastrophic damage. Unfortunately, rising sea levels and severe storms caused by climate change are being sidelined and smeared as a political wedge issue. The weather risks from a warming planet are raising insurance premiums for property both across the board in reinsurance rates and selectively in areas where flooding, wildfires, storms, droughts and pollution have caused damage and claims.
Models ranking address-level property risks from climate factors have been built by several firms and are being closely scrutinized by insurers who have their own databases on losses. As the property damage costs from increased global warming rise, so too will claims for reimbursement by the government; if and when the federal government is unwilling or unable to help people who incurred disaster losses, the private insurers will be left holding the bag.
According to data from the U.S. Senate Budget Committee, the rate of home insurance policy nonrenewal is rising in the U.S. and in Maine. If homeowners can’t afford insurance premiums big enough to share the costs of flood and storm damage with those unaffected, then they can’t afford to live in single-family homes and will have to share housing; the insurers must be doing the math that it’s better for their business to incentivize us to fortify our buildings against climate change than rachet up the premiums or stop renewing policies.
Here is the proof: the Maine Bureau of Insurance, which is responsible for regulating the insurance firms underwriting policies in the state, took it upon themselves to adopt a program designed in the hurricane and tornado belts by the Institute for Business and Home Safety.
Called Fortify, it collects money from insurers and distributes it to building owners in the form of substantial grants to add fortification to a new roof by sealing the roof deck and locking down the drip edge, measures proven in wind tunnel testing to keep the roof attached and the water out.
If insurers with sophisticated data think that enough increasingly scary weather is on its way to Maine to warrant adopting the program, shouldn’t we in the real estate and construction trades act like they are probably right?
What the heck are we doing here bickering about whether we should teach Realtors about sustainability, whether we should adopt stricter building energy codes that reduce emissions, or whether we need to take collective measures to make buildings more resilient to the risk of loss from worsening storms and floods? The answer is a resounding “yes.”
The real estate and construction industries can see this bubbling up like a manhole cover on a side street at the Portland Old Port during a sunny day king tide.
We need an all of us together approach to the transition to clean energy from fossil fuel combustion emissions in buildings, and we need it now.

title: AARP keeps Maine members informed
text:
As someone who has spent years working in civic engagement, I have seen firsthand what happens when people understand the power of their voice and use it.
In Maine, voters 50 and older are a powerful part of that voice. In the 2024 general election, they made up more than 59% of all voters in our state. That matters, not simply because of the size of this voting bloc, but because older Mainers consistently show up and participate in our democracy.
The issues important to older voters are also issues that touch entire families and communities. Social Security, affordable healthcare, support for family caregivers, housing and the ability to age with dignity and independence affect all of us, directly or through someone we love.
That is why staying informed matters. AARP provides information to help voters understand the issues and make their own decisions at the ballot box.
Democracy works best when people participate. When voters stay informed, ask questions, speak up, and ultimately vote, elected leaders and candidates listen.
Maine’s 50-plus voters have tremendous power. Let’s continue to use that power to strengthen our communities and help build a future where people of every generation can thrive.
Pious Ali
AARP Maine Volunteer
Portland

title: Para-athlete defies limits on the track, one push at a time
text:
LEE’S SUMMIT, Mo. (InvestigateTV) - Outside of Kansas City, a high school para-athlete is pushing past expectations and capturing track championships.
And Jeremiah Mangels is doing that while challenging himself and inspiring his team.
“I’d say just whenever I’m on the track, and I’m pushing, I’m just thinking next push, next push. Never thinking about quitting,” said Mangels. “I actually try to get to the Olympics for the events I do best in.”
He was recently named a Para High School All-American in the 100-meter dash by USA Track & Field, and his goals don’t stop there.
Born with spina bifida, Jeremiah initially anticipated a degree of separation from his able-bodied teammates.
“I was expecting to be more separated from them because I thought it would be difficult for me, as a para-athlete, to do things that they’re doing,” he said. “It surprised me how I could do everything that they were doing better than I thought.”
Jeremiah’s teammates don’t see him any differently from the others. Still, they want the team environment to feel safe and supportive for him.
“To me, he ain’t different. He’s just like me. He’s just like everybody else on the track team. And we want to create a space where everybody is welcome,” said senior teammate Jaisaiah Turner. “Track is for everybody. As long as you got the mental and the strength to do it, you all in.”
The Mangels family adopted Jeremiah from an orphanage in China when he was just six years old.
“He’s been through so much adversity in his life,” said his mom, Amy Mangels. “He grew up in an orphanage with no family, and to know that he’s able to pull that belief in himself out to do these things, it amazes us. I’m excited that we get to call him our son.”
Jeremiah has won 11 straight state championships. Not only does he excel at track, but he also plays basketball.
“He absolutely believes he’ll be in the Paralympics someday, whether it be for track or basketball or both,” his mom added. “He pushes himself every day to achieve that. I don’t think he would ever take no for an answer.”
Jeremiah has proven time and time again that sports are for everybody, no matter what you’re capable of.
“There was fear whenever I started because I didn’t know what I was getting into,” Jeremiah said. “But after I got to the practices and realized that it wasn’t as bad as I thought it was going to be, I just did everything I could to be as strong as I can.”

title: Chairlift rides return to Camden Snow Bowl for unique fall foliage experience
text:
CAMDEN, Maine (WABI) - A Midcoast offering is back again beginning this weekend, giving visitors a view of the fall foliage like no other.
Camden Snow Bowl is opening its chairlift every Sunday this October for foliage rides.
For $15 per person, you can take an approximately 25-minute ride up Ragged Mountain to the summit, with the changing trees lining the way.
From there, you can enjoy hot drinks and experience an ocean-view from the mountaintop, a feature only a few East Coast ski mountains have.
The Snow Bowl has been hosting the fall foliage rides for over a decade.
Organizers say it’s a great way to fundraise for the municipal mountain while also taking advantage of the beautiful scenery.
“We just love continuing the recreation opportunities all four seasons long. So, this is a really cool way to get people up on the mountain in the fall, folks that maybe might not come in the winter,” said Grace McMullen, assistant director for Camden Parks and Recreation and the assistant general manager at the Snow Bowl.
Rides run every Sunday this month from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.
Children must be three feet tall to ride, and children five and under get free entry.
Attendees get the choice to take the chairlift back down the mountain, or enjoy the trails to make their way back.

title: EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin tours Wesmac Custom Boats in Surry
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
SURRY, Maine (WABI) - On Thursday, Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin stopped in Surry to tour Wesmac Custom Boats.
Zeldin’s visit to Downeast Maine comes months after Maine fisherman were granted an exemption from EPA regulations, allowing certain commercial fishing vessels to utilize Tier 3 engines instead of Tier 4.
Zeldin stated that he felt it was important to have these discussions in person as opposed to over the phone.
“It’s very eye-opening when you actually stand on the boat, you look at the size of the tier 3 engine, you visualize the size of a tier 4 engine, how that impacts the design, what kind of physical limitations currently exist for a boat. I mean, we were all standing on a boat that was 50 feet long, but we’re hearing first-hand stories of operating on boats that are even smaller. The smaller the boat gets, the even less it makes sense, the more difficulty and challenge faced by those putting the boat together, the impact for the user. And also the practicality when you think of operations of a boat. You can’t assume that these lobstermen are full throttle their entire trip. It’s very much not not that reality. And you want to make sure that you have an engine that makes the most, it’s designed to make the most amount of sense, and you’re not making bad assumptions on how that engine is operated,” said Zeldin.
Zeldin said that immediately following his discussion he was going to make phone calls to the Office of Air and Radiation and work through options moving forward.
“As far as options go, is it an updated rulemaking? Is it an updated exemption, an updated exemption process? Is it new guidance that needs to come out of the agency?” said Zeldin.
Zeldin said that there will be further conversations with the office of general counsel to ensure any decisions made are durable and won’t be overturned.

title: Maine County Official of October, George Jabar II
text:
George Jabar II was selected as Maine County Official of October in honor of his community service by Spirit of America Foundation’s Maine Chapter. Jabar has served over 25 years as a commissioner of Kennebec County.
He has been president of and held other positions in Maine County Commissioners Association, and he currently serves on the Board of Directors of National Association of Counties.
An attorney by profession, Jabar was appointed to the Maine State Board of Corrections and was a liaison to the Judiciary for the Maine Board of Corrections.
Jabar is active in the Boys’ and Girls’ Club and has served as chair of its Board of Directors. He also served as chair of the Board of Directors for the Maine Youth Alliance.
Jabar has played a role in Kennebec County Spirit of America events and been helpful to the cause of volunteerism in other ways over the years.
Maine Spirit of America is a chapter of Spirit of America Foundation, an organization promoting community service.

title: Canine deputy 'Arch' hailed a hero after locating three children who wandered from campsite
text:
'I am very proud': Canine deputy 'Arch' locates three children who wandered from campsite
Thanks to the help of a canine deputy, three children are now back safely with their family after wandering off from a campsite in Colorado.
The Chaffee County Sheriff's Office in Colorado said on Saturday, Sept. 26, deputies were called to the Midland Bike Trail, east of Buena Vista, Colorado, for a report of three lost children.
When on scene, authorities learned around 9 a.m. that the children's family members noticed the kids, one being 9-years-old and another being 6-years-old, had wandered off and were missing.
Family members told officials they searched for two hours and notified police in desperation.
Additional resources were called in to assist, including Chaffee County Search and Rescue.
Multiple drones and a helicopter were put in the air, and several foot patrol search teams were deployed for grid searching, the department said.
In addition, the department deployed canine deputy Archie, “Arch,” to the area to look for the children.
"Canine Arch, almost immediately, picked up a scent from the camp and started leading searchers into the wilderness," the department said. "As Canine Arch was clearly on a mission and had the children’s travel direction pinpointed, Search and Rescue foot teams worked up and around in the same direction and were able to visually locate the missing children from a higher location."
Officials said the children were quickly reunited with their family and were found roughly 1.5 miles away from their camp around 2 p.m.
No injuries were reported.
“The teams worked amazingly quick and effective to bring these kids back to their worried families. I can only imagine the panic they must have felt. We are so fortunate in Chaffee County to have such a highly trained and dedicated search and rescue team of volunteers for these terrifying moments. Now adding our buddy Arch to the team, as a tool, I would match this team against any other in the state. I am very proud of them all," Sheriff Andy Rohrich said in the post.

title: Hurricane Rachel strengthens to Category 2 off of Mexico's Pacific Coast
text:
MEXICO CITY (AP) — Another storm strengthened into a Category 2 cyclone off Mexico’s Pacific coast on Thursday morning at the same time northern Mexico and parts of the southwest were reeling from flooding and damage from Hurricane Polo earlier this week.
Hurricane Rachel was located about 230 miles (370 kilometers) off the southern tip of Baja California on Thursday, chugging forward at 6 mph (9 kph) as a powerful hurricane, according to the National Hurricane Center. The center reported winds of 105 mph (165 kph.)
Rachel was projected to move along the Mexican coastline before veering west in the Pacific.
Mexican authorities said Thursday that, as Hurricane Rachel moves across the Pacific, they remain on alert because of forecasts of very heavy rain in the states of Baja California Sur, Sinaloa, and Jalisco, and the possibility of landslides, rising river levels, overflowing rivers and flooding in low-lying areas.
On Wednesday night, the U.S. Embassy in Mexico warned U.S. citizens in Cabos San Lucas, a popular vacation destination for Americans, of beach and port closures and deadly rip currents.
The Pacific has seen an unusually busy hurricane season, which experts have attributed to El Niño, which has fueled crippling droughts in Mexico and Central America and floods in other parts of the region. In the Pacific, it has resulted in warmer waters and wind patterns that act as fodder for hurricanes.
Storm remnants drench central U.S.
The region from eastern Colorado to northern Illinois, along with parts of Texas and Oklahoma, was still under flood watch Thursday as storm remnants continued to batter the region, flooding streets and neighborhoods and setting off water rescues.
Wednesday was the wettest day on record for Lincoln, Nebraska, which received 6.1 inches of rainfall, according to the University of Nebraska-Lincoln Climate Office. In Omaha, which received 4.7 inches of rain Wednesday, the fire department said it responded to 80 water rescues over a three-hour period ending early Thursday. Some floodwaters reached depths of 8 feet.
In Chicago, a wastewater treatment and stormwater management utility urged residents to conserve water use to prevent flooding and stormwater backup.
“We encourage everyone to conserve water when possible to create more capacity in our systems,” utility President Kari K. Steele said in a statement Wednesday.
In Kansas, Gov. Laura Kelly issued an emergency proclamation on Wednesday ahead of the storms that allows state resources to assist first responders in hard-hit communities.

title: Letter: Can’t imagine Maine under communism
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
My wife and I have visited Cuba three times in our 34-foot American-flagged sailboat. After spending time with local people, I wrote and published the book “Road to Havana.” Cuba has been under communist/socialist rule since Fidel Castro took power in 1959.
Recently, we were typically the only foreign boat at anchor in the shoreside communities we visited. We quickly became friends with the local people. They are resourceful and friendly but very poor: There is virtually no free enterprise, no private property rights and no freedom of speech in Cuba. The Cuban government owns and controls nearly everything, including what the people eat every day.
I can’t imagine Maine under a communist/socialist government.
Richard Vinal de Grasse
Islesboro

title: Mt. Blue field hockey captain back in action after emergency surgery
text:
FARMINGTON — On a scenic fall day in the western Maine mountains, there was hardly a patch of grass untouched by Keira Adams’ stick.
Between being active in front of goal, running from sideline to sideline, and tracking back when needed, the Mt. Blue field hockey captain was as lively as could be Tuesday when the Cougars hosted Bangor. She hardly looked like a player who, early in fall practices, was in the hospital rather than with her teammates.
“I’ve learned to be grateful to be here and for what I have,” said Adams, who played the full 60 minutes for Mt. Blue in a 2-1 victory. “I’m healthy, my body is working, and I’m moving around fine. I’m just so lucky that I’m able to be out here.”
That was far from guaranteed six weeks ago after the senior underwent an emergency appendectomy on the second day of preseason. Midway through the season, Adams has learned to see not just field hockey but life from a new perspective.
The fall season started like any other for Adams with the first preseason practice on Aug. 17. That evening, however, she began feeling a sharp pain in her lower chest. Not knowing what was wrong, she initially chose to “tough it out” through the night.
By morning, though, the pain hadn’t subsided, and Adams knew something was seriously wrong. She went to MaineHealth Medical Center in Portland, where she learned she had an inflamed appendix that required removal. Adams was hospitalized for approximately 12 hours.
“I had never had surgery, so of course I was scared — I had to go under anesthesia, obviously, so I was nervous,” Adams said. “I did cry a lot because my thought was, ‘I don’t want to get it; I don’t want to be taken out of the season,’ but I had no choice, really.”
The appendectomy kept Adams away from the team for four days. Although she rejoined the Cougars for the second week of fall practices, she was not cleared to resume practicing until Sept. 14. That meant, for three weeks, all Adams could do was watch as her teammates practiced and competed.
That was a tough experience, but it was also one that provided a chance for personal growth. Not once, Mt. Blue coach Julie Lajoie said, did Adams sulk or give off a “poor me” attitude. Instead, she became an encouraging voice from the sidelines — and learned the game from a new perspective.
“You want the kids to find some way they can continue to grow, and she found some ways on her own and really contributed more in a verbal way,” Lajoie said. “She was almost like an assistant coach for us in a lot of ways. … I think she became a better captain for us in the process.”
Although Adams, who had been working on her stick skills at home, felt ready to play upon her Sept. 14 return, she was not immediately able. Under Maine Principals’ Association rules, players must take part in five on-field practices before being eligible for competition. Adams, unfortunately, had only practiced once.
The senior made her return in Mt. Blue’s home game against Oxford Hills on Sept. 19. It was a triumphant return for Adams. One minute into the second quarter, she scored the opening goal in the Cougars’ 3-0 win.
“It was the best feeling in the world,” Adams said. “When I was going through that month of waiting, I felt like I kind of lost myself as an athlete because this is my pride and joy. So, when I came back and scored, I really got that spark and that fire. It made me so happy and grateful.”
Her absence from the lineup early in the season left a hole for Mt. Blue. The Cougars lost seven seniors from a strong 2025 squad, so the experience of Adams, who scored four goals last season, looked crucial for a younger 2026 team. Instead, Mt. Blue was missing a player who senior Reese Nye called “the glue that holds us together.”
“It was hard for us to see in her pain like that, especially so early in her senior year, but we knew she was going to come back stronger, and she did,” said Nye, Adams’ best friend and a fellow captain. “She took what she learned from it and applied it back to her game and has improved even more.”
Although Adams admits she’s a bit more tired than usual following games as a result of missing preseason conditioning, she is completely pain-free. Her stamina will return with time, and after everything she’s experienced, Adams isn’t about to complain about what she can and can’t do.
“There was nothing I could do other than support my team and be positive, so I focused on that instead of being sad all the time,” Adams said. “Playing the sport and watching it are so different, so that taught me a lot. … It could have been so much worse, so like I said, I’ve just learned to be grateful.”

title: Volunteer-led town hall gives city council and school board candidates platform

title: Enrolling in law school a decades long journey for Maine writer
text:
I just enrolled in law school.
It took me decades to get here.
I can trace the idea back to junior high, when a school trip to Washington, D.C., included a visit to Georgetown University. Somewhere around then, becoming a lawyer entered the realm of things I could imagine myself doing someday.
It wasn’t just a childhood idea. In the late 1990s, I took the LSAT and seriously considered going.
But law school wasn’t my biggest dream. My real dream was marrying my true love and growing a family together. As our family grew, I didn’t want to embark on law school while we were in the middle of raising our children.
Law school could wait. And it did, for decades.
I’ve enrolled in a four-year, part-time J.D. program conducted entirely online. The paperwork is signed, the initial payment has been made and my enrollment packet is on its way. Now I’m waiting to find out when I begin.
For me, law school was never simply a matter of deciding to go. The University of Maine School of Law, known as Maine Law, is in Portland, about an hour and a half from home. The University of New Hampshire Franklin Pierce School of Law is in Concord, New Hampshire, about two and a half hours away.
An hour and a half doesn’t sound terrible until you turn it into a regular commute. That’s roughly three hours of driving each time, before spending a minute in class. Concord would mean about five hours on the road. Add a Maine winter and what looks manageable on a map becomes a significant part of your life. I needed a way to add law school to my life, not dismantle my life to attend law school.
That’s where I see one of the biggest advantages of going to law school online. For people in western Maine and other places far from a law school, an online program can make law school an option when it might never have been practical before. It also opens the door to people with careers, families and established lives who can’t simply move away or reorganize everything around a campus.
Where you live no longer has to decide whether law school is even an option.
Then there is the money. I want to earn a J.D. I don’t want to take on an enormous amount of debt to do it. Four years of tuition will still require planning and some belt-tightening, but the program I’ve chosen is affordable enough that my goal is to pay for it as I go.
The cost changed the equation. So did the flexibility.
Instead of the traditional three-year J.D., mine is a four-year program considered part time. Each year is a yearlong course of study rather than the traditional fall-and-spring academic calendar. “Part time” doesn’t mean casually opening a casebook whenever I happen to have a free afternoon. There will be substantial reading, studying and coursework every week.
My first year, known in law-school shorthand as 1L, will include contracts, torts, criminal law and legal research, writing and analysis. There will be casebooks, briefs, exams and more reading than I probably want to contemplate right now. But the classroom will come to me.
Before applying, I also found someone on YouTube who had shared her experience going through the same program. Watching another student actually work her way through an entirely online law program made it seem less like an interesting possibility and more like something I could realistically do. I could see what the work looked like and how it might fit into a life that already existed.
I can study from home. I can work around writing deadlines and family life. Some studying can happen early in the morning. Even an hour on the treadmill can sometimes become review time. The flexibility doesn’t eliminate the work. It makes the work possible.
I actually had an opportunity to start this program before. I was accepted last year and decided not to enroll. A year later, I knew I was ready to do it. This time, I enrolled.
Getting accepted this time produced more suspense than I expected. College transcripts from decades ago suddenly came back into my life. My application required additional information about my educational history, followed by several days in which I spent entirely too much time checking my email.
Then the message finally arrived. “Congratulations!”
One word changed the question from whether I was going to law school to when I was starting.
So now the paperwork is finished. The payment is made. The books are almost all here. I’m enrolled.
And I’m waiting again. This time, though, I’m waiting for a start date. I’m hoping for mid-October. After that, the countdown changes completely. It becomes 1L, then 2L, 3L and 4L.
I’ll come back to this in the winter, once I have a few months of 1L behind me. By then, I should have a much better idea of what studying law from home in Maine actually looks like, rather than what I imagine it will look like before I’ve started.
For now, I have casebooks waiting, 1L approaching and four years of work ahead of me. Four years sounds like a long time. But I’ve been thinking about law school, on and off, for decades.
In between, I married my true love and we grew the family I dreamed about.
And if all goes according to plan, in 2030 our youngest will graduate from high school and I’ll graduate from law school. That sounds like a pretty good year to me.

title: Astronauts arrive at International Space Station on the quickest US express flight yet
text:
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. (AP) — Four astronauts pulled up at the International Space Station on Thursday after launching on an eight-hour express that set a U.S. speed record.
The fresh arrivals include a Canadian whose wife will give birth while he’s away.
SpaceX launched commander Jessica Watkins and her crew for NASA after a three-week delay to fix their Dragon capsule’s leaking fuel system. Thick clouds threatened all morning to halt the countdown but in the end, the skies cleared enough to allow for a safe liftoff.
Although their stay at the International Space Station will last a long six months, the flight there was the quickest yet not only for Elon Musk’s company, but any American entity, including NASA. The space station’s convenient location when the astronauts launched enabled the fast transit.
With the late morning liftoff from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Watkins became the first Black woman to lead a crew to orbit. A geologist who worked with NASA’s Mars rover Curiosity a decade ago, Watkins is making her second trip to the space station following a lengthy stay in 2022.
“Thanks for an amazing ride,” Watkins radioed following liftoff.
The others are newcomers to space: NASA’s Luke Delaney, a retired Marine; Canada’s Joshua Kutryk, a colonel in the Royal Canadian Air Force; and Russia’s Sergey Teteryatnikov, a former submariner. They will replace four astronauts who have been living at the orbiting laboratory since February.
This was the 13th crew launched by SpaceX for NASA, not counting 2020’s test flight. All four embrace their Crew-13 designation that pays homage in their mission patch to Apollo 13. The harrowing 1970 moonshot ended with the astronauts’ safe return.
References to the number 13 abounded Thursday. Watkins and her crew rode to the launch pad in black Teslas bearing plates that read “Lucky 13.” What’s more, they carried up a small crocheted golden dragon named Lucky with a four-leaf clover around its neck.
“We figured it wouldn’t hurt to bring a little of our own luck just in case, but clearly we don’t need it,” Watkins said from orbit, noting they were “four of the luckiest humans on or off planet Earth.”
Kutryk will become the fourth man to become a father while orbiting Earth. Wife Heather is due to give birth to their third child in late November. The Canadian Space Agency promises plenty of support for the entire family when the big day comes.
“A lot of life-changing things can happen over six months,” NASA manager Dana Weigel said on the eve of liftoff, noting that the space agency will do its best to keep Kutryk looped in to his family.
In 2004, NASA provided a radio link between space station astronaut Mike Fincke and his wife’s delivery room during the birth of their daughter. Five years later, Randy Bresnik, commander of next year’s Artemis III mission, dialed in to his wife’s hospital from orbit.
The happy news traveled more slowly for Austrian astronaut Franz Viehbock. His daughter was born a few hours after he launched to the Soviet Union’s Mir space station in 1991. He was not informed until the next day.
SpaceX, meanwhile, is on a roll. Three hours after Crew-13 blasted off, SpaceX launched a Falcon rocket from California with more than 100 mini satellites. Another Falcon was set to soar late Thursday night from Florida, with a classified satellite for the National Reconnaissance Office. All this comes the same week that the company’s massive Starship reached orbit for the first time.

title: Judge permanently dismisses case charging ex-Olympian with vandalizing Reflecting Pool
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A judge in the nation’s capital agreed on Thursday to permanently dismiss a criminal case charging a former Olympian with vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a move that could prevent federal prosecutors from reviving the case under political pressure from President Donald Trump.
D.C. Superior Court Judge Todd Edelman ordered the dismissal of David Hearn’s case with “prejudice,” which would block U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro’s office from refiling the felony charge against him. The judge ruled nearly a month after hearing attorneys’ arguments.
Hearn’s lawyers say Trump administration officials have continued to falsely accuse the Maryland resident of vandalizing the reflecting pool despite Pirro’s decision to drop the case on July 31. Trump responded by saying Pirro “choked” and “folded like an umbrella.”
In a court filing in July, Pirro said new evidence produced by the Interior Department showed Hearn wasn’t responsible for damage to the pool’s lining. Pirro’s office attributed the damage instead to a botched installation by a contractor as well as a rush to complete the project in time for this summer’s America 250 celebration in Washington.
Pirro’s admission was an embarrassing setback for the White House. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum has backed Trump’s claims that vandals damaged the pool.
Hearn has said he was on a bike ride on June 19 when he reached in to examine the pool’s newly peeled coating and briefly touched a chunk attached to the side of the pool. But he said he obeyed a park worker’s command to let go of it.
Hearn was charged with one count of property destruction, which carries a maximum prison sentence of 10 years. His lawyers questioned whether prosecutors properly presented the grand jury with adequate evidence to support the charge and the amount of damage alleged by the government.
Hearn, 67, of Bethesda, Maryland, competed in three Summer Olympics, earning his best finish, ninth, at the 1996 Atlanta Olympic Games, the U.S. Olympic and Paralympic Committee says on its website.
Trump, a Republican, appointed Pirro, a former Fox News host, to serve as the top federal prosecutor for the District of Columbia. Edelman was nominated to the bench by Democratic President Barack Obama.
Hearn’s attorneys said the ruling is “a victory for the rule of law and for an innocent American seeking justice” and allows Hearn to “move forward with his life as he deserves.”
“This administration chose to pursue an unjust prosecution against Mr. Hearn. It should not get repeated chances to wield the power of criminal prosecution against someone who should never have been prosecuted,” the lawyers said in a statement.
