title: Maine Tech Week returns to Portland with 'intersections' theme
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
After a successful inaugural event that drew hundreds of attendees and more than 100 speakers, Maine Tech Week will be back in Portland this month.
The event, scheduled for Oct. 19-22, will take place at Aura, Mechanics’ Hall, the Portland Museum of Art and other locations.
It will offer conversations, panels, workshops, demonstrations and hands-on sessions.
Intersections
This year’s theme, “Intersections,” reflects the idea that some of the most interesting innovation happens when industries, disciplines and perspectives come together in fields from ocean sciences to the future of work.
“Maine Tech Week started with a belief that Maine needed a place where people working across technology, business, creativity, research and industry could find one another,” said Torie DeLisle, the event’s founding director. “Last year showed us how much energy there is for that kind of connection. This year, we’re building on that momentum and creating even more opportunities for people and ideas that might not normally share the same room to intersect.”
Tech, work, creativity
Monday’s theme, “Where Maine Industries Meet the Future,” will explore how emerging technologies are reshaping industries that have long defined Maine, including the blue economy, agriculture, health care, manufacturing and the built environment.
Tuesday will tackle “The Space Between Creativity (Art) and Technology,” giving artists, storytellers, designers and technologists a chance to examine how technology is changing creativity.
“Maine, Technology and the Future of Work” will be the theme for Wednesday, with conversations about AI adoption, workforce development, education, investment, entrepreneurship and the skills Maine will need as technology changes how work is done.
On Thursday, programming will focus on “Emerging Voices and What Comes Next” with a focus on entrepreneurs, investors, emerging leaders and new voices shaping Maine’s innovation economy.
Maine’s global advantage
Highlights include:
- Theo Balcomb, creator of the Daily at the New York Times and former senior editor at the Atlantic, in a conversation about storytelling, technology and human attention
- Beth Orcutt, vice president for research at Bigelow Laboratory for Ocean Sciences, exploring the intersection of Maine’s ocean economy and innovation
- Wade Merritt, president of the Maine International Trade Center, moderating a conversation exploring where Maine’s next global advantage might lie.
Additional speakers include Torey Penrod-Cambra of HighByte, TimberHP CEO Matt O’Malia, Nina Scheepers of the Maine Venture Fund, Startup Boston founder Stephanie Roulic and Austin Williams, founding director of the Maine Blue Economy Center at Maine Technology Institute.

title: Judge denies defense motion asking Lindsay Clancy be found not guilty due to a lack of evidence
text:
EDITOR’S NOTE: This story includes discussion of suicide. If you or someone you know needs help, the national suicide and crisis lifeline in the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988.
BOSTON (AP) — The judge in the Lindsay Clancy murder case on Thursday refused to declare her not guilty, turning down a defense motion that had argued there wasn’t enough evidence to prove she was responsible for killing her three children.
During Clancy’s first trial, which ended Sept. 4 with a deadlocked jury, her defense argued that she was not criminally responsible because of a mental disease, specifically a rare condition called postpartum psychosis. As such, the defense didn’t dispute that the 36-year-old former labor and delivery nurse carried out the killings at her family’s Massachusetts home in 2023.
However, in a hearing earlier this week, Clancy’s attorney Kevin Reddington tried to persuade the judge that prosecutors had not offered any proof that Clancy did it. Prosecutors argued there was plenty of evidence, calling Reddington’s claim “laughable.”
Prosecutors have yet to decide whether they will put the case in front of a jury for a second time. They could choose to retry her on first-degree murder charges or seek to try her only on lesser charges, including second-degree murder or manslaughter, or drop the case entirely.
In his ruling Thursday, Judge William Sullivan noted that for the purposes of his decision, he was required to analyze the evidence in the light most favorable to prosecutors — and that it was up to the jury, not the judge, to decide whether to believe expert witnesses for the defense who testified that Clancy was not responsible for her actions because of mental illness.
“There was evidence introduced, both physical and circumstantial, that would permit a rational trier of fact to find beyond a reasonable doubt the elements of the charge of murder,” Sullivan wrote.
At the first trial, prosecutors acknowledged that Clancy had mental health problems that included months of treatment and a stay in a psychiatric hospital, but argued that she knew what she was doing when she strangled the children — the youngest just 8 months old — then tried to kill herself.
Sullivan had declared a mistrial with the jury split 11 to 1 in favor of acquitting Clancy of murder charges.
In Tuesday’s hearing, Reddington suggested the entire case “was based on speculation” and listed shortcomings in the prosecution’s case. There was almost no police investigation, he claimed, and significant questions revolving around Clancy’s condition outside the night of the killings and her lack of memory of what happened.
At the trial, jurors heard testimony that Clancy said she heard voices instructing her to kill 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan Clancy. Her DNA was found on exercise bands used to strangle them. Before the trial, Reddington himself filed a motion in which he said Clancy was willing to stipulate, in writing, to her involvement in the children’s deaths.
“For the first time, the defendant is arguing that there is no evidence she did this,” Prosecutor Shanan Buckingham told the judge. “I’d suggest to you the entire record is voluminous as to information supporting the fact that she did this.”
Clancy remains charged with murder and is expected to stay at a psychiatric hospital until her case is resolved.
Clancy could have been sentenced to life in prison if convicted of murder. If acquitted, the judge could have ordered her confined to a mental health facility.
Her former husband, Patrick Clancy, who discovered the children’s bodies, has said in interviews that he forgives her. The livestreamed trial generated intense public interest and drew attention to maternal mental health after childbirth.

title: Multi-generational family-owned lobster pound on MDI listed for $6M
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A historic, multi-generational family lobster pound on Mount Desert Island is for sale for $6 million.
Thurston’s Lobster Pound features a more than 3-decade-old restaurant overlooking Bass Harbor with signature bright yellow awnings and an 80-year-old wholesale operation. The business supports local fishermen by supplying fuel and bait while purchasing their daily lobster hauls.
The sale of the historic lobster pound follows the slow but steady decline of the region’s most quintessential profession: lobster fishing.
The lobster pound in the village of Bernard, on the quieter, southern edge of MDI was recently listed for sale Wednesday by LandVest realty group. The sprawling 1.53-acre property includes a restaurant, commercial lobster pound business, commercial wharves, a fuel dock, equipment to operate the business, an office and a two-bedroom employee apartment, among other amenities, according to the listing.
LandVest has received two inquiries on the property so far, according to listing agent Scott McFarland.
“We’re hoping that whoever buys it will keep it pretty much status quo,” McFarland said.
Thurston’s has some of Bass Harbor’s oldest structures, a few of which have existed since the 1860s, according to the Island Institute, a nonprofit that helps coastal communities navigate for climate and economic change.
Thurston’s was among dozens of commercial piers spread out along Maine’s coast to be damaged from back-to-back 2024 winter storms, which also battered Seawall Road near Southwest Harbor. That road will be closed through October to be permanently fixed.
Thurston’s received a share of a $250,000 Island Institute grant, split among 52 businesses, following the severe storms. It used the financial aid to rebuild sections of its damaged wharf, according to the institute.
The Bernard wholesale operation dates back to 1946, when Fred Thurston purchased the working waterfront property from a family member and began selling fuel and bait to local fishermen, according to the pier website.
Since then, the business has been passed down five generations, and is now owned by Michael and Elizabeth Radliffe. Their daughter and son-in-law, Christina and Derek Lapointe, oversee daily operations.
The Radcliffes opened the restaurant in 1993, and, barring a brief six year break between 2006 and 2012 when they leased the property to a longtime employee, have operated the shorefront seafood eatery ever since. The restaurant now seats 178 guests between several indoor and outdoor spaces.
“They put their heart and soul into that business for many years, and they’re getting up in age,” McFarland said of the Radcliffe owners. “It’s just time to make a transition.”
The popular seafood restaurant is set to close for the season Friday.
The restaurant’s traditional lobster roll is frequently listed among the island’s best by locals and travelling food bloggers.
News of the listing left locals hoping the treasured spot would remain as is following its sale.
“Oh nooooooo, whoever buys it please keep it the same,” one Facebook user wrote. “It will break my heart if it’s not.”
An employee who answered the restaurant’s phone Thursday morning declined to immediately comment on the property being for sale.

title: Narcotics unit investigating Ole Miss student deaths calls for ban on synthetic kratom
text:
LAFAYETTE COUNTY, Miss. (WMC/Gray News) - Law enforcement in Mississippi is calling on state lawmakers to ban synthetic kratom.
In a statement released Wednesday, Lafayette County Metro Narcotics discussed the drugs found at the scene of the deaths of two Ole Miss students last week.
Shortly after the deaths, Lafayette County Metro Narcotics issued a warning about kratom after packaging with the suspected substance was discovered.
“That warning was not a declaration that kratom or any specific substance caused either death. It was a proactive effort to inform the public of a potential danger while investigators worked to determine the facts,” the statement in response reads.
Court documents detail students’ activity before deaths
Toxicology tests are incomplete, but court documents filed Monday reveal what 18-year-old Aidan Hamilton and 20-year-old Robert Strang were doing in the hours and days before their suspected overdose deaths.
Investigators say both students purchased SMAX Pseudo-DHM pills, a chemically manipulated product, days before their deaths.
Investigators say records show Hamilton made multiple purchases at Puffs Vape Tobacco and Beer in Oxford. Two employees of that store were arrested and 500 units of kratom were seized.
The Metro Narcotics team also found an assortment of “THC cartridges, gummies, pre-rolls and other suspected THC substances.”
Recreational marijuana is still classified as an illegal Schedule I drug in the U.S.
Strang reportedly bought similar products from a store in Yalobusha County.
Narcotics unit calls for legislative action
“These investigations are far from over,” the statement released Wednesday reads.
The unit calls on Mississippi legislators to take immediate action to ban the synthetic kratom products.
“We need immediate legislative hearings, a thorough examination of the state’s controlled substance laws, and clear answers about how manufacturers, distributors and retailers can be held accountable when their actions put lives at risk,” the narcotics unit said.

title: What caused Spruce Mountain High School to hand out 19 different suspensions this year?
text:
Spruce Mountain High School has had 19 different student suspensions so far this school year
The school's principal says that the first couple of weeks have been tough for staff.
Spruce Mountain High School has had 19 different student suspensions so far this school year
The school's principal says that the first couple of weeks have been tough for staff.
Spruce Mountain High School's principal says that a month and a half into the school year, administration has already handed out 19 suspensions to students, six of which were related to civil rights and discrimination issues.
During a school board meeting, principal TJ Plourde broke down what caused the different suspensions. He said six involved incidents between students, five were for inappropriate language used towards staff, and one was a threat.
There were also six "civil rights violations" according to Plourde. A member of the school board asked the principal which protected classes, like race or gender, it involved, but he said the cases involved different ones.
Maine's Total Coverage reached out to RSU 73's superintendent for a further breakdown of all the suspensions, but they did not answer. However, based on the numbers from the school board meeting, 19 suspensions are 5.6% of the student body if there were no repeat suspensions for the same student.
The National Center of Education Statistics compiles out-of-school suspension data nationally and for individual states. The most recent year was the 2020-21 school year where numbers were low, likely due to virtual learning. However, looking at data from the 2017-18 school year, the rate of students who had out-of-school suspensions was 4.96% nationally, and 4.10% for Maine.
It's unclear if all of the 19 suspensions at Spruce Mountain High School were out-of-school suspensions.
"It's been a tough few weeks here, and I think we've dealt with it in the best way that we can," Plourde said at the school board meeting. "It's not a bad thing; it's just something that we're dealing with, and we're going to move through it."
The school plans on having the youth educational program Choices Matter at the school to talk to the students about making smart choices. According to the program's website, it puts a lot of focus on traffic safety, but Plourde said they will ask them to talk about how to better communicate with each other.

title: Very dense red tide confirmed along the Maine coast
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Dangerous red tide confirmed along the Maine coast
Dangerous red tide confirmed along the Maine coast
Maine has been dealing with a large algae bloom along the coast for weeks. On Thursday, testing of samples collected by a fisherman at about 12:30 p.m. on Wednesday off the coast of Harpswell confirmed the existence of a Karenia bloom, commonly known as red tide.
High-density blooms are generally considered those having a density of more than one million cells per liter. The testing in Maine found a density of 20 million cells per liter. Video shared by Harpswell Marine Resources & Harbor Management showed very brown and murky water.
The testing was done at the lab for Bowdoin College's Schiller Coastal Studies Center in Harpswell. The sample was collected after the weekend nor'easter moved away. There had been hope that the storm would move the algae bloom away from shore.
On Sept. 8, sampling confirmed the presence of Karenia mikimotoi in Portland Harbor at levels known to affect fish and shellfish.
On Sept. 10, Harpswell Harbormaster Darcie Couture told Maine's Total Coverage she had received reports of dead and dying clams and worms from clam harvesters.
She said this problem could impact shellfish harvesting in Harpswell for two years.
You can track all current shellfish closures online.
On Monday, Sept. 21, Harpswell Marine Resources & Harbor Management said that new readings that morning showed that dissolved oxygen (DO) levels in Maquoit Bay in Brunswick and Middle Bay in Harpswell were starting to crash, but were currently fine in the upper New Meadows River.
"We need to brace for the second wave of impacts from this event, which will come when low DO eventually causes suffocation mortalities in these areas if it doesn't turn around soon," management wrote.
For aquatic animals, dissolved oxygen in the water is like the air animals on land need to breathe. When DO levels get too low, there's a real risk of suffocation and death.
Officials say that when the high cell counts (chlorophyll) are on the way down, it is often followed by a bloom "crash" - the bloom cells start to die as they run out of nutrients and favorable growth conditions, and that decay drags down the DO in the water.

title: Obituary: Robert Barry Cumler
text:
WARREN – With hearts full of love and respect, the family of Robert Barry Cumler, 72, of Warren announces his passing on Sept. 23, 2026. Bob will be remembered as a respected attorney, a true sportsman and a loyal and generous man to family and friends.
Born in Cleveland, Ohio, to Robert and Ruth Barry Cumler, Bob was the second of six children. The family moved several times between Ohio and Maine and spent fun-filled summers at the family camp on Cobbossecontee Lake in Manchester. The property remained in the family for over 60 years and was loved by generations. Bob graduated from Granville High School in Granville, Ohio, where he played basketball and formed lifelong friendships.
He took undergraduate and postgraduate classes at the University of Maine at Orono and graduated from Colby College in 1977. In 1984, Bob obtained his law degree from Franklin Pierce Law Center, now known as the University of New Hampshire Franklin Pierce School of Law. Tuition was paid by running heavy equipment on construction sites in the summers in Ohio with his brother, Tom, and occasionally with his father. He also dug clams in Friendship, rowing from Garrison Island to his favorite spots on the Meduncook River.
While studying at Orono, Bob met his future wife, Holly Carlson, in the botany lab and they recently celebrated their 48th wedding anniversary. His legal career began in 1984 when he joined Jim Davidson’s practice in Waldoboro, continuing the practice with Peter Lynch under the name Cumler & Lynch. At the time of his retirement at the end of 2025, Nicholas Stiles had joined the firm, along with Rachel Klotz, under the name Cumler, Lynch & Stiles. Bob was a dedicated lawyer for 41 years who found the work and the relationships he formed there highly satisfying. Barbara, Jess, Jodi, and Abby were all loyal staff whom he depended on and counted among his friends. Boating in Friendship with Holly and Cranberry Island picnics with his entire family were favorite traditions for many years. Bob loved planning and cooking for all family gatherings. He cooked most dishes without using recipes, and was humble when people complimented his food.
Many weekends were spent with great friends partridge hunting and fishing for salmon and brook trout around Caratunk, Moosehead Lake, Wilson Pond and Grand Lake Stream. Dix Island provided more special times with friends to dig clams, deer hunt, and relax around blazing fires. At home, Bob stayed busy with yard work, growing vegetables and rooting for the Patriots and Celtics. In Florida, Bob would fish for tripletail for hours with Holly, and travel to different beaches by boat if the fish weren’t biting. He took up biking around the neighborhood in the past few years, and enjoyed making new friends. Bob’s last two memorable trips were to Portugal and Spain with most of his family, and extended trip to New Zealand with Holly to travel the wild backroads and fish. At the end of each vacation, Bob was always ready to get back to the office. His work, his family, and his many friends meant the world to him.
Bob is survived by his wife, Holly Cumler; brother, Tom Cumler and his wife Addy Cumler; sisters, Ruth Cumler, Cathy Cumler-Dennis and her husband Peter Dennis, Patty Cumler-Bryant and her husband, Bill Bryant; nephews, Joshua Cumler and his wife, Hannah Cumler; Colby Wieland and his fiance Nikki Hickey, Sam Bryant and his wife Carissa Bryant; nieces, Gillian Bryant, Hannah Cumler, Callie Arculeo and her husband Ryan; great nieces Zoe Cumler and Zara Arculeo; and great nephews Bobby Cumler and Phineas Cumler.
The family wishes to acknowledge the exceptional care that Bob received at Windward Gardens in Camden. We are incredibly grateful for the skilled care, the kindness and compassion shown by everyone, and the respect shown to Bob in his final days.
Please join us in remembering Bob on Tuesday, Oct. 13 for visiting hours and refreshments from 1 p.m. to 3 p.m. in the Fellowship Hall of the Broad Bay Congregational United Church of Christ at 941 Main Street in Waldoboro, Maine.

title: California helicopter crash kills 2 people and leaves 2 hospitalized and 1 missing
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — A medical helicopter crashed off Catalina Island near Los Angeles, killing two people and leaving two hospitalized, authorities said.
Rescuers early Thursday searched for a fifth person who was reported to be in the aircraft and was missing, the Los Angeles County Fire Department said in a social media post.
First responders were called to the crash shortly before 8 p.m. Wednesday and pulled four people from the water. Two were pronounced dead at the scene and two were brought in stable condition to hospitals on the mainland, the fire department said.
“This remains an active scene with search and rescue operations continuing throughout the night,” the department said.
The National Transportation Safety Board said it is investigating the crash.
Los Angeles County Supervisor Janice Hahn said in a post on X that she was told the medevac helicopter crashed shortly after takeoff from Catalina.
County firefighters and lifeguards responded to the scene, along with the U.S. Coast Guard and the sheriff’s department, officials said.
Authorities said the helicopter was submerged in 240 feet (73 meters) of water off Catalina, which is located about 22 miles (35 kilometers) off the mainland of Los Angeles County.
The helicopter was believed to be owned by REACH Air Medical Services of Sacramento, California, KTLA-TV reported.

title: Caribou City Council candidate wants to spur development and revitalization
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A Caribou city councilor is seeking reelection because she wants to see the city encourage economic development, grow housing and remain an affordable place to live.
Tamara Lovewell, 47, first joined the City Council in January 2024. 
She is running unopposed and is the only incumbent who’ll be on the ballot in November. Newcomers are running for the other two open council seats.
“As a taxpayer myself, I am keenly aware of the burden that increasing property taxes place on our residents,” Lovewell said. “I believe one of the best long-term ways to address this is by growing our tax base rather than continuing to place more of the burden on existing taxpayers.”
Lovewell and her husband, Lance, have been married for 22 years and have a blended family of 12 children and six grandchildren.
Family is the most important part of their lives and is her greatest motivation to make the community a better place, she said.
If elected, economic development and drawing new opportunities to Caribou would be among Lovewell’s top priorities. She also feels it’s important to spur community revitalization, invest responsibly in infrastructure and services and bring new housing into the city.
To accomplish that, she’d like to explore more grant-funded projects, seek public-private partnerships and promote fiscal responsibility within city departments.
City leaders need to create a community where people want to live and which gives new families a reason to make their home in Caribou.
“I believe we need to recognize what makes our community special and build upon it, while looking creatively at opportunities to revitalize our city, grow our tax base and improve quality of life,” Lovewell said.
Council service “comes with quite a learning curve,” she said, but she’s learned a lot about municipal policy and decision-making.
The council has delved into important issues during her tenure, including blight removal, cleanup projects and public safety improvements. Members have also enlarged small-business opportunities and promoted positive municipal working conditions, she said.
She’d like to see the group work more toward finding middle ground on important issues. Councilors bring their own perspectives, which is good, but should be open to changing their minds.
“We can respect each other’s viewpoints while also having the flexibility to listen, reconsider our own positions and think outside our own boxes when necessary,” she said.
Lovewell said her independent perspective has allowed her to make decisions based on common sense, reasoning and putting the needs of the community above political affiliation.
Though unaffiliated with a party, she often aligns with Republican values, she said.
Lovewell studied business and pre-law at Mt. Hood Community College, Columbia Gorge Community College and Central Washington University.
She is also a small-business owner: She and her husband operate Ruska Coffee Co. in Caribou.
Voters should know that councilors are community members, too, and most pursue the elected volunteer position because they genuinely want to help make the community a better place, Lovewell said.
“It is my heartfelt desire to make the best decisions I can, always considering the many people who may be impacted by those choices,” she said. “I will continue to serve Caribou thoughtfully and with integrity, common sense, an open mind and a willingness to work across differences for the people of our community.”

title: AARP Poll: Older Maine voters show sharp ticket-splitting in Senate, governor races
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - AARP has released its annual poll of Maine voters 50 and older.
Turnout is expected to be high once again among older voters, but pollsters report notable ticket-splitting among the nearly 1,000 Mainers surveyed.
While Sen. Susan Collins holds a 6-point lead over Troy Jackson among voters 50 and older, Democratic gubernatorial candidate Hannah Pingree is polling strongly across all age groups against Republican Bobby Charles and independent Rick Bennett.
Survey respondents ranked affordability, protecting Social Security, healthcare costs, and Medicare as their top concerns, with 60% of older Mainers reporting that they are worried about personal finances.
Voters 50 and older make up about 44% of Maine’s population, but casted 59% of all ballots in the 2024 presidential election.
Pollsters say that outsized turnout, paired with Maine’s status as both the nation’s oldest state and a key battleground, makes this voting bloc critical.
“Maine had the biggest gap between the Senate and gubernatorial votes, and it’s really 50+ voters that are driving that gap,” explained Matt Hogan, an AARP pollster partner from Impact Research. “We see a 10-point gap overall between the Senate margin and the gubernatorial margin, but among 50+, that gap grows to 16 points. Among seniors, it grows to 21 points, which I think just really, again, underscores the critical importance of the 50+ vote.“
Ultimately, AARP found a strong majority want candidates who pledge to protect Social Security from cuts for those who paid into it and take immediate action to lower healthcare costs.

title: Let’s not replay the tragedy of life without vaccinations
text:
I want to share how my family has been affected by vaccines. First, comic relief: when our baby began receiving the recommended shots, I was pleased but mystified by her reaction: she simply smiled at the nurse. Weren’t babies supposed to yell? Each time we returned to the medical office for follow-up vaccines, I witnessed happy interactions between my baby and the nurses. Was our kid normal, I wondered? Finally, a few years later, our child — then a toddler — loudly conveyed her opinion about that sharp “pinch.” Phew.
There are much sadder records in my extended family about a lack of medicines to help beloved siblings, parents and children. For example, before Penicillin was commonly available (in the 1940s) my grandmother’s sister died at age 21 (in 1930) of pneumonia. I’m glad that many other diseases have been controlled thanks to science. Smallpox, typhoid and diphtheria used to terrify communities. My ancestors also feared yellow fever, polio, mumps, measles and tetanus.
Let’s not replay those tragedies. Instead, let’s ensure that everyone gets to learn about the best medications available. My ancestors would have loved access to such medicines.
Mariana Tupper
Falmouth

title: Sen. King bill could speed up, reduce costs for some affordable housing projects
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
For more than a year, affordable housing developers in Maine have been wrestling with the requirements of a federal rule that they say is burying them in paperwork and making construction impossible.
Sen. Angus King thinks he can help.
On Wednesday, Maine’s independent senator introduced the Build American Efficiency Act, a bill encouraging the federal government to work with manufacturers on a publicly available database of certified American-made products that would meet the requirements of the Build America Buy America Act.
Also known as BABA, the program requires all building projects using certain government funds to source 95% of their construction materials from the United States.
Developers have said the administrative burden of simply tracking down domestic materials has been extreme and adds as much as $150,000 per project – and that’s not including the premium costs for American-made materials.
“It’s a perfect example of a well-meaning policy that turned out to have negative consequences,” King said in an interview Thursday. “You’ve got hundreds, if not thousands, of builders, each individually trying to sort through this maze, and now what our bill would do (is) create a simple, easy-to-access database so that they don’t have to do that.”
‘EXTENSIVE’ CHANGES NEEDED
The proposal, co-sponsored by Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, is a step in the right direction, but Laura Mitchell, executive director of the Maine Affordable Housing Coalition, said developers need more than a database to help projects move forward.
“BABA is really clogging the affordable housing development pipeline,” she said. “We’re really grateful for Sen. King being creative, and trying to find shortcut pathways to make it easier to comply with BABA, (but) this bill doesn’t offer the extensive level of changes that are needed.”
The National Electrical Manufacturer’s Association, identified in the bill as a possible standard to use, has the “Make It American BABA Registry,” which has a list of 68 manufacturing facilities spread across 15 companies that are certified to make 50-or-so products.
But compared to the roughly 1,600 parts that go into an affordable housing project, the few dozen products that are on that registry don’t carry much impact.
Mitchell said the Make it American system simply hasn’t certified enough products.
“There’s still going to be a lot of work put on these nonprofit affordable housing developers,” she said.
King, however, believes they can get certifications for all the hundreds, if not thousands of pieces.
“I think AI might help us on this,” he added.
THE WAIVER WAIT
For materials unavailable from American manufacturers, like HVAC systems or their components, developers can request a waiver from the Department of Housing and Urban Development.
And then they wait. And wait.
Laura Reading, director of affordable housing for Portland-based Developers Collaborative, waited for more than seven months for waivers for her two projects in Portland and Windham.
Both projects are set to close this month, but Reading found out last week that the waiver for her Portland project, a 110-spot childcare center for Youth and Family Outreach and 60 units of housing, needs to be resubmitted because it only covers funding from MaineHousing, not additional money from the city.
She’s hopeful it will be fast-tracked but noted that HUD has not given her a timeline.
A database wouldn’t help Reading’s current projects, but she said she could see one being useful in the future.
“The documentation for all of this has been a bit insane because all of these vendors want to use their own form and their own letter (of certification),” she said. “Some of them are not as clear as we need them to be.”
King said the list could also help speed up the waiver process, allowing HUD to more easily check whether something is available domestically and quickly approve or deny the request.
Reading added that it could potentially help HUD identify what products aren’t yet made in the U.S. (like an HVAC) system and create a universal waiver so developers aren’t forced to wait months for an approval on the same item for every project.
‘THE SILVER BULLET’
A general waiver is one of a handful of “administrative” changes that Mitchell, at the Maine Affordable Housing Coalition, said would be the most consequential. She’s hopeful to see HUD come out with one for HVAC by the end of the year.
Alternatively (or additionally), HUD could increase the allowable percentage of foreign materials from 5% to 10% or 15%. Or it could exempt affordable housing from BABA altogether.
“That would be the silver bullet addressing all of this,” Mitchell said.
The “Build Housing Affordably Act,” proposed in the House, would do so temporarily, while also instituting a 90-day window for waiver approvals.
Maine is one of the first states to come up against the BABA requirements, and affordable housing developers that have had their projects halted indefinitely are pushing to get the issue fixed before it spreads across the country.
Housing has recently become a bipartisan issue and King is optimistic that the bill can make it through Congress without any major setbacks and be enacted by the end of the year.

title: Donald Trump at center of feisty 1st Maine gubernatorial debate
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
President Donald Trump loomed large in an often testy debate Thursday that saw three gubernatorial candidates bicker on stage as much as they advocated bipartisanship and dove into the weeds of tax, housing and energy policy.
As she did in the Democratic primary, former Maine House Speaker Hannah Pingree invoked the president multiple times, citing rising prices in the wake of the Iran war, calling governors the front lines against an overreaching Trump administration and urging voters to boot Republicans out of Congress.
Independent state Sen. Rick Bennett of Oxford did not criticize the president directly, but linked the unpopular war to increased fuel and gas prices hurting Maine families and businesses. He also said he’d push Maine to reduce dependency on fossil fuels, and to work with other New England states to expand renewables, in stark contrast to the Trump administration’s pro-oil-and-gas posture.
And even Republican attorney Bobby Charles, who has long embraced Trump and was known for his similarly bombastic style during the GOP primary, highlighted two disagreements with the president: the Iran war and broad tariffs undercutting Maine consumers and businesses.
“I do not agree with him right now,” Charles said of Trump’s war, noting he did support previous U.S. attacks on Iranian nuclear facilities. He added that while he backed some targeted tariffs, he was “absolutely against” levies that were across the board or upended trade between the U.S. and Maine’s biggest trading partner in Canada.
The candidates laid out a number of economic, tax, housing, energy and addiction recovery plans in the Portland debate, hosted by News Center Maine and the Maine State Chamber of Commerce. And while moderators sought to rein them in amid crosstalk over policy and character, at many points the debate grew heated. None of them spared each other from attacks even as they all touted bipartisan bona fides.
“This is why we need women in charge,” Pingree said during a heated exchange between Bennett and Charles, drawing cheers and laughs in arguably the biggest line of the night.
Charles was fiery and aggressive on taxes, budget cuts and energy, pinning plenty of the state’s problems including high costs and a tough business environment on both Pingree’s and Bennett’s time in Augusta.
After Charles accused Pingree of a conflict of interest involving her family, she said, “Bobby has been spewing … misinformation,” lying about both her husband and taxes. She said she was not surprised by Charles’ negativity, while the attorney pushed back that he was presenting facts.
Bennett and Pingree both went after Charles for being a longtime Washington lobbyist, with Bennett questioning Charles’ ability to manage the budget based on previous reports of his work at the State Department. Charles argued Bangor Daily News reports on audits during his leadership were cherry picked and inaccurate.
Bennett at one point appeared unready for a question after arguing between Pingree and Charles, drawing laughs by saying it was hard to digest what was flying rapid-fire from the Republican. He later found his footing and pointed to partisanship as part of the reason government isn’t effective, citing the state budget growing significantly over the last decade.
“Nobody’s minding the store,” he said.
The debate capped off with each calling for bipartisanship. Bennett, a former Republican who often talked up his independence, said politicians should “start treating each other as human beings.”
Pingree said she’s learned how to agree to disagree and work together with lawmakers on both sides of the aisle. Mainers want elected leaders “to get things done to improve their lives,” she said.
Charles said “words are cheap,” arguing Democrats have stonewalled Republicans in Augusta and worked against the legacies of former Secretary of State Ed Muskie and former U.S. Sen. Margaret Chase Smith.
“I pledge to do my level best,” he said.

title: He travels the country foraging his food and medicine, here’s why
text:
HENDERSONVILLE, N.C. (InvestigateTV) — Robin Greenfield doesn’t buy his food. He finds it.
Greenfield is traveling the country foraging 100 percent of his food and medicine.
Greenfield said his lifestyle starts with his clothes, which are 100% compostable.
“This outfit is 100% homemade, natural fiber and natural dye,” Greenfield said. “I could just walk into those woods, die like a deer and there would be no littering.”
Fifteen years ago he changed the way he was living to minimize his impact on the earth and others. That starts with the food he eats.
During a 30-minute walk along a Hendersonville greenway, he found nearly a dozen edible plants.
“This right here is dock, this is a common edible,” Greenfield said.
Teaching others
Greenfield said he has spent the last decade learning and educating others about the grocery store that is in backyards.
“I think it is kind of revolutionary for people who think that food has to come from a grocery store, it has to cost money, but no food is growing all around us,” Greenfield said.
He doesn’t just eat plants.
He also forages meat anywhere he can find it, including roadkill. He fishes for his own food and forages starches like yams.
Health checkups
Greenfield checked with a doctor about whether this lifestyle is healthy. The doctor said he has no health concerns.
Greenfield doesn’t use a toothbrush or toothpaste because he only wants to use natural items. According to a dentist, he has some teeth staining, but no tooth decay.
His mission is to live in harmony with the earth and treat nature as a food pantry and pharmacy.
“A big part of that is through living simply. Just realizing what do I actually really need,” Greenfield said.
Greenfield’s lifestyle goes far beyond food and nutrition. He has sold almost all of his possessions and now lives below the federal poverty line on purpose.
You can watch the full interview with Greenfield on The Wellness Files with Kari Beal podcast.

title: Anesthesiologist explains what likely caused Christa Pike’s failed execution by lethal injection
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WVLT/Gray News) - A Tennessee anesthesiologist is weighing in on what may have gone wrong during the botched execution of Christa Pike.
Dr. Paul Allen, a professor of anesthesiology at the University of Tennessee Health Science Center, said the details coming out of Wednesday’s execution point to one likely explanation: the needle never properly made it into her vein.
According to Allen, for the lethal drug pentobarbital to make someone unconscious, it has to go directly into the bloodstream, meaning the needle has to be properly placed inside a vein.
Allen said finding a usable vein can be difficult for a number of reasons, including dehydration.
According to the Department of Corrections, Pike declined to pick a specialized last meal, though she did eat a meal during the period when her execution was stayed.
Allen added that veins can also be harder to access if they have been damaged over time.
“Not eating and drinking would make finding the vein and getting into the vein more difficult. Also, if she had bad veins to begin with, that were from either substance abuse or something of that nature, then it would be difficult to cannulate her vein,” Allen said.
In past appeals, Pike argued she had a vein condition that could make the lethal injection process difficult.
Allen said infiltration happens when a needle misses the vein or punctures through it, and the drug leaks into the soft tissue under the skin instead of circulating through the blood.
“What happened here, I would suspect, is that they infiltrated the vein,” Allen said. “That means that the drug, instead of going in the bloodstream, went into the peripheral tissues in the arm or wherever they put the needle in.”
Allen said that could explain a witness account that Pike described her arm throbbing in certain spots after the injections.
Allen said when the drug leaks into surrounding tissue instead of the bloodstream, it can still make someone drowsy, which could explain why Pike appeared sleepy and snoring, but the dose did not kill her.
The doctor stressed that his medical assessment was based on witness accounts, not a confirmed finding. The exact cause of what went wrong has not been officially released.
Allen said pentobarbital is not a new drug. It was once prescribed for sleep, and doctors have long known it can be dangerous in large doses.
According to Pike’s legal team, she survived the failed execution, but she has since been in critical condition, receiving life-saving medical care at an area hospital.
Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee has since halted executions in the state for the rest of the year.

title: Ex-officer Amber Guyger convicted of murdering neighbor in his own home granted parole after 7 years
text:
(AP) - The white Dallas police officer convicted of killing a Black man in his apartment that she mistook for her own was granted parole Thursday after serving seven years of her 10-year sentence.
The Texas Board of Pardons and Parole, which is appointed by Gov. Greg Abbott, rejected Amber Guyger’s initial parole request in 2024 but approved her case over the objections of victim Botham Jean ‘s family the first time she was eligible for release.
Guyger, 38, was convicted of murder in the 2018 killing of 26-year-old Jean, an accountant from the Caribbean island nation of St. Lucia, who had been eating a bowl of ice cream when Guyger entered his home and shot him. Guyger was arrested three days after the shooting and was fired before her murder trial.
She had faced up to life in prison or as little as two years. Prosecutors initially asked the jury for a sentence of 28 years.
The shooting drew widespread attention because of the strange circumstances and because it was one in a string of shootings of Black men by white police officers. Guyger’s sentencing hearing also included a stunning courtroom scene when Jean’s brother and the Black judge presiding over the case embraced the sobbing Guyger.
At trial, Guyger said that after a long shift at work and still in uniform, she walked up to Jean’s apartment — which was on the fourth floor, directly above hers on the third — and found the door unlocked. She said she thought the apartment was her own and that Jean was an intruder when she drew her service weapon and entered.
Civil rights attorney Lee Merritt said Thursday that Jean’s family “strongly opposed this parole.”
“They stood up again and again to ask that the full sentence be served. A 10-year sentence was already a fraction of what was lost. Releasing Ms. Guyger after seven years makes that loss feel even smaller in the eyes of the system. It is not smaller,” Merritt said.
In 2024, a jury ordered Guyger to pay Jean’s family nearly $100 million in a federal civil trial.
In granting her release, the board said it reviewed a “plethora” of information in her case.
The board said Guyger’s record did not include a documented pattern of violent or assaultive arrests or convictions, and showed she completed programs in her prison treatment plan to get and keep a job when she is released.
The board said the state prison system will determine when she is released. Texas Department of Criminal Justice officials did not immediately respond to requests for comment Thursday.

title: Christa Pike's Execution: Everything We Know
text:
Christa Pike’s Execution: Everything We Know About the Only Woman on Tennessee’s Death Row
Christa Pike is the only woman on Tennessee’s death row and was scheduled to be executed Wednesday for the 1995 killing of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer.
Pike, 50, was set to die by lethal injection at 10 a.m. Sept. 30 at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville.
Instead, a series of last-minute legal battles delayed the execution for hours.
Christa Pike's Execution Was Delayed for Hours
The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 6th Circuit issued a stay Wednesday morning, blocking Pike’s execution “until further order of this court.”
READ MORE: Mackenzie Shirilla Loses Final State Appeal in Double Murder Case
Tennessee’s attorney general’s office then asked the U.S. Supreme Court to overturn the stay and allow the execution to proceed.
The Supreme Court cleared the way shortly before 6 p.m., allowing Tennessee officials to begin the lethal injection process.
Christa Pike Remains Alive After Execution Attempt
Pike’s attorneys said prison officials administered two doses of lethal pentobarbital, but the drugs did not stop her heart.
“Ms. Pike has not lost consciousness and still has a heartbeat and is audibly snoring,” one of her attorneys wrote in an emergency motion.
A federal judge later ruled the motion moot after the state said medical personnel had begun providing care.
READ MORE: Oklahoma Mom Found Guilty After Husband Fathered 11-Year-Old Daughter’s Baby
Now, her attorney says Pike remains hospitalized on a ventilator and is “critically ill.”
Stephen Ferrell, a member of Pike’s legal team, made the comments during an appearance on CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday (Oct. 4). He said Pike’s legal team did not yet know her prognosis and “may not know for several days.”
Ferrell added that he had not personally seen Pike since she was hospitalized and said her hospital room is currently “guarded.”
READ MORE: These Five States Have Produced the Most Serial Killers
He also said Pike “may never recover” following the failed execution attempt.
What Did Christa Pike Say Before the Execution?
According to Associated Press reporter Kim Chandler, an official media witness, Pike said she was going to leave the world in the same way she had spent most of her life: “in love.”
Chandler said Pike expressed love for the people who were outside criticizing her and then said, “I’m at peace. I’m ready to be free.”
Pike ended her statement by calling it “a happy day.”
Why Was Christa Pike Sentenced to Death?
Pike and her boyfriend were convicted in the 1995 killing of Slemmer, who was their classmate at a job training facility in Knoxville.
READ MORE: ‘Dances With Wolves’ Actor Nathan Chasing Horse Sentenced to Life in Prison 
Slemmer was stabbed and beaten to death, and a pentagram was carved into her body. Other details of the case fueled fears surrounding the Satanic panic that spread across parts of the U.S. during the 1980s and 1990s.
Pike was sentenced to death, while her boyfriend received a life sentence.
Tennessee Pauses Executions After Christa Pike Survives
Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee is pausing all executions scheduled for the rest of the year after Christa Pike survived two doses of lethal pentobarbital during her execution attempt.
Carrying out a lawfully imposed sentence is among the State's most serious responsibilities, and the people of Tennessee expect it to be done in a manner that is not only legal and constitutional, but is effective.
Lee called for a “comprehensive, third-party review” of Pike’s execution, adding, “Therefore, the remaining scheduled execution will not be carried out this year.”

title: He’s 65 with a 100-year-old kidney, thanks to his mother’s lifesaving gift
text:
‘By my side all the time’: He’s 65 with a 100-year-old kidney, thanks to his mother’s lifesaving gift
He’s 65 and living with a 100-year-old kidney.
Calculating that math requires factoring in the intangible bond between parent and child that saved Raymond Vetuskey’s life at the age of 16.
“I’m a miracle, and I feel great every day,” Vetuskey said. “I know I’m lucky and I thank my mother.”
His mother, Elizabeth “Betty” Vetuskey, who would have turned 100 in June, stepped up to give her son a second chance when he was facing kidney failure.
Related video above | Siblings celebrate 50 years of life-saving kidney transplant
Vetuskey suffered from a virus as a teenager that severely damaged his kidney, according to officials with the University of Rochester Medicine Strong Memorial Hospital.
Dialysis was hard on his body and he was losing weight and strength. An organ transplant at the age of 16 was his only chance for survival.
Luckily, his mother was a near-perfect match, paving the way for a lifesaving surgery on March 2, 1978.
Vetuskey said he "felt great afterwards," and just weeks later, he attended a Genesis concert. He saved the ticket stub as a reminder for how quickly his life changed.
“Every day, I think of her," Vetuskey said in an interview with WHEC in Rochester, New York. "She’s right by my side, all the time."
Vetuskey said his mother has since died, but she would have turned 100 this year.
But 48 years later, officials with University of Rochester Medicine say his kidney is still thriving, making him the longest surviving kidney transplant recipient in the program.
“His story is an inspiration for organ transplant recipients and anyone awaiting a new organ,” said Miklos Z. Molnar, MD, PhD, director of Transplant Medical Services for URochester Medicine Transplant Institute.
The average survival is 15-to-20 years following living donor kidney transplantation, hospital officials said.
Advances in therapies and anti-rejection regimens have aided in prolonging lives for many recipients like Vetuskey.
Vetuskey’s young age combined with the familial match provided a strong foundation for this success, Molnar said.

title: Troy Jackson says sorry for comments on Jewish Mainers’ views on Gaza war
text:
Troy Jackson told media outlets across the country that he was sorry for saying Jewish Mainers “don’t like to” call Israel’s war against Hamas in Gaza a genocide, “only because they’re Jewish and what that means to them with the Holocaust.”
Jackson made the initial comments to News Center Maine on Tuesday. He called the three-year war — which began with Hamas terrorist attacks on Oct. 7, 2023, and has since resulted in the killing of 70,000 Palestinians by Israeli forces in Gaza — a genocide, and continued on to say Jewish Mainers “don’t like to use that term.”
“I apologize for the pain that caused,” Jackson said in a statement. “Mainers hold a range of deeply considered views, and I promise I will always listen and work to approach these conversations with the care and respect they deserve.”
Jackson reiterated his belief that “what’s happening in Gaza is a genocide.”
“In trying to acknowledge that, I misspoke and made a generalization about Jewish Mainers’ views that doesn’t reflect what I meant to say,” his statement continued.
In the News Center Maine interview, Jackson also called Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, a war criminal. The International Criminal Court, to which the U.S. is not a signatory, issued an arrest warrant against Netanyahu in 2024 for starving people in Gaza as a means of war and ordering the killing of civilians.
A United Nations commission first found that Israel was committing genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza strip in September 2025. More than 64,000 children have been killed or injured in Gaza since October 2023, the U.N. said in August.
Like his predecessor for the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate, Graham Platner, Jackson’s use of the word “genocide” to describe Israel’s actions in Gaza is part of a larger call to stop arms funding to Israel. Brown University found that the U.S. sent $21.7 billion in military aid to Israel from October 2023 to September 2025 — for which Republican Sen. Susan Collins, Jackson’s incumbent opponent, has consistently voted.
“I don’t want the United States sending money, a blank check to (Netanyahu) anymore, watching young children, innocent people die,” Jackson told News Center Maine. “I mean, I just disagree with that.”

title: MaineDOT converting high-crash Newburgh intersection into 4-way stop; local drivers divided
text:
NEWBURGH, Maine (WABI) - Motorists traveling between Newburgh, Hampden, and Winterport will soon face a major change to their daily commute as state transportation crews prepare to overhaul a notoriously dangerous intersection.
Beginning Tuesday, Oct. 6, the Maine Department of Transportation will convert the crossing of Route 9 (US-202) and Route 69 (Carmel Road North) into a permanent, all-way four-way stop.
The project includes new pavement markings, advance flashing “Stop Ahead” warning signs, flashing red LEDs on all stop signs, and reconfiguring the overhead beacon to flash red in all four directions.
A persistent ‘High Crash Location’
According to MaineDOT safety reports, the crossing has long been classified as a “High Crash Location”—an official state designation for intersections seeing crash rates substantially higher than the statewide average for comparable roads.
Recent state data indicates that crashes at the intersection are climbing:
- 2020–2022: 11 crashes
- 2021–2023: 13 crashes
- 2022–2024: 15 crashes
The state’s analysis revealed a Critical Rate Factor (CRF) topping 5.0, meaning collisions at the crossing occur at more than five times the expected statistical rate. Past visibility enhancements, including brush clearing and warning signs, failed to reduce the collision frequency.
Close calls spark calls for action
For local commuters who travel the corridor daily, the safety upgrades cannot come soon enough.
Bethany Tompkins of Hampden says near-misses are a regular occurrence, including a terrifying close call this past week while driving with her children.
“The one on the left was actually at a stop and the one on the right was coming up to the stop sign and then just gunned it and he just went straight through,” Tompkins said. “I slammed on my brakes, all the stuff in my car flew forward and he just went around me. Didn’t even look at me, he just kept driving. And of course I look back and my kids are back there, and my oldest one, her face is white.”
Truckers raise winter safety and traffic concerns
While drivers welcome added protection against high-speed T-bone collisions, commercial haulers warn that forcing heavy trucks to come to a complete stop could create a different set of road hazards.
Ernie Wallace, a Winterport resident who has driven commercial rigs for decades, says the geography and heavy freight volume on Route 9 make a four-way stop problematic—particularly as winter approaches.
“If you’re going towards Hampden, when they stop, the traffic behind them has to stop. Then he’s going to be two, three, four miles before he can ever get going again up to speed,” Wallace said. “The trucks coming the other way will have to start stopping probably way up by the golf course to get stopped at that stop sign safely, especially in the winter time.”
Drivers push for alternative solutions
While Tompkins and Wallace view the stop sign mandate through different lenses, both drivers agreed that another measure should have accompanied—or preceded—the stop signs: creating an enforceable, reduced speed zone to slow down approaching traffic.
Longer-term infrastructure studies from MaineDOT show that modern roundabouts provide significant safety benefits at high-speed rural crossings, historically delivering a 53% reduction in total crashes, a 74% drop in injury crashes, and a 92% reduction in overall crash costs.
Installation details
Town officials in Newburgh, Hampden, and Winterport are urging motorists to plan for extra travel time during the morning and evening commutes while drivers adjust to the new traffic pattern.
Work on the intersection is scheduled to take place on Tuesday, Oct. 6, weather permitting. In the event of inclement weather, the conversion will take place on Thursday, Oct. 8.

title: Phil Pressey back for second season as Maine Celtics coach
text:
Phil Pressey will return for a second season as the Maine Celtics head coach, the team announced Thursday.
Pressey is the first head coach to return for a second season with the Maine Celtics since Brandon Bailey was promoted to the Boston Celtics coaching staff after the 2018-19 season. Maine went 27-23 and reached the NBA G League playoffs for the fourth straight season.
Pressey replaced Tyler Lashbrook, who lead Maine to a 29-21 record in 2024-25 and a berth in the Eastern Conference finals before moving up to the Boston Celtics coaching staff.
Also returning to Maine this season are assistant coaches Mike Malat and Boaz Mensah. Devin Sweetney, Jacob Kester and Rich Kelly are joining the team’s staff.

title: Three Maine football storylines to follow against Sacred Heart
text:
One step forward, two steps back. That’s been the story of the University of Maine football team this season, and the Black Bears definitely went backwards Saturday in a 43-17 loss at Elon.
After a winless September, Maine (1-4, 1-1 Coastal Athletic Association) begins its October slate by hosting Sacred Heart (1-3, 1-1) at 3:30 p.m. Saturday (FloSports). Here are three storylines as the Black Bears look to snap a four-game losing streak.
Could change be coming at QB?
Starting quarterback Eddie Buehler struggled against Elon, completing 14 of 35 passes for just 88 yards. Caden Drezek, a junior, got his first action of the season in the fourth quarter, throwing a touchdown pass to Kevin Jackson to cap a 75-yard drive.
Maine coach Jordan Stevens was adamant that he never considered a QB change after Buehler’s less-than-stellar outing against Merrimack. But in Monday’s CAA news conference, Stevens was noncommittal when asked if Buehler would start.
“We’re just looking at that during the week here,” Stevens said.
Stay tuned.
Special teams, special teams, special teams
Without context, the total yardage in Maine’s most recent loss (Elon 376, Maine 315) doesn’t look all that bad. So, why the lopsided defeat? It’s because the Black Bears gave the Phoenix short fields, primarily via special teams miscues.
Elon blocked two punts in the first quarter, the first leading to a field goal and the second resulting in a safety. A 24-yard Elon punt return in the third quarter put the Phoenix at Maine’s 43, leading to a touchdown, and a muffed punt by the Black Bears late in that quarter resulted in another Elon field goal.
Throw in a 31-yard Elon touchdown drive after Maine turned it over on downs in the fourth quarter, and you see that the Phoenix offense didn’t have to do much to score. Sacred Heart (18.8 points per game) hasn’t lit up the scoreboard this year, but if Maine doesn’t clean up its special teams, that won’t matter.
A spark in the run game?
It wasn’t all bad news for Maine against Elon. After rushing for just 174 yards on 93 carries — 1.9 yards per carry — in three games since its season-opening win, the Black Bears rushed for 167 yards on 34 carries against Elon.
Can Maine repeat that? Well, consider that New Hampshire, which had averaged just 2.6 yards per carry prior to last week’s game at Sacred Heart, rushed for 181 yards on 29 carries (6.2 average) against the Pioneers. Perhaps the Black Bears can have similar success.

title: Thousands of eligible Mainers to automatically receive discounts on electric bills
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Thousands of low-income Mainers are slated to receive automatic discounts on their monthly electric bills.
Gov. Janet Mills announced on Thursday that $40 million in electricity discounts and other services would be distributed among eligible Maine households through the state’s Low Income Assistance Program, and many will be enrolled automatically this year.
Amounts vary by income, but eligible Central Maine Power customers could see discounts anywhere between 25% and 81%, while Versant customers could get between 17% and 83% off monthly, according to the announcement.
To qualify, customers must have a household income at or below 150% of the federal poverty guidelines. About 44,000 Maine ratepayers participated in the program last year, according to the announcement, but officials determined that roughly another 23,000 were eligible.
To increase participation, many households will now be enrolled automatically.
The Maine Department of Health and Human Services will use information from programs like SNAP and MaineCare to determine automatic eligibility, the announcement states. Those participating in the federally funded Home Energy Assistance Program will also be automatically enrolled in the program.
“Beneficiaries will have their information securely shared with participating utilities” to have the discounts applied to their monthly bills, the announcement said. Mainers not already participating in a DHHS program can apply for the Low Income Assistance Program.
The roughly $40 million in funding for the program is a leap from $22.5 million in 2025, with an additional $7.5 million being approved in a recent supplemental budget for this year. However, the program is largely funded by a ratepayer monthly surcharge of about $2, according to the announcement, with further support from New England Clean Energy Connect.
The monthly nature of the discount is also new to the program. Previously, program participants were given lump sums to offset their costs.
The program is part of “SupportLink,” a Mills initiative implemented through DHHS that connects Maine households with discounts and other forms of relief they are eligible for, unless they opt out, the announcement states.
“Maine families are being pushed to the brink by the president’s whipsaw tariffs and his reckless war in Iran,” Mills said of President Donald Trump in a written statement. “At a time when every dollar matters, my administration is making it easier for vulnerable Mainers to lower their electric bills without unnecessary paperwork or bureaucratic hurdles.”
SupportLink currently includes nine electric utilities, as well as Efficiency Maine and the Portland Water District, according to the announcement.
Mills credited the participating utilities as well as Maine’s Public Advocate, Public Utilities Commission, DHHS and MaineHousing for making the automatic process possible.
Leaders of those state entities praised the move in statements that were included in Thursday’s announcement.
Ian Yaffe, director of the Maine DHHS’ Office for Family Independence, said it’s “a meaningful step toward making services easier to access.”
“Families should not have to navigate multiple applications or send paperwork from one agency to another when we can securely share the information needed to connect them with help,” Yaffe stated.
Maine Public Advocate Heather Sanborn said it will “provide meaningful, predictable support” for struggling Mainers, while Dan Brennan, director of MaineHousing, said it will “help take some of the complications and pressures off our most vulnerable households.”
Eligible households can expect the discounts to begin taking effect on or soon after their November bill, according to the announcement, which notes the timing could be off due to electric bills not always following the calendar month.

Two major bills, including one addressing electricity costs tied to data centers, failed in the Senate Wednesday as lawmakers prepare for a six-week recess
Two major bills, including one aimed at addressing electricity costs tied to data centers, failed in the Senate Wednesday as lawmakers prepare for a six-week recess.
Polls show that many Americans are concerned about the impact data centers have on electricity prices, and the failure of the Ratepayer Protection Act could sway voters in November.
According to a recent Economist/YouGov poll, about half (51%) of Americans say that the construction of new data centers is a bad thing for the country.
A recent AP-NORC/University of Chicago poll found about 6 in 10 Americans support limiting the number of new data centers, while 63% are concerned about their impact on electricity prices.
On Wednesday, Senate Democrats blocked the Republican-backed Ratepayer Protection Act, which would have required state utility regulators to consider making large power users, such as data centers, pay for the grid upgrades needed to serve them. However, the bill would not have mandated states to adopt the standard.
The bill needed 60 votes to advance but fell shy of three votes, leading to finger-pointing from both parties.
"Let me be clear, this is nothing more than a messaging bill on the eve of an election," said Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M.
"If Democrats block this bill, they will prove beyond a shadow of a doubt that they do not care about affordability and that they will not do anything to take action to help," said Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio.
Senate Democrats also blocked the Stop Insider Trading Act, which would have prohibited lawmakers from buying individual stocks while in office. Critics argue the bill does not go far enough because it allows lawmakers to keep existing stock holdings.
The stock trading bill also included a separate measure requiring voters to present photo identification at the polls, part of the Save America Act, which Democrats have deemed a nonstarter.

title: Chairlift rides return to Camden Snow Bowl for unique fall foliage experience
text:
CAMDEN, Maine (WABI) - A Midcoast offering is back again beginning this weekend, giving visitors a view of the fall foliage like no other.
Camden Snow Bowl is opening its chairlift every Sunday this October for foliage rides.
For $15 per person, you can take an approximately 25-minute ride up Ragged Mountain to the summit, with the changing trees lining the way.
From there, you can enjoy hot drinks and experience an ocean-view from the mountaintop, a feature only a few East Coast ski mountains have.
The Snow Bowl has been hosting the fall foliage rides for over a decade.
Organizers say it’s a great way to fundraise for the municipal mountain while also taking advantage of the beautiful scenery.
“We just love continuing the recreation opportunities all four seasons long. So, this is a really cool way to get people up on the mountain in the fall, folks that maybe might not come in the winter,” said Grace McMullen, assistant director for Camden Parks and Recreation and the assistant general manager at the Snow Bowl.
Rides run every Sunday this month from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.
Children must be three feet tall to ride, and children five and under get free entry.
Attendees get the choice to take the chairlift back down the mountain, or enjoy the trails to make their way back.

title: Changes to SNAP benefits begin Thursday: Here’s what it means for your wallet
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Changes to SNAP benefits begin Thursday: Here’s what it means for your wallet
Major changes to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program go into effect Thursday for millions of Americans.
In the short term, most recipients will see a slight bump in payments to buy groceries. But in coming months, households could face stricter eligibility requirements.
Every year on Oct. 1, the federal government adjusts its monthly SNAP benefits to account for inflation.
In the 48 contiguous states and the District of Columbia, the maximum monthly benefit for a single-person household rises to $306 from $298. For a family of four, the maximum increases to $1,023 from $994. Actual benefits vary based on household income, size and expenses, and the maximum amounts are higher in Alaska, Hawaii, Guam and the U.S. Virgin Islands.
The annual adjustments are intended to account for changes in food costs.
Trump’s law shifts costs to states
At the same time, states must begin paying 75% of SNAP’s administrative costs, up from 50%, while the federal government’s share falls to 25%.
Those expenses include the work of running the program, rather than the food benefits deposited for recipients. Federal law is also scheduled to require some states to contribute toward benefit costs beginning in October 2027, based on their payment error rates.
The changes stem from a 2025 tax and spending law signed by President Donald Trump.
The benefit increases and state cost shift begin as the federal fiscal year starts Thursday.
Fewer people are receiving SNAP benefits
The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, known informally as food stamps, provides monthly payments to help low-income residents to buy food.
More than 37 million people nationwide received SNAP benefits in March, according to preliminary USDA figures.
That’s down nearly 5 million people — over 11% — from a year earlier.

title: Heating oil prices in Maine drop from record high

MAINE (WABI) - Heating oil prices in Maine dropped slightly this week after reaching record highs.
