title: Scarborough residents continue fight to push ICE out of its only facility in Maine
text:
The presence of Maine’s only Immigration and Customs Enforcement processing facility has brought a national conflict to Scarborough.
Scarborough representatives at the local, state and federal level cannot ignore the actions of ICE agents, many residents have argued in the wake of a Scarborough resident’s detention during a routine check-in in August, a 26-year-old man’s fatal shooting by an agent in Biddeford in July, and the January surge of federal immigration enforcement in Maine..
“Silence in the face of what ICE is doing in this town implies consent,” resident John Raby said during Wednesday’s Town Council meeting.
Residents have taken action — protesting, organizing, collecting information — and called for action from councilors and state representatives, who in turn have enacted legislation, demanded transparency, and called for ICE reforms. But questions remain about the efficacy of these actions and what power people have against a large federal agency.
“I join the widespread public frustration and outrage over ICE’s criminal behavior — and I say that as a lawyer,” Councilor Bill Donovan said. “Our authority is limited, but we’re mad. It’s wrong, and it’s happening in our town.”
Over the past few months, local and state officials have looked into what actions they can take against the ICE facility that opened in 2021, promising that this is just the beginning.
Last month, the Scarborough Democratic Town Committee submitted a petition to Maine’s congressional delegation requesting a meeting to review and remove the ICE facility at 40 Manson Libby Road.
About 700 Scarborough residents and 100 people from neighboring communities signed the petition, spurred by concerns about the conduct of ICE agents following the killing of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Biddeford.
The petition requested a meeting with the delegation and representatives from the U.S. General Services Administration — which is leasing the ICE building — the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and ICE, as well as state and local officials and Joshua Soley, the leasing and property manager for the ICE building. Rep. Chellie Pingree of Maine, D-1st District, also sent a letter to facilitate the request for a meeting at the end of September.
On Sept. 28, Scarborough Democratic Town Committee leadership met with representatives from Sen. Susan Collins’ and Angus King’s office, along with two representatives from Pingree’s office, according to a news release from the committee.
The committee asked the delegation to suspend operations at the facility until it is investigated, evaluate whether the facility is needed, commit to congressional action, request a civil rights investigation, request and provide updates on facility operations, and prevent expansion into Newport or elsewhere in Maine.
It also requested the delegation respond to the proclamation the Scarborough Town Council passed in July, calling on Maine’s congressional delegation to investigate. Only Pingree’s office had responded by the time of the September meeting, with a letter sent in July asking the Department of Homeland Security to seriously reconsider whether the facility should continue operating.
The delegation has already taken some actions regarding the ICE facility, but they noted it is difficult to get substantive responses from executive agencies, according to the committee.
Collins’ representative said they will relay the committee’s requests to the senator’s office in Washington, and King’s staff will ensure the office responds to the Town Council proclamation, according to the committee. Pingree’s staff will provide an update on the committee’s requests in two weeks, continue efforts to place testimony from the Biddeford shadow hearing into the official congressional record, and connect Scarborough advocates with resources related to funding for legal representation.
TOWN COUNCIL ACTIONS
On Wednesday, the Town Council had a first reading of a new ordinance that would expand limitations on cooperating with federal immigration enforcement to all town employees — a policy the Scarborough Police Department has followed for years. The second reading and vote will take place Oct. 21.
The ordinance was modeled on an ordinance Rockland passed last year, Councilor Jon Anderson said. It prohibits the use of town resources and employees to assist immigration enforcement, except where required by state or federal law or judicial order.
Other Maine communities have also passed similar ordinances, including Portland and Lewiston, and a state law that took effect in July restricts Maine’s police officers and sheriff’s deputies from coordinating with federal immigration agencies.
The council also unanimously authorized the council chair to send a letter to DHS, requesting a tour of the ICE facility. Some of the councilors were pessimistic about their chances of receiving a response from the agency, but they shared the belief that the town must take all actions at its disposal.

title: Attacker's motive remain unknown after FlyDubai flight to Israel escapes disaster
text:
Attacker's motive remain unknown after FlyDubai flight to Israel escapes disaster
The motive of the Omani copilot who stabbed his captain on a flight to Israel, causing the plane to plummet dangerously and forcing it to land in Saudi Arabia, remained unknown on Thursday as investigators across the region raced to learn more.
Video: Co-pilot of an Israel-bound Flydubai flight tried to hijack the plane after stabbing the captain
Israeli passengers who were on the FlyDubai aircraft carrying 174 people from the United Arab Emirates to Tel Aviv have described how the bloodied Indian captain managed to open the cockpit door to let them in before they grappled with the copilot and stabilized a descent so sharp that the plane’s rudder was torn away.
“We felt helpless, suspended in midair, and I didn’t know who to turn to. But it was all instinct to survive,” one of the responders, Asaf Rajuan, said in a new statement shared by Israel’s presidency.
A regional official briefed on the investigation said the suspect, an Omani citizen, was under arrest and confirmed that Saudi authorities were working with countries, including Israel, to try to determine a motive. He said the UAE, the United States and Oman also were involved. The official did not describe the extent of Israeli involvement.
“All possible scenarios, from terrorism to mental disorders, are being looked into. Nothing is ruled out for now,” said the official, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss the probe.
Israeli investigators will join the interrogation of the copilot
Israeli intelligence and security officials were investigating the copilot in Saudi Arabia, according to another regional official who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media.
Saudi Arabia does not have formal diplomatic ties with Israel, but there is longstanding security and intelligence cooperation through alternative channels.
Video shot inside the plane by Shota Musayev, a dentist who treated the captain, shows the copilot on his knees, with his hands tied behind his back. The copilot's name still has not been released.
The UAE government said its investigation team had begun its work into the motive and “whether it was linked to any terrorist purpose," adding that UAE law applies to crimes committed on board.
Capt. Smit Machchhar, widely praised as one of the heroes of the flight, was reportedly in stable condition, the Indian Embassy in Saudi Arabia said overnight. The condition of the copilot was not clear.
Asked if there is any indication of Iranian involvement, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Fox News "it’s too early to say.” The prime minister told CNN that Israel had received no specific warning.
U.S. President Donald Trump told reporters at the White House that he and Netanyahu discussed the incident “at length” by phone and it seemed as though the copilot “was perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack job."
Netanyahu said he also spoke with the UAE’s president, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, who agreed that Israel would join the interrogation of the suspect.
Netanyahu had warned in recent days of unspecified, heightened security threats. The country is a week away from the anniversary of the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel, which has triggered the war in Gaza.
Israel’s foreign ministry said the people on board were from Israel, India and the UAE. The U.S. State Department said four passengers had American citizenship.
FlyDubai has said its flights to and from Israel would be suspended.
School where captain trained calls the safe landing ‘miraculous’
In the chaos that unfolded about two and a half hours after leaving Dubai, the flight descended from 33,000 feet to 17,000 feet (around 10,000 meters to 5,100 meters) in about a minute, before making an erratic circle close to the Jordanian border and landing Tabuk about an hour later, according to Flightradar24, which identified the aircraft as a Boeing 737 Max 8.
The head of the New Zealand flight school where the Indian captain trained, Philip Kean, called it “miraculous in the way that the airplane was never, ever kind of designed for that sort of dive and survive that, the airplane actually didn’t break up completely.”
Already, Trump was praising the U.S.-based Boeing for producing a plane “that was able to withstand G Forces and Strain far beyond what it was designed.”
During the frantic search for a place to land, a person who heard the flight’s communications with air traffic control described the plane being turned away by Saudi Arabia and Jordan before eventually landing in Tabuk, while passengers screamed in the background. The pilot’s voice was trembling as he called “mayday” and said a hijacking was taking place.
The air control operators gave no reason for the refusals. The person who heard the communications spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media.
___
Magdy reported from Cairo and Anna from Jerusalem. Associated Press writer Josef Federman in Jerusalem contributed to this report.

title: It’s time for Mainers to put country first
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Many old-time Mainers, from all political parties, say they support Sen. Susan Collins because she brings money back to the state as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee. There is also a certain nostalgia many Mainers feel. “She’s done well for us in the past” and “she’s independent.” In truth, Collins has cost us more by following Donald Trump’s policies.
Collins has voted with Trump 95% of the time, resulting in extreme financial pain for most Mainers as well as Americans across the country. The war in Iran, tariffs, inflation, steep cost increases to gas and diesel, heat and groceries, the ballooning deficit, rising interest and mortgage rates, unaffordable housing, reduced SNAP benefits and $3 billion in Medicaid funding cuts in Maine alone to take effect in January — together with out-of-control immigration officers. These all have resulted from Trump’s policies, most of which Susan Collins has supported.
Until the Senate and the House are flipped, the unrestrained chaos, financial devastation and erosion to democracy will continue. What happens nationally affects Mainers too. It is time for Mainers to vote to push back against the impacts of Trump’s worst behaviors and put the country back on track. It’s time to put personal nostalgia aside, recognize that perfect is the enemy of good, and vote Susan Collins out and Troy Jackson in.
How will everyone feel if the Senate stays in Trump’s Republican control because Maine reelected Collins?
Susan Duncan
Phippsburg

title: Bobby Charles has received lobbyist money. But he’s trying to make an ‘Augusta’ distinction.
text:
He may run a firm that has lobbied in Washington, D.C., since the turn of the century, but in his bid to become Maine’s next governor, Republican Bobby Charles has said he is rejecting money from “Augusta lobbyists.”
Charles first made that pledge in June, when he called on Democrat Hannah Pingree and independent Rick Bennett to join him in also not accepting donations from Central Maine Power or “AI data center companies.”
He has occasionally left out the “Augusta” distinction, such as during an interview this summer. But he reiterated it in his latest digital ad, released Wednesday, in which he calls Augusta a “crime scene” and accuses Pingree and her family of profiting off her years leading Gov. Janet Mills’ policy and innovation office.
“I’m the only candidate in this race who has rejected Augusta lobbyist money,” Charles says in the ad.
But Charles has received money from lobbyists who live outside of Maine. He has received more than $13,000 in donations from current or former lobbyists and their family members, according to campaign finance records.
Still, Charles’ campaign, which has raised more than $1.8 million since launching last year, reiterated Wednesday that lobbyist donations to his campaign have not come from “Augusta lobbyists.”
That pledge has not changed the fact that Pingree, a former Maine House speaker from North Haven, has consistently led Charles by double digits in independent polling of the race to succeed Mills, a Democrat who is termed out of office after this year. Additionally, Charles has not received help from the Republican Governors Association in the form of ad spending — a sign that national leaders do not view the Maine race as very competitive.
Scrutiny over campaign donations across Maine’s high-profile races for the Blaine House, U.S. Senate and 2nd Congressional District is nothing new, though it ticked up this week when Pingree’s campaign said it would return $300 it received earlier this year from a former attorney for Jeffrey Epstein after the Portland Press Herald asked for comment on the donation.
Charles’ firm, The Charles Group, has lobbied on Capitol Hill for decades, though the Leeds lawyer and former assistant U.S. secretary of state says it mostly focuses on conducting studies, providing management guidance and evaluating performance for clients. Charles’ lobbying ties drew criticism even from his Republican primary opponents earlier this year, including Jonathan Bush, who dubbed him “Lobby Charles.”
Campaign finance records show he received contributions such as $4,150 from Van Hipp Jr. and his wife. Hipp Jr., a former South Carolina Republican Party chair, has a lobbying role as chair of American Defense International, a Washington-based consulting firm.
Among other donors, Rob Hartwell, a Virginia-based lobbyist and former chief of staff to several Republican members of Congress, chipped in $250. Bob Carlstrom, a former lobbyist who joined Charles in serving in former President Ronald Reagan’s administration, gave Charles more than $2,600. And Barry Caldwell, a former lobbyist for Cigna and other firms, donated $1,000.
Bennett, a former Maine Republican Party chair and state senator from Oxford who has been mired in the single digits in polls, and Pingree, who previously led Mills’ policy office and is the daughter of Democratic U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, mostly wrote off Charles’ pledge as performative. Each of them has received donations from people who work for lobbying firms that operate in Augusta, such as Preti Flaherty and Mitchell Tardy Jackson.
The lobbyist donations are not the only point of contention among the candidates. The Maine Democratic Party filed a complaint Thursday morning with the state’s ethics commission against Charles. The complaint said Charles reported 46 contributions totaling more than $25,000 over the legal contribution limit, including donors who gave thousands of dollars more than the $2,075 maximum amount allowed under law.
Charles gave the similar “no Augusta lobbyist” donations line in a campaign ad he released last week, featuring him and his daughter walking by apple trees while referring to Mills and Pingree as “Augusta’s bad apples.”
While not producing TV ads like Pingree, who has led the field in raising more than $4.2 million, Charles has projected confidence at his chances after he also used an array of lower-budget digital ads and social media videos to win a crowded Republican primary in June.
The three gubernatorial candidates will face off Thursday evening in a debate hosted by the Maine State Chamber of Commerce at Cross Insurance Arena in Portland.

title: Would ‘Medicare for All’ increase federal spending by roughly $3 trillion annually?
text:
Yes.
“Medicare for All” would increase federal spending by roughly $3 trillion annually, according to some estimates.
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Troy Jackson says he supports the idea, which would replace most private health insurance with federally funded “single-payer” coverage, in which the government pays most medical bills.
A 2019 Urban Institute study estimated that a comprehensive single-payer system would increase federal spending by $2.8 trillion annually, largely replacing expenditures by employers, households and states.
The Congressional Budget Office subsequently projected $1.5 trillion to $3 trillion in additional annual federal health care subsidies by 2030, depending on the program’s design.
But higher federal spending doesn’t necessarily mean higher overall costs: A recent Yale University analysis, which has not yet been peer-reviewed, estimated that Medicare for All could reduce total annual U.S. health spending by more than $1 trillion and save an estimated 114,000 lives a year.
This fact brief is responsive to conversations such as this one.
The Maine Trust for Local News partners with Gigafact to produce fact briefs — bite-sized fact checks of trending claims. Read our methodology to learn how we check claims.
Sources

- Congressional Budget Office: Testimony on a Single-Payer Health Care System That Is Based on Medicare’s Fee-for-Service Program
- Urban Institute: From Incremental to Comprehensive Health Reform
- Urban Institute: Don’t Confuse Changes in Federal Health Spending with National Health Spending

title: Presidents rarely visit Indian Country. Trump’s planned Choctaw Nation rally will be the latest
text:
ALBUQUERQUE, N.M. (AP) — President Donald Trump is holding a campaign rally on the Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma on Thursday, putting him in the company of just a handful of U.S. presidents who have visited tribal nations while in office.
The rally is part of Trump’s recent campaign push through deep red states, where he has been stumping for Republican candidates and promoting his agenda ahead of November’s midterm elections.
The Choctaw Nation is renting its venue for the rally but not sponsoring the event, it said.
“We hope his visit provides an opportunity to learn more about what we do as a sovereign nation for our members and for all people in southeast Oklahoma,” Choctaw Nation Principal Chief Gary Batton said in a statement.
It’s not the first time Trump has been to a tribal nation. In the homestretch of the 2020 election campaign, Trump visited the Lumbee Tribe of North Carolina and endorsed its push to secure federal recognition as a tribal nation, which he signed into law in 2025.
Tribal delegations have been meeting with presidents in Washington since the Early Republic, but presidential visits to reservations have been few and far between. The purpose and tone of those visits have changed dramatically as the relationship between the U.S. and tribal nations has evolved.
Early visits promoted assimilation
What was likely the first visit to a reservation by a sitting U.S. president occurred by happenstance. While traveling to Yellowstone National Park in the summer of 1883, President Chester A. Arthur met with Shoshone and Arapaho leaders on the Wind River Reservation and complimented the tribes’ “practice of industrial pursuits,” according to an account by Lt. Gen. Philip Sheridan at the time.
While there, Arthur’s delegation pressed Shoshone Chief Washakie and Arapaho Chief Black Coal to consent to breaking up the reservation they shared into private parcels — a move aimed at dismantling tribal sovereignty and solving what Arthur termed the “Indian problem.” Both chiefs refused.
Other early presidential visits to tribal land similarly reflected an era when the U.S. tried to undermine tribal sovereignty and assimilate Native people into white society. Theodore Roosevelt’s 1903 trek to Havasupai land at the bottom of the Grand Canyon preceded the forced removal of that tribe to make way for a national park.
During his 1927 visit to the Pine Ridge Reservation in South Dakota, President Calvin Coolidge promoted assimilationist boarding schools.
Recent presidential visits have focused on tribal sovereignty
President Bill Clinton made Pine Ridge a stop on his 1999 “New Markets Tour,” billing the visit as the first by a sitting president to tribal land since President Franklin Delano Roosevelt’s 1934 trip to the Blackfeet Nation in Montana. Clinton acknowledged the federal government failed to meet its obligations to hundreds of tribal nations and called for investment in Pine Ridge’s economy.
“We have tried to have a more respectful, more proper relationship with the tribal governments of this country, to promote more genuine independence, but also to give more genuine support,” Clinton said.
In 2014, President Barack Obama met with Dakota youths and attended a powwow on the Standing Rock Reservation in North Dakota, speaking about expanding economic and educational opportunities in Indian Country and promoting tribes’ inherent right to govern themselves. The following year, Obama spent time in the Iñupiaq village of Kotzebue in Alaska, highlighting the impacts of climate change on Arctic communities.
President Joe Biden made a somber apology
In 2024, President Joe Biden traveled to the Gila River Indian Community in Arizona to formally apologize for the federal government’s role in separating Indigenous children from their families and forcing them to attend boarding schools run by the U.S. and churches. A probe by Biden’s administration found that in addition to being stripped of their languages and cultures, many of those children experienced physical, emotional and sexual abuse. At least 970 died, and federal officials acknowledged the true number is likely higher.
Speaking alongside boarding school survivors and their descendants, Biden called that 150-year era a “blot on American history.”
“It’s a sin on our soul,” Biden said. “Quite frankly, there’s no excuse that this apology took 50 years to make.”
The visit marked a rare acknowledgment of the assimilationist policies that shaped some of the earliest presidential encounters with tribal nations.
___
This story is published through the Global Indigenous Reporting Network at The Associated Press.

title: Attorney says woman will plead not guilty in killing of son-in-law at California park
text:
DUBLIN, Calif. (AP) — The attorney for a Northern California woman who was charged along with her husband in the killing of their son-in-law said Thursday that she plans to plead not guilty and focus her defense on the abuse allegedly perpetrated by the victim.
Shili Chen and her husband Shouyong Zhang, both 77, appeared in court briefly to ask the judge for more time before entering formal pleas. They were both charged Wednesday with murder after authorities say they both shot their son-in-law, Jonathan McKinsey, to death Saturday in a public park. The killing came days before he and the couple’s daughter were set for a hearing in a bitter divorce and custody case.
Curtis Briggs, a court-appointed attorney assigned Thursday to Chen’s defense, said the court documents he has reviewed raised concerns that McKinsey was rageful and could not control his temper.
“Court documents show Mr. McKinsey was extremely violent and dangerous to his family,” he said.
Jennie Otis, a public defender representing Zhang, asked the judge on Thursday that he be medically evaluated, though she did not say for what. Otis declined to comment.
Both required Mandarin interpreters in the courtroom.
McKinsey, a 40-year-old gaming engineer for The New York Times, was killed in the parking lot of a sports complex in Dublin, a city east of San Francisco. A police sergeant was driving nearby and saw him on the ground as witnesses began calling 911 and pointing out the couple in their vehicle, who were still near the scene, Dublin Police Services said in a news release.
Police detained the couple as they were driving away in the parking lot and found a gun in Chen’s possession. Prosecutors said Zhang admitted to shooting McKinsey during a later interview, and another firearm was found in the car that he admitted to using during the crime. Prosecutors also said surveillance video was recovered showing both Chen and Zhang shooting the victim.
Court records show McKinsey’s killing came during a contentious divorce with his wife, Candice Jang, and a custody battle over the couple’s three young children. In petitions for restraining orders filed last year, the couple accused each other of physical, emotional and psychological abuse going back more than a decade. McKinsey, who is transgender, alleged that both Jang and her parents were verbally and physically abusive regarding a gender transition he underwent years ago.
McKinsey was arrested last October and charged with misdemeanor child abuse for allegedly hitting their oldest son. Police said he acknowledged having slapped the child. Prosecutors also charged him with endangering their youngest child after deputies responded to the family’s home to talk with him and found their 2-year-old had been left home alone, according to court documents.
McKinsey pleaded not guilty to the charges and alleged in court records that he had been set up by his wife, who had left the house without telling him the child was sleeping in a crib upstairs. He was released from jail on the condition that he complete 12 parenting classes. At the time of his killing, McKinsey was out on bail and had been trying to enter a mental health diversion program.
It was also in October that Jang obtained a domestic violence protection order against McKinsey.
Jang wrote a long list of alleged abuse by McKinsey in her filing, including an instance in 2010 when McKinsey allegedly had grabbed her by the forearms during an argument and caused her to hit the corner of a coffee table, fracturing a vertebra in her upper back. She also said that in 2023 she called the police to their home after McKinsey pushed their oldest son hard on the head. Jang also accused McKinsey of emotionally abusing her mother.
The Associated Press has been unable to reach Jang for comment.

title: ‘Still alive and snoring’: Christa Pike’s attorneys file emergency motion to halt execution
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV/Gray News) – Tennessee officials were unable to put Christa Gail Pike to death Wednesday for a 1995 murder after administering two doses of a lethal drug.
Her attorneys have filed an emergency motion to halt her execution after they say Pike was “still alive and snoring” after receiving her lethal injection on Wednesday.
“The vein in my arm feels like it’s about to bust,” one witness recalled her saying.
According to the emergency motion, the Tennessee Department of Correction began the execution of Pike at about 9 p.m. ET. The motion says that both syringes of pentobarbital were administered and that Pike “has not lost consciousness and still has a heartbeat and is audibly snoring.”
“It sounded like she was almost choking,” the witness recalled.
The emergency motion filed Wednesday night stated the execution is “causing Ms. Pike unnecessary agony and occurring in violation of [her] right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment.”
The motion also demanded the Tennessee Department of Correction immediately begin lifesaving measures.
The 50-year-old inmate was taken by ambulance from the prison, her attorneys said. She was being treated at a hospital.
“Tonight the State of Tennessee once again failed to carry out a lawful execution,” they said. “We take no pleasure in being right, but the concerns raised by Ms. Pike proved to be true: difficult vein access, blown veins, degraded pentobarbital, no emergency medical care available when things inevitably go wrong, all under a protocol that remains veiled in secrecy.”
As of 11:40 p.m. ET, they said they had not been informed about her condition.
Pike had been scheduled for execution at 10 a.m. Wednesday for the killing she committed at age 18 and would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.
An appeals court stopped the lethal injection just an hour before it was to start, and hours later the U.S. Supreme Court overturned that stay.

title: Longtime leader of Bucksport credit union to retire in 2027
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
“Serving as CEO for the past 31 years has been the greatest honor of my professional life,” said Kyle Casburn, president and CEO of Seaboard Federal Credit Union.
After more than three decades at the helm of Seaboard Federal Credit Union, Kyle Casburn plans to retire as president and CEO at the end of May 2027, the Bucksport-based credit union announced.
Casburn joined Seaboard in 1995 as an assistant manager and was promoted to CEO after three months. Under his leadership, the credit union grew from $42 million in assets to $248 million today.

Tony Manzo, who chairs the credit union’s board, credited Casburn’s “leadership, integrity and unwavering commitment to our employees and members” with positioning the credit union for long-term success.
To help find Casburn's successor, the credit union said its board has enlisted Houston-based Shanley Search Partners to evaluate internal and external candidates for the leadership role.

Founded in 1940, Seaboard has more than 14,000 members and 39 employees, with offices in Bucksport, Ellsworth and Hermon. It is ranked No. 22 among the largest Maine-based credit unions in the 2026 Mainebiz Book of Lists.

title: What’s in a name? Bernard
text:
TREMONT — As our nation’s 250th birthday year winds to a rather contentious close, it’s good to recall the men and women whose vision and courage made the birth of our nation possible. The whole Adams family, for instance, Ben Franklin, Nathan Hale, Thomas Paine and the like. But there are some less heroic historical figures whose hugely unpopular governance of the colonies, and the ever-increasing resentment they caused, served the purpose of driving a wedge between “we the people,” and the British sovereign, George III, and his Parliament.
One of these consequential nonheroes was Sir Francis Bernard, who was appointed Governor of New Jersey in 1758 and two years later the Massachusetts Bay Colony, which at that time included Maine. Apparently, Bernard’s tenure in New Jersey was unremarkable, but the colonists and local officials of the Massachusetts Assembly soon came to despise Bernard for his unflagging support of every tax act Parliament levied on colonial businesses and commodities — sugar, stamps, glass, paper, paint, tea, for example, the revenue of which paid the salaries of loyal judges and governors, such as Bernard himself.

title: Trump says Iran will be hit ‘very hard’ if it is behind copilot who tried to crash flight to Israel
text:
JERUSALEM (AP) — U.S. President Donald Trump said Thursday that if Iran is linked to the copilot who tried to crash an Israel-bound flight, the Islamic Republic would be struck “very hard” for the attempt on the lives of more than 180 people aboard the jet.
Trump issued the warning as investigators worked to determine why the copilot stabbed the flight’s captain, causing the FlyDubai plane to plummet before others on board stopped the attack and landed the airliner in Saudi Arabia.
The president was asked by reporters at the White House whether he had been briefed about any links between the pilot behind the attack and Tehran. He said, “We’re working on it right now.”
“I would say the answer, based on what I’m hearing, is yes, but we’re working on it right now,” Trump said. He did not elaborate about why he suspects Iran might be involved.
Asked if the U.S. would retaliate against Tehran if it was behind the attack, Trump said, “Oh they’ll be hit, very hard, don’t worry.”
“You just ask them,” he added. “They know what happened. They’ll be hit very hard.”
His remarks came as diplomatic efforts to end the war appear to have stalled.
Iranian officials indicated Wednesday that they received an official U.S. response to Tehran’s latest proposal to end the seven-month war, which Trump had publicly rejected just days earlier. The officials did not say what the response contained and whether it was a rejection.
Trump said in a Time magazine interview published Thursday that he will not accept proposals from Iran that “he wouldn’t have approved a year ago,” and left open the possibility of resuming bombing after the Nov. 3 election in the U.S.
Meanwhile, the American military has dispatched roughly 9,000 troops aboard a group of ships to the Middle East, a U.S. official said Thursday. That could mean three carriers will be in the region as soon as late October, according to the official, who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military operations.
Despite Trump’s public rebuff, mediators have continued working with Iran and the U.S. to try to broker a deal to end the fighting and open the Strait of Hormuz, according to officials who were not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity.
Passengers got into cockpit to take control of jet
Passengers on the plane — which was carrying 182 people, mostly Israelis, from the United Arab Emirates to Tel Aviv — have described how the bloodied Indian captain managed to open the cockpit door to let them in before they grappled with the copilot and stabilized a descent so sharp that the plane’s rudder was torn away.
“We felt helpless, suspended in midair, and I didn’t know who to turn to. But it was all instinct to survive,” Asaf Rajuan, who was among those who intervened, said in a statement shared by Israel’s presidency.
A regional official briefed on the investigation said the suspect, an Omani citizen, was under arrest and confirmed that Saudi authorities were working with countries, including Israel, to try to determine a motive. He said the UAE, the United States and Oman also were involved. Saudi Arabia said the copilot had been handed over to the UAE.
“All possible scenarios, from terrorism to mental disorders, are being looked into. Nothing is ruled out for now,” said the official, speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss an ongoing probe.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, without giving details, claimed the attacker underwent Islamist indoctrination. Asked who helped radicalize him, the prime minister told Fox News channel’s “Fox and Friends” he did not know.
When asked by AP how the prime minister knew the copilot underwent indoctrination, Netanyahu’s office said it would not comment.
Netanyahu told Fox that the suspect apparently got through a loophole in Israeli aviation rules that normally bar pilots from flying to Israel if they are from countries that do not have diplomatic relations with Israel, which Oman does not.
The copilot has not been publicly identified. Video shot inside the plane by Dr. Shota Musayev, a dentist who treated the captain, shows the copilot on his knees, with his hands tied behind his back.
Capt. Smit Machchhar, widely praised as one of the heroes of the flight, was recovering in the Emirati capital of Abu Dhabi, the Indian government said Thursday.
It was not clear what the copilot used as a weapon.
Israeli investigators will join the interrogation of the copilot
Israeli intelligence and security officials were in Saudi Arabia to help investigate the copilot, according to another regional official who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media.
Israel has requested that the copilot be sent to Israel for the investigation, though it was unclear if that request would be granted, the official said.
Saudi Arabia does not have formal diplomatic ties with Israel, but the countries have long cooperated on security and intelligence matters through alternative channels.
The UAE government said its own investigation team had begun looking into the attack and “whether it was linked to any terrorist purpose,” noting that Emirati authorities have jurisdiction because the plane is registered there and UAE law applies to crimes committed on board.
Asked if there is any indication of Iranian involvement, Netanyahu told Fox News it was “too early to say.”
Netanyahu earlier said he also spoke with the UAE’s president, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, who agreed that Israel would join the interrogation of the suspect.
On Wednesday, Trump told reporters at the White House that he and Netanyahu discussed the incident “at length” by phone. He said it seemed as though the copilot “was perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack job.”
Oman’s government has not commented.
Netanyahu had warned in recent days of heightened security threats, though he told CNN that Israel had received no specific warning. The country is a week away from the anniversary of the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel, which has triggered the war in Gaza, and weeks away from an election.
The Israeli Foreign Ministry said most of the people aboard the flight were from Israel, along with others from India and the UAE. The U.S. State Department said four passengers had American citizenship.
Someone in cockpit sent out discreet distress codes
Someone in the cockpit sent out two four-digit codes to discreetly signal distress while the plane flew erratically near the Jordanian border with Saudi Arabia, according to Flightradar24.com. The first code was “7700,” the universal “squawk” signal for an emergency, then “7500,” which indicates unlawful interference, including a possible hijacking.
The codes are used by pilots when speaking over the radio may not be possible or wise.
FlyDubai said Wednesday that the jet was secured by on-duty crew members “who diverted and landed the aircraft safely.” A regional official said the crew members were pilots in training. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media.
In the chaos that began about two and a half hours after takeoff, the Boeing 737 Max 8 descended from 33,000 feet to 17,000 feet (around 10,000 meters to 5,100 meters) in about a minute, before making an erratic circle close to the Jordanian border and landing in Tabuk, according to Flightradar24.
___
Magdy reported from Cairo. Price reported from Washington. Associated Press writers Josef Federman in Jerusalem and Laurie Kellman in London contributed to this report.

title: Third Wiscasset Education Budget Moves to November Referendum
text:
Wiscasset residents approved a $10,630,432 education budget proposal at a Tuesday, Sept. 29 special town meeting, setting the town up for a third attempt at validating the budget in November.
The third budget, approved with a vote of 52-14, is a decrease of $113,687 or 1.06% from last year’s education budget.
Wiscasset voters failed to validate two previous education budgets. The first, totaling $11,217,742, failed to meet validation at the annual town meeting by referendum on June 9, 547-535. title: Nokomis field hockey is the Varsity Maine Girls Team of the Week
text:
Varsity Maine Girls Team of the Week: Nokomis field hockey
Entering a game Wednesday at Camden Hills, the Nokomis field hockey team was off to a 6-1 start, including recent victories over Maine Central Institute and Erskine Academy by a combined margin of 10-0.
The Warriors were atop the Class B North Heal point standings, with notable victories over sixth-ranked Gardiner and second-ranked Cony.
“Our schedule has been really tough, but it’s been really fun,” said Nokomis sophomore Maeve Rush. “I think we’ve learned a lot about our game play from playing harder games.”
Nokomis has routinely been a contender in recent seasons but was put in a tough spot in August when coach Shaunessy Saucier left the program to become the head coach at Husson University.
The school moved quickly to hire former Nokomis standout Lauren Neal (formerly Lauren Burke), who played at Merrimack College from 2020-23.
“I’d say (the transition) has been interesting, but I don’t think it could have gone any smoother,” Neal said. “I think I got blessed to have a really good group of girls and a supportive staff. The parents have also been super supportive.”
The schedule doesn’t let up on the Warriors. They were supposed to play back-to-back games this week against unbeaten opponents, but a road game against two-time defending Class B champion Belfast was postponed Monday and will be made up Oct. 10. On Wednesday, Nokomis was visiting Camden Hills (9-0), the No. 1 team in Class A North.
“There’s just so much talent on this team,” Rush said. “I think we’re going to make some waves this season.”

title: Would ‘Medicare for All’ increase federal spending by roughly $3 trillion annually?
text:
Yes.
“Medicare for All” would increase federal spending by roughly $3 trillion annually, according to some estimates.
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Troy Jackson says he supports the idea, which would replace most private health insurance with federally funded “single-payer” coverage, in which the government pays most medical bills.
A 2019 Urban Institute study estimated that a comprehensive single-payer system would increase federal spending by $2.8 trillion annually, largely replacing expenditures by employers, households and states.
The Congressional Budget Office subsequently projected $1.5 trillion to $3 trillion in additional annual federal health care subsidies by 2030, depending on the program’s design.
But higher federal spending doesn’t necessarily mean higher overall costs: A recent Yale University analysis, which has not yet been peer-reviewed, estimated that Medicare for All could reduce total annual U.S. health spending by more than $1 trillion and save an estimated 114,000 lives a year.
This fact brief is responsive to conversations such as this one.

title: Bradley Cooper Set For Duke in Next ‘G.I. Joe’ Movie
text:
Bradley Cooper to Star as Duke in Next ‘G.I. Joe’ Movie
Yo, Joe.
You can’t have a G.I. Joe movie without team leader Duke, and according to Deadline, the upcoming franchise reboot has found the man for the job. That would be Bradley Cooper, who is reportedly set to star in the new Joe, which is directed and written by The Righteous Gemstones star (and Halloween legacyquel producer and co-writer) Danny McBride.
Their report contains zero details about McBride’s take on the G.I. Joe concept, which is based on the long-running toy line from Hasbro. The only concrete tidbit about the film is that it is “uncoupled from a previous crossover film with Transformers that is no longer in development.”
That was the movie that was teased in the post-credits scene of the most recent live-action Transformers movie, 2023’s Rise of the Beasts, when that movie’s human hero, played by Anthony Ramos, was recruited into the membership of G.I. Joe.
READ MORE: 20 Inexplicable Toy Lines Based on Movies
Whatever it is, McBride’s G.I. Joe will be divorced from the previous batch of live-action Joe movies. In that iteration, Duke was played by Channing Tatum, who starred in 2009’s The Rise of Cobra, and then played a supporting role in 2013’s G.I. Joe: Retaliation (where, uh, spoiler alert, Duke got killed off in a Cobra attack). The third and final film in that G.I. Joe cycle, Snake Eyes, was a prequel and did not feature that character.
Unless you count his voice role as Rocket in Guardians of the Galaxy, Cooper has not done many action movies on the scale of G.I. Joe. He did star as Face in the big-screen version of The A-Team from 2010, but otherwise, he’s generally tended to stick to more grounded comedies and dramas. But ... he kinda looks like a Duke type, right?
McBride’s G.I. Joe doesn’t have a release date yet.

title: See Lynne Drexler’s brilliant still lifes in a colorful new virtual exhibition
text:
In some ways, Lynne Drexler (1928–1999) was an outsider artist. While she took part in the New York City art scene in the 1950s and ’60s, Drexler ended up retreating to remote Monhegan Island off the coast of Maine, far from the madding crowd. She had little interest in playing the gallery game; she wanted to live her life and paint. The island proved the perfect spot for both.
Drexler’s island work included a series of still lifes created in the last decades of her life, between 1983 and 1997. They represent, if you will, a final flare of energy from a brilliant colorist and some of her most individual artworks.
“Lynne Drexler’s still life paintings are indeed gifts to us,” said Elizabeth Moss, owner and director of Moss Galleries. “They reflect her deep love of nature, her skilled yet intuitive connection with color and her knowledge of the European greats who came before.”
While flowers in a vase may represent a memento mori — the blooms will wilt and fade, reminding us of the fleeting nature of existence — not so Drexler’s floral studies. The five oils on canvas and nine crayon or colored pencil-on-paper pieces in “Interior Warmth: The Still Lifes of Lynne Drexler” at Moss Galleries give off a kind of radiance. Riffing on the show’s title, you could imagine gathering around them to warm yourself, a break from the sometimes-harsh island weather outside.
Each piece features a tabletop arrangement of flowers in a vase or planted in a pot. The title painting includes a totem-like liquor bottle in the center. Warmth, you could say, comes from a variety of sources.
Some of the pieces reflect the season. “Autumn Splurge,” 1989, captures a riot of flowers that bursts from the vase and reaches to the edges of the canvas. A pumpkin adds to the fall color scheme.
The abstract patterned fields that serve as backdrops tie these works to Drexler’s acclaimed mosaic-like paintings from earlier in her career. “Winter Arrangement,” 1986, places a flower arrangement against a wall of small geometric shapes. The bouquet has an aura, as if giving off energy.
If the crayon and colored pencil pieces are lighter in tone than the oils, they possess their own particular brilliance. Mostly untitled, they capture the glories of island gardens. The often decorative vases complement the colorful arrays.
In several, Drexler includes a household item — a mirror, a ceramic rooster — to add to the action. As with the oils, the patterned backgrounds bring abstraction into play. Wavy, spotted, splintered: these fields of color are an integral element of the lively compositions.
These works underscore Drexler’s early influences, most notably the Fauvist Henri Matisse and abstract artists Robert Motherwell and Hans Hofmann, with whom she studied. Matisse’s colorful freeform compositions, Motherwell’s inventive collages and Hofmann’s push-pull aesthetic add a special charge to her still lifes, lifting them from genre to a kind of genius.
Drexler fits into a vibrant line of flower painters, from Georgia O’Keeffe through Beverly Hallam and Carolyn Brady to such contemporaries as Samuel Gelber, Susan van Campen and Kayla Mohammadi. Like them, Drexler found light and joy in blooming things. Her paintings are a gift to all of us.
Art work available for viewing at Moss Galleries in Falmouth.

title: Patriots tight end Eli Raridon and wife announce death of newborn son
text:
(Gray News) - New England Patriots tight end Eli Raridon and his wife, Anna Raridon, announced the death of their newborn son.
“Our angel, Peter James Raridon, was born on September 11,” the couple announced on Instagram.
In the announcement, the couple said that they learned during the 20-week anatomy scan that their son had anencephaly, which they described as “a fatal condition in which he would not survive outside the womb.”
“While we are absolutely devastated that we were unable to bring our baby boy home, I am grateful to have loved him deeply, kept him safe, and had been his home for the past 9 months before he was called back to Heaven,” the post read.
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, anencephaly is a birth defect in which the baby forms without parts of the brain and skull. The CDC said that almost all babies with anencephaly die shortly after birth and there is currently no cure or treatment.
“I believe our little boy was lovingly knitted together in the womb by God, knowing how deeply he would be loved by our families, our friends, Eli, and me. Though his time with us was brief, his life still precious, his purpose still meaningful, and he will forever be a part of our story,” the post said.
Eli and Anna Raridon were married on May 25, 2025. They announced in an Instagram post on March 31 that they were expecting their first child.
“I have loved you every second of your life & will miss you every second of mine. What a sweet sweet reunion ours will be,” the couple’s post said.
This is Eli Raridon’s first season with the New England Patriots. He was picked by the team during the third round of the 2026 draft. Prior to that, he played for Notre Dame.

title: NTSB preliminary report reveals details of fatal Amazon-contracted cargo jet crash at Miami airport
text:
NTSB preliminary report reveals details of fatal Amazon-contracted cargo jet crash at Miami airport
The National Transportation Safety Board has released its preliminary report on the Amazon-contracted cargo jet crash at Miami International Airport, providing new details about the fatal accident.
The report states that the Boeing jet overshot a runway on Sept. 6, killing five people in a van on the tarmac.
The NTSB said the jet’s thrust reversers, which help slow the aircraft, did not deploy, though it remains unclear why they were not activated.
The agency also released an image from the cockpit, which officials said shows the speed brakes were stowed, meaning closed, when the pilot attempted to land. Speed brakes, which are panels on the wings that reduce lift and drag, were inexplicably retracted.
Federal crash investigators noted that a wheel brake was deployed and then released.
Voice data recorders revealed that one of the pilots called for a go-around— such as touching down and immediately take off again—15 seconds before the recording ends and impact.
The NTSB said the plane was traveling about 130 miles per hour when it went off the end of the runway.
The report is preliminary, meaning no cause for the fatal accident has been determined. A final report could take months or even years to complete.
21 Air, the company operating the jet, released a statement saying, in part, "We are reviewing the information in the NTSB preliminary report closely, alongside our own internal safety and operational protocols, and we will take all appropriate action to improve our safety based on the facts as they are established."

Four astronauts pulled up at the International Space Station on Thursday after launching on an eight-hour express that set a U.S. speed record.
The fresh arrivals include a Canadian whose wife will give birth while he's away.
SpaceX launched commander Jessica Watkins and her crew for NASA after a three-week delay to fix their Dragon capsule's leaking fuel system. Thick clouds threatened all morning to halt the countdown, but in the end, the skies cleared enough to allow for a safe liftoff.
Although their stay at the International Space Station will last a long six months, the flight there was the quickest yet not only for Elon Musk's company, but also any American entity, including NASA. The space station's convenient location when the astronauts launched enabled the fast transit.
With the late-morning liftoff from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Watkins became the first Black woman to lead a crew to orbit. A geologist who worked with NASA's Mars rover Curiosity a decade ago, Watkins is making her second trip to the space station following a lengthy stay in 2022.
"Thanks for an amazing ride," Watkins radioed following liftoff.
The others are newcomers to space: NASA's Luke Delaney, a retired Marine; Canada's Joshua Kutryk, a colonel in the Royal Canadian Air Force; and Russia's Sergey Teteryatnikov, a former submariner. They will replace four astronauts who have been living at the orbiting laboratory since February.
This was the 13th crew launched by SpaceX for NASA, not counting 2020's test flight. All four embrace their Crew-13 designation that pays homage in their mission patch to Apollo 13. The harrowing 1970 moonshot ended with the astronauts' safe return.
References to the number 13 abounded Thursday. Watkins and her crew rode to the launch pad in black Teslas bearing plates that read "Lucky 13." What's more, they carried up a small crocheted golden dragon named Lucky with a four-leaf clover around its neck.
"We figured it wouldn't hurt to bring a little of our own luck just in case, but clearly we don't need it," Watkins said from orbit, noting they were "four of the luckiest humans on or off planet Earth."
Kutryk will become the fourth man to become a father while orbiting Earth. His wife, Heather, is due to give birth to their third child in late November. The Canadian Space Agency promises plenty of support for the entire family when the big day comes.
"A lot of life-changing things can happen over six months," NASA manager Dana Weigel said on the eve of liftoff, noting that the space agency will do its best to keep Kutryk looped in to his family.
In 2004, NASA provided a radio link between space station astronaut Mike Fincke and his wife's delivery room during the birth of their daughter. Five years later, Randy Bresnik, commander of next year's Artemis III mission, dialed in to his wife's hospital from orbit.
The happy news traveled more slowly for Austrian astronaut Franz Viehbock. His daughter was born a few hours after he launched to the Soviet Union's Mir space station in 1991. He was not informed until the next day.
SpaceX, meanwhile, is on a roll. Three hours after Crew-13 blasted off, SpaceX launched a Falcon rocket from California with more than 100 mini satellites. Another Falcon was set to soar late Thursday night from Florida, with a classified satellite for the National Reconnaissance Office. All this comes the same week that the company's massive Starship reached orbit for the first time.

title: Child porn on cruise ships: dozens of crewmembers removed, including from ship that visited Maine
text:
PORTLAND, Maine (WMTW) - A cruise ship that makes frequent stops in Portland has been caught up in a U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) effort targeting the possession and distribution of child sexual abuse material and child sexual exploitation material among cruise ship crewmembers.
CBP says, as of Friday, it has removed 87 people at the Port of Boston from cruise ships as part of Operation Tidal Wave. That includes six citizens of the Philippines removed from a Norwegian Cruise Line ship called Breakaway in Boston on Sept. 20. CBP says all six admitted to previously having child sexual abuse material and child sexual exploitation material.
The Breakaway stopped in Portland twice in August and four times in September, including this week.
Our media partner, WMTW, is working to learn if any of the implicated crewmembers were in Maine or were detained here.
The Breakaway has a crew capacity of more than 1,600 and a guest capacity of about 3,900.
The Area Port of Boston plans to continue the operation through the end of the fiscal year.
“The success of Operation Tidal Wave reflects the unwavering dedication of our officers and partners to protect the most vulnerable,” said Acting Director of Field Operations Julio Caravia. “Let the removal of these 87 be a message to others: we will not accept this exploitation and CBP will not stop identifying and arresting the individuals who participate in it.”
Operation Tidal Wave also resulted in action against 27 crewmembers through the San Diego office and 15 people through the San Juan office this year.

title: Doctor in Christa Pike execution tied to earlier botched lethal injection
text:
NASHVILLE, TENN. (WSMV/WVLT/Gray News) - The doctor who oversaw Christa Gail Pike’s lethal injection was also involved in another botched execution earlier this year.
Pike was still alive after being administered a lethal injection, according to Luke Ihnen, an assistant federal defender on her defense team.
Ihnen confirmed that Pike had received two syringes of a lethal drug and said the team is filing a motion to stay the execution.
According to the motion, Pike did not lose consciousness and still had a heartbeat after receiving the lethal injection. It was reported that she was also audibly snoring.
The motion mentioned that the curtains went down twice.
Pike’s defense team had argued during a three-day hearing in August that she had a vein condition, which would make finding a vein to administer the lethal drug difficult.
Mark Fowler, the doctor who oversaw Pike’s botched execution, was also involved in the attempted execution of Tony Carruthers. His execution was abandoned in May after medical staff failed to establish IV access, a process that took more than an hour.
The petition filed by Pike’s attorneys is requesting an immediate stay of Pike’s execution and immediate medical care for her.
Her attorneys released a statement late Wednesday night that said Pike is being treated at a nearby hospital.
“Tonight the State of Tennessee once again failed to carry out a lawful execution,” they said. “We take no pleasure in being right, but the concerns raised by Ms. Pike proved to be true: difficult vein access, blown veins, degraded pentobarbital, no emergency medical care available when things inevitably go wrong, all under a protocol that remains veiled in secrecy.”
As of Wednesday night, they said they had not been informed about her condition.
Less than an hour before Pike was originally supposed to be executed at 11 a.m. Wednesday, the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals granted a stay pausing her execution. That prompted a response from the state, which asked the U.S. Supreme Court to intervene and allow the execution to continue.
The Supreme Court lifted the stay just before 7 p.m., which set in motion Pike’s execution.
Pike was found guilty in 1996 of the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer on the University of Tennessee campus.
Pike, along with 17-year-old Tadaryl Shipp and 18-year-old Shadolla Peterson, planned Slemmer’s torture and killing. The case later became known as the Job Corps Murder because both Pike and Slemmer were members of Job Corps at the time.
There’s no word on what the state’s next steps will be in Pike’s planned execution.
Her botched execution appears to be the latest failed attempt by the state of Tennessee to execute an inmate on death row. The state’s death penalty procedure has faced past scrutiny after botched executions prompted a pause from Gov. Bill Lee.
That said, Tennessee did successfully execute an inmate in August. Anthony Darrell Hines was executed at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville for the 1985 murder of Catherine Jean Jackson Jenkins.

title: There have been more than 340 mass shootings so far in 2026
text:
There have been more than 340 mass shootings so far in 2026
While 2026 has had record-low homicide numbers, the same decline has not been observed in mass shootings.
As of Sept. 24, there have been 343 mass shootings across the U.S. in which four or more victims were injured or killed, excluding the shooter(s).
At the same time last year, there had been 319 mass shootings. That's according to a Get The Facts Data Team analysis of Gun Violence Archive data provided by the Gun Violence Data Hub.
This year is on track to be the sixth worst year for mass shootings since 2014.
While there have been about 8% more shootings in 2026 compared to 2025, the nation still has not seen the high mass casualty numbers that plagued the early post-COVID-19 pandemic years.
Where the shootings took place
More than 320 people have been killed, and more than 1,440 people have been injured, in the mass shootings so far this year.
The shootings have spanned 40 states and Washington, D.C.
Texas has the highest number of mass shootings so far this year — 37. California, Illinois and Louisiana follow with 20 each.
The two deadliest mass shootings this year were both domestic violence incidents.
In Shreveport, Louisiana, eight children were killed and two adults were injured in a mass shooting in April. The suspect fathered seven of the children killed.
In Billings, Montana, a man killed eight of his relatives, including four children, in August.
Thursday marks the nine-year anniversary of the deadliest mass shooting in U.S. history. On Oct. 1, 2017, a shooter opened fire on an outdoor music festival in Las Vegas, killing 60 people and injuring more than 430 others.

title: Alleged drug dealer arrested after crashing into construction vehicle in Auburn
text:

Police say the crash happened at about 11:36 p.m. on Wednesday when Demetrius Starks, 45, drove a black BMW over a median, through a sign and then hit another vehicle near the intersection of Court Street and Minot Avenue.

While police were investigating, they say they determined that Starks was under the influence of narcotics. They say he had 153.8 grams of cocaine powder and crack cocaine, 9.8 grams of fentanyl powder, and a loaded 40-caliber pistol.

- Aggravated trafficking of fentanyl powder
- Unlawful possession of cocaine

title: Medical helicopter crash kills 2 people, leaves 2 hospitalized and 1 missing, report says
text:
A medical helicopter transporting a patient crashed off Catalina Island near Los Angeles, killing two people and leaving two hospitalized, authorities said Thursday. Rescuers continued searching for a fifth person who was aboard the aircraft and went missing after the Wednesday night crash.
The Coast Guard, firefighters and divers with the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department were among emergency personnel who searched through the night and into the afternoon.
The cause was not immediately clear. Coast Guard Capt. Stacey Crecy said the helicopter went down shortly after takeoff and hit the water a short distance from the island.
“We believe that the medical aircraft was transporting a person off the island for additional medical care on the mainland,” Crecy said.
Relatives of the missing person told ABC7 that the woman was being transported after having an allergic reaction. They also said her 20-year-old son went with her in the helicopter to help translate.
Sheriff Robert Luna said at an afternoon news conference that authorities were not yet identifying victims by name. But he described the two people that died as the male pilot and a female nurse. He also said another medic and a fourth person, a man, were hospitalized.
A memorial service was held on the island to honor the victims.
The crash came 11 days after a firefighting helicopter went down, killing two pilots in Yosemite National Park in California, and two weeks after a news helicopter crashed in Los Angeles, killing two people.
First responders were called to the Catalina crash shortly before 8 p.m. and pulled four people from the water. Two were pronounced dead at the scene, and two, in stable condition, were brought to hospitals on the mainland, the Los Angeles County Fire Department said.
Firefighters on the island were able to get to the scene quickly by boat, Crecy said.
The National Transportation Safety Board said it is investigating and identified the aircraft as a Eurocopter EC-135-P2. NTSB staff were expected to arrive on the scene later Thursday. The aircraft will be brought to a secure facility for evaluation, a board spokesperson said.
Authorities said the helicopter was submerged in 240 feet (about 70 meters) of water off Catalina, which is located about 22 miles (35 kilometers) off the mainland.
The helicopter landed on the island shortly after 7 p.m., following a 24-minute flight from an airport in Oceanside, according to the flight tracking service Flightradar24.
The helicopter was operated by REACH Air Medical Services of Sacramento.
“At this time, we are gathering information and coordinating with emergency responders and authorities,” the company said in a statement. “Our thoughts are with the families, loved ones and colleagues affected by this tragedy. We are focused on supporting our team and everyone impacted during this incredibly difficult time.”
The company said it was unable to share additional details out of respect for the people involved and the ongoing emergency response.

title: Senator introduces bill to protect workers during AI boom
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Artificial intelligence has become a recent hot topic of debate on Capitol Hill, as lawmakers consider how to move forward with the quickly changing technology. Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly (D) is one lawmaker proposing legislation that supports humans while also considering the relevance of the tech.
“This is something we have to tackle immediately,” Kelly said.
What to do about the rise and evolution of artificial intelligence has become a sticking point on Capitol Hill. With the technology both a benefit and a possible risk, Kelly says it’s important to get ahead of the trend.
“You know when I used to fly the space shuttle, the master alarms flashing on the instrument panel, you gotta take action. You look at the data, you come up with a plan, you execute the plan. That’s this moment with this technology,” Kelly said.
Kelly said AI has integrated itself into Americans’ everyday lives while also posing a risk to workers, who could soon see their positions filled by technological advancements.
Kelly introduced the Make AI Work for Americans Act, legislation that would guarantee companies benefiting most from AI invest in workers and pay their fair share, mitigating damage from technology poised to replace the human workforce.
“There are estimates out there that possibly millions of Americans lose their jobs because of this technology. We have to have an answer for that,” Kelly said.
The legislation is one proposal amid increased debate on artificial intelligence. The debate comes the same week President Donald Trump hosted top tech leaders at the White House to praise the development of what he calls “super intelligence.”
Kelly said any evolution must come with strict guardrails and should not rely on companies to self-police. He said that begins with an understanding of the basic workings of AI.
“So we can introduce good legislation that will work,” Kelly said.

title: Failed Tennessee execution renews the debate over death penalty methods
text:
Failed Tennessee execution renews the debate over death penalty methods
Tennessee officials have yet to explain what went wrong during the failed execution of Christa Pike, which was called off after she was given two doses of the drug meant to kill her.
Pike was taken to the hospital Wednesday night after she received a double dose of the drug Tennessee uses to execute prisoners but survived. Her lawyers said they were told her condition is critical, but they didn't know specifics.
She could be heard snoring loudly in the execution chamber Wednesday night more than an hour after the execution process began and nearly 30 minutes after a second dose of pentobarbital was administered.
Pike, who was sentenced to death for a gruesome 1995 murder, was taken by ambulance from the prison to a hospital, where she was being treated, her attorneys said.
May Martinez, whose daughter was murdered by Pike and her boyfriend and who traveled to Nashville to see the sentence carried out, told NBC News on Thursday that "it was a mess."
The failure, which one death penalty expert described as unprecedented, led Gov. Bill Lee to postpone Tennessee's lone remaining execution this year and to order a review "to determine exactly what occurred." It also raises questions again about the state's procedures and its use of single-drug lethal injections.
Pike, 50, had been scheduled for execution Wednesday morning for the killing she committed at age 18 and would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. An appeals court stopped the execution an hour before it was to start, but the U.S. Supreme Court overturned that stay hours later.
Officials gave Pike two doses of pentobarbital, her attorneys said in court filings late Wednesday.
The Tennessee Department of Correction said in a statement that it "followed every step of the State's lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General's Office."
The state's execution protocol calls for a secondary set of drug syringes to be administered "if the inmate is not deceased" after the first set. It does not spell out what happens if the subject is alive after the second set.
Tennessee announced in 2024 it was switching from a three-drug series for lethal injections to the single drug pentobarbital. That came more than two years after the state abruptly halted the execution of Oscar Smith and acknowledged it had failed to ensure its lethal injection drugs were tested properly.
Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said what Pike experienced is "singular and unparalleled."
Seven other people have survived medical problems due to an execution team's failure to access a vein to administer lethal injection drugs, but no one has stayed alive after receiving the drugs used in such executions, she said.
Pike would have been the 30th person executed in the U.S. this year after Florida carried out an execution on Tuesday.
Strapped to a gurney in the execution chamber, Pike described herself as at peace.
"I'm going to leave this world the way I spent most of my life and that is in love," she said in her "last" words.
But she remained awake and at one point raised her head, asking prison officials if her arm was supposed to feel that way. An hour after officials first raised the execution chamber's curtains, witnesses reported that a second dose of pentobarbital was administered.
Pike could still be heard snoring behind a closed curtain until the microphone was cut off almost 30 minutes later.
Lawyers for Pike filed an emergency motion late Wednesday with the Tennessee Supreme Court seeking to immediately halt and stay the execution, saying she was in "unnecessary agony" and the procedure violated her right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment. They also filed motions with the Sixth Circuit court and a district court.
It was the second time this year that Tennessee has been unable to complete an execution: In May state officials called off the lethal injection of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and killing three people in 1994, after executioners tried and failed for over an hour to place an IV to administer pentobarbital.
Pike and her boyfriend were convicted of the fatal stabbing and beating in 1995 of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a classmate at a job training facility in Knoxville. The killing gained attention because of a pentagram carved on Slemmer's body, stoking fears of Satan worship during the "satanic panic" of the 1980s and 1990s.
Pike's boyfriend wasn't eligible for the death penalty because he was 17 at the time of the killing and received a sentence of life in prison. He was denied parole last year.
Pike did not deny committing the killing, but her supporters argued that the state should consider her age at the time, her mental illness and her allegations of severe sexual abuse.
Assistant Federal Defender Stephen Ferrell said Pike's death sentence is an outlier because other 18-year-olds in Tennessee have had such sentences vacated.
After the killing, Pike was diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder. In her clemency petition, she said she only wanted to fight Slemmer but killed her in a frenzied attack when she couldn't "put the brakes on."
"It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I'd done," Pike said in a statement.
Associated Press writers Jeffrey Collins in Columbia, South Carolina, Ed White in Detroit, Hallie Golden in Seattle and Hannah Schoenbaum in Salt Lake City contributed.

title: Here’s what to know about political sign regulations in central Maine
text:
Across central Maine, more and more political signs are popping up in yards and along the region’s roads.
But what are the specific rules governing sign placement? And what happens if signs are tampered with?
Here are some key things to know.
WHERE CAN I PUT SIGNS?
Different rules apply to signs on private and public property.
Signs in the public right of way are prohibited from being placed on traffic control signs or devices, public utility poles or fixtures, rotary traffic islands, trees in the public right of way, control-of-access areas —areas where access is limited or prohibited— or medians less than 6 feet wide.
To avoid causing traffic hazards, signs in the public right of way cannot be placed along interstates, within 660 feet of the nearest edge of the interstate system or in a place that can be seen from an interstate highway.
In general, the Maine Department of Transportation will remove signs on either public or private property where they might block a driver’s sight line or cause traffic hazards.
Signs on private property must be outside of the right of way on public ways; how far that is depends on the road. People can contact their MaineDOT region office for more information.
Temporary signs on public property bearing the same or similar messages — like those supporting political candidates — must be placed at least 30 feet from one another.
Signs cannot be placed on public property within 250 feet of a polling location on election day.
WHEN CAN I PUT SIGNS UP?
Signs may be posted in rights of way six weeks before a primary or general election, and they must be removed in the week after the election.
Temporary signs can be placed within the public right of way for as long six weeks from Jan. 1 to June 30 and from July 1 to Dec. 31.
Signs on private property are not subject to any time restrictions.
HOW BIG CAN THEY BE?
Signs on private property are limited to 50 square feet. Temporary signs in the public right of way are limited to 4 feet by 8 feet.
Signs in the public way must be labeled with the name and address of the individual or organization that placed the sign and the date it was placed there.
Kelly Weissenfels, who is town manager and town clerk in Litchfield, said having contact information on signs is helpful, because if signs are placed improperly or are not collected after elections, those people can be alerted.
“I think (the rules) are broad enough to allow for plenty of freedom in placing signs,” Weissenfels said.
WHAT HAPPENS IF SIGNS ARE TAMPERED WITH?
Removing, damaging or disturbing a sign placed in the public right of way without authorization is a civil violation with a fine of up to $250.
Stealing a sign from private property is considered theft, a class E crime, while intentionally damaging or destroying the property of another would be considered criminal mischief, a class D crime.
Valerie Hanson, Pittston’s town clerk, said the town had to remove a political sign from a town road last year due to inappropriate content. Hanson said she’s surprised the town doesn’t receive more reports of people tampering with others’ political signs after hearing stories of theft and damage to signs in other towns.
WHERE CAN I LEARN MORE?
For more information about sign placement rules and town-specific restrictions, contact your local election official, who is generally a city or town clerk. More information about specific Maine laws regarding signs is available on the Maine State Legislature website.

title: High school teacher fired after offering students extra credit in return for cash donations, reports say
text:
(Gray News) - An Iowa high school teacher has been fired for offering students extra credit in return for cash donations to her personal GoFundMe account.
Stephanie Mullaley, a teacher at a high school in the Clinton Community School District, told students in spring 2026 that she had set up a GoFundMe page to raise money for what she described as “personal education goals,” the Iowa Capital Dispatch reported.
Mullaley allegedly told her students that she had set up a the fundraiser to help pay for her education, adding that if they made cash donations to her account they could earn extra credit toward their grade in her class.
Some students in the class contributed funds to the GoFundMe account, according to Administrative Law Judge Duane Golden. Because of the extra credit incentive, students felt pressured to donate money to the GoFundMe.
Donations, she allegedly wrote would be used to pay for “transportation, including flights, buses, and boats, food and hotel accommodations.”
She was fired on May 29, 2026, for allegedly violating the district’s ethics policy.
Golden denied Mullaley’s request for unemployment benefits, ruling that her conduct amounted to job-related misconduct and demonstrated a “willful or wanton disregard” of her employer’s interests, rendering her ineligible for benefits.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch could not reach Mullaley for comment.
The account had a fundraising goal of $1,800 and netted $140 through six donations ranging from $5 to $50 before activity on the account was paused.
