title: Letter: Susan Collins brings home money, but at what cost?
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
The other day, I read that a national poll showed Susan Collins with a 3-point lead over Troy Jackson. One of the things that many independents and even Democrats seemed to agree on was that Susan brings home the bacon: money, grants, and government contracts that are helpful to Maine businesses and people.
I guess that is true, but a bigger question for me is: “What is the real cost to Maine people and all of our American democracy if Susan Collins supports this president 95% of the time in order to get us that bacon?” I don’t want to let our need for federal money turn into a greed that rivals the greediness of this president and which is destroying the very democratic structures that made us a great country with enough wealth, not just for the lucky rich, but to share with middle-class workers, to share with people who can’t work, and to share with people who need a hand.
I believe Troy Jackson, Susan’s poorer Aroostook County compatriot, embodies the ideals that made America a great place to live, ideals that Susan seems somehow to have lost in her extended Senate career.
Michael A. Fasulo
Linneus

title: Obituary: Zachary Lawrence Barry
text:
SCARBOROUGH – Zachary Lawrence Barry, 22, of Scarborough, passed away far too soon on Sept. 16, 2026 in Storrs, Conn. Born in Washington, D.C., on April 28, 2004, Zach was the beloved son of Brian and Kristin Barry and the loving younger brother of Gwyneth Barry.
Zach graduated from Scarborough High School in 2022 and was a senior at the University of Connecticut, studying plant science with a concentration in turfgrass management. He recently completed an internship at Pine Valley Golf Club in Pine Hill, N.J., confirming his passion and excitement about working in golf course management.
From an early age, Zach was in constant motion and loved to be outdoors. He played and watched sports of every kind and was on soccer, baseball, basketball, lacrosse, cross country, and track teams, where he built life long friendships with his teammates. Nature was meaningful to Zach (especially frogs) and he explored the outdoors by camping and hiking, favorites including Sugarloaf, Katahdin, Sedona, and Switzerland. Scarborough was a special place for Zach and he loved to spend time with his friends in the high school student section, on the golf courses, and at places like Ferry Beach and Higgins Beach.
A defining characteristic of Zach was his good natured goofiness, which he shared freely with his friends, family, Finley (family dog), and teammates. Zach enjoyed being part of a team and showing up for his coaches and teammates. He contributed to seven state team titles with the Scarborough track and cross country teams and won four individual state championships. Zach especially loved the challenge of the 800 meter race.
Zach will be remembered for his distinctive laugh, making everyone around him laugh, his silly faces and voices, his movie quotes, tenacity, authenticity, and generous spirit.
Zach is survived by his loving parents, Brian and Kristin Barry; his sister, Gwyneth Barry; his grandparents, Lawrence and Marilyn Pierce; and his grandfather William V. Barry.
He was predeceased by his grandmother, Marilyn Barry.
A service and celebration of life will be held at Halo at the Point, 20 Van Aken Way, Portland, at 11 a.m. on Saturday, Oct. 10. A reception at Purpoodock Club, 300 Spurwink Ave., Cape Elizabeth, will immediately follow.
The Barry family would like to express their deepest gratitude to friends, family, and the local community for their love, prayers, and support during this incredibly difficult time.

title: ‘Because the Sky is Blue’ to open at Center for Main Contemporary Art
text:
An exhibition examining the histories of painting and its place as a critical practice today will open Friday at the Center for Maine Contemporary Art in Rockland. Bringing together artists strongly associated with Maine and voices from beyond the region, “Because the Sky is Blue” explores works that inhabit multiple histories, media and genres, challenging conventional distinctions between painting, sculpture, photography and film.
The opening reception at CMCA is from 4-7 p.m. on Oct. 2 during Rockland’s First Friday Art Walk, with music by DJ Alien Baby (Allison Cekala) and tacos from Taqueria Max in the courtyard.
The exhibition runs through Jan. 17, 2027, and features artists Clémentine Adou, Wilfrid Almendra, Bo Bartlett, Vija Celmins, Selena Kimball, Ryosuke Kumakura, Glenn Ligon, Sharon Lockhart, Matthew Metzger, Julie Poitras Santos and Miao Wang.
Organized by CMCA Curator Grant Wahlquist, the exhibition takes inspiration from Bo Bartlett’s Blue Sky Paintings and considers the sky as both subject and a point of departure for artistic inquiry.

title: Man accused of intentionally setting house fire that killed 15 dogs
text:
GENEVA, Fla. (WESH) - Authorities in Florida are investigating a house fire that left at least 15 dogs dead.
The Seminole County Sheriff’s Office says the man who lived in the home intentionally set the fire.
New body camera video shows deputies and firefighters responding to a fully engulfed house on Snow Hill Road in Geneva on Monday. At least 17 dogs were inside.
“Got one dog. The other ones are on the front cooked in the cage. They’re all upside down,” one responder said.
911 calls captured people describing what they saw and heard.
“There’s a fire. It’s fully engulfed. We were just driving by. There are dogs inside. There’s barking. It’s really bad,” one caller said.
In a separate 911 call, barking continued without stopping.
“Oh no, look at them. They are trying to go inside to get their babies ... they have a bunch of bullies,” the caller said.
On Monday, investigators found six dead dogs inside the house.
“Oh, it is so sad. The puppies are dead. Oh my God,” a caller said.
Animal services took in four more dogs, two of which died Monday night. On Tuesday, seven more dogs were found.
The sheriff’s office says Terrance Banks set his own house on fire by pouring gasoline on the floor in every room of the house. He then used a lighter to light a piece of paper on fire, which he used to ignite the gasoline.
Banks’ father can be heard calling 911 as he headed to his son’s home.
“I got a call from my son. I’m not there, but he rents the place, so I don’t know,” he said.
On Tuesday, a judge ordered that Banks remain in jail until he is mentally evaluated.
A neighbor who did not want to show his face or use his name for safety reasons spoke about Banks.
“He would normally try to keep to himself. I know he would not allow anybody other than, you know, the family he was with, approach the dogs,” the neighbor said.
The neighbor said it was clear Banks had some type of mental health issue.
“He would parade across the street from my house up and down and he would just be babbling on,” the neighbor said.
One of the two surviving dogs is now in the care of an emergency veterinarian for specialized treatment.

title: MaineHealth to ‘mentor next generation' with rural care grant
text:
MaineHealth has been awarded a five-year, $13.2 million federal research grant to improve acute care in rural areas.
Funding comes from the National Institute of General Medical Sciences, which is part of the National Institutes of Health in Washington, D.C.
The grant will allow the MaineHealth Institute for Research to build on its work over the past five years to establish a statewide research and care network addressing barriers associated with limited resources, expertise and access in rural areas.
The institute said the additional funding will build on that foundation by supporting promising clinician-scientists, advancing research underway and strengthening MaineHealth’s research facilities, support services, data management and national collaborations.
“We are excited about the progress we made in our first five years in helping our junior faculty develop while building academic relationships with collaborators across the country through this acute care COBRE,” or Center of Biomedical Research Excellence, said Dr. David Seder of MaineHealth Maine Medical Center in Portland, who will serve as the grant’s principal investigator.
“This new funding will provide direct health and economic benefits to the state of Maine as we leverage the relationships we developed to further our investigators’ current research and mentor the next generation of scientists,” he added.
Research plans
Among the new projects funded through the grant is a study aimed at improving treatment for patients with opioid use disorder while they are in the intensive care unit.
Another project builds on earlier research examining whether an innovative telesimulation program can improve neonatal resuscitation training in rural hospitals.
Rural hospitals with low birth volumes have significantly higher rates of brain injury and infant mortality when newborns require resuscitation, as clinicians have fewer opportunities to practice these emergency procedures.
A team led by Dr. Allison Zanno will work with colleagues at MaineHealth Mid Coast Hospital, Pen Bay Hospital, Lincoln Hospital, Franklin Hospital, Stephens Hospital and Maine Medical Center Biddeford to refine the training and evaluate its effectiveness in improving neonatal resuscitation, with a goal of expanding the program to more rural hospitals.
With more than 2,000 medical providers on staff and approximately 23,000 care team members, MaineHealth provides preventive care, diagnosis and treatment to 1.1 million residents across Maine and New Hampshire.

title: Manager Chad Tracy’s decisions questioned after Yankees eliminate Red Sox
text:
NEW YORK — With the Boston bats ice cold at Yankee Stadium again, a couple of quick hooks by Red Sox rookie manager Chad Tracy led to another early postseason exit.
And top starter Sonny Gray wasn’t happy about being lifted after only 70 pitches.
“I think I’m the best pitcher in the American League going through the order the third time. I think that’s a fact,” Gray said. “I would have liked to have been trusted in that moment.”
For the second consecutive season, the Red Sox were sent home for the winter by their biggest rivals as the New York Yankees rolled to a 9-2 victory Wednesday night and a two-game sweep of their Wild Card Series.
Boston was outscored 18-2 overall and left to lament a miserable finish to this roller-coaster ride of a season that included Tracy taking over when Alex Cora was fired in April.
Tracy’s decision-making came under scrutiny after both playoff games against the Yankees. In Boston’s 9-0 defeat a night earlier, Tracy pulled rookie starter Payton Tolle after 4 2/3 innings and 83 pitches in a 1-0 game.
Last year, the Red Sox won their Wild Card Series opener before losing to New York in a deciding Game 3 as they got overpowered by Cam Schlittler, who pitched another playoff gem against his hometown team Tuesday night.
“To have it end here two times in a row is tough,” shortstop Trevor Story said.
Facing a Yankees lineup missing injured slugger Aaron Judge, the Red Sox gave up 26 hits in two games despite a pair of effective performances from their starting pitchers.
At the plate, Boston mustered only seven hits and finally snapped a 26-inning postseason scoring drought that dated to last year when Willson Contreras homered just over the right-center fence in the sixth Wednesday.
“It’s obviously been an eventful year,” Tracy said. “In the moment right now you can’t think much more other than anything but the fact that we just lost a playoff series.”
Needing a victory to extend their season, the Red Sox sent Gray to the mound and the 18-game winner certainly gave them a chance. Boston trailed 1-0 in the fifth when the right-hander allowed a two-out single to Ben Rice that put runners at the corners.
Tracy then yanked Gray, eager to hand the ball to baseball’s best bullpen during the regular season.
“I felt good. You know, I felt crisp. I felt sharp. I felt like I was just out there competing. And yeah, I mean, I got clipped for a solo homer and then some singles, but I felt like I stayed on the attack throughout. I was just executing what I wanted to do,” Gray said. “I’m frustrated, for sure. You know, not ready for it to end. A lot of emotions.”
Asked about the move, Contreras put his finger over his lips to zip them shut.
“It’s not enough when you have talent or you have data or you have computers that’s telling you what to do, because this is baseball,” he said. “The data is here to help us, but at the end of the day you are going to have to need experience and veteran guys to win games.”
In both games of the series, Tracy gave the ball to left-handed reliever Erik Miller after taking out his starting pitcher.
On Tuesday, Rice greeted Miller with a 423-foot solo homer to straightaway center field.
On Wednesday, Tracy summoned Miller to face a different left-handed hitter, Cody Bellinger — who batted .274 against lefties this season and .259 versus right-handers. In fact, his .310 batting average against left-handers over the past two years was the best of any left-handed hitter in the majors.
Bellinger made Tracy and the Red Sox pay, lining an RBI single to right field.
“We’re struggling to score runs,” Tracy said. “And when you get in spots where you’re struggling to score runs and you’re already trailing, you feel like you’ve got to be aggressive and go.”
Back from a shoulder injury, ace starter Garrett Crochet entered in the sixth for his first outing since April 25 and first relief appearance since 2023 with the Chicago White Sox. The left-hander opened with a strikeout, but Spencer Jones reached safely on a wild pitch, and Crochet never got an out.
Bellinger’s three-run homer off right-hander Garrett Whitlock capped a six-run inning that made it 8-1, and the Red Sox were done. A bullpen that led the majors with a 3.00 ERA during the regular season finished this series with a 20.25 ERA after giving up 15 runs, 15 hits and seven walks in 6 2/3 innings, with a .484 opponents’ batting average.
Boston’s latest downfall in the Bronx was a crushing end to a wild 2026 season for the Red Sox, who stumbled to a 32-46 start. Tracy was the skipper at Triple-A Worcester before getting promoted to interim manager in Boston, and the team finally began to take off with a four-game sweep of the Yankees at Fenway Park in late June.
After clinching a wild-card spot last week, the Red Sox removed the interim tag and named Tracy the 49th manager in team history, signing him to a three-year contract that runs through the 2029 season, with a club option for 2030. The team also exercised the 2029 and 2030 options on chief baseball officer Craig Breslow.
“I wasn’t there for the highs and lows,” Crochet said. “For this team to do what it did do, to make it to this point, was nothing short of miraculous.”
Led by Gray and Contreras, among others, the Red Sox went on a 15-game winning streak in July that equaled a franchise record and used a 32-5 surge to climb back into contention. They became the fourth team in major league history to reach the postseason after falling 14 games under .500, and the first to qualify after losing as many as 44 of its first 75.
Gray, who can become a free agent after the World Series, went around the clubhouse to hug each of his teammates following Wednesday’s defeat.
“I’m proud of what we accomplished,” the pitcher said. “We were left for dead there for a while.”

title: Federal scholarship for private school and homeschooling opening to most kids in at least 30 states
text:
Nearly all schoolchildren in at least 30 states can apply for a new federal scholarship next year to help pay for private school, homeschooling and other educational expenses, according to regulations proposed Thursday by the Trump administration.
The first national school choice scholarship program, the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit, will launch Jan. 1, establishing a taxpayer-funded incentive for families to choose private or homeschooling in participating states. Taxpayers who donate to an organization passing out the scholarships will receive a federal tax credit, a perk expected to further fuel the conservative school choice movement.
About 96% of children in those states should be eligible, according to the department. Children attending public schools could use the scholarships for extra learning expenses.
School choice scholarships have been available for decades in conservative-led states and throughout the South, giving individual students taxpayer-funded grants ranging from a couple thousand dollars to more than $30,000 a year. In places where they are available to all students regardless of income, such as Florida and Arizona, the majority of students using the money were already in private or home school or were from affluent neighborhoods, an analysis by The Associated Press showed.
The federal program departs from most state programs by not forcing students to leave public school to qualify for the scholarship. Public school students could use the money for tutoring or special education therapies, although the Republican administration has not provided specific criteria for eligible expenses yet.
Regulators say they have set up the program in a way that will make it easier for poor students to apply, proposing to let students use proof of participation in a government assistance program in lieu of providing income documentation. Foster children would not have to provide any income verification when they apply, officials said.
Experiences with school choice scholarships in other states have shown barriers to using the programs go beyond paperwork hurdles. Many families often do not know scholarship programs exist. Federal officials have not said how they would tell taxpayers and students about the scholarships.
How the scholarship and tax credit will work
Taxpayers will have the chance to donate to a scholarship program in a participating state, even if they do not live there, starting Jan. 1. Individuals can donate up to $1,700 and receive a federal tax credit for the same amount in exchange. Federal officials propose a couple filing jointly could give as much as double that.
Scholarship organizations in each state would decide how much to grant to each child who applies, depending on available funds and student need. Children could qualify if they are in elementary through high school and their families earn up to three times the area’s median income.
Scholarship recipients could use their funding to pay for religious or private school tuition, homeschooling costs, tutoring and special education therapies, books, computers and other expenses connected to enrollment or attendance, according to officials at the Treasury Department.
At least 30 states have opted in and more may sign up
States could not turn to laws or regulations to narrow the uses for the scholarships or the type of organization that can grant them, federal officials said.
But states can choose whether to participate in to the program.
According to the most recent Treasury Department list, as of mid-September these states are in for 2027: Alabama, Alaska, Arkansas, Colorado, Florida, Georgia, Idaho, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, New Hampshire, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Virginia, West Virginia and Wyoming.
Governors from Arizona, Minnesota, Wisconsin, and Oregon have said their states will not join, with some arguing these programs divert resources from public schools.
More than two dozen states have yet to say what they will do. In New York, Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul has been supportive and the state is expected to sign up.
Governors deciding whether to participate face many competing objectives and interests. There is the opportunity to bring significant new education money to students who need extra support, such as tutoring or extra speech therapy that their public school does not provide. At the same time, large scholarship programs in states such as Florida and Arizona have accelerated a growing enrollment crisis in public schools.
Even so, the federal program is expected to bring taxpayer money for private school tuition to several states that have yet to embrace vouchers or education savings accounts.
In just a few years, after donations from taxpayers pick up, the IRS and the Treasury Department predict the program will direct nearly $26 billion into as many 2.2 million scholarships each year.
The federal tax-credit scholarship program was signed into law last year by President Donald Trump as his signature tax breaks and spending cuts bill. The public has 60 days to comment on the Treasury Department’s proposed regulations.

Partners for Peace celebrates Domestic Violence Awareness Month
text:
October is Domestic Violence Awareness Month and Partners for Peace, the domestic violence resource center for Penobscot and Piscataquis counties, has several events and opportunities for the community to get involved.
Domestic violence is a pervasive issue in Maine, with roughly half of homicides being domestic violence related. Each October, Partners for Peace amplifies the voices of survivors and remembers those taken too soon.
On Thursday, Oct. 8, Partners for Peace will host an awareness walk and vigil in Lincoln at the gazebo, 29 Main St. Prior to the walk and vigil, from 12 to 5 p.m., Partners for Peace advocates will be providing information, coordinate children’s activities and display the organization’s Clothesline Project. The walk and candlelight vigil in honor of those affected by domestic violence, including those taken too soon, will begin at 5 p.m. Sign up for the walk & vigil is preferred, but not required. Sign up online. This is a free event. T-shirts available for a suggested $10 donation.
Wednesday, Oct. 14 is recognized nationally as HealthCares About Domestic Violence Day, sponsored by FUTURES Without Violence to promote healthy relationships, address the health impacts of abuse and connect people to domestic violence advocates. This is an opportunity for healthcare providers, mental health providers and allied organizations to educate their teams and patients. Partners for Peace will be at Millinocket Regional Hospital during the day and invites other healthcare organizations to be in touch to schedule outreach opportunities.
Oct. 14 is Wear Purple Day sponsored by the Bangor Daily News. Purple is the awareness color of domestic violence. The community is encouraged to coordinate with their friends, families and coworkers to wear purple and show support on social media.
On Sunday, Oct. 25 there will be Family Movie Day at the Center Theatre in Dover-Foxcroft. Showtime is at 3 p.m. for “Hotel Transylvania: Transformania”. Doors open at 2:30 p.m. This event is free, no ticket necessary. There will be free popcorn, face painting, door prizes and kid-friendly Halloween costumes are encouraged.
Other community events and fundraisers include an Oct. 11 reading and signing with author Amber Hathaway at Bangor Beer Company; a dining fundraiser at Angler’s in Newport on Oct. 13; outreach at Old Town IGA on Oct. 14; the University of Maine March Against Domestic Violence on Oct. 16; and a dining fundraiser at Moe’s on Oct. 22. In Bangor, Dream Charm Bar is donating proceeds from its $5 purple ribbon charms year-round, and the Hannaford at 773 Stillwater Ave. will donate $1 for each specially marked Community Bag purchased throughout October.
Community members can also support survivors by donating to Partners for Peace, hosting a fundraiser or donation drive, sharing Domestic Violence Awareness Month information on social media or exploring ways for their businesses to participate. Partners for Peace offers a suggested reading list for adults and young people who want to learn more about domestic violence and abuse.
Details about events and ways to get involved are available on the organization’s Domestic Violence Awareness Month page: https://www.partnersforpeaceme.org/prevention/domestic-violence-awareness-month/.
Any questions about Domestic Violence Awareness Month can be directed to partnersforpeaceme@partnersforpeaceme.org.
Partners for Peace is the domestic violence resource center serving anyone affected by domestic abuse and violence in Penobscot and Piscataquis counties since 1973. For more information, visit www.partnersforpeaceme.org. To speak with a trained advocate, please call our 24-hour helpline at 1-800-863-9909. All Partners for Peace services are free, trauma-informed and confidential.

title: Rapper Rick Ross pleads not guilty to strangulation charge
text:
MIAMI BEACH, Fla. (AP) — Rapper Rick Ross was arrested in Miami Beach early Thursday and charged with battery related to a domestic violence accusation, authorities said.
Ross, whose legal name is William Roberts II, faces a felony charge of battery by strangulation, as well as a misdemeanor battery charge, according to online court records.
An attorney for Ross, 50, said in a statement that Ross is being wrongfully accused by an ex-girlfriend whose true motivations are unclear.
“The ex did not even file a police report until a month after the claimed incident allegedly took place,” defense attorney Steve Sadow said in the statement. “Mr. Roberts is innocent and has pled not guilty to the charges. He respectfully requests that his friends, fans and the general public not prejudge the situation and allow the judicial process to run its course.”
Jail records showed that Ross was being held Thursday morning on $5,000 bail. An arraignment is scheduled for Oct. 22.
Ross is a longtime South Florida resident who gained prominence in 2006 with his debut single “Hustlin.” He also has a home outside of Atlanta in Fayette County on a property he calls “The Promise Land.”
The rapper and entrepreneur helped put Miami on the musical map in the early 2000s, when most hip-hop fans looked to Atlanta and Houston as Southern rap headquarters. “Hustlin’” was certified platinum twice by the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) and sparked a bidding war for Ross. He eventually signed with Def Jam Records, headed by Jay-Z.
Ross’ debut album, “Port of Miami,” also went platinum, debuting at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 chart. It was the first in a series of chart-toppers, including 2008’s “Trilla” and 2009’s “Deeper Than Rap.” He has been nominated for nine Grammy Awards.
In 2008, he founded the influential label Maybach Music Group (MMG), boosting the careers of signees like Wale, Meek Mill and French Montana.
His most recent album, “Set In Stone,” was released in July.

title: A high-stakes fight for state political power heats up, with Trump's agenda on the line
text:
Political power in legislatures and governors’ offices is at stake in the November elections in more than one-third of the states, creating down-ballot drama in the midterms that could have significant implications for President Donald Trump’s agenda.
Outside groups aligned with the two major parties have pledged heavy spending in a battle for control of closely divided legislatures in at least a half-dozen states. But that’s just the tip of the spear in their political jousting.
In numerous other states, the parties are striving to make or break a legislative supermajority — an important threshold that allows them to enact laws with little regard to dissent. And in several states, competitive gubernatorial races could determine whether one party achieves a political trifecta, grasping hold of both legislative chambers and the top executive spot.
Party control of state governments can shape policies on contentious issues including abortion, school choice, data centers and the use of law-enforcement surveillance cameras. In a few states, the electoral outcomes this cycle could also have congressional redistricting implications for 2028.
The state races also carry significant implications for Trump’s agenda, because the elected officials can either aid or resist his immigration enforcement actions, social safety net limitations and efforts to alter voting procedures.
All told, voters in 46 states will choose more than 6,100 lawmakers in November, accounting for about 83% of all legislative seats nationwide, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. Thirty-six states will hold gubernatorial elections.
Trump’s approval ratings could swing state legislatures
Historically, the party of the president typically loses U.S. House seats in midterm elections. That also is true of state legislative seats.
In midterm elections over the past 50 years, the president’s party has lost an average of 7.9% of its house and assembly seats up for reelection in states, according to research by Steven Rogers, a political science professor at Saint Louis University. In Trump’s first midterm, in 2018, Republicans lost 8.7%, Rogers said.
A similar showing this year could spell the end of Republican control of legislative chambers in Arizona, Michigan, New Hampshire, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. Minnesota currently has the nation’s tightest margins, with an even split between Democrats and Republicans in the House and a one-seat Democratic edge in the Senate.
Trump’s poor public approval ratings could play a role in those states. For voters choosing state house and assembly candidates, presidential approval typically has three times the impact of state legislative approval, Rogers said.
Edith Jorge-Tuñón, president of the Republican State Leadership Committee, conceded that her party is in a defensive position.
“I think we knew going into this cycle, Democrats have an advantage,” said Jorge-Tuñón, whose group works to elect Republicans to legislative seats and statewide offices. But she argued that voter frustration with Democratic leadership in states like Minnesota or Oregon could provide a buffer against that advantage.
Racine could be key to Wisconsin political control
Wisconsin provides an example of how political power could swing. Democrats haven’t fully controlled Wisconsin’s government since 2010. But new legislative districts, ordered by the liberal-controlled Wisconsin Supreme Court, give Democrats a shot at flipping both Republican-led chambers.
Democrats’ hopes run through downtown Racine. Located along the shores of Lake Michigan north of Chicago and south of Milwaukee, Racine is a Democratic stronghold known both for its rich manufacturing past and as the kringle capital of Wisconsin. Danish immigrants brought the buttery, oval-shaped pastry to the area in the 1800s, and bakeries in downtown Racine continue to make the sweet treats and ship them around the country.
Under Republican-drawn maps enacted in 2011, most of Racine was removed from the 21st Senate District to make the seat safe for Republicans. But the new map added back the city’s north side and more Democratic-favorable areas in Milwaukee County and removed conservative rural areas.
The Republican incumbent decided to retire rather than seek reelection under the more competitive lines, further bolstering Democratic hopes.
Democrats are optimistic they will pick up the two seats needed to flip control of the Senate in November. They need to flip five seats to gain control of the Assembly. An open governor’s office, also on the ballot, gives them a shot at full control.
“In a year like this with the president and his war jacking up the prices of gas, Democrats are in a really strong position,” said Will Karcz, spokesperson for Wisconsin Senate Democrats.
A single seat could sway power in some states
In North Carolina, Republicans need to gain just one state House seat — without losing any Senate seats — to reestablish a three-fifths supermajority. That threshold is important because it gives Republicans the ability to override vetoes by Democratic Gov. Josh Stein without needing any Democratic votes.
Iowa Republicans face a similar math equation to regain a two-thirds legislative supermajority, which could matter even more if Democrats win the race to replace Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds, who chose not to seek reelection.
A loss of just one state Senate seat could cost Republicans a supermajority in Florida. Meanwhile, a pickup of one seat could result in a new Democratic supermajority in New York.
Among other battlegrounds, a swing of just a few seats could break a Republican supermajority in Missouri and gain Democratic supermajorities in Colorado and Nevada.
This year’s state elections could affect 2028’s congressional elections
If Democrats are able to win full control in Minnesota, Pennsylvania or Wisconsin, they could use their new trifectas to redraw U.S. House districts ahead of the 2028 elections. They would be copying tactics employed by Republicans ahead of this year’s elections in states such as Texas and Florida and by Democrats in California.
Republicans currently hold 20 of the 33 total congressional seats in those three northern states. So Democrats could make notable gains if they redraw districts to their advantage.
In Arizona and Michigan, where Republicans also hold an edge in congressional seats, redistricting would be more difficult because the task is assigned to an independent commission. California was in a similar situation. But Democratic lawmakers there placed an amendment on the statewide ballot last year allowing them to sidestep a commission to enact a new congressional map.
Both major parties are openly fundraising off the partisan redistricting stakes.
“Every election in this moment … potentially is about redistricting,” said Heather Williams, president of the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee.

title: Mountain Valley soccer is the Varsity Maine Boys Team of the Week
text:
Editor’s note: Each week during the fall sports season, Varsity Maine will highlight a boys and girls team of the week. The teams, picked by staff members, will take into account several factors, including success stories, bounce-back efforts and notable accomplishments, among others. Athletes, coaches and athletic directors can nominate teams by emailing sports editor Bill Stewart at [email protected] or Varsity Maine editor Lee Horton at [email protected].
Varsity Maine Boys Team of the Week: Mountain Valley boys soccer
The Falcons didn’t enter the fall as an expected contender in Class C South. In fact, in the past three years, the team has totaled four wins.
But after eight games, the Falcons own a 4-2-2 record and sit at No. 2 in the C South Heal point standings, just below defending state champion Hall-Dale (6-1).
“Last year, we only won one game. It was tough,” said Mountain Valley coach JT Taylor. “Sometimes you’ve got to take your licks before you can get to where you need to be.”
Last week, the Falcons picked up a 2-1 win over Maranacook and a 4-3 victory in a Class C/D crossover against Buckfield. Mountain Valley opened its season by showing it can hang with the division’s best teams, falling 2-1 to Mt. Abram.
“It’s so much more fun,” said Mountain Valley senior Cash Provencher. “We’re starting to become the team that other teams (don’t) want to play. … Change your expectations about us and watch out in the future.”
The Falcons still have a tough road ahead, including matches with Hall-Dale on Oct. 14 and Monmouth Academy in the regular-season finale on Oct. 19.

title: Morning Weather, Thursday, October 1st
It’s time for Mainers to put country first
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Many old-time Mainers, from all political parties, say they support Sen. Susan Collins because she brings money back to the state as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee. There is also a certain nostalgia many Mainers feel. “She’s done well for us in the past” and “she’s independent.” In truth, Collins has cost us more by following Donald Trump’s policies.
Collins has voted with Trump 95% of the time, resulting in extreme financial pain for most Mainers as well as Americans across the country. The war in Iran, tariffs, inflation, steep cost increases to gas and diesel, heat and groceries, the ballooning deficit, rising interest and mortgage rates, unaffordable housing, reduced SNAP benefits and $3 billion in Medicaid funding cuts in Maine alone to take effect in January — together with out-of-control immigration officers. These all have resulted from Trump’s policies, most of which Susan Collins has supported.
Until the Senate and the House are flipped, the unrestrained chaos, financial devastation and erosion to democracy will continue. What happens nationally affects Mainers too. It is time for Mainers to vote to push back against the impacts of Trump’s worst behaviors and put the country back on track. It’s time to put personal nostalgia aside, recognize that perfect is the enemy of good, and vote Susan Collins out and Troy Jackson in.
How will everyone feel if the Senate stays in Trump’s Republican control because Maine reelected Collins?
Susan Duncan
Phippsburg

title: Afternoon Weather, Thursday, October 1st
This city set a goal to end traffic deaths by 2050. Is it working?
text:
PHOENIX, Ariz. (InvestigateTV) — Experts have labeled car crashes as a public health concern. Every day, over 100 people in the United States are killed in a car crash.
But they also stress traffic collisions are preventable.
In 2021, the number of traffic-related deaths hit a record high of 43,230 in the country. Since then, there’s been a major shift toward improving road safety. In 2025, that number dropped to 36,640, one of the lowest rates in more than a decade.
One approach to creating safer streets is a national movement known as “Vision Zero.” The goal is to eliminate all traffic deaths and serious injuries by 2050.
In Phoenix, Arizona, the push is showing results, but also highlighting the limitations.
Phoenix recorded 278 traffic deaths in 2024, down from 307 the previous year, as the city’s Vision Zero program enters its third year with mixed results.
The city adopted Vision Zero in 2022 with the goal of eliminating all traffic deaths by 2050. Phoenix has one of the highest rates of traffic deaths among major U.S. cities.
Erik Gamino still struggles with the loss of his 13-year-old nephew JD, who was killed in July 2023 when Kyle Nobbley struck their car on Bell Road near 7th Street and fled the scene.
“It hurts a lot. I still go through the pain every day,” Gamino said.
Funding and staffing challenges
The city has spent $10 million annually on Vision Zero, improving dangerous intersections, adding lighting and building crosswalks and medians.
“These projects do make a difference. We can generally see at locations that we do see after a couple years that collision rates do come down,” said Carl Langford, traffic engineering supervisor.
However, the city continues to miss several goals, including reducing pedestrian-related fatal crashes, reducing nighttime crashes and increasing funding for road safety projects.
“Other strategies we are maybe lagging a little bit behind compared with what the plan was to begin with and some of that is potentially staffing shortages in some areas,” Langford said.
Police traffic unit reduced
Phoenix Police traffic unit has been reduced from more than 150 officers to about 40 due to staffing shortages, according to Councilwoman Debra Stark, who chairs the city’s Transportation, Infrastructure and Planning Subcommittee.
Phoenix installed 17 speed cameras — nine along road stretches and eight in school zones — as part of photo enforcement efforts.
The cameras have recorded more than 132,000 events as of May 31, with 17,600 of those resulting in traffic citations being mailed.
The program began issuing citations on March 25 after a 30-day trial period.
Officials say the system activates if you’re caught going 11 miles per hour over the speed limit. They say it’s not about making money, it’s about safety and slowing drivers down.
“Do I wish we had more money so that we could implement it quicker? You betcha. And that has been an issue,” Stark said.
When asked to grade the city’s Vision Zero performance, Stark said, “I would probably say a B.”
Family seeks justice, prevention
Nobbley took a plea deal in 2024, pleading guilty to manslaughter and failing to remain on scene. He was sentenced to eight and a half years in prison.
“It really doesn’t” bring closure, Gamino said of the sentence. “I feel like our justice system is not, it’s not right.”
Gamino got a tattoo of his nephew’s last heartbeat on his arm and hopes sharing their story can prevent other crashes.
“Just think about other people,” he said when asked what he wants other drivers to know.
Studies show speed, heavier vehicles, distracted driving and more people walking and biking contribute to traffic safety problems.
The city continues to apply for federal grants connected to Vision Zero despite uncertainty about future funding.

title: Narcotics unit investigating Ole Miss student deaths calls for ban on synthetic kratom
text:
LAFAYETTE COUNTY, Miss. (WMC/Gray News) - Law enforcement in Mississippi is calling on state lawmakers to ban synthetic kratom.
In a statement released Wednesday, Lafayette County Metro Narcotics discussed the drugs found at the scene of the deaths of two Ole Miss students last week.
Shortly after the deaths, Lafayette County Metro Narcotics issued a warning about kratom after packaging with the suspected substance was discovered.
“That warning was not a declaration that kratom or any specific substance caused either death. It was a proactive effort to inform the public of a potential danger while investigators worked to determine the facts,” the statement in response reads.
Court documents detail students’ activity before deaths
Toxicology tests are incomplete, but court documents filed Monday reveal what 18-year-old Aidan Hamilton and 20-year-old Robert Strang were doing in the hours and days before their suspected overdose deaths.
Investigators say both students purchased SMAX Pseudo-DHM pills, a chemically manipulated product, days before their deaths.
Investigators say records show Hamilton made multiple purchases at Puffs Vape Tobacco and Beer in Oxford. Two employees of that store were arrested and 500 units of kratom were seized.
The Metro Narcotics team also found an assortment of “THC cartridges, gummies, pre-rolls and other suspected THC substances.”
Recreational marijuana is still classified as an illegal Schedule I drug in the U.S.
Strang reportedly bought similar products from a store in Yalobusha County.
Narcotics unit calls for legislative action
“These investigations are far from over,” the statement released Wednesday reads.
The unit calls on Mississippi legislators to take immediate action to ban the synthetic kratom products.
“We need immediate legislative hearings, a thorough examination of the state’s controlled substance laws, and clear answers about how manufacturers, distributors and retailers can be held accountable when their actions put lives at risk,” the narcotics unit said.

title: Maine DHHS awards child development grant to out-of-state, private equity-backed firm
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A Maine organization that has provided training and assistance to educators for decades could close its doors after the state awarded a multimillion dollar contract to an out-of-state company backed by private equity and venture capital firms, officials confirmed Wednesday.
Maine Roads to Quality was created in 1999 by the Catherine Cutler Institute at the University of Southern Maine to offer professional development to child care providers across the state. The organization provides guidance to more than 10,000 Maine child care providers each year.
For much of its existence, Maine Roads has been funded by contracts provided by Maine’s Department of Health and Human Services. That lifeline evaporated last week.
The state offered a pair of contracts worth an estimated $10 million over two years to Shine Early Learning, a New York-based company that offers similar services to childcare centers, home-based providers and public schools in more than 30 states.
“The University of Southern Maine was notified on Sept. 21 that its proposals for two state contracts supporting the Maine Roads to Quality Professional Development Network were not selected for continued funding, thus ending a nearly three-decade partnership,” Samantha Warren, spokesperson for the University of Maine System, said in a statement.
Maine Roads employs more than 30 people. Warren said “layoffs are expected” without a renewal of the DHHS contracts.
The contracts specify Shine Early Learning must employ at least 10 staff members in Maine. Shine Early Learning’s proposals also specify it plans to use artificial intelligence to do much of the work Maine Roads’ human staffers currently perform.
The company plans to implement an “AI-powered family navigation assistant,” an AI-assisted employee vetting tool and an AI agent that will manage a provider registry, according to its applications.
Lindsay Hammes, a spokesperson for DHHS, noted the company has only been offered conditional awards and that no contracts have been ratified yet. The full value of the new contracts “will become public once they are finalized,” she said.
Shine Early Learning underbid Maine Roads by some $2 million between the two contracts, according to documents obtained by the Portland Press Herald. The company did not respond to a request for comment prior to publication.
One contract is for coaching, credentialing, and training of early childhood educators and care providers. The other is for providing a DHHS-approved training plan “designed to improve quality” of child care services and early childhood educators, according to the state’s request for proposals.
Those services have historically been housed under a single contract, Warren said.
When state offices ask for contract bids, they score each of the proposals on a scale from 0 to 100. Shine Early Learning’s bid for the coaching contract received a 97, while its proposal for the training plan got a perfect 100.
Maine Roads received about 73 points on each of its proposals. DHHS said the scores were issued in accordance with the processes laid out in its requests for proposals, but did not specify how Shine Early Learning received such high marks.
Shine Early Learning’s website touts the company’s “data-driven services and solutions” to “accelerate child and family outcomes.”
The company is owned by Acelero, Inc. — a firm seeded with a “strategic investment” from BlackRock, one of the world’s largest private equity companies. Several members from BlackRock and other venture capital firms who invested in Acelero subsequently joined the company’s board, according to a 2022 news release.
The private equity company’s investment in Acelero, and Shine Early Learning by extension, was made with the goal of “extending Acelero’s footprint and deepen(ing) its impact across communities,” BlackRock’s senior portfolio manager said at the time.
BlackRock handles more than $11 trillion in assets. The firm has been criticized for being “too big to fail,” purchasing everything from electric grids to billions’ of dollars of real estate across the country.
Activists have scrutinized BlackRock for investing in companies contributing to climate change and mass surveillance. The United Nations in 2025 issued a report saying BlackRock is complicit in Israel’s genocide in Gaza due to its investments in several weapons manufacturers.
In Maine, BlackRock acts as one of the primary investment managers for Maine’s Public Employee Retirement System.
Maine Roads plans to appeal DHHS’ decision on the contracts issued to Shine Early Learning, said Warren, the UMaine system spokesperson.
“In the meantime, the university is committed to continuing to provide high-quality services for Maine’s early childhood education community through the end of the current contract and supporting potentially affected employees, many of whom have served the field through the program for more than 15 years,” she said.

title: As heat becomes more extreme, inmates are increasingly threatened by rising temperatures
text:
Inmates increasingly threatened by rising temperatures as heat becomes more extreme
Steve Brooks' cell has no windows or air conditioning, so he relies on two 8-inch fans when it's stifling inside California's oldest prison. There's no access to ice or cold water, and during periodic power outages, there is no electricity.
"It's kind of like you're hyperventilating. The room's closing in," said Brooks, who is incarcerated in San Quentin Rehabilitation Center and has published articles about extreme heat behind bars.
During an eight-hour outage in 2024, the heat rose to between 90 and 100 degrees Fahrenheit (32 and 38 degrees Celsius). "It was just really scary." It felt, he said, like he was running out of oxygen.
As climate change fuels hotter temperatures, inmates are increasingly vulnerable.
Extreme heat can cause symptoms such as dizziness, nausea and headaches. Heat stroke, the most serious heat illness, can kill. When heat combines with humidity, it makes it harder for sweat to evaporate to cool the body.
Many prisons and detention centers in the U.S. are older buildings with antiquated, less efficient or nonexistent cooling systems. Many were built during a prison boom that started in the 1970s and were constructed with heat-trapping materials like concrete and steel. And many prisons are overcrowded.
Research shows the number of hot days has increased, and that hotter temperatures are linked to a higher risk of death for inmates, including from suicides.
Damon Gilbert, a staff attorney with New York Lawyers for the Public Interest, said heat-related deaths in prisons are underreported and often do not account for how high temperatures make chronic health issues worse. "It’s incredibly dangerous, and it’s only getting more dangerous. And so far, we are not keeping up as a country to adapting these facilities."
Prisons are getting hotter, increasing risk of death
One study by researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology found that most U.S. prisons had at least 10 days in the summer that were hotter than every previous summer, and several factors exacerbated the risks, including overcrowding and restrictions on movement.
Another study published in the National Library of Medicine found that hotter days mean more deaths from such things as heart disease and suicide — including among people who had been incarcerated for less than a year and those who were 65 or older.
Julie Skarha, who led the study on prison deaths linked to hotter days, said newly incarcerated people had a higher risk of dying, likely because they are not yet acclimated to the heat. "Some people are sentenced to serve in places they’ve never lived before. ... So suddenly, someone is having to adapt to this environment very quickly, something they’re not used to," she said.
‘It’s absolutely stifling. You can't breathe'
In the Minnesota prison at Lino Lakes, about 336 prisoners live in two medium-security units built in 1992 that the state acknowledges do not have effective cooling.
Greg Andreotti, who spent two summers in both units, said the facility’s design can exacerbate the heat. The cells hold up to two people and have large windows, and when Andreotti was there, they had no tinting or reflective film, "so your room bakes all day in the sun."
Inside the prison, people can buy small personal fans currently priced at $27.53, but many cannot afford them, he said. Other times they were not in stock. And while they might bring some relief, research shows fans are ineffective during heat waves.
The Minnesota Department of Corrections said those two housing units did not originally have air conditioning except for in common areas. It was added years later but struggles to control humidity during certain times of the year.
Aaron Swanum, a spokesman for the department, said in an email that there have been multiple repair efforts over the years but "they have not been able to effectively cool the housing units because the system is undersized for the space." The department is determining ways to better control inside temperatures and anticipates seeking state funding to make improvements.
For now, the facility uses large industrial fans in common areas and in the housing unit hallways, allows continuous access to ice, has painted skylights and takes other measures to help mitigate heat, the agency said. A recently completed window tinting project is expected to help.
"It’s oppressive. It’s like sitting in a tomb/sauna," recalled Josh Mcmillen, who was incarcerated in one of Lino Lakes' housing units without effective cooling. "You already feel like you’re being entombed when you shut that door. But when you shut that door, and it’s absolutely stifling, you can’t breathe. You feel no airflow."
In California, the Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation said it follows a heat illness prevention plan and that each prison monitors temperatures and provides additional cooling measures — including increased access to water stations, ice, showers and fans — during extreme heat.
Without adequate AC, cooling options are limited
Andreotti would cool off in the shower, use wet rags and sometimes lay on the concrete floor. Ice was only available outside his cell, and access was limited.
"When you’ve got 200 people attacking an ice machine over a three-hour period that you’re allowed out of your room, what do you think happens to it? There’s no ice," he said.
Mcmillen would stock up on aspirin for the tension headaches he would get from the heat.
In recent years, lawsuits related to heat in prisons have been filed in states including Missouri, Florida and Texas, where a federal judge called extreme heat in Texas prisons "plainly unconstitutional" and recently ordered the state to install air conditioning in all of its prisons by the end of 2029. Advocates allege temperatures inside can push above 120 degrees Fahrenheit (48.9 degrees Celsius), resulting in hundreds of inmate deaths in recent years.
On a summer day in 2023, Carlos Ramirez Bibiano was found vomiting and covered in a puddle of his own excrement in an outdoor cell in a Georgia prison, according to a lawsuit settled with his family recently for $3.25 million. He was left for five hours without water, shade or ice as temperatures climbed to 96 degrees Fahrenheit (35.6 degrees Celsius), and he was on medications that make it more difficult to regulate body temperature. That evening, the complaint says, Ramirez died of heart and lung failure caused by heat exposure.
Experts say more information, regulation is needed
It’s not much better for the prison guards and staff — though they get to go home after their shifts.
Lino Lakes Prison Warden Eddie Miles said they ensure prison staff have cold water, breaks and opportunities to cool off in climate-controlled areas to beat the heat.
Some states have rules to protect workers from extreme temperatures, but those do not apply to inmates. States like North Carolina, Vermont and Texas are spending millions to upgrade or install cooling systems. California says it could cost billions to make changes, though they might save millions in healthcare costs related to heat illnesses.
States have the power to protect inmates from the threat of extreme heat, experts said. It’s just a matter of political will.
"It’s going to take funding. It’s going to take attention and investment and collaborations between those agencies and the experts who are wanting to engage in this issue," said Carlee Purdum, assistant professor at the University of Houston who studies how disasters impact vulnerable people.

title: How to get or give help in Maine for housing, heating, food and more
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Across Maine, hundreds of nonprofits, churches and community groups offer help with food, household items and fuel assistance. Many of these programs cater to the most pressing needs in their communities and are often in need of support from those who can afford to donate.
If you are in need of help — or are in the position to offer support — below are some of the resources available.
Please send additional resource suggestions to [email protected].
HOW TO FIND HELP
Call 211 or go to 211Maine.org to connect with assistance programs near you. The service can also help with basic needs, such as directing people to shelter and transportation.
General Assistance is offered through town and city halls to help with rent, utilities and other expenses for people who qualify. Check with the town where you live for more information about how to apply.
The “Be There for Me” website helps parents and caregivers find a variety of support options, from housing and transportation to childcare and getting everyday items. Visit bethereforme.org to search for support.
FOOD ASSISTANCE
There are hundreds of food pantries and meal programs across the state. The Maine Food Access Map is an interactive tool to help people find resources near them.
To apply for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, visit a local Maine Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) Office for Family Independence, call 855-797-4357 or go to mymaineconnection.gov.
The federal Commodity Supplemental Food Program provides food boxes to low-income people 60 and older. For information about how to apply, visit the website for the Maine Department of Agriculture, Conservation & Forestry, which links to the local agencies that distribute the boxes.
HOUSING AND HEATING ASSISTANCE
The Home Energy Assistance Program (HEAP) helps qualified homeowners and renters pay for heating costs. Households are encouraged to apply for HEAP as soon as possible. Applications are handled by local Community Action Agencies. To apply online or to find information about how to apply by phone or in person, go to mainehousing.org.
Nearly two dozen wood banks operate across the state to provide households with firewood, including those in Cumberland, Freeport, Bethel, Kennebec County, Buxton, Waldo County and the Midcoast. For more information, visit the Maine Wood Banks website: woodbanks.org.
There are shelters in 11 counties for people experiencing homelessness. A list with contact information is available through MaineHousing. If you are currently homeless and need emergency shelter in Portland, call the 24/7 phone line at 207-761-2072. Veterans who are homeless or at risk can get immediate assistance by calling 800-377-5709 to connect with local programs.
The Maine Eviction Prevention Program helps cover past due rent and assistance for as long as a year to people who meet certain requirements. For more information, contact MaineHousing.
Pine Tree Legal Assistance provides free civil legal help to qualifying low-income Mainers with a variety of issues, including evictions and guidance on family matters. For more information, call 207-942-8322 or visit ptla.org.
HEALTHCARE ASSISTANCE
The Maine Medical Association maintains a list of clinics that offer free medical and dental care to people without insurance. To view the list and find contact information, visit mainephysicians.org.
The Maine Mobile Health Program’s mobile health clinics provide medical and behavioral health care on a sliding scale to farmworkers and others across the state. For more information, call 207-622-9252 or visit mainemobile.org.
HELP WITH HOUSEHOLD ITEMS
Several diaper banks operate in Maine. The Trinity Jubilee Center in Lewiston operates a diaper bank out of its food pantry and provides a 50-pack of diapers once a month. For more information, visit the website or call 207-782-5700.
In southern Maine, the Michael Klahr Jewish Family Services Diaper Bank in Portland does bi-monthly distributions. An essentials pantry also distributes household items that are not accessible with SNAP benefits. To sign up, call 207-772-1959.
For people with a case manager, help with furniture is available through Furniture Friends in Westbrook. Case managers can also request clothing and household items through Maine Needs in Portland.
HOW TO HELP
Maine Needs: The Portland nonprofit provides gently used clothing, boots, household items, diapers and other needed items to people across Maine and is accessed through case managers and social workers. Maine Needs accepts monetary donations and has detailed guidelines on its website for donating clothing and other requested items. It is also raising money to provide diapers through local food pantries to 8,500 babies. For more information, go to maineneeds.org
Keep ME Warm: The program, a partnership between United Way and community action agencies, is the only statewide fuel assistance fundraising effort in Maine. Donations support fuel assistance distributed across the state. To donate, visit uwsme.org/keep-me-warm.
Good Shepherd Food Bank: The Auburn-based nonprofit distributes food to more than 600 partner programs across the state. Good Shepherd accepts monetary donations to support its efforts. For more information, go to gsfb.org
Check with your local food pantry: Many local food pantries except donations of shelf-stable items, as well as money that can be used to buy food in bulk. Pantries also report a need for volunteers to help distribute and deliver food.
Furniture Friends: The Westbrook organization collects gently used furniture to give to community members who can’t afford to buy their own and who are referred through an agency or case manager. Information about how to donate furniture or money is posted on the Furniture Friends website. For more information, go to furniturefriends.org.

title: ‘Something to Chew On’ Series at Harbor Theater Starts Oct. 4

title: Maine Turnpike Authority plow debuts at Dempsey Challenge 2026
text:
LEWISTON, ME – Maine Turnpike Authority’s newest snow plow connected art, mission, and community at the 2026 Dempsey Challenge, where it made its event debut just one day after being unveiled. Positioned near the start line, The Defender immediately drew curiosity, questions, and conversation. As people approached the bright berry pink truck and yellow plow, many paused to take in the artwork celebrating everyday heroes who help clear the way to care.
The design reflects the Dempsey Center’s mission of supporting anyone impacted by cancer, while its ribbon and shield motif highlights the connection between patients, caregivers, Dempsey staff, and MTA crews who keep Maine’s busiest corridor safe.
“It really struck me how connected everything is,” said race participant Kim Cobb, who stopped for a selfie with her 5K team. “Knowing the roads are clear so we can get to our doctors and to the services at the Dempsey Center gives me real peace of mind. Seeing that message on a giant snowplow makes you think about all the folks working behind the scenes to make reaching my care possible.”
One of the morning’s most memorable moments came when Patrick Dempsey arrived by golf cart to see The Defender—named in his honor—for the first time at the event. He greeted MTA volunteers with a laugh, asking if he should “be expecting snow today,” before climbing into the driver’s seat at the invitation of snowplow operator Mike Somerset. Dempsey spent several minutes taking in the artwork and learning about the “beast of a vehicle” built for Maine’s harshest winter conditions. Later, he returned to congratulate auto racer Brandon Barker, winner of the 53rd Annual Nitro Trailers Oxford 250 and an MTA snowplow driver. The two talked about growing up in Maine, racing, and the unique overlap of racing cars and driving a snowplow.
Throughout race day, The Defender served as a visual anchor for the partnership—a reminder of the shared mission behind the collaboration: helping Maine people reach the emotional, physical, and social support offered by the Dempsey Center. The presence of The Defender underscored how reliable roads play a crucial role in connecting patients and caregivers to essential services year round.
Now returned and ready for duty within MTA’s winter fleet, The Defender will carry its message up and down the Turnpike over the winter. Hundreds saw it for the first time at the Challenge; in the months ahead, countless more will encounter it during winter storms as it continues its role as a moving symbol of care, connection, and community.
If you see The Defender out making the roads safe this winter, let it be a reminder that help in Maine is here. Learn more about the Dempsey Center at dempseycenter.org.
A full video recording of the press conference and unveiling from Friday, September 18 will be available on the MTA Youtube channel.

title: Man bleeds out, dies after punching through window at former elementary school, family says
text:
JACKSON, Miss. (WLBT/Gray News) - A Mississippi family is grieving a loved one who they say died after he punched through a window and seriously injured himself, possibly out of grief.
Jackson Public Schools says district law enforcement officers responded Sunday to the former Lake Elementary School. Upon arrival, they found a man with severe injuries who later died.
The man’s mother identified him as 38-year-old David Bridges. His family says Bridges punched through a window. The glass cut a main artery, and he bled out.
Bridges’ family says he was dealing with grief, and that may have led to the incident.
Loved ones gathered a few blocks from the building Monday afternoon to remember Bridges and share his legacy.
“An outspoken person, a respectful person, a loving person, but as humans, you know, we all got our share of flaws. But overall, he was a great person, a genuinely good person,” Calesha Esco said.
WLBT reached out to the Hinds County coroner for more information about the circumstances surrounding Bridges’ death.
JPS reported the building only sustained minor damage and that the area was secured and cleaned. The district said operations continued as normal Monday.
While the facility is a former elementary school, JPS currently uses it for its Re-Engaging for All to Progress or REAP Program, which provides an alternative pathway to a high school diploma for students who are at risk of dropping out of high school.

title: Meet Snow, our Adoptable Pet of the Week
text:
Meet Snow, our Adoptable Pet of the Week in Greater Portland
This week's featured adoptable pet from the Animal Refuge League of Greater Portland is Snow, a 2-year-old mixed-breed dog who is very friendly with people.
Matt Blanchard of the Animal Refuge League said Snow would make for a great family member, but would do best in a home that can provide structure and training since she still has a little bit of puppy energy.
"She gets a little jumpy for treats. When she gets worked up and excited, she might get on you and lick your face, that kind of thing," Blanchard said.
Blanchard added that Snow is a good mix of a playful pet and a cuddly companion.
"She's pretty active. She likes to wrestle with you a little bit and play. She likes to get a little excited, but she also seems like the kind of dog that is going to curl up right on top of you on the couch and get some good cuddles in. She loves to have her belly scratched and things like that," Blanchard said.
Snow does seem to enjoy being around other dogs, but Blanchard said any interested adopters who have a dog or child should have them meet Snow at the shelter. The Animal Refuge League does not believe Snow has had any exposure to cats.
More information about Snow is available on the Animal Refuge League's website, as long as she is still looking for her forever home.
Anyone who is interested in meeting Snow or other adoptable pets can visit the Animal Refuge League's shelter at 217 Landing Road in Westbrook between 11 a.m. and 4 p.m., except on Wednesdays, when the shelter is closed for adoptions.
The Animal Refuge League of Greater Portland does adoptions on a first-come, first-served basis. On the days the shelter is open, sign-in sheets will be placed on the front door at 9 a.m. to track the order of arrival of adopters who show up early. People who arrive early are asked to remain on the campus once they sign in.
Dog owners who are interested in adopting dogs that are older than 6 months, including Snow, are required to have their dogs meet the adoptable pet before a new pet can be brought home.

title: A Maine lobster turf war is over
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The local fishermen’s co-op in Spruce Head dropped its request for a court injunction after a neighboring seafood giant moved a boat that the co-op said was interfering with its ability to operate.
Attorney Patrick Mellor filed a notice with the state court in Knox County on Tuesday that it was withdrawing its request for injunctive relief after the vessel was removed from its previous location.
The lawsuit filed in April challenging the expansion of neighboring Maine Lobster and Processing LLC’s wharf system remains in effect. The two sides went through a court alternative dispute resolution process but no agreement was reached.
At stake is access to one of Maine’s most productive lobstering harbors — but also one of its smallest, with space exceedingly tight in its working waterfront on the south side of the island.
The Maine Department of Environmental Protection approved the expansion of Maine Lobster and Processing LLC’s wharf system on Jan. 8. But the co-op filed an appeal to the Board of Environmental Protection on Feb. 5, warning the expansion would block access to its own wharf — an appeal Maine Lobster contends is without merit.
The processor is a subsidiary of Mazzetta Co. LLC of Highland Park, Illinois, which bills itself as one of the world’s largest importers and producers of shrimp, mussels, lobsters, crab and finfish, selling more than 100 million pounds of finished seafood products annually. The conglomerate purchased the longtime family-owned Atwood Lobster business in Spruce Head in 2011. In addition to Atwood Lobster, Mazzetta owns and operates Beach Point Processing on Prince Edward Island in Canada and cold storage distribution facilities in Londonderry, New Hampshire.
The co-op is a fishing cooperative that has operated continuously since 1972 at its Spruce Head location. It serves about 40 lobstermen.
Maine Lobster wants to extend its bait storage building deck area, which the co-op contends would further constrict the navigational corridor used by its affiliated vessels. The expansion would increase navigational conflicts and safety risks, the co-op warns.
Maine Lobster also proposes constructing a new 16-foot-by-28-foot floating dock system. The co-op says this dock system would impede the only navigational access to its wharf.
Other parties have also pointed out that Maine Lobster installed a floating dock system in 2021 without a permit.
David Cousens of South Thomaston, president of the co-op and former longtime president of the Maine Lobstermen’s Association, warned regulators earlier this year that the expansion would lead to dire consequences for the local co-op.
“If the application is approved as currently configured, it would make it impossible for us to operate. We would go out of business,” Cousens said in an affidavit filed with the Board of Environmental Protection.
Spruce Head is one of the state’s top fishing ports, landing more than $20 million worth of seafood in 2025. That made it the fifth-biggest lobster port in Maine last year, following Stonington, Vinalhaven, Portland and Friendship.
The co-op and its neighbor have also argued over the placement of a disused lobster smack, which the co-op alleges has been intentionally parked in a manner that limits access to their own wharf.
Maine Lobster and Processing’s attorney, Thomas Federle, responded to the co-op’s appeal by noting the company scaled back its proposed expansion in response to the cooperative’s concerns.
“This substantial compromise by Maine Lobster was a sacrifice of operational needs, surrendering needed skiff space and additional workspace for its fishermen,” the company’s lawyer stated to the Board of Environmental Protection in his March 20 response.
Funding for the wharf expansion is being aided by a state working waterfront resiliency grant and a business resiliency grant to rebuild its wharf and raise it after the January 2024 storms.
The lawyer said the appeal puts the grant in jeopardy by delaying the project.
The Atwood Lobster company originated in 1920 when William Atwood’s grandfather, a lobster fisherman from Nova Scotia, moved his family to Boston. William Atwood’s father soon started a wholesale lobster business in Boston. That business was destroyed by fire in 1950 and his father decided to move the family and business to Maine to be closer to the supply of lobsters. The business stayed in the family until the sale to the Mazzetta subsidiary in 2011.

title: Phil Pressey back for second season as Maine Celtics coach
text:
Phil Pressey will return for a second season as the Maine Celtics head coach, the team announced Thursday.
Pressey is the first head coach to return for a second season with the Maine Celtics since Brandon Bailey was promoted to the Boston Celtics coaching staff after the 2018-19 season. Maine went 27-23 and reached the NBA G League playoffs for the fourth straight season.
Pressey replaced Tyler Lashbrook, who lead Maine to a 29-21 record in 2024-25 and a berth in the Eastern Conference finals before moving up to the Boston Celtics coaching staff.
Also returning to Maine this season are assistant coaches Mike Malat and Boaz Mensah. Devin Sweetney, Jacob Kester and Rich Kelly are joining the team’s staff.

title: Let’s not replay the tragedy of life without vaccinations
text:
I want to share how my family has been affected by vaccines. First, comic relief: when our baby began receiving the recommended shots, I was pleased but mystified by her reaction: she simply smiled at the nurse. Weren’t babies supposed to yell? Each time we returned to the medical office for follow-up vaccines, I witnessed happy interactions between my baby and the nurses. Was our kid normal, I wondered? Finally, a few years later, our child — then a toddler — loudly conveyed her opinion about that sharp “pinch.” Phew.
There are much sadder records in my extended family about a lack of medicines to help beloved siblings, parents and children. For example, before Penicillin was commonly available (in the 1940s) my grandmother’s sister died at age 21 (in 1930) of pneumonia. I’m glad that many other diseases have been controlled thanks to science. Smallpox, typhoid and diphtheria used to terrify communities. My ancestors also feared yellow fever, polio, mumps, measles and tetanus.
Let’s not replay those tragedies. Instead, let’s ensure that everyone gets to learn about the best medications available. My ancestors would have loved access to such medicines.
Mariana Tupper
Falmouth

title: Justice Department finds UCLA law school illegally used race in admissions
text:
The Justice Department found Thursday that the law school at the University of California, Los Angeles, illegally considered race in admissions.
The announcement follows a similar finding against the university’s medical school and comes as President Donald Trump’s administration ramps up scrutiny of colleges’ processes for selecting students. The administration also has accused the UC Berkeley Law School and the medical school at the University of California, San Diego, of illegally discriminating against white and Asian applicants.
The UCLA School of Law said in a statement that it was committed to making admissions decisions in compliance with all applicable laws.
“Students are admitted through a comprehensive, merit-based review process that considers each applicant’s achievements and experiences,” the statement said. “We are confident in our process.”
Affirmative action in college admissions has been illegal since a 2023 Supreme Court ruling forbade it. The same ruling said colleges could continue to assess how applicants’ backgrounds might speak to broader characteristics, but Trump has accused colleges of using applicants’ personal statements and other proxies to consider race in admissions — which conservatives view as illegal discrimination.
The Justice Department’s investigation found UCLA’s law school discriminated against white and Asian American students by favoring Black and Hispanic applicants in its 2023, 2024 and 2025 incoming classes. Its analysis found the mean LSAT score was lower for admitted Black applicants than for admitted white applicants.
The department also said admissions staff at the law school instructed applicants during recruitment efforts, including one called the “Diversity Admissions Open House,” how to reveal their race in essays.
“Like many of its peer institutions, UCLA Law School runs a two-tiered admissions system whose academic bar for acceptance shifts up or down depending on the color of your skin,” said Harmeet Dhillon, head of the department’s Civil Rights Division, in a news release.
California voters ended affirmative action in college admissions in a 1997 ballot measure. In a brief filed in the Supreme Court case, the UC system said the change led to a precipitous drop in underrepresented minorities, especially at the system’s most selective campuses. The brief said UC went on to implement a range of race-neutral measures to increase diversity.
The Trump administration also has sued over the main UCLA campus’s response to allegations of antisemitic harassment. The administration’s latest finding sets the stage for a voluntary resolution to bring UCLA into compliance with the Justice Department’s legal interpretation or, if none can be reached, potential legal action.
