title: Cheese recalled over suspected E. coli outbreak; 13 illnesses reported nationwide
text:
Cheese recalled after 13 illnesses linked to suspected multi-state E. coli outbreak, FDA says
A company is now halting production and recalling all of its raw milk cheese products that officials believe are linked to a multi-state E. coli outbreak.
Related video: How to stay ahead of recalls
According to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Sierra Nevada Cheese Company of Willows, California, voluntarily recalled its Graziers raw milk products on Sept. 29.
Officials said 13 illnesses have been linked to the products, believed to be contaminated with Escherichia coli O26:H11.
The FDA said the E. coli O26:H11 can cause "serious and sometimes fatal infections in young children, elderly people, and others with weakened immune systems."
"E. coli O26:H11 can cause acute diarrheal illness (often with bloody stools) within a few days of ingestion of the bacteria. Most people recover within a week," the FDA said. "However, a subset of infected individuals (especially children under 5 years of age, the elderly, and immunocompromised individuals) may develop Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS), a severe illness characterized by hemolytic anemia (red cell breakdown), thrombocytopenia (low platelet count) and renal failure. HUS can lead to death."
The recalled Graziers raw milk cheese products have not been linked to a specific lot, date code, or production date.
All lots of the Sierra Nevada Graziers Grass-Fed Raw Medium Cheddar, Raw Sharp Cheddar, Raw Monterey Jack, and Raw Jalapeño Jack have been recalled.
The company said the voluntary recall began after the FDA contacted them regarding reported illnesses linked to the products.
States linked to reported illnesses include California, Colorado, Georgia, Kentucky, Michigan, Nevada, Oregon, Tennessee and Utah.
Sierra Nevada Cheese Company has since issued notices on its website and social media and is cooperating with the FDA and the CDC.
Consumers who purchased the recalled products should not consume or serve them, and should return the products to the place of purchase for a refund, or dispose of it.
Anyone with questions can contact Sierra Nevada Cheese Company at (530) 934-8662, Monday through Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Pacific Time, or by email at recallinfo@sierranevadacheese.com.
"We sincerely appreciate the understanding and continued support of our customers and community as we work through this recall," the company said in a post on Instagram.

title: Water supply for Maine’s Navy shipyard is draining months ahead of schedule
text:
Water levels in ponds that supply Kittery remain 12 feet below normal heading into winter, and there is no end in sight to conservation measures now approaching their eighth week.
Recent rains raised levels in the Kittery Water District’s reservoirs only by about 3 inches. The district’s restriction, which it describes as “severe,” limits outdoor watering in Kittery and part of neighboring Eliot to nighttime and early morning on certain days of the week.
The rare shortage comes just as the district heads into its hardest period. Demand from Portsmouth Naval Shipyard, which uses more than half of the district’s water, rises in winter, while freezing temperatures lock up rain and snow that would refill the ponds. Kittery officials are asking the state to look at the shipyard’s plans for its water system.
The district gets its water from four ponds and uses about half of the ponds’ total capacity each year. The ponds have failed to refill this year amid an ongoing drought. Matthew Berube, the superintendent of Kittery Water District, said there is no end to the restrictions in sight.
Berube called the low water an “emergency,” saying the ponds are already where they would normally be in midwinter.
“I’m at levels in the pond that I would typically see in December and January after three months of my high-usage period,” he said. “I’m already advanced three months ahead of the schedule in water loss.”
Local officials said the drought that began last summer along with heavier development in southern Maine and rising demand from the shipyard caused the shortage. Leaks at the shipyard in April and July disrupted water service in the district. It’s not clear how much water was lost in the incidents.
The Navy is now starting a multimillion-dollar power and water project at the shipyard that includes a water tank and new water mains. Navy officials say the federally funded project’s on- and off-base utility improvements will benefit the area. They also say that the shipyard’s water usage has decreased from historic amounts.
“We deeply value our neighbors in Kittery and remain committed to transparent, proactive coordination to ensure that shipyard operations do not compromise the services our surrounding communities rely upon,” shipyard spokesperson Jessica Lamarre said in a statement.
The leaks and restrictions put pressure on the shipyard. In August, Kittery officials asked the state’s Board of Environmental Protection to examine the new project.
About a third of Eliot gets its water from the district. Because the restrictions apply to only part of town, they have caused some confusion, Town Manager Michael Sullivan said. He expects residents may have to get used to restrictions as the town grows.
“Water conservation is something that’s important, and it may be new to this region,” he said. “But you know, as there’s more development and the area gets more developed, it’s going to become more common.”
Berube also blamed development in the district.
“It’s got to be thought of differently,” he said. “We can’t just keep building to infinity because I don’t have infinite water.”
Daniel O’Connor is a Report for America corps member who covers rural government as part of the partnership between the Bangor Daily News and The Maine Monitor, with additional support from BDN and Monitor readers.

title: When running the Maine marathon, remember the journey
text:
Editor’s note: Assistant Sports Editor Scott Martin is training to run the Maine Marathon on Sunday. He has a goal and it’s within reach. He has been sharing his ups and downs and everything in between for what it takes to be ready to run 26.2 miles.
I took off my hydration vest and dropped it on the pavement next to my car at the Wainwright Sports Complex in South Portland. Three hours and 55 minutes after leaving this spot on Sept. 19, and nearly 10 months after signing up for the 2026 Maine Marathon, peak training was over. I was too tired and sore to celebrate, but as I leaned on my Subaru Impreza and chugged a vanilla protein shake, I couldn’t help but grin.
Training for my first marathon in seven years was not perfect, but training never is, and despite hiccups caused by illness, insomnia, work and other stress, I was able to do enough speed work and run enough miles to be prepared for a successful race on Sunday. For that, I am grateful.
The time on the clock when I finish will not be the sole factor in determining if my race was a success. There are way too many things that could happen that are out of my control to let my time alone determine if it was a good day or not.
My list of goals for the marathon on Oct. 4 has a number of times (A: 3:47:45; B: 3:49:44 — a PR; C: 3:59:59 — sub 4), but also has things like, “Don’t be a jerk,” “try to have fun,” and “don’t do anything crazy.”
If I accomplish those last three things and cross the finish line healthy, even if I don’t accomplish any of my time goals, race day will be a success.
Really, when I dropped my hydration vest in that parking lot, I had already won. I spent a lot of time this year (Garmin tells me I ran about 76 hours since July 1) working toward this goal. I ran more miles and harder workouts than I have since the COVID pandemic derailed my running habit. When I tore my calf on March 31, 2021, it started a cascade of health issues that forced me to stop running for nearly two months at the end of 2022.
I have spent the last four years building myself to this point. Making it to the starting line and having the opportunity to run a marathon is a huge win.
Maybe you think I am giving myself an out if I am unable to run my goal time. Maybe I am. I have a lot of doubts, despite what my running friends and my coaches tell me, about my ability to average 8:41 per mile for 26.2 miles. I ran close to that pace for 11 miles on Sept. 12, but it filled me with more questions than confidence.
“This feels so fast. Can I really do this for 26.2 miles? Am I fit enough? Will my achy knees put up with this?”
That’s just how my brain works. Confidence has never been my default. Doubt and pessimism are.
When I told my coach, Dan Frey of Finish Strong Physical Therapy and Endurance, about my doubts, he reminded me just how different the situation will be on race day.
“If you push aside race-day anxiety, that’s the only hard part about it,” Frey said. “It’s a supported race. There’s people running with you. There are people cheering you on. All of these things arguably make (the race) easier (than the workouts and the long runs).”
I’ll try to remember that on race day. I will also try to remember all the fun I had with my friends running this summer. Training has been a shared experience with a group of people I’ve grown quite fond of. What happens in the race won’t ruin what has happened over the last 10 months.
I hope I reach my goal in the race. I would love to erase the chalkboard in my apartment with 3:47 written on it because I finally ran that time after 12 years of trying. Even if I don’t, I’ll do my best to enjoy it, to not be a jerk, and remember the journey to get here.
Because no matter how long it takes to run 26.2 miles, the journey has been a lot longer.

title: Better planning could have headed off Lewiston hospital mess
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Douglas Rooks has been a Maine editor and columnist for 41 years. His biography of Gov. Ken Curtis, “Transformational,” is now available. He welcomes comment at [email protected].
The vote last week by Central Maine Medical Center nurses in Lewiston to unionize says a good deal about organizing prospects in the state, but even more about the mismanagement of Maine hospitals.
Driven by the perverse incentives of fee-for-service reimbursement, hospitals compete for a larger share of the revenue pie, ignoring opportunities for rational consolidation as care becomes increasingly specialized and high-tech.
The situation at CMMC, which has been under severe financial stress, has all the makings of a train wreck. Last year, Prime Healthcare of California, a for-profit chain, agreed to buy CMMC and formed a nonprofit subsidiary to make the acquisition — a maneuver that fooled no one. Nonetheless, the state issued a Certificate of Need approving the sale, in which Prime agreed to maintain designated staffing levels, invest in new services and — somehow — improve the financial balance sheet.
The immediate response by hospital employees? Nearly 20% of the staff resigned. Earlier this year, surgeries were briefly suspended and transferred elsewhere when the state found inadequate operating room sterilization.
The nurses’ campaign then came as no surprise — though hospital management’s response did. Just days before the union vote, Prime fired or suspended 20 nurses, most of them involved in the organizing drive, allegedly for neglecting their duties. Prime has employed similar union-busting tactics elsewhere, but it’s unprecedented in Maine hospitals.
The move drew a stern rebuke from Gov. Janet Mills, writing to Prime, “I strongly urge you to immediately reinstate every nurse who has been wrongfully fired or suspended.” To date, Prime has not responded — just as MaineHealth’s board in Portland ignored Mills’ plea, and that of the Democratic nominee for governor, Hannah Pingree, to delay closing the birthing center at Miles Memorial in Damariscotta, the 12th such closure statewide in recent years.
CMMC nurses voted 204-21 in favor of a union, a rate of 91% It followed a similarly successful effort to organize at Maine Medical Center in 2021 by the Maine Nurses Association, affiliated with National Nurses United, the third such attempt. Nurses at Northern Light Eastern Maine Medical Center in Bangor have had a union since 1976; labor will now have a seat at the management table in three of the state’s largest hospitals.
But the union campaigns reflect a larger reality — an apparent inability to adjust the state’s hospital structure to reflect changing demands for care within a community structure, as opposed to the often debilitating competition for patients and revenue.
Lewiston provides a case in point. Thirty years ago, Central Maine and St. Mary’s both had similar number of beds and budgets, and it was already clear that consolidation should be considered. Instead, CMMC embarked on an unwise expansion plan that led to the current crisis.
It briefly owned Parkview Hospital in Brunswick, which was then engaged in a highly public war of words with Mid Coast, itself a merger of hospitals in Brunswick and Bath, that ended only with Parkview’s bankruptcy. When Mid Coast took over operations, it declined to adjust or reduce any services and, overextended, had to sell to MaineHealth, which from its Portland headquarters now controls the majority of the state’s hospital services.
Or consider Waterville, where Inland, the state’s only osteopathic hospital, was closed by Northern Light last year. It’s possible it could have been saved. When the state approved the merger of Waterville’s other hospital, Mid Maine, with Augusta on the new MaineGeneral campus, it curiously allowed Waterville’s Thayer Hospital to retain a 24-hour ER, even though the facility downsized to outpatient care. Two emergency rooms in one small market vastly exceeded demand, with Inland the casualty.
Just as MaineHealth controls the majority of the state’s hospitals, under the Affordable Care Act federal and state governments have assumed the bulk of healthcare spending, well over half. This requires a larger state role in planning, and if necessary directing, the provision of services so patients and staff are protected, not forced out.
In the 1980s, the Maine Health Care Finance Authority regulated hospital charges, moderating rate increases while maintaining care standards, but was later abolished. Reviving it, while reviewing mergers and takeovers and offering alternatives, would be a good first step. The Prime Healthcare fiasco is exactly what the state must avoid repeating.
A national healthcare system, rising to prominence in this year’s campaigns, is ultimately the solution to many of our woes. The state can play an important role, however, and a new administration is the ideal place to start.

title: Obituary: Stephen T. Hughes
text:
AUBURN / NEW YORK CITY, N.Y. – Stephen T. Hughes passed away on Aug. 17, 2026. He was 83.
Steve lived a life marked by service to others — as an elected official, a trustee of the University of Maine, and an active member of several Episcopal parishes, most notably St. Bartholomew’s Church in New York City, N.Y. where he lived for the last 40 years of his life.
Born on July 26, 1943 to Albert W. “Beau” Hughes and Edith Bivens Hughes, Steve grew up in Auburn and graduated from Edward Little High School. He went on to attend Duke University in Durham, North Carolina, a state where members of his extended family lived. After being drafted, Steve served for two years in the United States Army before enrolling at the University of Maine.
At UMaine, Steve made many lifelong friends and served as president of the student body during a tumultuous era when the Vietnam War and the national debate surrounding it profoundly affected campus life. While still an undergraduate, he gained statewide recognition when Gov. Kenneth M. Curtis appointed him as the first student to serve as a trustee of the University of Maine.
Steve graduated from UMaine in 1970 and, while continuing his service as a trustee, attended the University of Maine School of Law. In 1974, voters in Auburn elected him to the Maine House of Representatives. He was reelected in 1976.
During his legislative career, Steve became closely identified with two landmark environmental measures. He sponsored legislation establishing Maine’s beverage-container deposit law, commonly known as the “Bottle Bill,” and championed the successful effort to eliminate most roadside billboards. Both measures helped shape Maine’s approach to environmental protection and preservation of its landscape and remain the law today. Steve was also a strong advocate for civil rights, reproductive freedom, and the rule of law.
After serving four years in the Legislature, Steve left Maine for New York City, N.Y. where he pursued a life of ministry. He enrolled at Union Theological Seminary and spent 15 years leading programs at the Cathedral Church of St. John the Divine. He later became deeply involved with St. Bartholomew’s Church, known as St. Bart’s, where he served in a variety of leadership roles for 25 years. His activities there were curtailed in later years by health issues related to COVID-19.
Throughout his life, Steve maintained a deep love of music, culture, and the arts. Blessed with an extraordinary tenor voice, he sang with numerous choirs in both Maine and New York. He also loved to travel and, over the years, explored much of the United States and Europe with his many friends.
Steve will be remembered for his lively conversation, intellectual curiosity, commitment to public and community service, love of music and the arts, and devotion to a wide circle of friends and an extended network of cousins scattered across the country.
Steve was predeceased by his parents, Albert W. “Beau” Hughes and Edith Bivens Hughes; and his brother, Nick Hughes.
A gathering of Steve’s Maine family and friends will be held 2 p.m., Sunday, Oct. 11, at Maple Hill Farm in Hallowell. A service celebrating Steve’s life will be held at 2 p.m. Nov. 6 at St. Bartholomew’s Church in New York City, N.Y. Interment will be in the Hughes family plot in Eno Presbyterian Church in Cedar Grove, N.C.
In lieu of flowers please donate to be made to the University of Maine Alumni Association. https://www.umainealumni.com/

title: Tanker crash causes delays on Maine Turnpike in Falmouth
text:
FALMOUTH, Maine (WABI) - Troopers responded to a two-vehicle crash on the Maine Turnpike southbound near mile marker 56 in Falmouth early Thursday.
The crash was reported at approximately 2:35 a.m.
The initial investigation indicates a SUV lost power and came to a stop in the travel lane, officials said.
A tractor-trailer tanker traveling southbound approached the stopped SUV and attempted to move into the right lane to avoid it. The tractor-trailer struck the rear passenger side of the SUV, pushing it toward the median. The tractor-trailer then tipped onto its right side.
Injuries and response
The driver and the passenger in the SUV and the driver of the tractor-trailer were transported to Maine Medical Center for evaluation. No serious injuries were reported.
A small amount of diesel fuel leaked from the tractor-trailer. The Maine Department of Environmental Protection responded to the scene.
Road closures
All southbound lanes in the area were closed following the crash, with traffic diverted at Exit 63.
The tractor-trailer has since been removed, and the scene has been cleared. All lanes are back open.
The crash remains under investigation.

title: Who’s afraid of Bobby Charles?
text:
Sam Patten has worked for Maine’s last three Republican senators, including Susan Collins’ first electoral campaigns, is a former managing editor of The Maine Wire and is the author of “Dangerous Company: The Misadventures of a Foreign Agent.”
Given the publicly available polling on Maine’s gubernatorial race going into the fall campaign season, it appears likely that Democrat Hannah Pingree is favored to win. So, with their nominee’s comfortable lead of more than 10 points, why is the state Democratic Party launching such furious attacks on Republican nominee Bobby Charles?
CNN recently released results of a poll that showed more than half — 52% — of likely
voters favoring Hannah Pingree as opposed to 39% saying they plan to vote for Bobby Charles (the poll did not include independent Rick Bennett, a former Republican). Last month, a Fox poll pegged Pingree at 49% compared to Charles’ 38% and Bennett’s 9%.
The answer is strikingly simple: it is not enough just to defeat Bobby Charles. In order to perpetuate their now eight-year stranglehold on power in the state, Maine Democrats must crush everything Charles represents, and to bury his call that Augusta actually be accountable for a change.
Taking a page out of an authoritarian’s handbook, the Democrats seem intent on obliterating Charles altogether — and stigmatizing those who might support him in November.
Charles’ sister authored an op-ed that was published in these pages on Sept. 9 and announced her intention to vote for Pingree. Based on a deeply personal revelation, the op-ed argued that her brother is too divisive and not sufficiently supportive of women to merit her vote.
It was a political body blow, reminiscent of women coming forward this summer alleging they’d been assaulted by then-Democratic senatorial nominee Graham Platner. While emotionally charged and undeniably brave in terms of public disclosure, there was something about both events that felt very political. After all, the synchronized press conference was held at the state Democrats’ Portland office.
Many of us disagree about politics around the family dinner table, but this was very different.
Also consider the peculiar press conference they staged late last month in a Portland park where one usually must tread carefully to avoid stepping on used hypodermic needles. It was there that former Maine CDC Director Nirav Shah — who but for ranked-choice voting would be squaring off against Charles this November — and two other Democrat-aligned public health figures inveighed against the Republican’s pledge to cut the state budget by $4 billion and insisted he would eliminate benefits for Maine’s senior citizens.
How dare he, Dr. Shah then seemed to sneer.
Then there is the candidacy of Rick Bennett itself. Fashioning himself a latter-day Bill
Cohen by walking around the state to put himself in various communities, Bennett —
once a chairman of the state GOP — seems to be a pressure release valve for old-
fashioned Maine Republicans who just wish people could be nice again and want to feel
good about their vote. But Bennett’s single-digit showing shows us how much times have
changed.
Why is he even running, I asked in a Maine Wire column a year ago, when sheer mathematics so
clearly indicated he has no path to victory? There are only two explanations I can
imagine today: either he wants to make a point, as Lindsey Graham did when he ran for
president in 2016 on the sole platform of defeating ISIS, or he wants to help someone
siphon away votes.
The only way to know which of these is Bennett’s motivation is to wait until Pingree announces her cabinet. “Look, Republicans,” Bennett’s candidacy seems to say, “this is what you are supposed to look like, pay attention!”
Maybe Maine Democrats are just so much better organized and resourced than their erstwhile counterparts at the state GOP that they can afford to spend as much attention on systematically attacking Charles as they have. But the persistence of their effort points to something different.
Cutting taxes and fighting crime are the wrong priorities, this effort insists. Despite the double-digit advantage Pingree seems to enjoy, crushing everything Charles stands for is important. Because, despite the breezy prettiness of Maine’s bucolic coast, they are afraid to discuss the rot that consumes Augusta today. Very afraid.

title: Several whales got entangled along the Maine coast in 2025, federal report finds
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Several whales got entangled along the Maine coast in 2025, federal report finds
A new report finds there were 76 confirmed entangled large whales documented along the coasts of the United States in 2025.
The report from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Fisheries says five of those entanglements were off the coast of Maine, with another unidentified whale in the Gulf of Maine. There were also two entanglements within the Gulf of Maine off the coast of Massachusetts.
The identified entangled whales off the Maine coast include three humpback whales, a fin whale and a minke whale. Both of the entangled whales off the northern coast of Massachusetts were humpback whales.
There was only one documented entanglement involving a North Atlantic right whale in 2025. That case was off the coast of Georgia.
NOAA says the 76 total entangled whales is slightly higher than the annual average of 72.7 between 2007 and 2024.
The report does not include reports of whales seen outside U.S. waters entangled in U.S. gear.
Entanglements off the northeast and mid-Atlantic coast dropped to the lowest total since 2013, when there were also 12.
Nearly 79% of all confirmed live whale entanglements were off the coasts of California, Alaska, Hawaii and Washington.
The NOAA report says approximately 46% of confirmed entanglement cases were verified as involving commercial or recreational fishing gear. The remaining cases involved line that could not be directly attributed to a fishery or other source.
"Although various marine industries use gear in the ocean, one of the most common sources of line is commercial or recreational fishing. It is likely some of the cases involving line that could not be identified to a specific source were related to fishing activities," the report said.
The report did not specify the nature of the entanglements in Maine.
If you encounter a whale that may be entangled, please contact your local network immediately via the 24/7 regional hotline or contact the United States Coast Guard on VHF CH-16 and keep a safe and legal distance from the animal. If you can stay with the animal at a safe distance until responders arrive, this will best help the animal and response team.
In Maine, the number to call is 866-755-NOAA (6622). You will need to provide certain information when making a report:
- Location of the animal
- Detailed description of the entangling gear or debris
- Location of the entanglement on the animal
- Direction and speed the whale is traveling, and whether it is solitary or with other whales
- Behavior of the whale
- Species of the whale, if known
- Approximate size and condition of the whale
- Photos and videos

title: Rapper Rick Ross denied special treatment in court as judge tells him ‘I don’t know who you are’
text:
MIAMI BEACH, Fla. (Gray News) — Rapper Rick Ross, born William Leonard Roberts, is facing charges for an alleged domestic violence issue in August.
But the judge Ross appeared in front of Thursday did not know who he was.
Brad Horenstein, Ross’ lawyer, wanted his client’s release expedited.
“Mr. Roberts is a celebrity, and so I don’t know...” Horenstein said.
“What does that mean?” the judge responded.
“I don’t know to whatever degree your honor can, but I’d ask that that his release be expedited. He’s in a red jumpsuit and for purposes of his safety. I don’t know what your honor can do, but, I don’t know,” Horenstein said.
The judge then said hello to Ross and said he would not get special treatment.
“Hi, Mr. Roberts. I have no idea who you are, except as somebody here in the court who’s going to be treated fairly just like everybody else here,” she said.
Ross faces a felony charge of battery by strangulation, as well as a misdemeanor battery charge, according to online court records.
An attorney for Ross, 50, said in a statement that Ross is being wrongfully accused by an ex-girlfriend whose motivations are unclear.
“The ex did not even file a police report until a month after the claimed incident allegedly took place,” defense attorney Steve Sadow said in the statement. “Mr. Roberts is innocent and has pled not guilty to the charges. He respectfully requests that his friends, fans and the general public not prejudge the situation and allow the judicial process to run its course.”
Jail records showed that Ross was being held Thursday morning on $5,000 bail. He was later released. An arraignment is scheduled for Oct. 22.

title: ‘Devastating’: Mother cremated before viewing, another’s body used in her place, families allege
text:
DETROIT (WDIV) - Two families are suing a Detroit funeral home, alleging one woman was cremated before her scheduled viewing and another’s body was used in her place.
Kimberly Moore died Sept. 3 after a battle with endometrial cancer. Her family alleges Hutchison Funeral Home cremated her and swapped her body with that of Sandra Miller before her viewing.
Ahead of the viewing, Moore’s daughter, Bianca Robinson, arrived at the funeral home to do her mother’s makeup – and quickly realized something was wrong, the family says. They were later told Moore had been accidentally cremated and that the body presented for viewing wasn’t hers.
“I didn’t get a chance to say goodbye, and I needed it so bad, just to keep going,” Robinson said. “This is devastating. I can’t sleep. We just want answers. Please.”
Moore’s family says they still have not received her ashes, which attorneys say will undergo DNA testing.
Miller died Sept. 13 after a battle with ovarian cancer. Her family says they were initially told by the funeral home that their mother was not involved in the incident. They later learned through Moore’s family that Miller’s body had allegedly been used as a “prop” during the former’s viewing.
“After everything she had been through, my mom deserved dignity, identification, protection and respect,” said Miller’s daughter, Cessley Walker. “She was somebody’s daughter. She was a sister. She was a wife. She was a mother. She was my mom.”
The funeral home says it launched an internal investigation into the incident, but James Harrington with Feiger Law says that’s not enough. His firm is now pursuing legal action on behalf of both families.
“What we know is that their process was woefully inadequate with the explanation that was told [being] the tag got wet and fell off. I don’t believe that for a second,” Harrington said. “I think it was just pure carelessness, recklessness.”
The funeral home, its owner, Jaimie Hutchison, and Southern Michigan Cremation Services were all named as defendants in the families’ lawsuits.
The funeral home’s vice president was not named. A family spokesperson says he was found dead in his Detroit home last Thursday. Details of his death have not been made public.

title: Maine hockey stars deliver young fan special birthday surprise
SpaceX launches 4 astronauts on a fast track to the International Space Station
text:
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. (AP) — Four astronauts rocketed into orbit Thursday on a space station mission that will stretch until spring, among them a Canadian whose wife will give birth while he’s away.
SpaceX launched commander Jessica Watkins and her crew for NASA after a three-week delay to fix the capsule’s leaking fuel system. Thick clouds threatened all morning to halt the countdown but in the end, the skies cleared enough to allow for a safe liftoff.
Although their stay at the International Space Station will last a long six months, the flight there promised to be the quickest yet for Elon Musk’s company: a mere eight-hour transit with an arrival well before bedtime.
With the late morning liftoff from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Watkins became the first Black woman to lead a crew to orbit. A geologist who worked with NASA’s Mars rover Curiosity a decade ago, Watkins is making her second trip to the space station following a lengthy stay in 2022.
“Thanks for an amazing ride,” Watkins radioed after reaching orbit.
The others are newcomers to space: NASA’s Luke Delaney, a retired Marine; Canada’s Joshua Kutryk, a colonel in the Royal Canadian Air Force; and Russia’s Sergey Teteryatnikov, a former submariner. They will replace four astronauts who have been living at the orbiting laboratory since February.
“We feel like some of the luckiest people in the world,” Kutryk said ahead of the launch.
This was the 13th crew launched by SpaceX for NASA, not counting 2020s test flight. All four embrace their Crew-13 designation that pays homage in their mission patch to Apollo 13. The harrowing 1970 moonshot ended with the astronauts’ safe return.
“We really wanted to honor their legacy, honor their resilience and their grit, and bring a little bit of that with us,” Watkins said. She and her crewmates rode to the pad in black Teslas bearing plates that read “Lucky 13.”
Kutryk will become the fourth man to become a father while orbiting Earth. Wife Heather is due to give birth to their third child in late November. The Canadian Space Agency promises plenty of support for the entire family when the big day comes.
“A lot of life-changing things can happen over six months,” NASA manager Dana Weigel said on the eve of liftoff, noting that the space agency will do its best to keep Kutryk looped in to his family.
In 2004, NASA provided a radio link between space station astronaut Mike Fincke and his wife’s delivery room during the birth of their daughter. Five years later, Randy Bresnik, commander of next year’s Artemis III mission, dialed in to his wife’s hospital from orbit.
The happy news traveled more slowly for Austrian astronaut Franz Viehbock. His daughter was born a few hours after he launched to the Soviet Union’s Mir space station in 1991. He was not informed until the next day.

title: New changes are coming to SNAP, including in Maine
text:
New changes are coming to SNAP, including in Maine
New changes are coming to SNAP, including in Maine
The start of October marks new changes to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, including adjustments here in Maine.
Going forward, the federal government will pay less to administer benefits, meaning that the State of Maine will have to foot more of the bill. While it used to be a 50/50 split between the state and federal government, states will now pick up 75% of the cost.
Per Maine’s DHHS, it will cost the state another $6 million to administer the program. That extra funding has already been allocated in the supplemental budget.
It’s the latest in many changes that have taken course after the Trump administration’s One Big Beautiful Bill became law. According to the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, more than 5 million people no longer use SNAP benefits.
“The goal of these benefits is not to keep people on them,” said Senate Republican Minority Leader Trey Stewart "The goal of these benefits is to help people out that are, you know, down on their luck, or, in a pinch, get them through that season of life, but ultimately help them to be self-sustaining and ideally thriving."
The state says changes this month also include some short-term relief. DHHS says most Mainers will see a little more each month to adjust for inflation.
Another update coming this month includes a new time limit period for Able‑Bodied Adults Without Dependents. The clock resets for certain participants to have three months of SNAP eligibility without meeting certain work requirements.
"SNAP is just one of those things that we call a win-win-win," said Amy Sassi, director of government affairs. "It ends hunger in communities because it allows families to go to the store and buy what they need. It decreases lines at food pantries."
The number of Mainers using SNAP has dropped. Our Get The Facts Data team found that about 13,000 Mainers who relied on the program no longer use it.

title: 2 more squishy toy products recalled due to ‘risk of serious injury or death’
text:
2 more squishy toy products recalled due to ‘risk of serious injury or death’
Two more squishy toy products have been recalled as federal officials warn of the "risk of serious injury or death."
The Consumer Product Safety Commission announced the new recalls Thursday, saying the products' water beads can grow larger than allowed under federal toy safety rules.
Related video above | Are squishy toys safe? Amazon removes some listings
If swallowed, the beads can cause choking or a dangerous intestinal blockage.
Officials said the risks include vomiting, dehydration and, in severe cases, death. No injuries have been reported.
Dozens of similar water bead toys have also been recalled in recent months over the same risk that the beads could expand if swallowed.
Here’s what to look for in the new recalls and how to get a refund.
Squishy Dumpling and Crazy Squib Ball Toys
ABC Trading is recalling about 37,000 toys: Squishy Dumplings, model 3655, and Crazy Squib Balls, model 3984.
The dumplings come in several translucent colors with glitter and water beads, in tan containers shaped like bamboo steamers.
The Crazy Squib Balls also come in several translucent colors and are wrapped in white netting.
Both toys violate the safety standard because their water beads can expand too much, federal officials said, posing a choking or intestinal blockage risk if swallowed.
They were sold nationwide from April through June for 41 cents to $1.25. Click here to view the full recall.
Mochi Malrang Mystery Dumpling Toys
LLK Trading is recalling about 480 Mochi Malrang Mystery Dumpling Toys.
The translucent red dumplings contain glitter and water beads, have cartoon faces and come in tan plastic containers shaped like bamboo steamers.
The packaging says “SOFT and SQUISHY” and “MOCHI MALRANG.” The beads can expand beyond the size allowed under safety rules, creating a risk of choking or intestinal blockage if swallowed.
Stop using the toy and email llktradinginc@gmail.com for a full refund. Click here to view the full recall.

title: Cumberland Fair holds annual apple pie contest
text:
Cumberland Fair holds annual State of Maine Apple Pie Contest
The annual State of Maine Apple Pie Contest was held Thursday at the 154th Cumberland Fair.
Maine's Total Coverage reporter Jim Keithley was asked back again to be one of the celebrity judges.
This year, there were 20 pies in all, with 18 baked by adults and two baked by local youth.
The pies are judged on presentation, recipe style, the flakiest crust and, of course, the apple filling.
This year's winner, Laurette Russell, said she has entered the competition for many years and finally snagged the blue ribbon this time around.

Russell, a New Gloucester resident, said she used red Gravenstein apples in her recipe. She said they are a very early heirloom apple.

title: Nurse bikes 926 miles from Maine to Massachusetts for healthcare worker mental health
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - An ICU nurse and endurance athlete has begun a 926-mile bike ride from the US-Canadian border in Madawaska to Provincetown, Massachusetts, to raise awareness for mental health struggles faced by healthcare workers.
Jenn Walsh, who spent years working at Boston’s Mass General Hospital and is now based in Dallas, started the ride in Aroostook County. She named the journey “The Pursuit.”
Journey begins with setback
The start of the ride was delayed for hours after Walsh experienced mechanical issues with her bike chain. Despite the setback, Walsh’s optimism remained as she continued through Mapleton, more than 60 miles from her starting point.
Walsh’s mother, Andy, is following her daughter closely through the finish.

title: October is pedestrian safety month
Supreme Court denies Arizona’s bid to delay start of takeover of healthcare in state prisons
text:
PHOENIX (AP) — The U.S. Supreme Court has rejected Arizona’s eleventh-hour bid to block the upcoming start of a court-ordered takeover of healthcare operations in its prisons after the state was found to have provided constitutionally inadequate care to incarcerated people and dragged its feet for over a decade in making required improvements. Justice Elena Kagan denied the state’s request Thursday, leaving an outside corrections professional set to take over healthcare management for 25,000 incarcerated people on Oct. 19.
Arizona had asked the courts to delay the takeover while it appealed that decision and the appointment of former Ohio corrections director Annette Chambers-Smith to lead the effort. The state sought the delay from the Supreme Court after lower courts rejected by the request.
Over the past 14 years, Arizona has been dogged by complaints that its prison healthcare system was run shoddily and callously and that it repeatedly failed to improve a system found to have exposed prisoners to harm and preventable deaths.
Under a 2014 settlement, the state pledged to overhaul medical and healthcare services for prisoners but was soon accused of failing to make promised improvements. That led to more than $2 million in contempt-of-court fines and the eventual revocation of the agreement by U.S. District Judge Roslyn Silver, who said corrections officials had shown little interest in making required changes.
After a 2021 trial, Silver ruled against the state, issuing an injunction that required corrections authorities to address the constitutional violations. Earlier this year, she ordered the takeover after concluding the state hadn’t gotten a semblance of compliance with court-ordered changes and the U.S. Constitution after more than a decade of litigation. Silver found that prisoners remained exposed to grave threats of harm and suffering because of systematic deficiencies in their health care.
The Arizona Department of Corrections, Rehabilitation and Re-entry did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Thursday’s decision.
In a statement, Corene Kendrick, an American Civil Liberties Union attorney who represents prisoners in the lawsuit, applauded the court’s refusal to delay the takeover, also known as a receivership. She said Arizona fought accountability at every turn while prisoners suffered. “Today’s decision clears the way for a receiver to do what the state has failed to do for more than a decade,” Kendrick said.
In seeking a delay, Arizona’s attorneys said Silver adopted a drastic takeover remedy without first trying intermediate fixes to speed compliance. They also said the judge hadn’t given the corrections department enough time to continue making progress and argued that the official appointed to run healthcare operations wouldn’t be politically accountable. They said the agency is committed to improving health care in prisons, has made significant progress since 2023 and that the prisoners won’t suffer harm if the start of the takeover were delayed by a few months.
Lawyers for prisoners said the state was minimizing its noncompliance, disputed its claim it had not been given enough time to comply after 14 years of litigation and said Silver had already tried less-intrusive remedies. They also said the state’s proposal of a months-long delay in the takeover “grievously minimizes” the harm prisoners face from the state’s inability to provide adequate care.
Complaints about health care in Arizona’s prisons have spanned both Republican and Democratic administrations.
The lawsuit was filed in 2012 during Republican Gov. Jan Brewer’s administration and continued under Republican Gov. Doug Ducey, when both contempt fines against the state were issued. Under Ryan Thornell, the corrections director in Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs administration, the department has complained that its progress in overhauling health care operations in recent years hasn’t been acknowledged.
The lawsuit over healthcare for incarcerated people covers Arizona’s nine state-run prisons but not the nearly 10,000 Arizona inmates held in private prisons.

title: Locals Already Reaching Out for Heating Assistance
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AROOSTOOK COUNTY, Maine (WAGM) - With this year’s high cost of heating fuel Avec Community Action is seeing a surge of calls from locals looking for heating assistance this season.
The agency says this year they expect 6 to 7 thousand households in Aroostook County to apply for LIHEAP funds. According to the Maine Department of Energy Resources, the average cost of heating oil in northern Maine is now $6.05 a gallon, up from just $3.34 a gallon last September. LIHEAP funds are usually available in mid-to-late November, but the agency says they’re seeing a need now.
Chief Program Officer Heidi Rackliffe says in her 18 years at the agency she’s never seen a need for heating assistance this early on in the season. “Every year seems to be a little bit of a new challenge, a new curveball thrown to us as the heating season approaches. This year, definitely the high costs are on everybody’s mind. Right now, we are having more phone calls than we have ever experienced this early in the season, and I think it’s just sheer panic and worry with the cost of fuel. Fuel tanks are low now and people are already in a position where they’re not able to financially put fuel in their tanks.
This will be the year where people will make determinations of do you get groceries? Do you do this? More so than ever before because the cost of living is just not equaling out to what people are bringing in to be able to afford comfortably to live. I just did a delivery for an individual who’s 87 with cancer right now. That delivery cost was $634 and when you’re looking at an individual who’s on a fixed income, has an income of $1,200 a month. That’s over half of her income for the month.”
Applications for LIHEAP are already open. Eligibility is based on household income. To schedule an appointment to apply, call Avec Community Action at (207)764-3721 or visit their website avecmaine.org.

title: 6 emergency RNs at Aroostook hospital resign amid dwindling morale
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Saturday was Kim Paradis’ last shift at Fort Kent’s Northern Maine Medical Center after working for 24 years at the hospital.
The emergency department registered nurse said she is among a growing number of staff who no longer recognize the hospital they had loved. In the last month and a half, six nurses — five full-time and one per diem — will have left the 13-nurse unit, she said.
“Communication was non-existent between bedside nurses and management administration. We had no say, not even a voice to talk about anything,” Paradis said Thursday. “Our manager was no longer our manager, and we were never told why when she was gone. The only time administration talked to us was because there was going to be a negative outcome for us.”
Hospital officials said that communication did change, as required by federal law, once the RNs voted to join the Maine State Nurses Association.
“The law limits what management can say to employees during a union campaign and, after employees vote to be represented by a union, management is generally prohibited from discussing wages, hours and working conditions directly with the represented RNs,” Pam Sime, hospital spokeswoman said.
The union and management ratified the long-negotiated three-year union contract in May.
The six emergency department registered nurses who resigned were represented by the Maine State Nurses Association and National Nurses Organizing Committee. Their resignations were first reported by The Maine Monitor.
Their departures were for multiple reasons, Sime said.
Two RN’s left for promotional opportunities into leadership positions at other facilities, one left to become a travel RN, one left to move out of state, one was a per diem RN used intermittently as needed, three of these RN’s asked to remain in a per diem status and/or applied for other positions within the hospital, she said.
“The ER remains staffed with fully qualified staff including RNs,” Sime added.
The nurses bargaining unit and hospital administrators have been battling over issues for the past two years at both the Fort Kent facility and Houlton Regional Hospital, which fall under the same management team. As contract negotiations appeared to drag on, especially related to emergency department staffing and patient safety concerns, several nurses expressed frustrations with leadership during multiple strikes and other public actions.
The critical access 25-bed hospital’s emergency department treats approximately 7,000 patients annually, averaging 19 patient visits per day. The issues for the nurses who left involved what they saw as the hospital’s lack of concern for patients and staff, Paradis said, adding that they were also concerned about the hospital’s decision to no longer staff a clerk for the 11 p.m. to 7 a.m. night shift.
On average, the hospital treats one to two patients during this time period and, without the clerk, there are still two registered nurses, one physician, one physician assistant and a security guard working, according to Sime.
The hospital regularly monitors patient volumes, quality indicators, and patient experience measures to ensure the emergency department continues to meet the healthcare needs of the community, she said.
When there are unexpected staffing shortages, the hospital hires experienced travel registered nurses to maintain coverage while recruiting qualified staff, Sime said.
According to Paradis, the discontent started when they filed to unionize in 2024.
“Things just got worse after that,” she said.
Paradis was one of the people on the bargaining committee and she became a target, she said.
“It just all went down after that and it wasn’t about the patients anymore,” she said. “That was the whole reason I became a nurse, to help people in my community. The environment was no longer conducive to that. I just couldn’t work with that anymore. It wasn’t going to be OK.”

title: Heat-trapping gas once frozen in Arctic ground is slowly leaking, warming the planet
text:
Heat-trapping gas once frozen in Arctic ground is slowly leaking and warming the planet
As Ted Schuur stepped along the edges of Smith Lake, a bubble surfaced from the muck underfoot. And then another.
Related video above: Trump administration lowers fuel efficiency standards in effort to lower car prices
They are bubbles of methane, a potent heat-trapping gas made from decomposing plants and animals that had once been stuck in Alaska's frigid permafrost. But that frozen ground is thawing because the Arctic is warming four times faster than the rest of the globe. For thousands of years, that frozen ground stored dead plants and animals, but the accelerating thaw is allowing them to decay into methane and carbon dioxide.
"Once you start leaking this carbon out, there’s so much in the ground that it’s not going to shut off," said Schuur, an ecologist at Northern Arizona University, calling it one of climate change's scary tipping points. "Essentially every year is setting a permafrost record."
There is three times as much carbon still frozen in permafrost than what is now in the air, but all over the Arctic, those heat-trapping gases are escaping into the atmosphere. Their release adds to what is already in the air from humanity's burning of coal, oil and natural gas, changing the delicate balance of how a warming world deals with the buildup of heat-trapping carbon, Schuur said.
Permafrost is ground that stays frozen — below 32 degrees Fahrenheit (zero degrees Celsius) — for at least two years and often for centuries and even millennia. That frozen ground — found in Alaska, Canada, Siberia, Antarctica and high mountain elevations elsewhere — has special advantages: trapping decaying matter, keeping it from turning into greenhouse gases, and just being firm enough for communities and industries to build their lives upon.
But warming is undercutting that.
Two different studies project that by the end of this century, those previously trapped gases in permafrost will add nearly half a degree of warming (about a quarter-degree Celsius) in addition to warming from the burning of fossil fuels. Over that time period, that will warm the Earth about as much as a major industrialized country like the United States or the whole of Europe, scientists said.
A sleeping giant awakens
"The permafrost system is really like a sleeping giant," said Gustaf Hugelius, a permafrost expert at Stockholm University.
For thousands of years, when the climate was somewhat stable, the Arctic helped Earth's delicate carbon cycle by acting as a sink. That means plants in the cold areas used to pull some heat-trapping gas out of the air and capture it in the frozen ground, with the Arctic essentially withdrawing more carbon from the air than it added, benefiting the entire globe. A few years ago, warming caused that balance to shift so that once-frozen ground is venting more heat-trapping gases than it takes in. Instead of reducing climate change, the Arctic is now adding to the problem, said Columbia University ecologist Duncan Menge.
Permafrost thaw, along with other "warming-induced emissions" from fires and changes to wetlands and lakes, is likely to increase warming by 20% by the end of the century, according to a September study co-authored by Arctic ecologist Sue Natali of the Woodwell Climate Research Center.
It may be a small amount, not worthy of scenarios of doom, but it’s something "that we’re going to have to deal with" on top of everything else, said University of Victoria climate scientist Andrew Weaver, who first calculated the half-a-degree of expected permafrost warming in a 2012 study.
What is troublesome is that when politicians and scientists talk about future warming, they are usually not accounting for the extra greenhouse gases from permafrost thawing, said Natali and Hugelius. So while the U.N. says without policy changes the world will warm 2.6 degrees C (4.7 degrees F) above preindustrial times by the end of the century, it leaves out a few tenths of a degree from thawing permafrost, they said.
A ground not so firm anymore
Thawing permafrost is not just messing with the planet's carbon balance; it's destabilizing the very land underfoot, making once-rigid ground collapse and sink, Natali said.
Frozen ground that is no longer firm became deadly this summer. Flooding in Nepal killed more than 1,000 people after part of a glacier collapsed, which happened after a heat wave that set records for the location and time of year, according to Berkeley Earth climate scientist Robert Rohde.
Ground that is solidly frozen holds up mountains and skyscrapers, but once the permafrost thaws, it’s no longer strong enough. That was likely one of several still-to-be-determined factors in the Nepal disaster, said George Washington University permafrost scientist Dmitry Streletskiy, lead author of an August study that found significant permafrost thawing in most of the Northern Hemisphere.
Permafrost in Alaska and other Arctic areas has long supported homes, roads and pipelines, but it’s no longer so reliable. For example, in Galbraith on Alaska’s North Slope, a recently formed 10-foot (3-meter) deep, crater-like hole was visible during a recent foray by scientists. These holes, known as slumps, occur when ice melts and the land collapses, releasing methane, Natali said. A Woodwell team has identified more than 40,000 of these slumps across the Arctic using satellites, according to scientist Kyle Arndt.
University of Alaska Fairbanks geophysicist Vladimir Romanovsky said when he first started studying permafrost in the 1970s, "everybody believed permafrost was very stable. People thought it was forever."
Not anymore, he said.
"It took some thousands and tens of thousands of years to sequester this carbon into permafrost," Romanovsky said. "You need a new ice age to put back this ice into the ground."
A time capsule to the last ice age is visible under a Fairbanks hill where the U.S. Army drilled a massive permafrost research tunnel. Artificially cooled and used for training, the tunnel's icy walls are dotted with bones of bison and mammoths, producing a sewage-like odor that vividly illustrates where the Arctic methane comes from.
"Every time I go there, I'm reminded of the magnitude of the problem. You smell it. You see it. You feel it all around you," Natali said. "You see how deep the ice is and just how the carbon is buried, and then when you go on top, and you see these large thaw features. ... This isn't a problem of 100 years from now. This is a problem of right now."

title: With youth gun violence plaguing Lewiston, the city will push for legislative reform
text:
Key Takeaways Key Takeaways are written by Maine Trust staff and highlight the most important points of this article so you can get the gist at a glance.
- The city’s Community Engagement and Accountability initiative has seen success with enforcement, but city officials say a lack of follow-through in the juvenile justice system means repeat offenders will continue to cycle back onto the city’s streets.
- City officials are seeking eight reforms to Maine’s juvenile justice system to combat rising youth gun violence and other crimes. Those include broader detention authority, expanded treatment for repeat offenders, and clarification or elimination of a rule called “chronological immunity” that often finds a juvenile incompetent to stand trial.
LEWISTON — As the city experiences an uptick in youth crime driven by teenage repeat offenders, officials will push the next Legislature to make reforms to the juvenile justice system.
City officials say police have increased their rates of solved crimes to nearly double the national average since the city implemented its Community Engagement and Accountability initiative. But, they say, the courts are not following through with accountability.
“We need to stop the repeated cycle and revolving door of juveniles being apprehended, released and apprehended again by ensuring meaningful accountability and intervention before another crime is committed,” City Administrator Bryan Kaenrath said.
Kaenrath said as part of its initiative the city is asking lawmakers to consider an eight-part reform plan for juvenile justice codes aimed at pulling the reins on repeat offenders revolving through the system. The reforms would, he said, hopefully lead to keeping repeat offenders detained, providing treatment while juveniles are in custody and changing competency procedures so juveniles can be held accountable.
Specifically, the reforms would:
- Give judges and Juvenile Community Corrections Officers more discretion in detaining repeat offenders.
- Expand programming at Long Creek Youth Development Center in South Portland.
- Give juvenile corrections officers more detention authority.
- Give District Attorneys more of a role in early releases.
- Require treatment for serious juvenile offenses.
- Put more responsibility on DHHS for court-ordered services.
- Create a competency restoration program.
- Change juvenile competency standards, namely clarifying or eliminating “chronological immunity” as a basis for finding a juvenile incompetent to stand trial.
Thus far this year in Lewiston, there have been 35 gun violence incidents involving 22 juveniles, with 11 of those juveniles involved in at least two incidents. Those cases led to 24 juvenile arrests and 67 seized firearms.
Police say the same teens are violating the law over and over again.
Late last month, two 15-year-olds were arrested in connection with gunshots fired near Horton and Ash streets, both of whom were on conditions of release for prior gun-related offenses. One had more than 70 police involvements in the past two years, police said.
Just two days prior, police arrested a 13-year-old on a gun charge and a 16-year-old on a drug charge. Both were repeat offenders, police said.
Over the past six weeks, police have conducted 96 hours of dedicated initiative patrols, collected over 900 community contacts, carried out 125 property site checks and conducted about 35 interviews, according to a city news release.
“Community policing is about building relationships and we’ve already seen positive progress,” Lewiston Mayor Carl Sheline said. “I’ve heard from officers on the ground that residents are starting to reach out to them while on patrol with helpful tips and information. Our officers absolutely care about Lewiston and neighbors are taking notice. Working together, we can keep our city safe.”
Police had 18 assists to patrol, carried out numerous arrests and had more than 75 residents engage them in conversation and with tips at their Mobile Command Unit. Police confirmed through initiative details what they have known for some time.
“We’re not talking about someone who’s just getting in trouble with the police once or twice,” Kaenrath said. “The case that the police department cited … is one teenager who’s had 70 contacts with the police in the last two years. So, we’re (talking about youths) who are back out in the same environment in a matter of days or weeks.”
Kaenrath, a former state legislator, said the city has already met with its legislative delegation about the proposals and plans to find broader support for the measures ahead of the Legislature’s next session in January.
“The legislative piece, we’re a little bit still early on … because bill submission is not until December,” Kaenrath said. “We want to be talking with other community partners and organizations (like) the Maine Prosecutors Association, the Maine Chiefs of Police Association, and even hoping to get some meetings with legislative leadership in Augusta to really talk about the situation Lewiston is in.”

title: Woman killed in Plymouth collision
text:
A woman died Wednesday evening after a collision in Plymouth.
A 67-year-old man was driving a sedan east on Moosehead Trail about 6:39 p.m. when he collided with a westbound pickup truck driven by a 69-year-old man, according to the Penobscot County Sheriff’s Office.
The crash sent both vehicles off the road and into Plymouth Pond, the sheriff’s office said.
The sedan’s driver was taken to the hospital with serious but not life-threatening injuries. His passenger, a 68-year-old woman, succumbed to her injuries at the hospital.
The pickup truck’s driver was taken to the hospital with injuries not considered life-threatening.
The crash remains under investigation.

title: Mortgage rate forecast: October 2026
text:
Mortgage rate forecast: October 2026
Mortgage rates surged in September, and they’ve reached their highest point since May 2024. The run-up in rates has left many consumers feeling less than eager to dive into the housing market.
The war in Iran sent oil prices soaring in recent months. Higher energy prices translate to both higher inflation and rising 10-year Treasury yields. And both of those things exert upward pressure on mortgage rates.
As of Sept. 30, the average 30-year mortgage rate was 7.38%, according to Bankrate’s weekly lender survey.
“With inflation still running well above target and no sustained relief from lower oil prices, the path of least resistance for rates remains higher,” says Nicole Rueth, senior vice president at CrossCountry Mortgage.
Will mortgage interest rates go down?
Most housing economists say mortgage rates are likely to stay elevated. The Mortgage Bankers Association and Fannie Mae both call for rates to stay near 7% for the rest of 2026 — although their latest forecasts were issued before the late September jump in mortgage rates and Treasury yields.
Mortgage rates are nothing if not volatile, though, and other factors are pushing them higher — especially the war in Iran.
Current mortgage rate trends
The median national home price clocked in at $429,100 in August, up 1.6% from a year earlier, according to the National Association of Realtors. But home sales volumes remain muted by the recent spike in mortgage rates.
“For the housing market, this increase in mortgage rates acts as a significant headwind,” says Lisa Sturtevant, chief economist at Bright MLS. “Sellers are having to adjust their pricing expectations and offer more concessions to buyers.”
Bankrate’s weekly mortgage rate averages differ slightly from the statistics reported by Freddie Mac, the government-sponsored enterprise that buys mortgages and packages them as securities. Bankrate’s rates tend to be higher because they include origination points and other costs, while Freddie Mac removes those figures and reports them separately. However, both Bankrate and Freddie Mac report similar overall trends in mortgage rates.

What to do if you’re getting a mortgage this year
- Shop around. With rates elevated, it’s more important than ever to shop around for a mortgage. Bankrate’s Hidden Homeownership Tax research found that 87% of Americans overpaid for their home loans in 2025 because they settled for the first offer they got. For the typical borrower, that added up to $3,343 in extra costs each year. The stakes are only higher when mortgage rates are rising quickly.
- Improve your credit score. The lowest mortgage rates go to borrowers with the highest credit scores, usually at least 780. A lower credit score won’t prevent you from getting a loan, but it can make all the difference between getting the best possible rate and more costly borrowing terms.
- Save up for a bigger down payment. Putting more money down upfront can help you obtain a lower mortgage rate, and if you put down at least 20% of the purchase price, you’ll avoid mortgage insurance, which adds costs to your loan. If you’re a first-time homebuyer and can’t cover a 20% down payment, there are loans, grants and programs that can help. Eligibility requirements vary by program but often depend on factors like your income.
- Understand your debt-to-income ratio. Your DTI ratio compares how much money you owe to how much money you make, specifically your total monthly debt payments against your gross monthly income. Not sure how to figure out your DTI ratio? Bankrate has a calculator for that.
Frequently asked questions
-  How are mortgage rates determined? Mortgage rates aren’t set by any one entity; they come from a complex mix of economic factors. Lenders typically set their rates based on the return they need to make a profit after accounting for risks and costs. The Federal Reserve gets a lot of attention, but it doesn’t directly set mortgage rates, either. The closest proxy for mortgage rates is the 10-year Treasury yield: Historically, the typical 30-year mortgage rate has been about 2 percentage points higher than the 10-year Treasury yield. But since the pandemic, that spread has been closer to 3 percentage points.
-  When should I refinance my mortgage? Deciding when to refinance is based on many factors. If rates have fallen since you took out your mortgage, refinancing might make sense. A refi can also be a good idea if you’ve improved your credit score and could lock in a lower rate.

title: Better planning could have headed off Lewiston hospital mess
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Douglas Rooks has been a Maine editor and columnist for 41 years. His biography of Gov. Ken Curtis, “Transformational,” is now available. He welcomes comment at [email protected].
The vote last week by Central Maine Medical Center nurses in Lewiston to unionize says a good deal about organizing prospects in the state, but even more about the mismanagement of Maine hospitals.
Driven by the perverse incentives of fee-for-service reimbursement, hospitals compete for a larger share of the revenue pie, ignoring opportunities for rational consolidation as care becomes increasingly specialized and high-tech.
The situation at CMMC, which has been under severe financial stress, has all the makings of a train wreck. Last year, Prime Healthcare of California, a for-profit chain, agreed to buy CMMC and formed a nonprofit subsidiary to make the acquisition — a maneuver that fooled no one. Nonetheless, the state issued a Certificate of Need approving the sale, in which Prime agreed to maintain designated staffing levels, invest in new services and — somehow — improve the financial balance sheet.
The immediate response by hospital employees? Nearly 20% of the staff resigned. Earlier this year, surgeries were briefly suspended and transferred elsewhere when the state found inadequate operating room sterilization.
The nurses’ campaign then came as no surprise — though hospital management’s response did. Just days before the union vote, Prime fired or suspended 20 nurses, most of them involved in the organizing drive, allegedly for neglecting their duties. Prime has employed similar union-busting tactics elsewhere, but it’s unprecedented in Maine hospitals.
The move drew a stern rebuke from Gov. Janet Mills, writing to Prime, “I strongly urge you to immediately reinstate every nurse who has been wrongfully fired or suspended.” To date, Prime has not responded — just as MaineHealth’s board in Portland ignored Mills’ plea, and that of the Democratic nominee for governor, Hannah Pingree, to delay closing the birthing center at Miles Memorial in Damariscotta, the 12th such closure statewide in recent years.
CMMC nurses voted 204-21 in favor of a union, a rate of 91% It followed a similarly successful effort to organize at Maine Medical Center in 2021 by the Maine Nurses Association, affiliated with National Nurses United, the third such attempt. Nurses at Northern Light Eastern Maine Medical Center in Bangor have had a union since 1976; labor will now have a seat at the management table in three of the state’s largest hospitals.
But the union campaigns reflect a larger reality — an apparent inability to adjust the state’s hospital structure to reflect changing demands for care within a community structure, as opposed to the often debilitating competition for patients and revenue.
Lewiston provides a case in point. Thirty years ago, Central Maine and St. Mary’s both had similar number of beds and budgets, and it was already clear that consolidation should be considered. Instead, CMMC embarked on an unwise expansion plan that led to the current crisis.
It briefly owned Parkview Hospital in Brunswick, which was then engaged in a highly public war of words with Mid Coast, itself a merger of hospitals in Brunswick and Bath, that ended only with Parkview’s bankruptcy. When Mid Coast took over operations, it declined to adjust or reduce any services and, overextended, had to sell to MaineHealth, which from its Portland headquarters now controls the majority of the state’s hospital services.
Or consider Waterville, where Inland, the state’s only osteopathic hospital, was closed by Northern Light last year. It’s possible it could have been saved. When the state approved the merger of Waterville’s other hospital, Mid Maine, with Augusta on the new MaineGeneral campus, it curiously allowed Waterville’s Thayer Hospital to retain a 24-hour ER, even though the facility downsized to outpatient care. Two emergency rooms in one small market vastly exceeded demand, with Inland the casualty.
Just as MaineHealth controls the majority of the state’s hospitals, under the Affordable Care Act federal and state governments have assumed the bulk of healthcare spending, well over half. This requires a larger state role in planning, and if necessary directing, the provision of services so patients and staff are protected, not forced out.
In the 1980s, the Maine Health Care Finance Authority regulated hospital charges, moderating rate increases while maintaining care standards, but was later abolished. Reviving it, while reviewing mergers and takeovers and offering alternatives, would be a good first step. The Prime Healthcare fiasco is exactly what the state must avoid repeating.
A national healthcare system, rising to prominence in this year’s campaigns, is ultimately the solution to many of our woes. The state can play an important role, however, and a new administration is the ideal place to start.

title: Sen. Susan Collins says her Maine home was recently egged
text:
Sen. Susan Collins says her home in Bangor was recently egged
U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, said her home in Bangor was egged about a week before the doors to her Biddeford office were vandalized.
Collins spoke about the incident at her Bangor home in an interview with WVOM that aired Tuesday.
"About a week ago, someone threw eggs all over our garage door, the front porch, window (and) front door," Collins said.
Collins said her husband, Tom Daffron, discovered the vandalism when he got up to go walk their dog.
"He said, 'Susan, come out here. You won't believe this.' And sure enough, the garage door was stained with broken eggs and eggshells on the ground," Collins said. "It was our dog, Pepper, who noticed, because she went over to start to lick it, that there were eggs that had been thrown at our front door, our window and our porch."
"That's just so unacceptable," the senator added. "I think it shows, unfortunately, the level that politics — even in the great state of Maine — have degenerated to."
On Monday, State Sen. Matt Harrington shared a photo showing that a vulgar insult about Collins and President Donald Trump had been spray-painted on the front doors to the senator's field office at 160 Main St. in Biddeford.
"Vandalism is unacceptable. Senator Collins and her staff will not be intimidated," Collins' chief of staff, Katie Brown, said in a statement regarding the Biddeford incident. "Our Biddeford constituent service office remains open, and we will continue serving the people of Maine."
On Thursday, Brown shared another statement with Maine's Total Coverage regarding the egging at Collins' Bangor home.
"This is another example of harassment against Senator Collins," Brown said. "Vandalism is unacceptable, and we will not be intimidated."
Collins is seeking her sixth term in the U.S. Senate, something no senator from Maine has done before. The Republican is facing a challenge from Democratic candidate Troy Jackson, the former president of the Maine Senate. There are six declared write-in candidates in the Senate race: unaffiliated candidate Brent Andrews, Democrat Sigrid Ann Olson, independent Gina Oswald, Faith in Humanity candidate Joseph Steinberger, unenrolled candidate Michael Turcotte and Democrat Ashley Webb.

title: Hurricane Rachel strengthens to a Category 3 storm off Mexico’s Pacific Coast
text:
MEXICO CITY (AP) — Hurricane Rachel has been upgraded to a Category 3 storm off Mexico’s Pacific coast as northern Mexico and parts of the U.S. Southwest were reeling from flooding and damage from the remnants of Hurricane Polo earlier this week.
The storm, located about 235 miles (380 kilometers) south off the southern tip of Baja California, was continuing west-northwest at 3 mph (6 kph) and expected to strengthen Friday before weakening this weekend, according to the National Hurricane Center.
The maximum sustained winds were 120 miles per hour (193 kph) as of Thursday evening. Rachel’s swells are expected to generate life-threatening surf and rip-current conditions off Mexico’s coast, the NHC warned.
Mexican authorities said Thursday they remain on alert because of forecasts of very heavy rain in the states of Baja California Sur, Sinaloa, and Jalisco, and the possibility of landslides, rising river levels, overflowing rivers and flooding in low-lying areas.
On Wednesday night, the U.S. Embassy in Mexico warned U.S. citizens in Cabos San Lucas, a popular vacation destination for Americans, of beach and port closures and deadly rip currents.
The Pacific has seen an unusually busy hurricane season, which experts have attributed to El Niño, which has fueled crippling droughts in Mexico and Central America and floods in other parts of the region. In the Pacific, it has resulted in warmer waters and wind patterns that act as fodder for hurricanes. Tropical Storm Nolo continued its northwest approach away from Hawaii on Thursday, though the National Weather Service said it could strengthen into a hurricane by the weekend.
Northern Mexico still reeling from Polo
Parts of northern Mexico were still reeling from floods and wider destruction left by Polo. Hundreds of people remained displaced or had their homes destroyed, and at least 13 municipalities remained flooded Thursday night, according to local authorities.
Lucía Vegas, who lives in the small town of Bacabachi in the border state of Sonora, said it was a miracle she survived severe flooding as it swept through her community. She, her husband and three children were left homeless.
Vegas said she and her family managed to survive thanks to their dog. In the middle of the night, as the floodwaters were rising, the dog woke her by shaking water off herself, giving the family enough time to climb a ladder onto the roof of their home just minutes before it was completely flooded.
“Right now, we have been left with nothing,” the 39-year-old woman said through tears.
Storm remnants drench central U.S.
Areas in Texas, Nebraska, Missouri and Iowa were still under flood watch Thursday afternoon as storm remnants continued to batter the region, flooding streets and neighborhoods and setting off water rescues.
Wednesday was the wettest day on record for Lincoln, Nebraska, which received 6.1 inches of rainfall, according to the University of Nebraska-Lincoln Climate Office.
In Omaha, which received 4.7 inches of rain Wednesday, the fire department said it responded to 80 water rescues over a three-hour period ending early Thursday. Some floodwaters reached depths of 8 feet. Schools remained open. But many buses never made it out of flooded parking lots, prompting officials to ask parents to transport their students to school.
San Antonio, Texas, was under a flash-flood warning through Thursday evening, and the city urged residents to avoid unnecessary travel. More than 19,000 residents across the state were without power Thursday afternoon, according to PowerOutage.us. Videos posted on social media showed floodwaters in Texas creating waves along Interstate 35 in Denton.
In Chicago, a wastewater treatment and stormwater management utility urged residents to conserve water use to prevent flooding and stormwater backup.
“We encourage everyone to conserve water when possible to create more capacity in our systems,” utility President Kari K. Steele said in a statement Wednesday.
In Kansas, Gov. Laura Kelly issued an emergency proclamation on Wednesday ahead of the storms that allows state resources to assist first responders in hard-hit communities.
___
Raza reported from Sioux Falls, South Dakota, and Castellón reported from Bacabachi, Mexico. Associated Press writer John Raby in Cross Lanes, West Virginia, contributed to this report.
