title: Older Mainers leaning toward Susan Collins in US Senate race, AARP poll shows
text:
A new battleground poll released by the AARP shows Democrat Troy Jackson with a narrow lead over Republican Susan Collins in Maine’s U.S. Senate race.
Jackson holds a 3 percentage point lead over Collins, 50% to 47%, which is within the survey’s margin of error of 3.1%.
But Jackson is trailing Collins among an important segment of Maine’s electorate — voters over 50 who are more likely to split their tickets than vote along party lines.
And Jackson is underperforming fellow Democrat Hannah Pingree, who holds a 13 percentage point lead over Republican Bobby Charles, 52% to 39%, in the governor’s race. Independent Rick Bennett drew 6%.
The survey of 982 likely voters was conducted from Sept. 20-22 by Fabrizio Ward and Impact Research. It offers insight into how older Mainers, who are among the most reliable voters in the state, are leaning in Maine’s closely watched race between Collins and Jackson.
The survey is further evidence that Collins remains a formidable opponent in a midterm cycle that is expected to be difficult for Republicans nationally, with President Donald Trump’s approval ratings at historic lows.
The AARP poll found that 61% of respondents disapproved of Trump’s job performance, while 37% approved. And 53% preferred Democrats on the generic congressional ballot, compared to the 43% for Republicans.
Maine’s older voters, Fabrizio Ward partner Bob Ward said, are “highly engaged. They’re paying attention and they’re looking for candidates who understand the issues that affect their daily lives.”
The top issue for all voters surveyed was affordability (44%). It was cited as the top issue by 33% of voters 50 and older, who said their main concerns were the price of gas and groceries.
Among older voters, 93% said they would be more likely to vote for a candidate that makes sure workers get the Social Security benefits they earned, 85% for someone who would protect the program from cuts and oppose increasing the retirement age, and 84% for someone who would lower the cost of healthcare and prescription drugs.
The poll found that voters 50 and older, who the AARP said comprised 60% or more of turnout in the last two federal election cycles, are breaking toward Collins and Pingree.
Collins holds a 9-point advantage among these older voters, about 20% of whom planned to split their tickets. Among these swing voters, Collins holds a 53-point advantage, while Pingree holds a 28-point advantage over Charles.
Bennett, meanwhile, drew 32% support among older swing voters in the governor’s race.
“It just speaks to how Sen. Collins is a different kind of Republican,” Ward said. “(She) maintains her base, but also reaches out to the center. This is going to be a really close race.”
Jackson holds a roughly two point lead over Collins, according to polling averages from the election website FiftyPlusOne.
A New York Times/Portland Press Herald/Siena poll conducted around the same time as the AARP’s survey found Collins with a 3 point lead over Jackson, 49% to 46%, which was also within the margin of error of +/- 4.9%.
That poll also found swing voters breaking toward Collins, including 8% of respondents that identified as Democrats.
The five-term Republican drew 13% support from people saying they wanted Democrats to won control the Senate, and 12% from people who voted for Democrat Kamala Harris for president in 2024.
The survey also found that Collins held a commanding leading among respondents aged 45-64. She led Jackson among that group 57% to 38%. But they practically split the 65 and over vote, with Jackson getting 48% to Collins’s 47%.
Both the NYT/Press Herald/ Siena and AARP polls were conducted before ProPublica reported that the Department of Justice and Federal Bureau of Investigation had been gearing up for bribery and corruption probe aimed at determining whether Collins was steering federal contracts to a defense contractor in exchange for political donations. That effort was dropped when Trump took office in 2025.
Collins has “vigorously” denied the allegations.

title: Three Maine football storylines to follow against Sacred Heart
text:
One step forward, two steps back. That’s been the story of the University of Maine football team this season, and the Black Bears definitely went backwards Saturday in a 43-17 loss at Elon.
After a winless September, Maine (1-4, 1-1 Coastal Athletic Association) begins its October slate by hosting Sacred Heart (1-3, 1-1) at 3:30 p.m. Saturday (FloSports). Here are three storylines as the Black Bears look to snap a four-game losing streak.
Could change be coming at QB?
Starting quarterback Eddie Buehler struggled against Elon, completing 14 of 35 passes for just 88 yards. Caden Drezek, a junior, got his first action of the season in the fourth quarter, throwing a touchdown pass to Kevin Jackson to cap a 75-yard drive.
Maine coach Jordan Stevens was adamant that he never considered a QB change after Buehler’s less-than-stellar outing against Merrimack. But in Monday’s CAA news conference, Stevens was noncommittal when asked if Buehler would start.
“We’re just looking at that during the week here,” Stevens said.
Stay tuned.
Special teams, special teams, special teams
Without context, the total yardage in Maine’s most recent loss (Elon 376, Maine 315) doesn’t look all that bad. So, why the lopsided defeat? It’s because the Black Bears gave the Phoenix short fields, primarily via special teams miscues.
Elon blocked two punts in the first quarter, the first leading to a field goal and the second resulting in a safety. A 24-yard Elon punt return in the third quarter put the Phoenix at Maine’s 43, leading to a touchdown, and a muffed punt by the Black Bears late in that quarter resulted in another Elon field goal.
Throw in a 31-yard Elon touchdown drive after Maine turned it over on downs in the fourth quarter, and you see that the Phoenix offense didn’t have to do much to score. Sacred Heart (18.8 points per game) hasn’t lit up the scoreboard this year, but if Maine doesn’t clean up its special teams, that won’t matter.
A spark in the run game?
It wasn’t all bad news for Maine against Elon. After rushing for just 174 yards on 93 carries — 1.9 yards per carry — in three games since its season-opening win, the Black Bears rushed for 167 yards on 34 carries against Elon.
Can Maine repeat that? Well, consider that New Hampshire, which had averaged just 2.6 yards per carry prior to last week’s game at Sacred Heart, rushed for 181 yards on 29 carries (6.2 average) against the Pioneers. Perhaps the Black Bears can have similar success.

title: Girl, 11, will learn her fate in trial over brutal rape and assault of a 5-year-old
text:
CLEVELAND (WOIO/Gray News) - The trial for the 11-year-old girl accused in the brutal rape and assault of a 5-year-old girl wrapped up in Cuyahoga County Juvenile Court Wednesday afternoon.
Judge Kristin Sweeney will release her decision on Friday.
What happened
Prosecutors said the 11-year-old, addressed as M.H. in court, and a now 10-year-old boy attacked the girl in a field in Cleveland on Sept. 13, 2025.
The victim’s clothes were removed, according to testimony, and she was strangled with her own shirt.
The 10-year-old boy, addressed as M.B. during the trial, pleaded guilty Monday to attempted rape and felonious assault.
He testified against the 11-year-old girl Wednesday and described what he claims M.H. said while strangling the victim with a shirt.
“This is what bad girls get for following people,” said M.B.
He says M.H. also ordered him not to tell anyone about what happened.
“How were you feeling when she told you that?” asked the prosecution. “Scared,” said M.B.
He is scheduled to be back in court on Nov. 20 and could face probation or placement in a residential treatment facility.
Victim’s mom takes the stand
On Tuesday, the mom of the victim took the stand and testified that her daughter spent several weeks in the hospital following the attack.
She also described the emotional toll the attack has had on her little girl.
“When we left the hospital, she went through severe behavioral changes. She kept saying she’s not pretty anymore. She kept saying earth is a bad place,” said the mom.
Previous coverage:
- Children charged in brutal attack on 5-year-old Cleveland girl to undergo competency restoration
- Cleveland police connect kid suspects to beating; mother describes 5-year-old as ‘unrecognizable’
- Prosecutors charge 2 children, 9 and 10, in brutal attack on 5-year-old Cleveland girl
Case background
The Cleveland Division of Police Sex Crimes and Child Abuse Unit investigated the case.
In October 2025, prosecutors charged the 11-year-old girl and then nine-year-old boy with attempted murder, rape, felonious assault, kidnapping and strangulation.
On April 1, Judge Sweeney ordered the two children to undergo competency restoration before they could stand trial.
According to court records, a change in the 11-year-old’s placement was necessary to get a true assessment of her competency.
When a placement was not found, prosecutors requested she be held in the detention center during the restoration process.
The court said returning to her home was not in her best interest, and the Court Diagnostics Clinic provided competency restoration services at the detention center.
Both children were previously held on home detention.
After a period of court-ordered rehabilitation, the children were later found competent to stand trial.

title: Woman told Cornell police 2 years ago she was 100% confident she was raped, transcript shows
text:
ITHACA, N.Y. (AP) - A woman who filed a lawsuit saying she was sexually assaulted by seven men at a Cornell University fraternity house told police weeks after the incident that she could “say with 100% confidence I was raped,” according to a report by CBS New York, which said it obtained a transcript of her interview with investigators.
The transcript, which has not been publicly released, raises new questions surrounding the local district attorney’s decision not to prosecute anyone at the time.
In recent days, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten has maintained the woman’s first account to police didn’t include allegations that she was drugged, incapacitated beyond the ability to consent, or forced into sex. Yet, he also said he had reopened the investigation based on new information in the woman’s lawsuit, which was filed this month.
Cornell has agreed to bring in outside lawyers to independently investigate how the university handled the woman’s allegations, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul announced Wednesday.
The woman initially went to Cornell’s campus police about three weeks after the alleged attack that began on Oct. 19, 2024, then went back on Nov. 14 and 15, 2024, to be interviewed.
“Yes. It was coercion, yes,” she told a campus police officer, according to the transcript obtained by CBS. According to CBS News, she said she was “completely and totally incapacitated” before some of the sexual abuse.
The woman acknowledged she had been drinking alcohol and used drugs the night she visited the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024, and that she had gaps in her memory.
She also told police she was comfortable with an initial sexual encounter with two of the men, but not with what happened later, when other men began to enter the room.
“And then, of course, I was being hit at the same time. Physically hit very, very hard,” she told police, according to the transcript. “I can say with 100% confidence I was raped,” it said she told investigators.
The woman, identified only by the pseudonym Jane Doe in the lawsuit, filed a complaint Sept. 16 saying she was sexually assaulted at the Chi Phi fraternity house after being pressured into snorting ketamine, smoking marijuana and drinking alcohol. She became completely incapacitated while fraternity members were sexually assaulting her, she said.
Van Houten didn’t immediately respond to emails and phone messages from The Associated Press on Wednesday, but he told CBS News he never saw the transcript of the woman’s interview when his office declined to bring charges, and relied instead on a statement written by a campus police officer but signed by the accuser.
Van Houten has released a summary of that statement, with some of her direct quotes included. He has defended his office’s decision not to do additional investigation after the woman first came forward.
“There were no question marks. There was no additional need to find information because we had all of the information that the police collected from Jane Doe through her very detailed, very comprehensive statement that she provided,” Van Houten told CNN earlier this week.
Cornell University first publicly disclosed that it was investigating the woman’s allegations on Nov. 8, 2024, the same day she first went to police. The school sent students an email warning them that a person had reported they had been sexually assaulted at a fraternity house and coerced into consuming drugs. Cornell suspended the Chi Phi fraternity the same day.
In another public statement to students in late November 2024, Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff said campus police were investigating “deeply disturbing allegations of drug abuse and sexual violence” at the fraternity house.
Later, Cornell appointed a task force designed to address sexual assault on campus. But with the district attorney’s decision not to pursue charges and the university’s internal disciplinary investigation shielded from the public, attention on the matter waned.
Cornell said in a statement this week that it supported the decision to reopen the criminal investigation, adding that its own investigation had led to some students being disciplined or expelled. The Chi Phi chapter remains barred from campus, but the university has declined to release more information on discipline for individual students, citing privacy rules.
Earlier this week, Hochul called for a new investigation into the university’s handling of the matter. In a post on social media Wednesday, she said she had spoken with Kotlikoff and he “agreed to bring in outside counsel for an independent investigation.” Cornell confirmed it had agreed but declined additional comment.
“This culture has to stop. And in New York, we’re going to do everything we can to stop it,” Hochul said.

title: Let’s not replay the tragedy of life without vaccinations
text:
I want to share how my family has been affected by vaccines. First, comic relief: when our baby began receiving the recommended shots, I was pleased but mystified by her reaction: she simply smiled at the nurse. Weren’t babies supposed to yell? Each time we returned to the medical office for follow-up vaccines, I witnessed happy interactions between my baby and the nurses. Was our kid normal, I wondered? Finally, a few years later, our child — then a toddler — loudly conveyed her opinion about that sharp “pinch.” Phew.
There are much sadder records in my extended family about a lack of medicines to help beloved siblings, parents and children. For example, before Penicillin was commonly available (in the 1940s) my grandmother’s sister died at age 21 (in 1930) of pneumonia. I’m glad that many other diseases have been controlled thanks to science. Smallpox, typhoid and diphtheria used to terrify communities. My ancestors also feared yellow fever, polio, mumps, measles and tetanus.
Let’s not replay those tragedies. Instead, let’s ensure that everyone gets to learn about the best medications available. My ancestors would have loved access to such medicines.
Mariana Tupper
Falmouth

title: Paul LePage touts ties to Donald Trump while hedging on tariffs, Iran and ICE
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Former Gov. Paul LePage promised in a Thursday debate that he could get President Donald Trump’s ear, voicing disagreements with the president on tariffs, immigration and the Iran war but opposing steps Congress could take to rein him in.
The Republican faced State Auditor Matt Dunlap, a Democrat, in the first of their two debates in the race for Maine’s open 2nd Congressional District. The WMTW debate showed LePage managing a delicate balance as the favorite in a seat Trump has won three times.
Trump carried the 2nd District by 9 points in 2024. But his approval rating in Maine was just 37% in an AARP poll released Thursday. The Iran war has helped push heating oil to above $6 per gallon heading into winter, an ominous figure for the state most reliant on that fuel source.
Dunlap went after the administration on Iran, immigration enforcement and Medicaid, but he largely avoided attacking Trump directly. Instead, he framed Congress as a check on the White House and focused on costs, a pitch aimed at district voters who still back the president.
“The job of Congress is to provide oversight of the executive branch,” Dunlap said.
When asked by moderator Jon Chrisos whether he had a direct line to the president, LePage noted that he worked with Trump as governor. During that time, he was one of Trump’s early endorsers and called himself “Donald Trump before Donald Trump became popular” in a reference to their bombastic styles.
“I know him personally, and I will say right now, I will be able to get into the Oval Office,” LePage said. “My opponent will not.”
It marked a shift from his 2022 run for governor, when he kept Trump at arm’s length in a statewide race. Asked then whether he wanted the former president’s help, LePage said, “If he comes, he comes.” Trump didn’t come. LePage lost to Gov. Janet Mills by 13 points.
On Thursday, LePage, who usually speaks off the cuff, read carefully from notes after being asked about Trump’s tariffs. Upon questioning, he said he does not support Trump’s tariffs on Canada in their current form. That was a softer line than last year, when LePage told Fox News he was “all for the tariffs” and said on WVOM that Trump was “doing the right thing” on trade.
He said he could help bring the president back to the table, pitching a continuation of a role he held in Trump’s first term, when Canadian officials saw LePage as a go-between with the White House during NAFTA talks. He opposed Trump’s tariffs on Canadian softwood lumber, putting him at odds with a pair of sawmill owners who accused him of a “Canada-first” trade policy.
“We need to de-escalate the rhetoric, and we need to get the president and the prime minister of Canada back to the negotiating table,” LePage said.
He also said he does not support the Iran war. But he opposed a war powers resolution, which Dunlap backs as a way to end the conflict and lower oil prices, saying it may hamstring the president in foreign policy
“I’m urging the president to finish the war in Iran as quick as possible,” he said.
LePage agreed with Dunlap that immigration agents have “run roughshod” in Maine, where an agent fatally shot a man in Biddeford in July. But he opposed new limits on the agency from Congress. Dunlap said LePage “changed his tune” after a relative faced deportation, which LePage called a personal matter.
LePage also said high earners should pay more into Social Security, a position most congressional Republicans oppose. Dunlap has tied him to Trump’s tax and spending law, which LePage embraced last year and U.S. Sen. Susan Collins voted against.
The candidates meet again for the second and final time on Oct. 15 at a forum hosted by WABI and WAGM. Dunlap had called for four debates, but LePage, the frontrunner in the race, agreed to two.

title: How common are botched executions? Here's what the data shows
text:
How common are botched executions? Here's what the data shows
Christa Pike survived two doses of lethal injection.
How common are botched executions? Here's what the data shows
Christa Pike survived two doses of lethal injection.
Death row inmate Christa Pike survived a failed attempt to execute her Wednesday in Tennessee.
Pike was set to be executed for a 1995 murder, officials gave her two doses of the lethal drug, pentobarbital. But, she continued breathing after the attempted lethal injection and was taken by ambulance from the prison, according to reports.
This is the second case of a botched execution in Tennessee this year. In May, Tony Carruthers was returned to his cell and issued a one-year reprieve after medical staff had trouble securing a primary IV line to administer the lethal drug.
How rare are botched executions?
The Death Penalty Information Center defines botched executions, like Pike's, as those involving unanticipated problems or delays that cause unnecessary suffering for the prisoner or reflected gross incompetence by the executioner.
While there is no official dataset on botched executions, Austin Sarat, a professor of jurisprudence and political science at Amherst College, wrote a book about botched executions.
Sarat looked at 8,776 executions from 1890 to 2010 and found that 276 were botched. These execution methods include lethal injection, lethal gas, hanging, electrocution and firing squad.
Lethal injection had the highest rate of botched executions, according to Sarat.
The Death Penalty Information Center compiled a list of well-known botched executions from the modern era, which started in 1982. There are 64 executions or attempted executions listed: three by asphyxiation, ten by electrocution, and 51 by lethal injection. Seven of the failed lethal injection executions were halted when execution personnel were unable to set an IV line.
Other times, inmates were given the wrong doses of the lethal drug. But none of the examples included a case similar to Pike's, where the inmate was still alive after two doses.

title: Changing the way you put your baby to bed can save their life, according to new CDC data
text:
Changing the way you put your baby to bed can save their life, according to new CDC data
Sudden unexpected infant death claimed the lives of about 3,400 babies in the United States in 2024.
Despite decades of public health efforts to promote safer sleep, these deaths remain a major cause of mortality during infancy.
A new report from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention found that nearly three-quarters of these deaths examined from 2020 through 2024 involved unsafe sleep factors.
Related video above | These are the best parenting products of 2026
That means there are steps parents and caregivers can take. The first one is knowing what a safe sleep environment looks like.
CNN spoke with wellness expert Dr. Leana Wen to learn what parents and other caregivers do to reduce an infant’s risk. Wen is an emergency physician and clinical associate professor at George Washington University. She previously served as Baltimore’s health commissioner and is the mother of two young children.
What did a new CDC report find about sudden unexpected infant death?
Dr. Leana Wen: Sudden unexpected infant death, or SUID, is a general term for the sudden and unexpected death of a baby younger than 1 year. It includes sudden infant death syndrome, or SIDS, as well as accidental suffocation and strangulation in bed, and infant deaths for which the cause remains unknown.
For this report, the CDC analyzed 4,861 SUID cases that occurred between 2020 and 2024 in 31 jurisdictions around the country that participate in its case registry. This registry provides detailed information about the circumstances surrounding deaths that is not available from death certificates alone.
The main finding is that 73% of the deaths were classified as having unsafe sleep factors. Looking at specific characteristics of the sleep environment, 78% involved soft bedding; 75% occurred on a sleep surface other than a crib or bassinet; 59% involved sharing a sleep surface with another person or animal; and 46% of infants were found sleeping on their stomach or side rather than their back. (These categories overlap, so an infant could have had several of these risk factors.)
There were also substantial racial disparities. Black infants accounted for 38% of the deaths in the registry, and the CDC noted that sudden unexpected infant death disproportionately affects Black and American Indian or Alaska Native infants. The reasons are complex and can include differences in access to resources in order to consistently implement safe sleep practices.
What should a safe sleep environment look like?
Wen: The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends babies be placed on their backs for every sleep, including naps. The sleep surface should be firm, flat and designed for infant sleep, such as a crib, bassinet or portable crib that meets current federal safety standards.
The crib should be empty or nearly empty. Use a firm mattress covered by a fitted sheet, without pillows, blankets, quilts, bumper pads or other soft objects. If parents are concerned about their baby being cold, they can use a wearable blanket or other well-fitting sleep clothing rather than putting a loose blanket in the crib.
The AAP recommends room-sharing without bedsharing, ideally for at least the first six months. That means the baby’s crib or bassinet can be next to the parents’ bed, which makes feeding and comforting easier, but the baby should sleep on a separate surface.
Babies should always be placed on their backs to sleep. Tummy time is important for developing strength and motor skills, but it should take place only when the baby is awake and being actively supervised. Once babies can roll from their backs to their stomachs and back again on their own, parents do not need to keep repositioning them during sleep, but they should still place them on their backs at the beginning of every sleep.
These recommendations apply every time and everywhere the baby sleeps. It is not enough to have a safe crib at home if the baby sleeps differently at a grandparent’s or babysitter’s house. Everyone caring for an infant should follow the same practices, and families should stick to the practices when traveling.
Why are soft bedding and sharing a bed with an infant dangerous?
Wen: Young infants have limited ability to move their heads and bodies if something interferes with their breathing. Soft bedding poses a particular danger because a pillow, blanket or other object can cover a baby’s nose and mouth, and the infant may not be able to reposition themselves to breathe.
Sharing a sleep surface creates additional risks. An adult, child or animal can unintentionally roll onto the baby or otherwise obstruct the baby’s airway. Infants can also become wedged between a mattress and a wall, headboard or other object. This is why adult beds are not considered safe sleep surfaces for infants. Couches and armchairs can be even more dangerous. A baby can become trapped between cushions or between the sleeping adult and the furniture.
The CDC data illustrate these dangers. Among the 919 deaths that investigators determined were caused by suffocation involving unsafe sleep factors, 74% involved soft bedding obstructing the airway. About one in four involved “overlay,” meaning another person or animal obstructed the infant’s airway, and 8% involved the baby becoming wedged between objects. Some deaths involved more than one mechanism.
What other steps can parents and caregivers take to reduce the risk of sudden unexpected infant death?
Wen: The most important step is to follow safe sleep practices every time the baby sleeps. That means placing the baby on their back in their own crib or bassinet, without soft bedding or other objects around them.
Parents should also avoid smoking and nicotine use during pregnancy and prevent the baby from being exposed to secondhand smoke after birth. Exposure to cigarette smoke increases the risk of SIDS, so no one should smoke or vape around the baby or in the home or car. They should also avoid alcohol, marijuana, opioids and illicit drugs during pregnancy and after delivery. These substances can increase risk during pregnancy, and their use by parents and other caregivers can impair their ability to wake up and respond to an infant.
In addition, AAP recommends breastfeeding and offering a pacifier at naps and bedtime, because these are also associated with a reduced risk of SIDS. Pregnant women should receive routine prenatal care, and babies should be sure to receive their recommended vaccinations.
What should parents do if their baby falls asleep in a car seat, stroller, swing or baby carrier?
Wen: Car seats are essential tools for protecting infants while traveling in vehicles, but they are not meant to be routine sleep spaces outside the car. Babies commonly fall asleep in car seats, strollers and baby carriers, and parents do not need to worry when that happens.
Once they reach their destination, parents should move the baby to an appropriate surface designed for infants. The main worry is the baby’s position. Young infants have relatively large heads and limited head and neck control. On an inclined or sitting surface, their heads can fall forward or their bodies can shift into a position that compromises breathing.
As far as swings, parents should be wary if it’s promoted as something that helps sleep. A product being sold for infants does not mean that it is appropriate for unsupervised sleep. The safest choice remains a firm, non-inclined surface that meets infant sleep safety standards.
What about exhausted parents who bring a baby into bed to feed or comfort them?
Wen: This is an important practical issue because nighttime feedings happen when parents are understandably exhausted. Parents can make it easier to follow safe sleep practices by keeping the baby’s crib or bassinet next to their bed. After feeding or comforting the baby, they should return the infant to this separate sleep space before going back to sleep themselves.
If a parent unintentionally falls asleep while feeding the baby in bed, they should return the baby to the crib or bassinet as soon as they wake. Pillows, blankets and other soft objects should be kept away from the baby during feeding in case the parent dozes off.

title: Obituary: Stephen T. Hughes
text:
AUBURN / NEW YORK CITY, N.Y. – Stephen T. Hughes passed away on Aug. 17, 2026. He was 83.
Steve lived a life marked by service to others — as an elected official, a trustee of the University of Maine, and an active member of several Episcopal parishes, most notably St. Bartholomew’s Church in New York City, N.Y. where he lived for the last 40 years of his life.
Born on July 26, 1943 to Albert W. “Beau” Hughes and Edith Bivens Hughes, Steve grew up in Auburn and graduated from Edward Little High School. He went on to attend Duke University in Durham, North Carolina, a state where members of his extended family lived. After being drafted, Steve served for two years in the United States Army before enrolling at the University of Maine.
At UMaine, Steve made many lifelong friends and served as president of the student body during a tumultuous era when the Vietnam War and the national debate surrounding it profoundly affected campus life. While still an undergraduate, he gained statewide recognition when Gov. Kenneth M. Curtis appointed him as the first student to serve as a trustee of the University of Maine.
Steve graduated from UMaine in 1970 and, while continuing his service as a trustee, attended the University of Maine School of Law. In 1974, voters in Auburn elected him to the Maine House of Representatives. He was reelected in 1976.
During his legislative career, Steve became closely identified with two landmark environmental measures. He sponsored legislation establishing Maine’s beverage-container deposit law, commonly known as the “Bottle Bill,” and championed the successful effort to eliminate most roadside billboards. Both measures helped shape Maine’s approach to environmental protection and preservation of its landscape and remain the law today. Steve was also a strong advocate for civil rights, reproductive freedom, and the rule of law.
After serving four years in the Legislature, Steve left Maine for New York City, N.Y. where he pursued a life of ministry. He enrolled at Union Theological Seminary and spent 15 years leading programs at the Cathedral Church of St. John the Divine. He later became deeply involved with St. Bartholomew’s Church, known as St. Bart’s, where he served in a variety of leadership roles for 25 years. His activities there were curtailed in later years by health issues related to COVID-19.
Throughout his life, Steve maintained a deep love of music, culture, and the arts. Blessed with an extraordinary tenor voice, he sang with numerous choirs in both Maine and New York. He also loved to travel and, over the years, explored much of the United States and Europe with his many friends.
Steve will be remembered for his lively conversation, intellectual curiosity, commitment to public and community service, love of music and the arts, and devotion to a wide circle of friends and an extended network of cousins scattered across the country.
Steve was predeceased by his parents, Albert W. “Beau” Hughes and Edith Bivens Hughes; and his brother, Nick Hughes.
A gathering of Steve’s Maine family and friends will be held 2 p.m., Sunday, Oct. 11, at Maple Hill Farm in Hallowell. A service celebrating Steve’s life will be held at 2 p.m. Nov. 6 at St. Bartholomew’s Church in New York City, N.Y. Interment will be in the Hughes family plot in Eno Presbyterian Church in Cedar Grove, N.C.
In lieu of flowers please donate to be made to the University of Maine Alumni Association. https://www.umainealumni.com/

title: K-9 sniffs out nearly 450 pounds of cocaine at northern border
text:
LEWISTON, N.Y. (Gray News) — Federal border officers seized an estimated $6 million worth of cocaine after discovering 174 packages concealed under the floorboards of a commercial truck bound for Canada, authorities said.
On Sept. 22, U.S. Customs and Border Protection officers at the Port of Buffalo’s Lewiston Bridge border crossing encountered a 21-year-old Canadian man driving a commercial truck and trailer.
After an initial physical inspection of the trailer, officers found the floorboard had been modified. A CBP canine then searched the empty trailer and alerted to the presence of narcotics. The truck and trailer were escorted to a secondary inspection area.
A detailed search uncovered 174 vacuum-sealed packages of cocaine concealed inside the floor, which field-tested positive for the drug. The narcotics weighed approximately 450 pounds and had an estimated street value of $6 million.
“This significant seizure highlights the exceptional vigilance, advanced training and relentless dedication of our CBP officers and canine teams at the Lewiston Bridge border crossing,” said Sharon Swiatek, acting port director for the Area Port of Buffalo. “While a large focus of our border security mission is on inbound threats, our officers remain equally sharp during outbound operations to dismantle transborder criminal networks, disrupt the flow of dangerous narcotics and protect communities on both sides of the border.”
The case was referred to Homeland Security Investigations for further review.

title: Red Clay Strays will play at the Bangor waterfront next summer
text:
The Red Clay Strays will play at the Bangor waterfront next summer.
The country rock band, along with St. Paul and the Broken Bones, will perform at the Maine Savings Amphitheater on July 23.

title: 2 nights, 2 worlds of music, 1 cozy space in Bath
text:
One of the things I love most about our Annex is its intimacy. There’s very little distance between artist and audience, which makes it a perfect room both for discovering something new and for hearing music you already love in a completely different way. Our next two concerts offer a little of both.
Thursday night, Oct. 8, at 7:30 p.m., we welcome Kouchera, a new group coming to us from the Portsmouth/Dover, New Hampshire area, blending Haitian Konpa with R&B, soul, funk and an infectious live energy. Konpa is a Haitian dance music with a driving, syncopated groove, and Kouchera brings that rhythmic foundation into conversation with the sounds of American soul and R&B. The band describes what they do as music with “emotional depth wrapped neatly in fun,” which seems like a pretty good invitation to a Thursday night.
Then on Saturday, Oct. 10, we turn toward one of the great American musical rabbit holes: the Grateful Dead.
Dead to the Core is an acoustic celebration of the Dead led by musician and writer Jeffrey Pepper Rodgers, founding editor of Acoustic Guitar magazine. Rather than trying to recreate Grateful Dead performances note for note, the group takes the songs apart and rebuilds them through acoustic instruments, vocal harmonies and their own musical personalities.
For me, this gets at something essential about the Dead. Underneath the psychedelic experimentation and sprawling electric jams was a band deeply connected to American folk, country, bluegrass, blues and roots music. You can hear it beautifully on records like “American Beauty” and “Workingman’s Dead.” Dead to the Core taps into those roots while also taking songs we may associate with electric guitars and big jams and cooking them down into something more intimate. In a room like the Annex, you can really listen to the architecture of these songs — the lyrics, harmonies, melodies and wonderful strangeness of them.
And Saturday begins before the concert.
At 4 p.m., Dead to the Core will host a free Grateful Dead Hootenanny, open to anyone who wants to sing or play. Bring an acoustic instrument — or simply bring your voice. The band will provide lyric and chord sheets and lead everyone through classic Dead songs together.
Then at 7:30 p.m., they take the stage.
Two nights, two very different musical traditions, and one little room built for listening, gathering and getting a little closer to the music. Oh, and there’s a roster of new beers and drinks to choose from!
Matthew Glassman is executive and artistic director of the Chocolate Church Arts Center in Bath.

title: Tanker crash causes delays on Maine Turnpike in Falmouth
text:
FALMOUTH, Maine (WABI) - Troopers responded to a two-vehicle crash on the Maine Turnpike southbound near mile marker 56 in Falmouth early Thursday.
The crash was reported at approximately 2:35 a.m.
The initial investigation indicates a SUV lost power and came to a stop in the travel lane, officials said.
A tractor-trailer tanker traveling southbound approached the stopped SUV and attempted to move into the right lane to avoid it. The tractor-trailer struck the rear passenger side of the SUV, pushing it toward the median. The tractor-trailer then tipped onto its right side.
Injuries and response
The driver and the passenger in the SUV and the driver of the tractor-trailer were transported to Maine Medical Center for evaluation. No serious injuries were reported.
A small amount of diesel fuel leaked from the tractor-trailer. The Maine Department of Environmental Protection responded to the scene.
Road closures
All southbound lanes in the area were closed following the crash, with traffic diverted at Exit 63.
The tractor-trailer has since been removed, and the scene has been cleared. All lanes are back open.
The crash remains under investigation.

title: Texts show how Cornell accuser became convinced she had been raped, report says
text:
ITHACA, N.Y. (AP) — A former Cornell University student who alleges she was gang raped at a fraternity in 2024 received a text-message apology from one of the brothers soon afterward. After initially saying she didn’t see what happened as illegal, she became convinced within weeks that she had been violated, according to a newspaper report citing records from the university’s private investigation.
The documents, as described by The New York Times, trace the woman’s shift from seeing the alleged encounter as a dismaying embarrassment to seeing it as a sexual assault — one she then reported to campus police, discussed with the university’s internal investigators and is pursuing in a lawsuit filed in September. The case has roiled the Ivy League campus and has raised questions about why no criminal case was brought.
According to the Times’ report of records and statements gathered during the inquiry:
The day after the Oct. 19, 2024, party at the Chi Phi fraternity house, the woman got back to her room and told her roommates she’d taken ketamine — a powerful anesthetic sometimes used as a party drug — and had sex with multiple men. The roommates said that at that point, the woman didn’t describe the events as rape or assault, but one roommate noted: “I don’t really remember her ever kind of citing that she had said yes to anything that occurred,” the newspaper reported.
Texts between accuser and one of the accused
The following day, the woman got a text message from one of the men she would later accuse in her sexual assault lawsuit. He texted that he “just wanted to apologize for how things went down the other night” and regretted that he and a fellow fraternity brother — also now a defendant in the woman’s lawsuit — had been too intoxicated to “shut it down and kick people out before it got way out of hand.”
The woman texted back that “at the end of the day non of the sexual stuff was illegal” and that she had liked being with the two men.
But by Oct. 23, 2024, she was growing distraught that word of the episode had spread around campus. Soon, she saw a post in an online forum about campus Greek life that asserted that Chi Phi brothers had gang raped a sophomore and should be reported.
“That’s the first time I had ever heard the narrative change that I wasn’t a whore and that I was assaulted,” she later told investigators.
Over the days after that post, her tone became more aggrieved — “how could you let this happen?” — as she kept communicating with the first Chi Phi brother who’d texted her after the party. Still, she planned to attend the fraternity’s Halloween Party, until she was disinvited.
On Nov. 3, 2024, she texted the man: “let’s be clear that 90% of what happened that night was not consensual,” saying she’d been given a lot of ketamine. While her memories were patchy, they included a humiliating, drug-laced sexual act, she wrote.
“I know that i told u i felt uncomfortable and i didn’t know anyone in the room,” she added.
She went to Cornell campus police five days later and spoke to them again on Nov. 14 and 15, 2024, telling them: “I can say with 100% confidence I was raped,” according to a report by CBS New York, which said it obtained a transcript of her police interview.
Cornell plans a forum Thursday night
Cornell’s student government planned a public forum Thursday on sexual violence to allow students to demand “institutional accountability” and talk about their own experiences on campus.
Cornell has said it suspended the Chi Phi fraternity indefinitely and disciplined or expelled some students, but the university has declined to provide specifics, citing student privacy rules.
The local district attorney, Matthew Van Houten, declined at the time to bring any criminal charges, but this week said he would reopen the investigation based on new information in the woman’s lawsuit, which identifies her only by the pseudonym Jane Doe.
He has maintained the woman’s first account to police didn’t include allegations that she was drugged against her will, incapacitated beyond the ability to consent, or forced into sex. After CBS News this week revealed details from the police interview transcript, he told the network he’d never seen her detailed account and had relied instead on a statement written by a campus police officer and signed by the accuser.
She’s suing seven men who she said participated in the assault, as well as the university, the fraternity, and others.
Lawyers for two of the men she is suing have denied they participated in a sexual assault. One said his client hadn’t touched the woman or engaged in any drug use. Attempts by The Associated Press to reach the other men or their representatives have been unsuccessful.
Under pressure from the public and politicians, including Gov. Kathy Hochul, the private university agreed Wednesday to bring in outside lawyers to independently investigate how it handled the woman’s allegations.

title: Nash Callahan shows up for Augusta
text:
Whether you vote early in person, by mail, or in person on Nov. 3, please join me in voting for Saunders “Nash” Callahan for Augusta City Council.
As an at-large city councilor, part of my job is taking calls from our entire community. Each time Nash Callahan calls me, I am impressed with his understanding of the issues, the depth and nuance of his thinking, and the practicality of his ideas. It was not difficult to write this letter for Nash — I think it may have been our second conversation when I commented that if he kept this up, he’d soon be having these discussions with me as a fellow city councilor. I hope that prediction becomes a reality this November.
Nash has a long history of involvement in the city and a perspective that would serve the council well, the thing that makes me most sure of my decision to vote for Nash is his independent mind.
I don’t necessarily want to sit at that table with a person who will agree with me in every discussion; I want people there who bring up points I would have missed, who are willing to make difficult decisions, and who help the council engage in healthy dialogue and problem-solving. Nash has consistently shown these characteristics through his committee service, engagement in the community and public comment at council meetings. I think it’s well past time to put his talents to work for Augusta in another capacity: at-large city councilor.
Stephanie-Ann Sienkiewicz
Augusta

title: Maine DHHS awards child development grant to out-of-state, private equity-backed firm
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A Maine organization that has provided training and assistance to educators for decades could close its doors after the state awarded a multimillion dollar contract to an out-of-state company backed by private equity and venture capital firms, officials confirmed Wednesday.
Maine Roads to Quality was created in 1999 by the Catherine Cutler Institute at the University of Southern Maine to offer professional development to child care providers across the state. The organization provides guidance to more than 10,000 Maine child care providers each year.
For much of its existence, Maine Roads has been funded by contracts provided by Maine’s Department of Health and Human Services. That lifeline evaporated last week.
The state offered a pair of contracts worth an estimated $10 million over two years to Shine Early Learning, a New York-based company that offers similar services to childcare centers, home-based providers and public schools in more than 30 states.
“The University of Southern Maine was notified on Sept. 21 that its proposals for two state contracts supporting the Maine Roads to Quality Professional Development Network were not selected for continued funding, thus ending a nearly three-decade partnership,” Samantha Warren, spokesperson for the University of Maine System, said in a statement.
Maine Roads employs more than 30 people. Warren said “layoffs are expected” without a renewal of the DHHS contracts.
The contracts specify Shine Early Learning must employ at least 10 staff members in Maine. Shine Early Learning’s proposals also specify it plans to use artificial intelligence to do much of the work Maine Roads’ human staffers currently perform.
The company plans to implement an “AI-powered family navigation assistant,” an AI-assisted employee vetting tool and an AI agent that will manage a provider registry, according to its applications.
Lindsay Hammes, a spokesperson for DHHS, noted the company has only been offered conditional awards and that no contracts have been ratified yet. The full value of the new contracts “will become public once they are finalized,” she said.
Shine Early Learning underbid Maine Roads by some $2 million between the two contracts, according to documents obtained by the Portland Press Herald. The company did not respond to a request for comment prior to publication.
One contract is for coaching, credentialing, and training of early childhood educators and care providers. The other is for providing a DHHS-approved training plan “designed to improve quality” of child care services and early childhood educators, according to the state’s request for proposals.
Those services have historically been housed under a single contract, Warren said.
When state offices ask for contract bids, they score each of the proposals on a scale from 0 to 100. Shine Early Learning’s bid for the coaching contract received a 97, while its proposal for the training plan got a perfect 100.
Maine Roads received about 73 points on each of its proposals. DHHS said the scores were issued in accordance with the processes laid out in its requests for proposals, but did not specify how Shine Early Learning received such high marks.
Shine Early Learning’s website touts the company’s “data-driven services and solutions” to “accelerate child and family outcomes.”
The company is owned by Acelero, Inc. — a firm seeded with a “strategic investment” from BlackRock, one of the world’s largest private equity companies. Several members from BlackRock and other venture capital firms who invested in Acelero subsequently joined the company’s board, according to a 2022 news release.
The private equity company’s investment in Acelero, and Shine Early Learning by extension, was made with the goal of “extending Acelero’s footprint and deepen(ing) its impact across communities,” BlackRock’s senior portfolio manager said at the time.
BlackRock handles more than $11 trillion in assets. The firm has been criticized for being “too big to fail,” purchasing everything from electric grids to billions’ of dollars of real estate across the country.
Activists have scrutinized BlackRock for investing in companies contributing to climate change and mass surveillance. The United Nations in 2025 issued a report saying BlackRock is complicit in Israel’s genocide in Gaza due to its investments in several weapons manufacturers.
In Maine, BlackRock acts as one of the primary investment managers for Maine’s Public Employee Retirement System.
Maine Roads plans to appeal DHHS’ decision on the contracts issued to Shine Early Learning, said Warren, the UMaine system spokesperson.
“In the meantime, the university is committed to continuing to provide high-quality services for Maine’s early childhood education community through the end of the current contract and supporting potentially affected employees, many of whom have served the field through the program for more than 15 years,” she said.

title: Here are heating assistance resources for Mainers using oil, electricity or wood
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
While fall is always a beautiful time of year here in Maine, it also means that Mainers must start planning for higher home heating costs. And while the forecast shows a couple more days of warm weather ahead, the cooler temperatures are here to stay. Heating oil costs are always a concern for Maine families, but this year is especially worrying, as the war in Iran has driven oil prices up significantly. The price of heating oil has risen roughly 60% since the war began, meaning hardworking Mainers will have to spend even more of their paychecks just to stay warm. Beyond heating our homes, Mainers will face additional financial hardship this year, as rising oil prices have driven up costs for groceries and all transported goods.
While my colleagues and I in the Maine Legislature cannot control oil prices or foreign conflicts launched by the current federal administration, we work hard to ensure that help is available to those who need it. If you heat your home with oil and worry about affording a fill-up, I recommend contacting heating assistance resources as soon as possible. Applications for the Home Energy Assistance Program (HEAP) are now open and can help those who qualify pay for heating costs such as fuel. Assistance through this program is available through May, or until funds run out. I want to stress again the importance of applying early to ensure you do so before funds run out. Go to MaineHousing’s website (mainehousing.org) for more information on the program and to view the application. Beginning in November, you can also contact the Midcoast Maine Community Action Program (MMCA) if you need emergency energy assistance. MMCA’s Energy Crisis Intervention Program helps Mainers who urgently need fuel to heat their home. They can be contacted at 207-442-7963.
This past session, we also worked hard to ensure that we provided relief to Mainers who heat with electricity for the upcoming fall and winter seasons. We passed LD 1936, which lowered electricity rates for people in northern and eastern Maine who previously paid unnecessarily high prices for electricity compared to those in southern Maine. People in those regions who rely on electricity to heat their homes should see a decrease in utility costs this season. We also limited how much utility companies can charge low-income households with the passage of LD 2203. Now, providers may not charge low-income customers anything greater than the standard-offer service rate. Additionally, we passed a law that makes plug-in solar systems available to both homeowners and renters, so Mainers can generate electricity at home, reducing the electricity delivered to their homes and lowering their monthly heating bill.
For Mainers who have a woodstove but may need help affording firewood, the Midcoast Wood Bank (MWB) is a terrific resource for the municipalities of Bath, West Bath, Bowdoin, Bowdoinham, Topsham, Brunswick, Harpswell, Lisbon and Woolwich. MWB offers up to two cords of firewood per household in need per season. Those who can pick up the wood themselves will receive help loading it. If you cannot transport the firewood yourself, MWB offers a limited delivery service. You can contact MWB at -207-800-1658 or email them at [email protected] for help and for additional resource options.
Many towns also have General Assistance or specific local heating assistance programs. You can contact your local town office or call the toll-free Maine General Assistance hotline at 1-800- 442-6003 for more information. Efficiency Maine also has guides on their website with tips on saving energy and money for homeowners and renters. On their website, you can also find tools to compare costs, learn about rebates for energy-efficient home upgrades and more. Bath Housing’s Comfortably Home Program has resources to help people button up their homes for colder weather.
If you would like to learn more about any of these programs or if you would like help applying, please do not hesitate to reach out. My office has contacts at nearly all of these programs and organizations that we can speak with. You can always email me at [email protected] or you can call my office at 207-287-1515.
Sen. Denise Tepler represents Maine Senate District 24, which includes all of Sagadahoc County, plus Dresden in Lincoln County.

title: Lewiston invites residents to Red Shop conversation Oct. 5
text:
LEWISTON, ME – The City of Lewiston invites residents to learn about the past, present and future of the Red Shop during a Community Conversation on Mon., Oct. 5, from 5:30 PM to 7 PM at the Hampton Inn, 15 Lincoln St. The City will conclude with a tour of the nearby building.
The city is holding the conversation to explain how it plans to activate Simard-Payne Memorial Park and hear what residents would like to see and do there. Participants will learn about plans for the former Bates Mill complex machine shop, including how it could support community events and concerts.
Built in 1938, the Red Shop served as a machine shop for the Bates Mill complex and helped control water flow in the canal system. Its location at 38 Water St. connects Lewiston’s industrial history with the riverfront’s growing role as a gathering place.

title: Mainers are stretched thin. In Oxford County, many can’t afford enough food.
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
This is the first story in the series Stretched Thin: The cost of getting by in Maine, which looks at the financial hardships Mainers face. Social services reporter Gillian Graham reported this story as a USC Annenberg Center for Health Journalism 2026 National Fellow and a participant in the Center’s engagement initiative.
MEXICO — By the time the first people arrived for lunch on a warm July day, Michelle Williams and the volunteers at the River Valley’s only soup kitchen had been at work for hours.
They stretched out clean white tablecloths and arranged baskets of fruit and snacks on the buffet line. They filled large orange coolers with lemonade and water and set out napkins and utensils. They stirred baked beans bubbling in a warmer, the scent wafting out of the kitchen.
Williams, a retired hospice nurse who founded Good Samaritan Missionary Services, had started cooking the day before. The menu included barbecue pulled chicken sandwiches, street corn pasta salad and her famous lemon icebox cake.
Her motivation, she said, is simple: “Food is a necessity, not a luxury.”
In Oxford County’s River Valley — where the towns that hug the Androscoggin River have long been known for their deep ties to paper manufacturing — many working families have a hard time covering their everyday expenses. The hunger rate is among the highest in the state.
The financial situation can be even more bleak for people who are retired, unemployed or homeless.
Some families have been in poverty, or hovering just above it, for generations.
Before the soup kitchen opened, there were few options in the area for food assistance. Three years ago, Williams started an emergency food pantry at town hall. Within six months, it morphed into the soup kitchen because of the high demand, she said.
It’s not uncommon to hear about people working 12-hour days but still struggling to make ends meet, said Joleen Bedard, president and CEO of United Way of Western Maine. Some have seasonal jobs with inconsistent incomes, while others grapple with how to get to work and appointments in a region without widely accessible public transportation.
“It’s certainly a struggle and I don’t see it changing any time soon,” she said. “There are two Maines: the haves and the have-nots.”
‘BARRIER AFTER BARRIER’
Every day, thousands of Mainers face the hardest choices: buy food or pay for a prescription; drive far for healthcare or risk going without; toil to afford childcare or stop working; go to a homeless shelter or sleep in a tent.
Across the state, data from 2024 shows, 40% of households fell below the federal poverty line or just above the threshold, where people struggle to afford basic expenses, but don’t always qualify for assistance.
“There is an enormous number of hardworking families throughout the state who are one unexpected expense away from crisis,” said Dan Coyne, who heads the United Way of Southern Maine.
This summer, the United Ways of Maine released new data they say shows traditional measures of poverty have undercounted the number of households in the state experiencing financial hardship.
Many have incomes above the federal poverty line and are part of a population called ALICE — Asset Limited, Income Constrained, Employed. The threshold for each county is calculated using household income and a survival budget that includes the cost of housing, childcare, food, transportation, healthcare and technology.
It does not include room for savings, debt payments or emergency expenses.
In Rumford, 66% of households struggle to afford basic expenses — the most of any town in the county, according to the United Way. Census data shows 15% are below the poverty line.
Half of the households in Mexico and 41% in neighboring Dixfield also fall below the ALICE threshold.
For decades, people in Maine’s rural areas have experienced financial hardship and poverty at higher rates. But even in coastal areas, where more wealth is concentrated, there are pockets of residents struggling.
For many in the Oxford County region, improving their financial outlook seems nearly impossible, even if they’re working, said Melissa McEntee, who runs Rumford Group Homes, the only homeless shelter program in the county.
“We see hard-working families who do everything they can to get out of that poverty cycle. Everything in River Valley keeps sucking them back in,” she said. “Everything is a barrier. It’s barrier after barrier after barrier.”
FALLING THROUGH THE CRACKS
Sue Grace remembers the heyday of Rumford, when the town was booming and there wasn’t an empty storefront downtown. There was a big hotel that hosted fancy weddings, a hat shop she’d visit with her grandmother, and a police officer with a whistle and white gloves directing traffic.
“Talk about a Norman Rockwell portrait,” the lifelong Rumford resident said.
Grace, 72, worked at the local hospital for years and raised her four kids in town. In the ’80s, as manufacturing at the paper mill declined and the workforce shrank, businesses on Congress Street started to close. Unemployment ticked up and there was less going on to keep kids entertained, she said.
The paper mill in Rumford employed more than 3,000 people at its peak, but today it employs just over 500. The steep decline in manufacturing created economic uncertainty in the communities, according to Friends of the River Valley, which supports a range of nutrition, education, health and social services programs in the area.
Grace said she never considered leaving, even after she retired from her job as a phlebotomist and two of her adult children moved out of town. She was doing fine on her Social Security and small pension for a while, but things have become tougher in the past few years as the cost of everything seemed to go up.
Now, she feels like she’s falling through the cracks.
Grace gets about $24 a month in federal food assistance benefits and the $417 monthly rent for her apartment is based on her income. In August, she was eagerly awaiting her $300 affordability check from the state so she could replace her six-year-old cell phone.
She’s grateful for the help and said she’s fortunate to be better off than many, but she still has to make tough choices.
Most days, Grace eats two meals to save on groceries.
She goes to the soup kitchen in Mexico for lunch because that is food she doesn’t have to figure out how to pay for.
“I was raised that you don’t ask for help. I had to learn to do that,” she said, while sitting in her dining room under a wall sign encouraging visitors to “Live well, laugh often, love much.”
After working hard for 40 years, Grace doesn’t think she should have to struggle so much.
FILLING THE GAP
A half-dozen people carrying reusable shopping bags lingered in the dirt parking lot outside of the Old School Food Pantry in Mexico on a gloomy day in June. They chatted quietly as raindrops started to fall, adding to the unseasonable chill.
They were an hour early for the weekly distribution, but wanted to make sure they could get what they needed.
The two-room food pantry in the bottom floor of an old school building sits on a hill facing the river. The white plumes from the mill stacks drift over the trees.
Just inside the door, volunteer William Gallant sat at a table, lists of pantry regulars laid out in front of him and clipboards with checklists of grocery items neatly stacked to the side. Every time someone came in, he clicked a counter dangling from his neck to keep track of how many people showed up for groceries.
Oxford County has one of the highest food insecurity rates in the state, with nearly a quarter of all children in the region experiencing hunger, according to Feeding America, which tracks the issue across the country.
The number of Mainers experiencing hunger continues to rise. It’s the highest it’s been in a decade, according to a report released this summer.
More than 11,000 Mainers have lost access to the federal Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program because of sweeping changes that began rolling out last fall, according to state officials.
Rural areas of Maine, where more people tend to rely on SNAP, are being hit especially hard by the changes, according to hunger prevention advocates. Work exemptions were removed for rural areas with low employment options, leaving some people struggling to find work or volunteer opportunities to maintain access to food assistance.
Food pantries trying to fill the gap are reporting record numbers of visits. In August, nearly 300 families came in to pick up fresh produce, meat and boxes of shelf-stable groceries from the Old School Food Pantry.
Gallant, 77, grew up in Rumford when the paper mill was the biggest employer and the company’s owner pumped money into the town, including the community center where kids gathered for dances and bowling in the basement.
Gallant, who has been volunteering at the food pantry for four years, sees the impact every week from behind his check-in table.
There are always new people coming in for the first time — older retirees whose pensions don’t cover the bills anymore, working parents who can’t afford groceries, people who are out of work and piecing together whatever they can to get by.
As the pantry gets busier, he worries there won’t be enough food to go around.
“I don’t ever want to be the person who has to tell them we ran out of food,” he said, as he handed a clipboard to the next person in line.
FEEDING THE COMMUNITY
The school district that serves Rumford and Mexico decided in late June that it did not have the staff to distribute free lunch to kids during the summer, a move that Williams, from the soup kitchen, said was particularly hard on families already struggling to provide food.
In the first days after school let out, she said there was a noticeable increase in families with kids coming in for lunch.
“Holy smokes, we are getting our butts handed to us,” Williams said in early July. One day the previous week, she served 45 people in less than an hour. Half of them were children.
As the outside temperature pushed into the high 80s, Angela Dean, her husband and their 1-year-old daughter were among the first to arrive for lunch on July 6.
“We just want to live here, Michelle,” Dean called out as she walked into the air-conditioned room and headed for a table in the back corner.
Dean, who was staying at the homeless shelter, comes in for lunch most days the soup kitchen is open. She knows everyone by name.
“It’s a huge relief,” she said, after settling her daughter into a highchair and filling their plates. “It might seem like one meal three days a week isn’t a big deal, but when you’re a mom trying to survive, it’s so important.”
Dean has lived in the River Valley for more than 20 years. She doesn’t think there are enough resources available to help residents. She said she’s watched rents shoot up higher than she thought possible.
“A lot of people struggle here,” Dean said. “There are a lot of people who don’t have anywhere to go. People are overworked and underpaid.”
Alisha Holtorf, of Mexico, came into the soup kitchen a few minutes later with four of her five children. They’re regulars, too, and have grown especially close to Williams and the volunteers who serve lunch. Williams keeps applesauce pouches on hand for the youngest Holtorf, 2-year-old Ember.
Holtorf, 34, runs the food pantry at her church, Praise Assembly of God in downtown Rumford, and sees firsthand how many people in the community are living on the edge financially.
“People are doing all they can, but it still doesn’t seem like enough for this area,” she said.
Holtorf homeschools her kids and works two part-time jobs. Her husband has a manufacturing job in Auburn, but she said they still don’t make enough and don’t qualify for any assistance programs. To stretch her budget, Holtorf grows vegetables, swaps the clothes her kids have outgrown for new sizes at the church’s clothing closet, and is careful about spending at the grocery store.
The Holtorfs saved for several years to pay for a road trip to see family in Iowa in September.
She said people often come to the church for help, but the congregation is small and many of its members are on fixed incomes and can’t afford to give more.
“It’s hard,” she said, “telling people we don’t have the funds.”
‘ROBBING PETER TO PAY PAUL’
While it’s clear many people — including older residents who rely on Social Security and young families burdened by childcare expenses — are struggling to get by, Rumford Town Manager George O’Keefe sees progress in addressing some of the critical needs laid bare in the years following the decline in manufacturing.
The service sector has grown substantially and there has been “really drastic” growth in energy production and storage businesses, O’Keefe said.
Rumford, the largest town in the county, has a hospital and the Black Mountain of Maine ski resort. Larger ski resorts nearby attract thousands of people every winter.
For the last few years, the town has been focused on encouraging the construction of more housing — from neighborhoods of single-family homes to affordable apartments for older residents. O’Keefe believes this will go a long way toward addressing some of the financial pressure on River Valley residents.
“There are a lot of families that struggle to stay on the rung of the economic ladder they’re on, let alone make upward progress,” O’Keefe said.
Courtney Johnson finds herself facing the same choice every winter: keep the lights on or heat the house. The Mexico resident always chooses heat because the power company can’t easily disconnect service during the coldest months of winter under state law.
“The saying ‘Robbing Peter to pay Paul’ never meant anything to me as a kid,” she said. “Now, I do it all the time.”
Johnson is blunt when she describes her family’s financial situation: “It sucks to be poor.”
Johnson, 39, and her husband, Jason, met while growing up in York County, but didn’t start dating until after they were out of school and she had two children. They had five more children together, including a baby girl born this summer. They moved to the River Valley about eight years ago to live with his mother’s boyfriend. For nearly four years, the family stayed crammed together in two bedrooms.
Johnson said she asked her husband to pick up a scratch-off lottery ticket when he was at the store a few years ago. The $5 ticket he bought was a winner, a stroke of luck that she said sent him running down the street in celebration.
They decided to use the money to create more stability for the family and Johnson said they were able to buy a house in Mexico for $55,000 in 2023. Some of the kids still have to share bedrooms, she said, but they’re not crowded into small rooms. The property came with apple trees and a picnic table, just like the house she had always dreamed of owning.
But owning a home hasn’t alleviated their financial constraints.
Johnson recently left her job as a direct support professional at a local nonprofit to care for her new baby. Childcare, if she could find it, would cost more than she made. Her husband is a subcontractor, but work can be inconsistent. Sometimes, she said, he works on homes of older members of their church who can only afford to pay him with thanks, prayer and homemade cookies.
The Johnsons, who work part-time leading the youth ministry at Praise Assembly of God, found their way to the church a few years ago after attending its annual Culture of Compassion event, where people can get a free lunch, groceries and clothing.
Johnson is grateful her family is insured through MaineCare and receives benefits from the Women, Infants and Children program. Most months, the $1,300 they get from SNAP is enough to cover groceries, but sometimes they have to use a local food pantry.
“We’re very frugal because we know what it’s like to go without,” she said. “We try not to take from this church (food pantry) because we know people around here need it more.”
The Johnsons try to help where they can. When they heard a young person in their church was using dish soap to brush his teeth, they bought him toothpaste. Recently, they scraped together $200 to buy meat for a family short on food.
“We will go without to help another family,” she said.
FINDING A WAY TO HELP
In the River Valley, many support systems are informal. If one group can’t help someone, they often know where to point them for assistance, said McEntee, the homeless shelter director.
“People who care and want to help have found a way to band together,” McEntee said. “We feel lucky that in Oxford County we are small and all the providers know each other.”
At Good Samaritan, helping goes beyond the food laid out on the buffet table.
On Thursdays, a retired social worker sits in the back of the soup kitchen, helping people sign up for assistance programs. The back room is stocked with basic toiletries, household items and pet food. When someone faces an unexpected hardship, Williams is known to jump in.
“Michelle will always find a way to help,” said Carol Violette, a retired seamstress who has volunteered at the soup kitchen since it opened.
Williams and the Good Samaritan board do it all on a shoestring budget.
They apply for grants and put a small donation jar out during every lunch. When a grant payment was delayed, Williams used some of her own Social Security check to cover expenses until it came in. A supporter gives $400 every month from her Social Security income.
As summer waned, Williams spent hours canning sauerkraut, pickled beets, tomato sauce and vegetables to get the soup kitchen through the long winter.
“It’s a tiring week,” she said, “but it’s nice to go into the weekend knowing you’ve helped people.”
When the new school year started, Williams decided to cut back to two lunches each week. When winter sets in, she plans to open the soup kitchen on the coldest days as a refuge for people living outside and those whose homes aren’t warm enough.
There won’t always be lunch, but the coffee will be hot.

title: 35% of undergraduate women at Cornell University say they have been sexually assaulted on campus
text:
ITHACA, N.Y. (WTSM) — More than a third of undergraduate women polled in a Cornell University survey reported experiencing nonconsensual sexual contact since arriving on campus, according to data released by Cornell.
Cornell has surveyed its student body since 2021 to learn more about sexual assaults on campus.
Survey results show increase since 2023
Cornell’s 2025 Survey of Sexual Assault and Related Misconduct found 35% of undergraduate women and 15% of the entire student body polled reported experiencing nonconsensual sexual contact since coming to Cornell. In 2023, that total number was 11%.
Laura Palumbo, communications director for the National Sexual Violence Resource Center, said the surveys provide information beyond campus safety reports or reports made to campus law enforcement.
“They can tell us a lot more about what’s happening on a campus than just looking at the number of campus safety reports or reports that have come through to campus law enforcement,” Palumbo said.
Survey participation declined
Only 15% of students invited to Cornell’s 2025 survey participated, less than half the respondents from two years earlier. Palumbo said that raises questions about whether students believe sharing their experiences will lead to change.
Fraternity investigation raises questions
In the case of an investigation into Cornell fraternity members allegedly raping and drugging a student, the district attorney has said the survivor’s initial account differed from allegations made later.
Palumbo said changes or additional details in a survivor’s account aren’t necessarily unusual following trauma.
“It’s very normal for survivors to, one, delay their disclosure. And then as they are ready to come forward, it’s very normal for survivors to not have a linear recollection of their traumatic experience, especially if there were intoxicants involved,” Palumbo said.
University and criminal investigations differ
The case has also raised questions about the difference between university and criminal investigations. Palumbo said Title IX proceedings, which mandate universities to respond to, investigate and resolve reports of sexual assault, are separate from criminal investigations conducted by law enforcement.
Cornell’s own survey found only 23% of respondents who experienced nonconsensual sexual contact contacted a formal resource.
“It’s not at all clear where that breakdown may have happened in this case, but I will tell you that is something that survivors commonly struggle with,” Palumbo said.

title: Descendants of Civil War Veteran Invited to Oct. 11 Service
text:
Waldoborough Historical Society and Cpl. George Samuel Cobb Camp #68 of Camden will hold a commemorative service for Civil War veteran John W. Palmer at 2 p.m. on Sunday, Oct. 11.
The ceremony will take place at the Rural Cemetery, at 561 Washington Road in Waldoboro. Any descendants of Palmer are welcome to join.
Palmer served with the 32nd Maine Infantry and passed away in 1944. He was the last Civil War veteran to be buried in Lincoln County.

title: Maine men’s basketball team starts season with eight new players
text:
ORONO, Maine (WABI) - The Maine men’s basketball team is picked to finish eighth of nine teams in the conference preseason poll.
The Black Bears spoke about what this year’s lineup will look like with eight new players.
“We play Maine basketball. Those kind of keys are unselfish, be a team player, that’s kind of what Maine basketball is,” said Ace Flagg, sophomore forward.
“We’ll really be able to space the floor a lot more this year. We got a lot of guys that can knock down shots, hit open shots. A lot of guys that can create for others, so it’ll be similar but a little different,” said Caleb Crawford, junior guard.
“Our guards all the way through our five men, I think this team has a chance to be one of the better passing teams we’ve had. So the way we play, we really value that at a high level. Hopefully that generates some really easy looks at the rim,” said Chris Markwood, head coach.
Maine tips off the season by hosting Husson on Sun. Oct. 25 at 4:30 p.m.
The America East opener comes with a trip to Bryant on Sat. Jan. 2.
