title: Better planning could have headed off Lewiston hospital mess
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Douglas Rooks has been a Maine editor and columnist for 41 years. His biography of Gov. Ken Curtis, “Transformational,” is now available. He welcomes comment at [email protected].
The vote last week by Central Maine Medical Center nurses in Lewiston to unionize says a good deal about organizing prospects in the state, but even more about the mismanagement of Maine hospitals.
Driven by the perverse incentives of fee-for-service reimbursement, hospitals compete for a larger share of the revenue pie, ignoring opportunities for rational consolidation as care becomes increasingly specialized and high-tech.
The situation at CMMC, which has been under severe financial stress, has all the makings of a train wreck. Last year, Prime Healthcare of California, a for-profit chain, agreed to buy CMMC and formed a nonprofit subsidiary to make the acquisition — a maneuver that fooled no one. Nonetheless, the state issued a Certificate of Need approving the sale, in which Prime agreed to maintain designated staffing levels, invest in new services and — somehow — improve the financial balance sheet.
The immediate response by hospital employees? Nearly 20% of the staff resigned. Earlier this year, surgeries were briefly suspended and transferred elsewhere when the state found inadequate operating room sterilization.
The nurses’ campaign then came as no surprise — though hospital management’s response did. Just days before the union vote, Prime fired or suspended 20 nurses, most of them involved in the organizing drive, allegedly for neglecting their duties. Prime has employed similar union-busting tactics elsewhere, but it’s unprecedented in Maine hospitals.
The move drew a stern rebuke from Gov. Janet Mills, writing to Prime, “I strongly urge you to immediately reinstate every nurse who has been wrongfully fired or suspended.” To date, Prime has not responded — just as MaineHealth’s board in Portland ignored Mills’ plea, and that of the Democratic nominee for governor, Hannah Pingree, to delay closing the birthing center at Miles Memorial in Damariscotta, the 12th such closure statewide in recent years.
CMMC nurses voted 204-21 in favor of a union, a rate of 91% It followed a similarly successful effort to organize at Maine Medical Center in 2021 by the Maine Nurses Association, affiliated with National Nurses United, the third such attempt. Nurses at Northern Light Eastern Maine Medical Center in Bangor have had a union since 1976; labor will now have a seat at the management table in three of the state’s largest hospitals.
But the union campaigns reflect a larger reality — an apparent inability to adjust the state’s hospital structure to reflect changing demands for care within a community structure, as opposed to the often debilitating competition for patients and revenue.
Lewiston provides a case in point. Thirty years ago, Central Maine and St. Mary’s both had similar number of beds and budgets, and it was already clear that consolidation should be considered. Instead, CMMC embarked on an unwise expansion plan that led to the current crisis.
It briefly owned Parkview Hospital in Brunswick, which was then engaged in a highly public war of words with Mid Coast, itself a merger of hospitals in Brunswick and Bath, that ended only with Parkview’s bankruptcy. When Mid Coast took over operations, it declined to adjust or reduce any services and, overextended, had to sell to MaineHealth, which from its Portland headquarters now controls the majority of the state’s hospital services.
Or consider Waterville, where Inland, the state’s only osteopathic hospital, was closed by Northern Light last year. It’s possible it could have been saved. When the state approved the merger of Waterville’s other hospital, Mid Maine, with Augusta on the new MaineGeneral campus, it curiously allowed Waterville’s Thayer Hospital to retain a 24-hour ER, even though the facility downsized to outpatient care. Two emergency rooms in one small market vastly exceeded demand, with Inland the casualty.
Just as MaineHealth controls the majority of the state’s hospitals, under the Affordable Care Act federal and state governments have assumed the bulk of healthcare spending, well over half. This requires a larger state role in planning, and if necessary directing, the provision of services so patients and staff are protected, not forced out.
In the 1980s, the Maine Health Care Finance Authority regulated hospital charges, moderating rate increases while maintaining care standards, but was later abolished. Reviving it, while reviewing mergers and takeovers and offering alternatives, would be a good first step. The Prime Healthcare fiasco is exactly what the state must avoid repeating.
A national healthcare system, rising to prominence in this year’s campaigns, is ultimately the solution to many of our woes. The state can play an important role, however, and a new administration is the ideal place to start.

title: AARP keeps Maine members informed
text:
As someone who has spent years working in civic engagement, I have seen firsthand what happens when people understand the power of their voice and use it.
In Maine, voters 50 and older are a powerful part of that voice. In the 2024 general election, they made up more than 59% of all voters in our state. That matters, not simply because of the size of this voting bloc, but because older Mainers consistently show up and participate in our democracy.
The issues important to older voters are also issues that touch entire families and communities. Social Security, affordable healthcare, support for family caregivers, housing and the ability to age with dignity and independence affect all of us, directly or through someone we love.
That is why staying informed matters. AARP provides information to help voters understand the issues and make their own decisions at the ballot box.
Democracy works best when people participate. When voters stay informed, ask questions, speak up, and ultimately vote, elected leaders and candidates listen.
Maine’s 50-plus voters have tremendous power. Let’s continue to use that power to strengthen our communities and help build a future where people of every generation can thrive.
Pious Ali
AARP Maine Volunteer
Portland

title: MDIRSS joins national cohort studying AI in K-12 education
text:
BAR HARBOR — The Mount Desert Island Regional School System took another step in its efforts to codify a sound policy regarding the use of artificial intelligence in the classroom, becoming one of 14 new school districts and eight state-level education organizations to join a national community of practice dedicated to building clear, effective, and responsible artificial intelligence policies.
MDIRSS, along with Cape Elizabeth and the Maine State Department of Education, were recently announced as members of the 2026-2027 District and State Policy Lab cohort under the EDSAFE AI Alliance, a project of InnovateEDU. EDSAFE is a global coalition started in 2020 out of the growing need for structure surrounding AI implementation in education. The nonprofit organization works in the United States with K-12 school districts, state agencies, and policymakers, centered around its SAFE framework for AI implementation — Safety, Accountability, Fairness and transparency, and Efficacy.
“Whether a policymaker is looking at creating rules and regulations around an AI product to be used in education or a school district is looking to create an AI policy to help their students and staff use AI in their work, the SAFE framework is meant to guide that,” said Andrea Claver, the project manager for the EDSAFE AI Alliance.
The organization began with a steering committee consisting of 33 of the nation's leading AI nonprofit organizations doing policy work. But the team felt the need to connect with school districts and state agencies to better inform its work, so, in 2024, the organization launched the Policy Labs initiative to do just that. The labs are a free service, with funding provided through a multi-year grant from Google.org, that provides deep technical assistance for districts to help them create a policy stack, or a plan for AI implementation from the ground up.
“[The plans] focus on the fact that it's human-centered. It's not meant to replace human thinking, and it’s future-driven, so preparing students and staff members even for the future of work and skills that they'll need in the future,” Claver said. “But then it goes all the way up the chain through acceptable use policies, AI literacy plans, all the way to procurement, where they're really looking at the tools that they'll purchase to use within a school system.”
The EDSAFE AI Alliance Policy Lab network now encompasses 36 school districts and 15 states, impacting over 654,300 educators and millions of K-12 students across the U.S. The goal is to help school and state leaders as they face pressing questions regarding data privacy, civil rights, instructional efficacy, and ethics as generative AI rapidly reshapes the educational landscape.
“We know that AI needs to be addressed. There needs to be policy around it to protect students, to protect staff, but there also needs to be deep education around it. So, that includes AI literacy in the classroom as well as professional development for staff because it's not going away,” said Claver, “and if we just ignore it, then we're going to have another problem like we have with social media. So, our whole philosophy is that we need to address it, but we need to do it with intention, and, and we need to ground it in those pillars of the SAFE framework. Because if we're not doing it safely, if we're not naming how and who is responsible for the different pieces, and if we're not measuring efficacy — that's a huge one right now — if we're not stating how this is truly driving positive outcomes in education, then we're not doing our students justice, and they're really the ones that we need to do all of this for.”
It’s a philosophy that meshes with MDIRSS’s approach to AI so far, with the joining of the cohort by no means being the first time that anyone in the district has thought about the issue. The district formed an AI leadership team in 2023 that has spent a lot of time learning about the technology and the different tools available. It has also started to write the district's statement of beliefs about AI, which focuses on keeping humans in the lead of the technology, as well as a framework for the mindful and intentional use of AI in the learning process.
“The question now is: how do we educate all of our educators in order to educate our students about the mindful and intentional use of AI?” asked Kate Meyer, an instructional innovation specialist/ELA teacher at MDI High School. “And it's not necessarily about the technology aspect of it, like how AI works. There's a little bit of that, but it's really about how do we monitor the output for bias? We know there's bias in there, and so how do we monitor for that? How do we monitor it for accuracy? How do we, if we're going to use AI output in our work, how do we make sure that that's our own work and we're not offloading to AI? How do we reflect on our use of it, right? How do we decide if this is the right tool? So, it's really all these critical thinking questions about if we choose to engage with this tool, how do we do so, so that we are using it to push our thinking and not to offload our thinking?”
The goal for the district’s work in the cohort is to take the next step in their AI policy process, which is to craft a handbook to guide the technology's implementation. The final product will hopefully not only provide information for people who want to use the tool, but also help them understand the ethical issues behind it. The district leadership team will work on parent communication about what's happening in the schools in terms of AI literacy, how educators are talking to students about using the tool mindfully. The team will accomplish this through meetings at least once a month with other members of the cohort, in large and small groups, in order to share resources and information based on where the other entities are in their process.
If other districts already have a handbook made, MDIRSS can use it as a basis for their own. The district will be asked to share the work they have done on their statement of intent and policy framework, which are steps that some of the other members in the cohort may have yet to take. The goal is to not have individual districts continually having to “reinvent the wheel,” according to the team at EDSAFE, who will be available for regular check-ins during the year-long cohort process and beyond.
“It’s been on the minds of educators since ChatGPT came to be, and they were seeing student work come in that was clearly not their own,” Claver said of the need for policy around AI use in the classroom. “The problem is the capacity and expertise to do the work, you know, ‘where do we start? Who is the person that's going to do this?’ … So that's usually where we meet people. Either they have been asked by their board to address AI, or they just know that it's important to do so, but they're not sure where to start.”
Meyer, along with Anne Swann, the high school tech lead, and Cindy Lambert, the education technology lead for K-8, are members of the AI Leadership team and will represent the district during its work with the policy cohort. For Meyer, this represents the continuation of the work she has been doing since taking a distinguished educator position with the Maine DOE several years ago that focused on digital instructional design and digital citizenship. In the second year of that two-year program, ChatGPT came out, which shifted Meyer’s focus to AI and AI issues in education. "So, I had a great advantage that most educators don't have, which is the advantage of time,” Meyer said. “A full year really to learn the tool and to think about what it might look like in the classroom. And then when I came back to my classroom, I started implementing that work.”
What Meyer saw in the classroom after that point mirrored the country’s approach to AI, with some students who had no conversation with adults in their lives about how to use the tool appropriately and were therefore using it inappropriately, and some students who didn’t want to use it at all for various reasons. But one unifying factor Meyer said she has heard from her students is that they believe it's the job of educators to teach them how to use the tool properly.
“The first step really has to be thinking about, 'is this something that you even want to use AI for?' Is the outcome that you might get appropriate for the task that you're trying to do, like, do you want to use AI to write a letter to your grandma, or should you probably do that yourself?” Meyer said. “And then, 'is this an ethical use of AI?' So, before you even touch the tool, it's really thinking about, 'is this the best tool for the task?' Because it's just a tool that sometimes is really helpful, and sometimes it's not the right tool at all. And that can be applied, you know, the, the national conversation or the global conversation about screen time … If we're going to do a task and I say, ‘Let's pull out our laptops,’ then you're trusting that I have decided that that's the right tool for the task. When sometimes I say, 'Hey, pull out a pencil and your notebooks,’ it’s because that's the right tool for the task. So this is just one more tool in the toolbox as far as I'm concerned.”
A big issue facing schools is that the tool itself is evolving faster than any learning tool has before, necessitating constant relearning by educators who have enough to focus on in the classroom as it is. Joining the cohort is expected to help the district keep up with the latest guidance on AI by putting them in constant contact with professionals in the field and other districts, but MDIRSS’s main antidote to the rapid advancement of AI tools is to take it slow.
“The district AI leadership team, is focused on not getting caught up in the hype of whatever the next new big thing might be in AI, but really being very intentional about what it is that we want from this tool and how to get that from the tool, and then choosing tools that are safe,” Meyer explained.
The AI leadership team does not currently have many tools that it recommends everybody use, according to Meyer. Right now, the district is using Google Suite because it is connected to its Google workspace. The team also recommends Magic School, because Magic School has safety guardrails for educators and students, so data and privacy is 100% protected. The chatbots on the student-facing side are specifically trained to not act as companion chatbots, said Meyer, which are chatbots that interact with humans as if they are a friend or a partner.
“We’re finding tools that are here to support teaching and learning and not for any other use,” Meyer said. “I think the most important thing for the community to understand about the district's approach is that we are really approaching it with curiosity, but also with caution. And to understand that there is a team of people who are informed by educator and student voices on what that might look like, but that we are not trying to barrel ahead and use AI in places where it's not appropriate.”

title: Sen. King bill could speed up, reduce costs for some affordable housing projects
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
For more than a year, affordable housing developers in Maine have been wrestling with the requirements of a federal rule that they say is burying them in paperwork and making construction impossible.
Sen. Angus King thinks he can help.
On Wednesday, Maine’s independent senator introduced the Build American Efficiency Act, a bill encouraging the federal government to work with manufacturers on a publicly available database of certified American-made products that would meet the requirements of the Build America Buy America Act.
Also known as BABA, the program requires all building projects using certain government funds to source 95% of their construction materials from the United States.
Developers have said the administrative burden of simply tracking down domestic materials has been extreme and adds as much as $150,000 per project – and that’s not including the premium costs for American-made materials.
“It’s a perfect example of a well-meaning policy that turned out to have negative consequences,” King said in an interview Thursday. “You’ve got hundreds, if not thousands, of builders, each individually trying to sort through this maze, and now what our bill would do (is) create a simple, easy-to-access database so that they don’t have to do that.”
‘EXTENSIVE’ CHANGES NEEDED
The proposal, co-sponsored by Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, is a step in the right direction, but Laura Mitchell, executive director of the Maine Affordable Housing Coalition, said developers need more than a database to help projects move forward.
“BABA is really clogging the affordable housing development pipeline,” she said. “We’re really grateful for Sen. King being creative, and trying to find shortcut pathways to make it easier to comply with BABA, (but) this bill doesn’t offer the extensive level of changes that are needed.”
The National Electrical Manufacturer’s Association, identified in the bill as a possible standard to use, has the “Make It American BABA Registry,” which has a list of 68 manufacturing facilities spread across 15 companies that are certified to make 50-or-so products.
But compared to the roughly 1,600 parts that go into an affordable housing project, the few dozen products that are on that registry don’t carry much impact.
Mitchell said the Make it American system simply hasn’t certified enough products.
“There’s still going to be a lot of work put on these nonprofit affordable housing developers,” she said.
King, however, believes they can get certifications for all the hundreds, if not thousands of pieces.
“I think AI might help us on this,” he added.
THE WAIVER WAIT
For materials unavailable from American manufacturers, like HVAC systems or their components, developers can request a waiver from the Department of Housing and Urban Development.
And then they wait. And wait.
Laura Reading, director of affordable housing for Portland-based Developers Collaborative, waited for more than seven months for waivers for her two projects in Portland and Windham.
Both projects are set to close this month, but Reading found out last week that the waiver for her Portland project, a 110-spot childcare center for Youth and Family Outreach and 60 units of housing, needs to be resubmitted because it only covers funding from MaineHousing, not additional money from the city.
She’s hopeful it will be fast-tracked but noted that HUD has not given her a timeline.
A database wouldn’t help Reading’s current projects, but she said she could see one being useful in the future.
“The documentation for all of this has been a bit insane because all of these vendors want to use their own form and their own letter (of certification),” she said. “Some of them are not as clear as we need them to be.”
King said the list could also help speed up the waiver process, allowing HUD to more easily check whether something is available domestically and quickly approve or deny the request.
Reading added that it could potentially help HUD identify what products aren’t yet made in the U.S. (like an HVAC) system and create a universal waiver so developers aren’t forced to wait months for an approval on the same item for every project.
‘THE SILVER BULLET’
A general waiver is one of a handful of “administrative” changes that Mitchell, at the Maine Affordable Housing Coalition, said would be the most consequential. She’s hopeful to see HUD come out with one for HVAC by the end of the year.
Alternatively (or additionally), HUD could increase the allowable percentage of foreign materials from 5% to 10% or 15%. Or it could exempt affordable housing from BABA altogether.
“That would be the silver bullet addressing all of this,” Mitchell said.
The “Build Housing Affordably Act,” proposed in the House, would do so temporarily, while also instituting a 90-day window for waiver approvals.
Maine is one of the first states to come up against the BABA requirements, and affordable housing developers that have had their projects halted indefinitely are pushing to get the issue fixed before it spreads across the country.
Housing has recently become a bipartisan issue and King is optimistic that the bill can make it through Congress without any major setbacks and be enacted by the end of the year.

title: More than a dozen sickened in parasite outbreak linked to hotel pool, health officials say
text:
BOTHELL, Wash. (KPTV/Gray News) — Public health officials say more than a dozen people were sickened by a parasite linked to a hotel swimming pool.
Health officials in King County shared that an investigation was opened earlier this summer after 14 people reported falling ill after swimming in the pool at McMenamins Anderson School, an entertainment destination and boutique hotel built inside a converted junior high school, in late August.
The investigation found that an outbreak of cryptosporidiosis was linked to the hotel pool, with laboratory tests confirming the illness was caused by cryptosporidium, a microscopic parasite.
Those who were sickened were said to have symptoms such as diarrhea, stomach cramps, nausea and fever that started days after visiting the pool area.
Investigators suspect the parasite spread when an infected swimmer entered the pool.
Officials noted that the facility was well-maintained, followed all county health and safety regulations, and had no violations during a September inspection.
But because the microscopic parasite is highly chlorine-resistant, it can survive in properly treated pools for several days.
No hospitalizations or deaths were reported in this case, with Washington health officials saying the outbreak now appears to be over.
Cryptosporidium was also the parasite that caused an outbreak of explosive diarrhea across the U.S. also earlier this year.
Health officials emphasized that swimmers should avoid public pools for at least two weeks after recovering from diarrhea or vomiting and should shower with soap before swimming.

title: Bobby Charles has received lobbyist money. But he’s trying to make an ‘Augusta’ distinction.
text:
He may run a firm that has lobbied in Washington, D.C., since the turn of the century, but in his bid to become Maine’s next governor, Republican Bobby Charles has said he is rejecting money from “Augusta lobbyists.”
Charles first made that pledge in June, when he called on Democrat Hannah Pingree and independent Rick Bennett to join him in also not accepting donations from Central Maine Power or “AI data center companies.”
He has occasionally left out the “Augusta” distinction, such as during an interview this summer. But he reiterated it in his latest digital ad, released Wednesday, in which he calls Augusta a “crime scene” and accuses Pingree and her family of profiting off her years leading Gov. Janet Mills’ policy and innovation office.
“I’m the only candidate in this race who has rejected Augusta lobbyist money,” Charles says in the ad.
But Charles has received money from lobbyists who live outside of Maine. He has received more than $13,000 in donations from current or former lobbyists and their family members, according to campaign finance records.
Still, Charles’ campaign, which has raised more than $1.8 million since launching last year, reiterated Wednesday that lobbyist donations to his campaign have not come from “Augusta lobbyists.”
That pledge has not changed the fact that Pingree, a former Maine House speaker from North Haven, has consistently led Charles by double digits in independent polling of the race to succeed Mills, a Democrat who is termed out of office after this year. Additionally, Charles has not received help from the Republican Governors Association in the form of ad spending — a sign that national leaders do not view the Maine race as very competitive.
Scrutiny over campaign donations across Maine’s high-profile races for the Blaine House, U.S. Senate and 2nd Congressional District is nothing new, though it ticked up this week when Pingree’s campaign said it would return $300 it received earlier this year from a former attorney for Jeffrey Epstein after the Portland Press Herald asked for comment on the donation.
Charles’ firm, The Charles Group, has lobbied on Capitol Hill for decades, though the Leeds lawyer and former assistant U.S. secretary of state says it mostly focuses on conducting studies, providing management guidance and evaluating performance for clients. Charles’ lobbying ties drew criticism even from his Republican primary opponents earlier this year, including Jonathan Bush, who dubbed him “Lobby Charles.”
Campaign finance records show he received contributions such as $4,150 from Van Hipp Jr. and his wife. Hipp Jr., a former South Carolina Republican Party chair, has a lobbying role as chair of American Defense International, a Washington-based consulting firm.
Among other donors, Rob Hartwell, a Virginia-based lobbyist and former chief of staff to several Republican members of Congress, chipped in $250. Bob Carlstrom, a former lobbyist who joined Charles in serving in former President Ronald Reagan’s administration, gave Charles more than $2,600. And Barry Caldwell, a former lobbyist for Cigna and other firms, donated $1,000.
Bennett, a former Maine Republican Party chair and state senator from Oxford who has been mired in the single digits in polls, and Pingree, who previously led Mills’ policy office and is the daughter of Democratic U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, mostly wrote off Charles’ pledge as performative. Each of them has received donations from people who work for lobbying firms that operate in Augusta, such as Preti Flaherty and Mitchell Tardy Jackson.
The lobbyist donations are not the only point of contention among the candidates. The Maine Democratic Party filed a complaint Thursday morning with the state’s ethics commission against Charles. The complaint said Charles reported 46 contributions totaling more than $25,000 over the legal contribution limit, including donors who gave thousands of dollars more than the $2,075 maximum amount allowed under law.
Charles gave the similar “no Augusta lobbyist” donations line in a campaign ad he released last week, featuring him and his daughter walking by apple trees while referring to Mills and Pingree as “Augusta’s bad apples.”
While not producing TV ads like Pingree, who has led the field in raising more than $4.2 million, Charles has projected confidence at his chances after he also used an array of lower-budget digital ads and social media videos to win a crowded Republican primary in June.
The three gubernatorial candidates will face off Thursday evening in a debate hosted by the Maine State Chamber of Commerce at Cross Insurance Arena in Portland.

title: Eligible low-income CMP and Versant customers to get automatic discounts
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Eligible low-income CMP and Versant customers will receive automatic discounts, Gov. Mills says
Maine Gov. Janet Mills announced Thursday that eligible low-income customers of Central Maine Power and Versant Power will soon begin receiving automatic discounts on their electric bill.
Mills said that starting Thursday, the Maine Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) will use existing information from programs such as the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) and MaineCare to identify households that qualify for $40 million in electric discounts through Maine's Low Income Assistance Program (LIAP).
Beneficiaries will have their information securely shared with participating utilities, which will automatically apply discounts to their monthly electric bills. Households participating in the federally funded Home Energy Assistance Program (HEAP) will also automatically be enrolled in LIAP through a secure information sharing arrangement facilitated by MaineHousing.
The discount amounts vary by income, but a Central Maine Power customer could receive a monthly discount between 25% and 81% off of their monthly bill. Versant Power customers could see a monthly discount between 17% and 83%. The Office of the Public Advocate created fact sheets for CMP and Versant customers on the breakdown of discounts.
"Maine families are being pushed to the brink by the president's whipsaw tariffs and his reckless war in Iran. At a time when every dollar matters, my administration is making it easier for vulnerable Mainers to lower their electric bills without unnecessary paperwork or bureaucratic hurdles," Mills said in a statement. "I thank Maine's Public Advocate, Public Utilities Commission, the Department of Health and Human Services, MaineHousing, and Maine's electric utilities for their partnership to make this automatic enrollment possible."
LIAP funds were applied to a customer's bill as a lump sum in previous years, meaning that customers might be hit with higher bills at the end of the winter. Funds will now be applied by CMP and Versant as a monthly discount, while LIAP participants who get their power from Maine's smaller consumer-owned utilities will continue to have their discount applied as a lump sum.
To qualify for LIAP, customers must have household income at or below 150% of the federal poverty guidelines or be eligible for HEAP.
Returning LIAP participants who were enrolled as a result of participating in a DHHS program do not need to do anything to enroll, but officials said they should pay close attention to their electric bills to ensure their discount has been applied.
Mainers who do not participate in a DHHS program can apply for LIAP through their local Community Action Agency.
Officials said returning LIAP participants who were enrolled through a Community Action Agency should contact their local agency again to apply.
Because electric bills do not always follow the calendar month, eligible customers should expect to see discounts take effect on or soon after their November bill. Customers who have questions about their discount or enrollment should contact their electric company.
Mills said the arrangement for the automatic discounts is part of SupportLink, a new administration initiative through DHHS that will securely connect eligible Maine households with discounts and relief programs they may qualify for, unless they have otherwise opted out. SupportLink currently includes nine electric utilities, Efficiency Maine and the Portland Water District. The governor said there are plans to expand the program to include additional services and benefits over time.

title: Robert H. B. Cox (1931-2026)
Ex-officer Amber Guyger convicted of murdering neighbor in his own home granted parole after 7 years
text:
(AP) - The white Dallas police officer convicted of killing a Black man in his apartment that she mistook for her own was granted parole Thursday after serving seven years of her 10-year sentence.
The Texas Board of Pardons and Parole, which is appointed by Gov. Greg Abbott, rejected Amber Guyger’s initial parole request in 2024 but approved her case over the objections of victim Botham Jean ‘s family the first time she was eligible for release.
Guyger, 38, was convicted of murder in the 2018 killing of 26-year-old Jean, an accountant from the Caribbean island nation of St. Lucia, who had been eating a bowl of ice cream when Guyger entered his home and shot him. Guyger was arrested three days after the shooting and was fired before her murder trial.
She had faced up to life in prison or as little as two years. Prosecutors initially asked the jury for a sentence of 28 years.
The shooting drew widespread attention because of the strange circumstances and because it was one in a string of shootings of Black men by white police officers. Guyger’s sentencing hearing also included a stunning courtroom scene when Jean’s brother and the Black judge presiding over the case embraced the sobbing Guyger.
At trial, Guyger said that after a long shift at work and still in uniform, she walked up to Jean’s apartment — which was on the fourth floor, directly above hers on the third — and found the door unlocked. She said she thought the apartment was her own and that Jean was an intruder when she drew her service weapon and entered.
Civil rights attorney Lee Merritt said Thursday that Jean’s family “strongly opposed this parole.”
“They stood up again and again to ask that the full sentence be served. A 10-year sentence was already a fraction of what was lost. Releasing Ms. Guyger after seven years makes that loss feel even smaller in the eyes of the system. It is not smaller,” Merritt said.
In 2024, a jury ordered Guyger to pay Jean’s family nearly $100 million in a federal civil trial.
In granting her release, the board said it reviewed a “plethora” of information in her case.
The board said Guyger’s record did not include a documented pattern of violent or assaultive arrests or convictions, and showed she completed programs in her prison treatment plan to get and keep a job when she is released.
The board said the state prison system will determine when she is released. Texas Department of Criminal Justice officials did not immediately respond to requests for comment Thursday.

title: Lethal drug that failed to execute Christa Pike was already under scrutiny
text:
(AP) - The lethal drug administered in Tennessee’s failed attempt to execute Christa Pike has been used in multiple states that carry out the death penalty and by the U.S. government after President Donald Trump resumed federal executions during his first term.
Pike, 50, remained alive Wednesday after two doses of pentobarbital were administered, according to her attorneys and media witnesses. On Thursday afternoon, her legal team confirmed that she was still alive and receiving “life-saving medical care.”
Tennessee officials haven’t explained yet what went wrong.
Republican Gov. Bill Lee ordered a third-party review to determine what happened and said another scheduled execution in Tennessee will not take place this year.
What is pentobarbital?
Pentobarbital is a barbiturate, a class of drugs that depresses the central nervous system.
Approved medical uses include sedation, short-term treatment of insomnia, preparation for anesthesia and emergency control of certain severe seizures. It is also used in veterinary euthanasia.
In an overdose, it can produce coma, suppress breathing and cause circulatory collapse and death.
Why is it used in executions?
For years, lethal injections commonly used three drugs: an anesthetic, a paralytic that stopped breathing and potassium chloride to stop the heart.
That method drew criticism because if the anesthetic failed, the paralytic could prevent a prisoner from communicating pain. It also became difficult to maintain after drugmakers restricted distribution for executions.
The pentobarbital protocol was adopted at the federal level during Trump’s first term to replace a three-drug mix used in the 2000s.
As with Tennessee’s guidelines, the federal death penalty protocol calls for administering a 5-gram dose of pentobarbital; in medical settings, patients typically receive a fraction of a gram.
Trump resumed the federal death penalty after an informal moratorium during previous administrations. The federal government used pentobarbital in 13 executions between 2020 and 2021, contributing to making Trump the most prolific execution president in over 130 years.
During the Biden administration, the Justice Department stopped executions with pentobarbital after a government review raised concerns about the potential for “unnecessary pain and suffering.”
After Trump came back to power, the Justice Department in 2026 reauthorized the use of lethal injections with pentobarbital.
How do guidelines vary in different states?
Georgia and Texas use a similar protocol to Tennessee, administering a second dose only if the first is unsuccessful. South Carolina, which turned to pentobarbital in 2024, automatically gives inmates two 5-gram doses spaced about 10 minutes apart.
Lawyers for people on death row have argued that giving such a large dose twice was proof the condemned were dying a lingering death, still conscious and feeling like they were drowning when fluid rushed into their lungs.
But a South Carolina Department of Corrections attorney said inmates are unconscious in well under a minute and can’t feel anything. The heart may show an occasional flicker on a monitor, but that’s because it is the last organ to use the body’s stored oxygen and has residual electrical impulses.
When past lethal injection executions have gone wrong, it is usually because an IV line can’t be properly inserted and the execution is stopped before the drugs are given. There have also been cases of violent reactions or prolonged time passing before death when a new combination of drugs is used.
Wednesday’s failed pentobarbital execution appeared to be the first time problems happened with that drug. Witnesses frequently report that inmates stop breathing and become still less than a minute after getting the drug.
What have experts said about the drug?
Experts quoted in the 2025 federal review argue pentobarbital can cause pulmonary edema, a buildup of fluid in the lungs that may create a sensation of suffocating.
The review concluded that “there remains significant uncertainty about whether the use of pentobarbital as a single drug lethal injection causes unnecessary pain and suffering” and advised that the government should “err on the side of humane treatment.”
Other specialists quoted in a report released by the second Trump administration said a lethal dose causes unconsciousness before that occurs.
Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

title: Doctor in Christa Pike execution tied to earlier botched lethal injection
text:
NASHVILLE, TENN. (WSMV/WVLT/Gray News) - The doctor who oversaw Christa Gail Pike’s lethal injection was also involved in another botched execution earlier this year.
Pike was still alive after being administered a lethal injection, according to Luke Ihnen, an assistant federal defender on her defense team.
Ihnen confirmed that Pike had received two syringes of a lethal drug and said the team is filing a motion to stay the execution.
According to the motion, Pike did not lose consciousness and still had a heartbeat after receiving the lethal injection. It was reported that she was also audibly snoring.
The motion mentioned that the curtains went down twice.
Pike’s defense team had argued during a three-day hearing in August that she had a vein condition, which would make finding a vein to administer the lethal drug difficult.
Mark Fowler, the doctor who oversaw Pike’s botched execution, was also involved in the attempted execution of Tony Carruthers. His execution was abandoned in May after medical staff failed to establish IV access, a process that took more than an hour.
The petition filed by Pike’s attorneys is requesting an immediate stay of Pike’s execution and immediate medical care for her.
Her attorneys released a statement late Wednesday night that said Pike is being treated at a nearby hospital.
“Tonight the State of Tennessee once again failed to carry out a lawful execution,” they said. “We take no pleasure in being right, but the concerns raised by Ms. Pike proved to be true: difficult vein access, blown veins, degraded pentobarbital, no emergency medical care available when things inevitably go wrong, all under a protocol that remains veiled in secrecy.”
As of Wednesday night, they said they had not been informed about her condition.
Less than an hour before Pike was originally supposed to be executed at 11 a.m. Wednesday, the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals granted a stay pausing her execution. That prompted a response from the state, which asked the U.S. Supreme Court to intervene and allow the execution to continue.
The Supreme Court lifted the stay just before 7 p.m., which set in motion Pike’s execution.
Pike was found guilty in 1996 of the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer on the University of Tennessee campus.
Pike, along with 17-year-old Tadaryl Shipp and 18-year-old Shadolla Peterson, planned Slemmer’s torture and killing. The case later became known as the Job Corps Murder because both Pike and Slemmer were members of Job Corps at the time.
There’s no word on what the state’s next steps will be in Pike’s planned execution.
Her botched execution appears to be the latest failed attempt by the state of Tennessee to execute an inmate on death row. The state’s death penalty procedure has faced past scrutiny after botched executions prompted a pause from Gov. Bill Lee.
That said, Tennessee did successfully execute an inmate in August. Anthony Darrell Hines was executed at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville for the 1985 murder of Catherine Jean Jackson Jenkins.

title: Maine gubernatorial hopefuls trade barbs in first televised debate
text:
The first televised debate between the three candidates vying to become Maine’s next governor featured several testy exchanges, many of which involved Republican Bobby Charles.
The hourlong debate, hosted by the Maine Chamber of Commerce and moderated by News Center Maine, sought to cover a wide range of topics, including taxes, state revenue, housing, substance use, energy costs and healthcare. But moderators had trouble keeping the candidates on topic and within their allotted time.
The forum was an opportunity for Charles and independent Rick Bennett to shake up a race in which Democrat Hannah Pingree has been the clear front-runner in polling and fundraising.
Bennett, a longtime Republican who unenrolled from the party when he entered the race in June, repeatedly went after Charles, accusing him of not understanding the state budgeting process, and attacking his record serving in the U.S. State Department under President George W. Bush.
“It’s hard to digest all I’ve just heard here, particularly from Bobby Charles,” Bennett, 63, said about 20 minutes into the debate in response to a question about state spending.
“He just doesn’t simply understand how the fiscal process works, which doesn’t surprise me because inspector generals and auditors at the federal government cited him dozens of times for mismanagement of federal spending.”
Bennett was referring to a Bangor Daily News article about how federal audits raised concerns about poor management, spending and ineffectiveness during Charles’ 18-month tenure leading the Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs.
“The Bangor Daily News doesn’t always report the facts,” Charles shot back. “We showed them, ‘Hey, here is the unbelievable record,’ and they decided that they’re gonna take the little paragraph down here that didn’t look like it was the best paragraph.”
Charles, meanwhile, portrayed himself as a political outsider. He said Bennett and Pingree are part of the current political system that has led to the present affordability and housing crises. And he said he’d use his experience as a former investigator to conduct a top-to-bottom review of state agencies to root out fraud and waste.
“I find it ironic that two people who’ve served both 30 years and 25 years are saying that we need to fix the system,” Charles said.
After one exchange, Pingree, who was flanked by both men, said, “This is why we need women in charge.” The line drew laughter and applause from the audience.
Throughout the night, Pingree and Bennett tried to put Charles on the defensive.
At one point, Pingree referred to Bennett as “my friend.” She later called out Charles’ previous work as a federal lobbyist and repeatedly highlighted his support for President Donald Trump, whose low approval rating is creating headwinds for Republicans across the county.
“(Charles is) somebody who has supported Donald Trump at every turn,” Pingree said. “His tariffs, his war in Iran, his big, beautiful bill that has cut our healthcare system. We’re facing economic headwinds because of this president.”
Later, Charles, a 66-year-old Leeds lawyer and former assistant U.S. secretary of state, sought to distance himself from Trump on tariffs and the Iran war.
“I have been very clear, at the outset, that the hitting of the nuclear program was great (but), I do not agree with him right now, in terms of the extended engagement over there,” Charles said about Iran. “I’ve never met the guy (Trump), but I have appealed publicly that we need to get back to the negotiating table and get tariffs down.”
It’s unclear whether the debate will change the trajectory of the race.
Pingree, a 49-year-old Democrat from North Haven who led a policy office under Gov. Janet Mills and is the daughter of U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, has held a steady lead in both fundraising and polling.
Pingree led Charles 48% to 36% in a New York Times/Portland Press Herald/Siena poll released last week, while Bennett drew 8%.
The Democrat has a significant money advantage as well. She has raised more than $4.3 million, compared to Charles’ $1.8 million and Bennett’s nearly $924,000.
The candidates will meet for three more debates, including one Thursday hosted by Maine Public, News Center Maine and the Portland Press Herald. WGME CBS 13 will host a debate on Oct. 13, followed by WMTW the next day.

title: Lincoln Academy golf wins tight battle for KVAC B title, state bid
text:
ROCKLAND — Considered the favorites to win the Kennebec Valley Athletic Conference Class B Shootout, the Lincoln Academy golf team had to work for it Thursday.
In the end, the Eagles did prevail, beating out Nokomis and Medomak Valley to win the conference title at Rockland Golf Club. The win secured Lincoln a spot in the Class B championships next Saturday at Natanis Golf Course in Vassalboro.
“Our boys have had a great season — they really have — and they did excellent today,” said Lincoln coach Todd Brackett. “Nokomis has a really good team, and they beat us in the regular season. Medomak, we have a good rivalry with them. We knew it was going to be close.”
Lincoln’s top-four players shot a combined nine-hole score of 162, beating out the Warriors (166) and the Panthers (167) in a tight battle for first. Belfast (181), Leavitt (183) and Erskine Academy (188) rounded out the team scoring.
Lincoln junior Drew Nichols (38) shot the second-best score of the day, finishing a stroke behind medalist Caden Chretien of Nokomis (37). Colin Mitchell shot a 39 for the Eagles to tie Medomak Valley’s Seb Mank and Joseph Wilcox for third.
“My short game was really solid,” Nichols said. “Off the tee, I was a little iffy — I actually topped my driver twice, so that was interesting — but with how good my short game was, I was able to get around the golf course. … I had a really rough go of it this season, so I’m glad I brought it around here.”
Max Blake added a 41 for Lincoln, while Dylan Lomas shot a 44. That was enough to outduel Nokomis, which also got a 42 from Atticus Haining, a 43 from Will Hayes and a 44 from Jake Paradis, and Medomak Valley, which got a 44 from Andrew Flanders and a 45 from Wyatt Hood.
“If anybody was going to steal it from us today, I thought it was going to be Medomak,” Brackett said. “Like I said, we just played great today. It was a good day for us out there.”
A warm October day that saw temperatures reach the upper 60s even on the coast made for an enjoyable round of golf. The winds from earlier in the week had largely subsided, though some stiffer gusts did arrive later into the afternoon.
Medomak Valley had the fortune of playing the round on its home course, though coach Kevin Richardson pointed out that changing greens throughout the week mitigated that advantage. Richardson, too, said the three-way race between Medomak Valley, Lincoln and Nokomis played out as expected.
“In all 10 regular-season matches that we played (until today), we had the medalist, which shows you that Lincoln and Nokomis both have some really good players,” Richardson said. “We played well all year, and I had a feeling we were going to play well today. We did, but it just wasn’t quite enough.”
Nokomis, Medomak Valley, Belfast, Leavitt and Erskine will still get chances to book berths at states at the KVAC qualifier Tuesday at Natanis. Lincoln can rest easy that its state championship participation is assured, though Nichols said the Eagles’ absence Tuesday will also have some drawbacks.
“We’d like to go to the qualifier to get that extra round in, but it’s also quite the plus that we get to have that auto-bid,” Nichols said. “We’re a good group of guys that play a lot and put the work in over the summer, so it feels great.”
Jason Thurston of Belfast tied for seventh individually, shooting a 42. James Brisson shot a 44 to lead Leavitt, while Blake Morrow and Nolan Pierce also shot 44s to lead Erskine.

title: Americans are using buy now, pay later more than ever. Here’s what to know if you’re one of them
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Americans spent more than $160 billion last year using buy now, pay later plans, according to research published by Federal Reserve economists.
Experts say they’re increasingly seeing people use the plans for everyday expenses like groceries, bills, transportation and, sometimes rent.
“It has been very hard out there for a lot of people,” said Sara Rathner, NerdWallet’s credit card expert. “It’s a tough job market, and it’s a rough economy, and the cost of the things that we buy every day has been going up, in some cases more than people’s incomes.”
Pay-in-four plans, which generally allow consumers to pay for purchases in four installments over six weeks, accounted for about half of the $160 billion in buy now, pay later spending last year, according to the study. Use of those plans has increased nearly 80% since 2023.
The rest of the plans were either longer- or shorter-term loans.
How consumers are using buy now pay later
When Elizabeth Brown first used buy now, pay later, she had just started living by herself and was earning a salary that made it hard to afford basic expenses. She would buy groceries and, once she got her paycheck, pay for them through buy now, pay later. Six years later, things haven’t changed much.
“I used buy now, pay later so I can have the furniture I need. I have groceries in my fridge because of it. I don’t necessarily feel shameful for using it because at the end it’s very beneficial to me at this point of my life,” said Brown, 26, of Columbia, South Carolina, who works as a clinical service member at an optical store.
Buy now, pay later products have evolved. Rent now, pay later services are one form, which break rent into multiple payments.
“It isn’t really just a convenience element anymore; it really is becoming a cash flow challenge,” said Mark Elliott, chief customer officer at Happen Bank, a financial services company formerly known as Lending Club.
Jordan Williams, 28, first used buy now, pay later to get concert tickets to Hozier. Then, when she experienced financial hardship after her daughter was born, she started leaning on it to pay for some of her groceries.
“There’s just not a lot of resources, and that makes me angry because this shouldn’t be something I have to do,” said Williams, a lecturer and content creator from Greensboro, North Carolina. ”We should be able to just afford groceries. I feel angry and then I feel embarrassed.”
For a long time, Williams felt ashamed about having to use buy now, pay later for basic expenses. She now feels less alone after talking with other people who also have debt.
If you’re going to use buy now, pay later plans, here are some expert recommendations:
Read the fine print
The most well-known buy now, pay later product is pay-in-four, where you can pay back what you owe in four payments, one every two weeks, with a 0% annual percentage rate, or APR. However, not every buy now, pay later loan has the same terms. Before you commit to buying something using buy now, pay later, Ed deHaan, a professor at the Stanford Graduate School of Business, recommends that you read your contract carefully.
“So-called buy now, pay later products are popping up that are not good deals at all,” deHaan said. “Some of them charge hefty fees, both upfront and if you miss a payment.”
In general, if you miss a buy now, pay later payment, you can face fees, interest or the possibility of being banned from using the services in the future.
Know how it impacts your credit score
In the past, buy now, pay later loans didn’t impact your credit score, but that has changed. Buy now, pay later agencies now report credit lending activity to one of the three major credit bureaus, Equifax, Experian and TransUnion.
“Entering into a buy now, pay later plan for now isn’t going to affect your credit in any way, but missing a payment can, so that’s where you really want to be careful,” Rathner said.
Credit reporting depends on the company and its policies. For example, both Affirm and Klarna report to Experian and TransUnion. Afterpay does not report to any credit bureau.
Only borrow what you can pay back
Before purchasing something with buy now, pay later, deHaan recommends pausing to consider whether it’s an amount you can pay back.
“The general advice for credit is that it’s very easy to spend and hard to pay off,” deHaan said. “And most of us, many of us, are not good at making good predictions about what we will be able to pay in the future.”
When using buy now, pay later, Brown set herself a limit of $100 a month across payments, and she avoids signing up for payments every two weeks and instead chooses the monthly payment options.
Avoid stacking plans
As with credit cards, you can sign up for multiple buy now, pay later plans. These loans can quickly balloon until they become unmanageable. If you don’t want to risk snowballing into debt, avoid stacking buy-now, pay later loans, said Carla Sanchez-Adams, senior attorney at the National Consumer Law Center.
“Avoid multiple purchases because then it gets really hard to track, especially if they’re with different companies,” Sanchez-Adams said.
If you have to utilize multiple loans, make sure you keep track of the payment amounts and dates so you avoid late fees, she added.
Seek out additional resources
Looking into additional resources such as food banks, SNAP or hardship help programs in your area can be helpful, Rathner said.
“If you are stretched thin for affording food and going into debt to do so, it could be time to seek out additional help,” she said. “So this is hopefully less of a struggle for you and your family while you’re going through this difficult time.”
Seek help from a nonprofit credit counseling agency
If you’ve reached a point where you have too many buy now, pay later loans and maybe some credit card debt too, it might be time to seek help from a credit counseling agency. Two well-known resources for finding nonprofit credit counseling agencies are the National Foundation for Credit Counseling and the Financial Counseling Association of America. Both can help you connect with certified agencies and counselors.
“You have financial stress, you have work stress, you have family stress,” Rathner said. “Get help with the financial stress because that can help you feel more in control of this area of your life. And it can help take one step at a time toward paying down your debts and feeling more in control.”

title: Older Mainers leaning toward Susan Collins in US Senate race, AARP poll shows
text:
A new battleground poll released by the AARP shows Democrat Troy Jackson with a narrow lead over Republican Susan Collins in Maine’s U.S. Senate race.
Jackson holds a 3 percentage point lead over Collins, 50% to 47%, which is within the survey’s margin of error of 3.1%.
But Jackson is trailing Collins among an important segment of Maine’s electorate — voters over 50 who are more likely to split their tickets than vote along party lines.
And Jackson is underperforming fellow Democrat Hannah Pingree, who holds a 13 percentage point lead over Republican Bobby Charles, 52% to 39%, in the governor’s race. Independent Rick Bennett drew 6%.
The survey of 982 likely voters was conducted from Sept. 20-22 by Fabrizio Ward and Impact Research. It offers insight into how older Mainers, who are among the most reliable voters in the state, are leaning in Maine’s closely watched race between Collins and Jackson.
The survey is further evidence that Collins remains a formidable opponent in a midterm cycle that is expected to be difficult for Republicans nationally, with President Donald Trump’s approval ratings at historic lows.
The AARP poll found that 61% of respondents disapproved of Trump’s job performance, while 37% approved. And 53% preferred Democrats on the generic congressional ballot, compared to the 43% for Republicans.
Maine’s older voters, Fabrizio Ward partner Bob Ward said, are “highly engaged. They’re paying attention and they’re looking for candidates who understand the issues that affect their daily lives.”
The top issue for all voters surveyed was affordability (44%). It was cited as the top issue by 33% of voters 50 and older, who said their main concerns were the price of gas and groceries.
Among older voters, 93% said they would be more likely to vote for a candidate that makes sure workers get the Social Security benefits they earned, 85% for someone who would protect the program from cuts and oppose increasing the retirement age, and 84% for someone who would lower the cost of healthcare and prescription drugs.
The poll found that voters 50 and older, who the AARP said comprised 60% or more of turnout in the last two federal election cycles, are breaking toward Collins and Pingree.
Collins holds a 9-point advantage among these older voters, about 20% of whom planned to split their tickets. Among these swing voters, Collins holds a 53-point advantage, while Pingree holds a 28-point advantage over Charles.
Bennett, meanwhile, drew 32% support among older swing voters in the governor’s race.
“It just speaks to how Sen. Collins is a different kind of Republican,” Ward said. “(She) maintains her base, but also reaches out to the center. This is going to be a really close race.”
Jackson holds a roughly two point lead over Collins, according to polling averages from the election website FiftyPlusOne.
A New York Times/Portland Press Herald/Siena poll conducted around the same time as the AARP’s survey found Collins with a 3 point lead over Jackson, 49% to 46%, which was also within the margin of error of +/- 4.9%.
That poll also found swing voters breaking toward Collins, including 8% of respondents that identified as Democrats.
The five-term Republican drew 13% support from people saying they wanted Democrats to won control the Senate, and 12% from people who voted for Democrat Kamala Harris for president in 2024.
The survey also found that Collins held a commanding leading among respondents aged 45-64. She led Jackson among that group 57% to 38%. But they practically split the 65 and over vote, with Jackson getting 48% to Collins’s 47%.
Both the NYT/Press Herald/ Siena and AARP polls were conducted before ProPublica reported that the Department of Justice and Federal Bureau of Investigation had been gearing up for bribery and corruption probe aimed at determining whether Collins was steering federal contracts to a defense contractor in exchange for political donations. That effort was dropped when Trump took office in 2025.
Collins has “vigorously” denied the allegations.

title: Chellie Pingree’s going after Trump. Why are so few of us listening?
text:
Hardly anyone seems to be paying attention to the increasingly sharp and powerful case made by Rep. Chellie Pingree against President Trump. They should.
Pingree, a Democrat who represents Maine’s 1st District, rips into Trump daily on an astonishing variety of issues, never mincing words. The House representative has been more or less screaming about the importance of saving America while we still can.
Consider just a handful of her many comments in the past two months.:
On corruption: “Trump’s personal wealth has ballooned by more than $2 billion in just the past 18 months, thanks to a combination of insider trading, shady crypto schemes, and brazen backroom deals. He’s the most corrupt president in history — and it ain’t close.”
On farming: “Trump says he wants to help American farmers but then plans to flood the American market with foreign beef. There is nothing ‘America First’ about his dumbass plan.”
On using tax money for campaign ads: “Let’s be clear: It is ILLEGAL to pay for campaign ads with taxpayer money. Period. … He really does see himself as above silly things like ‘the law’ and ‘campaign ethics.’”
On Iran: Trump “casually threatening to ‘annihilate’ another country in front of the entire U.N. General Assembly. What he’s saying would constitute war crimes. And this man has the nuclear codes. It’s astounding how hellbent he is on violating domestic and international law practically every time he opens his mouth. American foreign policy cannot revolve around destabilizing global peace and stability, the world economy, and our role as the leader of the free world. Horrifying.”
On the Kennedy Center: “Trump says the Kennedy Center is bankrupt and that only he can save it. BULLSHIT. The only problem with the Kennedy Center is Donald J. Trump.”
On the Arch: “Republicans are sitting back and letting Trump desecrate the hallowed landscape of Arlington National Cemetery. This hideous, massive vanity project is such an affront to veterans and Gold Star families. … Republicans in Congress could stop this and every other vanity project Trump is obsessed with. They need to grow a damn spine and remember their duty to the taxpayer. Pathetic.”
Pingree isn’t just concerned, not even very concerned. She’s actively trying to shake this nation from its torpor and get people riled up enough to prevent Trump from destroying what generations before him have built.
Pingree told me this week, “Whether it’s social media rants made with AI slop or threatening to annihilate entire civilizations, none of what Trump is saying and doing is normal or OK. I will keep speaking out, calling attention to this administration’s abuses and incompetence, and making sure people have the information they need to act.”
Maine’s independent senator, Angus King, issues eloquent statements opposing the president’s most stupid proposals and projects. King’s words are more measured, in keeping with the rational debate of our country at its best.
Regrettably, this isn’t a moment for polite disagreement. With so much at stake, Pingree has become too damn angry for calm appeals.
“My hope is that speaking out, consistently and plainly, helps turn justified frustration into engagement, organizing and, ultimately, change at the ballot box in November,” Pingree said.
Why she isn’t getting through to more people, I don’t know. As far as I’m concerned, Pingree is a hero in these dark times.

title: Woman Dies After Sedan And Pickup Collide On Moosehead Trail
text:
Updated as of 10/02/2026
The Penobscot County Sheriff's Office has identified the three individuals involved in a deadly crash that took place just before 7 PM on Wednesday, September 30th.
According to authorities, 67-year-old Kendall Thompson of Dixmont was driving a Chrysler sedan, with 68-year-old Patricia Thompson in the passenger's seat. They were heading east on or near Route 7 near Plymouth Pond. 69-year-old Timothy Malo of Newport was driving his Hyundai Santa Cruz west when the vehicles collided.
"An early investigation indicates Malo's vehicle crossed the center line and struck the Thompson's vehicle in the eastbound lane. As a result of the crash, both vehicles left the roadway and came to rest in Plymouth Pond. All three occupants were transported to the hospital; sadly, Mrs. Thompson passed away from her injuries sustained during the crash."
The Sheriff's office is still looking into the matter and trying to "determine what charges will be filed in this investigation."
We will update this story once those decisions are made.

title: Obituary: Constance Barbara Ortolani
text:
CAPE ELIZABETH –
Constance Barbara Ortolani, 78, passed away on Sept. 22, 2026, surrounded by her family and near her longtime home of Cape Elizabeth, Maine. Connie was a teacher, dancer, mother, sister and friend. She was committed to her communities, dedicated to helping others, and a devoted Boston sports fan. 
Connie was born in the Back Bay Fens neighborhood of Boston, Mass., to Nicholas Rassias, a bartender and postal worker, and Christine Rassias, a hairdresser. Her family later moved to the Boston neighborhood of Jamaica Plain. Her brother, Peter, loved baseball and his big sister, but at the age of 11, he passed away from leukemia. Connie honored his spirit throughout her life by supporting the Dana Farber Cancer Institute.
Connie was a third-generation Greek American and was raised with a strong Greek tradition, including attending Hellenic school. Every year, she liked to attend Portland’s Greek festival for the mousaka, koulourakia cookies and, of course, the dancing.
As a young woman, Connie excelled at school and athletics, especially dance. She performed in the Nutcracker, cast as “one of the boys” because she was tall. A straight-A student, she attended Boston State College and received a Bachelor of Science in elementary education. Early in her career, she taught gym and health at Copley Square High School.
During college, Connie worked at an Anderson-Little clothing store. There, she met Philip Ortolani. For one of their first dates, they went to a Bruins game, where Connie fell in love with another Boston sports team, and also Philip. They got married in 1971, moved to Randolph, Mass., and started a family, having two children, Nikki and Alex.
In 1982, Philip was considering a job in southern Maine and brought Connie to see the Pine Tree State. Her response was lukewarm. Connie always called herself a “Boston Girl,” but she soon came to love Maine—its coastline, its birds, its lobster rolls, and its people.
She began teaching at local schools while also working as a dance instructor. In 1991, she got a master’s degree in special education from the University of Southern Maine with a near-perfect GPA.
Connie went on to teach at Hall School and later Lincoln Middle School, where she was known as a dedicated teacher with a talent for getting her kids to engage in lessons and respond to her. In the mid-2000s, she started working for Even Start, a literacy and education program to help families break out of poverty. She became a program director and child education specialist, further deepening her bonds with the local community and other educators. Her mother, Christine, also eventually moved to the area, allowing Connie and her family to be close to Christine in her final years.
After retiring, Connie took on volunteering. Some of it was formal, such as becoming a regular volunteer at soup kitchens and Reiche School, often working with children who were just starting to learn English. Some volunteering was informal, such as delivering a meal to a family or connecting them with a local furniture charity. Of this volunteering, she would always say that she “got back more than she gave.”
In 2015, Connie and her family were struck by tragedy. A car ran off the road and took Philip’s life, while injuring Connie. She stayed close to Philip by taking frequent trips to Fort Williams, where they loved to walk, and by hanging hearts around her home to keep him close.
Despite her loss, Connie went on to build an active life. In the mornings, she would often attend a dance, Zumba, or gym class, and then volunteer in the afternoon at a school or with the Wayside Food Programs. In the evenings and weekends, she’d often connect with a much-loved group of friends in the Portland area. They would go to plays, dance in Congress Square, and explore new restaurants. In her neighborhood, she’d go on “walk and talks,” where she always said she ended up doing more talking than walking. In these ways, she shared her spirit and love for life despite its hardships, and took solace in the strength and endurance of others.
She also hosted her children in Maine and took frequent trips to New York City, N.Y., to visit them, go to Broadway shows and museums, and attend holiday gatherings. She reveled in her role as grandmother to her grandson, Enzo, including taking him on a trip to Universal Studios and to basketball games in Brooklyn. In her final year, her daughter Nikki moved up to Maine, bringing Connie great happiness and comfort.
Even after being diagnosed with glioblastoma in June, Connie carried a smile on her face and always had a word of kindness or gratitude. She constantly said how lucky she was.
Connie is survived by her daughter, Nikki Ortolani of South Portland; son, Alex Ortolani, daughter-in-law, Kate, and grandson, Enzo of Brooklyn; and cousins Arthur and his wife Judy Carakatsane of Portsmouth, N.H., Michael and wife Pam Carakatsane of Lynnfield, Mass., and Bill and wife Sharon Carakatsane of Lowell, Mass.
To view Connie’s memorial page or to leave an online condolence for the family please visit http://www.hobbsfuneralhome.com
In lieu of flowers, donations can be made to the Dana Farber Cancer Institute (danafarber.jimmyfund.org) or
Wayside Food Programs (https://www.waysidemaine.org/home).
