title: The laws tied to the Susan Collins-Navatek allegations are ‘crystal clear.’ Enforcing them is another matter.
text:
The allegations of a “pay-to-play” scheme and bribery outlined in the recent ProPublica report on U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, and a contractor may not lead to any further consequences beyond serving as campaign fodder, but experts said the piece highlighted some key facts.
Existing laws are clear on banning such behavior, but it takes a federal agency to investigate any alleged wrongdoing, campaign finance experts noted.
That seems to be what happened with the case involving Hawaiian defense contractor Navatek, its former CEO-turned-convicted-felon Martin Kao and an illegal donation to a pro-Collins super PAC through a shell company. But an FBI investigation focusing on Collins and Kao — along with other potential corruption involving members of Congress — died after President Donald Trump returned to office in 2025 and purged the anti-corruption unit that had been handling the probe, ProPublica reported.
So it appears unlikely that more penalties will come as a result of the alleged interactions detailed in the Sept. 22 piece, though ProPublica said it was only “the first in a series of stories drawn from our reporting.” The fallout is instead mostly coming in the form of fresh criticism of Collins as she seeks a sixth term against former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson in a race that appears neck and neck ahead of the Nov. 3 election.
Still, the report opened up various questions regarding campaign finance and what is allowed in an American political system that both sides of the aisle agree is awash in money.
Collins and her campaign staff, who have never been charged in connection with Kao’s case, have bashed the new reporting as covering old allegations from Kao, who was sentenced to 87 months in prison last year after he pleaded guilty to funneling more than $200,000 to Collins’ 2020 reelection campaign and an affiliated super PAC that Collins and the PAC returned in light of the criminal proceedings against Kao.
But ProPublica rebutted the Collins camp’s criticism by noting its story focused on previously unreported claims Kao made between 2022 and 2024, and on how a trove of records and emails the news organization obtained show the FBI was still investigating Kao’s relationship with Collins, her staffers and employees of the super PAC up until early 2025.
The Portland Press Herald spoke with several campaign finance experts who have worked in law and for the federal government about various questions raised by the ProPublica reporting. Without rehashing all the details in the ProPublica story, the interviews revealed a few tweaks that could fix broader finance loopholes. But the experts agreed the existing laws in place to protect against pay-for-play schemes and bribery are clear. Enforcing them is another matter.
What are the laws on contractor donations and bribery of public officials? What are the penalties for breaking them? How easy it is to prosecute?
Both the Hatch Act amendments of 1940 and Federal Election Commission regulations ban federal government contractors from donating to — or promising to donate to — federal candidates, political parties, political committees and super PACs. Civil fines are common penalties, but prison sentences occur in more serious cases that also involve other violations.
Kao received his 87-month prison sentence in 2025 because of a series of violations, rather than illicit campaign donations. His crimes included COVID-19 pandemic wire fraud, money laundering and bank fraud, with a judge also ordering him to pay back about $12.8 million in Paycheck Protection Program funds he fraudulently obtained.
Anti-bribery statutes prohibit “quid pro quo” dealings and ban public officials from giving or receiving anything of value if it is given “with intent to influence” an official act or received “in return for being influenced.” A bribery conviction is punishable by up to 15 years in prison, but a separate case of giving a “gratuity” after the fact as “thanks” for an act, but not in exchange for it, can result in up to two years. A “gratuity” does not include campaign contributions.
The current laws make it “crystal clear that certain behaviors are unlawful,” said Erin Chlopak, who worked for the FEC in litigation and policy roles for nearly a decade and now serves as the nonprofit Campaign Legal Center’s senior director of campaign finance. The Campaign Legal Center had filed a complaint with the FEC after getting suspicious about what turned out to be the $150,000 straw donation to the pro-Collins super PAC in 2020 that Kao reportedly told PAC officials he would give through the “Society of Young Women Scientist and Engineers.”
But proving bribery is not easy, campaign finance experts noted, and Supreme Court rulings have narrowed what counts. For contractor violations, the FEC has lacked a four-member quorum during Trump’s second term and thus cannot start investigations or issue penalties.
“It is incredibly difficult for prosecutors to prove that sort of quid pro quo exchange,” said Eric Petry, counsel in the left-leaning Brennan Center for Justice’s Elections and Government Program. “And oftentimes, it really boils down to a ‘he said versus she said,’ which is really difficult for courts and juries to get to the bottom of.”
A jury in 2024 found former U.S. Sen. Bob Menendez, a New Jersey Democrat who was seeking reelection that year as an independent, guilty of acting as a foreign agent for Egypt amid a yearslong bribery scheme involving him, his wife and three New Jersey businesspeople. Menendez is appealing his 11-year prison sentence.
On the topic of illicit federal contractor donations, FEC commissioners were equally divided in 2024 and thus closed a complaint from the Campaign Legal Center that a federal contractor violated the law by giving more than $236,000 to a super PAC supporting Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis’ presidential campaign.
What are the gray areas? What about business leaders who donate and whose companies win contracts?
The ban on federal contractor donations does not apply to several categories of people, including stockholders, officers or employees of a corporation, and it does not apply to donations in state or local elections. And when it comes to campaign money, the U.S. Supreme Court’s Citizens United ruling in 2010 essentially paved the way for corporations to spend unlimited funds on elections.
Petry said Congress could seek to boost low levels of public trust in the government by at least expanding the federal contractor donation ban to cover those other affiliated individuals, such as stockholders and officers. He also flagged how federal contractors and corporations can give to presidential inauguration funds or projects such as Trump’s White House ballroom.
Other examples of giving are allowed and easier to spot, though experts noted that voters have cited them in surveys when expressing disgust with the amount of money floating around the political system.
New Balance’s owner and chairman, Jim Davis, gave $1 million to Collins’ super PAC last year. The senator proudly held one of the company’s shoes when announcing her reelection campaign in February. And earlier in September, she touted a nearly $60 million contract the company got to produce military footwear at its Skowhegan plant.
Did Collins actually call Kao to thank him?
Scott Reed, who leads the pro-Collins Pine Tree Results PAC, was mentioned repeatedly in the recent ProPublica piece because of Kao’s testimony, FBI records and emails showing his interactions with Kao. That included a 2019 meeting in Washington in which Reed allegedly asked Navatek executives for a $500,000 campaign donation after Collins had helped the company win a multimillion dollar Navy research contract in Maine.
ProPublica viewed an email in which Kao told Reed he planned to donate $150,000 through a shell company. “Very smart,” Reed replied.
(ProPublica reached out to Reed for comment, and he said via email that, “I understand Martin Kao is now sitting in federal prison,” along with saying he “never had any communications with Senator Collins (or) her staff about Martin Kao and/or Navatek.”)
Seven days after the super PAC cashed the check from Kao’s shell company, one of Reed’s subordinates emailed a Navatek lobbyist asking for Kao’s phone number and said Collins “would like to call Martin to thank him,” ProPublica reported.
The Collins campaign and its manager, Steve Abbott, responded last week by saying they do “not believe” the senator ever called Kao. When the Portland Press Herald asked Wednesday if Collins herself would comment on whether she called Kao, campaign spokesperson Blake Kernen said it “does not appear in any of our records that this call was made.”
“Neither Susan Collins nor anyone who worked for her believes that she made a call,” Kernen said.
Would a federal investigation get reopened?
Since the ProPublica story came out, The New York Times and Washington Post have also each reported that the FBI in 2025 shut down its investigation revolving around Reed, Kao and Collins. The Times reported that senior bureau officials questioned Kao’s truthfulness, but ProPublica said that by the end of 2024, agents had “enough evidence to pursue a sweeping bribery probe that could ensnare top lawmakers of both political parties.”
Campaign finance experts said a renewed investigation is unlikely under Trump, who is serving his second and final term through 2028. Craig Holman, a government affairs lobbyist for the left-leaning consumer advocacy group Public Citizen, has helped states such as Illinois, New Jersey and Connecticut write their own “pay-to-play” legislation but said the Justice Department has the chief responsibility to prosecute bribery or contractor-related corruption.
“It is very unfortunate, though not surprising, that the Trump administration would step in and stop that investigation,” Holman said. “They just accept this as normal behavior.”

title: Para-athlete defies limits on the track, one push at a time
text:
LEE’S SUMMIT, Mo. (InvestigateTV) - Outside of Kansas City, a high school para-athlete is pushing past expectations and capturing track championships.
And Jeremiah Mangels is doing that while challenging himself and inspiring his team.
“I’d say just whenever I’m on the track, and I’m pushing, I’m just thinking next push, next push. Never thinking about quitting,” said Mangels. “I actually try to get to the Olympics for the events I do best in.”
He was recently named a Para High School All-American in the 100-meter dash by USA Track & Field, and his goals don’t stop there.
Born with spina bifida, Jeremiah initially anticipated a degree of separation from his able-bodied teammates.
“I was expecting to be more separated from them because I thought it would be difficult for me, as a para-athlete, to do things that they’re doing,” he said. “It surprised me how I could do everything that they were doing better than I thought.”
Jeremiah’s teammates don’t see him any differently from the others. Still, they want the team environment to feel safe and supportive for him.
“To me, he ain’t different. He’s just like me. He’s just like everybody else on the track team. And we want to create a space where everybody is welcome,” said senior teammate Jaisaiah Turner. “Track is for everybody. As long as you got the mental and the strength to do it, you all in.”
The Mangels family adopted Jeremiah from an orphanage in China when he was just six years old.
“He’s been through so much adversity in his life,” said his mom, Amy Mangels. “He grew up in an orphanage with no family, and to know that he’s able to pull that belief in himself out to do these things, it amazes us. I’m excited that we get to call him our son.”
Jeremiah has won 11 straight state championships. Not only does he excel at track, but he also plays basketball.
“He absolutely believes he’ll be in the Paralympics someday, whether it be for track or basketball or both,” his mom added. “He pushes himself every day to achieve that. I don’t think he would ever take no for an answer.”
Jeremiah has proven time and time again that sports are for everybody, no matter what you’re capable of.
“There was fear whenever I started because I didn’t know what I was getting into,” Jeremiah said. “But after I got to the practices and realized that it wasn’t as bad as I thought it was going to be, I just did everything I could to be as strong as I can.”

title: Spend an evening with creator of ‘Duck of Justice’ at Rockland library
text:
Join Rockland Public Library for a evening with Maine author Tim Cotton from 6-7:30 p.m. Thursday, Oct. 8, in the Community Room.
Cotton retired after 34 years in law enforcement, but is better known, for some reason, as the creator of the marginally world-famous Bangor Police Department Facebook page, where the “Duck of Justice” was born. The page went from 9,000 followers to over 350,000 during his tenure. He gave it up in 2022. The iconic Duck of Justice was Cook’s idea, but he simply didn’t expect it to become so popular, so he ran with it.
“It’s not science, after all,” Cotton said.
Cotton’s writing, lauded by some and panned by others, has led him to author four popular books, all collections of his essays from social media and beyond. He is working on his first fiction novel, something “a bit darker, with no ducks,” he said. He is the recipient of the Erma Bombeck Award for humor writing, and has been featured by NPR Morning Edition, USA Today, People, 207 and a bunch of others that he doesn’t recall all that well now. Cotton has been a two-time guest on Mike Rowe’s podcasts and a few others, but still has not been asked to be the grand marshal in any parades — for that he’s thankful.
Cotton’s daily writings on Facebook and his website focus on Maine life in general and are complimentary to his favorite place on earth, Downeast Maine. His dog Ellie, an 11-year-old box-a-dor, is prominently featured in his daily musings, but she doesn’t travel with him to library talks. He is sure she doesn’t bite but sometimes questions the way she looks at people who don’t buy his books.
Cotton does fewer appearances at libraries these days, mostly because he strongly believes that he says it all, every day, on the “interwebs,” but he has agreed to visit Rockland Public Library because he doesn’t get to Rockland all that much since the “incident.” He refuses to share any further details.
Cotton’s talks are unrehearsed, unscripted, and feature stories and anecdotal observations, and he loves question-and-answer sessions, but refuses to talk about politics or sporting events. He also believes that the word “no” is a complete sentence, so don’t be angry when he says it when you ask about politics or sporting events.
His books will be available for sale at the Oct. 8 event, but he urges folks to buy them from someone else because they are usually cheaper. He will sign books you have or books you buy from him, but his penmanship is poor, and he has a difficult time discerning which spelling of “Megan” you use if your name is Meghan, so just tell him upfront.
All are welcome to attend. The Rockland Public Library is located at 80 Union St. For more information, contact Jeannie Sullivan at [email protected].

title: ‘Shouldn’t have taken 31 years’: Victim’s niece voices frustration before Christa Pike’s botched execution
text:
KNOXVILLE, Tenn. (WVLT/Gray News) - Colleen Slemmer’s niece said the process of executing Christa Pike should not have taken 31 years.
After learning the state was fighting to lift the stay, Seeley expressed both frustration with the delay and hope that the high court would finally deliver closure.
“It didn’t make sense how they stopped it an hour before she was supposed to go,” Seeley said. “I think that they had enough time out of the 31 years to be able to do this. Colleen is going to get justice today.”
Slemmer was 19 years old when she was killed in January 1995 after being lured to an isolated area on the University of Tennessee agricultural campus. Both Slemmer and Pike were enrolled in Job Corps at the time.
Pike and two co-defendants, Tadaryl Shipp and Shadolla Peterson, were convicted in 1996. Testimony showed the trio tortured Slemmer, carved a pentagram into her chest, and Pike kept a piece of Slemmer’s skull as a souvenir.
Members of Slemmer’s family traveled to the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville on Wednesday morning expecting the execution to take place, but the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals suddenly granted a stay.
Seeley said she spoke with her grandmother, May Martinez, by video call earlier in the day while the family prepared for what they hoped would be the end of a decadeslong legal fight.
Seeley’s mother, who was Slemmer’s sister, passed away in 2021, and Seeley’s stepfather traveled to the prison to stand in her place.
Seeley pushed back against Pike’s repeated legal attempts to overturn her death sentence or obtain clemency.
“It shouldn’t have taken 30, 31 years to be able to get this,” Seeley said. “Allowing somebody, what Christa did to my aunt, to allow her to live 31 years longer than her is heartbreaking.”
Tennessee officials were unable to execute Christa Gail Pike on Wednesday for the 1995 murder after administering two doses of a lethal drug.
Her attorneys filed an emergency motion to halt the execution, saying Pike was “still alive and snoring” after receiving the lethal injection Wednesday.
“The vein in my arm feels like it’s about to bust,” one witness recalled her saying.
According to the emergency motion, the Tennessee Department of Correction began the execution of Pike at about 9 p.m. ET. The motion says that both syringes of pentobarbital were administered and that Pike “has not lost consciousness and still has a heartbeat and is audibly snoring.”
The emergency motion filed Wednesday night stated that the execution was “causing Ms. Pike unnecessary agony and occurring in violation of [her] right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment.”
The motion also demanded the Tennessee Department of Correction immediately begin lifesaving measures.
The 50-year-old inmate was taken by ambulance from the prison, her attorneys said. She was being treated at a hospital.

title: Reflecting Pool vandalism case against three-time Olympian permanently dismissed
text:
Judge permanently dismisses case charging three-time Olympian with vandalizing Reflecting Pool
A judge in the nation's capital agreed on Thursday to permanently dismiss a criminal case charging a three-time Olympian with vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a move that could prevent federal prosecutors from reviving the case under political pressure from President Donald Trump.
Related video above: What really caused the damage to the Reflecting Pool?
D.C. Superior Court Judge Todd Edelman ordered the dismissal of David Hearn's case with "prejudice," which would block U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro's office from refiling the felony charge against him. The judge ruled nearly a month after hearing attorneys' arguments.
Hearn's lawyers say Trump administration officials have continued to falsely accuse the Maryland resident of vandalizing the reflecting pool despite Pirro's decision to drop the case on July 31. Trump responded by saying Pirro "choked" and "folded like an umbrella."
In a court filing in July, Pirro said new evidence produced by the Interior Department showed Hearn wasn't responsible for damage to the pool's lining. Pirro's office attributed the damage instead to a botched installation by a contractor as well as a rush to complete the project in time for this summer's America 250 celebration in Washington.
Pirro's admission was an embarrassing setback for the White House. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum has backed Trump's claims that vandals damaged the pool.
Hearn has said he was on a bike ride on June 19 when he reached in to examine the pool's newly peeled coating and briefly touched a chunk attached to the side of the pool. But he said he obeyed a park worker's command to let go of it.
Hearn was charged with one count of property destruction, which carries a maximum prison sentence of 10 years. His lawyers questioned whether prosecutors properly presented the grand jury with adequate evidence to support the charge and the amount of damage alleged by the government.
Hearn, 67, of Bethesda, Maryland, competed in three Summer Olympics, earning his best finish, ninth, at the 1996 Atlanta Olympic Games, the U.S. Olympic and Paralympic Committee says on its website.
Trump, a Republican, appointed Pirro, a former Fox News host, to serve as the top federal prosecutor for the District of Columbia. Edelman was nominated to the bench by Democratic President Barack Obama.

title: 100+ Women Who Care Androscoggin support Meals on Wheels
text:
AUBURN, ME – On August 3, 100+Women Who Care Androscoggin held their quarterly fundraising meeting at Central Maine Community College in Auburn. At that meeting, the membership voted to support Meals on Wheels with their donations. The donation, totaling $8100, was delivered to Meals on Wheels on Sept. 9.
The SeniorsPlus’ Meals on Wheels (MOW) program serves homebound individuals over the age of 60 and those with disabilities that reside in Androscoggin, Franklin and Oxford counties. MOW is designed to help older adults age in place in the comfort of their home. The program is needs based rather than means tested and uses a weighted scale to serve those most in need – the most vulnerable – first. Nutrition is a basic building block for health maintenance and illness recovery. Registered Dietician-approved meals provide 1/3 of the Recommended Dietary Allowance. Provision of meals enables older adults to remain in the comfort of their own home rather than be cared for in a long-term care facility, ultimately reducing tax-payer burden.
MOW is a three-pronged approach: a nutritious meal, safety check, and social interaction. Delivery drivers provide a brief social visit, are trained to identify safety risks and observe wellness changes. Most clients live alone, are socially isolated, and often have no one regularly checking on them – factors that increase the risk of disease, depression, and mortality. Our program helps reduce these risks.
Last year, SeniorsPlus provided 146,483 home delivered meals to 868 unduplicated clients. 596 of those individuals were residents of Androscoggin County who received a total of 87,515 meals.
100+ Women Who Care Androscoggin is a collaboration of local women who invest in the community by pooling their donations for the greatest impact. They meet four times a year. Members can nominate organizations or projects that are working to address community needs. At each meeting they hear from 3 of the nominated organizations and then vote for one group to receive their donation. The members then write a check to that organization. To date, 100+ Women Who Care Androscoggin has raised and donated $76,610. With a matching grant, the community impact is $96,015.
100+ Women Who Care Androscoggin currently has more than 160 members and welcomes others to join to enlarge their community impact. For more information or to join, email 100womenwhocareandroscoggin@gmail.com.
100+ Women Who Care present a check to Meals on Wheels. Pictured, l to r, are Carol Goyette, Eric Robenstine and Janis Walker from Meals on Wheels, and Marty McIntyre, Founder of 100+ Women Who Care Androscoggin.

title: Maine gubernatorial hopefuls trade barbs in first televised debate
text:
The first televised debate between the three candidates vying to become Maine’s next governor featured several testy exchanges, many of which involved Republican Bobby Charles.
The hourlong debate, hosted by the Maine Chamber of Commerce and moderated by News Center Maine, sought to cover a wide range of topics, including taxes, state revenue, housing, substance use, energy costs and healthcare. But moderators had trouble keeping the candidates on topic and within their allotted time.
The forum was an opportunity for Charles and independent Rick Bennett to shake up a race in which Democrat Hannah Pingree has been the clear front-runner in polling and fundraising.
Bennett, a longtime Republican who unenrolled from the party when he entered the race in June, repeatedly went after Charles, accusing him of not understanding the state budgeting process, and attacking his record serving in the U.S. State Department under President George W. Bush.
“It’s hard to digest all I’ve just heard here, particularly from Bobby Charles,” Bennett, 63, said about 20 minutes into the debate in response to a question about state spending.
“He just doesn’t simply understand how the fiscal process works, which doesn’t surprise me because inspector generals and auditors at the federal government cited him dozens of times for mismanagement of federal spending.”
Bennett was referring to a Bangor Daily News article about how federal audits raised concerns about poor management, spending and ineffectiveness during Charles’ 18-month tenure leading the Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs.
“The Bangor Daily News doesn’t always report the facts,” Charles shot back. “We showed them, ‘Hey, here is the unbelievable record,’ and they decided that they’re gonna take the little paragraph down here that didn’t look like it was the best paragraph.”
Charles, meanwhile, portrayed himself as a political outsider. He said Bennett and Pingree are part of the current political system that has led to the present affordability and housing crises. And he said he’d use his experience as a former investigator to conduct a top-to-bottom review of state agencies to root out fraud and waste.
“I find it ironic that two people who’ve served both 30 years and 25 years are saying that we need to fix the system,” Charles said.
After one exchange, Pingree, who was flanked by both men, said, “This is why we need women in charge.” The line drew laughter and applause from the audience.
Throughout the night, Pingree and Bennett tried to put Charles on the defensive.
At one point, Pingree referred to Bennett as “my friend.” She later called out Charles’ previous work as a federal lobbyist and repeatedly highlighted his support for President Donald Trump, whose low approval rating is creating headwinds for Republicans across the county.
“(Charles is) somebody who has supported Donald Trump at every turn,” Pingree said. “His tariffs, his war in Iran, his big, beautiful bill that has cut our healthcare system. We’re facing economic headwinds because of this president.”
Later, Charles, a 66-year-old Leeds lawyer and former assistant U.S. secretary of state, sought to distance himself from Trump on tariffs and the Iran war.
“I have been very clear, at the outset, that the hitting of the nuclear program was great (but), I do not agree with him right now, in terms of the extended engagement over there,” Charles said about Iran. “I’ve never met the guy (Trump), but I have appealed publicly that we need to get back to the negotiating table and get tariffs down.”
It’s unclear whether the debate will change the trajectory of the race.
Pingree, a 49-year-old Democrat from North Haven who led a policy office under Gov. Janet Mills and is the daughter of U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, has held a steady lead in both fundraising and polling.
Pingree led Charles 48% to 36% in a New York Times/Portland Press Herald/Siena poll released last week, while Bennett drew 8%.
The Democrat has a significant money advantage as well. She has raised more than $4.3 million, compared to Charles’ $1.8 million and Bennett’s nearly $924,000.
The candidates will meet for three more debates, including one Thursday hosted by Maine Public, News Center Maine and the Portland Press Herald. WGME CBS 13 will host a debate on Oct. 13, followed by WMTW the next day.

title: Walmart recalls nearly 4.5 million grill wire brushes. Here are the impacted brushes
text:
(Gray News) - Walmart is recalling nearly 4.5 million grill brushes because small metal wire bristles can detach, stick to grills or food, and cause severe internal injuries requiring surgery if swallowed.
The recall covers approximately 4,477,655 Expert Grill metal wire bristle brushes sold individually and as part of grilling tool sets, according to the Consumer Product Safety Commission.
The brushes feature black plastic or stainless steel handles, and several models include an attached metal scraper.
Products were sold at Walmart stores nationwide and online at Walmart.com from January 2021 through August 2026 for between $1 and $28.
No injuries or incidents have been reported, according to the CPSC notice.
Recalled models
The recall includes five specific models. Consumers can locate the model number on the product packaging or on a sticker or tag attached directly to the brush:
- EX5607031616002: Expert Grill 16-inch Steel Fiber Scrub Brush and Scraper for Grills (sold January 2025 to August 2026)
- EX5607031616003: Expert Grill Handheld Steel Fiber Scrub Brush with Ergonomic Handle for Grill Cleaning (sold January 2025 to August 2026)
- XG1310700206: Expert Grill 21-inch 3-Head Grill Brush with Stainless Steel Bristles and Soft-Grip Handle (sold January 2022 to August 2026)
- XG1136178597003: Expert Grill Long Handle Grill Brush with Scraper, 17.7-inch (sold January 2021 to August 2026)
- XG1410700124: Expert Grill Grilling Accessories BBQ Grill Tools Set, 10-Piece Stainless Steel Grill Kit (sold December 2023 to August 2026)
Refund and contact information
Consumers should immediately stop using the recalled brushes and contact Walmart to receive a full refund or store credit valid in stores or online. Customers will be instructed to either return the product to a store or discard it.
Walmart can be reached toll-free at 800-925-6278 from 7 a.m. to 9 p.m. CT Monday through Friday, or online through the company’s product recalls page.

title: Three Maine football storylines to follow against Sacred Heart
text:
One step forward, two steps back. That’s been the story of the University of Maine football team this season, and the Black Bears definitely went backwards Saturday in a 43-17 loss at Elon.
After a winless September, Maine (1-4, 1-1 Coastal Athletic Association) begins its October slate by hosting Sacred Heart (1-3, 1-1) at 3:30 p.m. Saturday (FloSports). Here are three storylines as the Black Bears look to snap a four-game losing streak.
Could change be coming at QB?
Starting quarterback Eddie Buehler struggled against Elon, completing 14 of 35 passes for just 88 yards. Caden Drezek, a junior, got his first action of the season in the fourth quarter, throwing a touchdown pass to Kevin Jackson to cap a 75-yard drive.
Maine coach Jordan Stevens was adamant that he never considered a QB change after Buehler’s less-than-stellar outing against Merrimack. But in Monday’s CAA news conference, Stevens was noncommittal when asked if Buehler would start.
“We’re just looking at that during the week here,” Stevens said.
Stay tuned.
Special teams, special teams, special teams
Without context, the total yardage in Maine’s most recent loss (Elon 376, Maine 315) doesn’t look all that bad. So, why the lopsided defeat? It’s because the Black Bears gave the Phoenix short fields, primarily via special teams miscues.
Elon blocked two punts in the first quarter, the first leading to a field goal and the second resulting in a safety. A 24-yard Elon punt return in the third quarter put the Phoenix at Maine’s 43, leading to a touchdown, and a muffed punt by the Black Bears late in that quarter resulted in another Elon field goal.
Throw in a 31-yard Elon touchdown drive after Maine turned it over on downs in the fourth quarter, and you see that the Phoenix offense didn’t have to do much to score. Sacred Heart (18.8 points per game) hasn’t lit up the scoreboard this year, but if Maine doesn’t clean up its special teams, that won’t matter.
A spark in the run game?
It wasn’t all bad news for Maine against Elon. After rushing for just 174 yards on 93 carries — 1.9 yards per carry — in three games since its season-opening win, the Black Bears rushed for 167 yards on 34 carries against Elon.
Can Maine repeat that? Well, consider that New Hampshire, which had averaged just 2.6 yards per carry prior to last week’s game at Sacred Heart, rushed for 181 yards on 29 carries (6.2 average) against the Pioneers. Perhaps the Black Bears can have similar success.

title: Poland native to headline October Side Door Coffeehouse in Brunswick
text:
October’s Side Door Coffeehouse will feature Sigrid Sibley, a native of Poland Spring, on Oct.9 at the Unitarian Universalist Church of Brunswick.
Open mic starts at 7 p.m., with signups beginning at 6:45 p.m. Sibley will headline the evening at 8:30 p.m. Admission is $12 for adults and free for children 17 and under. Purchase tickets in advance at ticketstripe.com/events/557109338542554.
Sibley was raised on a small homestead with backyard chickens, fruit trees and a busy family garden. She began songwriting at age 14, finding roots in bluegrass, Americana and traditional music. Her songs draw on common folk themes, as well as her love for nature, agriculture and life in Maine.
As a solo artist and with her band, Sibley performs across the state and beyond. Past performances include the Common Ground Fair in Unity; the Maine Cheese Festival in Pittsfield; the Word Barn, in Exeter, New Hampshire; and the Poland Spring Resort summer concert series. Sibley studied music education with a focus in composition at the University of Southern Maine. During her time at college, she met and collaborated with local musicians in Southern Maine, including several who contributed to her debut album, “Old Faithful Dreams,” released in May 2025. The first single of her album, “Never Knew Love,” was selected as a finalist for the 2025 Maine Songwriters Association contest. Sibley is currently a member of One Longfellow Square’s inaugural class of LEAF fellowship. Information on upcoming shows can be found online on her website or by joining her monthly newsletter.
The Side Door Coffeehouse is a venue for local musicians and others (professional and amateur) to share their talents, and for residents and visitors of the Midcoast community to enjoy great entertainment and conversation in a relaxed setting. Organized by a group of volunteers from the UUCB, the Side Door Coffeehouse operates on the second Friday of every month except August.

title: Wiscasset Machinist Able to Use Engineering Background in Craft
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
After a life in boat repair, a business owner in Wiscasset is producing parts that are unavailable elsewhere, using computer numerical control manufacturing.
Joseph Gillespie, the 22-year-old owner and operator of Gillespie Machine, grew up learning how to repair boats from his father, Mike Gillespie, at the Wiscasset business Gillespie Marine.
“I was always a marine diesel mechanic with my dad,” Gillespie said. “That’s how I started out with building engines and transmissions. And then, he’s always running into parts that are unavailable for years from the original manufacturer, and so I kind of played with the idea of getting into machining.”

title: What to know about Christa Gail Pike's failed lethal injection attempt
text:
What to know about Christa Gail Pike's failed lethal injection attempt
Christa Pike remained alive after Tennessee tried to put her to death by lethal injection, making her the only inmate to have survived after the drugs were administered.
Video above: Media witnesses recall what happened during Christa Pike’s failed execution
What happened to Pike on Wednesday is “singular and unparalleled,” said Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center.
The failed execution also came after an eight-hour delay while the U.S. Supreme Court considered whether to postpone her execution.
Pike, 50, was still in the hospital Thursday afternoon in critical condition, and her lawyers said they did not know her long-term chance for recovery.
Here's what to know about Pike's execution:
Video below: 'Hear her snoring': WKRN journalist Tori Gessner describes Christa Pike's lethal injection
What happened?
Pike's execution was supposed to start at 10 a.m., but a federal appeals court stopped it about an hour before. The state appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court, and it took eight hours for the conservative majority to overrule the lower court and let the lethal injection with the barbiturate pentobarbital proceed.
About 90 minutes later, prison officials raised the curtain to the execution chamber, where media witnesses saw Pike strapped to a gurney with an IV in her arm. She said she was leaving the world with love.
“I’m ready to be free,” she said. This is a happy day.”
She sang a song with her spiritual adviser, looked around and after several minutes said her arm was hurting or burning and asked if it was supposed to feel that way.
The curtain to the witnesses was closed then opened again around the time a second dose of pentobarbital would be administered. Pike appeared to lose consciousness, but she continued breathing and at times made snoring-like noises for the next hour.
Prison officials closed the curtain for good about 40 minutes after they first opened it. Pike's attorney demanded a telephone to ask a court to stop the execution.
It's unknown what was happening to Pike from the time the curtain closed for good at 8:06 p.m. until her attorney was told an ambulance was coming and witnesses were told to leave around 8:50 p.m.
“We at this point do not know the ramifications of the chemical torture that she has endured," Pike's attorney Randy Spivey said.
Prison officials have not said when their attempt to kill Pike turned into life-saving efforts. They have only released a statement saying their lethal injection protocols were followed.
Tennessee governor stops December execution to investigate
Within hours, Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee canceled the state's last execution of 2026, scheduled for Dec. 3, and ordered a comprehensive third-party investigation into what went wrong with Pike.
“It needs to be done thoroughly and however long that takes, whatever process is required to make sure we get to the very end of it and all the questions are answered,” Lee said.
It's not the first time Lee has ordered an investigation into capital punishment in Tennessee. Four years ago, an independent review found the state didn't follow its own execution rules and failed to properly test lethal injection drugs. That probe came after an April 2022 execution was stopped because of mishandling of drugs.
In May, Tennessee stopped the execution of Tony Carruthers after medical workers who got an IV into his right arm couldn't get a secondary IV line after trying his other arm, his left hand and his left foot, then failing to establish a central line. The governor ordered officials to wait at least a year before trying to execute Carruthers again.
Pike's lawyers called for the governor to now spare her life.
“Christa has endured punishment greater than any other person in the history of the American death penalty. The governor must commute Christa's sentence now,” Spivey said.
Pike's lawyers warned of medical conditions
Pike’s legal team told the courts and Tennessee prison officials that she had medical conditions that would make death by lethal injection agonizing.
They said Pike suffered from a condition with elevated platelets known as thrombocytosis. They argued the condition could cause issues with blood clotting at injection sites or bleeding that could affect her lungs.
Medical workers also had trouble drawing blood from her, and setting an IV line is a harder process, her lawyers said. Spivey said he counted at least seven spots where needles were put into her left arm Wednesday and that at least one needle bent on an unsuccessful attempt.
Pike’s biggest fear from being executed wasn’t “a fear of dying. It was a fear of a prolonged, painful, traumatic death. And that’s what happened minus the death,” said Stephen Ferrell, an attorney for Pike.
What was Christa Gail Pike convicted of?
Pike didn't deny she killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer in 1995. The two were classmates at Knoxville Job Corps.
Prosecutors said Pike feared Slemmer was a romantic rival and lured her to a secluded area where she and her boyfriend slashed Slemmer with a box cutter and beat her with a large chunk of asphalt. The case got widespread attention because of the brutality of the killing, the ages of the people involved and because a satanic symbol was carved into the victim’s body.
Video below: Roane County News journalist Damon Lawrence reads Christa Pike's last words
Pike said she was sexually abused starting from when she was a toddler and that she was raped at ages 11 and 17. Her lawyers said her death sentence was unfair because she was 18 at the time of the crime and the jury wasn't told about the abuse and how that might have affected her behavior.
Slemmer's mother witnessed the execution attempt and said her daughter didn't get justice.
“I watched the whole thing. She was awake. She was laughing. She was moving her head, moving her feet. She was trying to sit up. Didn’t work the first time they gave her a shot. It didn’t work the second time so she’s in the hospital and alive," May Martinez said by telephone.
Tadaryl Shipp, Pike’s boyfriend, has admitted that he was the one who carved a pentagram, a star-shaped symbol associated with Satanism, into her body. He was 17 at the time of the killing and was sentenced to life with the possibility of parole because of his age.

title: ‘Like I won the lottery’: Army veteran battling leukemia surprised with mortgage-free home
text:
RICHMOND HILL, Ga. (WTOC/Gray News) - A retired Army veteran who suffered severe injuries during his military service and is now battling leukemia received a life-changing surprise: a brand-new, mortgage-free home.
Retired Army Chief Warrant Officer Steve Smith and his wife, Jenifer, were welcomed into their custom, three-bedroom home in the Del Webb Savannah at Heartwood community during an emotional ceremony surrounded by community leaders, veterans and family.
“It’s like you literally go out, get a lottery card, and you’re like, ‘I won,’” Smith said.
Service and life-altering injuries
Smith enlisted in the U.S. Army in 1990, dedicating 13 years of service before being medically and honorably discharged in 2003.
While deployed to Kuwait that same year, Smith was performing a high-altitude night parachute jump when his chute became entangled and partially collapsed. Unable to deploy his reserve chute in time, he plummeted roughly 200 feet to the ground in a semi-assisted fall.
The impact fractured bones across his back, shoulders, collarbone, femur, pelvis and right arm, leaving him with permanent paralysis in his hand. He also lives with a traumatic brain injury, post-traumatic stress disorder, hearing and vision loss, tinnitus and ongoing mobility complications. Smith has since been diagnosed with leukemia.
“To be injured in the way I was, it was a mental blow, because you feel like you can no longer be who you were,” Smith said.
For years, the couple faced mounting questions about the future.
“It’s surreal, you dream, you think, ‘What’s gonna happen?’” Jenifer Smith said.
Built for accessibility and family
The home was gifted through a partnership between national nonprofit Building Homes for Heroes and PulteGroup’s Built to Honor program.
The house was constructed with specialized accommodations for Smith’s physical recovery, featuring zero-entry doorways, a roll-in shower and full main-level living spaces.
PulteGroup Coastal Carolinas Division President Matthew Raines said crews wanted to ensure the home was completely stress-free from day one.
“We’re gonna provide them a fully furnished house, move-in ready, with things in the pantry,” Raines said, noting the home includes “the amazing things that they put throughout this house to make your life wonderful, easier, happier.”
During the ceremony, U.S. Rep. Buddy Carter presented Smith with an American flag that previously flew above the U.S. House of Representatives.
“A community that cares about each other, and that’s why we’re here today,” Carter said. “We’re here to welcome home Steve and Jenifer Smith, a true American hero.”
For the Smiths, Richmond Hill offers not just physical stability, but proximity to loved ones. The home splits the distance between family living in Virginia and Florida.
“Being able to go an hour and a half to go see them, that means everything to me, it really does,” Smith said.

title: Islander Adventure: Eliot Mountain Trail
text:
The Eliot Mountain Trail offers a quick, 2-mile hike on Mount Desert Island. This accessible getaway takes you across bog bridges, along narrow trails lined with thick green moss, and to wide-open views of Northeast Harbor and Some Sound.
The trailhead is located on Route 3, between the Asticou and Seal Harbor, but you need to look closely to see the sign that says Eliot Mt. Trail/Thuya Garden at the edge of the woods. Parking is available for about four cars at the trailhead.

title: Veggies to Table Releases Fall Events Schedule
text:
Veggies to Table is opening the farm this fall for more learning, gathering and giving back.
Community members are invited for guided farm tours and workshops for gardeners of all experience levels. The season also includes a special harvest dinner and fundraiser at The Contented Sole, benefiting Veggies to Table’s work growing and donating organic produce and flowers to neighbors in need.
“Education is more and more at the heart of what we do.” said Erica Berman, executive director of Veggies to Table. “We love welcoming people to the farm to learn, connect, and see this work up close. It gives us a chance to share practical growing skills and celebrate the joy and purpose behind everything we grow.”

title: InvestigateTV+: Is poor vision sabotaging students?
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Poor vision could be sabotaging young students as they learn to read. InvestigateTV+ looks at how a lack of access to screenings could play a part.

How poor vision could be impacting reading skills
Knowing how to read is vital to everyday life whether you’re at work, home, or in school.
In classrooms across the country, a growing number of children struggle with learning this critical skill. Part of the reason could be because they can’t see clearly.
Ending traffic deaths
One approach to creating safer streets is a national movement known as “Vision Zero.” The goal is to eliminate all traffic deaths and serious injuries by 2050.
In Phoenix, Arizona, the push is showing results, but also highlighting the limitations.
Living off the land
Robin Greenfield doesn’t buy his food. He finds it.
Greenfield is traveling the country foraging 100 percent of his food and medicine.
Defying limits on the track
Outside of Kansas City, a high school para-athlete is pushing past expectations and capturing track championships.
And Jeremiah Mangels is doing that while challenging himself and inspiring his team.

title: National Institutes of Health Awards MaineHealth $4.5M to Study Impacts of PFAS
text:
MaineHealth will expand its research into the health impacts of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, known as PFAS, with funding from a five-year, $4.5 million grant by the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences of the National Institutes of Health.
The study at the MaineHealth Institute for Research, led by principal investigator and MaineHealth pediatrician Dr. Abby Fleisch, will build on her previous findings that children with higher levels of PFAS in their blood experienced a later onset of puberty and had lower bone mineral density, putting them at risk for osteoporosis later in life.

title: Chellie Pingree’s going after Trump. Why are so few of us listening?
text:
Hardly anyone seems to be paying attention to the increasingly sharp and powerful case made by Rep. Chellie Pingree against President Trump. They should.
Pingree, a Democrat who represents Maine’s 1st District, rips into Trump daily on an astonishing variety of issues, never mincing words. The House representative has been more or less screaming about the importance of saving America while we still can.
Consider just a handful of her many comments in the past two months.:
On corruption: “Trump’s personal wealth has ballooned by more than $2 billion in just the past 18 months, thanks to a combination of insider trading, shady crypto schemes, and brazen backroom deals. He’s the most corrupt president in history — and it ain’t close.”
On farming: “Trump says he wants to help American farmers but then plans to flood the American market with foreign beef. There is nothing ‘America First’ about his dumbass plan.”
On using tax money for campaign ads: “Let’s be clear: It is ILLEGAL to pay for campaign ads with taxpayer money. Period. … He really does see himself as above silly things like ‘the law’ and ‘campaign ethics.’”
On Iran: Trump “casually threatening to ‘annihilate’ another country in front of the entire U.N. General Assembly. What he’s saying would constitute war crimes. And this man has the nuclear codes. It’s astounding how hellbent he is on violating domestic and international law practically every time he opens his mouth. American foreign policy cannot revolve around destabilizing global peace and stability, the world economy, and our role as the leader of the free world. Horrifying.”
On the Kennedy Center: “Trump says the Kennedy Center is bankrupt and that only he can save it. BULLSHIT. The only problem with the Kennedy Center is Donald J. Trump.”
On the Arch: “Republicans are sitting back and letting Trump desecrate the hallowed landscape of Arlington National Cemetery. This hideous, massive vanity project is such an affront to veterans and Gold Star families. … Republicans in Congress could stop this and every other vanity project Trump is obsessed with. They need to grow a damn spine and remember their duty to the taxpayer. Pathetic.”
Pingree isn’t just concerned, not even very concerned. She’s actively trying to shake this nation from its torpor and get people riled up enough to prevent Trump from destroying what generations before him have built.
Pingree told me this week, “Whether it’s social media rants made with AI slop or threatening to annihilate entire civilizations, none of what Trump is saying and doing is normal or OK. I will keep speaking out, calling attention to this administration’s abuses and incompetence, and making sure people have the information they need to act.”
Maine’s independent senator, Angus King, issues eloquent statements opposing the president’s most stupid proposals and projects. King’s words are more measured, in keeping with the rational debate of our country at its best.
Regrettably, this isn’t a moment for polite disagreement. With so much at stake, Pingree has become too damn angry for calm appeals.
“My hope is that speaking out, consistently and plainly, helps turn justified frustration into engagement, organizing and, ultimately, change at the ballot box in November,” Pingree said.
Why she isn’t getting through to more people, I don’t know. As far as I’m concerned, Pingree is a hero in these dark times.

title: Witnesses to Christa Pike’s failed execution say their view was blocked multiple times
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WVLT/Gray News) - Witnesses to the failed execution of Christa Pike said their view of her attempted execution was often obscured, raising questions about Tennessee’s already scrutinized execution process.
Several witnesses were told by Tennessee’s Department of Correction that they would be granted access to watch Pike’s execution for the murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer.
During a news conference, witnesses confirmed TDOC staff had closed a curtain over the viewing window multiple times, blocking their view of the room where Pike was being put to death.
Tennessee’s official execution witness policy does not mention when, if at all, a curtain is supposed to be drawn over the window.
One witness to the failed execution outlines how often the curtain came down. Times are reported in Eastern time.
- 7:41 p.m. - Witnesses enter the viewing chamber
- 8:26 p.m. - Curtains open for the first time
- 8:46 p.m. - Curtains close for the first time
- 8:49 p.m. - Curtains open
- 9:05 p.m. - Curtains close
- 9:53 p.m. - Witnesses escorted out of viewing room
Another witness said, “I cannot mention enough how much happened behind a closed curtain as Christa Pike was still alive. A lot of this execution, or attempted execution, happened when we could not see what was going on.”
Tennessee is required by state law to allow media to witness an execution. Those witnesses act as representatives for the public and enable checks and balances when the state decides to execute someone in the public’s name.
Pike’s legal team said it had not been given an update on her condition after she was taken from the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution to a nearby hospital.
“The Tennessee Department of Correction followed every step of the State’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General’s Office,” the Tennessee Department of Correction said in a statement. “The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening. Christa Pike has been transported to an off-site medical facility.”
The failed execution marked the end of a chaotic day for Pike, Tennessee and several federal authorities.
Less than an hour before Pike was originally supposed to be executed at 11 a.m. Wednesday, the 6th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals granted a stay pausing her execution. That pause then prompted a response from the state, which asked the U.S. Supreme Court to intervene and allow the execution to continue.
Pike was convicted in 1996 in the “Job Corps Murder,” a name that came about because both Pike and Slemmer were members of the Job Corps at the time of the 1995 killing. Prosecutors have said in testimony that Pike conspired with two others, 17-year-old Tadaryl Shipp and 18-year-old Shadolla Peterson, to kill Slemmer over relationship issues. During the case, it was discovered that the offenders had carved a pentacle into Slemmer’s chest and taken a piece of her skull as a souvenir of the grisly murder.
There is no word on what the next steps will be in Pike’s planned execution.

title: Bangor warming shelters prepare for winter as state awards record grants
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - MaineHousing has announced $2.7 million in grants for winter warming shelters across the state — the largest funding round in the program’s history.
The Bangor Area Homeless Shelter on Main Street and The Brick Church on Union Street are among the organizations receiving funding. Following a freeze in state funding last year, The Brick Church will receive direct support from the state as it enters its seventh operating season.
“I’ve never been paid, and we all just volunteer here,” said Pastor Leon Licata. “This year we’ll be able to give out some stipends and help some people along the way that way.”
Licata says while they are excited to be a recipient of this year’s funding, the church still faces issues related to capacity.
“I’m okay to hold 70 people, but last year there was 120 to 130 people out on the street,” Licata said. “That makes a big difference, especially if that’s your son, daughter, mother, father, grandparent.”
Licata said discussions are already underway to help support warming shelters that were not awarded state funds, including the neighboring Together Place and The Mansion Church on Center Street.
“They’ve always funded us in the past. I was a little set back by that. I really expected that we would get the funding again,” said Mansion Church Pastor Terry Dinkins.
Despite not receiving state funding, Dinkins plans to keep the warming center open and is turning to the community for support.
“We’re not going to let a lack of funds keep people from coming into the church to be warm and fed. We’ll just have to change some things around, maybe ask the community or our congregation to step up and donate finances,” Dinkins said, “Just because we didn’t get funding, we’re still going to open up the doors.”
Community members can support The Mansion Church by visiting its Facebook page.
The Brick Church is also seeking volunteers to help overnight and with crowd management this season.

title: Mainers are stretched thin. In Oxford County, many can’t afford enough food.
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
This is the first story in the series Stretched Thin: The cost of getting by in Maine, which looks at the financial hardships Mainers face. Social services reporter Gillian Graham reported this story as a USC Annenberg Center for Health Journalism 2026 National Fellow and a participant in the Center’s engagement initiative.
MEXICO — By the time the first people arrived for lunch on a warm July day, Michelle Williams and the volunteers at the River Valley’s only soup kitchen had been at work for hours.
They stretched out clean white tablecloths and arranged baskets of fruit and snacks on the buffet line. They filled large orange coolers with lemonade and water and set out napkins and utensils. They stirred baked beans bubbling in a warmer, the scent wafting out of the kitchen.
Williams, a retired hospice nurse who founded Good Samaritan Missionary Services, had started cooking the day before. The menu included barbecue pulled chicken sandwiches, street corn pasta salad and her famous lemon icebox cake.
Her motivation, she said, is simple: “Food is a necessity, not a luxury.”
In Oxford County’s River Valley — where the towns that hug the Androscoggin River have long been known for their deep ties to paper manufacturing — many working families have a hard time covering their everyday expenses. The hunger rate is among the highest in the state.
The financial situation can be even more bleak for people who are retired, unemployed or homeless.
Some families have been in poverty, or hovering just above it, for generations.
Before the soup kitchen opened, there were few options in the area for food assistance. Three years ago, Williams started an emergency food pantry at town hall. Within six months, it morphed into the soup kitchen because of the high demand, she said.
It’s not uncommon to hear about people working 12-hour days but still struggling to make ends meet, said Joleen Bedard, president and CEO of United Way of Western Maine. Some have seasonal jobs with inconsistent incomes, while others grapple with how to get to work and appointments in a region without widely accessible public transportation.
“It’s certainly a struggle and I don’t see it changing any time soon,” she said. “There are two Maines: the haves and the have-nots.”
‘BARRIER AFTER BARRIER’
Every day, thousands of Mainers face the hardest choices: buy food or pay for a prescription; drive far for healthcare or risk going without; toil to afford childcare or stop working; go to a homeless shelter or sleep in a tent.
Across the state, data from 2024 shows, 40% of households fell below the federal poverty line or just above the threshold, where people struggle to afford basic expenses, but don’t always qualify for assistance.
“There is an enormous number of hardworking families throughout the state who are one unexpected expense away from crisis,” said Dan Coyne, who heads the United Way of Southern Maine.
This summer, the United Ways of Maine released new data they say shows traditional measures of poverty have undercounted the number of households in the state experiencing financial hardship.
Many have incomes above the federal poverty line and are part of a population called ALICE — Asset Limited, Income Constrained, Employed. The threshold for each county is calculated using household income and a survival budget that includes the cost of housing, childcare, food, transportation, healthcare and technology.
It does not include room for savings, debt payments or emergency expenses.
In Rumford, 66% of households struggle to afford basic expenses — the most of any town in the county, according to the United Way. Census data shows 15% are below the poverty line.
Half of the households in Mexico and 41% in neighboring Dixfield also fall below the ALICE threshold.
For decades, people in Maine’s rural areas have experienced financial hardship and poverty at higher rates. But even in coastal areas, where more wealth is concentrated, there are pockets of residents struggling.
For many in the Oxford County region, improving their financial outlook seems nearly impossible, even if they’re working, said Melissa McEntee, who runs Rumford Group Homes, the only homeless shelter program in the county.
“We see hard-working families who do everything they can to get out of that poverty cycle. Everything in River Valley keeps sucking them back in,” she said. “Everything is a barrier. It’s barrier after barrier after barrier.”
FALLING THROUGH THE CRACKS
Sue Grace remembers the heyday of Rumford, when the town was booming and there wasn’t an empty storefront downtown. There was a big hotel that hosted fancy weddings, a hat shop she’d visit with her grandmother, and a police officer with a whistle and white gloves directing traffic.
“Talk about a Norman Rockwell portrait,” the lifelong Rumford resident said.
Grace, 72, worked at the local hospital for years and raised her four kids in town. In the ’80s, as manufacturing at the paper mill declined and the workforce shrank, businesses on Congress Street started to close. Unemployment ticked up and there was less going on to keep kids entertained, she said.
The paper mill in Rumford employed more than 3,000 people at its peak, but today it employs just over 500. The steep decline in manufacturing created economic uncertainty in the communities, according to Friends of the River Valley, which supports a range of nutrition, education, health and social services programs in the area.
Grace said she never considered leaving, even after she retired from her job as a phlebotomist and two of her adult children moved out of town. She was doing fine on her Social Security and small pension for a while, but things have become tougher in the past few years as the cost of everything seemed to go up.
Now, she feels like she’s falling through the cracks.
Grace gets about $24 a month in federal food assistance benefits and the $417 monthly rent for her apartment is based on her income. In August, she was eagerly awaiting her $300 affordability check from the state so she could replace her six-year-old cell phone.
She’s grateful for the help and said she’s fortunate to be better off than many, but she still has to make tough choices.
Most days, Grace eats two meals to save on groceries.
She goes to the soup kitchen in Mexico for lunch because that is food she doesn’t have to figure out how to pay for.
“I was raised that you don’t ask for help. I had to learn to do that,” she said, while sitting in her dining room under a wall sign encouraging visitors to “Live well, laugh often, love much.”
After working hard for 40 years, Grace doesn’t think she should have to struggle so much.
FILLING THE GAP
A half-dozen people carrying reusable shopping bags lingered in the dirt parking lot outside of the Old School Food Pantry in Mexico on a gloomy day in June. They chatted quietly as raindrops started to fall, adding to the unseasonable chill.
They were an hour early for the weekly distribution, but wanted to make sure they could get what they needed.
The two-room food pantry in the bottom floor of an old school building sits on a hill facing the river. The white plumes from the mill stacks drift over the trees.
Just inside the door, volunteer William Gallant sat at a table, lists of pantry regulars laid out in front of him and clipboards with checklists of grocery items neatly stacked to the side. Every time someone came in, he clicked a counter dangling from his neck to keep track of how many people showed up for groceries.
Oxford County has one of the highest food insecurity rates in the state, with nearly a quarter of all children in the region experiencing hunger, according to Feeding America, which tracks the issue across the country.
The number of Mainers experiencing hunger continues to rise. It’s the highest it’s been in a decade, according to a report released this summer.
More than 11,000 Mainers have lost access to the federal Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program because of sweeping changes that began rolling out last fall, according to state officials.
Rural areas of Maine, where more people tend to rely on SNAP, are being hit especially hard by the changes, according to hunger prevention advocates. Work exemptions were removed for rural areas with low employment options, leaving some people struggling to find work or volunteer opportunities to maintain access to food assistance.
Food pantries trying to fill the gap are reporting record numbers of visits. In August, nearly 300 families came in to pick up fresh produce, meat and boxes of shelf-stable groceries from the Old School Food Pantry.
Gallant, 77, grew up in Rumford when the paper mill was the biggest employer and the company’s owner pumped money into the town, including the community center where kids gathered for dances and bowling in the basement.
Gallant, who has been volunteering at the food pantry for four years, sees the impact every week from behind his check-in table.
There are always new people coming in for the first time — older retirees whose pensions don’t cover the bills anymore, working parents who can’t afford groceries, people who are out of work and piecing together whatever they can to get by.
As the pantry gets busier, he worries there won’t be enough food to go around.
“I don’t ever want to be the person who has to tell them we ran out of food,” he said, as he handed a clipboard to the next person in line.
FEEDING THE COMMUNITY
The school district that serves Rumford and Mexico decided in late June that it did not have the staff to distribute free lunch to kids during the summer, a move that Williams, from the soup kitchen, said was particularly hard on families already struggling to provide food.
In the first days after school let out, she said there was a noticeable increase in families with kids coming in for lunch.
“Holy smokes, we are getting our butts handed to us,” Williams said in early July. One day the previous week, she served 45 people in less than an hour. Half of them were children.
As the outside temperature pushed into the high 80s, Angela Dean, her husband and their 1-year-old daughter were among the first to arrive for lunch on July 6.
“We just want to live here, Michelle,” Dean called out as she walked into the air-conditioned room and headed for a table in the back corner.
Dean, who was staying at the homeless shelter, comes in for lunch most days the soup kitchen is open. She knows everyone by name.
“It’s a huge relief,” she said, after settling her daughter into a highchair and filling their plates. “It might seem like one meal three days a week isn’t a big deal, but when you’re a mom trying to survive, it’s so important.”
Dean has lived in the River Valley for more than 20 years. She doesn’t think there are enough resources available to help residents. She said she’s watched rents shoot up higher than she thought possible.
“A lot of people struggle here,” Dean said. “There are a lot of people who don’t have anywhere to go. People are overworked and underpaid.”
Alisha Holtorf, of Mexico, came into the soup kitchen a few minutes later with four of her five children. They’re regulars, too, and have grown especially close to Williams and the volunteers who serve lunch. Williams keeps applesauce pouches on hand for the youngest Holtorf, 2-year-old Ember.
Holtorf, 34, runs the food pantry at her church, Praise Assembly of God in downtown Rumford, and sees firsthand how many people in the community are living on the edge financially.
“People are doing all they can, but it still doesn’t seem like enough for this area,” she said.
Holtorf homeschools her kids and works two part-time jobs. Her husband has a manufacturing job in Auburn, but she said they still don’t make enough and don’t qualify for any assistance programs. To stretch her budget, Holtorf grows vegetables, swaps the clothes her kids have outgrown for new sizes at the church’s clothing closet, and is careful about spending at the grocery store.
The Holtorfs saved for several years to pay for a road trip to see family in Iowa in September.
She said people often come to the church for help, but the congregation is small and many of its members are on fixed incomes and can’t afford to give more.
“It’s hard,” she said, “telling people we don’t have the funds.”
‘ROBBING PETER TO PAY PAUL’
While it’s clear many people — including older residents who rely on Social Security and young families burdened by childcare expenses — are struggling to get by, Rumford Town Manager George O’Keefe sees progress in addressing some of the critical needs laid bare in the years following the decline in manufacturing.
The service sector has grown substantially and there has been “really drastic” growth in energy production and storage businesses, O’Keefe said.
Rumford, the largest town in the county, has a hospital and the Black Mountain of Maine ski resort. Larger ski resorts nearby attract thousands of people every winter.
For the last few years, the town has been focused on encouraging the construction of more housing — from neighborhoods of single-family homes to affordable apartments for older residents. O’Keefe believes this will go a long way toward addressing some of the financial pressure on River Valley residents.
“There are a lot of families that struggle to stay on the rung of the economic ladder they’re on, let alone make upward progress,” O’Keefe said.
Courtney Johnson finds herself facing the same choice every winter: keep the lights on or heat the house. The Mexico resident always chooses heat because the power company can’t easily disconnect service during the coldest months of winter under state law.
“The saying ‘Robbing Peter to pay Paul’ never meant anything to me as a kid,” she said. “Now, I do it all the time.”
Johnson is blunt when she describes her family’s financial situation: “It sucks to be poor.”
Johnson, 39, and her husband, Jason, met while growing up in York County, but didn’t start dating until after they were out of school and she had two children. They had five more children together, including a baby girl born this summer. They moved to the River Valley about eight years ago to live with his mother’s boyfriend. For nearly four years, the family stayed crammed together in two bedrooms.
Johnson said she asked her husband to pick up a scratch-off lottery ticket when he was at the store a few years ago. The $5 ticket he bought was a winner, a stroke of luck that she said sent him running down the street in celebration.
They decided to use the money to create more stability for the family and Johnson said they were able to buy a house in Mexico for $55,000 in 2023. Some of the kids still have to share bedrooms, she said, but they’re not crowded into small rooms. The property came with apple trees and a picnic table, just like the house she had always dreamed of owning.
But owning a home hasn’t alleviated their financial constraints.
Johnson recently left her job as a direct support professional at a local nonprofit to care for her new baby. Childcare, if she could find it, would cost more than she made. Her husband is a subcontractor, but work can be inconsistent. Sometimes, she said, he works on homes of older members of their church who can only afford to pay him with thanks, prayer and homemade cookies.
The Johnsons, who work part-time leading the youth ministry at Praise Assembly of God, found their way to the church a few years ago after attending its annual Culture of Compassion event, where people can get a free lunch, groceries and clothing.
Johnson is grateful her family is insured through MaineCare and receives benefits from the Women, Infants and Children program. Most months, the $1,300 they get from SNAP is enough to cover groceries, but sometimes they have to use a local food pantry.
“We’re very frugal because we know what it’s like to go without,” she said. “We try not to take from this church (food pantry) because we know people around here need it more.”
The Johnsons try to help where they can. When they heard a young person in their church was using dish soap to brush his teeth, they bought him toothpaste. Recently, they scraped together $200 to buy meat for a family short on food.
“We will go without to help another family,” she said.
FINDING A WAY TO HELP
In the River Valley, many support systems are informal. If one group can’t help someone, they often know where to point them for assistance, said McEntee, the homeless shelter director.
“People who care and want to help have found a way to band together,” McEntee said. “We feel lucky that in Oxford County we are small and all the providers know each other.”
At Good Samaritan, helping goes beyond the food laid out on the buffet table.
On Thursdays, a retired social worker sits in the back of the soup kitchen, helping people sign up for assistance programs. The back room is stocked with basic toiletries, household items and pet food. When someone faces an unexpected hardship, Williams is known to jump in.
“Michelle will always find a way to help,” said Carol Violette, a retired seamstress who has volunteered at the soup kitchen since it opened.
Williams and the Good Samaritan board do it all on a shoestring budget.
They apply for grants and put a small donation jar out during every lunch. When a grant payment was delayed, Williams used some of her own Social Security check to cover expenses until it came in. A supporter gives $400 every month from her Social Security income.
As summer waned, Williams spent hours canning sauerkraut, pickled beets, tomato sauce and vegetables to get the soup kitchen through the long winter.
“It’s a tiring week,” she said, “but it’s nice to go into the weekend knowing you’ve helped people.”
When the new school year started, Williams decided to cut back to two lunches each week. When winter sets in, she plans to open the soup kitchen on the coldest days as a refuge for people living outside and those whose homes aren’t warm enough.
There won’t always be lunch, but the coffee will be hot.

title: Renee Good’s family sues US government, immigration officials over her killing
text:
MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — Renee Good’s family sued the U.S. government and several immigration officials Thursday, alleging wrongful death and other violations of federal law in the 37-year-old woman’s killing by an immigration officer during a federal crackdown in Minneapolis.
The two lawsuits were filed by Good’s partner, Becca Good, and Renee’s brother Brent Ganger.
One lawsuit, filed against “the United States of America,” alleges the wrongful death of Renee Good under Minnesota law predicated on claims of battery, assault, false imprisonment, intentional infliction of emotional distress and negligence that caused her death.
The other lawsuit alleges a conspiracy to interfere with civil rights. It names as defendants: Jonathan Ross, the immigration officer who shot her; White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller; former Homeland Security head Kristi Noem; former U.S. Border Patrol commander-at-large Gregory Bovino, Corey Lewandowski, President Donald Trump’s campaign manager, and others.
Renee Good, a mother of three, was fatally shot Jan. 7 as protests against immigration raids flared across the city. According to Becca Good, her partner stopped their car in a street to support neighbors during an immigration operation.
Bystander video shows Renee Good in the driver’s seat of a red SUV blocking part of the road and repeatedly honking her horn.
Two immigration officers get out of a truck, their faces covered, and one orders Good to get out of the car. She reverses briefly, then turns the steering wheel as the officer says again, “get out of the car.”
Almost simultaneously, Becca Good, standing in the street, shouts: “Drive, baby, drive!”
One officer standing in front of the vehicle pulls his weapon and fires into the windshield. He lurches back as the car turns away from him. The officer, who is now very close to the open window on the driver’s side, opens fire two more times, fatally shooting Renee Good, according to an analysis of the videos by The Associated Press and others.
Federal officials at the time said the officer acted in self-defense and that Good had engaged in “an act of domestic terrorism.”
The killing of Good and another U.S. citizen, Alex Pretti, in Minneapolis just weeks later sparked outrage across the country and calls to rein in immigration enforcement. At least 10 people have died in encounters with immigration officers during President Donald Trump’s second term.
In July, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer with a history of violent behavior fatally shot a 25-year-old Colombian man, Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, in his car in Biddeford, Maine. Durán Guerrero was not the target of an immigration enforcement action.
Last week, immigration enforcement agents shot and wounded a Venezuelan delivery driver in Austin, Texas. Wilber Rafael Garces-Perez, 28, survived but was charged with sideswiping an officer with his car mirror and later attempting to strike an officer with the vehicle.
Becca and Renee Good were not legally married, according to a family lawyer, but referred to one another as wives. They had only recently relocated to Minneapolis from Kansas City, Missouri.
In social media accounts, Renee Good described herself as a “poet and writer and wife and mom.” On Pinterest, a profile picture shows her smiling and holding a young child, alongside posts about tattoos, hairstyles and home decorating.
In an interview shortly after her death, Renee Good’s mother, Donna Ganger, told The Associated Press: “She had this way of making you feel special and loved that I didn’t even understand that until we lost her.”
