title: Troy Jackson ahead of Susan Collins in AARP poll, but she's dominating swing voters
text:
Politics
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
Democrat Troy Jackson leads U.S. Sen. Susan Collins by 3 points in an AARP poll released Thursday, but no Republican in the group’s battleground Senate surveys this year is doing better with voters who split their tickets than the five-term incumbent.
The survey shows Jackson winning a base election that pits young voters against old ones. His 25-point lead among voters under 50 is outweighing Collins’s 9-point edge with older voters. But Collins, who trailed in every public poll in 2020 before winning by nearly 9 points, has more swing-voter support than any Republican in AARP’s seven battleground Senate polls.
The same pollsters found Democrats leading or tied in all seven races dating back to June, including in Republican-leaning Texas and Ohio. Collins’ hold on ticket-splitters is what keeps her within striking distance in a terrible environment for President Donald Trump and her party.
“Susan Collins is the thing that differentiates this battleground from many of the others that we’re looking at this cycle,” said Bob Ward of Fabrizio Ward, the Republican firm that works for Trump and conducts AARP surveys with Democratic-aligned Impact Research. “She is not a traditional Republican.”
Jackson, a former Maine Senate president from Allagash, led Collins 50% to 47% in the survey of 982 likely voters taken Sept. 20-22. The margin of error was plus or minus 3.1 percentage points. The survey was taken concurrently with three others released last week, two of which had Jackson narrowly ahead.
The age split in AARP’s poll is stark. Jackson led voters 18 to 34 by 47 points. Collins led voters 50 to 64 by 12, the widest margin with that group for any Republican in AARP’s Senate polls. She led those 65 and older by just 7, the smallest senior margin among them. Yet even that lead reflects crossover support, because Maine seniors favored Democrats for Congress by 6 points.
There may be a turnout edge in Collins’ base. Only 69% of the youngest voters rated their motivation to vote at a 10 out of 10, compared with 89% of voters 65 and older. Younger voters may not turn out in the numbers the survey assumes, Ward cautioned.
Collins’ path runs through swing voters 50 and older, according to the AARP survey. These voters didn’t pick the same party in the Senate, governor and generic congressional races, making up 20% of the poll’s older voters and backing the Republican 70% to 17%.
The 53-point margin within that demographic is the widest of any Senate candidate in AARP’s polls of Alaska, Georgia, Michigan, North Carolina, Ohio, Texas and Maine this cycle. The next-best showing was former Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers’ 33-point lead in Michigan. Every other Republican was losing swing voters.
Collins was also the only candidate in the series with a positive image among those voters, at 59% favorable to 32% unfavorable. Jackson was underwater at 23% to 60%, the worst of any major-party Senate candidate AARP tested.
Her crossover appeal extends beyond that group. Collins won 11% of Democrats, the most for any Republican in the series. Democrats led the generic congressional ballot here by 10 points, yet she ran 7 points ahead of her party. That was also the most of any Republican AARP polled.
She’s doing this in the most anti-Trump electorate AARP surveyed this cycle. Trump’s job approval in Maine was 37% to 61%, worse than in any of the other six states.
But the electorate still isn’t sold on Collins. Voters viewed her favorably by 44% and unfavorably by 53%, while Jackson’s image was 47% to 44%.
Few voters are left to persuade. Only 3% were undecided, the lowest of any Senate race in AARP’s battleground polls this cycle. The rest ranged from 5% in Georgia, Michigan and North Carolina to 8% in Texas. Ward said many of these voters may not ultimately turn out.

title: Older Mainers leaning toward Susan Collins in US Senate race, AARP poll shows
text:
A new battleground poll released by the AARP shows Democrat Troy Jackson with a narrow lead over Republican Susan Collins in Maine’s U.S. Senate race.
Jackson holds a 3 percentage point lead over Collins, 50% to 47%, which is within the survey’s margin of error of 3.1%.
But Jackson is trailing Collins among an important segment of Maine’s electorate — voters over 50 who are more likely to split their tickets than vote along party lines.
And Jackson is underperforming fellow Democrat Hannah Pingree, who holds a 13 percentage point lead over Republican Bobby Charles, 52% to 39%, in the governor’s race. Independent Rick Bennett drew 6%.
The survey of 982 likely voters was conducted from Sept. 20-22 by Fabrizio Ward and Impact Research. It offers insight into how older Mainers, who are among the most reliable voters in the state, are leaning in Maine’s closely watched race between Collins and Jackson.
The survey is further evidence that Collins remains a formidable opponent in a midterm cycle that is expected to be difficult for Republicans nationally, with President Donald Trump’s approval ratings at historic lows.
The AARP poll found that 61% of respondents disapproved of Trump’s job performance, while 37% approved. And 53% preferred Democrats on the generic congressional ballot, compared to the 43% for Republicans.
Maine’s older voters, Fabrizio Ward partner Bob Ward said, are “highly engaged. They’re paying attention and they’re looking for candidates who understand the issues that affect their daily lives.”
The top issue for all voters surveyed was affordability (44%). It was cited as the top issue by 33% of voters 50 and older, who said their main concerns were the price of gas and groceries.
Among older voters, 93% said they would be more likely to vote for a candidate that makes sure workers get the Social Security benefits they earned, 85% for someone who would protect the program from cuts and oppose increasing the retirement age, and 84% for someone who would lower the cost of healthcare and prescription drugs.
The poll found that voters 50 and older, who the AARP said comprised 60% or more of turnout in the last two federal election cycles, are breaking toward Collins and Pingree.
Collins holds a 9-point advantage among these older voters, about 20% of whom planned to split their tickets. Among these swing voters, Collins holds a 53-point advantage, while Pingree holds a 28-point advantage over Charles.
Bennett, meanwhile, drew 32% support among older swing voters in the governor’s race.
“It just speaks to how Sen. Collins is a different kind of Republican,” Ward said. “(She) maintains her base, but also reaches out to the center. This is going to be a really close race.”
Jackson holds a roughly two point lead over Collins, according to polling averages from the election website FiftyPlusOne.
A New York Times/Portland Press Herald/Siena poll conducted around the same time as the AARP’s survey found Collins with a 3 point lead over Jackson, 49% to 46%, which was also within the margin of error of +/- 4.9%.
That poll also found swing voters breaking toward Collins, including 8% of respondents that identified as Democrats.
The five-term Republican drew 13% support from people saying they wanted Democrats to won control the Senate, and 12% from people who voted for Democrat Kamala Harris for president in 2024.
The survey also found that Collins held a commanding leading among respondents aged 45-64. She led Jackson among that group 57% to 38%. But they practically split the 65 and over vote, with Jackson getting 48% to Collins’s 47%.
Both the NYT/Press Herald/ Siena and AARP polls were conducted before ProPublica reported that the Department of Justice and Federal Bureau of Investigation had been gearing up for bribery and corruption probe aimed at determining whether Collins was steering federal contracts to a defense contractor in exchange for political donations. That effort was dropped when Trump took office in 2025.
Collins has “vigorously” denied the allegations.

title: Father of newborn triplets kidnapped, murdered in case of mistaken identity, authorities say
text:
SAN JOAQUIN COUNTY, Calif. (KCRA) - Three suspects wanted in the kidnapping and murder of a California father who authorities say was a victim of mistaken identity have been identified.
Avtar Singh, a 57-year-old father of newborn triplets, was kidnapped Feb. 17 from a Sikh temple in Tracy. His body was found three days later more than 100 miles away.
Investigators with the San Joaquin County Sheriff’s Office believe Singh was a victim of mistaken identity. On Wednesday, they identified the three suspects indicted in connection with his death as 25-year-old Alberto Alencastro, 20-year-old Alfonso Segura and 22-year-old Barnabe Segura.
All three suspects have been indicted on charges that include murder with special circumstances and kidnapping. The men are from Vallejo, have ties to Mexico and remain at large.
Surveillance footage showed Singh had been kidnapped by three people in a white crossover-style SUV. The suspect vehicle was identified by Flock license plate reader technology, tracked to Vallejo and seized on Feb. 19, the sheriff’s office said.
Authorities say Singh was not the intended target of the kidnapping but instead mistaken for someone else. Between Feb. 25 and Feb. 27, investigators traveled to Canada to interview the man identified as the intended target. He and his family had been receiving threats related to a stolen trailer, the sheriff’s said.
Investigators say that stolen trailer was enough for the three suspects to want to chase him down and kill him.
Singh had lived on the Sikh temple’s grounds with his wife and children. San Joaquin County Sheriff Patrick Withrow remembered him as a pillar in his community.
“He was such a good person. He cooked for everybody at the temple, and he took care of anything that was broken,” Withrow said. “This man was taken from a place of worship in broad daylight because of a theft that had nothing to do with him.”
Withrow says investigators made a promise to Singh’s wife.
“We gave her our word then and we give her our word now that we will not let this go by without finding these individuals,” he said.
The three suspects all face a life sentence without the possibility of parole. The Sikh community is offering a $50,000 reward for information that may lead to their arrests.

text:
PHILADELPHIA (KYW) -- A woman shot and killed a man who police say broke into her apartment Wednesday morning.

title: Pres. Trump begins midterm campaign tour in three red states
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump left the White House on Thursday afternoon to start a monthlong midterm campaign tour, beginning in Texas, Oklahoma and Alabama, three Republican-leaning states.
The tour aims to build support for members of the president’s party who are running in the November elections.
The president’s first stop was the Peterbilt truck factory in Denton, Texas. He is also expected to appear at a rally in Durant, Oklahoma on Thursday night and another rally in Mobile, Alabama on Friday.
RNC Central Regional Communications Director Zach Kraft said the campaign events give Trump a chance to reach voters in two states with significant races.
“[It] gives President Trump the opportunity to speak to voters both in Oklahoma and in Texas, where we have tons of critical races,” he said.
The decision to have the president campaign in traditionally Republican-leaning states, rather than more competitive areas, has drawn attention from political observers and Democratic opponents, who say it may indicate that the GOP is playing defense in areas where the party typically performs well.
“I do think it’s interesting that we constantly see Donald Trump in these red states. Texas specifically. He was just here for the midterm conventions, said Texas state Rep. Mihaela Plesa, a Democrat.
Plesa said she thinks the president’s visit suggests that Democrats have more opportunities to win in Texas during this election cycle, compared to previous years.
“I think that not just the Trump brand, but really Republican policies are facing the scrutiny of what people are feeling right now,” she said. “And I think that Democrats have an opportunity to talk about what it is that they’re going to do for working Americans, whether we’re talking about helping them pay for their healthcare, making sure they can support the American dream, that homeownership is a reality for young people.”
The Cook Political Report has labeled the Texas U.S. Senate race and three U.S. House races in the state as “toss ups.”
The group has rated nearly every congressional race in Oklahoma and Alabama as “Solid R,” with the exception of Alabama’s 2nd Congressional District, which is been labeled as “likely R.”
Earlier this week on Capitol Hill, Sen. Tommy Tuberville, R-Ala., said the Mobile stop does not signal concern from the president.
“What he’s doing is he’s starting his tour. And he did the same thing back what 2015. That’s where he started. Senator Sessions introduced him that night. I will introduce him this week,” Tuberville said, who is running for governor during this election cycle.
Trump is also expected to campaign in Ohio, Iowa and Alaska this month.

title: What scares me about real estate in Maine right now
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Julia Bassett Schwerin of Cape Elizabeth has been a real estate broker since 2005.
The real estate market is approaching a balanced market where supply and demand are in equilibrium and moving away from the seller’s market it has been in since 2020. After the pandemic, demand surged, prices rose and inventory dropped, but now the number of homes for sale has finally started to recover.
My prediction is that prices, which have doubled the value of most homes over the last seven years, will soften as sellers spend some of their massive equity to attract fewer buyers, but will not result in anything like the crash we had in 2008.
The issue that does scare me is that the operating expenses of owning a home represent a larger contributor to the unaffordability of housing than the first cost, which is getting all the attention. Specifically, I am referring to the cost of heating and homeowner’s insurance.
Maine has been doing well transitioning off heating with oil, going from 70% down to 50% of homes burning oil in the last seven years, but oil costs are expected to increase 30% this winter compared to last due to the Iran war. Buyers of more efficient buildings using clean energy are much more able to benefit from paying less in fuel cost than the small increase in mortgage payments for better insulation and air sealing.
For help paying utility bills, check out the consumer assistance information on the websites of the Public Utilities Commission, the Office of the Public Advocate and Efficiency Maine.
Maine has also enjoyed affordable insurance until recent storms caused catastrophic damage. Unfortunately, rising sea levels and severe storms caused by climate change are being sidelined and smeared as a political wedge issue. The weather risks from a warming planet are raising insurance premiums for property both across the board in reinsurance rates and selectively in areas where flooding, wildfires, storms, droughts and pollution have caused damage and claims.
Models ranking address-level property risks from climate factors have been built by several firms and are being closely scrutinized by insurers who have their own databases on losses. As the property damage costs from increased global warming rise, so too will claims for reimbursement by the government; if and when the federal government is unwilling or unable to help people who incurred disaster losses, the private insurers will be left holding the bag.
According to data from the U.S. Senate Budget Committee, the rate of home insurance policy nonrenewal is rising in the U.S. and in Maine. If homeowners can’t afford insurance premiums big enough to share the costs of flood and storm damage with those unaffected, then they can’t afford to live in single-family homes and will have to share housing; the insurers must be doing the math that it’s better for their business to incentivize us to fortify our buildings against climate change than rachet up the premiums or stop renewing policies.
Here is the proof: the Maine Bureau of Insurance, which is responsible for regulating the insurance firms underwriting policies in the state, took it upon themselves to adopt a program designed in the hurricane and tornado belts by the Institute for Business and Home Safety.
Called Fortify, it collects money from insurers and distributes it to building owners in the form of substantial grants to add fortification to a new roof by sealing the roof deck and locking down the drip edge, measures proven in wind tunnel testing to keep the roof attached and the water out.
If insurers with sophisticated data think that enough increasingly scary weather is on its way to Maine to warrant adopting the program, shouldn’t we in the real estate and construction trades act like they are probably right?
What the heck are we doing here bickering about whether we should teach Realtors about sustainability, whether we should adopt stricter building energy codes that reduce emissions, or whether we need to take collective measures to make buildings more resilient to the risk of loss from worsening storms and floods? The answer is a resounding “yes.”
The real estate and construction industries can see this bubbling up like a manhole cover on a side street at the Portland Old Port during a sunny day king tide.
We need an all of us together approach to the transition to clean energy from fossil fuel combustion emissions in buildings, and we need it now.

title: Hurricane Rachel strengthens to a Category 3 storm off Mexico’s Pacific Coast
text:
MEXICO CITY (AP) — Hurricane Rachel has been upgraded to a Category 3 storm off Mexico’s Pacific coast as northern Mexico and parts of the U.S. Southwest were reeling from flooding and damage from the remnants of Hurricane Polo earlier this week.
The storm, located about 235 miles (380 kilometers) south off the southern tip of Baja California, was continuing west-northwest at 3 mph (6 kph) and expected to strengthen Friday before weakening this weekend, according to the National Hurricane Center.
The maximum sustained winds were 120 miles per hour (193 kph) as of Thursday evening. Rachel’s swells are expected to generate life-threatening surf and rip-current conditions off Mexico’s coast, the NHC warned.
Mexican authorities said Thursday they remain on alert because of forecasts of very heavy rain in the states of Baja California Sur, Sinaloa, and Jalisco, and the possibility of landslides, rising river levels, overflowing rivers and flooding in low-lying areas.
On Wednesday night, the U.S. Embassy in Mexico warned U.S. citizens in Cabos San Lucas, a popular vacation destination for Americans, of beach and port closures and deadly rip currents.
The Pacific has seen an unusually busy hurricane season, which experts have attributed to El Niño, which has fueled crippling droughts in Mexico and Central America and floods in other parts of the region. In the Pacific, it has resulted in warmer waters and wind patterns that act as fodder for hurricanes. Tropical Storm Nolo continued its northwest approach away from Hawaii on Thursday, though the National Weather Service said it could strengthen into a hurricane by the weekend.
Northern Mexico still reeling from Polo
Parts of northern Mexico were still reeling from floods and wider destruction left by Polo. Hundreds of people remained displaced or had their homes destroyed, and at least 13 municipalities remained flooded Thursday night, according to local authorities.
Lucía Vegas, who lives in the small town of Bacabachi in the border state of Sonora, said it was a miracle she survived severe flooding as it swept through her community. She, her husband and three children were left homeless.
Vegas said she and her family managed to survive thanks to their dog. In the middle of the night, as the floodwaters were rising, the dog woke her by shaking water off herself, giving the family enough time to climb a ladder onto the roof of their home just minutes before it was completely flooded.
“Right now, we have been left with nothing,” the 39-year-old woman said through tears.
Storm remnants drench central U.S.
Areas in Texas, Nebraska, Missouri and Iowa were still under flood watch Thursday afternoon as storm remnants continued to batter the region, flooding streets and neighborhoods and setting off water rescues.
Wednesday was the wettest day on record for Lincoln, Nebraska, which received 6.1 inches of rainfall, according to the University of Nebraska-Lincoln Climate Office.
In Omaha, which received 4.7 inches of rain Wednesday, the fire department said it responded to 80 water rescues over a three-hour period ending early Thursday. Some floodwaters reached depths of 8 feet. Schools remained open. But many buses never made it out of flooded parking lots, prompting officials to ask parents to transport their students to school.
San Antonio, Texas, was under a flash-flood warning through Thursday evening, and the city urged residents to avoid unnecessary travel. More than 19,000 residents across the state were without power Thursday afternoon, according to PowerOutage.us. Videos posted on social media showed floodwaters in Texas creating waves along Interstate 35 in Denton.
In Chicago, a wastewater treatment and stormwater management utility urged residents to conserve water use to prevent flooding and stormwater backup.
“We encourage everyone to conserve water when possible to create more capacity in our systems,” utility President Kari K. Steele said in a statement Wednesday.
In Kansas, Gov. Laura Kelly issued an emergency proclamation on Wednesday ahead of the storms that allows state resources to assist first responders in hard-hit communities.
___
Raza reported from Sioux Falls, South Dakota, and Castellón reported from Bacabachi, Mexico. Associated Press writer John Raby in Cross Lanes, West Virginia, contributed to this report.

title: Pilot escapes with minor injuries after crashing extremely rare plane in Maine
text:
Pilot escapes with minor injuries after crashing extremely rare plane in Brunswick, Maine
A pilot from Windham, New Hampshire, walked away with only minor injuries after crashing a plane while landing at the Brunswick Executive Airport in Brunswick on Thursday.
The Brunswick Police Department says the 82-year-old pilot was flying a 1930s Kinner Sportwing airplane when the plane flipped over after landing.
The pilot was the only person on board and was treated at the scene for what police said were minor injuries.
The plane was headed to Owls Head from Lawrence, Massachusetts. Owls Head is home to the Owls Head Transportation Museum.
The museum released a statement on Thursday afternoon saying they were still assessing the situation and gathering information.
"We have been told the pilot is safe, and the incident occurred during taxi rather than while landing. We remain optimistic that the vintage Kinner aircraft will be properly assessed and operable soon," the museum said.
The Federal Aviation Administration is investigating the cause of the crash.
The Kinner Sportwing was only made for a few years in the 1930s by the Kinner Airplane & Motor Corporation in California. Only eight of this model were ever made and only one is known to still exist.
According to the Aircraft Owners and Pilots Association, it was purchased by a man from Windham, New Hampshire, in 2016 and taken to a hangar in Lawrence.

title: Who’s afraid of Bobby Charles?
text:
Sam Patten has worked for Maine’s last three Republican senators, including Susan Collins’ first electoral campaigns, is a former managing editor of The Maine Wire and is the author of “Dangerous Company: The Misadventures of a Foreign Agent.”
Given the publicly available polling on Maine’s gubernatorial race going into the fall campaign season, it appears likely that Democrat Hannah Pingree is favored to win. So, with their nominee’s comfortable lead of more than 10 points, why is the state Democratic Party launching such furious attacks on Republican nominee Bobby Charles?
CNN recently released results of a poll that showed more than half — 52% — of likely
voters favoring Hannah Pingree as opposed to 39% saying they plan to vote for Bobby Charles (the poll did not include independent Rick Bennett, a former Republican). Last month, a Fox poll pegged Pingree at 49% compared to Charles’ 38% and Bennett’s 9%.
The answer is strikingly simple: it is not enough just to defeat Bobby Charles. In order to perpetuate their now eight-year stranglehold on power in the state, Maine Democrats must crush everything Charles represents, and to bury his call that Augusta actually be accountable for a change.
Taking a page out of an authoritarian’s handbook, the Democrats seem intent on obliterating Charles altogether — and stigmatizing those who might support him in November.
Charles’ sister authored an op-ed that was published in these pages on Sept. 9 and announced her intention to vote for Pingree. Based on a deeply personal revelation, the op-ed argued that her brother is too divisive and not sufficiently supportive of women to merit her vote.
It was a political body blow, reminiscent of women coming forward this summer alleging they’d been assaulted by then-Democratic senatorial nominee Graham Platner. While emotionally charged and undeniably brave in terms of public disclosure, there was something about both events that felt very political. After all, the synchronized press conference was held at the state Democrats’ Portland office.
Many of us disagree about politics around the family dinner table, but this was very different.
Also consider the peculiar press conference they staged late last month in a Portland park where one usually must tread carefully to avoid stepping on used hypodermic needles. It was there that former Maine CDC Director Nirav Shah — who but for ranked-choice voting would be squaring off against Charles this November — and two other Democrat-aligned public health figures inveighed against the Republican’s pledge to cut the state budget by $4 billion and insisted he would eliminate benefits for Maine’s senior citizens.
How dare he, Dr. Shah then seemed to sneer.
Then there is the candidacy of Rick Bennett itself. Fashioning himself a latter-day Bill
Cohen by walking around the state to put himself in various communities, Bennett —
once a chairman of the state GOP — seems to be a pressure release valve for old-
fashioned Maine Republicans who just wish people could be nice again and want to feel
good about their vote. But Bennett’s single-digit showing shows us how much times have
changed.
Why is he even running, I asked in a Maine Wire column a year ago, when sheer mathematics so
clearly indicated he has no path to victory? There are only two explanations I can
imagine today: either he wants to make a point, as Lindsey Graham did when he ran for
president in 2016 on the sole platform of defeating ISIS, or he wants to help someone
siphon away votes.
The only way to know which of these is Bennett’s motivation is to wait until Pingree announces her cabinet. “Look, Republicans,” Bennett’s candidacy seems to say, “this is what you are supposed to look like, pay attention!”
Maybe Maine Democrats are just so much better organized and resourced than their erstwhile counterparts at the state GOP that they can afford to spend as much attention on systematically attacking Charles as they have. But the persistence of their effort points to something different.
Cutting taxes and fighting crime are the wrong priorities, this effort insists. Despite the double-digit advantage Pingree seems to enjoy, crushing everything Charles stands for is important. Because, despite the breezy prettiness of Maine’s bucolic coast, they are afraid to discuss the rot that consumes Augusta today. Very afraid.

title: Susan Collins’ Bangor home egged
text:
U.S. Sen. Susan Collins’ house in Bangor was egged last month.
The eggs showed up at Collins’ Bangor home in the early morning hours of Sept. 18, according to a Bangor Police Department report obtained by the Bangor Daily News.
Collins first mentioned the egging during an interview on WVOM. Her husband, Tom Daffron, saw the splattered eggs on the garage door, as well as on the front door, window and porch, she said.
It’s the second report of vandalism at a place Collins lives or works in recent weeks. With just over a month until a pivotal election, someone painted a vulgar message about Collins and President Donald Trump on the doors of her Biddeford office.
The Bangor Police Department has checked on Collins’ home more than 500 times since her 2018 vote to confirm Justice Brett Kavanaugh to the U.S. Supreme Court, according to data reviewed by the BDN in August.
“This is another example of harassment against Senator Collins,” the senator’s Chief of Staff Katie Brown said. “Vandalism is unacceptable, and we will not be intimidated.”
There were no eggs visible on the property at 4:45 a.m. that day but they could be seen at 5:10 a.m., according to camera footage reviewed by the Bangor Police Department. No footage of a suspect was captured, the report said.
The Bangor police officer drove through the neighborhood and Collins’ home was the only one that had been egged, the report said.
The report, which redacts the couple’s names, said the man did not want to pursue criminal charges but did want the vandalism documented.

title: 'United States' misspelled in accord signed by Trump and AI executives
text:
'United States' misspelled in accord signed by Trump and AI executives
President Donald Trump’s “White House Accord on Super Intelligence” with six tech leaders contained a typo in the country’s name.
Six executives from companies with leading artificial intelligence models signed the document, along with Trump — whose title was misspelled as “President of the Unites States” under his signature.
The White House X account shared photos of the document and signatures. It’s not clear whether it’ll appear the same way in the Federal Register, the government journal that publishes agency rules, proposed rules and public notices.
The voluntary document encourages companies making “frontier models” — meaning the most advanced AI models available at a given time — to develop “robust internal processes and controls to ensure that their technology behaves as intended.”
Trump called the document “morally binding” and said it’s “almost like a constitution, in a way,” telling reporters it's "going to be great."
He has been a staunch advocate for the emerging technology, most recently signing an executive order instructing the executive branch to refer to artificial intelligence as "super intelligence," or SI. "The word super is the best word of all and it's the simplest," he said in explaining the change.
Many politicians and citizens have raised concerns about the risks posed by AI, ranging from security to privacy to questions over military use. Tech CEOs have recently become some of the loudest voices of caution, raising the alarm about their own companies' technology.
“If managed poorly, I even believe AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole,” Dario Amodei, chief executive officer of Anthropic, told the U.N. Security Council last month. He has written about his concerns that AI could be used for “cyberattacks and bioterrorism, and serious economic disruption.” Specifically, he said AI has been developing faster and has become capable of making itself better.
Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, told the Security Council, “We could lose control of the future to AI.” He has said that slowing the pace of AI development could give society time to adjust to it.
Trump, however, has broadly dismissed those concerns, claiming they are part of a "HOAX" and "SICK conspiracy" that would benefit China, another global leader in AI.
The executives who signed the document are Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Greg Brockman of OpenAI, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.
The document suggests that companies pursue oversight through internal controls that monitor AI’s capabilities and through external auditors to check those internal processes. But it doesn’t set explicit requirements, phrasing these measures as ones companies “should implement.”
It notes that “over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws or regulations,” but leaves that possibility as an open question and doesn’t specify what circumstances would make regulation necessary.

title: The Latest: Trump hits the campaign trail as a new AP-NORC poll shows his deepening unpopularity
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Americans are deeply frustrated with President Donald Trump’s handling of the economy and rising prices. A new poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research finds that only 17% of U.S. adults approve of his handling of the cost of living. Just 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall, marking a new low.
The new numbers come as Trump and Vice President JD Vance hit the campaign trail on Thursday, heading to heavily Republican areas to shore up lagging enthusiasm in their party ahead of next month’s midterm elections. Trump will go to Texas and Oklahoma while Vance stumps in Florida, areas where GOP candidates were once expected to glide to victory but are now facing tougher races.
The Latest:
DC judge permanently dismisses case charging ex-Olympian with vandalizing Reflecting Pool
D.C. Superior Court Judge Todd Edelman dismissed the case against David Hearn with “prejudice,” which would block U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro’s office from refiling the felony charge under political pressure from Trump.
Hearn’s lawyers say Trump administration officials have continued to falsely accuse the Maryland resident of vandalizing the reflecting pool despite Pirro’s decision to drop the case on July 31. Trump responded by saying Pirro “choked” and “folded like an umbrella.”
In an embarrassing setback for the White House, Pirro informed the court that new evidence produced by the Interior Department showed the damage resulted from a botched installation by a contractor rushing to complete the project in time for this summer’s America 250 celebration in Washington.
Rising bond yields rattle markets worldwide and overshadow hopes for AI stocks
The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 5.32% on Thursday, near its highest level since 2002. It was less than 4% before the war with Iran began. The higher borrowing costs are helping to overshadow optimism that the artificial-intelligence industry can keep climbing.
The S&P 500 is heading toward its seventh loss in the last eight days. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and Nasdaq composite are trading downward. The losses were even sharper in Europe, where bond yields saw a significant jump overnight.
High yields slow the overall economy by making it more expensive for everyone to borrow money, while undercutting prices for stocks and other investments. Worries about high inflation are festering as oil prices climbed again Thursday. The price for a barrel of Brent crude jumped 3.3% to $101.24, swinging on uncertainty about any end to the U.S. war with Iran.
Renee Good’s family describes a Trump administration conspiracy
The civil rights suit says the shots fired by Jonathan Ross, the immigration officer who killed Good, “were the predictable and intended product of the operation.”
A news release from the family’s lawyers says the lawsuit describes as a “carefully planned, coordinated effort between senior federal officials and private actors to make two ethnic communities — Minnesotans of Somali and Hispanic descent and origin — the object of aggression and abduction, and to silence by intimidation, arrest and violence the neighbors and allies of those targeted communities who observed, documented and warned of that campaign.”
The lawsuit also alleges “collaboration of federal agencies and individuals with private entities for an operation with discriminatory design, racially targeted pursuit and seizure of individuals without regard to their legal status, and each defendant’s participation in the conspiracy.”
The Justice Department didn’t immediately respond to an email seeking comment on the lawsuits.
Renee Good’s family sues US government and immigration officials
The family of the 37-year-old woman killed by an immigration officer during a federal crackdown in Minneapolis is alleging wrongful death and other violations of federal law.
The two lawsuits were filed by Good’s partner, Becca Good, and Renee’s brother Brent Ganger. One says her death was caused by battery, assault, false imprisonment, intentional infliction of emotional distress and negligence. The other alleges a conspiracy to interfere with civil rights.
The named defendants include Jonathan Ross, the immigration officer who shot her; White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller; former Homeland Security head Kristi Noem; former U.S. Border Patrol commander-at-large Gregory Bovino, Corey Lewandowski, President Donald Trump’s campaign manager, and others.
Supreme Court grants review of Trump administration’s mandatory detention policy for immigrants
The Supreme Court on Thursday agreed to review a Trump administration policy denying bond hearings for immigrants as the government carries out a sweeping immigration crackdown.
The justices will consider whether immigrants who have been living in the U.S. have a right to a hearing to determine if they should remain detained while challenging their possible deportation.
Appeals court judges from nine of 11 federal circuits have concluded that detaining immigrants without a bond hearing violates federal law.
Those decisions conflict with rulings by the 5th and 8th circuits, which held that immigrants accused of illegally entering and remaining in the U.S. must be detained while their deportation cases are pending.
Trump says he’d pardon administration officials
In the Time magazine interview, the president indicated he’s open to issuing pardons for members of his administration.
“Yeah, sure I’d do that,” he said.
Scrutiny is sure to ramp up on key members of the Trump administration should Democrats take one or both chambers of Congress in this fall’s midterm elections.
Trump justified his thinking by pointing to former President Joe Biden’s preemptive pardons he issued for key government officials and family members as he was departing the White House.
Trump exaggerated what Biden did, saying: “Sleepy Joe Biden, he gave pardons to everyone.”
Trump says his low poll numbers are ‘fake numbers’
The president said in an interview with Time magazine conducted on Monday that “pollsters are corrupt” and the bad polls “are fake.”
Trump, in the interview published Thursday, said his own pollster told him his numbers “are much higher than the numbers.”
“I would beat anybody running today by 20 points,” he said.
Trump dismisses reports that Netanyahu was warned about Hamas operation days before Oct. 7 attack
The president said in an interview with Time magazine conducted on Monday that he was hearing about those weeks-old reports for the first time that day and said, “I can’t imagine this.”
If Netanyahu had known about it, “he would have done something about it. Certainly, he would have had people at least alert,” Trump said in the interview published Thursday.
An Israeli newspaper reported in early September that Netanyahu was directly warned by the president of the United Arab Emirates that Hamas was planning a major offensive just days before the militant group attacked on Oct. 7, 2023.
Trump dodges on whether Netanyahu deserves reelection
In the Time magazine interview, Trump repeatedly avoiding answering directly whether Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu should be reelected later this month.
“I can only say that I’m not involved in politics anymore,” said the U.S. president, who is ramping up his campaigning for Republicans in the November midterms.
Trump then touted his own record on Israel rather than answering directly whether Netanyahu should be reelected, despite several attempts from Time journalists.
Trump finally answered: “Well, people have written off Bibi many, many times, just like they’ve written off me many, many times. I wouldn’t underestimate Bibi.”
Of Netanyahu’s opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, Trump said: “I don’t hear bad things about him.”
More bombing of Iran ‘possible’ after midterms, Trump says
Trump said in a Time magazine interview published Thursday morning that it’s “possible” he’ll ramp up bombing in Iran after the Nov. 3 midterms.
When pressed further by Time journalists, Trump continued: “I can’t tell you that because look, you know, you’re asking, where are you going to bomb?”
He said in the interview, conducted Sept. 28, that he rejected the latest ceasefire proposal from Iran because “things that I wouldn’t have approved a year ago I wouldn’t have today.”
Trump cited as an example an offer from Iran to “open up the Strait” of Hormuz, but said the overall proposal was “not good enough.”
Inside Ken Paxton’s jet-setting lifestyle: California wineries, European hot spots and ski resorts
An Associated Press records review shows Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton has traveled frequently and spent less time in Texas as the state’s attorney general since becoming a star in Trump’s MAGA universe.
When the conservative firebrand launched his Senate campaign on Fox News, he cleared his calendar for a trip to the Masters golf tournament in Georgia that cost Texas taxpayers at least $25,000. Overall since assuming office in 2015, Paxton left about 730 workdays blank on his official calendars and took over 275 out-of-state trips to places such as California wine country, Caribbean resorts and European tourism hot spots.
Records show Paxton’s travel cost Texas taxpayers a minimum of $1.9 million to cover expenses charged by his security detail. It’s unclear how Paxton has financed much of his portion of the travel.
Trump praises Boeing-made FlyDubai aircraft for remaining airborne
The president, in an early morning social media post, credited the “GREAT Boeing Company” with building a plane “that was able to withstand G Forces and Strain far beyond what it was designed and expected to do.”
On Wednesday, a copilot stabbed his captain and attempted to crash a flight bound for Israel from the United Arab Emirates that was carrying 174 people. Passengers, most of them Israelis, feared for their lives as the FlyDubai aircraft lost half its altitude in about a minute.
Aviation experts were also surprised the plane did not crash after a descent so extreme that most of the rudder was ripped off the tail.
“It is about time that The Boeing Company, which builds, by far, the finest commercial airliners in the sky, was given credit for this airplane’s incredible ‘genius!’” Trump added in his posting about the Arlington, Virginia-based aircraft manufacturer.
Trump’s economic approval hits a new low as midterms approach
Just 26% approve of Trump’s handling of the economy overall, marking a new low in AP-NORC polling.
Trump’s numbers on the economy represent a 14-point drop from March 2025, just after he took office for the second time. His struggles on the issue mark a significant departure from his first term, when the economy was often a point of strength.
Trump’s low grade on the economy rivals President Joe Biden’s economic approval rating in June 2022, when there was record-high inflation during the COVID-19 pandemic.
But Americans were less likely to blame Biden in the lead-up to that year’s midterm elections, a sharp contrast to the solid majority who hold Trump responsible now.
Costs drag on Trump as the economic pain keeps coming
Americans have grown more worried about being able to afford basics like groceries and gas over the last few months, the new AP-NORC poll shows.
About half of U.S. adults say they are “extremely” or “very” concerned about being able to afford gas in the coming months, up from 39% in July.
And about half are highly concerned about being able to afford food.
Pedro Sanchez, a 52-year-old from California who voted for Trump told the AP: “I used to have a lot more disposable income. I don’t have that anymore. It’s gotten eaten up because of all these increases in the cost of everything.”
AP-NORC Poll: Most Republicans now disapprove of Trump on costs
Americans are deeply frustrated with rising prices under President Trump, according to a new AP-NORC poll.
Only 17% of U.S. adults approve of the president’s handling of the cost of living. That frustration is also reaching Republicans. About 6 in 10 Republicans now disapprove of how Trump is handling costs, up from about half in April.
Robert Gault, a 66-year-old from Bradford, Pennsylvania, told the AP about Trump: “He said, ’Make America Great Again.′ And I have not seen him do that.”
Despite the overall frustration, about two-thirds of Republicans don’t blame Trump personally for high prices and say factors outside of his control are more to blame.
But Americans overall disagree. A majority, 65%, of U.S. adults blame Trump’s policies for persistently high costs more than factors outside of his control.
Trump and Vance hit the campaign trail in deep-red areas where GOP candidates seek a boost
President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance will both hit the campaign trail on Thursday, but they will be heading to heavily Republican areas to shore up lagging enthusiasm in their party ahead of next month’s midterm elections.
Trump’s travel on Thursday to Texas and Oklahoma kicks off what the president said will be a 32-day campaign blitz leading up to Nov. 3. Vance will be stumping in Florida, putting the Republican Party’s highest-ranking officials in areas where GOP candidates once expected to have glide paths to victory but are now facing tougher races.
Republicans have expressed growing pessimism about their chances in the election, which will determine control of Congress, as the president has repeatedly dismissed concerns about high costs and gas prices as his unpopular war in Iran drags on.
According to Trump, his party’s headwinds are merely a matter of poor public relations about a job he says is well done.
“We’re not getting the word out,” he told reporters on Wednesday. “I mean, we’re just not getting it.”

title: These are the most popular side hustles people are taking on to boost a budget
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PHOENIX (Aging Untold) — Rob Macgregor has a full-time job, running a small car dealership in Phoenix. He spends at least 40 hours a week selling cars. Then he works on his side hustle, giving golf lessons.
He’s been playing golf since he was a kid, and teaching the game he loves has become a passion.
“[I} won a state championship in Michigan and then turned pro shortly after that, decided to teach golf lessons for money,” he said.
Macgregor connects with students on Teachme.To. The platform matches students with local instructors for lessons in all kinds of activities, including golf, pickleball, tennis and guitar.
Macgregor has come to rely on the extra income he earns as a golf instructor.
“I have six kids and they all like their own little hobbies, so I get to use the money that I create from this side income,” he said. “It covers some of it.”
Macgregor is like a lot of people, working to increase income. A recent LendingTree survey shows 38% of American adults have a side hustle.
“That’s actually down a little bit from a few years ago but it’s still a really big number, and I think it really indicates how much people need a little bit of help in extending their monthly budget,” Matt Schulz with LendingTree said.
Popular side hustles
According to LendingTree, the most popular side hustles are food and grocery delivery and online freelancing. Another 14% of side hustlers report doing part-time or seasonal work, 13% do house cleaning and 13% make and sell items. E-commerce resale, social media influencing, babysitting, pet sitting, rideshare driving, day trading and teaching also made the list.
On average, according to the survey, side hustlers say they’re making an extra $1,215 per month.
“The main thing to understand about a side hustle is that it takes a lot of work,” Schulz said. “This isn’t free money. This isn’t just a switch that you flip and all of a sudden, you’re bringing in money.”
Macgregor opens his online schedule whenever he can for students like Mateo Frances, who found Macgregor on the Teachme.to platform.
“He had great ratings, Frances said. “I saw it as an opportunity to learn a game that I’m sort of falling in love with that I can play for the rest of my life.”

title: ‘Devastating’: Mother cremated before viewing, another’s body used in her place, families allege
text:
DETROIT (WDIV) - Two families are suing a Detroit funeral home, alleging one woman was cremated before her scheduled viewing and another’s body was used in her place.
Kimberly Moore died Sept. 3 after a battle with endometrial cancer. Her family alleges Hutchison Funeral Home cremated her and swapped her body with that of Sandra Miller before her viewing.
Ahead of the viewing, Moore’s daughter, Bianca Robinson, arrived at the funeral home to do her mother’s makeup – and quickly realized something was wrong, the family says. They were later told Moore had been accidentally cremated and that the body presented for viewing wasn’t hers.
“I didn’t get a chance to say goodbye, and I needed it so bad, just to keep going,” Robinson said. “This is devastating. I can’t sleep. We just want answers. Please.”
Moore’s family says they still have not received her ashes, which attorneys say will undergo DNA testing.
Miller died Sept. 13 after a battle with ovarian cancer. Her family says they were initially told by the funeral home that their mother was not involved in the incident. They later learned through Moore’s family that Miller’s body had allegedly been used as a “prop” during the former’s viewing.
“After everything she had been through, my mom deserved dignity, identification, protection and respect,” said Miller’s daughter, Cessley Walker. “She was somebody’s daughter. She was a sister. She was a wife. She was a mother. She was my mom.”
The funeral home says it launched an internal investigation into the incident, but James Harrington with Feiger Law says that’s not enough. His firm is now pursuing legal action on behalf of both families.
“What we know is that their process was woefully inadequate with the explanation that was told [being] the tag got wet and fell off. I don’t believe that for a second,” Harrington said. “I think it was just pure carelessness, recklessness.”
The funeral home, its owner, Jaimie Hutchison, and Southern Michigan Cremation Services were all named as defendants in the families’ lawsuits.
The funeral home’s vice president was not named. A family spokesperson says he was found dead in his Detroit home last Thursday. Details of his death have not been made public.

title: Whale sinks yacht in Pacific Ocean, sailors rescued 18 hours later
text:
Whale sinks yacht in Pacific Ocean, sailors rescued 18 hours later
A whale strike sank an Australian yacht in the South Pacific, leaving its four crew members adrift in a life raft for about 18 hours before a cargo ship rescued them.
The 51-foot Tai Tam was about 250 nautical miles north of Norfolk Island when it hit a whale and began taking on water, according to a release from the Royal New Zealand Air Force.
Related video above | Scientists are learning the basic building blocks of sperm whale language after years of effort
The crew activated an emergency beacon, abandoned the yacht and climbed into a life raft.
Sailors on board the ship told New Zealand’s 1News that a pod of what appeared to be four or five sperm whales was nearby before the ship was struck. The yacht’s owners also said they believed sperm whales were involved.
New Zealand’s Rescue Coordination Centre sent a Royal New Zealand Air Force P-8A Poseidon to locate the sailors and make radio contact.
The aircraft helped direct nearby vessels to the scene.
The cargo ship Sofrana Surville reached the crew around 6 a.m. Sunday. A private sailing vessel also assisted, officials said.
The four sailors — two Australians, a New Zealander and a French national — were taken aboard the cargo ship.
“It was a massive relief, stepping on board the container ship,” New Zealander Terry Hetherington told 1News.
Skipper Jeremy Cooper told the Australian Broadcasting Corporation that the crew tried to limit the damage, but soon realized the yacht could not be saved.
Rescue officials credited the crew’s preparation and quick activation of their emergency beacon. The New Zealand Defence Force said the operation involved New Zealand, Australian and New Caledonian rescue agencies, as well as the vessels that responded.

title: ‘America’s Most Wanted’ rerun leads to tip, arrest in hit-and-run after 29 years
text:
DES MOINES, Iowa (KCRG/Gray News) - Thanks to a rerun of “America’s Most Wanted,” police in Iowa have made an arrest in a deadly hit-and-run cold case from nearly 30 years ago.
The Des Moines Police Department announced a breakthrough Tuesday related to the case of 64-year-old Leslie Ruby, who was killed in a hit-and-run outside his Des Moines home on Sept. 29, 1997.
Ruby was a retiree, a grandfather and a veteran of the Korean War. Police say he was described by everyone who knew him as a very loving and caring family man.
Investigators were able to identify the suspect as then-28-year-old Gerardo Garcia-Michel, but police say he fled the state before he could be arrested.
Despite attempts to find Garcia-Michel, the case ran dry as investigators exhausted their leads.
The popular TV show “America’s Most Wanted” aired an episode on the Ruby case in 1998. Almost 29 years later, police say a rerun of that episode led someone to send a Crime Stoppers tip to investigators, saying Garcia-Michel was his neighbor.
That tip helped detectives find Garcia-Michel in New Jersey. He was arrested by U.S. Marshals, and Des Moines Police are working to extradite him to Iowa.
“It doesn’t matter if it’s 29 minutes or 29 days or 29 years after a crime. Getting answers for the family is one of the most important things that we can do,” Police Sgt. Paul Parizek said.

title: Mainers are stretched thin. In Oxford County, many can’t afford enough food.
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
This is the first story in the series Stretched Thin: The cost of getting by in Maine, which looks at the financial hardships Mainers face. Social services reporter Gillian Graham reported this story as a USC Annenberg Center for Health Journalism 2026 National Fellow and a participant in the Center’s engagement initiative.
MEXICO — By the time the first people arrived for lunch on a warm July day, Michelle Williams and the volunteers at the River Valley’s only soup kitchen had been at work for hours.
They stretched out clean white tablecloths and arranged baskets of fruit and snacks on the buffet line. They filled large orange coolers with lemonade and water and set out napkins and utensils. They stirred baked beans bubbling in a warmer, the scent wafting out of the kitchen.
Williams, a retired hospice nurse who founded Good Samaritan Missionary Services, had started cooking the day before. The menu included barbecue pulled chicken sandwiches, street corn pasta salad and her famous lemon icebox cake.
Her motivation, she said, is simple: “Food is a necessity, not a luxury.”
In Oxford County’s River Valley — where the towns that hug the Androscoggin River have long been known for their deep ties to paper manufacturing — many working families have a hard time covering their everyday expenses. The hunger rate is among the highest in the state.
The financial situation can be even more bleak for people who are retired, unemployed or homeless.
Some families have been in poverty, or hovering just above it, for generations.
Before the soup kitchen opened, there were few options in the area for food assistance. Three years ago, Williams started an emergency food pantry at town hall. Within six months, it morphed into the soup kitchen because of the high demand, she said.
It’s not uncommon to hear about people working 12-hour days but still struggling to make ends meet, said Joleen Bedard, president and CEO of United Way of Western Maine. Some have seasonal jobs with inconsistent incomes, while others grapple with how to get to work and appointments in a region without widely accessible public transportation.
“It’s certainly a struggle and I don’t see it changing any time soon,” she said. “There are two Maines: the haves and the have-nots.”
‘BARRIER AFTER BARRIER’
Every day, thousands of Mainers face the hardest choices: buy food or pay for a prescription; drive far for healthcare or risk going without; toil to afford childcare or stop working; go to a homeless shelter or sleep in a tent.
Across the state, data from 2024 shows, 40% of households fell below the federal poverty line or just above the threshold, where people struggle to afford basic expenses, but don’t always qualify for assistance.
“There is an enormous number of hardworking families throughout the state who are one unexpected expense away from crisis,” said Dan Coyne, who heads the United Way of Southern Maine.
This summer, the United Ways of Maine released new data they say shows traditional measures of poverty have undercounted the number of households in the state experiencing financial hardship.
Many have incomes above the federal poverty line and are part of a population called ALICE — Asset Limited, Income Constrained, Employed. The threshold for each county is calculated using household income and a survival budget that includes the cost of housing, childcare, food, transportation, healthcare and technology.
It does not include room for savings, debt payments or emergency expenses.
In Rumford, 66% of households struggle to afford basic expenses — the most of any town in the county, according to the United Way. Census data shows 15% are below the poverty line.
Half of the households in Mexico and 41% in neighboring Dixfield also fall below the ALICE threshold.
For decades, people in Maine’s rural areas have experienced financial hardship and poverty at higher rates. But even in coastal areas, where more wealth is concentrated, there are pockets of residents struggling.
For many in the Oxford County region, improving their financial outlook seems nearly impossible, even if they’re working, said Melissa McEntee, who runs Rumford Group Homes, the only homeless shelter program in the county.
“We see hard-working families who do everything they can to get out of that poverty cycle. Everything in River Valley keeps sucking them back in,” she said. “Everything is a barrier. It’s barrier after barrier after barrier.”
FALLING THROUGH THE CRACKS
Sue Grace remembers the heyday of Rumford, when the town was booming and there wasn’t an empty storefront downtown. There was a big hotel that hosted fancy weddings, a hat shop she’d visit with her grandmother, and a police officer with a whistle and white gloves directing traffic.
“Talk about a Norman Rockwell portrait,” the lifelong Rumford resident said.
Grace, 72, worked at the local hospital for years and raised her four kids in town. In the ’80s, as manufacturing at the paper mill declined and the workforce shrank, businesses on Congress Street started to close. Unemployment ticked up and there was less going on to keep kids entertained, she said.
The paper mill in Rumford employed more than 3,000 people at its peak, but today it employs just over 500. The steep decline in manufacturing created economic uncertainty in the communities, according to Friends of the River Valley, which supports a range of nutrition, education, health and social services programs in the area.
Grace said she never considered leaving, even after she retired from her job as a phlebotomist and two of her adult children moved out of town. She was doing fine on her Social Security and small pension for a while, but things have become tougher in the past few years as the cost of everything seemed to go up.
Now, she feels like she’s falling through the cracks.
Grace gets about $24 a month in federal food assistance benefits and the $417 monthly rent for her apartment is based on her income. In August, she was eagerly awaiting her $300 affordability check from the state so she could replace her six-year-old cell phone.
She’s grateful for the help and said she’s fortunate to be better off than many, but she still has to make tough choices.
Most days, Grace eats two meals to save on groceries.
She goes to the soup kitchen in Mexico for lunch because that is food she doesn’t have to figure out how to pay for.
“I was raised that you don’t ask for help. I had to learn to do that,” she said, while sitting in her dining room under a wall sign encouraging visitors to “Live well, laugh often, love much.”
After working hard for 40 years, Grace doesn’t think she should have to struggle so much.
FILLING THE GAP
A half-dozen people carrying reusable shopping bags lingered in the dirt parking lot outside of the Old School Food Pantry in Mexico on a gloomy day in June. They chatted quietly as raindrops started to fall, adding to the unseasonable chill.
They were an hour early for the weekly distribution, but wanted to make sure they could get what they needed.
The two-room food pantry in the bottom floor of an old school building sits on a hill facing the river. The white plumes from the mill stacks drift over the trees.
Just inside the door, volunteer William Gallant sat at a table, lists of pantry regulars laid out in front of him and clipboards with checklists of grocery items neatly stacked to the side. Every time someone came in, he clicked a counter dangling from his neck to keep track of how many people showed up for groceries.
Oxford County has one of the highest food insecurity rates in the state, with nearly a quarter of all children in the region experiencing hunger, according to Feeding America, which tracks the issue across the country.
The number of Mainers experiencing hunger continues to rise. It’s the highest it’s been in a decade, according to a report released this summer.
More than 11,000 Mainers have lost access to the federal Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program because of sweeping changes that began rolling out last fall, according to state officials.
Rural areas of Maine, where more people tend to rely on SNAP, are being hit especially hard by the changes, according to hunger prevention advocates. Work exemptions were removed for rural areas with low employment options, leaving some people struggling to find work or volunteer opportunities to maintain access to food assistance.
Food pantries trying to fill the gap are reporting record numbers of visits. In August, nearly 300 families came in to pick up fresh produce, meat and boxes of shelf-stable groceries from the Old School Food Pantry.
Gallant, 77, grew up in Rumford when the paper mill was the biggest employer and the company’s owner pumped money into the town, including the community center where kids gathered for dances and bowling in the basement.
Gallant, who has been volunteering at the food pantry for four years, sees the impact every week from behind his check-in table.
There are always new people coming in for the first time — older retirees whose pensions don’t cover the bills anymore, working parents who can’t afford groceries, people who are out of work and piecing together whatever they can to get by.
As the pantry gets busier, he worries there won’t be enough food to go around.
“I don’t ever want to be the person who has to tell them we ran out of food,” he said, as he handed a clipboard to the next person in line.
FEEDING THE COMMUNITY
The school district that serves Rumford and Mexico decided in late June that it did not have the staff to distribute free lunch to kids during the summer, a move that Williams, from the soup kitchen, said was particularly hard on families already struggling to provide food.
In the first days after school let out, she said there was a noticeable increase in families with kids coming in for lunch.
“Holy smokes, we are getting our butts handed to us,” Williams said in early July. One day the previous week, she served 45 people in less than an hour. Half of them were children.
As the outside temperature pushed into the high 80s, Angela Dean, her husband and their 1-year-old daughter were among the first to arrive for lunch on July 6.
“We just want to live here, Michelle,” Dean called out as she walked into the air-conditioned room and headed for a table in the back corner.
Dean, who was staying at the homeless shelter, comes in for lunch most days the soup kitchen is open. She knows everyone by name.
“It’s a huge relief,” she said, after settling her daughter into a highchair and filling their plates. “It might seem like one meal three days a week isn’t a big deal, but when you’re a mom trying to survive, it’s so important.”
Dean has lived in the River Valley for more than 20 years. She doesn’t think there are enough resources available to help residents. She said she’s watched rents shoot up higher than she thought possible.
“A lot of people struggle here,” Dean said. “There are a lot of people who don’t have anywhere to go. People are overworked and underpaid.”
Alisha Holtorf, of Mexico, came into the soup kitchen a few minutes later with four of her five children. They’re regulars, too, and have grown especially close to Williams and the volunteers who serve lunch. Williams keeps applesauce pouches on hand for the youngest Holtorf, 2-year-old Ember.
Holtorf, 34, runs the food pantry at her church, Praise Assembly of God in downtown Rumford, and sees firsthand how many people in the community are living on the edge financially.
“People are doing all they can, but it still doesn’t seem like enough for this area,” she said.
Holtorf homeschools her kids and works two part-time jobs. Her husband has a manufacturing job in Auburn, but she said they still don’t make enough and don’t qualify for any assistance programs. To stretch her budget, Holtorf grows vegetables, swaps the clothes her kids have outgrown for new sizes at the church’s clothing closet, and is careful about spending at the grocery store.
The Holtorfs saved for several years to pay for a road trip to see family in Iowa in September.
She said people often come to the church for help, but the congregation is small and many of its members are on fixed incomes and can’t afford to give more.
“It’s hard,” she said, “telling people we don’t have the funds.”
‘ROBBING PETER TO PAY PAUL’
While it’s clear many people — including older residents who rely on Social Security and young families burdened by childcare expenses — are struggling to get by, Rumford Town Manager George O’Keefe sees progress in addressing some of the critical needs laid bare in the years following the decline in manufacturing.
The service sector has grown substantially and there has been “really drastic” growth in energy production and storage businesses, O’Keefe said.
Rumford, the largest town in the county, has a hospital and the Black Mountain of Maine ski resort. Larger ski resorts nearby attract thousands of people every winter.
For the last few years, the town has been focused on encouraging the construction of more housing — from neighborhoods of single-family homes to affordable apartments for older residents. O’Keefe believes this will go a long way toward addressing some of the financial pressure on River Valley residents.
“There are a lot of families that struggle to stay on the rung of the economic ladder they’re on, let alone make upward progress,” O’Keefe said.
Courtney Johnson finds herself facing the same choice every winter: keep the lights on or heat the house. The Mexico resident always chooses heat because the power company can’t easily disconnect service during the coldest months of winter under state law.
“The saying ‘Robbing Peter to pay Paul’ never meant anything to me as a kid,” she said. “Now, I do it all the time.”
Johnson is blunt when she describes her family’s financial situation: “It sucks to be poor.”
Johnson, 39, and her husband, Jason, met while growing up in York County, but didn’t start dating until after they were out of school and she had two children. They had five more children together, including a baby girl born this summer. They moved to the River Valley about eight years ago to live with his mother’s boyfriend. For nearly four years, the family stayed crammed together in two bedrooms.
Johnson said she asked her husband to pick up a scratch-off lottery ticket when he was at the store a few years ago. The $5 ticket he bought was a winner, a stroke of luck that she said sent him running down the street in celebration.
They decided to use the money to create more stability for the family and Johnson said they were able to buy a house in Mexico for $55,000 in 2023. Some of the kids still have to share bedrooms, she said, but they’re not crowded into small rooms. The property came with apple trees and a picnic table, just like the house she had always dreamed of owning.
But owning a home hasn’t alleviated their financial constraints.
Johnson recently left her job as a direct support professional at a local nonprofit to care for her new baby. Childcare, if she could find it, would cost more than she made. Her husband is a subcontractor, but work can be inconsistent. Sometimes, she said, he works on homes of older members of their church who can only afford to pay him with thanks, prayer and homemade cookies.
The Johnsons, who work part-time leading the youth ministry at Praise Assembly of God, found their way to the church a few years ago after attending its annual Culture of Compassion event, where people can get a free lunch, groceries and clothing.
Johnson is grateful her family is insured through MaineCare and receives benefits from the Women, Infants and Children program. Most months, the $1,300 they get from SNAP is enough to cover groceries, but sometimes they have to use a local food pantry.
“We’re very frugal because we know what it’s like to go without,” she said. “We try not to take from this church (food pantry) because we know people around here need it more.”
The Johnsons try to help where they can. When they heard a young person in their church was using dish soap to brush his teeth, they bought him toothpaste. Recently, they scraped together $200 to buy meat for a family short on food.
“We will go without to help another family,” she said.
FINDING A WAY TO HELP
In the River Valley, many support systems are informal. If one group can’t help someone, they often know where to point them for assistance, said McEntee, the homeless shelter director.
“People who care and want to help have found a way to band together,” McEntee said. “We feel lucky that in Oxford County we are small and all the providers know each other.”
At Good Samaritan, helping goes beyond the food laid out on the buffet table.
On Thursdays, a retired social worker sits in the back of the soup kitchen, helping people sign up for assistance programs. The back room is stocked with basic toiletries, household items and pet food. When someone faces an unexpected hardship, Williams is known to jump in.
“Michelle will always find a way to help,” said Carol Violette, a retired seamstress who has volunteered at the soup kitchen since it opened.
Williams and the Good Samaritan board do it all on a shoestring budget.
They apply for grants and put a small donation jar out during every lunch. When a grant payment was delayed, Williams used some of her own Social Security check to cover expenses until it came in. A supporter gives $400 every month from her Social Security income.
As summer waned, Williams spent hours canning sauerkraut, pickled beets, tomato sauce and vegetables to get the soup kitchen through the long winter.
“It’s a tiring week,” she said, “but it’s nice to go into the weekend knowing you’ve helped people.”
When the new school year started, Williams decided to cut back to two lunches each week. When winter sets in, she plans to open the soup kitchen on the coldest days as a refuge for people living outside and those whose homes aren’t warm enough.
There won’t always be lunch, but the coffee will be hot.

title: WMHS Nurse Arrested for Operating Under the Influence
text:
A Wiscasset Middle High School nurse was arrested shortly after the end of the school day for operating under the influence on Tuesday, Sept. 22.
Wiscasset Police Chief Lawrence Hesseltine said he received a call about an erratic vehicle at 2:48 p.m. He located the driver, Sommer Harding, of Bath, at 3:05 p.m. and arrested her in the parking lot of the Marketplace Plaza on Bath Road.
Hesseltine said she measured a .38% blood alcohol content. The legal limit for operating a vehicle in Maine is .08%.

title: ICE is moving Maine detainees more quickly and farther away, report says
text:
Most people detained and processed by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in Maine are quickly moved out of state, according to a new analysis by an immigrant advocacy group.
After processing at the agency’s facility in Scarborough, 98% of the individuals detained this year amid the agency’s expanded efforts have been swiftly moved to facilities outside Maine, mostly in Massachusetts and New Hampshire, before commonly being transferred to sites in the South, the report says.
Detainees are also spending less time at any given facility, and so far this year, 90% of those processed in Scarborough have been moved within six hours of their initial detention.
The new data, which comes through public records requests to ICE from the Deportation Data Project and was analyzed by the Maine Immigrants’ Rights Coalition, underscores long-standing concerns by the attorneys and loved ones of those detained.
Those groups have argued that the agency swiftly moves detainees out of state, and even shifts them several times to several different facilities, making it harder to stay in contact or legally advocate.
ICE significantly grew its operations in Maine this year amid the Trump administration’s push to increase deportations. Immigration agents arrested hundreds during a surge in January, most with no criminal convictions, despite the agency’s claim that it only targets the “worst of the worst.”
In July, an agent in Biddeford fatally shot Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a 25-year-old father, who didn’t have a criminal history and wasn’t the target of enforcement that day, sparking widespread protest.
The Scarborough facility — ICE’s only one in Maine, since the agency pulled detainees from the Cumberland County Jail following criticism by the sheriff — has been the subject of frequent protest from residents advocating for its closure.
Hunter Cropsey, the programs and engagement manager at the coalition and a co-author of the report, said it was born out of requests from individuals in Scarborough who wanted more data to understand the relationship between the facility and their town.
The data also comes amid reports of a new forthcoming ICE facility in the Penobscot County town of Newport, although details remain scarce.
The report shows 293 detentions at the Scarborough facility between Jan. 1 and Aug. 5 of this year, a significant increase over prior years.
An analysis of data from 2024 to 2026 shows that while most people held at the Scarborough facility used to be held elsewhere in Maine after being processed, that shifted sharply in the last two years. Now, more than half go to Massachusetts as their next location, while 40% go to facilities in New Hampshire.
The most common next stops this year were in Plymouth, Massachusetts; Dover, New Hampshire; and Burlington, Massachusetts.
Later transfers often took detainees far from New England, primarily to Louisiana and Texas, but also to Arizona, Georgia and Ohio. Forty percent of those first processed in Scarborough spent some time in the Gulf states, according to the report.
After being processed in Maine, detainees this year spent time in a total of 30 facilities across 11 states, for an average of just 12.6 days at each site. That’s a significant change from 2024, when detainees spent an average of 46 days in a given facility.
Cropsey, the co-author, said the movement to those southern states is particularly notable because it’s less likely detainees would be released on bond and, statistically, an applicant’s likelihood of approval for asylum is lower.
But even just a move across the border to New Hampshire can cut off detainees from their support systems and their chances of a good legal defense, he said.
“This accelerated and widespread movement removes Mainers from their communities and support systems, creating severe hurdles for legal representation and family contact,” the report concludes. With planned increases in ICE enforcement and the proposed Newport facility, those patterns are likely to intensify, the report says.

title: Bangor man faces kidnapping, assault charges after indictment
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A Bangor man accused of kidnapping a woman in July has been indicted by a Penobscot County grand jury.
Harold English, 25, has been charged with several crimes including kidnapping, domestic violence stalking, and domestic violence assault.
English put his hands on a woman, forced her into his car, and drove off, according to Bangor Police.
The incident happened on Basketball Court. Officials said English was found later on Cynthia Avenue and was eventually detained after refusing to submit to arrest.
