title: 3 people sent to hospital after tanker truck crashes on Maine Turnpike in Falmouth
text:
3 people sent to hospital after tanker truck crashes on Maine Turnpike in Falmouth
Emergency crews have cleared a tanker truck that had been blocking all southbound lanes of the Maine Turnpike in Falmouth after a two-vehicle crash early Thursday morning.
3 people sent to hospital after tanker truck crashes on Maine Turnpike in Falmouth
Emergency crews have cleared a tanker truck that had been blocking all southbound lanes of the Maine Turnpike in Falmouth after a two-vehicle crash early Thursday morning.
Three people were taken to Maine Medical Center for evaluation after a tractor-trailer tanker hit an SUV that had stopped in a travel lane on the Maine Turnpike in Falmouth early Thursday morning.
Maine State Police said the crash happened around 2:35 a.m. near mile marker 56 on the southbound side.
Investigators said a 2020 GMC SUV lost power and stopped in the travel lane. A 2019 Freightliner tanker traveling southbound approached the SUV and tried to move into the right lane to avoid it.
The tanker struck the rear passenger side of the SUV, pushing it toward the median. The tractor-trailer then tipped onto its right side.
The SUV's driver and passenger, along with the tanker driver, were taken to Maine Medical Center. Police said no serious injuries were reported.
A small amount of diesel fuel leaked from the tanker, prompting a response from the Maine Department of Environmental Protection.
All southbound lanes were closed following the crash, and traffic was diverted at Exit 63. By around 5:30 a.m. the tanker had been removed, the scene cleared and all southbound lanes reopened.
The crash remains under investigation.

title: Catholic Charities Maine adds a large-capacity freezer for food donations
text:
MONTICELLO, Maine (WAGM) - Catholic Charities Maine now has room for up to 320,000 pounds of frozen food.
A new freezer in Monticello is about five times larger than the organization’s previous frozen-food storage capacity. The added space means Catholic Charities can accept larger donations when available and store that food until it’s needed by pantries across northern Maine.
Jon Blanchard, director of hunger and relief services, said the freezer allows the organization to accept and distribute protein-based donations more easily.
“The frozen food is where the protein comes from. So to be able to just always accept donations and be able to dole it out in sizes to our pantries that they can accept because they’ve got to have refrigeration to keep it frozen too is huge for us,” Blanchard said.
Steve Letourneau, CEO of Catholic Charities of Maine, said the expanded storage capacity allows the organization to accept donations from a wider area.
“We’ve gotten requests for food donations from other parts of the whole country and with the large food bank that we have now, we can really take on a lot of those donations and that’s going to benefit everybody in the county,” Letourneau said.
The freezer cost more than $400,000 for work and materials. Officials said the money came from donations and fundraising efforts.

title: Dressing up for CLT production of ‘Cabaret’
text:
AUBURN, ME – Cast and crew for Community Little Theatre’s upcoming production of the musical “Cabaret” have been busy lately getting fitted for costumes, no small task for a show like this.
Since its Broadway debut in 1966, “Cabaret” has captivated audiences with its subversive plot and groundbreaking storytelling. Set in Berlin in the final years of the Weimar Republic, the musical portrays a society on the brink of collapse, using the Kit Kat Club as both a space of liberation and a harbinger of impending authoritarianism. As fascism rises outside its doors, the club’s revelers dance in a haze of sex, cynicism, and cabaret. Costume design has played a crucial role in shaping audience interpretations of the show’s themes, characters, and historical context.
Performances of “Cabaret” will be held on October 16, 17, 22, 23, and 24 at 7:30 p.m., and October 18 and 25 at 2:00 p.m. All shows will be held at CLT on 30 Academy Street in Auburn. Tickets are available online at www.laclt.com.
“Cabaret” director Brandon Chaloux, at left, is pictured here with cast member Nex Staples, who plays one of the Kit Kat Boys. Nex has just tried on a possible addition to his wardrobe for the show. “Cabaret” will open at CLT on October 16.

title: SNAP benefit changes are in effect for millions of recipients. Here’s what you need to know
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray News) - Millions of Americans who depend on the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program will be seeing changes Thursday, including a slight cost-of-living increase.
Every year on Oct. 1, the federal government adjusts its monthly SNAP benefits to account for inflation.
For the upcoming fiscal year, the maximum SNAP benefit for a one-person household will rise by about $8 per month, while the maximum benefit for a household of four will increase by about $29 per month.
Those numbers translate to a maximum monthly benefit of $306 for a single-person household and $1,023 for a household of four.
Federal officials note that benefits vary based on different household circumstances, and residents in Alaska, Hawaii, Guam and the U.S. Virgin Islands will see higher maximums.
The inflation adjustments are intended to help families with the rising cost of food.
Food prices in the United States have increased by about 2.7% between August 2025 and August 2026, according to the United States Department of Agriculture.
The USDA reported earlier this year that more than 37 million people received SNAP benefits, with the program also seeing a drop of nearly 5 million recipients from a year earlier.
More information for those interested in applying for SNAP benefits can also be found online.

title: Dunlap, LePage take the debate stage for first time in 2nd Congressional District race
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Democrat Matt Dunlap and Republican Paul LePage went toe-to-toe Thursday night in their first debate in the 2nd Congressional District race.
LePage, 77, the former governor, and Dunlap, 61, the state auditor and former secretary of state, are just over a month away from the Nov. 3 election to decide who will succeed Democratic Rep. Jared Golden, who did not seek reelection.
A recent poll conducted by the University of New Hampshire Survey Center found Dunlap with a 51% to 45% edge over LePage, with 5% of respondents undecided.
Unsurprisingly, Dunlap and LePage disagreed on a number of topics during Thursday night’s debate televised by WMTW, but both continuously argued their agendas would be more effective in meeting a common goal: affordability.
Healthcare took the spotlight on many occasions throughout the debate. On questions regarding MaineCare, the state’s Medicaid program, LePage said he would attempt to raise reimbursement rates, while Dunlap said he supports expanding the program.
Early on, both candidates were asked what bill they’d introduce first, if elected. Dunlap said his first piece of legislation would focus on healthcare access and affordability, such as restoring tax subsidies for the Affordable Care Act. LePage said he would introduce a bill to increase access to dental care for veterans.
A number of Democratic candidates this cycle have made a Medicare for All system a cornerstone of their campaign, but Dunlap didn’t fully embrace it Thursday night. He highlighted some of the benefits and said he would “certainly encourage the country to go in that direction,” while cautioning it would take a long time to fully implement.
LePage, meanwhile, bashed the idea, claiming it would do away with private healthcare and services would get “rationed.”
They also disagreed on tariffs. Dunlap argued that the trade war with Canada is detrimental to American citizens, while LePage argued “we’ve gotten a bad deal for many years,” but the two allies need to come to a resolution.
The two differed even while finding common ground on several topics, including the war in Iran. Both, for instance, said they don’t support the war, but LePage said he doesn’t support a war powers act, while Dunlap does.
Both agreed that housing production could be boosted by better supporting those who make the housing. However, Dunlap said he’d help make finances more accessible for housing developments, while LePage said he’d focus on improving the permitting process and regulations.
Dunlap and LePage also agreed that caps on Social Security contributions should be raised, and that Congress should have at least some oversight on the development of artificial intelligence. They differed on data centers, with LePage saying that should be decided on the local level and Dunlap arguing federal, state and local governments need to work together on the issue.
Perhaps the most stark difference between the two candidates was their attitudes toward President Donald Trump.
Multiple times throughout the debate, including in his opening statement, LePage touted his ability to call upon Trump. He said the first thing he’d do, if elected, would be to request that Trump “put restrictions on sending diesel to foreign countries.” He also said he’d call him before the election to make that suggestion.
During a response to a question on the trade war with Canada, LePage suggested, “I can help the president because I can speak French to the prime minister.”
“I will be able to get into the Oval Office; my opponent will not,” LePage said.
As for Dunlap, he repeatedly critiqued Trump’s policies and argued Congress needs to reel the president in.
“The job of Congress is to provide oversight of the executive branch,” he said regarding the war in Iran.

title: Renee Good's family sues US government and immigration officials over her killing in Minneapolis
text:
MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — Renee Good’s family sued the U.S. government and several immigration officials Thursday, alleging wrongful death and other violations of federal law in the 37-year-old woman’s killing by an immigration officer during a federal crackdown in Minneapolis.
The two lawsuits were filed by Good’s partner, Becca Good, and Renee’s brother Brent Ganger.
One lawsuit, filed against “the United States of America,” alleges the wrongful death of Renee Good under Minnesota law predicated on claims of battery, assault, false imprisonment, intentional infliction of emotional distress and negligence that caused her death.
The other lawsuit alleges a conspiracy to interfere with civil rights. It names as defendants: Jonathan Ross, the immigration officer who shot her; White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller; former Homeland Security head Kristi Noem; former U.S. Border Patrol commander-at-large Gregory Bovino, Corey Lewandowski, President Donald Trump’s campaign manager, and others.
Renee Good, a mother of three, was fatally shot Jan. 7 as protests against immigration raids flared across the city. According to Becca Good, her partner stopped their car in a street to support neighbors during an immigration operation.
Bystander video shows Renee Good in the driver’s seat of a red SUV blocking part of the road and repeatedly honking her horn.
Two immigration officers get out of a truck, their faces covered, and one orders Good to get out of the car. She reverses briefly, then turns the steering wheel as the officer says again, “get out of the car.”
Almost simultaneously, Becca Good, standing in the street, shouts: “Drive, baby, drive!”
One officer standing in front of the vehicle pulls his weapon and fires into the windshield. He lurches back as the car turns away from him. The officer, who is now very close to the open window on the driver’s side, opens fire two more times, fatally shooting Renee Good, according to an analysis of the videos by The Associated Press and others.
Federal officials at the time said the officer acted in self-defense and that Good had engaged in “an act of domestic terrorism.”
The killing of Good and another U.S. citizen, Alex Pretti, in Minneapolis just weeks later sparked outrage across the country and calls to rein in immigration enforcement. At least 10 people have died in encounters with immigration officers during President Donald Trump’s second term.
In July, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer with a history of violent behavior fatally shot a 25-year-old Colombian man, Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, in his car in Biddeford, Maine. Durán Guerrero was not the target of an immigration enforcement action.
Last week, immigration enforcement agents shot and wounded a Venezuelan delivery driver in Austin, Texas. Wilber Rafael Garces-Perez, 28, survived but was charged with sideswiping an officer with his car mirror and later attempting to strike an officer with the vehicle.
Becca and Renee Good were not legally married, according to a family lawyer, but referred to one another as wives. They had only recently relocated to Minneapolis from Kansas City, Missouri.
In social media accounts, Renee Good described herself as a “poet and writer and wife and mom.” On Pinterest, a profile picture shows her smiling and holding a young child, alongside posts about tattoos, hairstyles and home decorating.
In an interview shortly after her death, Renee Good’s mother, Donna Ganger, told The Associated Press: “She had this way of making you feel special and loved that I didn’t even understand that until we lost her.”

title: How to sex and age your harvested ruffed grouse
text:
October is grouse season. The woods are orange, red and yellow, and as the nights get colder, more birds will start showing up along the roads.
While some hunters are simply happy to have game meat for dinner, there are certainly those inquisitive folks who want to know more about the birds they harvest. They dig into the crop to determine what the bird was eating and want to know its age and sex.
Knowing whether a grouse was a juvenile or adult and a male or female can give hunters a little more insight into the birds they are finding in the woods. It can also help them better understand the grouse population in the areas they hunt.
The feathers provide several clues that can be used to determine a harvested ruffed grouse’s sex and whether it is a juvenile or adult.
Determining sex of a ruffed grouse
Start with the rump feathers above the base of the tail. One white dot at the tip of the feather indicates a female, while two white dots indicate a male.
Another method is to pull one of the two central tail feathers and measure it. A fully grown feather 6 inches or longer indicates a male, while one shorter than 5½ inches indicates a female. Tail feathers measuring between 5½ and 6 inches cannot reliably determine the bird’s sex on their own.
For birds with central tail feathers measuring between 5½ and 5⅞ inches, the Ruffed Grouse Society describes another method. Compare the central tail feather with the second primary flight feather. If the two are about the same length, the bird is a female. If the tail feather is more than ⅜ inch longer, the bird is a male.
The dark band near the end of the tail can provide another clue. About 77% of males have an unbroken dark band, according to the Ruffed Grouse Society, but some males have broken bands, so this characteristic should not be used by itself to determine sex.
Determining age of a ruffed grouse
Examine the ninth and 10th primary wing feathers. Juvenile grouse have narrowed, pointed feathers with frayed edges, while adult grouse have rounded feathers with smooth, intact edges.
Early in the season, while some adult grouse are still molting their primary feathers, you can also determine age by looking at which feathers are growing. Adult grouse replace their primary feathers in sequence, while juveniles are growing their first set. A growing ninth or 10th primary indicates an adult, while a growing seventh or eighth primary indicates a juvenile.
There is an important limitation when aging grouse: You can distinguish a juvenile from an adult, but you cannot determine the exact age of an adult grouse from its feathers. After the first complete molt of a 14- to 15-month-old adult, there are no known physical characteristics that reliably determine the bird’s age, according to the Ruffed Grouse Society.
A helpful video by the RGS demonstrates these techniques on birds in hand.

Worried about the tenor of Troy Jackson’s campaign
text:
Why is the Maine Democratic Party allowing the Troy Jackson campaign to sink?
Why are Jackson and the party succumbing to external pressure, reversing Jackson’s position on the Palestinian question (it is genocide in Gaza) and on universal healthcare? Polls have shown support for Palestine and universal healthcare are popular among voters.
Where is the passion, reason, commitment of the Troy Jackson of two months ago? Why has he been muzzled? Why is he standing down from issues Mainers care about? Instead of focusing on yard signs, we suggest the Jackson campaign let the current Collins story play itself out.
Jackson needs to focus on what will make Maine and the country a better place. There is little time left.

title: Personal bankruptcy filings up nearly 50% since 2022, analysis finds
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Personal bankruptcy filings have jumped nearly 50% since 2022, according to a new LendingTree analysis, as inflation on housing, insurance, groceries and health care, combined with high interest rates, pushes families deeper into credit card debt.
About 1,400 people a day are now turning to the courts for relief. The biggest spikes are in the South, and most filings are the more severe Chapter 7 bankruptcies, which wipe out many debts but also significantly damage credit.
Matt Schulz, with LendingTree, said reaching the point of filing for bankruptcy typically follows a long period of financial strain.
“Anytime you’re talking about bankruptcy, it’s a really big deal, because bankruptcy is generally the end of a long, difficult period that somebody has faced over the course of months or years, and they’ve decided that they really have no other choice,” Schulz said.
Schulz said filing for bankruptcy can create financial challenges that last seven to 10 years. He recommends addressing missed or late payments as early as possible.
“It’s a whole lot easier to go to a creditor when you are saying, ‘Hey, I think I may be late with a payment this month or in the coming months,’ than to go to them and say, ‘Hey, I haven’t paid you in three months, can you help me?’” Schulz said.
Schulz said it is easy to feel powerless when facing serious debt, but resources are available. Creditors can be contacted directly, and nonprofit credit counselors are available for guidance at any time. Schulz said third-party organizations, including local government programs and religious organizations, may also be able to help.

title: Court documents detail hours leading up to 2 Ole Miss students’ suspected overdose deaths
text:
OXFORD, Miss. (WMC/Gray News) — Mississippi leaders and lawmakers are calling for a crackdown on kratom and kratom-like products after two Ole Miss students died last week.
Toxicology tests are incomplete, and the autopsies on both young men are still pending.
But court documents filed Monday reveal what 18-year-old Aidan Hamilton and 20-year-old Robert Strang were doing in the hours and days before their suspected overdose deaths.
Investigators with Lafayette County Metro Narcotics previously said store-bought kratom was found in both students’ rooms.
On Sept. 30, Metro Narcotics clarified the information in an earlier statement to WMC:
“During the investigations, packaging associated with kratom-related products was discovered at both locations. This information prompted law enforcement to issue a public safety warning out of an abundance of caution.
That warning was not a declaration that kratom or any specific substance caused either death. It was a proactive effort to inform the public of a potential danger while investigators worked to determine the facts.”
Authorities were able to determine where the young men bought the drugs. The investigation now stretches from Lafayette County into neighboring Yalobusha County at a convenience store about 20 miles from the Ole Miss campus.
What investigators found in Hamilton’s dorm room
Hamilton died in his on-campus dorm room on Sept. 21.
Court documents show the coroner and medical personnel on the scene said the young man “could have died due to a pulmonary edema, consistent with a drug overdose.”
Hamilton’s roommate told investigators that Hamilton “smoked a lot of marijuana from pens and pipes,” “would keep his marijuana in a safe,” and “used it a lot, so much so, he had a terrible cough.”
But investigators are focusing on SMAX Pseudo-DHM pills, a chemically manipulated product, found on Hamilton’s dresser in his room at Stewart Hall.
Statements filed by Caleb East, an agent with the Lafayette County Metro Narcotics Unit, noted that “agents are aware that these are often sold as a kratom-like substance at gas stations or tobacco shops.”
Mississippi Department of Public Safety Commissioner Sean Tindell said, “We’re wanting to test those and make sure that anything that’s in there… it’s not being laced with any other chemicals, or there’s no other harmful chemicals in that product.”
What investigators found at Strang’s home
At the scene of Strang’s death, inside his off-campus home on Van Buren Avenue, investigators said they found 20 to 30 nitrous oxide cans.
His roommates said Strang “would use whippets daily,” the street term given to the popular party drug. Strang’s housemates also said he would use “sometimes two to three cans a week.”
Investigators also found a packet of SMAX on his nightstand in packaging similar to what was found in Hamilton’s dorm.
Roommates said Strang took a Xanax bar around 4 p.m. Sunday. He was last seen in the kitchen around midnight. His body was discovered the next day in his bedroom at 3:30 p.m.
Doctors warn about kratom and synthetic kratom-like products
Following the student deaths, Mississippi doctors are again warning about the dangers of products marketed as kratom, a natural leaf that can be tainted with other chemicals or offered in versions that are made synthetically with illegal substances, referred to as “gas station heroin.”
Dr. Lucas Trautman, medical director at the Oxford Treatment Center, told WMC, “It’s being sold in gas stations as sort of ‘natural’... that’s the buzz you hear with it... in order to help you with pain or sleep. Well, it’s just an opioid, so people get addicted to it, too, and have severe withdrawals.”
Family physician Dr. Jennifer Bryan said, “I would urge the public that if you see ‘natural,’ natural does not mean safe. It’s not synonymous. We still don’t know what’s inside that package. No matter what the label says, you don’t know what’s inside that package. The regulation is very loose.”
SMAX Pseudo-DHM is a synthetic drug marketed as a kratom-like substance. But investigators say it has a “significantly higher potency compared to natural leaf products.”
In the affidavit filed in the Third District Circuit Court of Mississippi on Sept. 28, following undercover operations at two retail stores, drug agents said the ingredients can be “produced fully synthetically in clandestine laboratories.”
The affidavit lists the ingredients of SMAX Pseudo-DHM as pseudoindoxyl, MGM-15 and 7-hydroxymitragynine.
The DEA temporarily placed mitragynine, pseudoindoxyl and MGM-15 on the Schedule I list on Aug. 26, 2026.
Schedule I drugs, including heroin, LSD and ecstasy, are illegal in the U.S. under federal law.
“Synthetic mitragynine compounds can be significantly stronger than morphine,” East wrote in the affidavit, “and carry a high risk of severe addiction, overdose and death.”
Where the drugs were purchased
Investigators with Metro Narcotics say Strang bought his SMAX product at Express Mart #7 in Water Valley in Yalobusha County. Bank records show he visited the store twice — once on Sept. 9 and again on Sept. 11.
The store is about a 20- to 30-minute drive from the Ole Miss campus.
Undercover officers bought more of the product a day after his death.
Court documents say the clerk said the store was out of the 200-mg version but sold “another form of the SMAX Pseudo-DHM pills consistent with the packages found at the Strang scene.”
The pills were sent to a forensic lab in Columbus, Mississippi, for analysis.
Agents returned to Express Mart #7 on Sept. 23 and bought more of the pills, this time sending them to a crime lab in Florida for analysis.
Investigators say records show Aidan Hamilton made multiple purchases at Puffs Vape Tobacco and Beer in Oxford. Bank records provided by his parents showed he visited the store and made purchases on Sept. 9, Sept. 14 and Sept. 20, one day before his death.
On Sept. 24, Metro Narcotics agents sent a confidential informant into the store, equipped with audio and video equipment. The informant tried to buy nitrous oxide, but the clerk told him that the store didn’t have any.
The affidavit says the clerk then offered to sell the informant marijuana from a jar and pre-rolled joints. The informant declined, but later asked if the store sold “7 O Kratom based pills.” The clerk said yes.
Records show an employee told an undercover informant to “be careful taking the pills because people are dying from them.”
Two employees of that store were arrested, and 500 units of kratom and kratom-like products were seized. The Metro Narcotics team also found an assortment of “THC cartridges, gummies, pre-rolls and other suspected THC substances.”
Recreational marijuana is still classified as an illegal Schedule I drug in the U.S.
Possible legislative action
The scope and impact of the Ole Miss deaths investigation could lead to legislative change.
Commissioner Tindell said, “Once kratom is banned locally, it’s still only a misdemeanor. And so I think one of the things the legislature is going to look at and consider next year… is, are we at the point where we need a statewide ban on kratom?”
Kratom is currently banned in the City of Oxford and Lafayette County. And again, the ingredients in the SMAX products found in the students’ rooms — products sold by two retail establishments — are illegal under federal law.
The students’ toxicology reports are being expedited and could come back as soon as this week. Until that happens, their causes of death are pending.
The American Kratom Association held a news conference in Oxford on Wednesday to defend natural kratom and differentiate it from the manufactured products that authorities said were found in the students’ rooms.

title: Bakery pairs pastries with a path to employment
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
MEMPHIS, Tenn. (Aging Untold) — Lucy J’s, a bakery in Memphis, is providing jobs and training opportunities for people who need a fresh start, according to head baker Josh Burgess.
Burgess is also Lucy J’s executive director. The bakery is named after his daughter and eldest son.
“Our fresh bread is some of the best in the city,” Burgess said. “Our sourdough and our cheddar jalapeno bread are very, very popular. We have the best cinnamon roll in the world.”
The bakery also sells savory and sweet pockets, croissants, cupcakes and cookies.
Jobs for families in need
The jobs pave a path forward for many of Lucy J’s employees.
“Just depends on what they need, and we try to find a slot for them to fill,” Burgess said.
Josh Burgess’ wife, Tracy Burgess, is executive director of Dorothy Day House, a Memphis nonprofit that provides temporary housing and support services, including jobs at Lucy J’s, for families experiencing homelessness.
“There is a huge need here in the city, and it really is an invisible problem,” Tracy Burgess said. “They have to be able to sustain their family life after they move out.”
Dorothy Day House was founded in 2006 and named after a late journalist who advocated for the poor. The organization operates three locations in Memphis for families working toward stability while gaining a network of support.
Living wage and expansion plans
Lucy J’s provides jobs for some Dorothy Day House families and pays workers $15 an hour.
“It’s just a community that needs help,” Josh Burgess said. “And they’re here to help us, and we’re here to help them.”
With steady demand for Lucy J’s baked goods at groceries, restaurants and food trucks, Josh and Tracy Burgess hope to raise money to expand the bakery and hire more workers.
“It’s a big mission that we’re trying to tackle, and we could use everybody’s help,” Josh Burgess said. “Come in, buy something, donate if they’re available, volunteer if they’re available, and just become part of the community.”

title: Woman arrested after cocaine, guns are seized from Cornish home
text:
Maine woman arrested on trafficking charges after cocaine, guns seized from Cornish home
The Maine Drug Enforcement Agency (Maine DEA) says a woman has been arrested after agents seized cocaine, diverted prescription pills and several guns while searching a Cornish home.
Adele Rogers, 52, of Cornish, has been charged with four counts of aggravated trafficking in Schedule W drugs following Thursday's operation.
The Maine DEA said that for the past several months, the agency has been investigating a suspected drug trafficking organization in the town of Cornish. The investigation included undercover purchases of crack cocaine from a home on Main Street, according to authorities.
On Thursday, Maine DEA agents executed a search warrant at the Main Street residence with assistance from the Maine State Police and U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration.
Agents seized 49.5 grams of cocaine, hydrocodone pills, three firearms and $1,760 in suspected drug proceeds as a result of the search. Officials said the seized drugs have an estimated street value of $5,000.
Rogers was taken into custody at the home without incident. She is being held on $50,000 bail at the York County Jail.
The Maine DEA said the drug trafficking investigation will continue and that additional arrests are expected in the case.
Authorities are asking anyone who has information about this investigation or the illegal sale of drugs in their community to contact the Maine DEA office closest to them, call the Maine DEA tip line at 1-800-452-6457 or text "MDEA" to 847411.
The Maine DEA also encouraged people who are suffering from substance use disorder to call 211 or text their zip code to 898211 for a list of resources available in their area.

title: Lewiston looks to Augusta for help addressing repeat youth violence
text:
Lewiston looks to Augusta for help addressing repeat youth violence
City officials say they've increased police enforcement citywide, but more needs to be done to break the cycle of violence.
Lewiston looks to Augusta for help addressing repeat youth violence
City officials say they've increased police enforcement citywide, but more needs to be done to break the cycle of violence.
In August, the city of Lewiston put into motion its Community Engagement and Accountability initiative as a way to curb youth violence in the city. The first part of the initiative was increasing police presence, but now it’s looking to make changes in Augusta.
City officials say that so far this year there have been 35 instances of gun violence in Lewiston, and 25 of those were committed by juveniles. Breaking that number further down, all but two of those juveniles were repeat offenders.
“There's one individual who's had 70 events with the police department just in the last two years,” said Bryan Kaenrath, Lewiston's city administrator.
As an immediate response, police have used the overtime funding to increase targeted patrols while also doing more police details in the city, where officers are walking or biking around and engaging with community members.
“The more you're present, the more you're engaged, the more deterrence there is for future crimes happening,” Kaenrath said.
Despite the high levels of youth violence, Lewiston officials say that they have been successful in investigating the crimes, resolving more than than 60%.
However, gun violence numbers have continued to climb during the targeted enforcement.
Lewiston police Chief Carly Conley said these are just band-aid fixes.
"For there to be significant change, it's in Augusta's hands, 100%. That being said, you know, we're still going to do everything within our control and within our means and our power to approach these issues in any kind of creative way we can to try to limit them," Conley said.
Community Engagement and Accountability is pushing eight policy proposals to lawmakers, combating what it calls a “revolving door” of high-risk juveniles returning into the community after detainment.
The city says current detention criteria often require the release of juveniles despite a history of dangerous behavior. The city would have this amended so that judges and Juvenile Community Corrections Officers can consider serious and repeated violations when determining if detention is necessary.
Many programs at Long Creek Youth Development Center are only available to committed juveniles, rather than detained juveniles who may end up staying in the facility for some time. The city wants those programs to be opened up so even kids who are detained can start taking part as soon as they get there.
Other policy proposals involve requiring treatments for serious juvenile offenses, and holding the Department of Health and Human Services accountable for carrying out treatments.
The next legislative session doesn't start until the winter, so it could be some time for these to get written into law, and they could look very different before then.
Still, Kaenrath is optimistic they will move forward.
"You may not get 100% of what you want, but if we can get a large share of it or we can get something done, that's going to be a huge accomplishment, and it's going to make a real difference on the ground here in the city of Lewiston," Kaenrath said.
The city also wants to continue funding the increased patrols for officers, something it does have control over. Conley said the station is understaffed, which is why the money is being put towards overtime.
"Many times our patrol officers don't have the time to stop and just sit and engage in the community because they're going to call to call to call to call," Conley said.

title: Child porn on cruise ships: dozens of crewmembers removed, including from ship that visited Maine
text:
PORTLAND, Maine (WMTW) - A cruise ship that makes frequent stops in Portland has been caught up in a U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) effort targeting the possession and distribution of child sexual abuse material and child sexual exploitation material among cruise ship crewmembers.
CBP says, as of Friday, it has removed 87 people at the Port of Boston from cruise ships as part of Operation Tidal Wave. That includes six citizens of the Philippines removed from a Norwegian Cruise Line ship called Breakaway in Boston on Sept. 20. CBP says all six admitted to previously having child sexual abuse material and child sexual exploitation material.
The Breakaway stopped in Portland twice in August and four times in September, including this week.
Our media partner, WMTW, is working to learn if any of the implicated crewmembers were in Maine or were detained here.
The Breakaway has a crew capacity of more than 1,600 and a guest capacity of about 3,900.
The Area Port of Boston plans to continue the operation through the end of the fiscal year.
“The success of Operation Tidal Wave reflects the unwavering dedication of our officers and partners to protect the most vulnerable,” said Acting Director of Field Operations Julio Caravia. “Let the removal of these 87 be a message to others: we will not accept this exploitation and CBP will not stop identifying and arresting the individuals who participate in it.”
Operation Tidal Wave also resulted in action against 27 crewmembers through the San Diego office and 15 people through the San Juan office this year.

main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A Madawaska motel is on the market for the third time in less than a decade.
The Gateway Motel, a 33-room motel with an on-site restaurant, was listed for $650,000 on Sept. 28.
The facility is among the most northeastern lodging establishments in the U.S., situated along Route 1 toward the eastern edge of Madawaska.
The 5.13-acre property also has a three-bedroom owner’s residence and 12 additional rooms that could become rentable if renovated, according to the listing.
Formerly named Four Corners Inn and Suites, the motel was last sold in late 2022 for $650,000, and before that in 2019, transfer tax records show. The current listing price is below the property’s assessed value, which tax records list at $674,500.
Built in 1959, the establishment is just minutes from a Canadian border crossing, and a trail from its parking lot connects to ITS 81, which has made the motel at times a hub for traveling snowmobilers.
The motel’s owners did not respond to a request for comment Wednesday.

title: Sen. King bill could speed up, reduce costs for some affordable housing projects
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
For more than a year, affordable housing developers in Maine have been wrestling with the requirements of a federal rule that they say is burying them in paperwork and making construction impossible.
Sen. Angus King thinks he can help.
On Wednesday, Maine’s independent senator introduced the Build American Efficiency Act, a bill encouraging the federal government to work with manufacturers on a publicly available database of certified American-made products that would meet the requirements of the Build America Buy America Act.
Also known as BABA, the program requires all building projects using certain government funds to source 95% of their construction materials from the United States.
Developers have said the administrative burden of simply tracking down domestic materials has been extreme and adds as much as $150,000 per project – and that’s not including the premium costs for American-made materials.
“It’s a perfect example of a well-meaning policy that turned out to have negative consequences,” King said in an interview Thursday. “You’ve got hundreds, if not thousands, of builders, each individually trying to sort through this maze, and now what our bill would do (is) create a simple, easy-to-access database so that they don’t have to do that.”
‘EXTENSIVE’ CHANGES NEEDED
The proposal, co-sponsored by Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, is a step in the right direction, but Laura Mitchell, executive director of the Maine Affordable Housing Coalition, said developers need more than a database to help projects move forward.
“BABA is really clogging the affordable housing development pipeline,” she said. “We’re really grateful for Sen. King being creative, and trying to find shortcut pathways to make it easier to comply with BABA, (but) this bill doesn’t offer the extensive level of changes that are needed.”
The National Electrical Manufacturer’s Association, identified in the bill as a possible standard to use, has the “Make It American BABA Registry,” which has a list of 68 manufacturing facilities spread across 15 companies that are certified to make 50-or-so products.
But compared to the roughly 1,600 parts that go into an affordable housing project, the few dozen products that are on that registry don’t carry much impact.
Mitchell said the Make it American system simply hasn’t certified enough products.
“There’s still going to be a lot of work put on these nonprofit affordable housing developers,” she said.
King, however, believes they can get certifications for all the hundreds, if not thousands of pieces.
“I think AI might help us on this,” he added.
THE WAIVER WAIT
For materials unavailable from American manufacturers, like HVAC systems or their components, developers can request a waiver from the Department of Housing and Urban Development.
And then they wait. And wait.
Laura Reading, director of affordable housing for Portland-based Developers Collaborative, waited for more than seven months for waivers for her two projects in Portland and Windham.
Both projects are set to close this month, but Reading found out last week that the waiver for her Portland project, a 110-spot childcare center for Youth and Family Outreach and 60 units of housing, needs to be resubmitted because it only covers funding from MaineHousing, not additional money from the city.
She’s hopeful it will be fast-tracked but noted that HUD has not given her a timeline.
A database wouldn’t help Reading’s current projects, but she said she could see one being useful in the future.
“The documentation for all of this has been a bit insane because all of these vendors want to use their own form and their own letter (of certification),” she said. “Some of them are not as clear as we need them to be.”
King said the list could also help speed up the waiver process, allowing HUD to more easily check whether something is available domestically and quickly approve or deny the request.
Reading added that it could potentially help HUD identify what products aren’t yet made in the U.S. (like an HVAC) system and create a universal waiver so developers aren’t forced to wait months for an approval on the same item for every project.
‘THE SILVER BULLET’
A general waiver is one of a handful of “administrative” changes that Mitchell, at the Maine Affordable Housing Coalition, said would be the most consequential. She’s hopeful to see HUD come out with one for HVAC by the end of the year.
Alternatively (or additionally), HUD could increase the allowable percentage of foreign materials from 5% to 10% or 15%. Or it could exempt affordable housing from BABA altogether.
“That would be the silver bullet addressing all of this,” Mitchell said.
The “Build Housing Affordably Act,” proposed in the House, would do so temporarily, while also instituting a 90-day window for waiver approvals.
Maine is one of the first states to come up against the BABA requirements, and affordable housing developers that have had their projects halted indefinitely are pushing to get the issue fixed before it spreads across the country.
Housing has recently become a bipartisan issue and King is optimistic that the bill can make it through Congress without any major setbacks and be enacted by the end of the year.

title: Graphic timeline now on display at the Chapman-Hall House
text:
To further enhance visitors’ experience at the 1754 Chapman-Hall House in Damariscotta, a Timeline of Events has been installed in the ell of the historic cape at the head of Main Street. “The 100” chronology, depicted in art and photos, takes one from the first visits of European explorers and fishermen in the 1580s through 1960, when the house was saved from demolition, and 2008 when it was deeded to Lincoln County Historical Association. David Griffin, a graphic designer with MoranGriffin, Inc., Dresden, designed the timeline, using research details and original illustrations of Chapman-Hall House by Paul C. Bates and Maurice “Jake” Day.
Bates and his wife retired to South Bristol in 1972, and in 1982 they moved to Damariscotta. As an artist, he worked in pen and ink and watercolors. His pieces, many of local Midcoast sites, are noted for their attention to detail.
Day is well known locally for his paintings of Maine wilderness, animal caricatures, his work on “Bambi” for Disney and for his dioramas, which are displayed by his family in Damariscotta every December holiday season.
The house will be open on Saturdays and Sundays from noon to 4 p.m. through Pumpkinfest. Located at 270 Main St., the Chapman-Hall House Museum is on the National Register of Historic Sites and Places. Admission is charged; children under 16 are free.

title: Zoo Atlanta shares new video of giant panda Fu Shuang settling in
text:
Zoo Atlanta shares new video of giant panda Fu Shuang settling in
Panda lovers are getting a glimpse into the life of Fu Shuang, one of two pandas gifted to the United States by China as part of Beijing's long tradition of "panda diplomacy."
In a video posted on Zoo Atlanta's Facebook page, Fu Shuang was seen settling into her new home and munching on bamboo.
Watch the video above.
The pandas — a male named Ping Ping and a female named Fu Shuang — arrived on a FedEx flight Sunday from Chengdu, in southwestern China. Their arrival at Zoo Atlanta came with great fanfare, especially since the bears are a rarity in U.S. zoos.
"Atlanta’s newest arrivals are exceeding the team’s expectations in terms of their acclimation," the zoo said in the post. "Both Ping Ping and Fu Shuang are eating well and adjusting more and more each day."
In 2024, Zoo Atlanta returned four pandas who had lived at the zoo to China, marking the end of a 25-year agreement between the zoo and China.
Zoo Atlanta said the pandas are not ready for visits from the public yet, telling panda lovers to "stay tuned for future announcements about when you’ll be able to meet them!"

title: Patriots tight end Eli Raridon and wife announce death of newborn son
text:
(Gray News) - New England Patriots tight end Eli Raridon and his wife, Anna Raridon, announced the death of their newborn son.
“Our angel, Peter James Raridon, was born on September 11,” the couple announced on Instagram.
In the announcement, the couple said that they learned during the 20-week anatomy scan that their son had anencephaly, which they described as “a fatal condition in which he would not survive outside the womb.”
“While we are absolutely devastated that we were unable to bring our baby boy home, I am grateful to have loved him deeply, kept him safe, and had been his home for the past 9 months before he was called back to Heaven,” the post read.
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, anencephaly is a birth defect in which the baby forms without parts of the brain and skull. The CDC said that almost all babies with anencephaly die shortly after birth and there is currently no cure or treatment.
“I believe our little boy was lovingly knitted together in the womb by God, knowing how deeply he would be loved by our families, our friends, Eli, and me. Though his time with us was brief, his life still precious, his purpose still meaningful, and he will forever be a part of our story,” the post said.
Eli and Anna Raridon were married on May 25, 2025. They announced in an Instagram post on March 31 that they were expecting their first child.
“I have loved you every second of your life & will miss you every second of mine. What a sweet sweet reunion ours will be,” the couple’s post said.
This is Eli Raridon’s first season with the New England Patriots. He was picked by the team during the third round of the 2026 draft. Prior to that, he played for Notre Dame.

title: A Russian drone hits a Kyiv school as Moscow presses its aerial campaign against Ukraine
text:
A Russian drone hits a Kyiv school as Moscow presses its aerial campaign against Ukraine
A Russian drone struck a school in Kyiv on Thursday, city officials said, as the Ukrainian capital endured another night and day of relentless aerial attacks.
Related video: A pregnant soldier mourns her 21-year-old husband at his funeral in Ukraine
Children and staff at the school were in shelters when the drone hit, Kyiv Mayor Vitalii Klitschko said, although the drone's warhead didn’t explode. There was no immediate report of casualties. The building’s brick frontage showed a large hole and black burn mark alongside smashed windows.
Kyiv has in recent weeks lived through repeated air raid alerts, punctuated by loud bangs and palls of black smoke as drones and missiles hit, making it feel like a city under siege. The Russian onslaught aims to terrorize civilians, officials and analysts say, and break their will to resist 4 ½ years after Moscow’s full-scale invasion.
The strain is showing among Kyiv residents. Maryna Lystopad, 35, said her hair has started falling out due to the strain of escalating attacks and never knowing where a drone or missile will hit.
"It’s really horrible. I can’t take it anymore. I think, I think that soon we’re all going to leave. I’m really not doing well,” she told The Associated Press.
“I’m constantly anxious. I can’t relax,” she said. “I keep thinking that if something happens, if something hits, one of my relatives could be killed.”
She recently had to go to another part of the city, she said, and was “genuinely stressed the whole way there.”
“I kept checking, like, whether anything was flying in, where it was going, where am I supposed to go? Where am I supposed to run?”
Russia's missiles and drones are stretching Ukraine's air defenses
The war on the ground hasn’t seen major shifts since last year, but Ukraine is struggling to fend off Russia’s intensified aerial attacks on cities that include speedy ballistic missiles and high-flying jet-powered drones.
In response, Ukraine has fired its long-range drones at manufacturing plants deep inside Russia and has targeted Russia’s drone launch sites. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Thursday that Kyiv’s forces struck a site in Russia’s southwestern Oryol region that is used to store and launch attack drones.
To turn the tide, Ukraine needs U.S.-made Patriot missiles that can effectively defend against ballistic missiles, but they are in short supply since the Iran war began. A plan to produce them inside Ukraine could take years to bear fruit.
Kyiv is currently racing to produce new interceptors that can bring down fast-moving jet-propelled drones as the swift cycle of military innovation during the war continues.
Ukraine also wants tougher sanctions imposed on Russia to prevent it from getting key high-tech components for its arsenal.
Moscow, meanwhile, is pressing its advantage before Ukraine comes up with an answer to the latest challenges.
Russia steps up its campaign against Ukraine's power grid
Ukrainian officials didn’t report any energy infrastructure being hit Thursday, a day after what officials said was the biggest Russian attack on the power grid since last spring.
The Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank, said Wednesday's barrage marked “the beginning of Russia’s strike campaign aimed at degrading Ukraine’s energy security ahead of winter … and forcing Ukraine to capitulate.”
Russia is expected to step up attacks on the electricity supply as the weather gets colder. It was 19 degrees Celsius (66 F) in Kyiv on Thursday, and mild temperatures were set to continue.
In a surprise development, Russia used a new jet-powered drone for the first time Wednesday, fitting it with a warhead designed to sever high-voltage pylons, said Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Ukraine’s president on defense technology.
___
AP reporter Volodymyr Yurchuk contributed to this story from Kyiv, Ukraine.

title: Anesthesiologist explains what likely caused Christa Pike’s failed execution by lethal injection
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WVLT/Gray News) - A Tennessee anesthesiologist is weighing in on what may have gone wrong during the botched execution of Christa Pike.
Dr. Paul Allen, a professor of anesthesiology at the University of Tennessee Health Science Center, said the details coming out of Wednesday’s execution point to one likely explanation: the needle never properly made it into her vein.
According to Allen, for the lethal drug pentobarbital to make someone unconscious, it has to go directly into the bloodstream, meaning the needle has to be properly placed inside a vein.
Allen said finding a usable vein can be difficult for a number of reasons, including dehydration.
According to the Department of Corrections, Pike declined to pick a specialized last meal, though she did eat a meal during the period when her execution was stayed.
Allen added that veins can also be harder to access if they have been damaged over time.
“Not eating and drinking would make finding the vein and getting into the vein more difficult. Also, if she had bad veins to begin with, that were from either substance abuse or something of that nature, then it would be difficult to cannulate her vein,” Allen said.
In past appeals, Pike argued she had a vein condition that could make the lethal injection process difficult.
Allen said infiltration happens when a needle misses the vein or punctures through it, and the drug leaks into the soft tissue under the skin instead of circulating through the blood.
“What happened here, I would suspect, is that they infiltrated the vein,” Allen said. “That means that the drug, instead of going in the bloodstream, went into the peripheral tissues in the arm or wherever they put the needle in.”
Allen said that could explain a witness account that Pike described her arm throbbing in certain spots after the injections.
Allen said when the drug leaks into surrounding tissue instead of the bloodstream, it can still make someone drowsy, which could explain why Pike appeared sleepy and snoring, but the dose did not kill her.
The doctor stressed that his medical assessment was based on witness accounts, not a confirmed finding. The exact cause of what went wrong has not been officially released.
Allen said pentobarbital is not a new drug. It was once prescribed for sleep, and doctors have long known it can be dangerous in large doses.
According to Pike’s legal team, she survived the failed execution, but she has since been in critical condition, receiving life-saving medical care at an area hospital.
Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee has since halted executions in the state for the rest of the year.

title: MaineDOT converting high-crash Newburgh intersection into 4-way stop; local drivers divided
text:
NEWBURGH, Maine (WABI) - Motorists traveling between Newburgh, Hampden, and Winterport will soon face a major change to their daily commute as state transportation crews prepare to overhaul a notoriously dangerous intersection.
Beginning Tuesday, Oct. 6, the Maine Department of Transportation will convert the crossing of Route 9 (US-202) and Route 69 (Carmel Road North) into a permanent, all-way four-way stop.
The project includes new pavement markings, advance flashing “Stop Ahead” warning signs, flashing red LEDs on all stop signs, and reconfiguring the overhead beacon to flash red in all four directions.
A persistent ‘High Crash Location’
According to MaineDOT safety reports, the crossing has long been classified as a “High Crash Location”—an official state designation for intersections seeing crash rates substantially higher than the statewide average for comparable roads.
Recent state data indicates that crashes at the intersection are climbing:
- 2020–2022: 11 crashes
- 2021–2023: 13 crashes
- 2022–2024: 15 crashes
The state’s analysis revealed a Critical Rate Factor (CRF) topping 5.0, meaning collisions at the crossing occur at more than five times the expected statistical rate. Past visibility enhancements, including brush clearing and warning signs, failed to reduce the collision frequency.
Close calls spark calls for action
For local commuters who travel the corridor daily, the safety upgrades cannot come soon enough.
Bethany Tompkins of Hampden says near-misses are a regular occurrence, including a terrifying close call this past week while driving with her children.
“The one on the left was actually at a stop and the one on the right was coming up to the stop sign and then just gunned it and he just went straight through,” Tompkins said. “I slammed on my brakes, all the stuff in my car flew forward and he just went around me. Didn’t even look at me, he just kept driving. And of course I look back and my kids are back there, and my oldest one, her face is white.”
Truckers raise winter safety and traffic concerns
While drivers welcome added protection against high-speed T-bone collisions, commercial haulers warn that forcing heavy trucks to come to a complete stop could create a different set of road hazards.
Ernie Wallace, a Winterport resident who has driven commercial rigs for decades, says the geography and heavy freight volume on Route 9 make a four-way stop problematic—particularly as winter approaches.
“If you’re going towards Hampden, when they stop, the traffic behind them has to stop. Then he’s going to be two, three, four miles before he can ever get going again up to speed,” Wallace said. “The trucks coming the other way will have to start stopping probably way up by the golf course to get stopped at that stop sign safely, especially in the winter time.”
Drivers push for alternative solutions
While Tompkins and Wallace view the stop sign mandate through different lenses, both drivers agreed that another measure should have accompanied—or preceded—the stop signs: creating an enforceable, reduced speed zone to slow down approaching traffic.
Longer-term infrastructure studies from MaineDOT show that modern roundabouts provide significant safety benefits at high-speed rural crossings, historically delivering a 53% reduction in total crashes, a 74% drop in injury crashes, and a 92% reduction in overall crash costs.
Installation details
Town officials in Newburgh, Hampden, and Winterport are urging motorists to plan for extra travel time during the morning and evening commutes while drivers adjust to the new traffic pattern.
Work on the intersection is scheduled to take place on Tuesday, Oct. 6, weather permitting. In the event of inclement weather, the conversion will take place on Thursday, Oct. 8.

title: Obituary: Marc R. Robichaud
text:
AUBURN – Marc R. Robichaud, 50, passed away Friday, Sept. 25, 2026, in Auburn. He was born March 29, 1976, in Lewiston, the son of Richard R. Robichaud and Claire J. (Ayotte) Barclay. He was a 1994 graduate of Edward Little High School in Auburn. Marc was a member of the U.S. Army and worked as a laborer in the roofing industry upon his discharge. He enjoyed playing hockey, golfing, softball and scuba diving.
From an early age, Marc was active in sports. He played hockey for St. Peter’s, Auburn Youth Hockey, and Edward Little High School, forging many lasting friendships. As an adult, he maintained his love for sports, playing in local softball and hockey men’s leagues. He was also an avid scuba diver and loved exploring what he referred to as “God’s aquarium.” However, Marc’s truest passion was spending every moment he could with family. He treasured family vacations to Camp Ellis and Bonaire, as well as quieter moments spent having dinner and playing cribbage together. His nieces and nephews especially adored him, and he was affectionately known as “Uncle Mahhhhc.”
Marc brought so much light into the lives of his family and everyone fortunate enough to know him. He had a way of making people laugh and feel at ease, because he was never afraid to be himself. A big kid at heart, Marc was kind, funny, and welcoming. He was also an amazing hugger who might accidentally break your ribs or hand when he gave you a bear-sized hug or handshake. Marc’s vibrant presence was evident when he entered a room, and his absence will be deeply felt.
He is survived by his mother, Claire Barclay of Auburn, his children, Ben Lane-Robichard of Greene, Keri Anne Tiner of Minot, twins, Marc Robichaud II and Regina Robichaud both of Florida., siblings, Chris Robichaud of Naples, Fla.., Timothy Barclay II (Hanna) of Belchertown, Mass., and Elizabeth Collins (Matthew) of Longmeadow, Mass., nieces and nephews, Alyssa Robichaud, Timothy “Rex” Barclay III, Sophie Collins and Oliver Collins, and many loving aunt, uncles, and cousins. He was predeceased by his biological father, Richard Robichaud, dad, Timothy “Pops” I. Barclay, Sr. and sister, Jeanne Barclay. Messages of condolence may be sent to: http://www.finleyfuneralhome.com.
A graveside service will be held at 11 a.m., Saturday, October 3, at Moose Hill Cemetery, 31 Record Road, Livermore Falls. Arrangements by FINLEY FUNERAL HOME, 15 Church Street, Livermore Falls.
In lieu of flowers, donations can be made to the Greater Androscoggin Humane Society, 55 Strawberry Ave, Lewiston. https://gahumane.org/give/general-donations/

title: ‘I was wrong’ is hard to say. But many Trump voters need to say it.
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
James C. McGuire Jr. lives in Waldoboro and is the author of the four-book “American Crossroads” series. His writing examines democracy, political division, citizenship, and the search for common ground.
Across Maine, some voters who once supported Donald Trump enthusiastically now respond very differently when asked about him. They do not defend his conduct or explain why they still support his decisions. Instead, they may say, “I don’t follow politics anymore,” “I’m sick of both parties,” or “I hate all politicians.”
Sometimes that frustration is genuine. Washington has given Americans plenty of reasons to distrust government. But sometimes these declarations sound less like political independence and more like an escape hatch — a way to avoid saying three difficult words: “I was wrong.”
These voters probably followed politics when Trump told them what they wanted to hear. They followed when he promised lower prices, better jobs, safer communities, and an end to wars. They followed when he identified enemies to blame and presented himself as the only person strong enough to rescue the country.
They wore the hats, planted the signs, repeated his accusations, and excused behavior they would never have tolerated from another president. Some dismissed every warning as fake news and treated criticism of Trump as a personal attack against themselves.
Now, as promises collide with reality and the results become harder to defend, some have suddenly stopped following politics.
That is convenient.
Saying “all politicians are crooks” spreads responsibility so widely that nobody has to accept any personally. If every officeholder is equally corrupt, then supporting Trump was no worse than supporting anyone else. Every broken promise disappears into a swamp of generalized cynicism.
But everyone is not equally responsible for every decision. We cannot cheer for one person while he is gathering power, then blame the entire political system when we dislike what he does with it. We cannot demand credit for victories while assigning every failure to Congress, the courts, the media, Democrats, immigrants, or some hidden “deep state.”
Our ballots belong to us. So does the responsibility to examine what follows from them.
That does not mean every Trump voter is a bad person. Many decent, hardworking Mainers believed his promises. Some felt ignored by Washington. Some were worried about the cost of living, their jobs, immigration, or the direction of the country. Those concerns were real, even when the proposed answers were not.
People can be deceived by slogans, frightened by propaganda, and persuaded by candidates who know how to turn genuine anxiety into personal loyalty. None of us is immune from making a poor political choice.
There is no disgrace in recognizing a mistake. In fact, changing one’s mind when confronted with evidence is a sign of judgment and character. The greater failure is recognizing the damage but refusing to acknowledge any responsibility for it.
“I was wrong” requires courage.
“I don’t follow politics anymore” requires nothing.
Walking away does not erase a vote or its consequences. Workers who lose jobs, veterans who lose services, farmers who lose markets, seniors who fear for their benefits, and families struggling to pay bills cannot simply tune politics out. They must live with what elected leaders do.
Democracy does not demand perfection from voters. It demands attention, honesty, and a willingness to reconsider when the evidence proves us wrong. Citizenship continues after Election Day.
If you supported Trump and now regret it, I urge you to say so. Say, “I believed him. I defended him. I was wrong.”
Then help repair the damage. Question the next grand promise. Reject the next convenient lie. Judge leaders by their actions instead of their party labels. Warn others about the tactics that once persuaded you.
Changing your mind is not weakness. Admitting a political mistake does not make you foolish.
It makes you an honest citizen — and honesty is something Maine and America desperately need.

title: More than a dozen sickened in parasite outbreak linked to hotel pool, health officials say
text:
BOTHELL, Wash. (KPTV/Gray News) — Public health officials say more than a dozen people were sickened by a parasite linked to a hotel swimming pool.
Health officials in King County shared that an investigation was opened earlier this summer after 14 people reported falling ill after swimming in the pool at McMenamins Anderson School, an entertainment destination and boutique hotel built inside a converted junior high school, in late August.
The investigation found that an outbreak of cryptosporidiosis was linked to the hotel pool, with laboratory tests confirming the illness was caused by cryptosporidium, a microscopic parasite.
Those who were sickened were said to have symptoms such as diarrhea, stomach cramps, nausea and fever that started days after visiting the pool area.
Investigators suspect the parasite spread when an infected swimmer entered the pool.
Officials noted that the facility was well-maintained, followed all county health and safety regulations, and had no violations during a September inspection.
But because the microscopic parasite is highly chlorine-resistant, it can survive in properly treated pools for several days.
No hospitalizations or deaths were reported in this case, with Washington health officials saying the outbreak now appears to be over.
Cryptosporidium was also the parasite that caused an outbreak of explosive diarrhea across the U.S. also earlier this year.
Health officials emphasized that swimmers should avoid public pools for at least two weeks after recovering from diarrhea or vomiting and should shower with soap before swimming.

title: Witnesses describe Christa Pike ‘snoring’ and ‘looking around’ during botched execution attempt
text:
KNOXVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV/Gray News) - Christa Pike remains alive after officials attempted to execute her by lethal injection, with witnesses describing “haunting” moments during the failed attempt.
The state tried to execute her by lethal injection on Wednesday, but neither the initial nor backup dose of pentobarbital killed her.
“Christa is alive right now. We don’t have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment,” Spivey said during a news conference.
Witnesses say she was snoring when the execution chamber’s microphone was cut off more than an hour into the attempt.
Attorneys say at least seven needles were used in her left arm alone. They described her physical reactions, including ragged breathing, looking around and complaining of a burning sensation.
The failed execution amounted to “torture,” her lawyers said, and they called for her death sentence to be commuted.
“I’m haunted by last night,” he said. “What I saw last night is not something that should ever, ever happen again.”
Pike, 50, was sentenced to death for killing Colleen Slemmer in 1995.
Slemmer was 19 years old when she was killed after being lured to an isolated area on the University of Tennessee agricultural campus. Both Slemmer and Pike were enrolled in Job Corps at the time.

The Department of Defense has announced the creation of a new office of religious affairs to oversee religious policy, funding and "spiritual readiness" across the military.
"Our department is, you might say, putting on the full armor of God because while we wage physical war, we all know the real battle is spiritual," Secretary Pete Hegseth said.
Hegseth announced the new office this week, stating that its director will report directly to him.

Hegseth said religious support has been underfunded and overlooked.
Critics of the initiative have expressed concerns that it risks blurring the line between church and state.

title: Nearly 60 years after his adoption, man learns Grammy Award-winning musician Michael McDonald is his biological father
text:
ST. LOUIS (KMOV/Gray News) - A man who was placed for adoption as a baby nearly 60 years ago learned that his father is five-time Grammy Award winner Michael McDonald.
Michael Goessling said he always knew he was adopted and had a “wonderful childhood.”
“I could not pick two finer folks to raise me,” he said.
Goessling always wondered about his biological parents and said the mystery began unraveling after one of McDonald’s children took a 23andMe DNA test.
“Within 36 hours, he got an email notifying him, ‘Michael Gossling, half brother, St. Louis,’” Goessling said. “And that’s how this all began.”
On his 58th birthday, Goessling met his birth mother in person. Later, he spoke with his biological father over the phone. Goessling asked what he did for a living, and his biological father mentioned he was a musician preparing to tour through St. Louis that summer.
“And I said, ‘Are you Michael McDonald?’” Goessling said. “And he said, ‘Yeah, I’m afraid so.’”
Goessling’s biological mother and McDonald were 14 years old when Goessling was conceived.
McDonald is a singer-songwriter and Doobie Brothers member known for songs including “What a Fool Believes” and “I Keep Forgettin.’”
The fact that Goessling and McDonald share the same first name is purely coincidental.
McDonald and Goessling’s biological mother have remained close friends over the years.
McDonald described the emotional weight of not knowing what happened to his son.
“We always talked about him. And it always came down to our greatest fear was, how did life treat him?” McDonald said. “I always carried that guilt with me. But just to know that he was OK and that he had a good life, and a life certainly that I wouldn’t have been able to afford him at that time, was a great reward. The real rock stars in this story are his adoptive parents.”
Goessling and McDonald have since met in person.
“When he first saw me, he put his arms out, gave me a big old bear hug and told me he loved me, and I told him the same,” Goessling said.
The reunion also made McDonald a grandfather.
“Yeah, I’m still wrapping my head around that,” McDonald said with a laugh. “My daughter-in-law is just the daughter-in-law you’d hope for. And the kids are two of the greatest kids you’d ever meet. I’m just so proud of them.”

title: Cape Elizabeth recognizes historical burial site
text:
A path winds around and through two grassy areas in a shady grove behind the Riverside Cemetery in Cape Elizabeth, bounded by marshy wetlands. Long grasses cover roots. And stones.
Some of these stones poke up no more than a few inches from the ground. They’re suspiciously rectangular, local history enthusiast Diane Brakeley thinks.
There are dozens of these stones, which would seem like a normal occurrence on any other wooded area or trail. But here, it could mark the remains of previous Cape Elizabeth residents.
They were farmers and fishermen, perhaps, who toiled on the same marshes, plains and coasts we enjoy today, but didn’t have the means to inscribe their names.
There are 51 markers of burials in this shady grove surrounded by the Greenbelt trail, remnants of old Jordan family plots, according to Town Planner Maureen O’Meara.
Less than 10 years ago, an archaeologist discovered the markers when they did a survey, a required step to building a new bridge over the marshy brook.
The town knew there were burials nearby — six graves on the cemetery side of the brook and four engraved headstones deeper along the path. They mark the spots where Revolutionary War veteran John Jordan, his wife and two daughters lie, their feet pointed east, ready to rise with the sun.
But the rest of the stones don’t have names, epitaphs or birth and death dates.
“Unless you know what to look for, you’re not going to realize it’s a burial ground,” O’Meara said. She’d walked by that area many times, and it wasn’t until she was accompanied by an archaeologist that she realized the extent of it. She thinks there are at least 50 people buried there, likely the descendants of Nathaniel Jordan, himself a descendant of John Jordan.
“Fifty-one burial sites feels like a pretty significant number to me,” she said.
She thought it would be respectful to build a memorial to those buried so close to the trail. It took the conservation committee — the body responsible for town trail stewardship — years to acquire the boulder and have the plaque made.
On a sticky recent Wednesday evening, about 30 residents, including town staff, councilors and curious neighbors, gathered to unveil the memorial. The shiny silver plaque displays a map of the markers and some history about the Jordans. Nathaniel and Mary Jordan were married in 1793, and they had at least 10 children by 1820.
“It’s a really special moment and place marking an intersection of the distant past and today,” Town Council Chair Elizabeth Scifres said.
Some, like O’Meara, see this plaque as a form of closure, a fitting recognition. Others want more.
Brakeley thinks the town should remove the path that bisects these burials.
“We’re stepping on dead bodies,” she said as she traversed the path. She said that it’s one thing to have a perimeter trail surrounding the burials. It’s another to have a thoroughfare running through it. She pointed out stones on the trail that she believes are markers.
O’Meara said that will be an ongoing conversation with the conservation committee, along with other aspects to consider.
Giving people a place to walk, she said, would deter off-trail activity. Without a designated trail through the burial area, there could be more trampling and damage to the site.
A local Boy Scout troop built the path a few years ago so that people would be able to access the four engraved headstones closer to the wetlands.
“A place where the present can intersect with the past is a good thing,” O’Meara said.
In the meantime, Brakeley will continue combing through archives and online resources to try to find information about the people buried there. Their names and stories might be lost to history, she said. But they will be recognized.

title: Federal report says pilots weren’t warned about wind before Amazon cargo plane crashed in Miami
text:
(AP) - Despite regulations requiring it, an air traffic controller failed to tell the pilots of an Amazon cargo plane about the potential for strong tailwinds as they landed in Miami, careening off the runway and killing five people last month, according to a preliminary report Thursday from the National Transportation Safety Board.
Just four minutes before clearing the plane for landing, an air traffic controller had provided a wind advisory to a different flight, noting gusts of up to 25 mph (40 kph) from the south. But the controller “did not issue information about the wind” to the pilots of the Amazon cargo plane, the report said.
According to federal regulations, “both wind direction and velocity were required to be stated when authorizing use of a runway when a tailwind component exists,” the NTSB report said.
The airplane, carrying packages of contact lenses for Amazon, came in fast after a flight from Puerto Rico and barreled roughly 1,200 feet (366 meters) past the end of the runway at Miami International Airport on Sept. 6. It smashed into a van carrying workers for a company that cleans airplanes. Five people who were in the van died. Two others in the van sustained serious injuries, as did the driver of a car that was hit by the plane. The two pilots had minor injuries.
A summary of cockpit voice recordings previously released by the NTSB said one of the pilots repeatedly warned his counterpart that they were going too fast as they approached for landing and after touchdown. But the fellow pilot never gave “a consistent verbal response” to the warnings, the NTSB has said. The two pilots had flown together for the first time just earlier that day, according to the preliminary NTSB report.
The cockpit audio recordings also captured a series of automated warnings from the plane about the speed of descent and the approaching terrain.
The plane was well down the runway when its right and nose landing gear first touched down, reducing how much distance it had on the runway to stop. Experts have said strong winds from approaching storms could have created a tailwind that helped propel the plane forward.
After the crash, Amazon suspended its partnership with 21 Air, which operated the plane. The North Carolina carrier had flown packages for Amazon since 2024. The Boeing 767 that crashed was 32 years old and originally built to carry passengers. It was converted to a cargo plane in June 2016, the preliminary NTSB report said.
The Miami crash came less than a year after a UPS cargo plane crashed at Louisville’s Muhammad Ali International Airport after losing its engine while accelerating down the runway. That crash killed all three pilots and 12 people on the ground. Twenty-three more were injured.
