title: Free Acoustic Concert at Sasanoa Brewing Oct. 11
text:
World-traveling acoustic singer-songwriter Bryan Bielanski, of Charlotte, N.C., will perform a free concert from 3-6 p.m. on Sunday, Oct. 11 at Sasanoa Brewing.
This performance was rescheduled from Sunday, Sept. 27.
Bielanski has entertained audiences all over the world with his catchy songs and relentless touring. His unique style is inspired by rock and folk music, for sounds that are excitingly fresh yet instantly familiar at the same time.
This globetrotting musician has been touring the United States and the world for years and has performed in 49 of the 50 states plus 28 countries in Europe, Asia, and Central America.

title: Phil Pressey back for second season as Maine Celtics coach
text:
Phil Pressey will return for a second season as the Maine Celtics head coach, the team announced Thursday.
Pressey is the first head coach to return for a second season with the Maine Celtics since Brandon Bailey was promoted to the Boston Celtics coaching staff after the 2018-19 season. Maine went 27-23 and reached the NBA G League playoffs for the fourth straight season.
Pressey replaced Tyler Lashbrook, who lead Maine to a 29-21 record in 2024-25 and a berth in the Eastern Conference finals before moving up to the Boston Celtics coaching staff.
Also returning to Maine this season are assistant coaches Mike Malat and Boaz Mensah. Devin Sweetney, Jacob Kester and Rich Kelly are joining the team’s staff.

title: These are the most popular side hustles people are taking on to boost a budget
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PHOENIX (Aging Untold) — Rob Macgregor has a full-time job, running a small car dealership in Phoenix. He spends at least 40 hours a week selling cars. Then he works on his side hustle, giving golf lessons.
He’s been playing golf since he was a kid, and teaching the game he loves has become a passion.
“[I} won a state championship in Michigan and then turned pro shortly after that, decided to teach golf lessons for money,” he said.
Macgregor connects with students on Teachme.To. The platform matches students with local instructors for lessons in all kinds of activities, including golf, pickleball, tennis and guitar.
Macgregor has come to rely on the extra income he earns as a golf instructor.
“I have six kids and they all like their own little hobbies, so I get to use the money that I create from this side income,” he said. “It covers some of it.”
Macgregor is like a lot of people, working to increase income. A recent LendingTree survey shows 38% of American adults have a side hustle.
“That’s actually down a little bit from a few years ago but it’s still a really big number, and I think it really indicates how much people need a little bit of help in extending their monthly budget,” Matt Schulz with LendingTree said.
Popular side hustles
According to LendingTree, the most popular side hustles are food and grocery delivery and online freelancing. Another 14% of side hustlers report doing part-time or seasonal work, 13% do house cleaning and 13% make and sell items. E-commerce resale, social media influencing, babysitting, pet sitting, rideshare driving, day trading and teaching also made the list.
On average, according to the survey, side hustlers say they’re making an extra $1,215 per month.
“The main thing to understand about a side hustle is that it takes a lot of work,” Schulz said. “This isn’t free money. This isn’t just a switch that you flip and all of a sudden, you’re bringing in money.”
Macgregor opens his online schedule whenever he can for students like Mateo Frances, who found Macgregor on the Teachme.to platform.
“He had great ratings, Frances said. “I saw it as an opportunity to learn a game that I’m sort of falling in love with that I can play for the rest of my life.”

title: Man accused of intentionally setting house fire that killed 15 dogs
text:
GENEVA, Fla. (WESH) - Authorities in Florida are investigating a house fire that left at least 15 dogs dead.
The Seminole County Sheriff’s Office says the man who lived in the home intentionally set the fire.
New body camera video shows deputies and firefighters responding to a fully engulfed house on Snow Hill Road in Geneva on Monday. At least 17 dogs were inside.
“Got one dog. The other ones are on the front cooked in the cage. They’re all upside down,” one responder said.
911 calls captured people describing what they saw and heard.
“There’s a fire. It’s fully engulfed. We were just driving by. There are dogs inside. There’s barking. It’s really bad,” one caller said.
In a separate 911 call, barking continued without stopping.
“Oh no, look at them. They are trying to go inside to get their babies ... they have a bunch of bullies,” the caller said.
On Monday, investigators found six dead dogs inside the house.
“Oh, it is so sad. The puppies are dead. Oh my God,” a caller said.
Animal services took in four more dogs, two of which died Monday night. On Tuesday, seven more dogs were found.
The sheriff’s office says Terrance Banks set his own house on fire by pouring gasoline on the floor in every room of the house. He then used a lighter to light a piece of paper on fire, which he used to ignite the gasoline.
Banks’ father can be heard calling 911 as he headed to his son’s home.
“I got a call from my son. I’m not there, but he rents the place, so I don’t know,” he said.
On Tuesday, a judge ordered that Banks remain in jail until he is mentally evaluated.
A neighbor who did not want to show his face or use his name for safety reasons spoke about Banks.
“He would normally try to keep to himself. I know he would not allow anybody other than, you know, the family he was with, approach the dogs,” the neighbor said.
The neighbor said it was clear Banks had some type of mental health issue.
“He would parade across the street from my house up and down and he would just be babbling on,” the neighbor said.
One of the two surviving dogs is now in the care of an emergency veterinarian for specialized treatment.

title: Court documents detail hours leading up to 2 Ole Miss students’ suspected overdose deaths
text:
OXFORD, Miss. (WMC/Gray News) — Mississippi leaders and lawmakers are calling for a crackdown on kratom and kratom-like products after two Ole Miss students died last week.
Toxicology tests are incomplete, and the autopsies on both young men are still pending.
But court documents filed Monday reveal what 18-year-old Aidan Hamilton and 20-year-old Robert Strang were doing in the hours and days before their suspected overdose deaths.
Investigators with Lafayette County Metro Narcotics previously said store-bought kratom was found in both students’ rooms.
On Sept. 30, Metro Narcotics clarified the information in an earlier statement to WMC:
“During the investigations, packaging associated with kratom-related products was discovered at both locations. This information prompted law enforcement to issue a public safety warning out of an abundance of caution.
That warning was not a declaration that kratom or any specific substance caused either death. It was a proactive effort to inform the public of a potential danger while investigators worked to determine the facts.”
Authorities were able to determine where the young men bought the drugs. The investigation now stretches from Lafayette County into neighboring Yalobusha County at a convenience store about 20 miles from the Ole Miss campus.
What investigators found in Hamilton’s dorm room
Hamilton died in his on-campus dorm room on Sept. 21.
Court documents show the coroner and medical personnel on the scene said the young man “could have died due to a pulmonary edema, consistent with a drug overdose.”
Hamilton’s roommate told investigators that Hamilton “smoked a lot of marijuana from pens and pipes,” “would keep his marijuana in a safe,” and “used it a lot, so much so, he had a terrible cough.”
But investigators are focusing on SMAX Pseudo-DHM pills, a chemically manipulated product, found on Hamilton’s dresser in his room at Stewart Hall.
Statements filed by Caleb East, an agent with the Lafayette County Metro Narcotics Unit, noted that “agents are aware that these are often sold as a kratom-like substance at gas stations or tobacco shops.”
Mississippi Department of Public Safety Commissioner Sean Tindell said, “We’re wanting to test those and make sure that anything that’s in there… it’s not being laced with any other chemicals, or there’s no other harmful chemicals in that product.”
What investigators found at Strang’s home
At the scene of Strang’s death, inside his off-campus home on Van Buren Avenue, investigators said they found 20 to 30 nitrous oxide cans.
His roommates said Strang “would use whippets daily,” the street term given to the popular party drug. Strang’s housemates also said he would use “sometimes two to three cans a week.”
Investigators also found a packet of SMAX on his nightstand in packaging similar to what was found in Hamilton’s dorm.
Roommates said Strang took a Xanax bar around 4 p.m. Sunday. He was last seen in the kitchen around midnight. His body was discovered the next day in his bedroom at 3:30 p.m.
Doctors warn about kratom and synthetic kratom-like products
Following the student deaths, Mississippi doctors are again warning about the dangers of products marketed as kratom, a natural leaf that can be tainted with other chemicals or offered in versions that are made synthetically with illegal substances, referred to as “gas station heroin.”
Dr. Lucas Trautman, medical director at the Oxford Treatment Center, told WMC, “It’s being sold in gas stations as sort of ‘natural’... that’s the buzz you hear with it... in order to help you with pain or sleep. Well, it’s just an opioid, so people get addicted to it, too, and have severe withdrawals.”
Family physician Dr. Jennifer Bryan said, “I would urge the public that if you see ‘natural,’ natural does not mean safe. It’s not synonymous. We still don’t know what’s inside that package. No matter what the label says, you don’t know what’s inside that package. The regulation is very loose.”
SMAX Pseudo-DHM is a synthetic drug marketed as a kratom-like substance. But investigators say it has a “significantly higher potency compared to natural leaf products.”
In the affidavit filed in the Third District Circuit Court of Mississippi on Sept. 28, following undercover operations at two retail stores, drug agents said the ingredients can be “produced fully synthetically in clandestine laboratories.”
The affidavit lists the ingredients of SMAX Pseudo-DHM as pseudoindoxyl, MGM-15 and 7-hydroxymitragynine.
The DEA temporarily placed mitragynine, pseudoindoxyl and MGM-15 on the Schedule I list on Aug. 26, 2026.
Schedule I drugs, including heroin, LSD and ecstasy, are illegal in the U.S. under federal law.
“Synthetic mitragynine compounds can be significantly stronger than morphine,” East wrote in the affidavit, “and carry a high risk of severe addiction, overdose and death.”
Where the drugs were purchased
Investigators with Metro Narcotics say Strang bought his SMAX product at Express Mart #7 in Water Valley in Yalobusha County. Bank records show he visited the store twice — once on Sept. 9 and again on Sept. 11.
The store is about a 20- to 30-minute drive from the Ole Miss campus.
Undercover officers bought more of the product a day after his death.
Court documents say the clerk said the store was out of the 200-mg version but sold “another form of the SMAX Pseudo-DHM pills consistent with the packages found at the Strang scene.”
The pills were sent to a forensic lab in Columbus, Mississippi, for analysis.
Agents returned to Express Mart #7 on Sept. 23 and bought more of the pills, this time sending them to a crime lab in Florida for analysis.
Investigators say records show Aidan Hamilton made multiple purchases at Puffs Vape Tobacco and Beer in Oxford. Bank records provided by his parents showed he visited the store and made purchases on Sept. 9, Sept. 14 and Sept. 20, one day before his death.
On Sept. 24, Metro Narcotics agents sent a confidential informant into the store, equipped with audio and video equipment. The informant tried to buy nitrous oxide, but the clerk told him that the store didn’t have any.
The affidavit says the clerk then offered to sell the informant marijuana from a jar and pre-rolled joints. The informant declined, but later asked if the store sold “7 O Kratom based pills.” The clerk said yes.
Records show an employee told an undercover informant to “be careful taking the pills because people are dying from them.”
Two employees of that store were arrested, and 500 units of kratom and kratom-like products were seized. The Metro Narcotics team also found an assortment of “THC cartridges, gummies, pre-rolls and other suspected THC substances.”
Recreational marijuana is still classified as an illegal Schedule I drug in the U.S.
Possible legislative action
The scope and impact of the Ole Miss deaths investigation could lead to legislative change.
Commissioner Tindell said, “Once kratom is banned locally, it’s still only a misdemeanor. And so I think one of the things the legislature is going to look at and consider next year… is, are we at the point where we need a statewide ban on kratom?”
Kratom is currently banned in the City of Oxford and Lafayette County. And again, the ingredients in the SMAX products found in the students’ rooms — products sold by two retail establishments — are illegal under federal law.
The students’ toxicology reports are being expedited and could come back as soon as this week. Until that happens, their causes of death are pending.
The American Kratom Association held a news conference in Oxford on Wednesday to defend natural kratom and differentiate it from the manufactured products that authorities said were found in the students’ rooms.

title: Dom Huntington is Portland football’s ironman
text:
PORTLAND — Dom Huntington has been playing tackle football since the second grade. He’s loved the game from the start. The competition. The discipline. His brotherhood with teammates.
“It just makes me happy to play,” Huntington said.
To the Portland High senior right guard and defensive lineman, it just makes sense that he would want to play football whenever possible.
But Huntington is unusual. He is a high school football ironman.
Huntington has played in every Portland varsity football game since Week 1 of his freshman season. Because Portland has been to three straight Class A championship games, there have been a lot of games.
Entering a Class A showdown at Thornton Academy (4-0) on Saturday, Huntington has played in 39 varsity football games — 42 if you include Portland’s annual Thanksgiving Day exhibition game against Deering.
“I never really thought about it like that,” Huntington said. “I just go week-by-week and look at every game the same. I don’t really keep track. I just love the brotherhood and winning.”
Portland (4-0) is in the driver’s seat to win a fourth straight Class A North title. If that happens, Huntington could play 47 high school games (51 with the Turkey Day tussle included).
“He’s a pretty dang good player. Terrific as a lead blocker when he’s pulling,” said Dylan Rottkov, Portland’s third head coach during Huntington’s career. “Dom’s a monster on the D-line.”
AVAILABILITY MATTERS
“The most important ability is availability.” The sports adage is often credited to NFL coaching legend Bill Parcells. Regardless of who said it first, there is much to appreciate in that statement.
Being ready, healthy, and talented enough to play in every varsity high school football game over four seasons is an achievement.
The Press Herald sent an email to the state’s head coaches asking if their team had a senior who fit the ironman description. While far from a perfect survey method, the results are illustrative. Just three coaches responded.
Poland linebacker Gavin Gilbert and Dirigo defensive end/tight end/fullback Kaeden Swan have each played in 32 games entering this weekend. Gilbert is a four-year starter at linebacker. Swan, who also runs for Dirigo’s cross country team, is a three-year starter who played varsity special teams as a freshman. Greely quarterback/free safety Luke Piper has played in 35 varsity games, 34 as a starter on at least one side of the ball, including state championship game wins in 2024 and 2025. Piper could max out at 43 games if Greely returns to the Class C final.
HUNTINGTON’S PATH
Huntington is 5-foot-11 (“6 foot on a good day,” he said) and about 225 pounds. He was the same height and just a few pounds lighter as a freshman, when first-year Portland coach Sean Green put Huntington on varsity special teams right away. Because of injuries, Huntington started several games at nose guard in a 10-1 season.
“I think it helped me a lot, starting a few games as a freshman,” Huntington said. “It really gave me the experience I needed.”
Huntington has been a two-way starter at right guard and across the defensive line since his sophomore year.
As a sophomore, Portland went 10-2 and won its first state championship in 22 years with a decisive victory against Thornton Academy. Last season, with Nick Cliche as the head coach, Portland went 9-3, including a title game loss to Thornton.
With Huntington on the field, Portland is 33-6. He’s played many of those games, especially the past two seasons, with fellow seniors Law Nguyen at left guard, Dan Gallagher at center and Bailey Jordan at fullback.
“I think we have a chance this year to win it all,” Huntington said.
Huntington’s ironman streak nearly ended last season in a Week 5 loss to Thornton. He broke his wrist when he hit Thornton running back Connor Ayoob’s face mask while trying to punch the ball free.
“He was so low and I tried to go for him and he just dug down, and I hit him directly in the face,” Huntington said.
Huntington was outfitted with a cast for everyday wear, and a protective club-like cast for football.
“I had to wear it the rest of the season. I tried to use it to my advantage,” Huntington said.
NEXT IN LINE?
The Huntington family’s consecutive-games streak could continue after this season.
Portland’s starting left tackle is freshman Liam Huntington, Dom’s 6-2, 245-pound “little” brother. There are times when Dom pulls to his left from his right guard position and he’s side-by-side with his brother, combo blocking an unfortunate defender.
“I never thought he was going to play right next to me,” Dom Huntington said. “It’s pretty cool. And my parents love it, of course.”

title: How Tennessee's failed execution of Christa Pike unfolded, minute-by-minute
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — Christa Pike was scheduled to be executed. But after two injections, she kept breathing. She made snoring sounds, she talked, she said her arm was hurting.
Pike, sentenced to die for torturing and killing 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer in 1995, said as her scheduled lethal injection began that she was at peace.
Strapped to a gurney around 7:30 p.m. Wednesday, Pike, who was allowed to give a final statement, said she was leaving the world with love.
“I’m ready to be free,” she said. This is a happy day.”
Leaving prison in an ambulance, not a hearse
Pike, now 50, was 18 when she committed the murder and would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.
But instead she survived two doses of the pentobarbital meant to kill her. She left the prison in an ambulance instead of a hearse.
The Associated Press was among those who witnessed her failed execution. She was already strapped to the gurney, with IV inserted in her arm, when prison officials raised the curtain to the execution room at 7:27 p.m.
Her spiritual adviser was standing beside the gurney near her head. He spoke to her. They sang a song. The lyrics were not audible, but included repeating the phrase — “I love you.” The spiritual adviser stroked her forehead.
Minutes ticked by. She raised her head and looked around; she smiled. Then she said her arm was hurting and asked a prison official in the room if it was supposed to feel that way.
Ten minutes in, at 7:37 p.m., she sighed, the IV in her arm fed from a control room adjacent to the death chamber, separated by a ledge. At 7:41 p.m., a rock or paper weight about the size of a golf ball was placed on the ledge. Prison officials have not confirmed what it means, but its placement appeared to coincide with a direction in the protocol that says after the drugs are administered, a five-minute countdown begins until the curtain is closed.
At 7:46 p.m., officials closed the curtain, blocking the witnesses’ view of the death chamber. Pike’s spiritual adviser left the chamber and sat briefly with her attorney in the media witness room.
The curtain rose again three minutes later. The Tennessee lethal injection protocol calls for a second round of pentobarbital if the inmate is not deceased after the first round.
An hour-plus of what sounded like snoring
Her spiritual adviser returned to the chamber and stood beside Pike with his hands folded. Pike appeared to begin to lose consciousness at some point and started making a sound like snoring. She continued to do so for the next hour, a sign that she was alive long after she was expected to be dead.
Her head raised slightly off the gurney and turned to the side at about 7:56 p.m. She kept breathing.
Officials closed the curtain again at 8:06 p.m.
For the next 40 minutes, Pike could be heard from behind the curtain. She sounded like she was snoring, a rhythmic, regular breathing pattern.
Inside the prison, Pike’s attorney, Randy Spivey, later told the media that at about 8:22 p.m. he demanded access to a telephone to contact other lawyers on the team. He said he demanded the execution be halted and that life-saving medical care be given to Pike. He said he received confirmation at about 8:50 p.m. that an ambulance was on the way.
At 8:53 p.m., an announcement came: “Will witnesses please exit the area.” The media was escorted out, and a prison spokesperson said she had no information to provide about what had happened.
Fire trucks and ambulances arrived in front of the prison at around 9:14 p.m. Pike’s attorneys later issued a statement that she had been taken to a hospital and was being treated, though they did not know the specifics of her condition. On Thursday afternoon, they said she was in critical condition receiving medical care.
Governor orders a review
The Tennessee Department of Correction issued a statement saying the department followed protocol.
“The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening,” the agency wrote. “Christa Pike has been transported to an off-site medical facility.”
The agency has not said what went wrong. It was the second time this year that Tennessee has been unable to complete an execution, though in the other case, officials couldn’t find a suitable vein for an IV line so the drugs weren’t administered.
Gov. Bill Lee ordered a review and postponed another execution scheduled for later this year, calling what happened in the death chamber “deeply disturbing.”
Slemmer’s mother, May Martinez, had traveled to Nashville to see the sentence carried out.
“I didn’t get justice for my daughter,” Martinez told the AP by telephone.
“I watched the whole thing. She was awake,” Martinez said. “She was moving her head, moving her feet. She was trying to sit up. Didn’t work the first time they gave her a shot. It didn’t work the second time so she’s in the hospital and alive.”
“This isn’t justice for Colleen.”

title: International bridge in Calais to close for six weeks
text:
CALAIS, Maine (WABI) - Those traveling between Calais and Canada may need to find an alternate route for an extended period of time.
The Ferry Point Bridge which connects Calais and New Brunswick over the St. Croix River will be closed for six weeks, according to the MaineDOT.
The closure will begin on Tuesday, October 13th. Crews will be working to rehabilitate the bridge during the closure.
Drivers trying to cross the border will have to either take the Milltown International Bridge or the International Avenue Bridge. Commercial drivers are being asked to take the International Avenue Bridge

title: Mainers feel the pinch of surging food prices
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
This story appears as part of a collaboration to strengthen investigative journalism in Maine between the BDN and The Maine Monitor. Read more about the partnership.
Mandy Belanger of Lewiston could once afford three meals a day for herself, her two children and her mother, but she had to make difficult cuts in recent years while navigating the biggest surge in grocery prices in a half century.
On weekly trips to a nearby Hannaford, she started buying pork instead of red meat and chicken, and less meat overall, trying to stretch the disability income her family relies on. Belanger said she no longer purchases snack foods. She also buys fewer fruits and vegetables, getting cheaper Hannaford-brand boxed foods instead. But replacing the items in her cart with cheaper alternatives has only done so much.
Eventually, she had to cut her family’s daily meals from three to two — and her own to one.
“Being the adult in the house, you go without more than you do,” she said on Aug. 26. “I eat one meal a day.”
Grocery prices have grown about 28% in the Northeast since 2020, slightly less than the increase seen nationwide. But the average weekly wage in Maine has stayed consistently lower than the national average and has continued to lag behind. In a state where nearly half of residents struggle to pay for basic needs, Mainers are feeling the pinch.
Maine shoppers are avoiding certain foods, traveling farther to buy in bulk and purchasing fewer items overall to save a little money each week. Still, many are finding their dollars are not stretching as far as they used to, and, in many areas of the state, residents do not have the option to shop around.
National grocery corporations, meanwhile, are maintaining stable or growing profit margins, while food and beverage sales grow each year.
Hannaford spokesperson Caitlin Cortelyou said it’s important to the company to keep groceries affordable and that Hannaford has made investments in recent years at the majority of its stores to lower prices.
The Maine Monitor also reached out to Costco; BJ’s Wholesale Club; Target; Walmart, which owns Sam’s Club; and Albertsons, which owns Shaw’s. They did not respond to questions about how they have been able to grow sales.
Mainers already experience food insecurity at higher income levels than the national average. An estimated 28% of Maine households in 2024 fell under the ALICE threshold, which refers to homes that earn more than the federal poverty level but still cannot afford basic needs in their county. These homes do not qualify for public assistance programs, such as food stamps, called the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program.
Other homes that used to qualify for government help no longer do. Last month, nearly 22,000 fewer people in Maine received food stamps compared with the same month last year, after President Donald Trump’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act restricted who qualified for the program and shifted more costs to states.
For residents such as Belanger, who said she relies on food stamps and whose grocery expenses account for 65% of her overall monthly budget, higher grocery prices mean difficult choices.
During the winter, her choice lay between food or heat for her son, 17; her daughter, who is 23 and disabled; and her mother, who lives with them. During this past summer season, she chose between food and personal items, such as laundry detergent, cleaning supplies and toothpaste.
“It’s frustrating. It’s unhealthy,” she said.
Changing habits to no avail
Shoppers and local grocery store owners from around the state told The Monitor the same thing: Everything is more expensive now.
General inflation and shocks from the production-side of the grocery market caused both gradual increases and significant price spikes, said Jonathan Malacarne, assistant professor of agricultural economics at the University of Maine.
Although increases driven by industry shocks — such as the avian flu that made the price of eggs jump last year — tend to come back down, prices raised by general inflation do not, he said.
The price of beef in particular has steadily risen as the U.S. cattle herd has shrunk to the smallest size in 75 years. In Maine supermarkets, shoppers said they are steering clear.
Jordan Sherman of Portland regularly shops at the Portland Food Co-op. She now avoids red meat and chicken because of the price, she said, instead getting her protein from other sources such as pork, sausage, beans or tofu.
Sherman has also started going to multiple stores during her weekly shopping runs, she said. She hunts for deals at Hannaford and Trader Joe’s, and goes to the farmers market for cheaper, longer-lasting produce. Her budget to eat out at restaurants has shrunk, she said.
Others, such as Brian Bowler, are traveling farther each month to buy in bulk.
Bowler, who lives in Harpswell and recently graduated from St. Joseph College, travels an hour each month to shop at Maine’s only Costco in Scarborough. He purchased his membership about a year and a half ago, shortly after the Costco location opened, and said purchasing items in bulk helps him save some money overall.
Still, shoppers are finding their efforts are making little meaningful difference.
Barbie Dow of Lewiston expected her weekly grocery spending to slow when the last of her four boys moved away to college. But five years into the empty-nester life with her husband, their grocery bill has remained about the same at $200 to $300 each week, sometimes higher.
“You go from feeding six people, plus all their friends and everybody else coming over, to feeding two, and the price did not hardly move down at all,” Dow said.
“I feel bad when I’m at the grocery store and see people with children,” said Stephanie Fullam, a retired special education teacher. “I look at what they’ve got in her basket, and I think, ‘I don’t know how people can afford it.’”
Fullam of Augusta rarely deviates from her shopping list, she said, and purposely shops around to get the best quality for the price. She also makes the hour-long drive to the state’s only Trader Joe’s in Portland and Costco in Scarborough.
Fullam recalled a three-year stretch in 1978 when her husband was out of work and needed surgery, and money was tight while raising three teenage children.
“Hamburger was cheap; chicken was cheap,” and “you stretched it,” she said.
“We get by, but, if we were raising the kids now, I don’t know how we would do it,” Fullam said.
Behind store shelves
Local grocers told The Monitor that higher gas prices, which account for 15 to 30% of the total cost of food, have been a primary driver of the price increases their customers see.
The price of regular unleaded gas in the Northeast spiked nearly 39% since the start of the U.S. war with Iran last February. It’s gone up about 56% since 2020.
To account for higher gas prices, freight companies often charge additional shipping costs on top of their base price. Some local grocers are seeing higher additional costs for every delivery.
The Portland Food Co-op, which gets about 40% of its retail items from within the state, began seeing fuel surcharges from their largest distributors on top of their normal transportation costs about six months ago, around the start of the Iran war, John Crane, the general manager, said. The recent surcharges typically range from an extra $30 to $50, but can be as much as $70.
Harvest Time Natural Foods, a local grocer that has operated in Augusta since 1974, has also seen freight charges increase from a typical $5 to $10 charge per delivery to around $50, store owner Lewis Purinton said.
The latest jump in costs are the largest Purinton has seen since he founded the store 50 years ago, he said.
Lina Raye, a longtime manager at Harvest Time, said the store stopped carrying certain items, such as raw red-skinned peanuts that came from the west or black rice from Minnesota, about a year ago because of shipping costs.
Because of extra costs absorbed by the store, the price of most retail items at the Portland Co-op have increased, Crane said, particularly coffee. Coffee beans from Equal Exchange Coffee, based in Massachusetts, are now $11.99 per pound. Three years ago, the Portland Food Co-op sold them for about $7.99 per pound.
To protect customers but still cover his costs and maintain a profit, Crane shifted markup rates among different items and avoided spiking the cost of grocery basics, he said.
For instance, he has marked up milk, eggs, potatoes and other essentials by about 20%; diapers by about 10%; and specialty items such as chocolate by about 30% or higher.
“That’s really how we look at it, just thinking about the poorest among us — what they actually need and making sure that we’re not applying markups to the staples that people need,” he said.
In addition to stores, Maine farms are also feeling the pain of higher prices for gas, alongside high seed and fertilizer prices, said Serynn Nowlin, a manager at Pine Root Farm in Steep Falls.
At their spot at the Portland Farmers Market in August, Pine Root Farm was the only vendor selling ears of sweet corn. The cost to grow corn each season — taking into account seed, land, water and fertilizer — now outweighs the benefits of selling what once was a lucrative product, Nowlin said.
“Corn used to be more of a cash crop for us, and now it’s like, ‘We have the space to grow it, so we do,’” they said.
In remote areas of the state such as Jackman, customers can’t easily shop around for a better price.
Some Jackman locals travel 50 miles south to Jimmy’s Market in Bingham or 70 miles to Walmart in Skowhegan. But mostly they rely on the Mountain Country Market, a small grocery store and the only one in Jackman. Food prices there, however, have gone up just as they have everywhere else, said store owner Scott Smith, who was raised in Jackman.
The situation is a delicate one as the Jackman community might not survive without a grocery store, he said.
“Talking about it isn’t going to help,” Smith said. “It’s got to change in our government.”
Grocer giants
At the same time, large grocery corporations are pulling in greater profits each year from grocery sales. U.S. Walmart locations’ net sales for groceries have increased by nearly $100 billion since 2020, a nearly 50% increase.
Data from Macrotrends, a market research firm for investors, shows that major U.S. grocers with a presence in Maine have been able to maintain stable or growing profit margins as cost-drivers continue to worsen.
Large grocery corporations have advantages over local stores that allow them to better safeguard and generate profits. One such advantage is the capability to sell private labels — products that are sold under a store’s own brand name, such as Walmart’s “Great Value” brand — where stores make more money off each sale than with other products.
Customer attitudes have shifted favorably toward private labels in recent years, which made up about 21% of profits from the total U.S. market sales last year, according to the Private Label Manufacturers Association. In food and beverage aisles, private label sales accrued nearly a quarter of all sales, according to the market analytics firm Circana.
For Hannaford, one of the most prominent grocery store chains in the state, private-brand sales are an important part of business, Cortelyou said.
Lately the company has seen “robust private brand growth” in fresh items such as chicken and broccoli, alongside other staples such as frozen pizza and canned beans, she said.
Large grocery store companies also proved during the pandemic they are better able to protect their supply chains amid disruptions because they have stronger negotiation standing than local stores.
The surge in grocery food prices shows no signs of slowing, according to Axios, which cited numbers from J.P. Morgan. The company projected that food prices will stay elevated, with the inflation rate accelerating from 2.8% earlier this year to 5% in the first half of next year.
In the long run, companies may be reluctant to lower prices even if the drivers of grocery costs come down, said Malacarne of UMaine.
“If consumers are used to paying a certain price, the sellers have little incentive to lower that price unless they face significant competition,” he said.
